# Commodore 64 (breadbin, ASSY 250407) `c64`

A home computer sold from 1982. This tree traces every physical component back through the industrial processes of the early 1980s to the ore, crude oil and quartz sand it began as. Roughly 320 discrete parts from about twenty distinct manufacturing industries. The chips were designed in Pennsylvania and fabricated there; the board was populated and the machine was boxed in Hong Kong, with some runs contract-manufactured in Japan.

## Breadbin case: two-piece ABS shell `c64.case`

The C64 'breadbin' housing is a rear shell and a front bezel, both injection-moulded general-purpose ABS in a warm beige-brown. The rear shell carries the ventilation ribs, moulded screw bosses, connector cut-outs and the rubber feet; the bezel carries the keyboard window with its square key openings, the two knurled thumbscrews, the rainbow badge and the fine 'leather' grain. A foil-on-board RFI shield sits inside over the motherboard.

### Rear shell (bottom half) `c64.case.rear-shell`

The larger of the two mouldings. It forms the base pan, the raised side walls, the wrap-over top with its row of ventilation slots, the rear and side connector cut-outs, the internal ribs that stiffen the pan, the moulded screw bosses and standoffs, and the feet pads.

#### Ventilation slots in the top wrap `c64.case.rear-shell.vents` _(medium)_

A row of moulded louvre slots in the curved top panel behind the cartridge port, letting convective air out of the case over the SID and VIC-II. They are negative features: slots cut into the tool, not separate ribs. Because they run across a thick section they leave visible flow lines and are a classic sink-mark site.

##### Ribs and bosses behind the vent slots `c64.case.rear-shell.vents.rib-bosses`

Internal cross-ribs tying the top panel to the pan, moulded 1.5-2.5 mm thick at roughly the same gauge as the outer wall so the whole panel cools and shrinks as one. Where the ribs are thicker than the wall the extra melt freezes later and pulls a faint sink mark onto the visible surface.

#### Moulded bosses and standoffs `c64.case.rear-shell.bosses`

Integral cylindrical bosses on the pan floor that carry the four case screws, the motherboard mounting screws, the keyboard PCB screws and the RF shield tabs. Each is a thick section relative to the 3 mm pan, so the tool must be cored or cored-and-gauged to keep them from sinking, and each has a blind hole with a drafted self-tapping thread.

##### Self-tapping thread form in plastic `c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.steel-thread`

A 1980s cost trick: instead of a moulded-in metal insert, the boss is cored with a shallow single-start helical flute of the same nominal diameter as a self-tapping screw. The screw's flank cuts its own thread on first insertion, giving a metal-in-plastic thread that will not strip.

#### Rear and side connector openings `c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts`

Rectangular and keyed cut-outs for the cartridge port, user port, cassette port, serial port, video DIN, power DIN and the two DE-9 control ports. Cut with knife-edged steel on the tool; the moulded lip around each port also acts as a draft and a finger stop, and the mouldings carry the connector bodies as separate inserts.

### Front bezel (top half) `c64.case.bezel`

The dished front panel with the keyboard window. It is the visible part of the machine, so it carries the fine leather-grain texture, the rainbow badge recess, the two knurled thumbscrews and the moulded-in 'COMMODORE' lettering on the lower lip.

#### Keyboard window and key openings `c64.case.bezel.key-well` _(medium)_

A single rectangular opening spanned by thin webs between the key holes; the caps push through and their plungers sit on the keyboard PCB below. The webs are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between 66 holes that are only about 10 mm across.

#### Moulded-in leather grain `c64.case.bezel.leather-texture`

The fine random pebble texture on the visible faces of the bezel and the rear shell. It is cut into the hardened tool steel by EDM from a positive pattern, then the whole cavity is polished and chrome-plated so the grain reads as a soft satin rather than as sharp metal. On genuine surviving Commodore tooling the flow pattern beneath the texture is still faintly visible, which is how restorers authenticate an original mould.

#### Knurled thumbscrews for contrast/brightness `c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews` _(medium)_

Two moulded plastic thumbscrews on the bezel that carry small metal shafts to the contrast and brightness potentiometers on the board. The caps are ABS, the shafts are plated steel, and the knurl is moulded rather than cut.

### Rainbow Commodore badge `c64.case.logo` _(medium)_

The seven-bar rainbow 'commodore' logo on the bezel. On the breadbin it is a raised area of the case itself, decorated by a run of coloured and metallised ink rather than being a separate appliqué; on later machines it is a flat printed decal.

#### Raised badge area on the bezel `c64.case.logo.raised-area` _(medium)_

A shallow raised island on the bezel where the logo sits, moulded as part of the bezel tool. It gives the pad printer a flat, non-textured island so the ink sits proud of the leather grain and the colours read cleanly.

### Case feet `c64.case.feet` _(medium)_

Four small anti-vibration feet on the underside of the rear shell, moulded in a soft dark rubber or a flexible PVC, that stop the machine skating on a desk and stop the moulded ABS case from ringing against the desk.

#### Foot elastomer compound `c64.case.feet.elastomer` _(medium)_

A soft, low-durometer elastomer drop-in-moulded over a small ABS boss, or a moulded-in flexible nub. The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: it is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS.

### RFI shield: aluminium foil on a board spacer `c64.case.shield`

The C64 needed a conductive screen over the motherboard because a 1 MHz machine with a video oscillator radiates through a plastic case. Commodore used a die-cut sandwich of aluminium foil laminated to a cardboard or plastic-fibre spacer, bent into a box and stapled or taped to plastic standoffs, rather than a full metal can.

#### Aluminium foil `c64.case.shield.foil`

Household or semi-rugged aluminium foil, 0.03-0.06 mm, slit and die-cut. Its job is not to be a Faraday cage in the strict sense but simply to be a continuous, grounded-ish conductor over the board so the radiated field collapses.

##### Aluminium slab casting and rolling `c64.case.shield.foil-casting`

Bauxite is refined to alumina, smelted to primary aluminium in a Hall-Heroult potline at 950 C, then cast into rolling ingots and hot-rolled to foil gauge. Foil rolling is astonishingly aggressive: a 600 mm slab becomes 0.006 mm sheet after thousands of reduction passes.

#### Shield spacer (board core) `c64.case.shield.spacer` _(medium)_

A rigidising core so the foil does not crumple and short against the board. Cheap versions use thin greyboard; better ones use a plastic-fibre or corrugated spacer. This is the part that makes the shield stand off the motherboard so it cannot touch solder joints.

### Case fasteners `c64.case.fasteners` _(medium)_

The screws that hold the C64 together: a handful of case-assembly screws plus the motherboard and keyboard mounting screws. They are cheap zinc-plated self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, with occasional brass inserts.

#### Cold heading and thread cutting `c64.case.fasteners.cold-heading`

Steel wire is drawn, cut to length, cold-headed on a multiple-spindle header, the thread is cut or rolled, and the head is slotted or Phillips-formed. This is one of the most automated manufacturing processes on earth: a header makes tens of thousands of screws an hour with essentially no machining.

#### Zinc electroplating of fasteners `c64.case.fasteners.zinc-plating`

Small parts are barrel-plated in an acid or alkaline zinc solution, then often chromate-passivated for corrosion resistance. Zinc is chosen because it is sacrificial and cheap, and because a partly-depleted zinc coat on a thirty-year-old screw looks like rust rather than like a defect.

#### Moulded-in brass insert (later practice) `c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert` _(medium)_

Modern repro cases and late Commodore tools mould a brass or stainless insert into the boss and use a real machine screw. The insert is placed by hand or by gravity feed and captured by the ABS on the next shot, giving a reusable metal thread.

### ABS resin, general-purpose injection grade `c64.case.abs-resin`

Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a SAN matrix rigidified by acrylonitrile, toughened by grafted polybutadiene and given surface gloss by styrene. Commodore bought commodity ABS pellets in 25 kg bags, compounded them with colour masterbatch in a merchant compounder, and shipped them to case factories in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

#### Emulsion graft polymerisation to ABS `c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisation`

The dominant ABS route since the 1960s and still the one that makes the resin in the C64. Butadiene is polymerised in water to a polybutadiene latex; styrene and acrylonitrile are graft-polymerised onto that latex; the graft latex is coagulated, dewatered, dried and compounded with separately made bulk-SAN resin.

##### Monomer triad fed to the ABS plant `c64.case.abs-resin.monomers`

Styrene supplies gloss and mouldability, acrylonitrile supplies rigidity and chemical resistance, butadiene supplies the rubber phase that survives the drop the machine takes off a desk. All three arrive as cracker or reformer products, not as laboratory reagents.

###### Styrene monomer `c64.case.abs-resin.styrene`

Vinylbenzene, made by catalytic dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene or by styrene monomer recovery from a cracker. 1980s ABS plants bought it at 99.5%+ into stainless bulk tanks.

###### Ethylbenzene dehydrogenation to styrene `c64.case.abs-resin.styrene-dehydrogenation`

Endothermic vapour-phase dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over shell-type alumina-iron catalysts at 600-700 C, giving styrene plus hydrogen. Modern plants add a styrene monomer recovery loop to recycle unreacted ethylbenzene; 1980s plants ran single-pass at roughly 50-60% conversion and burned the rest.

###### Ethylbenzene `c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene`

Benzene alkylated with ethylene (or propylene) over a solid acid to make the styrene feedstock, with diethylbenzene and triethylbenzene as the by-products that have to be separated out.

###### Benzene alkylation with ethylene `c64.case.abs-resin.ethylbenzene-alkylation`

Friedel-Crafts alkylation over amorphous silica-alumina or a zeolite at 200-350 C and 5-20 bar, giving ethylbenzene plus polyalkylated heavies removed by fractionation.

###### Benzene `c64.case.abs-resin.benzene`

A C6H6 aromatic produced either by catalytic reforming of naphtha or by hydrodealkylation of toluene. Benzene is the entry point to styrene, and via cumene to phenol, epoxy resin and polycarbonate.

###### Catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction `c64.case.abs-resin.aromatics-extraction`

Naphtha is vaporised and passed over platinum (often with rhenium) on gamma-alumina at 450-520 C and 5-30 bar. Naphthenes and paraffins dehydrocyclise to aromatics; the C6+ aromatics are then split by extractive distillation with sulfolane or by azeotropic distillation with NMP.

###### Platinum-alumina reforming catalyst `c64.case.abs-resin.platinum-catalyst` _(medium)_

0.3-0.5 wt% platinum with rhenium, chloride and fluoride promoters dispersed on synthetic gamma-alumina. The platinum comes from PGM ores or from spent refinery catalyst; the alumina support is sintered from calcined bauxite.

###### Platinum-group metal concentrate `c64.case.abs-resin.pgm-ore` _(medium)_

Sulfide ore mined in South Africa's Bushveld complex or Russia's Norilsk, concentrated and smelted to a matte, then leached and refined. The platinum fraction is a fraction of a percent of the ore, which is why reclaiming spent catalyst is a real industry.

###### Bauxite (alumina precursor) `c64.case.abs-resin.bauxite`

Hydrated alumina rock, mined and Bayer-refined to alumina. It is the source of the alumina support for the reforming catalyst, and also the ore that becomes the aluminium in the EMI shield.

###### Acrylonitrile (vinyl cyanide) `c64.case.abs-resin.acrylonitrile`

CH2=CH-CN, the polar monomer that gives ABS its rigidity and resistance to solvents. Almost all of it is made by catalytic ammoxidation of propylene with ammonia and air over a bismuth-molybdate catalyst in a fluidised bed.

###### Sovereign/BP ammoxidation of propylene `c64.case.abs-resin.ammoxidation`

Propylene, ammonia and air are fed together into a turbulent fluidised-bed reactor over a bismuth-molybdate-on-silica catalyst at 400-510 C and only 1.5-3 bar. Acrylonitrile comes out together with acetonitrile, HCN and COx; the gases are quenched in a countercurrent water absorber, the AN is distilled, and the residual ammonia is neutralised with sulphuric acid to ammonium sulphate fertiliser.

###### Ammonia `c64.case.abs-resin.ammonia`

Made by steam-methane reforming natural gas to synthesis gas (CO+H2) and then Haber-Bosch synthesis over promoted iron. Every tonne of acrylonitrile needs roughly a quarter tonne of ammonia, and the byproduct ammonium sulphate goes straight back onto farmland.

###### Steam-methane reforming (primary reformer) `c64.case.abs-resin.steam-methane-reforming`

Natural gas and steam are burned over nickel at 800-900 C to give synthesis gas, CO plus H2. The high-temperature endothermic step is fired by burning part of the gas itself, so an ammonia plant is really a gas-fired furnace with a chemistry attached.

###### Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis `c64.case.abs-resin.haber-bosch`

Nitrogen and hydrogen react at 400-500 C and 150-300 bar over an iron catalyst promoted with K2O and Al2O3. This is where the era shows: 1980s plants ran the classic packed-bed, and modern plants use much more efficient ruthenium catalysts at lower pressure.

###### Bismuth phosphomolybdate ammoxidation catalyst `c64.case.abs-resin.mo-bi-catalyst`

The heart of the ammoxidation. A mixture of bismuth, molybdenum, iron, cobalt and other metal oxides, typically supported on silica or silica-alumina. It works by a redox cycle: the lattice oxygen of the molybdate grabs an allylic hydrogen from propylene, ammonia inserts, the nitrile is desorbed, and air re-oxidises the bismuth.

###### Bismuth ore and bismuth compounds `c64.case.abs-resin.bismuth-source` _(medium)_

Bismuth comes mainly as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from bismuthinite (Bi2S3) or as native bismuth in tin/tungsten veins. The oxo-nitrate is precipitated from an acid solution and calcined to bismuth oxide for the catalyst.

###### Molybdenum ore (molybdenite) `c64.case.abs-resin.molybdenum-source` _(medium)_

Molybdenite, MoS2, mined mostly as a by-product of porphyry copper. It is roasted to technical-grade molybdic oxide and then purified to the high-purity metal or oxidised for catalyst use.

###### Silica / silica-alumina support `c64.case.abs-resin.silica-support` _(medium)_

The porous carrier for the bismuth molybdate, made from diatomaceous earth or by co-precipitating silica from sodium silicate. Diatomaceous earth is a filter-aid mineral mined from ancient diatomite deposits.

###### Butadiene (1,3-butadiene) `c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene`

The rubber monomer. 1980s butadiene came almost entirely from the C4 fraction of the steam cracker, extracted by extractive distillation (or by older acetylene-dimerisation routes still running in Europe).

###### Recovery of butadiene from the C4 cut `c64.case.abs-resin.butadiene-extraction`

The C4 stream from the cracker contains butenes, isobutene and butadiene. Because butadiene boils at -4 C and its neighbours at +1 to +13 C, it is separated by extractive distillation with a heavy solvent such as NMP or furfural in a tall column, or by older acetonedimethylformamide absorption.

###### Steam cracking of naphtha (the source of all four monomers) `c64.case.abs-resin.steam-cracking`

Naphtha or gas oil is vaporised, mixed with steam and flashed through coils in a radiant furnace at 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second. The gas is quenched fast to stop further cracking, then fractionated into hydrogen, ethylene, propylene, a C4 cut and an aromatics cut. Almost every polymer in the C64 - ABS, SAN, SBR feet, polystyrene foam - starts as a cut out of this one column.

###### Cracker coil casting in high-nickel alloy `c64.case.abs-resin.naphtha-cracker-coil` _(medium)_

Radiant furnace coils are investment-cast from HK40 or 35Cr-45Ni alloy in twenty to forty segments, then thermally expanded into the tube supports. The nickel content is what keeps the coil from coking and creeping at 850 C.

###### Refractory fibre block lining `c64.case.abs-resin.refractory` _(medium)_

The furnace interior is lined with castable alumina and calcium-aluminate refractory or ceramic fibre blanket to hold 850 C and survive thermal cycling. It is a consumable and a real maintenance cost.

##### Emulsifier (fatty-acid soap) `c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisation.emulsifier` _(medium)_

The ABS latex is not made with a synthetic surfactant but with cheap soap - typically a sodium or potassium salt of a C16-C18 fatty acid, sometimes blended with a sulfosuccinate for stability. This is the 1980s process: fully synthetic surfactants were still expensive.

##### Free-radical initiator (persulfate) `c64.case.abs-resin.emulsion-polymerisation.initiator` _(medium)_

Potassium persulfate or sodium persulfate, thermally decomposed in the aqueous reactor to start the radical chain. Cheap, and the resulting sulphate is later washed out during coagulation.

###### Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash) `c64.case.abs-resin.potassium-hydroxide`

Made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, the potassium salt crystallising from the sodium-rich liquor. It is what turns the fatty acid into the soap emulsifier and the persulfate precursor into the initiator.

###### Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine `c64.case.abs-resin.chlor-alkali`

Electrolysis of saturated brine in a membrane or mercury cell splits salt water into chlorine, sodium (or potassium) hydroxide and hydrogen. This is one of the foundational 20th-century chemical processes and it feeds PVC, solvents, and every chlorinated intermediate.

###### Halite (rock salt) `c64.case.abs-resin.halite`

Sodium chloride, mined or solution-mined from evaporite deposits and dissolved to make the brine that is electrolysed. Pure salt is the raw material for the entire chlor-alkali chemical complex.

#### SAN resin (styrene-acrylonitrile) matrix component `c64.case.abs-resin.san-resin`

Most ABS is a blend: grafted rubber plus a separately polymerised SAN. The SAN is the continuous, glossy, rigid phase; the grafted rubber is the dispersed, toughening phase. The SAN is usually made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation in a separate plant and shipped to the ABS compounding line as pellets or as latex.

##### Bulk polymerisation of SAN (plug flow) `c64.case.abs-resin.bulk-polymerisation`

A monomer mixture of styrene and acrylonitrile is polymerised thermally in a series of stirred, jacketed plug-flow reactors - classic 'prepolymerise then finish' with the reactor temperature ramped from ~130 C to ~230 C to convert 95-99% of the monomer. The SAN is devolatilised and extruded to pellets.

#### Additives package added at compounding `c64.case.abs-resin.additives`

ABS pellets as delivered are a straw-coloured, unpigmented polymer. The beige-brown of the C64 case is added downstream at the compounder as a colour masterbatch, along with stabilisers, a release agent and, in some grades, a flame retardant. A 1982 C64 case is almost certainly pigmented at the compound line, not at the moulder.

##### Pigment masterbatch (colour concentrate) `c64.case.abs-resin.pigment-masterbatch`

A high-loading pellet of pigment dispersed in an ABS or PE carrier resin, let down at 1-4% into the natural ABS. The colour masterbatch is itself a compounding product, made on its own twin-screw line.

###### Phthalocyanine blue pigment `c64.case.abs-resin.phthalo-blue` _(medium)_

Copper phthalocyanine (PB15), an intensely coloured, heat-stable, lightfast blue used for the cool grey-blue tones on some cases. Copper plus four phthalonitrile rings, assembled in a violent exotherm.

###### Phthalic anhydride `c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride`

Made by air oxidation of o-xylene over vanadia-titania catalysts at ~450 C. It is the classic route to phthalocyanine pigments and to glycidyl ester epoxy resins.

###### o-Xylene `c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene`

One of the three xylene isomers separated out of the mixed aromatics from the reformer by adsorption (UOP Parex-type) or by distillation. The ortho isomer is the one that gets oxidised to phthalic anhydride.

###### C8 aromatics separation (UOP Parex) `c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separation`

Para-xylene is selectively adsorbed from the mixed C8 aromatics onto a zeolite molecular sieve, desorbed with a purge, leaving o- and m-xylene. It is a swinging adsorption unit with hundreds of adsorbent beds and rotating valves.

###### Copper for the phthalocyanine centre `c64.case.abs-resin.copper`

Copper(II) salts, from electrorefined copper. Copper comes from chalcopyrite CuFeS2 ore or from ore sorted to a copper concentrate, then smelted, converted and electrorefined.

###### Chalcopyrite (copper ore) `c64.case.abs-resin.chalcopyrite`

CuFeS2, the dominant copper ore, mined underground or in large open pits and concentrated by flotation before smelting. The smelter's job is to strip the iron into slag so that copper matte can be converted and electrorefined.

###### Froth flotation of copper ore `c64.case.abs-resin.flotation`

Crushed and ground ore is conditioned with xanthate collectors and frothers, and the copper sulfide particles are floated to the surface in a bank of rectangular flotation cells. This is how most of the world's copper is separated from its host rock.

###### Flash smelting and converting `c64.case.abs-resin.flash-smelting`

Sulfide concentrate is blown with oxygen-enriched air in a flash furnace at ~1250 C, so that the sulfur burns and autogenous heat smelts the copper. The resulting matte is oxidised in converters, slagged of its iron, and the blister copper is electrorefined.

###### Titanium dioxide (white pigment) `c64.case.abs-resin.titanium-dioxide`

The workhorse white pigment, present in almost every beige or grey ABS and in most white packaging ink. Rutile is the industrial grade: made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile ore to TiCl4, then oxidising it in a 1000 C flame to pure white rutile pigment.

###### Ilmenite and rutile ore `c64.case.abs-resin.rutile-ore`

Titanium ore, mined from beach sands and hard-rock deposits. Ilmenite (FeTiO3) is the dominant feed; it is reduced to titanium slag, or chlorinated to TiCl4.

###### Metallurgical coke `c64.case.abs-resin.coke`

The reductant in the chlorinator (TiO2 + 2C + 2Cl2 -> TiCl4 + 2CO) and the fuel of the flame reactor. Coke is a by-product of coking coal in a coke oven battery, not a mined material in itself.

##### Release agent / lubricant `c64.case.abs-resin.release-agent` _(medium)_

A trace of an internal lubricant such as a metal stearate (zinc or calcium stearate, or a fatty-acid ester) is compounded into the ABS so the mould releases cleanly. Too much and it bloats the surface of the textured area.

###### Stearic acid `c64.case.abs-resin.stearic-acid`

C18 saturated fatty acid, made by hydrogenating tallow (or palm stearin) or by pressing stearic acid out of beef tallow. It is the base of the metal stearate lubricants and also of many cosmetic-grade waxes.

###### Tallow (rendered fat) `c64.case.abs-resin.tallow`

Rendered bovine or ovine fat, a slaughterhouse byproduct, used historically as a soap and lubricant feedstock and as a fatty-acid source.

##### Flame retardant additive (optional) `c64.case.abs-resin.flame-retardant` _(medium)_

Not all ABS is flame retardant, but electronics housings were often specified with a UL94 HB or V-2 grade, which is achieved by adding a halogenated additive - typically brominated epoxy or an aliphatic bromine-chlorine compound at 5-15 parts per hundred. It slows burning but costs toughness and colour, so a textured beige housing usually avoided it.

#### Twin-screw compounding and pelletising `c64.case.abs-resin.compounding`

Natural ABS pellets are let down with the colour masterbatch and additives on a co-rotating twin-screw extruder, degassed, filtered through a screen pack, and pelletised - chopped strands or underwater cut. This is a 1980s standard plastic-compounding line.

### Case tooling: H13 family mould with EDM texture `c64.case.tooling`

The two breadbin case moulds are large two-plate tools in pre-hardened or hardened hot-work steel, with the leather-grain texture cut by electrical discharge machining and the cavity polished and hard-chromed. A single mould produces thousands of C64 cases; its cost is amortised over millions of parts, so Commodore could afford a 5-cavity family tool.

#### Tool steel (P20 pre-hardened or H13/SKD61 hardened) `c64.case.tooling.tool-steel`

Most 1980s housing tools were cut from pre-hardened P20-type steel (about HRC 30-35) so the tool could be finished-machined without distortion. Tools needing more polish cycles or more heat went to H13/SKD61, vacuum-hardened and tempered to HRC 44-50.

##### H13 / SKD61 hot-work tool steel `c64.case.tooling.h13`

A 5% Cr, 1% Mo, 1% V, 0.4% C alloy. Chromium gives hardenability and polishability, molybdenum and vanadium give secondary hardness and temper resistance. Also sold as DIN X40CrMoV5-1, JIS SKD61 or AISI H13.

###### Ferrochrome from chromite ore `c64.case.tooling.ferrochrome`

Chromite, FeCr2O4, is smelted in a submerged-arc or submerged-top furnace with coke and lime to give high-carbon ferrochrome, then refined to low-carbon ferrochrome. Almost all the chromium in a tool steel charge comes in as ferrochrome.

###### Chromite ore `c64.case.tooling.chromite-ore`

The only economic chromium ore, mined mostly in South Africa's Bushveld complex and in Zimbabwe, Kazakhstan and Turkey. Sold as a lumpy or sintered lump, or as a fines fraction.

###### Ferromolybdenum from molybdite `c64.case.tooling.ferromoly`

Molybdenite is roasted to technical molybdic oxide (MoO3) and then reduced with aluminium or in a submerged-arc furnace with coke to ferromolybdenum, which is dosed into the steel melt.

###### Ferrovanadium from vanadiferous slag `c64.case.tooling.vanadium-ferroalloy`

Vanadium is not mined as a vanadium ore at all in most of the world. It is recovered as a byproduct: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag from iron ore smelting is re-smelted, or slag is leached with soda ash, and vanadium is precipitated and reduced to ferrovanadium.

###### Iron ore (vanadiferous magnetite) `c64.case.tooling.iron-ore`

The ore is smelted in a blast furnace; when it carries vanadium the slag is deliberately kept for vanadium recovery. So the same lump of ore yields the iron for the press frame and, later, the vanadium in the tool steel.

###### Vacuum hardening and tempering of the tool `c64.case.tooling.heat-treatment`

H13 is austenitised at 1000-1050 C, quenched in air or in vacuum, then double-tempered at 500-600 C to get secondary hardness. Vacuum is preferred because it avoids decarburisation and the distortion that salt baths cause. In 1982 salt baths were still very common for smaller tools.

###### Nitriding of the polished cavity `c64.case.tooling.nitriding`

A short nitriding treatment after polishing diffuses nitrogen into the surface, growing a hard, low-friction skin on the cavity that resists the corrosive effect of styrene monomer. Standard on hot-runner tools and increasingly used on ABS housings.

##### P20 pre-hardened tool steel `c64.case.tooling.p20`

A 0.38% C, 0.9% Cr, 0.4% Mo, 0.2% V steel supplied at HRC 30-35. Because it arrives hard, the whole cavity can be machined and polished with no risk of distortion from a later heat treatment, which is why it dominated housing tooling in 1982.

#### Machining of the cavity and core `c64.case.tooling.machining`

A 1982 tool shop would rough the cavity with large carbide or HSS milling cutters, leaving 0.3-0.5 mm, then finish-mill, then grind the critical faces flat and parallel, then EDM the texture, then lap and polish. Rough and finish were both done on machining centres or on conventional mills and grinders - CNC was normal but not universal.

##### Surface grinding and the parting line `c64.case.tooling.grinding`

The two plates are ground parallel and the parting plane is lapped. A visible flash line around the case seam is the parting line: on a housing tool it is put exactly at the joint line of the two halves so it disappears into the joint.

##### EDM cutting of the leather grain `c64.case.tooling.edm`

The texture is the one feature that cannot be milled: a random stochastic pattern of overlapping spherical dimples. It is cut by sinking a shaped graphite or brass electrode into the hardened, ground cavity, or by wire-EDM scanning. Sinking EDM gives a whole panel at once; wire EDM gives resolution but is slower.

###### Graphite electrode for EDM texturing `c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode`

Isostatic-pressed fine-grain graphite, turned or milled to the negative of the texture panel, or a CNC-shaped graphite block. Graphite is used because it is easy to machine, wears predictably as the electrode erodes, and does not damage the workpiece the way a metal electrode would.

###### Natural graphite flake `c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore`

Flake graphite is mined in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, China and Brazil, purified by acid (or in the 1980s by chlorination) and pressed with pitch binder into tooling graphite.

###### Brass electrode for fine detail `c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode`

Copper-zinc alloy electrodes are used where the texture has fine features, because brass machines more accurately than graphite and can be reworked. Brass comes from copper and zinc ores smelted together.

#### Lapping and polishing the cavity `c64.case.tooling.polishing`

The cavity is progressively polished - progressively finer abrasives on cloth and stone - to a mirror. On a textured tool the polish is done to the whole surface and the texture simply stays; on flat surfaces it goes to Ra 0.05-0.1 um, which is what makes the plated ABS read as glossy.

##### Abrasive polishing compounds `c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound`

Aluminium oxide for the bulk work, green chromium oxide for the final mirror. Both are made from bauxite or from chromite.

###### Synthetic alumina abrasive `c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina`

Bauxite is refined to alumina and sintered or fused into corundum, then crushed and graded into abrasive powders. Hardness ~9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, and the workhorse of metal finishing.

#### Hard chrome plating of the cavity `c64.case.tooling.plating`

The polished cavity is electroplated in a hexavalent chromium bath to a few microns. Chrome is much harder than the tool steel, so the tool wears far better; it is also what gives the moulded ABS its character - the gloss of a C64 case is the gloss of chrome, not of steel.

##### Chromic acid for the plating bath `c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid`

Made by roasting chromite with soda ash and limestone, leaching the sodium chromate, and acidifying. So the chromium in the plating bath comes from the same chromite that came into the tool steel.

#### Mould assembly: guide pins, ejectors, cooling `c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly`

The finished plates are set into a mould base with guide pillars or bushes, an ejector-plate assembly with pins under every feature that would imprint on the visible face, and water lines carrying coolant through the cores and plates to remove the heat of plasticisation.

### Injection moulding of the case `c64.case.moulding`

The bezel and rear shell are moulded on a large toggle or hydraulic press in a multi-cavity family tool. The ABS is dried, melted at around 250 C, injected at high pressure through a gate on the parting line, cooled against water channels, and ejected with pin marks and a visible gate vestige.

#### Injection press (300-600 t) `c64.case.moulding.press`

A toggle or direct-hydraulic injection moulding machine with a screw plasticiser, a heated barrel with three or four zones, an oil or water temperature controller, and a mould base. Toggle machines clamp faster and are what most housing tools ran on.

##### Plasticising screw and barrel `c64.case.moulding.injection-screw`

A flighted screw turns in a heated barrel, conveying and melting pellets on the way back and injecting on the way forward. The screw is nitrided 33CrMoV or 40Cr steel, bimetallic-lined at the tip in later designs.

##### Hydraulic clamp unit `c64.case.moulding.hydraulics`

Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector. A hydraulic press is the reason injection pressure reached 1000+ bar - compared with the ~500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.

#### Drying the ABS before moulding `c64.case.moulding.drying`

ABS is hygroscopic: even a little absorbed water hydrolyses the nitrile groups at melt temperature, causing splay streaks and reduced molecular weight. Pellets are dried before use - typically 2-4 hours at 80-90 C in a hot-air, dehumidifying hopper dryer - to below about 0.05% moisture.

##### Desiccant for the drying hopper `c64.case.moulding.desiccant`

Either silica gel or, better, a synthetic zeolite molecular sieve (3A/4A) that adsorbs water at low partial pressure and regenerates at 200-300 C. Zeolites are made from kaolin or from amorphous silica and alumina.

###### Kaolin (china clay) `c64.case.moulding.kaolin`

A white clay, essentially kaolinite Al2Si2O5(OH)4, washed from a kaolin pit, calcined and reacted with sodium aluminate or caustic to make a 4A zeolite molecular sieve. Kaolin is a dug mineral, not a petrochemical.

#### Melting and plasticising the ABS `c64.case.moulding.plasticisation`

The screw melts and homogenises the pellets as it retracts. Back pressure and screw speed set the melt temperature. For ABS the barrel zones run roughly 200 (feed) to 250-260 C (nozzle); the melt must be well above the 100 C Vicat softening point but below the ~270 C where ABS starts to degrade.

#### Injection and packing under pressure `c64.case.moulding.injection`

The mould is closed, the screw drives forward and the melt is forced into the cavity through the gate at high pressure, then held under pressure to pack the part to full density and to control sink marks. The pressure must exceed the pressure drop along the flow path, so thin, long, textured flows need very high injection pressure - this is why C64 cases show flow marks (the '2-point flow pattern' that Commodore's revived tooling still carries).

#### Cooling and controlled crystallisation `c64.case.moulding.cooling`

The mould is water-cooled, or temperature-controlled, and the part is held until it has shrunk to the tool dimension. Cooling is the dominant term in the cycle time for a large ABS housing, and controlling the rate matters as much as the total: cool too fast on one side and the part distorts; too slow and the cycle stretches.

#### Ejection, pin marks and gate vestige `c64.case.moulding.ejection`

Ejector pins push the part off the core and off the gate. They leave small round marks, usually inside the case where nobody sees them. The gate leaves a small scar on the parting line that is trimmed or simply hidden by the two halves of the case meeting over it.

#### Insert moulding of metal and plastic fittings `c64.case.moulding.inserts` _(medium)_

Things that cannot be moulded in - metal shields, posts, threads - are placed in the cavity before the shot and over-moulded. In a C64 case the shield standoffs and sometimes threaded metal inserts are insert-moulded this way.

#### Multi-shot / two-colour moulding `c64.case.moulding.two-shot` _(medium)_

A second shot in a second cavity moulds a second colour or material over the first, giving a hard-wearing colour layer or a soft-touch overmould. The technique existed and was used in 1982, but the breadbin case is essentially a single-colour ABS shell: the colour comes from the pigment in the resin, not from a second shot. Multi-shot became the norm for later keyboards and for grip surfaces.

##### Two-colour / two-material injection machine `c64.case.moulding.two-shot-machine` _(medium)_

A press with two injection units and a rotating or shuttle plate so the second shot is made into the already-moulded first shot. The tooling must be indexable so the transfer happens while the part is still hot, which is why multi-shot tools are very expensive and hard to maintain.

### Other polymers inside the case `c64.case.other-polymers` _(medium)_

The ABS case shares the machine with several other plastics. This node groups the second- and third-generation polymers in the C64's plastic parts so their feedstocks are traceable too.

#### Polystyrene (GPPS / HIPS foam, trays) `c64.case.other-polymers.polystyrene`

General-purpose and impact polystyrene appear in the C64's plastic inventory as packaging foam and tray material rather than in the case itself. The case is ABS, not polystyrene - a common misconception.

##### HIPS (impact-modified styrene) `c64.case.other-polymers.hips-rubber`

Styrene polymerised in the presence of a polybutadiene graft rubber, exactly the same chemistry as ABS but with styrene replacing acrylonitrile. Made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation.

#### Polycarbonate `c64.case.other-polymers.polycarbonate` _(medium)_

Bisphenol A polycarbonate appears in clear covers, lens and shroud parts and in some clear case variants. It is made from bisphenol A and phosgene, and from the same BPA that comes out of cumene/benzene oxidation.

##### Cumene (for bisphenol A) `c64.case.other-polymers.cumene`

Propylene benzene alkylation product, separated from the C9 aromatics by distillation, then oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and cleaved to phenol and acetone. Phenol + acetone -> bisphenol A -> phosgene + BPA -> polycarbonate.

#### Polyoxymethylene (acetal / POM) `c64.case.other-polymers.pom` _(medium)_

Acetal homopolymer and copolymer appear in precision mechanical parts - key plungers, small gears, latches - because POM is stiff, self-lubricating and dimensionally stable. It is made by polymerising formaldehyde from purified methanol.

##### Methanol (from synthesis gas) `c64.case.other-polymers.methanol`

Made by reacting carbon monoxide and hydrogen from natural-gas reforming, a few hundred C and 50-100 bar over a copper/zinc oxide catalyst. Formaldehyde comes from methanol oxidation over silver or iron-molybdenum catalyst.

#### Nylon 6 / 6 (connector latches, clips) `c64.case.other-polymers.nylon`

Nylon is the classic connector and latch material: tough, slightly elastic, and it takes a good insert or press-fit without cracking. It appears in the latch tabs and clips that hold connectors in the case.

##### Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine `c64.case.other-polymers.adipic-acid`

Both are made from benzene or cyclohexane in the chemical chain: adipic acid by nitric oxidation of KA oil (cyclohexanol/cyclohexanone), and HMDA from butadiene via the NBS route (chlorination, ammonolysis, hydrogenation). Nylon 6,6 salt is then condensed.

#### PVC (cable jackets, sleeving) `c64.case.other-polymers.pvc`

The wire jackets, cable boots and some insulators in a C64 are PVC. PVC is made by polymerising vinyl chloride, and vinyl chloride comes from the chlor-ethylene route (EDC cracking to VCM plus HCl) or from oxychlorination of ethylene. The ethylene and the chlorine both come out of the same crackers and chlor-alkali plants that feed everything else.

##### Vinyl chloride monomer `c64.case.other-polymers.vinyl-chloride`

Made by cracking EDC to VCM and HCl, then recombining HCl with ethylene (oxychlorination) or recovering HCl from the cracker. Then polymerised in a suspension autoclave - the classic 20-50 bar autoclave with a suspension agent - to PVC.

#### Polyester / PET film (insulation, overlay) `c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film` _(medium)_

Polyester film is used as thin insulation, as overlay film on some keycap legends, and as the amber capacitor sleeve material in the power supply. It comes from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, both of which come out of the aromatics and olefin chains already used elsewhere in the machine.

##### Terephthalic acid (for PET film) `c64.case.other-polymers.terephthalic-acid`

Made by air oxidation of para-xylene over cobalt-manganese acetate at 150-250 C and 10-40 bar, in a process that is a classic example of good process engineering: the oxidation is exothermic and the acetic acid byproduct is recycled.

#### Natural rubber (feet, grommets) `c64.case.other-polymers.natural-rubber` _(medium)_

Some C64 feet and small grommets are natural rubber, cis-1,4-polyisoprene, made by coagulating latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis. Natural rubber has excellent resilience and grip and ages to a tacky amber.

##### Natural rubber latex `c64.case.other-polymers.hevea-latex`

Tapped from the rubber tree; the latex is preserved with ammonia, coagulated with acid, and the coagulum is pressed into sheets and smoke-cured. The tree is a plantation crop - rubber trees only yield for about 25 years and need a tropical climate.

#### Neoprene (chloroprene rubber) `c64.case.other-polymers.neoprene` _(medium)_

Polychloroprene is used where oil and weather resistance matter - cable jackets on some Commodore leads, feet, and gasket material. It comes from chloroprene, made by chlorination of butadiene from the same C4 cracker cut.

#### Epoxy (potting, die attach) `c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy`

Epoxy resin is not a case material but appears as a potting and die-attach compound inside the machine - gluing the heat sink to the regulators and, in places, encapsulating a noisy analogue section. Epoxy comes from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both aromatic-derived.

## Keyboard module: 66 keycaps on hybrid switches `c64.keyboard`

The C64's keyboard is a separate wired module that drops into the bezel: a steel backplate, a single-sided PCB carrying the matrix, 66 individually moulded ABS keycaps, and beneath each cap a Mitsumi-style hybrid switch - a moulded plunger with a conductive rubber pad and a metal return spring, closing a printed-circuit board contact when pressed. Legendas are printed onto the cap tops with a two-colour pad printer.

### Keycaps (66 individual moulded ABS caps) `c64.keyboard.keycaps`

Not a single dished sheet: 66 separate rectangular caps, each moulded in dark brown-grey ABS with a slightly concave top, each dropping through its own square opening in the bezel onto its own plunger. Some breadbin sets had tan-coloured function keys, others grey.

#### ABS grade for keycaps `c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs`

A housing-grade ABS, low rubber content so the moulded texture stays crisp and the cap does not feel gummy. Keycap ABS is usually a slightly higher-gloss, higher-flow grade than the case resin because the caps are thin and have to fill a short, tight flow path.

##### Flow and fill of a thin keycap `c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs-flow`

A keycap is one of the shortest flows in moulding: a shallow, thin-walled box filled through a single gate. It is a classic short-shot candidate, which is why keycap tools are small multi-cavity tools with a well-placed gate and a warm mould so the flow front does not freeze before the last corner fills.

#### Keycap tool (small multi-cavity, hardened steel) `c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool`

Keycaps are made in small high-cavity tools - 4, 8 or 16 cavities in one block - because a cap is cheap and the tool has to be small enough to fit a small press. The tool is hardened tool steel, and the caps come off a common gate so the visible faces are identical.

#### Printed keycap legends `c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend`

Legends are printed on the cap top with a two-colour pad printer (pad printing / tampo printing): a soft silicone pad picks up ink from a cliche, deforms against the slightly crowned cap, and transfers the character. White legends on the dark caps; the RETURN and SHIFT caps in some sets get legends on the front face too.

##### Front-face legends (shifted / graphic characters) `c64.keyboard.keycaps.front-legends` _(medium)_

On sets that carry the shifted and graphic characters, these are printed on the small front wall of the cap. Printing a vertical face with a pad printer needs the pad tilted and a second fixture, which is why early sets avoided it and used a bolder single top legend.

#### Keycap colours and any colour coding `c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours` _(medium)_

Breadbin C64 caps are almost uniformly a dark brown-grey, with function keys sometimes a lighter grey or tan. There is no per-number colour coding on the breadbin keyboard - that idea belongs to some other machines (the C64C and later Commodore sets vary, and the VIC-20 had differently coloured function keys). What a C64 keycap has is a moulded-in colour, not a printed colour.

#### Cross-point fitting and cap underside `c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point`

The underside of the cap carries a moulded cross that clips onto the matching cross-post on the plunger - about 5 mm on early breadbin caps, about 3 mm on later ones. The two are not interchangeable. The underside also has guide ribs that keep the cap square as it travels.

### Hybrid switches (Mitsumi-style plunger, rubber dome, spring) `c64.keyboard.switches`

The C64 does not use a rubber-dome-only membrane like a calculator, nor a mechanical switch like a typewriter. It uses a hybrid: a moulded plunger carrying a conductive rubber pad rides on a coil spring, and pressing it drives a gold or carbon contact onto a PCB pad. That gives a real click, a light touch and a definite bottom-out - which is why a C64 keyboard still feels 'mechanical' in the 1980s sense.

#### Switch plunger (moulded, with conductive rubber) `c64.keyboard.switches.plunger`

A small moulded body with a cross-post on top that the keycap clips onto, one or more arms that carry a conductive rubber pad, and a stem that slides in the keyboard body. Type 2 plungers have four prongs and carry a loose grey 'bubble' contact.

##### Plunger polymer (acetal / filled nylon) `c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer` _(medium)_

The plunger has to be dimensionally stable over millions of strokes and low-friction against the spring and the body. Acetal (POM) is the classic choice for its low friction and stiffness; glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate are also used. All three are moulded on small multi-cavity tools.

#### Conductive rubber contact (carbon-loaded silicone) `c64.keyboard.switches.conductive-rubber`

The contact is a small pad of silicone rubber loaded with conductive carbon black. The carbon particles touch each other and carry a small current across the PCB pad when the pad is pressed down, closing the switch. It needs to be conductive enough to bridge the gold contact but resistive enough not to be a dead short.

##### Silicone rubber (the matrix of the conductive pad) `c64.keyboard.switches.silicone`

Polydimethylsiloxane. The base polymer is made by ring-opening polymerisation of octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane or by equilibration of a silanol-terminated PDMS; fillers (silica, silicone oil) tune the hardness and the tear strength.

###### Fumed / precipitated silica filler `c64.keyboard.switches.silica-filler`

Reinforcing silica for the silicone rubber. It is made either by fuming silicon tetrachloride in a flame or by precipitating from a sodium silicate solution. Both routes end at quartz sand or silicon metal.

###### Silicon metal (from quartz) `c64.keyboard.switches.silicon-metal`

Quartz sand (SiO2) is reduced with carbon in a submerged-arc furnace at about 2000 C to give 98-99% silicon. This is the starting point for the whole silicon chemistry, and here it ends up in a rubber pad rather than in a chip.

##### Carbon black filler `c64.keyboard.switches.carbon-black`

The conductive filler. Furnace black is made by feeding oil or gas to a hot refractory-carbon reactor in a stream of air at 1200-1500 C, quenching the soot, then pelletising and grinding it. It is the same carbon black family used in tyre rubber.

##### Compounding the conductive silicone pad `c64.keyboard.switches.rubber-compounding`

Silicone rubber, conductive carbon black, a peroxide cure and a filler are mixed on a two-roll mill, then the pad is either transfer-moulded or printed as a dot on the plunger. Getting the carbon black well dispersed without overworking it is the whole trick: too little mixing leaves lumps that do not conduct, too much breaks down the carbon network and the pad stops conducting.

###### Two-roll compounding mill `c64.keyboard.switches.two-roll-mill`

Two counter-rotating chilled rolls nip the compound and disperse the filler. It is the oldest and still the most reliable way to get a clean dispersion, and every rubber and plasticiser maker owns one.

###### Cure system (peroxide crosslinker) `c64.keyboard.switches.cure-system`

Silicone rubber needs a crosslinker. Dicumyl peroxide is the classic general-purpose choice for a compression-moulded pad; addition-cure (platinum-catalysed) systems came later and cure faster with less shrink.

###### Dicumyl peroxide `c64.keyboard.switches.dicumyl-peroxide`

The commonest silicone crosslinker of the era. It is made from cumene: cumene is oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and then condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to give dicumyl peroxide.

###### Alpha-methylstyrene `c64.keyboard.switches.alpha-methylstyrene`

A C9 vinylbenzene used as a chain-transfer agent and as the co-reactant in dicumyl peroxide. It is made by dehydrating cumene over alumina or acid at ~300-400 C - a direct route from the same C9 aromatics that make cumene itself.

###### Cumene to hydroperoxide and alpha-methylstyrene `c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-oxidation`

Cumene is air-oxidised in a stirred liquid-phase reactor at ~100-140 C to cumene hydroperoxide. Part is condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to make dicumyl peroxide; part is acid-cleaved to phenol and acetone, which goes on to bisphenol A and epoxy. One plant, three products.

###### Cumene from benzene and propylene `c64.keyboard.switches.cumene-source`

Propylene is alkylated onto benzene over phosphoric acid on silica (or a zeolite) at 300-450 C and 20-60 bar to give cumene, which is separated from its polyalkylated heavies by distillation.

#### Return spring (music wire) `c64.keyboard.switches.spring`

A small coil spring under each key that returns the plunger. It is drawn from music wire (a high-carbon, low-carbon-content steel with a tight tensile range) and wound on a automatic spring coiler. Type 1 keyboards spring every key; Type 2 springs only the space bar and relies on the rubber dome elsewhere.

##### Music wire (patented steel) `c64.keyboard.switches.music-wire`

A high-carbon, low-carbon-content alloy steel with very tight mechanical properties and a very clean surface - patented in the 1880s for piano wire. It is drawn to fine gauge on a bull-block or continuous wire drawer and patented through a multi-step process.

#### The snap: force-displacement curve of the switch `c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve` _(medium)_

The 'feel' of a C64 key is a curve, not a number. The plunger rides down the spring, then the rubber dome on the PCB has to collapse (or the contact arm has to snap over), producing a peak in force; past the peak the force drops as the dome collapses, then rises again into the bottom-out. Peak-to-valley difference of maybe 20-30 gf is what the finger reads as 'clicky'.

### Keyboard PCB (matrix and contacts) `c64.keyboard.pcb`

A single-sided PCB carrying the 8x8 matrix traces and one contact pad per switch, sitting under the plungers. The keyboard PCB plugs into a 24-pin header on the mainboard (CN1) and carries no logic of its own - it is just a switch matrix that the CIA scans.

#### Matrix topology and the two odd keys `c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix`

The CIA drives one of eight rows low and reads the eight columns; a pressed key connects one row to one column. Sixty-four positions are scanned. RESTORE is wired straight to the NMI line, bypassing the matrix, which is why RESTORE works even while the CPU is jammed. SHIFT LOCK is a mechanically latching switch wired to the same two lines as the left SHIFT.

#### Contact pads (gold or carbon) `c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts`

Each switch lands on a printed pad. On gold-plated keyboards the pad is gold over nickel; on cheaper sets it is a carbon/graphite coating on the copper. The contact on the plunger is the conductive rubber; the pad is the fixed electrode.

### Steel backplate `c64.keyboard.backplate`

A sheet-steel plate under the PCB with punched openings for the plungers and rolled or pressed stiffening beads. It carries the springs and holds the plungers' travel, and it is screwed to the keyboard body with about twenty small gold-coloured screws.

#### Piercing and forming of the backplate `c64.keyboard.backplate.punching`

The openings are pierced on a punch press in a single stroke across the whole sheet; the stiffening beads are then roll-formed. This is a high-volume sheet-metal process: a tonne of steel punched this way costs a fraction of a machined equivalent.

### Keyboard body and its fasteners `c64.keyboard.body`

A moulded ABS body that holds the plungers, the PCB and the backplate, and carries the cable. It is retained by about twenty small gold-coloured screws, and on the shift-lock position it has a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB.

#### Shift-lock keyswitch `c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch`

A tiny mechanically-latching slide switch (a black plastic body with a metal leaf contact) that holds itself in the shifted position until pressed again. It is not a matrix key at all - it is a separate latch that closes the shift lines.

#### Keyboard retaining screws (gold-coloured) `c64.keyboard.body.screws`

Roughly twenty small self-tapping screws with a gold or brass finish hold the keyboard backplate and body together. The gold colour is a zinc-nickel or brass-look plating, chosen because it reads as 'quality' on a part the customer never sees.

### Keyboard ribbon cable and connector `c64.keyboard.cable`

A short flat ribbon or discrete-lead cable from the keyboard to the 24-pin header (CN1) on the front-left edge of the mainboard, terminating in a moulded connector housing. It carries the eight matrix rows, the eight columns, the RESTORE line and the power rails - twenty-four conductors.

#### Ribbon conductors `c64.keyboard.cable.conductor` _(medium)_

Either a laminated flat-flex ribbon (etched copper on polyimide film) or discrete stranded wires. Ribbon is thinner; discrete leads are more flexible at the fold and are what most Commodore keyboard cables used.

## Rear and side I/O panel `c64.io-panel`

Everything you can plug into the machine. The back carries the 8-pin DIN video output, the 6-pin DIN serial (IEC) port, the 6-pin edge-connector datasette port, the user-port edge connector, the 7-pin DIN power input and the RF modulator's coax socket; the side carries two DE-9 control ports for joysticks and paddles; the bottom edge of the board exposes the 44-pin expansion socket. The video output is composite plus separate luma and chroma on an 8-pin DIN — which is one reason the RF modulator existed and one reason it did not need to be as good as it was.

### Front and rear I/O connectors `c64.connector-jacks`

Every plug-in interface on a C64: the 24-pin user port, the 2x6 cassette port, the 44-pin cartridge socket, the 8-pin DIN video/audio and 6-pin DIN serial connectors, the two DE-9 control ports, the 7-pin PSU inlet and the keyboard ribbon header. They share one manufacturing sequence: stamped-and-formed brass contacts, nickel underplate, gold flash, and an injection-moulded thermoplastic or glass-filled phenolic insulator.

#### Shared contact manufacturing: stamping, forming, plating `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking` _(medium)_

Almost every connector here is made the same way at the front end: a brass or phosphor-bronze strip is blanked, pierced, bent and formed in a multi-slide tool, then plated in a nickel bath and given a thin gold flash on the contact areas.

##### Four-slide die forming (blank, pierce, form, cut) `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die`

Contacts are made on a multi-slide machine: a brass or copper-alloy strip is fed as a continuous coil, and each station in the slide performs one operation - piercing the terminal slot, forming the spring barrel, bending the solder tail, then cutting off the finished contact. Hundreds of thousands of identical contacts per hour, which is why connectors are cheap.

###### Tool steel of the stamping die `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die.tool-steel`

The progressive die is made from hardened tool steel - P20 for the body, D2 or H13 for the cutting edges - with the contact geometry machined and ground. A stamping die outlasts tens of millions of strokes, which is why the contact is a commodity.

###### Iron ore behind the die steel `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die.tool-steel.iron-ore`

Tool steel is made in the same integrated plants as everything else: ore to blast furnace to basic oxygen furnace to alloyed bar.

###### Coiled contact strip `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die.coil-stock`

The blank comes off the coil as a continuous ribbon of brass strip, the cheapest way to feed a high-speed press. The whole 44-position cartridge socket's 88 contacts are stamped from one coil.

###### Copper rod to contact strip `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die.coil-stock.copper`

Brass strip is rolled from drawn copper-tin rod on a Sendimir mill. The copper is refined to cathode, cast to wire rod and drawn; the tin and zinc are added in the melt.

###### Copper ore `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-slide-die.coil-stock.copper.ore`

Chalcopyrite or native copper, refined and drawn. The chain from ore to contact strip is two or three steps.

##### Brass strip (Cu-Zn) `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock`

Cartridge brass, usually 70/30 copper-zinc, drawn into strip. Brass is used because it is easy to form, springs usefully, and takes nickel plating well; a strip's mechanical properties are set by the zinc content and by work hardening from the drawing die.

###### Copper of the brass `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-copper`

Refined from chalcopyrite, mined underground or in porphyry open pits, smelted and then electrorefined to 99.99 % and cast into a wire rod. The same copper appears in the connector shells, the board's traces and the coils of the RF modulator.

###### Copper electrorefining `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-copper.electrorefining`

Blister copper from the smelter is refined electrolytically to 99.99 % cathode, which is then cast to wire rod and rolled into foil. Electrorefining is what makes the uniform, sulphur-free copper that both brass contact strip and solderable connector plating require.

###### Blister copper from the smelter `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-copper.electrorefining.blister`

Fire-refined copper at 96-98 % purity, still carrying enough precious metals and impurities to pay for its own electrorefining. Modern smelters in 1982 moved to direct-to-blister continuous casting, cutting the fire-refining step.

###### Zinc of the brass `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-zinc` _(medium)_

Zinc is recovered from sphalerite ore, roasted to the oxide and either smelted to crude zinc or leached and electrowon; it is the element that makes copper springy and hard-working.

###### Sphalerite (zinc blende) `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-zinc.sphalerite`

The dominant zinc ore, usually a cubic sulphide with variable iron content, mined underground in limestone-hosted replacement deposits. Concentrates are roasted to the oxide or leached.

###### Roasting and calcination `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-stock.brass-zinc.roasting`

The concentrate is fluid-bed roasted, oxidising ZnS to ZnO with SO2 recovered as sulphuric acid. The oxide is then either smelted with coke to crude zinc or leached and electrowon.

##### Nickel underplate then gold flash `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating`

Two plating baths in sequence. First a nickel underplate (electroless nickel-phosphorus on some parts, barrel or rack electrolytic nickel on others) is laid down; this is the barrier layer that stops the base copper or brass diffusing into the gold, and nickel is also what the solder actually wets. Then a thin gold flash - typically 0.05-0.5 um over nickel - goes on the mating contact areas only, masked by selective plating or by tabbing the contact.

###### Electroless nickel-phosphorus deposition `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.electroless-nickel`

A hypophosphite bath plates nickel onto the parts without an external current, by catalytic reduction on the brass surface. Because the deposit is amorphous nickel containing a few per cent of phosphorus, it is harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure electrolytic nickel and it does not need to be masked. It became the standard underplate for the whole connector industry by the mid-1980s.

###### Phosphorus from phosphate rock `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.electroless-nickel.phosphorus` _(medium)_

The hypophosphite reducing agent is made from white phosphorus, which was still produced in the 1980s by the electric-furnace reduction of phosphate rock - a route that consumed very large tonnages of low-grade apatite for a few tens of kilograms of elemental phosphorus.

##### Gold for the contact flash `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold`

Gold is deposited from a cyanide or sulphite bath, by immersion displacement onto the nickel or by electroplating with a gold strike. It is the one precious metal on an entire C64's connector set, applied as a sub-micron skin over several square centimetres - a deliberate economics of just enough gold to make the contact.

###### Gold cyanide plating bath `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cyanide-bath` _(medium)_

Gold is plated from an alkaline cyanide bath with a gold anode that dissolves to replenish the bath. The bath is deliberately kept extremely low in free cyanide and gold so that the gold itself is plated preferentially rather than the underlying base metal.

###### Sodium cyanide from salt `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cyanide-bath.cyanide` _(medium)_

The plating bath chemistry, and the reason the cyanide gold plating shops needed strict effluent control and why the industry carried a persistent safety and pollution burden through the period.

###### Immersion gold flash `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.immersion`

A displacement process: the nickel surface is briefly attacked by a cyanide solution and gold plates itself out by substitution, in a few tenths of a micron, with no current. It is fast, cheap and exactly the right thickness for a connector flash.

###### Doré bullion as the metal feed `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.dore` _(medium)_

Most industrial gold plating in 1982 was fed from dore bullion - a semi-pure gold-silver alloy - refined to the fine gold the plating shops bought. The dore itself was mostly refinery production from anode slimes and mined doré bullion, so the plating gold is not a separate supply chain from jewellery gold.

###### The silver in dore `c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.dore.silver-ore`

Dore bars are mostly gold but carry 10-30 % silver, because silver is far cheaper to recover alongside gold than on its own account. That silver in turn came largely from lead-zinc and copper concentrates.

#### Connector housing: injection-moulded thermoplastic or phenolic `c64.connector-jacks.moulding`

The insulator every connector sits in. Card-edge and card-guide style connectors used black glass-filled polyester or phenolic because it machines cleanly, has almost no moulding flow and stands soldering temperatures; D-sub and DIN shells used glass-filled nylon or PBT. All were injection-moulded in multi-cavity tools.

##### Glass-filled phenolic (thermoset) `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic`

Phenol-formaldehyde resin reinforced with chopped glass fibre and moulded under heat and pressure. Extremely dimensionally stable, heat resistant and flame retardant, which is why black glass-filled phenolic is the classic black body of terminal blocks, card-edge sockets and relay bases. The disadvantage is that it cannot be melted and reformed, so every detail - including the card guide slot - has to be in the tool.

###### Chopped E-glass fibre `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.glass-fibre`

The reinforcement in a glass-filled phenolic or PBT housing. E-glass is a drawn alkali-free borosilicate, and the fibre is chopped to ~3-15 mm, sized with a coupling agent and blended into the resin just before the tool closes.

###### Silica sand for the glass fibre `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.glass-fibre.sand`

The glass fibre in a connector body begins as silica sand melted with limestone and dolomite. The same sand is used for window glass, and it is the same quartz that the crystal reactors grow from.

###### Phenolic compression press `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.compression-press`

A heated platen press with matched metal dies, pressing the thermoset compound to shape and curing it in the same operation. Compression rather than injection is what makes phenolic bodies cheap: the flow is short and the die is simple.

###### Phenol and formaldehyde `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.resin-source`

Phenol comes from cumene or chlorobenzene, both benzene derivatives; formaldehyde from methanol oxidation. So a black phenolic connector body is, like everything else on this board, two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.

###### Phenol from cumene `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.resin-source.phenol`

Phenol was made almost entirely by the cumene process: cumene oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide, then acid-split to phenol and acetone. Both products of that split fed the phenolic and the epoxy chains.

###### Benzene from a steam cracker `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.resin-source.phenol.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

##### PBT thermoplastic housing `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt` _(medium)_

Polybutylene terephthalate is moulded at normal injection temperatures, so a connector body can carry snap-fit features, pivot pins and cable strain-relief arms that a thermoset cannot. Glass-filled PBT was the standard D-sub and DIN shell material of the era, chosen for stiffness and low creep.

###### Dimethyl terephthalate and butanediol `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt` _(medium)_

PBT is a condensation polymer of DMT and 1,4-butanediol. DMT comes from paraxylene; butanediol came in the 1980s largely from maleic anhydride hydrogenation (a coal/route) or from butanediol dehydrogenation. Both are petrochemical or coal-chemical intermediates.

###### Paraxylene and DMT `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.px`

Paraxylene is oxidised to terephthalic acid, esterified with methanol to DMT, then condensed with butanediol. Methanol was itself a cheap synthesis-gas product of that period, so DMT carries coal and gas chemistry as well as oil.

###### Naphtha `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.px.naphtha`

The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

###### UV stabiliser and glass filler `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.uv-stabiliser` _(low)_

PBT needs an ultraviolet absorber because it yellows and embrittles in light, plus a glass filler for stiffness. The absorber is a benzotriazole, and both additives are minor mass but were cost-relevant in a moulded part sold in tens of millions.

##### Injection moulding press and tool `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-press`

A multi-cavity tool clamped between the platens of a screw injection moulder. The housing is a commodity: the same part is made in hundreds of thousands for the entire electronics industry, which is why connector housings cost less than the contacts inside them.

###### Injection screw and barrel `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-press.screw`

A nitrided steel screw and barrel, heated to 230-280 C, plastifying the polymer and injecting it into the tool. The screw is itself a wear part made from tool steel, so the moulding industry is a steady consumer of alloy steel.

###### Mould tool steel `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-press.tool-steel`

P20 stainless tool steel was the industry standard cavity steel in 1982, hardened to ~48-52 HRC and polished to a fine finish. A connector housing's surface is entirely a function of the cavity polish.

###### Iron ore behind P20 tool steel `c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-press.tool-steel.iron-ore` _(medium)_

AISI P20 is a low-alloy tool steel: iron with about half a per cent of chromium and a similar amount of molybdenum, made in the same alloy-steel shops as every other industrial tool.

#### User port, 24-pin card edge `c64.connector-jacks.user-port`

The C64's expansion bus. A 24-position double-row card-edge socket, 3.96 mm pitch, carrying the address, data and control lines plus regulated and unregulated power out to user-port peripherals. Spare parts for this connector are specified as gold-over-nickel contacts in a PBT UL94 V-0 insulator, which is a fair description of the period part.

##### Gold-over-nickel card-edge contacts `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts`

Each contact is a formed spring leaf whose nose protrudes from the insulator and sweeps the mating card's copper edge as it slides in. The wiping action means the gold never has to be thick to stay clean, and the nickel beneath carries the solder joint to the board.

###### Spring leaf alloy `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.leaf-alloy`

The leaf has to both wipe the mating edge and hold a contact force, so it is a hard-worked copper alloy - phosphor bronze or a brass-tempered strip. It is the same material family as the switch contacts and the cartridge socket.

###### Copper ore for the leaf `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.leaf-alloy.copper-ore`

Chalcopyrite and native copper, refined to cathode and rolled. The contact-leaf and switch-leaf trades drew on the same copper rod as the winding wire and the board traces.

###### Solder tail and wave-solder attachment `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.solder-tail`

The tail is formed flat and pierced so it takes a fillet in the wave-solder bath, giving a mechanically strong joint that also resists the repeated flexing of a plugged-in peripheral cable.

###### Through-hole tail and wave joint `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.solder-tail.wave-joint`

A pierced rectangular tail that takes a large fillet in the wave bath. The joint has to survive a peripheral cable being pulled.

##### User-port pin functions `c64.connector-jacks.user-port.pinout` _(medium)_

Pins 1-12 carry +5 V out, ground, /RESET, /PPASS (the CPU-select line), the cassette sense/write/read lines and the cassette motor line, plus 9 V AC; pins 13-24 carry the user port's serial bus lines (/EOT, /SERCLK, /ATN IN, /ATN OUT) and the speaker and cassette-slot lines. The C64 6510's on-chip I/O port is wired straight into this connector, which is why a printer interface or a modem could hang directly off it.

#### Cassette (datasette) port, 2 x 6 card edge `c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port`

The port that reads and writes Commodore DATAsette tapes. It is a 12-position card-edge socket - six contacts on each face, 3.96 mm pitch - that mates with a 6-pin connector on the datasette lead. Carrying analogue audio, motor control and a sense line, it is a reminder that in 1982 'I/O' still meant tape.

##### Cassette read pull-up resistor `c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-up`

The /FLAG input of CIA #1 that senses a keypress is pulled up through a 3.3 kOhm resistor, part of the resistor array family described under mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks. It is a tiny detail that shows the whole board's design logic: discrete resistors where few are needed, a printed array where many identical ones are.

###### The 3k3 pull-up as a discrete part `c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-up.resistor`

The datasette sense/flag line is held high by a single 3.3 kOhm 1/4 W resistor on the board. It is one of the values shared with the bussed resistor arrays, which is a good illustration of how the board mixes array and discrete for the same resistance.

###### Same carbon film supply chain `c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-up.resistor.source`

The 3k3 is one of the ordinary carbon film resistors whose chain is described at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.

###### Why the port exists at all `c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-up.signal`

The port carries analogue audio plus three DC control lines. The C64 read FSK-encoded data by timing transitions on the read line and generating the tones on the write line - the whole tape interface is three transistors, a resistor and two electrolytics, which is why it is so sensitive to capacitor leakage.

#### Cartridge / expansion port, 44-pin dual card edge `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port`

The slot along the bottom of the case into which cartridges plug. A 44-position dual female card-edge socket in a black glass-filled polyester body, with phosphor-bronze contacts gold-flashed over nickel. It is the single most-scrutinised connector on the machine: its contacts carry the entire address and data bus and have to survive thousands of cartridge insertions.

##### Moulded card guide and polarising key `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-guide` _(medium)_

The socket body doubles as the mechanical guide: a moulded channel sets the card's insertion depth, and an asymmetric keyway stops a cartridge being inserted the wrong way round. Because the body is a thermoset, the guide is machined or moulded in one piece and cannot flex.

###### Machined guide features `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-guide.machining` _(medium)_

Because the socket body is a thermoset, the card channel, the stop face and the polarising key cannot be melted into place - they have to be present in the compression tool or machined afterwards. Both were normal for this part in 1982.

###### Glass fibre of the filled phenolic `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-guide.machining.filler`

Chopped glass fibre in the phenolic is what stops the guide wearing when a cartridge is pushed and pulled thousands of times. It is the same filler as in the connector housings.

###### Contact alignment and pitch `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.alignment` _(medium)_

At 2.54 mm pitch across 44 positions, the accumulation of tolerance is what makes or breaks a card-edge socket: the tool and the plating process have to hold the contacts on a common plane so no single contact is left proud and taking all the wear.

##### Contact wear and the 'dead cartridge' problem `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contact-wear`

A card-edge socket is a wear item: each insertion plucks the leaf contacts and sweeps the mating gold edge. Dust, oxide from the cartridge's board and accumulated plasticiser eventually make one or two contacts intermittent, which is the classic 'dead cartridge' symptom. Contact cleaning and, on a well-used machine, contact replacement were the routine repair.

###### Contact cleaning regime `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contact-wear.cleaning` _(medium)_

The routine service answer to a marginal cartridge socket: an alcohol swab on the contacts, a foam rod through the slots, and a bend of the leaf if it has lost tension. It is one of the few repairs on a 1982 machine that needs no parts.

##### Commodore expansion port specification `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.spec` _(medium)_

The 44-pin socket's pin assignment, pitch and card thickness were Commodore's own definition rather than a JEDEC standard, which is why cartridges for the C64, C128 and VIC-20 are interchangeable and C64C cartridges are not.

##### Phosphor bronze contacts `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contacts-alloy`

Phosphor bronze was the standard card-edge contact alloy for this connector, gold-flashed over nickel. It is springy, fatigue-resistant and takes a good plating - the combination a card-edge socket needs, because it is wiped hard on every insertion.

###### Tin in the bronze `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contacts-alloy.tin`

The tin that makes the contact alloy springy came from cassiterite, mined and smelted.

###### Cassiterite workings `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contacts-alloy.tin.cassiterite`

Heavy, chemically inert tin oxide that concentrates in placers below pegmatites and in alluvial gravels. Because it is so dense it also turns up in gold placer concentrates, where it was historically an impurity to be discarded.

###### Selective gold plating of the contact area `c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.contacts-alloy.plating-bath` _(medium)_

The contact is selectively plated by tabbing: the terminal is masked or wired as a cathode so only the mating area is gold-flashed.

#### Video/audio connector, 8-pin round DIN `c64.connector-jacks.av-din`

One round DIN on the rear panel carrying composite video, separate luma and chroma (for a Commodore 1701 monitor's RGB-with-separate-luma input), mono audio, and the RF modulator's composite and audio out. Very early 1982 boards used a 5-pin version instead, with luma and chroma combined.

##### Sprung split-tulip centre pin `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin`

The centre contact is a thin slotted pin that is sprung into a slight taper, so it plugs into a matching conical socket and self-aligns. The slot lets it flex elastically and also means a slightly undersized mating hole still makes contact at two lines rather than at a point - which is why DIN connectors are famously forgiving.

###### Conical mating socket `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mating-socket` _(medium)_

The socket the tulip pin plugs into has a matching taper, usually machined or stamped with a broach, so the two surfaces self-align on insertion. The taper is the reason a DIN plug feels forgiving and a plain pin-and-socket does not.

###### Broached taper `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mating-socket.broach` _(medium)_

The mating socket's cone is broached rather than turned, so the surface finish is controlled by a single multi-form tool. The broach was hardened steel, so this was another tool-steel consumer.

###### Iron ore `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mating-socket.broach.iron-ore`
