Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

###### Contact plating of the DIN pin `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.contact-plating` _(medium)_

The centre pin is nickel-plated with a gold or silver flash; the signal level here (composite video and line-level audio) is high enough that nickel alone would work, but gold was used for consistency with the other connectors.

###### Nickel underplate plus precious flash `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.contact-plating.electrolytic` _(medium)_

The same nickel-then-gold sequence as every other contact in the machine, on a tin or nickel base.

##### Nickel-plated steel shell and shield can `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell`

The outer barrel is a drawn steel shell, nickel-plated for corrosion resistance and solderability, and crimped around the insulator. On a metal-panel or rear-case mounting it doubles as the shell ground. Nickel plate on steel is the standard 1982 finish for a mains-adjacent chassis connector.

###### Drawn steel shell stock `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.steel-strip`

The barrel is deep-drawn from nickel-plated steel strip - a two-and-a-half type can be drawn in a few progressive strokes. The nickel plate carries the shell ground and resists the corrosion a rear-panel connector sees.

###### Iron ore to strip steel `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.steel-strip.iron-ore`

Hot-rolled strip from a continuous caster, cold-rolled and annealed. The strip trade is downstream of the same ore-to-pig-iron chain as everything else ferrous.

###### Shell knurl and bayonet ring `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.knurl`

The knurled ring on a DIN plug is what a user grips to unscrew it; on a socket the threaded barrel screws into the panel. The knurl is rolled into the shell in the same draw.

###### Knurl rolling `c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.knurl.knurling` _(medium)_

The knurl is rolled into the shell in the drawing die by a knurled wheel, because knurling a drawn can after plating would cut through the nickel.

#### Serial bus connector, 6-pin round DIN `c64.connector-jacks.serial-din`

The IEC serial bus that daisy-chained the 1541 disk drive, printers and the rest of Commodore's peripheral family. Same body and same stamping technology as the video connector, smaller pin count, and the same sprung centre pin.

##### IEEE-488-style handshake on 6 wires `c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.protocol` _(medium)_

Commodore's bus ran clock and data in both directions with attention lines and handshaking on every transfer - an IEEE-488 descendant. That is why a C64 could sit between two 1541 drives and still address the right one: the addressing is on the bus, not in the drive.

#### Control ports, 2 x DE-9 subminiature D `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports`

The two nine-pin D-sub sockets on the rear panel for joystick or paddle controllers, a light pen or a mouse. Each is a DE-9 female in a plastic D-shaped shell with gold-flashed brass contacts dimpled for reliable mating - the connector everyone remembers from Atari, Commodore and Amiga alike.

##### Dimpled contact and shell-ground design `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.dimple`

Each female contact carries a dimple on its mating face. Dimpling pushes the two contact surfaces into a defined line contact rather than a random point contact, which lowers the contact resistance and stops the surfaces rolling on each other. The plug's outer shell also contacts the socket shroud, so the plug's ground comes from its metal shell rather than from its pins.

##### D-subminiature (MIL-DTL-24308) standard `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.d-sub-standard`

The D-sub was standardised for military/aerospace use in the 1950s and became universal electronics furniture. Its 2.77 mm pitch, D-shaped polarised shell and 2.5 mm panel-mount screw pattern are defined by the standard; the C64's control ports are ordinary commercial DE-9 sockets.

##### DE-9 insulator `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insulator` _(medium)_

A black glass-filled thermoplastic insulator carrying the nine contacts, keyed to the metal shell. It has to hold position to a few hundredths of a millimetre because the contacts must all engage simultaneously in a stiff nine-pin plug.

###### Glass-filled nylon insulator `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insulator.nylon`

Glass-filled PA66 holds nine contact positions to a few hundredths of a millimetre over a plastic D-shell, and it takes the insertion force of a stiff nine-pin plug without cracking.

###### Caprolactam `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insulator.nylon.caprolactam`

Nylon-6-6 from caprolactam, itself from benzene-derived cyclohexanone. The same chain as the switch body and the keycap.

###### Benzene from a steam cracker `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insulator.nylon.caprolactam.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

##### Metal shell shroud and strain relief `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.shroud` _(medium)_

On the machine side the socket is a plastic-shell type with no metal shroud; the shroud is on the cable plug, where it is what provides the plug's shell ground and its mechanical strength. Both were stamped and plated the same way.

###### Shroud stamping and plating `c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.shroud.stamping`

The cable plug's metal shroud is stamped from brass strip and nickel-plated; it provides the plug's shell ground and its mechanical strength, and it is what the user grips.

#### Power inlet, 7-pin round DIN `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet`

The rear-panel socket the external PSU brick plugs into. A 7-pin round connector in a large 'type C' shell, following the DIN 45329 / IEC 10 form: pins 1 and 5 carry the regulated +5 V DC and pins 6 and 7 the 9 V AC from the transformer, with the switched side feeding the board through L5, C97, C100 and SW1.

##### Friction-lock and pull-proof contacts `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction-lock` _(medium)_

A mains-adjacent DC supply connector needs its contacts to survive being tugged by the cable. The mating pins are a friction type with a deliberately stiff crimp barrel so a pull is taken by the metal, not the solder fillet; some Commodore supplies additionally used a friction-lock retention ring on the plug body.

###### Crimp barrel construction `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction-lock.crimp`

The pin is a hollow brass tube with an interference crimp onto the conductor rather than a solder joint. That is the actual meaning of a friction-lock contact: the metal grips the metal, so a tug on the cable is carried by a mechanical interference fit and not by the solder fillet.

###### Brass pin stock `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction-lock.crimp.brass`

Cartridge brass drawn wire, the standard material for crimp contacts because it is springy enough to hold an interference fit yet soft enough to take the crimp without cracking.

###### Copper ore to brass `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction-lock.crimp.brass.copper-ore`

Brass is a copper-zinc alloy, so it begins at a copper ore and a zinc ore. Both are ancient mined materials and both were still being mined rather than synthesised in 1982.

###### The pin 5 damage fault `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fault` _(medium)_

One of the best-known Commodore power faults: a partially populated or incorrectly wired supply lead damages the 5 V pin in the machine's socket, so the machine will not power up even with a known-good supply. It is a wear-and-misalignment problem on a friction contact carrying a DC load that the connector was not designed to be unplugged under.

##### SW1 switching of the 5 V rail `c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.switching`

The socket feeds straight into the board's main filter (L5, C97, C100) and then through switch SW1, so SW1 breaks the load current rather than the supply - which is why the switch's contact rating looks absurdly high for the job. The external brick's own rocker does the real mains isolation; SW1 only breaks DC at a few amps.

#### Keyboard ribbon header `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header` _(low)_

A soldered pin header at the front-left edge of the mainboard carrying the keyboard's flat ribbon cable. The keyboard's matrix lines and the shift-lock return run out of the machine this way; it is the one connector on the board that is not an industry-standard part but a plain 2.54 mm row of pins.

##### Wave-soldered pin header `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint` _(medium)_

The header's pins were pushed into the board and wave-soldered in one pass with the rest of the components, in 63/37 lead-tin solder. That is why the pin material is brass with a tin plate rather than nickel: it wets tin-lead, and it does not need the corrosion resistance a gold-plated control-port contact does.

###### 63/37 lead-tin solder `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.solder`

The alloy that joined every part on the board. Snelled with a small amount of lead to make it flow better at a low temperature, it has a eutectic at 183 C. The lead came from galena, the ore of lead, and the tin from cassiterite - two of the oldest traded metals, both still mined rather than synthesised in 1982.

###### Galena (lead ore) `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.solder.galena`

Lead came from galena, PbS, a dense cubic mineral mined underground often as a by-product of silver and zinc. It is roasted and sintered to litharge and reduced in a blast furnace - the same cupellation metallurgy that has produced lead for three thousand years.

###### Flux and its origin `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.flux` _(medium)_

Rosin flux, dissolved in alcohol, cleaned the board in the wave-solder bath. Rosin is the sticky residue of pine trees, and the cleaning step after soldering removes it because ionic residue is what makes a board drift or corrode.

###### Pine rosin `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.flux.pine` _(medium)_

Rosin is the fossilised sticky resin of conifers, dissolved in alcohol as the soldering flux and then washed off because ionic residue causes drift and corrosion.

###### Softwood resin `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.flux.pine.wood` _(medium)_

Collected from pine and conifer stands; the tree that keeps the board clean.

###### Wave-soldering machine `c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.solder-joint.wave-solder`

A pumped solder pot with a travelling wave, a heated conveyor and pre- and post-heating tunnels. The whole C64 board went through one wave in about ten seconds; that is why the pins were tinned and the leads formed for a flat joint.

### Switches and slide potentiometers `c64.switches`

Three human-operated controls on a C64: the mains-free power slider SW1 on the right-hand case panel, and the two slide potentiometers for volume/tone and brightness on the top surface. The power switch gates the incoming 5 V rail; the two potentiometers are wired directly into the SID audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.

#### SW1 power slider switch `c64.switches.power-slider`

A single-pole, double-throw or single-throw slide switch on the mainboard, actuated by a moulded slider that protrudes through a rectangular cut-out in the right-hand side of the case. Its only job in the C64 is to interrupt the incoming +5 V rail - everything else on the board runs off the switch's output side.

##### Moulded switch body (melamine / phenolic / nylon) `c64.switches.power-slider.body`

The insulator the whole mechanism lives in. Small slide switches of this generation used a filled thermoset (melamine-formaldehyde or glass-filled phenolic) or a glass-filled nylon; both mould well in simple two-plate tools and stand a soldering iron's heat. Melamine was the industry default because its arc resistance in a mains-adjacent switch is better than polystyrene's.

###### Melamine-formaldehyde thermoset `c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine`

A thermoset built from melamine and formaldehyde, filled with cellulose or glass fibre, and compression-moulded hot. It is rigid, arc-resistant, dimensionally stable and cheap - the standard insulator for mains switches and domestic electrical accessories of the period.

###### Melamine resin from urea and formaldehyde `c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.melamine-resin`

Melamine is made by condensing urea with formaldehyde. Urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide, both cheap industrial gases; formaldehyde comes from oxidising methanol, which comes from the catalytic conversion of synthesis gas. Both halves were pure petrochemical by 1982.

###### Glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF) `c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon` _(medium)_

A tough, self-lubricating engineering thermoplastic used where a moving slider needs low friction and good wear resistance against the moulded track. Injection-moulded into the actuator and often into the switch's own guide body.

###### Glass filler in the nylon `c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.filler`

30 % chopped glass fibre in the PA66, for stiffness at a thin wall and for dimensional stability against the moulded detent. The same filler as in the connector housings.

###### Nylon-6-6 polymer (caprolactam) `c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nylon-6-6` _(medium)_

The base polymer of PA66, made by hydrolytic ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam, itself made from benzene via phenol and cyclohexanone. It replaced silk and nylon-6 for mechanical parts because of its moisture stability and higher melting point.

###### Caprolactam to nylon-6-6 `c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nylon-6-6.caprolactam`

Caprolactam is polymerised hydrolytically, or converted to the salt and polymerised as a nylon salt, in a continuous process at ~250-280 C. The caprolactam itself comes from phenol or cyclohexanone - both benzene derivatives from a steam cracker or catalytic reformer.

###### Benzene from the cracker `c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nylon-6-6.caprolactam.benzene`

Benzene is one of the oldest commercially useful petrochemicals: it was isolated from coal tar long before 1982, but by then most industrial benzene came from the aromatics complex of a steam cracker, made by catalytic reforming of naphtha. It is the root of the styrene, phenol, nylon and epoxy trees.

###### Solder terminals and anchor `c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal`

The pins of the switch are brass, either solid or a brass tube over a steel mandrel with a solder tail. Brass is used because it wets tin-lead solder reliably and does not need nickel underplate for a low-voltage contact.

###### Brass pin stock `c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.brass-stock`

Solid brass wire or a brass tube over a steel mandrel, cut and headed. Brass is chosen because it is springy enough to survive the assembly line and soft enough to take a solder joint.

###### Case screws and panel mounting `c64.switches.power-slider.body.screws` _(medium)_

The switch body was riveted or snapped into the mainboard and located by the case's moulded boss. The moulded boss and its snap feature are part of the case tooling, not the switch tooling.

##### Slide mechanism, actuator and detent `c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism` _(medium)_

The actuator is a moulded slider with ribs that engage moulded detent ramps in the body, so it clicks into a definite position at each end rather than resting ambiguously. A moulded spring or a bent leaf spring inside supplies the return force and the over-centre snap that gives the switch its tactile 'click'.

###### Return leaf spring `c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf-spring` _(medium)_

A bent spring steel leaf that provides the over-centre force and the return to OFF. It is the part that fatigues: after enough actuations it loses tension and the switch no longer snaps crisply.

###### Spring steel strip `c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf-spring.steel`

A high-carbon strip steel, hardened and tempered, cut and blanked. Blade and coil spring steel of this quality came from the same integrated steel plants as the razor blades and the automotive leaf springs.

###### Moulded detent ramp `c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.detent-ramp` _(medium)_

A stepped ramp moulded into the nylon body or actuator over which the slider rides, giving a definite position at each end. Moulding the detent rather than machining it is what keeps the part cheap at the volumes a consumer switch sold in.

##### Leaf contacts and contact plating `c64.switches.power-slider.contacts`

A pair of formed leaf springs - phosphor bronze or stainless - carry the current; one is fixed and one moves with the slider, wiping against its mate over a small spring pressure so the electrical contact area is always fresh. The wipe is the whole reason slide switches do not corrode: an oxide film is continuously displaced.

###### Phosphor bronze leaf stock `c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosphor-bronze`

A copper-tin alloy with a few tenths of a per cent of phosphorus, valued for springiness, fatigue resistance and a low and stable contact resistance. Drawn strip, blanked, pierced and formed in a progressive die; the standard contact alloy of the whole electronics industry.

###### Tin in the bronze (from tin ore) `c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosphor-bronze.tin`

The tin that makes phosphor bronze springy and corrosion-resistant came from cassiterite, the ore of tin, worked since the Bronze Age and still a major traded commodity in 1982.

###### Copper of the bronze (from copper ore) `c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosphor-bronze.copper`

Refined from chalcopyrite or native copper, smelted, converted and electrolytically refined, then drawn, rolled and annealed into the contact strip. The same copper, more or less, appears in the C64's traces, connectors and windings.

#### Volume and brightness slide potentiometers `c64.switches.level-sliders` _(medium)_

Two miniature slide potentiometers on the mainboard whose sliders protrude through the top of the case. One sets the audio level at the SID output; the other sets the analogue video brightness level. Both use a printed resistive track and a spring-loaded wiper.

##### Printed carbon track on a ceramic substrate `c64.switches.level-sliders.track`

The resistive element is a track of carbon ink printed onto a flat ceramic or phenolic substrate, with metal end lands at each end. Printing is what makes a slide pot cheap: the geometry of the track, its length and its taper, sets both the total resistance and the law.

###### Carbon ink for the printed track `c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-ink`

Carbon black ground into a binder to a printable ink, screen-printed along the substrate and cured in a tunnel oven. The track length sets the nominal resistance and its taper sets the law; the two C64 sliders are linear, so the printed geometry is constant width.

###### Furnace black in the pot track `c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-ink.furnace-black`

The printed track uses a fine carbon black, finely ground so it prints smoothly and fires into a hard conductive film. The same powder, ground finer, is in the resistor film and the rubber dome.

###### Substrate and end lands `c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvature` _(medium)_

The carbon track is printed between two metallic end lands, usually fired silver, one at each end of the travel. The wiper bridges them; the centre terminal taps the wiper. All three terminals are solder pins on the pot's tail.

###### Firing of the printed substrate `c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvature.substrate-firing`

The carbon or cermet track is fired into the ceramic substrate in a tunnel oven at several hundred degrees, fusing the binder and the glass frit so the track cannot be scratched off by the wiper.

##### Spring-loaded wiper `c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper`

A small sprung metal clip or blade, usually a copper-nickel-plated spring steel or nickel strip, presses onto the carbon track and taps the voltage off at whatever point along it the slider has dragged it to. It must carry current through a sliding contact, so its plating and its spring force are the two design limits.

###### Plated spring-steel strip `c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-strip`

The wiper is stamped from spring strip and plated in a nickel or precious-metal bath so that it both springs correctly and carries current across a sliding contact without galling the carbon track.

###### Nickel plating bath `c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-strip.nickel`

The same nickel chemistry as the resistor lead plating and the connector underplate: a sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, or electroless nickel-phosphorus where the deposit had to be hard.

###### Pre-contact break and noise `c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.precontact`

A resistive track and a sliding contact inherently generate noise, and a cheap carbon track generates a lot. C64 volume pots are a well-known source of a faint hiss or crackle in the audio output - a real consequence of the printed-carbon technology, not a fault.

##### Moulded housing and slider knob `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing` _(medium)_

A small injection-moulded thermoplastic body with the moulded detent rails for the slider, and a moulded knob with the finger rib that protrudes through the case cut-out. The same polymer families as the switch body: nylon, ABS or a filled phenoxy.

###### Injection moulding of the pot body `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injection`

The body is injection moulded with the three terminal slots, the detent rails and the wiper guide all in one shot, in a multi-cavity tool shared with the rest of the world's miniature slide pot production.

###### ABS or PBT housing polymer `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injection.polymer` _(medium)_

Either the same ABS as the keycaps or a glass-filled PBT. Both are chosen for stiffness at a thin wall - a pot body has to hold a wiper alignment over millimetres of travel without creeping.

###### Moulded slider knob `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob` _(medium)_

A small moulded knob with a moulded-in guide rib that engages the body's rails, protruding through the case cut-out. The knob and the body were often moulded in the same tool family so the fit is guaranteed.

###### ABS for the slider knob `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.abs`

The knob is ABS because it has to be moulded thin, in a gloss finish, with a fine rib. It is the same polymer as the keycaps a few inches away on the same machine.

###### Styrene for the ABS `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.abs.styrene`

The styrene monomer that gives ABS its rigid, gloss-forming phase.

###### Benzene from a steam cracker `c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.abs.styrene.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

##### Single and ganged (twin) sections `c64.switches.level-sliders.section`

A potentiometer is made in two or three mechanically independent sections that share a common wiper shaft, so one slider knob moves the end terminal, the wiper and the middle terminal together. A 'ganged' pair means two complete potentiometers on one shaft; the C64's two sliders are physically separate parts rather than a ganged pair, since they control completely unrelated signals in different parts of the machine.

###### Common wiper shaft `c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft` _(medium)_

A drawn steel shaft pressed through the moulded wiper carriers, so all the potentiometer sections move together. Drawing the shaft from steel rather than moulding it in plastic is what keeps the alignment over millions of slider cycles.

###### Steel for the shaft `c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.iron-ore`

Mild steel drawn bar. The chain from iron ore to drawn bar is the same one behind every other steel part on the machine.

###### Self-lubricating bushing `c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushing` _(medium)_

A moulded nylon or PTFE-impregnated bushing in the chassis that the shaft runs in. Dry, it is what makes a slider pot feel smooth rather than gritty.

###### PTFE-impregnated bushing `c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushing.ptfe` _(medium)_

A nylon or bronze-impregnated bushing with a PTFE (Teflon) lubricant. PTFE is made by polymerising tetrafluoroethylene, whose monomer is made from fluorspar via hydrofluoric acid and chloroform.

###### Fluorspar for the fluorine `c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushing.ptfe.fluorspar` _(medium)_

Fluorspar, calcium fluoride, was the world's main source of fluorine for PTFE and refrigerant fluorocarbons. Its acid-grade material was a genuine traded mineral in 1982.

## Mainboard ASSY 250407 `c64.mainboard`

A single two-layer FR-4 board carrying the whole computer. Eight 4164 DRAMs make the 64 KB of main RAM; a 1 KB static RAM holds screen colour; the 6510 processor, the VIC-II, the SID, two CIAs, the PPI, a mask-programmed PLA and three mask ROMs do the rest, wired together with a dozen 74-series parts, three CMOS parts and a handful of small-signal transistors. Everything is through-hole DIP. About 320 components and 20 integrated circuits.

### C64 mainboard ASSY 250407 - bare double-sided FR-4 board `mb.pcb`

The unpopulated logic board of a 1983 Commodore 64. A 1.6 mm two-layer epoxy-glass laminate about 390 x 180 mm carrying 35 um copper on both faces, roughly 1200 unplated through-holes for component leads, NO plated-through holes and NO vias at all, green epoxy solder mask on both sides and a white screen-printed legend. Made by an outside printed-circuit-board house, not by Commodore.

#### FR-4 copper-clad laminate panel, 1.6 mm `mb.pcb.laminate` _(medium)_

The structural core of the board: woven E-glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin, sandwiched between two 35 um copper foils. It leaves the laminate mill as a rigid panel roughly 1.2 x 2.4 m which the PCB house cuts into working blanks.

##### Woven E-glass cloth `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth` _(medium)_

Continuous glass filaments woven into a plain-weave cloth that becomes the mechanical skeleton of the laminate. In 1983 the cloth would be roughly 0.1-0.2 mm thick, woven from yarn of about 9-22 tex with 8-18 filaments per centimetre. It is the structural, not the dielectric, member of the board.

###### Air-jet or rapier weaving `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.weave` _(medium)_

Warp and weft yarn are interlaced on a loom. Air-jet looms dominate because they run fast with few picks per inch; rapier looms use a rapier to carry the weft. Some cloth for laminate is stitched rather than woven, which is cheaper and adequate for reinforcement.

###### Glass yarn `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.yarn` _(medium)_

Hundreds of continuous filaments twisted together into one yarn, then wound onto a package for the loom. Sizing holds the filaments in place so they do not fuzz or separate.

###### Continuous E-glass fibre `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre` _(medium)_

The elementary filament of the reinforcement, drawn from molten glass. E-glass is a borosilicate/aluminosilicate carrying 15-19 % of non-glass oxides, mainly boron and lime, which lower the melting point enough for cheap fine-diameter drawing.

###### Bushing filament drawing `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.draw` _(medium)_

Molten glass is fed to a platinum-rhodium bushing plate perforated with hundreds to thousands of 4-9 um holes and pulled downward at enormous speed. Surface tension, not a die, forms each filament. The fibres gather into a ribbon, are cooled and wound.

###### Glass batch (frit) `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.batch` _(medium)_

A dry blend of silica sand, limestone or dolomite, and boron compounds, with a trace of carbon black so the glass comes out faintly green rather than water-clear. Melting the batch is what feeds the bushing.

###### High-purity silica sand `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica` _(medium)_

Low-iron, low-alumina quartz sand, the main glass former. Fibre-grade sand must be very clean, so deposits are washed, floated and acid-leached before melting. This is the terminal raw material of the whole glass chain.

###### Sand purification (beneficiation) `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.purify` _(medium)_

Washing, density separation and flotation remove heavy mineral and clay impurities; an acid leach removes iron, which would otherwise darken the glass. Drying and sieving follow.

###### Quartz sand / sandstone deposit `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.silica.rock` _(medium)_

Weathered quartz grains from unconsolidated deposits or friable sandstone, dug and screened. This is where the board's glass, and therefore a large fraction of its mass, begins as a mineral taken out of the ground.

###### Limestone / dolomite `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.lime` _(medium)_

Adds lime and magnesia to E-glass, lowering the melt temperature and improving the chemical durability of the drawn fibre.

###### Boron oxide compounds (colemanite, borax) `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.boron` _(medium)_

B2O3 lowers the working temperature of the melt, which is what makes fine-diameter drawing practical on ordinary platinum-rhodium equipment.

###### Glass melting furnace and bushing `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.melt` _(medium)_

A regenerative gas furnace melts the batch to a red-hot glass at roughly 1400-1600 deg C, with a nickel-alloy bushing plate riding on the sump. Fuel is almost always natural gas or oil.

###### Sizing and binder on the fibre `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size` _(medium)_

Fresh glass fibre is slippery and fragile. Filaments are coated while hot with a thin organosilane sizing plus a film-former such as starch or PVA that holds the ribbon together and stops the yarn fuzzing. For laminate the silane is chosen to form the chemical bond to the epoxy; that interface is the classic site of delamination failure.

###### Organosilane coupling agent `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.size.silane` _(medium)_

A bifunctional molecule with an alkoxy end that bonds to the glass surface and a reactive organic end that copolymerises with the epoxy. It is the molecular glue that turns a loose glass cloth into a chemically bonded laminate, and it is what makes copper-to-glass peel strength measurable.

###### Silane chemistry `chem.silane`

Two chemically unrelated families share the name, and both come off the same silicon-chlorine-hydrogen chemistry. Monosilane SiH4 is the gas used to deposit polysilicon in CMOS fabrication. Organosilanes — silane coupling agents — are the surface chemistry that makes glass fibre bond to epoxy resin, and they end up in every FR-4 board. Both are pyrophoric, and monosilane is acutely toxic in a way that made it one of the more awkward gases to handle before the industry moved to DCS.

###### Monosilane (SiH4) for polysilicon deposition `chem.silane.monosilane`

The workhorse polysilicon precursor for gate oxide, doped poly gates, lightly doped source/drain and passivation films in 1982-84 CMOS. A silicon fab in that era ran a silane or dichlorosilane plant, usually on site, because the gas is dangerous to ship and to store.

###### Disproportionation of trichlorosilane with hydrogen `chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route` _(medium)_

Trichlorosilane plus hydrogen, catalysed, yields monosilane and hydrogen chloride. This is the route most fabs used in the early 1980s because trichlorosilane was already being distilled in bulk for the polysilicon itself, so the silane plant was a small add-on to the same distillation train. The hydrogen chloride is recycled back into the chlor-alkali plant.

###### Low-pressure CVD deposition of polysilicon `chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd`

Silane decomposes on hot silicon wafers at 600-850 C in a diffusion tube, laying down a conformal layer. Poly gates made this way replaced the older aluminium gate, which is the change that made NMOS CMOS manufacturable at all — and the reason a 6510's logic gate is polysilicon rather than aluminium.

###### Silane coupling agents for glass fibre sizing `chem.silane.coupling-agent`

Organosilanes with two different ends: a hydrolysable alkoxy or chloro group that bonds to the glass surface hydroxyls, and a functional group — vinyl, amino, epoxy, methacrylate — that reacts with the resin. Aminopropyltriethoxysilane and vinyltrimethoxysilane are the workhorses. Applied to woven cloth after desizing, they are the reason epoxy bonds to glass rather than merely wetting it, and therefore the reason a C64 mainboard does not delaminate when it is soldered.

###### Flame-drawn fibre (roving) `mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.flame` _(medium)_

The cheaper alternative to bushing fibre: glass is remelted in a small furnace and blown through a plate with a few larger holes into 20-30 um fibres. Coarser, so it is used as a surface mat or chopped strand, not as the woven reinforcement itself.

##### Brominated DGEBA epoxy resin `mb.pcb.laminate.resin` _(medium)_

The diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A blended with a brominated epoxy co-resin so the cured laminate self-extinguishes. That blend is the FR in FR-4. This is the board's dielectric and its flame-retardant system, and it is where almost all of the board's non-glass, non-metal mass ends up.

###### Bisphenol A backbone `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bpa` _(medium)_

Condensed from two molecules of phenol with acetone under acid catalysis. This is the reaction that makes the epoxy a thermoset rather than a thermoplastic, and it is the point where petrochemical aromatics enter a material people imagine as 'plastic'.

###### Phenol `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.phenol` _(medium)_

Aromatic feedstock for bisphenol A. The cumene process alkylates benzene with propylene to cumene, oxidises it to cumene hydroperoxide, then cleaves with sulfuric acid to give phenol and acetone together.

###### Cumene and cumene hydroperoxide `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cumene` _(medium)_

The intermediate whose acid cleavage is the cheapest industrial route to phenol. Benzene plus propylene over phosphoric or sulfuric acid, then air oxidation.

###### Benzene `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.benzene` _(medium)_

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from heavy naphtha or made by catalytic reforming; the universal starting point for the phenol/cumene chain.

###### Heavy naphtha `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.naphtha` _(medium)_

A mid-boiling petroleum fraction from which benzene is extracted by solvent recovery. Crude oil is the ultimate source.

###### Crude oil `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.crude` _(medium)_

The hydrocarbon mixture pumped out of a sedimentary reservoir that ultimately supplies every aromatic and olefin feedstock on this branch of the tree.

###### Petroleum reservoir `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.reservoir` _(medium)_

Porous sandstone or fractured carbonate holding crude oil under pressure. Produced through steel casing and perforated liner into a gathering system, often by water or steam injection to hold down the pressure.

###### Propylene `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.propylene` _(medium)_

The C3 olefin used both here and for epichlorohydrin. From steam cracking of propane or naphtha, or as a co-product of ethylene.

###### Naphtha steam cracker `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cracker` _(medium)_

Naphtha vapour pyrolysed at 800-900 deg C in coils to make ethylene, propylene and butenes. A high-temperature furnace that is the gateway from crude to the whole plastics chemistry.

###### Epichlorohydrin `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.epichlorohydrin` _(medium)_

Reacts with bisphenol A in aqueous caustic to give the diglycidyl ether liquid that becomes the binder. Made by chlorohydrin reaction of propylene, then dehydrochlorination.

###### Chlorohydrin and dehydrochlorination `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorohydrin` _(medium)_

Propylene is chlorohydrinated with hypochlorous acid at low temperature to 1-chloro-2-propanol, which is treated with caustic lime to epichlorohydrin. The caustic also does the ring-opening condensation with bisphenol A.

###### Chlorine from brine `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.chlorine` _(medium)_

Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution in diaphragm or membrane cells yields chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. The same caustic soda serves the resin reaction.

###### Brine `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.brine` _(medium)_

Concentrated salt solution evaporated from sea water or saline groundwater.

###### Rock salt / evaporite salt `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.halite` _(medium)_

Halite mined from evaporite deposits or sun-dried from sea water, then dissolved to brine.

###### Tetrabromobisphenol-A epoxy co-resin `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.retardant` _(medium)_

The brominated co-resin that gives FR-4 its self-extinguishing behaviour. Bromine radicals released in the gas phase quench the combustion chain, so the laminate passes the UL-94 V-0 burn test.

###### Elemental bromine `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromine` _(medium)_

A heavy red-brown liquid and the source of the retardant bromine. Made by oxidising bromide-rich brines with chlorine, or by blowing air and steam off seawater treated with chlorine.

###### Bromide-rich brine (bittern) `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.bromide` _(medium)_

Mother liquor left from salt manufacture, historically rich enough in bromide to strip bromine from; today also drawn from underground brines.

###### Curing agent and cure chemistry `mb.pcb.laminate.resin.cure` _(medium)_

An amine or anhydride that opens the epoxide rings and cross-links them. The period laminate system was typically a bisphenol-A / diaminodiphenylsulfone blend, which is what set the elevated glass transition temperature of FR-4 sheet.

##### B-stage prepreg and core sheet `mb.pcb.laminate.prepreg` _(medium)_

Glass cloth pulled through epoxy, squeezed between metering nips to a controlled resin content and dried at 120-160 deg C until only partly cross-linked. The result is a dry, slightly tacky, board-like sheet that can be stacked and stored. The residual cure is completed under heat and pressure in the press.

##### Hot platen press and the lamination cycle `mb.pcb.laminate.press` _(medium)_

A stack of foil, prepreg, core and prepreg is pressed between heated platens. Pressure squeezes out the excess resin and forces it into the weave, and the heat completes the cure. This one step turns loose foil and cloth into a single homogeneous 1.6 mm sheet with copper bonded to both faces.

###### Heated platens `mb.pcb.laminate.press.platen` _(medium)_

Cast iron platens heated by embedded steam or electric resistance elements and ground flat. The cast iron is the reason a 1980s laminate press can hold a flatness tolerance tighter than anything the component designer asked for.

###### Cast iron platen body `mb.pcb.laminate.press.iron` _(medium)_

Grey cast iron, machined and surface-ground, chosen for dimensional stability and thermal mass rather than strength.

###### Pig iron from blast furnace `mb.pcb.laminate.press.pigiron` _(medium)_

Made by smelting iron ore with coke in a blast furnace, with limestone flux. The same ore and coke that make the platen also make the drill spindles and the wave-solder machine frame.

###### Iron ore (hematite/magnetite) `mb.pcb.laminate.press.ironore` _(medium)_

Run-of-mine ore crushed and concentrated before the blast furnace. The metal backbone of every machine tool on the board line comes from here.

###### Iron ore body `mb.pcb.laminate.press.orebody` _(medium)_

A concentration of iron oxides in banded iron formation or massive hematite, mined by open pit or underground room-and-pillar, then crushed and washed.

###### Hydraulic press pack and oil `mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic` _(medium)_

Pressure is applied by a hydraulic press pack with multiple heated platens so several laminate books can be pressed at once. The hydraulic oil is refined from crude.

###### Hydraulic oil `mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.oil` _(medium)_

A petroleum-derived lubricating fluid circulating through the press. Traced to crude oil like almost every other lubricant on the line.

###### Release paper between books `mb.pcb.laminate.press.release` _(medium)_

Bleached or unbleached kraft paper laid between each laminate book so resin does not bond one book to the next and the platen stays clean. Kraft paper is lignin-rich cellulose pulp.

###### Press heat source `mb.pcb.laminate.press.heat` _(medium)_

Steam coils or electric resistance elements in the platens. Gas- or oil-fired central steam was the norm in a laminate plant of this era.

##### Foil bonding and copper-clad laminate `mb.pcb.laminate.ccl` _(medium)_

Treated copper foil, prepreg and core are stacked and press-bonded to give the copper-clad laminate the PCB house buys. The foil is pre-treated so the epoxy keys into it during the press rather than peeling away.

###### Copper foil bonding treatment `mb.pcb.laminate.ccl.foilbond`

ED foil carries a natural fine-pebble surface that grips epoxy. Rolled foil is smooth and must be deliberately roughened or given a nodular peckled treatment so the laminate does not delaminate along the copper interface. This interface is what the peel-strength test measures.

#### Copper foil, 35 um, electro-deposited `mb.pcb.foil`

The conductive skin on both faces of the laminate. In 1983 most consumer laminate was clad with electro-deposited foil because it is cheap and its rough surface bonds well to epoxy. Rolled annealed foil was used where thermal or dimensional stability mattered more.

##### Electrodeposition onto a cathode drum `mb.pcb.foil.ed` _(medium)_

Cathode copper is dissolved into a sulfuric acid copper sulfate bath and electroplated onto a slowly rotating titanium or stainless drum. Brighteners and suppressors in the bath control grain so the stripped foil is a dense film rather than a powdery deposit.

###### Nodular (peckled) deposition `mb.pcb.foil.ed.nodule` _(medium)_

The final plating stage deposits fine nodules instead of flat copper. This nodular surface is what gives ED foil its grip on the resin during lamination.

##### Drum winding, stripping and slitting `mb.pcb.foil.wind` _(medium)_

The drum winds until the foil reaches 35 um, then the foil is peeled off and slit into rolls 1.0-1.4 m wide, the width the laminator needs.

##### Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts `metal.copper`

The most-used metal after iron, and in a C64 it is everywhere the electricity goes and everywhere the heat has to leave. The PCB tracks are 35 um copper foil on 1.6 mm FR-4; the switch-mode transformer is wound with 0.2-0.4 mm enamelled magnet wire; the rectifiers and the regulator leadframes are copper; the edge connector fingers and the heatsink mounts are copper alloy. All of it starts as porphyry ore at 0.4-1% Cu, which is why copper smelters are, in the 1980s, as much sulfuric acid plants as they are metal plants.

###### Porphyry copper ore (0.4-1% Cu) `metal.copper.ore`

A porphyritic intrusion - a granite-textured quartz monzonite that has been split by its own crystallisation and had its cracks filled with hot copper-bearing fluids. The copper minerals are chalcopyrite CuFeS2, bornite and chalcocite Cu2S, covellite and enargite Cu3AsS4. The ore body is graded by porphyry systems but the grade is low and getting lower, which is the whole problem with the industry. In 1982 the great producers were Chuquicamata and El Teniente in Chile, Bingham Canyon in Utah, Butte, the Arizona porphyry belt, Oyu Tolgoi and the Escondida development, and the copper belt of northern Zambia.

###### Open-pit copper mine `metal.copper.mine`

An enormous terraced pit. Ore is drilled and blasted on 15 m benches, loaded into haul trucks by 3-6 cubic metre shovels or loaded onto a conveyor, and hauled in 100-150 tonne trucks out of the pit on ramps. The waste:ore ratio at a mature porphyry pit is often 2-5:1, which is why the waste dumps are larger than the pit. As the pit deepens into the ore, block caving takes over: a fracture zone is undercut and the ore caves into a series of drawpoints, and the mining cost per tonne collapses - El Teniente in Chile was the world's largest block-cave operation from 1958 onwards.

###### Block cave drawpoints and ore pass `metal.copper.block-cave` _(medium)_

The block cave is the deepest and most sophisticated piece of 1980s mining engineering anywhere near a C64: a slot is cut along the base of the ore block, the slot is blasted, the overlying ore fractures and subsides into the void, and a finger stoper trains stop releasing ore once the cave front has moved past a drawpoint, to stop surface subsidence from outrunning the cave. Ore falls 100-1000 m to a conveyor at the bottom. Throughput per drawpoint is low - a few hundred tonnes a day - so a big block cave has hundreds of them.

###### Tertiary porphyry intrusion `metal.copper.intrusion`

The leaf: a granodiorite or quartz monzonite stock, once liquid and now frozen, with the copper-bearing sulphide veins filling fractures and disseminated grains through it. Under a 100 m of leached, iron-stained capping lies the transition ore and then the primary sulphides, so the pit's first 50-150 m of material is nearly worthless and has to be hauled anyway.

###### The haul road, the ramp and the truck cycle `metal.copper.haulage` _(medium)_

The economics of an open pit are a haulage problem. A 130-tonne truck on a 2 km round trip from the loading point to the crusher, at about 25 km/h loaded and 40 km/h empty, takes 3-5 minutes per cycle including spotting and loading, so a shovel with a 4-second loading cycle needs about 6-8 trucks to keep it fed. The ramp grade matters enormously - every 1% of extra grade costs roughly 1-2% of the truck's payload - and so does where the crusher is put. A large porphyry pit moves 100,000-400,000 tonnes a day, and the fleet is 100-400 trucks.

###### Dust suppression and the environmental limit `metal.copper.dust-suppression` _(medium)_

A 100,000 t/day pit with unsuppressed haul roads produces a very large tonnage of airborne dust, and by the 1970s that had become a legal problem: the Clean Air Act of 1970 and the 1974 federal mine-safety inspection regime both applied to metal mines, and the pit had to water its roads, restrict the speed on unpaved haulage, and in the worst cases stop blasting in a high wind. So the environment is a genuine node in the middle of the ore chain, not a decoration at the end of it, and it is the same regulation that produced the sinter-plant dust precipitator in the steel branch.

###### Crushing and grinding to 100-150 um `metal.copper.grinding`

The ore arrives at 1 m. It goes through a gyratory crusher, then a semiautogenous mill (which uses the ore itself as the grinding medium, so no steel balls to pay for at that stage), then one or two ball mills in a closed circuit with a spiral classifier and then a cyclone. Autogenous grinding came in during the 1970s and was fully established by 1982 because it both saved the grinding media cost and produced a much cleaner surface - less steel contamination matters when you are about to float it. The grind has to be fine enough to liberate chalcopyrite but not so fine that the froth washes out.

###### Forged steel grinding balls `metal.copper.steel-grinding-media` _(medium)_

Even in an autogenous circuit the ball mills need some steel, and the balls themselves are a ferroalloy product: rail steel or scrap forged and quenched. Hardness matters more than anything - a 1982 ball mill ran 100-150 mm balls in the harder grind, and the wear rate was the plant's second-biggest cost after power. Nickel and chromium in the steel were deliberately kept low here, unlike in a crusher liner.

###### Froth flotation of chalcopyrite `metal.copper.flotation`

The slurry is conditioned with lime to a pH of 8-9.5 and with a xanthate collector, then aerated in a bank of 20-50 cubic metre rectangular cells. Air bubbles pick up the particles of chalcopyrite that the collector has made water-repellent and float them into a froth; the gangue stays in the water. Each cell in a bank is stage-controlled, with a froth of 100-300 mm. In 1982 the workhorse collector was sodium or potassium ethyl xanthate, made from carbon disulphide, caustic soda and ethanol, and the frother was pine oil or a synthetic such as methyl isobutyl carbinol.

###### Ethyl xanthate collector from carbon disulphide `metal.xanthate` _(medium)_

Xanthate is the workhorse flotation reagent, and it is a petrochemical in disguise: carbon disulphide (from natural gas or from coke-oven gas and methane) reacts with ethanol and caustic soda. Potassium and sodium ethyl xanthates were the standard 1980s collectors for sulphide copper, with a frother on top. So the flotation chemistry that recovers copper in 1982 depends on a sulphur-and-alcohol chain that ends in a gasworks, not a mine.

###### Lime and soda ash as pH regulators `metal.caustic-lime-flotation` _(medium)_

Flotation needs the ore surfaces clean of slime and the water at a controlled alkaline pH, or the xanthate decomposes to xanthic acid and carbon disulphide and evaporates. Lime from a limestone kiln is the cheapest and most common regulator; soda ash where lime is unavailable; and in the deep concentrators of Chile and Arizona the process water has to be lime-treated hard before use because the Andean water is very soft and very acid.

###### Pine oil and MIBC frothers `metal.pine-oil-frother` _(medium)_

Frothers are oily surfactants that stabilise the air-water interface. Until the 1970s the standard was pine oil distilled from pine stumps and mill residues - a forestry residue, not a mineral. Pine oil was being displaced by methyl isobutyl carbinol, a petrochemical, precisely because the natural supply was limited and the synthetic one gave a more stable froth.

###### Carbon disulphide from natural gas `metal.cs2-synthesis` _(medium)_

Carbon disulphide, the feedstock for every xanthate collector and for the rayon and cellophane industries, was made in 1982 almost entirely from natural gas or from methane recovered from coke-oven gas: the gas and a fraction of hydrocarbon oil are passed over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C, and the carbon disulphide is condensed out. So the flotation collector that separated copper from a porphyry in Nevada was made from gas, and the same molecule went into the rayon that was in the 1980s' idea of a flame-retardant textile. It is a leaf of the copper branch that is unambiguously a chemical plant rather than a mine.

###### Natural gas: the atmosphere-derived feedstock `natural-gas`

The leaf of this branch and of several others in this file. Natural gas is not mined, it is the accumulated hydrocarbon gas of ancient life that was trapped under an impermeable rock, and where it reaches the surface unburned it is burned off as a safety flare. In 1982 it fed the Haber-Bosch ammonia for the gold cyanide, the CS2 for the copper xanthate, the hydrogen for the ferrosilicon, the reforming for the direct reduction of iron ore, and the methanol for the phenol-formaldehyde and the epoxy. So the deepest shared leaf of the metals tree is not a rock at all: it is a gas that came out of the ground.

###### Copper flotation concentrate (~25-30% Cu) `metal.copper.concentrate`

A damp, fine, almost black powder shipped by rail or truck to the smelter. What the smelter really wants is not the copper but the sulphur, because that is what makes the smelter a sulfuric acid plant. A 25% Cu concentrate is roughly 50% sulphur and 10% iron, and the smelter's job is to burn out the iron, keep a copper-iron matte, and send every tonne of SO2 to an acid plant.

###### Thickening, filtration and the concentrate shipment `metal.copper.concentrate-handling` _(medium)_

The flotation concentrate at 25-30% Cu arrives as a pulp at 10-20% solids and has to be dewatered to 8-12% moisture to be shipped, because shipping water is shipping money. A 30,000 t/day concentrator produces 1,000-3,000 t of concentrate a day, and it is thickened in a 30-50 m diameter tank, filtered on a vacuum belt or a plate-and-frame press, and often dried to 8% on a steam belt dryer so it does not cake in a railcar. Copper concentrate that arrives wet is worth less per tonne and smelters charge for the water.

###### Flash smelting of concentrate to copper matte `metal.copper.smelting`

Concentrate, silica flux and limestone are dropped into a vertical reverberatory shaft where a hot gas blast, 40-60% oxygen-enriched, burns the concentrate as it falls. Three reactions happen simultaneously: the sulphides oxidise to copper oxide and iron oxide, the oxides react with each other to form a copper-iron matte, and the iron oxide reacts with the silica flux to make a slag. The furnace runs at 1250-1400 C and the products settle into three layers - matte at the bottom, slag above it, and offgas above that - which are tapped separately. By 1982 the flash furnace had largely displaced the reverberatory furnace: it is smaller, faster and needs less fuel, and it works on concentrate straight from the flotation circuit with only a small amount of dried concentrate added as fuel.

###### Silica flux from a sand quarry `metal.silica-flux`

The smelter adds sand or quartzite so that the iron in the concentrate can be thrown off as a slag instead of entering the matte. The quartz is often a cheap nearby dune sand - which is exactly the same material the glass industry buys, and the reason a copper smelter in the 1980s had a sand dryer and a small silica prep plant. The flux is dosed so the slag's silica content matches what the concentrate brings.

###### Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand) `metal.silica-sand`

Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.

###### Aeolian dune sand and beach placer `metal.silica-sand.dune`

The leaf: quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges - a sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

###### Sulphuric acid, 93-99%, from smelter SO2 `metal.sulphuric-acid`

The most-produced inorganic chemical in the world, and about half to three fifths of it was made not from burning sulphur but from the offgas of the copper, zinc and lead smelters in this file. The plants are the same: gas cleaning, drying, 10-14% SO2, 400-450 C over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, absorption in 98-99% acid in the first absorber, and then a second absorber with fresher acid - the double contact, double absorption process that was the industry standard by 1982. This node is the deliberate convergence point: the copper flash furnace, the zinc sinter plant, the lead sinter plant, the copper tankhouse and the zinc leach all feed or draw from the same acid plant.

###### Where the smelter acid goes `metal.sulphuric-acid.uses`

Roughly half of world sulfuric acid production is made from smelter offgas. In 1982 the biggest single use was fertiliser: phosphoric acid from Florida apatite, then superphosphate. The second was metal refining - the copper tankhouse electrolyte, the zinc plant leach circuit and the iron and steel pickling line, all of which are in this tree. The third was hydrofluoric acid. So a great deal of the world's phosphate rock was fertilised with acid made from the sulphur in somebody else's copper ore.

###### Apatite ore for phosphoric acid `metal.phosphate-ore`

The Florida pebble phosphate - a marine sedimentary phosphorite of fossil bones and excreta - is the classic source, and it is the end consumer of most of the sulfuric acid made in the copper and zinc branches of this file. It is mined by dragline or bucket-wheel stripping of 5-15 m of overburden over a 3-6 m ore layer, then crushed and slurry-piped to a beneficiation plant. Almost no phosphate rock in 1982 came from a chemical process: the whole fertiliser industry downstream of the copper and zinc smelters is a sedimentary rock mined out of a swampy coastal plain.

###### Marine phosphorite bed `metal.phosphate.rock`

The leaf: a 1-10 m bed of unconsolidated, often glauconitic phosphatic sand and clay in a marine or coastal plain sequence, sitting directly on limestone. It is dug, washed in a slurry pipeline, and floated or gravity-separated.

###### The flash furnace, its tuyeres and the concentrate burn `metal.copper.flash-furnace`

The furnace is a 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter vertical shaft with a refractory lining, fed by a few hundred tonnes an hour of dried concentrate through a hopper, and blown at the bottom by 30-60% oxygen-enriched air through tuyeres. The concentrate burns as it falls - it is the fuel as well as the charge - so the furnace needs almost no external heat. The reaction happens in the first metre above the tuyeres, the particles are spent, and the matte and slag settle into the two-deep bath at the bottom. The shaft above is used to preheat the charge with the rising offgas, and a flash furnace treats more tonnage in less volume than anything else in smelting.

###### Peirce-Smith converter to blister copper `metal.copper.converting`

The matte from the flash furnace is charged into a horizontal cylindrical steel converter with refractory lining and is blown with air through tuyeres along the side. The iron in the matte oxidises preferentially and goes into a slag that is skimmed off the top every few hours; once the iron is gone the copper sulphide itself oxidises to copper metal and gives off SO2. The blow takes 4-8 hours and takes 1 t of 60% matte to roughly 0.85 t of blister copper at 98-99% purity, still containing iron, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. The converter is a batch process and by the 1980s it was the target of the new continuous technologies (Noranda, Inductokemco) that were not yet commercial.

###### Fire refining and the anodic slimes of arsenic `metal.copper.fire-refining` _(medium)_

Blister copper still carries arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and every one of them is a nightmare for the electrolytic tankhouse because they float to the cathode and destroy the deposit. So the blister is ladle-refined: an oxidising slag of sodium carbonate with the impurities skims off, and then the copper is under-oxidised by dropping in green charcoal to reduce the whole mass back to copper, with the arsenic floatationised out. Where the arsenic is high, the refinery buys a second, smaller furnace.

###### The Peirce-Smith converter and its tuyeres `metal.copper.converter` _(medium)_

The converter is a cylindrical steel shell, 3.5-4.8 m inside diameter and 8-10 m long, on trunnions so it can be tilted, lined with magnesite brick, with 20-40 tuyeres along one side at the trunnion line. Air at 30-50% oxygen is blown in at 5-10 bar through water-cooled tuyeres that must be cleared and re-cleared by hand every few hours as the lining erodes - and a tuyeres that is not cleared becomes a plug and the whole heat is lost. The operator tilts the converter so the slag runs out of the mouth, then charges back, and there is no continuous process anywhere else in smelting with quite that much manual involvement. It is the machine that has been unchanged since 1865, and it is still the standard.

###### Blister copper anode, 99.9%+ `metal.copper.anode`

Blister is poured into a horizontal straight-mould casting machine - a ladle of molten copper that pours into a row of cast-iron moulds on a moving chain, giving a rectangular anode of 200-500 kg, roughly 700-1000 mm long, 400-800 mm wide and 30-50 mm thick, with a hanging loop cast on top. In 1982 the standard anode assay was 99.5-99.9% copper, and the gold and silver in it - typically 5-30 g/t gold equivalent - is why anodes are not made to 99.99%: that would be throwing away money.

###### Electrolytic refining of copper to 99.99% `metal.copper.tankhouse`

The refinery's tankhouse is a building a couple of hundred metres long containing rows of concrete or rubber-lined steel cells. Each cell holds a 150-250 g/L copper, 200-250 g/L free sulfuric acid solution at 55-65 C, with one or two anodes and one cathode per cell. Current at 20,000-40,000 A per cell is passed through; copper dissolves off the anode and plates onto the cathode at 98-99% efficiency, and gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and the platinum group fall out as a sludge on the bottom of the cell - the anode slime - which is worth more per tonne than the copper. A refinery producing 100,000 t a year has 300-500 cells and about 100,000 MWh of DC power.

###### Electrolytic copper cathode, 99.99% `metal.copper.cathode`

The end product of the mine-to-metal chain and the shape in which essentially all world copper trades. A flat plate grown on a stainless steel or copper starter sheet, with a characteristic slightly rough surface because too many nucleation sites make a soft, dull deposit. Cathode mass is 45-125 kg depending on the refinery. Weighed, sampled, stamped and shipped. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tankhouse branch, the foil branch and the wire branch.

###### Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper `metal.anode-slime`

The sludge on the tankhouse cell floor, 5-20 kg per tonne of copper refined, containing gold, silver, platinum, palladium, selenium and tellurium. It is dried and shipped to precious-metals refineries, where the gold is separated by cupellation, the selenium by roasting to SeO2 and volatilising, and the platinum group metals by solvent extraction and precipitation. By 1982 the anode slime was typically worth more per tonne than the copper in the anode, and a copper mine with good gold credits could be a gold mine that happened to have copper in it. This is a deliberate convergence node: the copper, gold and silver branches all meet in it.

###### Platinum-group metals from the anode slime `metal.palladium` _(medium)_

The anode slime also carries platinum, palladium, ruthenium, iridium, rhodium and osmium, at grams per tonne of copper rather than kilograms, so the volumes are tiny and the values are astronomical. In 1982 most of the world's refined palladium came from the nickel-copper ores of the Sudbury and Norilsk basins and from the Bushveld's platinum mines rather than from the copper anode slimes, but the slimes were a real secondary source for platinum and rhodium. The refining route is a solvent extraction and precipitation circuit followed by a final electrolytic or thermal refining, and by 1982 the platinum-group market was dominated by South Africa and the Soviet Union, whose platinum was the ore of choice for autocatalyst converters in the 1970s - which is a genuine and slightly absurd piece of industrial history, since the autocatalyst is a device for cleaning up the exhaust of a car and the platinum came out of the same layered intrusion as the chrome in the ignition plugs.

###### Cupellation of the gold-silver dross `metal.anode-slime.cupellation`

The slime is smelted with lead and flux into a litharge, then the litharge is blown with air in a cupellation furnace. The lead and everything else oxidises and is absorbed by a bone-ash or magnesite cupel, and what is left on the cupel is gold and silver together. This is the oldest refinery process in the book and it was still standard in 1982, because it is simple and it works.

###### Bone ash cupel from animal bone `metal.cupellation.cupel` _(medium)_

Traditional cupels are made of calcined bone - tricalcium phosphate - ground and pressed into a shallow cup with a porous, low-density surface that absorbs the molten litharge. Bone ash is the reason cupellation is called what it is, and by the 1982 industry the major refineries had largely moved to magnesia and alumina cupels for the big furnaces, though bone ash was still in use. So a refinery furnace foot was, historically, a rendering-house product.

###### Copper ingot and rod casting `metal.copper.ingot-casting`

The cathode is melted in an induction furnace or a reverberatory with a controlled sulphur addition, then cast - either continuously into wire rod by the Properzi upcast method or into 250-450 kg ingots for further processing. The 1980s standard route to rod was continuous casting; the alternative, longer route was a DC casting machine feeding a wire rod mill. Melting loses almost nothing because copper does not oxidise appreciably; the real problem is gas absorption.

###### Upcast wire rod line `metal.copper.upcasting` _(medium)_

In the Properzi upcaster the melt runs out of a horizontal holding furnace into a vertical casting trough behind a steel die that is being drawn upward by a rotating carousel; the trough is water-cooled and the copper solidifies against the moving die face, giving a controlled solidification structure. It makes 6-9 mm rod very cheaply and was standard in the 1980s, though the resulting cast structure needs patenting before drawing.

###### Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings `metal.copper.wire`

The switch-mode transformer in a C64's power supply - and any small mains-frequency transformer - is a coil of enamelled copper wire. The wire starts as 6-8 mm rod, is patented (heated to 200-350 C so the work-hardening from drawing anneals out), then drawn through a series of diamond dies to 0.15-0.5 mm, then enamelled and baked. 1982's magnet wire was overwhelmingly polyurethane enamel, sometimes with a nylon or polyester overcoat; polyurethane is the classic because it strips cleanly from the copper and does not need a flame to remove. This is a deliberate convergence node: the transformer winding, the ferrite core and the soldered joint all come off it.

###### Patenting: annealing the rod before drawing `metal.copper.patenting`

Copper work-hardens fast: a few percent of reduction raises the tensile strength enormously and the wire simply snaps in the die. So the rod is heated - in steam, in air, or in a fluidised bed - to about 200-350 C, which recrystallises the elongated drawing structure back to equiaxed grains, and then quenched. The black oxide that air patenting leaves is actually helpful, because it stops the wire rusting in the draw bin. Patenting is the cheapest trick in the whole wire business.

###### Drawing lubricant: copper sulfonate or oil emulsion `metal.copper.wire-lubricant` _(medium)_

The die must be lubricated or the copper galls and the die wears out. In the 1980s the standard was a water-based emulsion or a copper-sulfonate-and-fatty-acid concentrate, applied in a die box or as a once-through bath. Lubricant chemistry is also the friction and galling story in the die, which is why the drawing lubricant industry is a small speciality chemical business rather than an oil business.

###### Multiwire drawing through diamond dies `metal.copper.multiwire-drawing`

Since the 1960s the industry stopped drawing one wire at a time and started drawing 7-19 wires simultaneously through a cone of dies, so the die size needed for a 0.2 mm wire is much larger and lasts much longer. The dies are natural diamond - or, as synthetic diamond tooling matured through the 1980s, polycrystalline diamond compact - set in a steel holder with a hardened steel casing. Drawing to 0.15 mm means the copper has been elongated by a factor of order 1600, which is why magnet wire is made only from low-oxygen, low-sulphur electrolytic cathode and never from cast copper.

###### Enamelling and cure of magnet wire `metal.copper.enamelling`

The drawn wire is passed through a die and coated with liquid polyurethane enamel in a continuous length of 10-20 coats, each flash-dried, then cured in a vertical oven at 150-220 C for up to an hour. The result is a wire whose insulation survives a 155 C winding temperature and whose dielectric strength is 5-10 kV between turns. Enamelling is a chemical coating line rather than a metallurgy process, but the wire underneath it is this branch's problem.

###### Polyurethane enamel from a di-isocyanate `metal.copper.enamel-resin` _(medium)_

The wire enamel is a thermosetting urethane, made from a diol and a di-isocyanate such as toluene di-isocyanate, with a blocked-isocyanate cure so the coating is stable in the coating bath and only reacts in the cure oven. Its advantage over phenolic (vinyl formal, the pre-war standard) and polyester is that it strips cleanly and bonds without a heat gun. So a C64 transformer's insulation is a chemical product of the polyurethane industry, not a distillation product.

###### The enamelling line and the cure oven `metal.copper.enamelling.furnace` _(medium)_

A magnet-wire enamelling line is a 20-40 m long machine: a pay-off, a bunch of dies applying 10-20 coats with flash-off between them, a vertical cure oven 8-15 m tall, a capstan, a take-up. The cure oven is gas or electric at 150-220 C with the wire passing through it in a helix, and it is the cure schedule and not the coating that decides the wire's class. A class 155 wire needs a full hour at temperature; a class 130 wire can get away with less. In 1982 the whole world's magnet wire was made on lines of exactly this design, whether the wire came from Japan, France or the United States.

###### Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil `metal.copper.foil`

Two completely different foils with the same name, and this is a deliberate convergence node. The PCB foil is 35 um copper (70 um on very old boards) electrolytically deposited or rolled; the C64's board is single-sided, so it is one sheet of foil laminated to 1.6 mm FR-4. The capacitor foil is electro-deposited drum foil, deposited 6-18 um onto a rotating stainless or titanium drum from a copper sulphate bath, stripped and wound, then roughened again for etching just like aluminium foil.

###### Electro-deposited drum foil `metal.copper.foil.ed-drum`

A rotating drum cathode, 1-2 m diameter and 1-1.5 m wide, dips into an acid copper sulphate bath and turns; copper plates onto it at 20-100 A/dm2. A scraper peels the foil off at the top of the drum as a continuous 6-18 um web, which is then slit and wound. The deposit is not bulk metal: it is a columnar, sometimes dendritic growth, which is exactly why it etches into foil capacitors so well and why, for PCBs, it needs a bonding treatment before the laminate resin will stick to it.

###### Nodular treatment for PCB foil adhesion `metal.copper.foil.bonding` _(medium)_

Bare copper foil will not bond to epoxy; it delaminates. So the foil is treated in a warm sulfuric acid bath with a silicofluoride or a silane - historically sodium silicofluoride, later silanes - which grows a forest of microscopic oxide nodules on the surface. The resin flows into the forest and locks in, and the peel strength goes from a few N/cm to about 20 N/cm. This etching of the foil surface is the single most important step in making a copper-clad laminate, and the silicofluoride comes from the same fluorochemical industry as the hydrofluoric acid in the aluminium and tantalum branches.

###### Rolled annealed copper foil `metal.copper.foil.ra` _(medium)_

The traditional foil: heavy copper strip rolled on a Sendimir mill to 35-105 um and slit. It has a rolled, fibrous grain that is anisotropic, so it is easy to form and easy to drill, and it was the foil of record for anything that needs to be bent rather than etched. By 1982 electronic-grade rolled foil had been mostly displaced by electro-deposited foil for PCBs because deposition was cheaper and the bonding treatment was more reliable, but rolled foil remained the foil of choice for fine pitch and for capacitor cathodes.

###### Anode casting and the anode scrap stream `metal.copper.anode.casting` _(medium)_

About 10-20% of the anode never makes it into a cell - it is broken in handling, or the bars are too thin, or the busbar is corroded away - and it goes back to be remelted and recast. Every tankhouse therefore has a stub and an anode scrap yard and a melt, and the plant's anode book is a mass balance between the smelter's output and the tankhouse's demand. At the end of its life an anode is a thin, perforated, gold-bearing skeleton of iron and lead oxide that goes back to the smelter, so the gold in the anode is in a closed loop with the refinery and the melt is where the loop is closed.

            - *Anode slime: the real reason to smelt copper* `metal.anode-slime` *(seen above)*
###### Starter sheets, seeding and the tankhouse floor `metal.copper.tankhouse.starters` _(medium)_

Everything in a tankhouse depends on nucleation. The cathodes start on stainless steel or titanium starter sheets, or on copper seed plates that have been roughened. If too many nuclei start, the deposit is dull and soft and hard to strip; if too few, it is bright and hard and needs a big shear force. The whole art is seeding the right number. The electrolyte is also circulated at 200-400 mm/s across the cell face, because the anode slime would otherwise build up and short.

          - *Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings* `metal.copper.wire` *(seen above)*
          - *Copper foil: 35 um PCB and 6-18 um capacitor foil* `metal.copper.foil` *(seen above)*
###### Crushing, the copper-in-sulphide test and the mine call `metal.copper.crushing` _(medium)_

Ore that has been crushed and assayed is worth what its copper is worth, and the assay is the contract between the mine and the mill. A fire assay of a 100 g charge gives the total copper, and a leach assay of the fines gives the recoverable copper, and the difference between them - the oxide and locked-up copper - is what makes a mill's flowsheet design difficult. The crush is a gyratory at 1500 t/h followed by a screen, and nothing about a porphyry ore is subtle except this.

#### Dry-film photoresist, negative working `mb.pcb.photoresist` _(low)_

A dry film about 25-40 um thick, on a PET carrier, laminated onto the copper. Where the artwork film lets UV through, the acrylate resist cross-links and hardens; the hardened areas stand up to the ferric chloride. Everything else dissolves away and the copper under it etches out.

##### PET carrier film `mb.pcb.photoresist.carrier` _(medium)_

The polyester backing the resist is laminated from. Peeled off after lamination and before exposure, leaving the resist on the copper.

##### Film lamination of the resist `mb.pcb.photoresist.laminate` _(medium)_

The board is baked dry, the film is fed from a spool, heated, and pressed onto the copper by rubber-covered nip rollers. The rubber hardness matters: too hard and it embosses the fragile foil.

##### Surface clean and tack-free prep `mb.pcb.photoresist.coat` _(medium)_

Before the resist goes on, the board is degreased and dried so the film lies flat. A tack-free prep was unusual on period boards; wet resist had an easier time of it, which is one reason modern processes moved.

##### Photoresist chemistry `chem.photoresist`

The organic photoresists of 1983 were almost all positive-working diazonaphthoquinone resins on a novolac: the light-sensitive group is a diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate ester on a phenolic novolac made from phenol and formaldehyde. Exposing the resist converts the ester to a carboxylic acid, which makes the exposed resin soluble in the alkaline developer, so the image is positive. It is a strictly positive image because of the mechanism, not because of anything clever - the exposure destroys the very group that was holding the resin together.

###### Novolac resin from phenol and formaldehyde `chem.photoresist.novolac`

Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid to a thermoplastic, low-molecular-weight resin with no epoxide or methylol functionality left. The resin is not the photosensitive part; it is the part that gives the film its mechanical integrity and its dissolution behaviour in the developer. Its phenolic hydroxyl groups are why the novolac dissolves so readily in TMAH - and why an alkaline developable resist could not have worked with the old novolac-epoxy resists of the early 1960s.

###### Diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate `chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone`

The photosensitive ester: 1,2-naphthoquinone-2-diazide-5-sulphonic acid esterified onto the phenolic hydroxyls of the novolac. The 1,4-isomer was the one the 1980s photoresist industry settled on because it gives the higher photospeed and less outgrowth. The whole resist is about 20-30% diazo compound by weight; the rest is novolac and a small amount of sensitiser.

###### Alkaline development with TMAH `chem.photoresist.development`

0.2-0.3 N TMAH, at 20-25 C, by spray or immersion, for 30-60 seconds. The developer has to be controlled to a fraction of a degree and to a fraction of a percent of TMAH because the image is only about half a micrometre deep and the process window is correspondingly narrow. Spray development, introduced in the early 1980s, removed the meniscus and the particle problems of immersion and became the industry standard within a few years.

###### Dehydration bake and hard bake `chem.photoresist.hard-bake`

A dehydration bake at 150-200 C to drive the water out of the spin-coated film before exposure, and a post-exposure hard bake at 120-180 C to crosslink or densify the remaining image. The hard bake is what makes the resist resistant to the plasma etch and to the buffered HF, and it is also what makes it harder to strip - which is why the industry moved to plasma stripping and to ozonised water by the late 1980s, and why the old solvent strippers (phenol and sulphuric acid) disappeared from the process.

###### Resist stripping `chem.photoresist.hard-bake.stripping` _(medium)_

The 1980s progression: a phenolic-plus-sulphuric-acid liquid strip, then an ozone/water clean and an oxygen plasma ashing step to remove the hardened resist. The move was driven by the ion contamination of the liquid strippers and by the fact that the hard-baked resist was becoming impossible to remove in a controlled way. Plasma ashing uses an oxygen plasma at about 1 mbar and 250-400 C.

###### Negative resists and image reversal `chem.photoresist.negative` _(medium)_

A small share of 1980s production was negative-working - the exposed areas crosslink and stay - and image-reversal resists, where a photoacid generator makes a carboxylic acid in the exposed areas and an amine in the top layer diffuses into them and makes the exposed areas soluble, so a positive image is made with a negative resist chemistry. The reversal chemistry existed in 1983 because of the contrast it gave with the deep-ultraviolet exposure tools of the late 1980s.

###### Polysilane and plasma-polymerised resists `chem.photoresist.plasma-resist` _(low)_

The silicon-containing resists, in which a Si-Si backbone absorbs the deep ultraviolet and generates a silyl radical that crosslinks the exposed area. In 1983 they were in development for the 1 micron and sub-micron layers, and they are the reason the industry needed a deep-ultraviolet lithography tool at all. Their problem was exactly the same as everything else in this branch: a new chemistry with a contamination story attached.
