#### UV exposure through the artwork film `mb.pcb.exposure` _(medium)_

The artwork negative is laid against the resist and the board is flood-exposed. In 1983 this was a mercury-vapour or metal-halide lamp in a vacuum-frame exposure unit. Fibre-optic exposure systems that pipe collimated light into a bed of glass rods were spreading through the later 1980s and gave far more even illumination.

##### Vacuum exposure frame `mb.pcb.exposure.vacframe` _(medium)_

A hinged platen with a rubber diaphragm. Film and resist are clamped and then evacuated so the film sits hard against the resist with no bubbles and no shadowing.

##### Mercury-vapour exposure lamp `mb.pcb.exposure.lamp` _(medium)_

A quartz envelope filled with mercury vapour struck by an arc, rich in the near UV where the acrylate resists are sensitive. Needs a water-cooled jacket and a choke.

#### Ferric chloride etching `mb.pcb.etch`

The masked laminate goes into warm ferric chloride solution, which dissolves the unmasked copper and leaves traces, pads and ground pour standing. Copper removed along the way is recovered, and the etchant is periodically replenished or dumped.

##### Ferric chloride etchant `chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chloride`

FeCl3 at 35-42 degrees Baume (about 3-5 molar), which is an oxidising acid: the ferric ion takes an electron from the copper and the cupric ion falls back to ferrous. Regeneration is done either with chlorine (the industrial way, in a cell) or with hydrogen peroxide and acid. The byproduct is copper chloride, which in the 1980s was becoming a problem in its own right because of the copper discharge limits.

###### Regenerating the ferric chloride etchant `chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chloride.regeneration`

Spent ferric chloride is ferrous chloride and copper chloride, and it has to be oxidised back to ferric before it can etch again. The industrial way was a chlorination cell: chlorine into the ferrous solution at 60-80 C, converting ferrous back to ferric and precipitating the copper as cuprous chloride. The cell was a piece of the chlor-alkali plant's technology, and the chlorine in it was often the same chlorine that the plant bought for its own electroplating line.

###### Chlorination and the copper problem `chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chloride.regeneration.chlorine-regeneration` _(medium)_

Chlorine regenerates the ferric ion, and the copper comes out as a precipitate. In 1983 the industry was having to deal with two consequences: the chloride concentration climbed and had to be bled off, and the copper sludge was a waste with its own disposal limits. The alkaline persulphate etch solved both - it regenerated with hydrogen peroxide and sodium hydroxide, and the copper came out as cuprous oxide - and it was the reason the ferric chloride process was on its way out by 1990.

#### Resist stripping and clean-up `mb.pcb.strip` _(medium)_

The cross-linked resist film is dissolved away in a caustic or amine stripper, then the board is rinsed, given a mild acid clean to knock back any last residue, dried, and inspected.

##### Water for a factory `facility.water`

Every 1980s electronics and metals plant drank more water than it realised. Two distinct demands: ordinary industrial water (cooling, rinsing, process, human) and, in the fab, water pure enough to grow an oxide on silicon without introducing a defect.

###### Raw water intake `facility.water.raw-intake`

Either a surface intake from a river or reservoir, or a deep well into a confined aquifer. Surface water for cooling, well water for the ultrapure plant - because groundwater is already filtered by geology and low in organics.

###### Deep well and well pump `facility.water.well`

A 150-300 mm steel or PVC casing to 100-300 m with a deep-turbine or submersible pump. In the Lehigh Valley the sand-and-gravel aquifer gave soft, iron-bearing water that had to be degreased; in Taiwan the wells hit 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel.

###### Well screen and gravel pack `facility.water.well-screen` _(medium)_

Wire-wound or slotted screen with a graded silica-sand or garnet gravel pack, wrapped in geotextile. Stops the well pumping sand and the aquifer silting up the pump.

###### Aquifer sand and gravel `facility.water.aquifer-gravel`

Glacial outwash and alluvial gravel forming the confined aquifer; the raw material of the well itself and the source of the hardness and iron.

###### Confined sand-and-gravel aquifer `facility.water.aquifer`

The buried glacial and alluvial gravel bed saturated under pressure. Ends at the ground.

###### River / reservoir intake and pump house `facility.water.surface-intake`

A screened intake structure with travelling-bar screens, coarse screens and a low-lift pump house on the bank. In practice many 1980s plants - including Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones - bought municipal or industrial-zone water from the local authority and paid a tariff, rather than taking their own.

###### The river or reservoir `facility.water.river-intake`

Turbid, hard, seasonally variable. The Schuylkill at Norristown, the Sham Chun at Hong Kong, the Tamsui at Taipei, the Keelung river, and the many dams that supplied Hong Kong from the 1960s (Plover Cove, 1973).

###### Pretreatment for the ultrapure plant `facility.water.pretreatment`

Coagulation, clarification, multimedia filtration and activated carbon, all in one reinforced-concrete block that dominated the plant footprint. The purpose is to strip the water of the things that would poison an ion-exchange resin or foul an RO membrane: suspended solids, colour, hardness, chlorine, organics and silica.

###### Coagulation and clarification `facility.water.coagulation`

Alum or ferric chloride plus lime and a coagulant aid is flash-mixed, then the floc is grown in a flocculation bay and settled out over 2-4 hours in a clarifier. Residual turbidity had to be under about 1-2 NTU for the sand filters to be worth having.

###### Alum (hydrated aluminium sulfate) `facility.water.alum`

The workhorse coagulant. Made from bauxite (or domestic low-grade bauxite/clay) digested in sulphuric acid and crystallised. Ended at the bauxite mine by way of the same chain that makes the aluminium in the grid conductor.

###### Bauxite ore for the alum plant `facility.power.bauxite-mine-alum`

High-digestion alumina-grade bauxite, crushed and digested. The same input as the Bayer process. Ends at the ore body.

###### Sulphuric acid `facility.water.sulphuric-acid`

Made by burning sulphur or roasting pyrite and absorbing the SO2 in a contact plant to 93-98% oleum-free acid. The single most-produced industrial chemical in the world, and the raw material for lead-acid batteries, phosphates and most water treatment.

###### Sulphur (from recovered petroleum gas) `facility.water.sulphur`

By 1983 nearly all of the world's sulphur came from desulphurising high-sulphur crude and natural gas with Claus converters - i.e. it came out of the same crude oil that made the fuel oil.

###### Multimedia (sand) filtration `facility.water.multimedia-filtration`

Pressure filters in lead/catalysed iron tanks, 3.5-4.5 m diameter, containing 600-700 mm of graded media - typically 100 mm anthracite on 50 mm sand on 25 mm garnet. Backwashed with air scour plus water at 20-40 m/h.

###### Silica filter sand `facility.water.filter-sand`

Washed, graded, nearly pure SiO2 sand with effective size 0.5-0.7 mm. A large, unglamorous, and genuinely scarce mineral input to any waterworks.

###### Sand and gravel extraction pit `facility.water.sand-quarry`

Sand and gravel pit, usually a river dredging operation. Ends at the sand deposit.

###### Anthracite filter coal `facility.water.anthracite`

Hard, coarse anthracite crushed to 1-2 mm as the coarse top layer. Same material as the boiler fuel, just graded differently.

###### Activated carbon adsorption `facility.water.activated-carbon`

A tall bed of coconut-shell, coal or lignite carbon catalytically activated in a furnace, removing humic colour, trihalomethane precursor, pesticide and industrial organics. In the ultrapure plant it was the last chance to remove organics before the ion-exchange resin and the RO membrane.

###### Coconut-shell activated carbon `facility.water.coconut-carbon`

The premium grade, made in Sri Lanka, India or the Philippines by carbonising shell and steam-activating. The same material appears in the 8-bit filter section of a home computer.

###### Coconut shell (husk) `facility.water.coconut-shell`

The waste husk of the coconut palm, dried in the sun and carbonised. Ends at the coconut plantation.

###### Ultrapure water for the fab `facility.water.ultrapure`

The water that rinses a silicon wafer between every process step, and the water in which the thermal oxide grows. Target in 1983 was 10-15 MOhm-cm (roughly 1 ppb total ionic impurities) held at 20-25 C, distributed in 304 stainless or PVDF-lined piping.

###### Demineralisation by ion exchange `facility.water.ion-exchange`

Strong-acid cation then strong-base anion exchange, then a mixed-bed polish. Removed >95% of the ionic load of the filtered water and got to 10-15 MOhm-cm. It could not remove silica, organics or colloids, and the resin was a huge organic load in itself.

###### Mixed-bed deioniser `facility.water.mixed-bed`

A resin bed with cation and anion beads thoroughly mixed, polishing the effluent to sub-ppb. It was the top of the 1980s purity curve and was standard offtake to the wet benches.

###### Reverse osmosis `facility.water.ro`

Cellulose acetate or thin-film composite spiral-wound elements in 6-inch pressure vessels rejecting 90-99% of dissolved ions, 95-98% of organics and, importantly for the 1980s plant, most of the silica and hardness. The first RO units were installed at plants like this from the mid-1970s; by 1983 they were displacing two beds of ion exchange ahead of the polishers.

###### Cellulose acetate / TFC membrane `facility.water.ro-membrane` _(medium)_

A 0.2-1.5 micrometre-thick selective layer on a polysulphone support, wound into a spiral and potted with epoxy. This is the same membrane family as the 1541 floppy's read/write head gap in spirit - a nanoscale selective barrier - but the RO element was 1 m long.

###### UV sterilisation `facility.water.uv` _(medium)_

A 254 nm germicidal lamp in a stainless vessel, dosing typically 30-40 mJ/cm2, to kill bacteria and oxidise the last of the organics. Added in the late 1980s onward, mostly for the reclaim loop, because a 1970s fab did not sterilise its ultrapure water at all.

###### Low-pressure mercury lamp `facility.water.uv-lamp`

A quartz envelope with a low-pressure mercury vapour discharge emitting 254 nm, immersed in a quartz sleeve in the water. Same lamp chemistry as the germicidal fittings in hospitals.

###### Ultrafiltration `facility.water.ultrafiltration` _(medium)_

Hollow-fibre or dead-end membranes with a 1-100 nm cut-off, pressurised at 1-4 bar, stripping colloids, bacteria and endotoxin from the DI loop and from the reclaim stream. Rare in the 1980s; the state of the art then was a 0.2 micrometre-rated 'final filter' on the last loop, or nothing.

###### Ultrapure distribution loop `facility.water.di-loop`

Slotted 316L stainless or PVDF-lined pipework in a continuous recirculating loop, running hot at 60-80 C to suppress bacteria, with take-off points at each wet bench. A loop that is not constantly moving will grow biofilm within a day - the single hardest problem in 1980s ultrapure water.

###### PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) `facility.water.pvdf`

A fluoropolymer from vinylidene fluoride, chemically inert to ultrapure water and to most process acids, used as a liner or as solid pipe in ultrapure service. Melting point about 170 C, and it will not support microbial growth.

###### Polypropylene piping `facility.water.pp`

Polypropylene was the cheapest acid- and chemical-resistant pipe for wet-bench waste lines and reclaim, and (as spun-bonded fabric) the material of the 1980s 'class 100' air filter pre-filter.

###### Water reclaim and recovery loop `facility.water.reclaim` _(medium)_

Acid and solvent rinses, dump rinses and cooling-tower blowdown collected, neutralised, filtered and fed back to the pretreatment inlet. Water conservation in a 1983 fab was a cost decision, not an environmental one, and typically recovered 50-70% of the plant's demand.

###### Effluent treatment and discharge `facility.water.effluent`

Neutralisation, settling and (where the acidity and fluoride demanded it) lime neutralisation with fluoride precipitation, then discharge to a municipal sewer under a permit or to an outfall. See facility.hazardous-waste for the solid side.

###### Ordinary industrial water `facility.water.industrial`

The 99% of the plant's water use: cooling, washing, rinsing, boiler feed, human use. Deliberately not ultrapure, deliberately recycled.

###### Induced-draught cooling tower `facility.water.cooling-tower`

A 20-60 m concrete or steel shell packed with fill, with fan blades in the base drawing air up through the falling film of circulating water. Water evaporates, concentrates the dissolved solids, and is purged to the drain or the recovery plant.

###### Tower fill and eliminator `facility.water.tower-filling`

Cellulose (Kraft), PVC or polystyrene film fill media in a lattice or dendritic pack, plus a drift eliminator of PVC chevron sheets at the top. Cellulose fill was being replaced by flame-retardant PVC in the mid-1980s for fire reasons.

###### Cooling-water chemical treatment `facility.water.chem-treatment` _(medium)_

Chromate-based corrosion inhibitors (the dominant, and environmentally toxic, 1980s chemistry), or the newer phosphate/phosphonate/zinc formulations, plus biocide (chlorine or an organomercurial/isothiazolinone blend) and an antiscalant acid. This is where a large share of the plant's chemical consumption went.

###### Sodium chromate inhibitor `facility.water.chromate`

A dichromate/chromate film former that passivates the steel of the cooling system. Enormously effective, and the reason thousands of 1980s cooling towers are a chromate source in the groundwater.

###### Chromite ore (FeCr2O4) `facility.water.chromite`

The only economic source of chromium. Mined by underground stoping in the Bushveld Complex of South Africa and elsewhere, then smelted to ferrochrome.

###### Chromite mine `facility.water.chromite-mine`

A stratiform chromite seam (UG2 in the Bushveld) worked by stoping or by open pit. Ends at the chromitite layer in the ground.

###### Evaporative (swamp) cooler `facility.water.evaporative-cooling`

A finned coil with water sprayed over it and an induced-draft fan. Far cheaper than a chiller and it worked well in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore, where the wet-bulb temperature was already low; useless in a humid July in Pennsylvania.

###### Reciprocating chiller `facility.water.chiller`

A compressor, condenser and evaporator in a packaged unit, cooling water or air cooled. The alternative to evaporative cooling wherever the wet-bulb was too high. 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11, and therefore both a refrigerant-ozone problem and a safety problem.

###### Water in the leaching plants `facility.water.leach-plant-water` _(medium)_

Where this tree passes through the metal and silicon trees, the water system is completely different: an agitated heap or tank leaching circuit with a counter-current rinse, a pregnant-liquor clarifier and a counter-current decant (CCD) wash, using acidic sulfate or alkaline cyanide liquor. The cyanide circuit consumed a large water volume and generated a cyanide-bearing tailings pond.

#### Routing and outline cutting `mb.pcb.mill` _(medium)_

In 1983 the board outline, internal cut-outs and the edge-connector routing slot were milled mechanically on a CNC router with a carbide cutter. Laser routing existed but was not yet the commodity default for a board with no fine geometry.

##### Edge-connector routing slot `mb.pcb.mill.slot`

The expansion-port slot is milled so that a thin projecting ear of laminate is left with copper on both faces. That ear is the board edge connector, and its copper is then selectively plated. The slot geometry sets the finger width and spacing that the case connector must mate with.

##### Carbide router cutter `mb.pcb.mill.cutter` _(medium)_

A tungsten-carbide end mill, often with a diamond-like coating, cutting laminate that is mostly glass fibre. Glass dust is abrasive, so tool life is short and the cutter is changed on a schedule.

#### Drilling every component hole `mb.pcb.drill`

The board is drilled on a numerical-control drill for every component lead, jumper, jack and mounting hole. Because there are no vias, the drill programme is just a component position list; there is no barrel to plate afterwards.

##### NC drill and tool change `mb.pcb.drill.ncd` _(medium)_

A tape-fed drill head steps through the tool table, swapping bits for the several diameters the board needs, over pinned or vacuum-held fixtures. A bit-management and drill-jig system holds sub-millimetre position accuracy; drill wander is what breaks a fine-pitch DIP row.

##### Carbide drill bit `mb.pcb.drill.bit` _(medium)_

Tungsten-carbide or high-speed-steel bits, ground and resharpened. Laminated glass plus copper is abrasive and the hole is the one feature that cannot be reworked once drilled wrong.

#### How this board changed layer with NO vias `mb.pcb.vias`

The most distinctive fact about the C64 mainboard. There are no vias and no plated-through holes. A connection that has to move from the component side to the solder side does it by passing through the hole of a component lead: every resistor, capacitor, diode and DIP pin doubles as a via. Where a layer change was needed with no component available, the board carried a short single-core tinned wire jumper, hand-fitted and hand-soldered after wave soldering.

##### Ground pour instead of a ground plane `mb.pcb.vias.plane` _(medium)_

With no internal plane layer, the two signal layers carry return current on their own copper, so the layout used wide ground pours and heavy copper wherever return current had to flow. Modern boards solve the same electromagnetic problem with a dedicated plane, which is the main reason vias became universal.

#### Surface finish: pads and edge contacts `mb.pcb.finish` _(medium)_

After etching the copper is protected, made solderable, and given a wear-resistant finish where it will be touched. On this board, because there are no plated barrels, the finish job is far simpler than on a modern via board.

##### HASL solder level on the pads `mb.pcb.finish.hasl` _(medium)_

Exposed copper is coated in molten solder by carrying the board through a wave or a drag of 63/37 tin-lead and blowing or brushing off the excess, leaving a flat solderable layer that will not corrode. This is the period default for a two-sided consumer board with no vias, and it lines up with the solder the wave machine is already using.

###### 63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste `metal.solder`

The alloy that makes electronics manufacturable. 63% tin, 37% lead is a true eutectic, so it melts and freezes at one temperature, 183 C, with no mushy interval - which means a joint goes from solid to liquid in milliseconds and the reflow time window can be measured in seconds. That property is why a decade of copper thicknesses and lead-free anxiety has not displaced it from the bench. A C64 has roughly 3,500 through-hole joints; at about 30 mg of solder per joint that is around 100 g of alloy per machine, in wire fed from spools and in a few kilos of bar in the wave-solder tank.

###### Casting the 63/37 bar `metal.solder.alloy-making`

The alloy is made in a handful of ways, all of them embarrassingly simple. The best is the cored wire method: rods of high-purity tin are cast inside a steel tube pre-filled with molten lead at exactly 37%, so the tube's own wall meters the lead; the tube and the core are then rolled and drawn out to wire in one operation, and the core forms down the middle as the flux. This is how most electronics solder wire is still made. The alternative, and what the solder manufacturer would do for its own bar stock, is simply to melt the two ingots together in a grease pot with a little antimony or phosphorus and pour into ingot moulds.

###### Antimony addition to stiffen the alloy `metal.solder.antimony` _(medium)_

Pure Sn-Pb solder creeps. A 1982 instrument or a through-hole joint under a hot component would push itself out of the joint over a few years, and the classic failure was a capacitor that walked out of its pads. Two tenths of a percent of antimony, as an Sb-Sn hardener or as a lead-antimony master alloy, makes the alloy's creep resistance about an order of magnitude better with only a small rise in melting point. So the solder in the C64 very probably contained 0.1-0.5% antimony, and none of it is on the bill of materials.

###### The cored-wire manufacturing method `metal.solder.cored-wire` _(medium)_

The standard way to make electronics solder wire, and the reason the alloy composition is so consistent. A steel tube with a wall thickness calculated for 37% lead by volume is filled with molten high-purity tin - actually with the exact alloy, but the wall does the metering - and the tube is cold-drawn and then drawn to wire in the same multiwire machine the copper industry uses. The core forms down the middle as the tube collapses. The result is a wire in which the flux core is in the middle of the metal rather than smeared along it, which is what stops the flux from being wiped off during handling. The alternative - extruding a bar of flux and then jacketing it in molten alloy - gives a worse wire and was being displaced by the cored method through the 1980s.

###### How the flux core is filled `metal.solder.flux-core-fill` _(low)_

The flux core is a paste, not a powder: rosin dissolved in a solvent - turpentine, or in the 1980s increasingly a mild-rosin paste - with the zinc chloride activator, made viscous enough to hold a column. It is injected into the tube with a hydraulic filler in a batch, and the tube's ends are crimped and drawn closed. The viscosity and the shrinkage matter, because the core has to survive being drawn to 0.5 mm without either splitting out of the wire or shrinking away from the axis. So the flux chemistry in a C64's solder wire is a colloid and a rheology problem as much as it is a chemical one.

###### 63/37 solder wire with a rosin core `metal.solder.wire`

The wire that went through a C64 assembly line: a solid 63/37 core inside a flux core inside a tin-lead sheath, made by the cored-wire method and drawn on the same kind of multiwire machine the copper industry uses, in a smaller and more delicate setup. This is a deliberate convergence node: the solder alloy branch, the rosin branch and the wave-solder branch all meet here, and it is the single most identifiable material in the whole tree - it is why the C64 is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

###### Wave soldering with the alloy pot `metal.solder.wave-solder`

The board assembly method for a 1982 C64. The bottom of the board is swept across a standing wave of molten 63/37 at 250-280 C, the excess drains through a hot-air knife, and the whole board lives in a hood full of the vapour of flux decomposition products. A few kilograms of solder in the pot are held at a temperature just above the 183 C liquidus, and the pot is kept clean with a rotating skimmer. Wave soldering is why solder consumption in electronics manufacturing was measured in kilograms per day per line rather than grams per board, and why the flux vapour was a genuine occupational exposure that the electronics industry was only beginning to quantify in the late 1980s.

###### The solder joint itself and lead leaching `metal.solder.joint-microscopy` _(medium)_

A good 1982 through-hole joint is a shallow concave meniscus filling the pad hole about 70-90%, with a fillet at the lead. The metallurgical reason it works is the intermetallic: copper and tin react to form Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn, and the joint is a composite of unreacted solder and intermetallic compound. On the PCB side the pad is tin-plated and forms a Cu-Sn intermetallic too. What nobody in 1982 was measuring was how much lead leached out of a solder joint into the copper land when the joint was at 200 C for an hour - and it is a lot, which is the mechanism behind the later 'solder fatigue' literature.

###### The hot-air knife and the solder wave `metal.solder.wave-solder.knife` _(medium)_

A pump throws molten solder up a nozzle to form a standing wave 3-8 mm high, and the board is dragged across it on a conveyor with fingers. As the board leaves, a 'hot-air knife' - a duct blowing 200-300 C air across the solder line - blows the excess solder off the pads and off the solder side of the board, and what runs off goes back into the pot through a trough. The whole operation is a temperature profile in space: preheat, flux activation, wave, drain, and the knife. Getting the four temperatures right - preheat, pot, board and cleaning - is the entire craft.

###### Preheater, fluxer and the thermal profile `metal.solder.preheater` _(medium)_

Before the wave, the board goes through a preheater - infrared lamps, a hot plate or hot air - to 100-150 C, and through a fluxer that lays a foam or sprayed layer of flux on the solder side. The reason for preheating is thermal expansion: a FR-4 board with a big hole pattern expands by a different amount in different directions, and if the solder side heats faster than the component side the board warps and the joints crack. A C64's mainboard is a large single-sided board with a lot of heat-generating parts on one side, so warp was a real yield problem. The preheater is the cheapest fix and it is a temperature-control problem.

###### Board warp, thermal stress and the epoxy `metal.solder.board-warp` _(medium)_

Why preheat exists at all. A single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 board with a large hole pattern expands and contracts with a coefficient of about 14-18 x 10^-6 per K, and it is not isotropic - the copper layer and the epoxy cloth have different coefficients, and the weave gives the board different stiffness in the warp and weft directions. Warm the solder side faster than the component side and the board bows; cycle it and the board stays bowed; and on a double-sided board it can delaminate the copper from the epoxy. So the preheater is really an epoxy-handling device, and the epoxy is the resin agent's problem while the solder pot is the metals one, and they meet at the warp.

###### Solder paste: powder in flux `metal.solder.paste` _(medium)_

Solder paste is a mixture of atomised alloy powder at 60-90% by weight in a flux vehicle, and in 1982 it was the technology for surface-mount parts, which Commodore did not really use on the mainboard but which every other electronics maker in the world was. The powder particle size is controlled by the printing stencil: a 0.5 mm gap needs 20-45 um powder so the powder does not bridge the gap with two particles. Alloy powder is not made by atomising finished solder; it is made by atomising the melt and then the 63/37 particles are aged so they develop an oxide shell of a controlled thickness, so that paste sits on a pad for minutes without the paste shrinking or the surface going dull.

###### The leaded-solder problem in the 1980s `metal.solder.lead-hazard`

Lead in solder was the first workplace poison to arrive with electronics. It was already deeply regulated for the smelter workers - the whole lead industry is under air-monitoring and blood-lead surveillance - and by the early 1980s occupational-health attention had turned to the solder bench: solder fume is an aerosol of lead oxide particles, and the flux fumes carry it. The US OSHA lead standard covered soldering. The C64 is the emblem of this because it was sold by the million with a leaded-solder supply chain: the solder manufacturer, the wave-solder pot, the washing machines that washed the flux off, the drain water, and finally the landfill. Every one of those is a different regulatory jurisdiction and none of them was solved in 1982.

###### Silver-bearing solder and silver paste `metal.solder.silver-solder-paste` _(medium)_

A distinct and important thing in the 1980s electronics industry, which is easy to confuse with the lead-tin eutectic: high-temperature silver solder - 62Ag/38Cu, 50Ag/50Cd, 70Ag/30Sn - melts at 600-750 C and is brazed, not soldered. Silver-tin solder melts at 217-220 C and is used where lead-free behaviour is wanted. Silver brazing is how the heat sinks and the chassis joints were made. And separately there is the silver-filled epoxy and silver-filled ink of the electronics industry: real silver powder at 60-80% by weight in an epoxy or an organic vehicle, screen-printed or stencil-printed and fired, used for die attach and for the conductive ink of the keyboard membrane. That is a genuine and separate use of silver in a C64, and it is a chemistry, not a metallurgy.

###### The wave-solder pot and its dross `metal.solder.pot` _(medium)_

A 5-20 kg pot of 63/37 at 250-280 C with a pump and a wave-forming nozzle, plus a rotating skimmer and an oil skimmer. The surface of a working solder pot accumulates a metre of black oxide dross - tin oxide, lead oxide and flux residue - and it has to be skimmed off every shift and every night, and it is a genuine metallurgical waste stream: the dross contains most of the lead and a lot of the tin, and in 1982 the recovery options were poor. A dross reclaimer sold a few percent of the metal back and the rest went out as lead-containing waste. This is the point at which the solder chain and the lead chain close on each other.

###### The solder pot oxide and why it forms `metal.solder.dross-oxide` _(medium)_

At 250-280 C the surface of molten Sn-Pb oxidises continuously - tin oxide forms preferentially because it has the lower oxidation potential - so the pot grows a skin of SnO2 with lead oxide and flux in it. The skimmer takes it off, but the formation is unavoidable, which is why wave-solder lines had a person whose whole job was pot maintenance and why the flux was designed to keep the oxide mobile and floatable rather than letting it crust over.

###### Cleaning the flux residue off the board `metal.solder.cleaning` _(medium)_

A rosin-fluxed board is covered in a sticky, slightly acidic film of flux decomposition products that will corrode the copper and will not accept a conformal coating. In 1982 it was removed in an aqueous machine - a conveyor with spray bars and drying ovens - often followed by a trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degreaser. The cleaning water left the factory through the drain with the lead in it, which is the other half of the 1982 leaded-solder problem and the reason the electronics industry spent the late 1980s arguing about what to do about it.

###### The solder wash-water waste stream `metal.solder.waste-water` _(medium)_

A C64 assembly line's cleaning water carried dissolved lead, tin, flux residues and a lot of suspended solids. In 1982 the standard practice was dilute and discharge: a settling tank and a pH adjustment, then to the drain. The lead was almost all in the sludge, so the sludge went to a hazardous-waste landfill and the liquid went out. This is the last place the C64's lead leaves the factory, and it is the reason leaded solder became a regulatory object rather than merely an occupational one.

###### Lead in landfill leachate `metal.solder.waste-leachate` _(low)_

The leaf of the solder branch, and it is not a rock but a fate: the lead sludge in the landfill, and the leachate it makes. It is included because a chain that ends at 'the drain' is not a chain, and because this is the point at which the C64's mass ultimately becomes a chemical in the ground.

###### The hazardous-waste landfill `metal.landfill` _(low)_

Where the last of the C64's lead ends up in 1982: a permitted hazardous-waste landfill, an RCRA cell lined with clay and plastic, with a leachate collection system and a monitoring well array. That is the modern answer. In 1982 the answer was usually a pit - an unlined pit, in many states, because the RCRA regulations only began to bite around 1980-1984 and the small-quantity generator exemption that most electronics factories claimed put them below the line. So the leaf of this tree is a hole in the ground, and the specific hole is either a permitted cell or an unlined pit depending on the state and the year, and I cannot tell you which without knowing the factory.

###### The solder factory's own waste streams `metal.solder.waste` _(medium)_

A solder pot, a dross heap, a flux residue stream, a wash-water drain and a baghouse for the flux fumes. The dross goes to a reclaimer or to a hazardous-waste disposal contract; the baghouse dust is lead oxide and rosin and is genuinely hazardous; and the wash water goes to the drain with the lead in it. In 1982 this was the least regulated part of the whole electronics industry, and it is the reason the United States' lead exposure limits for electronics workers - which were set at a time when electronics was not a regulated industry - exist at all. The waste stream is a leaf of this tree and a genuinely uncomfortable one.

###### The flux fume baghouse and its dust `metal.solder.waste-baghouse` _(medium)_

The wave-solder hood has an extraction duct and a baghouse, because the fume is an aerosol of lead oxide and of rosin-acid degradation products. The dust is 30-60% lead oxide and it is collected as a hazardous waste. A big 1982 line threw away tens of kilograms a week. The control measure was local exhaust ventilation with a capture hood about 100 mm from the wave, and the compliance measure was an area respirator, which was why electronics assembly was one of the more heavily respirated occupations of the period.

##### Selective plating of the edge contacts `mb.pcb.finish.selective` _(medium)_

Only the edge-connector contact surfaces get a hard, wear-resistant metal. The usual route is a nickel underplate followed by electrolytic gold applied through a fountain plater or a selective rack, with everything else masked. Sometimes the entire board is immersion gold-plated instead, which is simpler and gives softer gold.

###### Selective masking `mb.pcb.finish.selective.mask` _(medium)_

The board is plated overall and the gold is stripped from everywhere except the contact surfaces, or the contacts alone are exposed to the bath with the rest of the board shielded by a fountain-plater weir or a plating rack.

###### Cyanide gold bath `mb.pcb.finish.selective.cyanide` _(medium)_

Gold dissolves in a cyanide complex with a fine gold anode; the cathode is the board rack. Cyanide plating baths are still the standard because they are stable and fast, and still require the same destruction-and recovery regime.

##### Anti-tarnish treatment `mb.pcb.finish.antitarnish` _(medium)_

A benzotriazole-type organic protectant is applied to stop the non-plated copper from darkening in storage and handling. Cheap, invisible, and easy to skip until someone notices the boards going brown in the box.

##### Plated-barrel line - NOT on this board `mb.pcb.finish.pth`

The C64 mainboard skips the entire through-hole plating sequence a via board runs: hole desmear, electroless copper seed, electrolytic copper build, nickel, gold. This node exists to make the absence explicit, because it is a common and wrong assumption about this board.

#### Epoxy solder mask on both sides `mb.pcb.mask` _(medium)_

Green epoxy ink is screen-printed over the whole board with apertures left over every pad and hole. It is the green the C64 has always been. Without it the board shorts from a fingerprint, a solder splash or a screw, and the white legend would disappear under bare copper.

#### White silkscreen legend and compartment boxes `mb.pcb.legend` _(medium)_

Reference designators, block outlines and assembly notes are printed in white epoxy ink over the cured mask and baked. Commodore drew boxes around functional blocks, the so-called compartments, and used extra ink colours in bands and outlines to colour-code regions of the board and mark the television standard.

##### Screen printing and bake `mb.pcb.legend.screen` _(medium)_

A fine-mesh screen coated with photosensitive emulsion is stretched and tensioned over the board, epoxy ink squeegeed through, and the board then baked to cure the ink onto the mask.

##### Coloured silkscreen bands `mb.pcb.legend.colour` _(low)_

A separate pass in each extra colour, with its own screen, to draw the colour bands and outlines that mark functional regions and the PAL or NTSC variant. A modern cosmetic imitation of this is a coloured solder mask; in 1983 it was extra ink passes.

#### Electrical test of the bare board `mb.pcb.inspection` _(medium)_

Before any component goes on, the blank is checked for shorts between nets and for opens in the artwork. In 1983 this was a continuity and insulation-resistance tester plus a careful visual check under a lamp and a loupe; automated optical inspection was available but too expensive to be assumed on every commodity line.

#### Finished bare board, fab no. 250406 `mb.pcb.bareboard` _(medium)_

A drilled, etched, stripped, masked, legended and finished blank ready for component insertion. At 1983 commodity prices a two-layer 1.6 mm consumer board of this size cost on the order of one to two dollars.

### MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP `mb.cpu`

8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.

#### Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.cpu.wafer` _(medium)_

The starting substrate for the die: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished mirror finish on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat.

##### 9N-11N electronic-grade polysilicon `mb.cpu.wafer.polysilicon`

Chunky polycrystalline silicon chunks loaded into the Czochralski crystal puller. Made by the Siemens process: high-purity trichlorosilane is reduced with pure hydrogen over electrically heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C, depositing polycrystalline silicon on the hot wires until a rod ~150-250 mm diameter and about 1 m long is grown.

###### Siemens wire-heated deposition reactor `mb.cpu.wafer.siemens-reactor`

A vertical bell-jar or can reactor holding 40-80 U-shaped silicon filaments wound from vapor-grown poly. A few hundred amps of DC is passed through the filaments to hold them at ~1150 C while SiHCl3 vapour decomposes on them. These reactors were the standard ultra-purity route until the late 1980s.

###### Trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), 9N-11N `mb.cpu.wafer.tcs`

The intermediate that carries silicon from cheap metallurgical-grade metal to electronics grade. Made by passing dry HCl over crushed metallurgical silicon at 250-350 C in a fluidised or bubbling bed: Si + 3 HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2. Rectified by fractional distillation to a boiling point of 31.8 C until metal, B and P contaminants are below 1 ppb.

###### Hydrogen chloride from salt and chlorine `mb.cpu.wafer.hcl`

Dry HCl gas made by chlorinating hydrogen over a bed of rock salt, or by burning hydrogen in chlorine, then condensing and drying it with concentrated sulfuric acid. The chlorine itself comes from electrolysis of brine.

###### Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis `mb.cpu.wafer.brine`

Salt dissolved in water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen; the hydrogen is what reacts with the salt to make HCl and what reduces the trichlorosilane.

###### Rock salt for the chlor-alkali cell `mb.cpu.wafer.salt`

Halite mined by room-and-pillar or solution mining in the Michigan basin, Louisiana's Salt Dome, the Cheshire salt field (which is why a US chlor-alkali industry sat on top of salt), and the Zechstein basin of northern Germany. Brine is made by pumping water into the salt and pumping out saturated brine.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.cpu.wafer.msi`

Rough grey lumps of silicon produced in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and petroleum coke at 1900-2200 C. This is the ore-like starting point: roughly 300 kg of 98% silicon per 6510-class wafer batch. Boron and phosphorus ride along at hundreds of ppm and must be removed later.

###### Submerged arc furnace, 20-40 MVA `mb.cpu.wafer.saf`

A refractory-lined steel shell 10-12 m deep with three graphite electrodes lowered into a charge of quartz lump, petroleum coke and wood chips. Electric current (200-400 kA at 40-70 V) maintains an arc that melts the charge in the 'submerged zone' at 1900-2200 C, tapping grey metallic silicon out of the bottom every 1-2 hours. Up to 4 t/day in a modern furnace; a 1982-era unit made a few hundred tonnes per year.

###### Quartz (SiO2) lump for the arc furnace `mb.cpu.wafer.quartz`

High-purity quartz, ideally with under 200 ppm aluminium and iron, crushed to 5-30 mm. Because aluminium in the metal feeds straight through to every device, silicon makers specify vein quartz or purified lump.

###### Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2 `mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-sand`

The geologic end of the whole tree. Sand washed from a high-purity quartzite or sandstone deposit, then purified for semiconductor use by acid leaching (HF + HNO3 to strip Al and Fe) and by chlorination, yielding quartz that can be melted into crucibles or reacted with HCl.

###### Pegmatite / quartzite ore, mined and crushed `mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore`

The actual dig: a hard-rock pegmatite or high-purity quartzite vein, blasted and jaw-crushed, then screened and hand-sorted to 5-30 mm lump for the arc furnace. Only a fraction of a deposit is white enough to be metallurgical-grade.

###### Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away `mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-ore.mica` _(medium)_

The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite/K-feldspar and muscovite/BIOTite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallization - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.

###### Semiconductor-grade quartz purification `mb.cpu.wafer.quartz-leach`

Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible rather than the arc furnace is crushed to sand, then hot-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 to dissolve surface aluminium and iron, chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip B, P, As and alkali metals, and finally annealed in vacuum. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.

###### Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar `mb.cpu.wafer.hf`

HF is made by treating finely ground fluorspar (CaF2) with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead/cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. It attacks glass and is the standard etchant for thermal oxide; huge quantities of it went through the same silicon supply chain.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.cpu.wafer.fluorspar`

Acid-grade fluorspar mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits, beneficiated by flotation to 97%+ purity. Large deposits in Mexico (San Luis Potosi), South Africa (Plettenberg Bay) and China. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching, no quartz purification and no cleaning chemistry.

###### Sulfuric acid from sulfur, from pyrite or natural gas `mb.cpu.wafer.h2so4`

Contact-process sulfuric acid: sulfur (mined as Frasch-free elemental sulfur, or roasted from pyrite ore) is burned and catalytically oxidised over V2O5 to SO3, absorbed in 98% H2SO4. Used both for HF manufacture and for the Piranha clean.

###### Petroleum coke as the carbon reductant `mb.cpu.wafer.coke`

Needle coke or calcined petroleum coke from a petroleum coke calciner, used as both reductant and fuel in the arc furnace. Also the ancestor of the graphite electrodes and of the epoxy resin later on in the package.

###### Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke `mb.cpu.wafer.coke.calciner`

Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours, then the green coke is calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave 0.5-2% sulphur needle coke. In the silicon industry a blend of petroleum coke and anthracite coal is used instead.

###### Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled `mb.cpu.wafer.coke.crude`

Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C / 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms, a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, are the feed for coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.

###### Anthracite coal as a coke substitute `mb.cpu.wafer.coke.anthracite` _(medium)_

The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.

##### Czochralski growth of the boron-doped ingot `mb.cpu.wafer.cz`

The puller melts polysilicon chunks in a fused quartz crucible at ~1420 C in a flowing helium or argon atmosphere, dips a seed crystal, and rotates and slowly withdraws it while a raw boule ~100 mm across and 1-1.5 m long grows. Boron trichloride or diborane is dosed into the melt to set the 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity. The constant rotation and the thermal gradient grow a dislocation-free, uniform cross-section with a slight oxygen precipitate peak near the seed end.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.cpu.wafer.crucible`

A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm ID, holding several kilos of molten silicon and dipping into it several cm at 1420 C. It is itself grown from quartz sand in a flame-fusion electric furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel, annealed slowly to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out. Crucibles were the dominant silicon-metal loss source and were scrapped after a handful of pulls.

###### Quartz sand melted into crucible glass `mb.cpu.wafer.crucible-sand`

High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame/arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C into a clear annealed vitreous silica blank. Graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.

###### Seed crystal for CZ pulling `mb.cpu.wafer.seed`

A short (100 mm) (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and defect-free growth of the new boule.

###### Float zone alternative (silicon for other parts, not the 6510) `mb.cpu.wafer.fz`

In float-zone growth a poly rod is converted to monocrystal by dragging a molten silicon zone down it in an inert atmosphere, touching no crucible at all. Yield is higher and oxygen is lower, but the crystals were narrow (<30 mm) and slow, so FZ in 1982 was for power rectifiers and some bipolar parts, not CPU wafers.

###### Helium as the CZ growth atmosphere `mb.cpu.wafer.he`

High-purity helium (6N) bled over the melt to carry off the intense blackbody heat and to sweep volatile boron compounds away. Argon or a helium/argon mix was a cheaper alternative and produced more oxygen precipitation.

##### Ingot slicing: ID or OD saw + laser scribe `mb.cpu.wafer.slicing`

The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed (ruby or Nd:YAG) before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw (blade up to 2.2 m diameter, rotating at 2000 rpm, ~0.30 mm kerf) or, on more advanced 1982 machines, by ID saw (blade inside the crystal, ~0.25 mm kerf). The result is ~0.7 mm wafers, far too warped and marked to print on.

###### Diamond-impregnated saw blade `mb.cpu.wafer.blade`

A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at 2-3 wafers a minute relies on that grit: natural or synthetic industrial diamond, 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.

###### Industrial diamond from graphite `mb.cpu.wafer.diamond` _(medium)_

Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered into a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co, Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

##### Double-sided lapping `mb.cpu.wafer.lapping`

Saw-cut wafers are lapped on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate using a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to ~300 um with a mirror surface but still several micrometres of total thickness variation across the wafer.

##### Wet chemical polish (not CMP) `mb.cpu.wafer.polish`

1982 practice: the wafer was chemically polished in hot alkaline or acidic peroxide solution - for example hot dilute NaOH/H2O2, or HNO3/HF/acetic - which removed ~10 um of damage layer and left an atomically flat surface. Chemical-mechanical polishing with a soft pad and slurry did not reach volume production until the late 1980s.

##### Edge profiling / edge chamfer `mb.cpu.wafer.edge`

The wafer rim was rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch, removing the razor edge so later photoresist could not build up and so the wafer would not chip in handling.

##### Pre-diffusion wafer clean: Piranha and RCA SC-1 `mb.cpu.wafer.clean`

Every wafer entering the furnace was cleaned. The workhorse step was Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C, boiling off organics and metal), followed by RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) and SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), then a megasonic rinse in deionized water and a short HF dip to strip native oxide. Megasonic (1.6 MHz sonic) cleaners and particle-count-filtered N2 blow-off were standard.

###### Ultrapure deionized process water `mb.cpu.wafer.water`

City water passed through sand, activated carbon, cation and anion exchange resins, a 1.5 micron filter and finally UV sterilization to reach 10-18 Mohm-cm and under 100 ppt dissolved solids. Every C64 die consumed thousands of litres of this water across its ~50 dip and rinse steps.

#### Photomask set, ~10 levels `mb.cpu.mask-set` _(medium)_

The 6510 pattern was drawn as polygons on a Calma/Computervision layout system, converted through a mask database to mask data, and cut into 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates for a 100 mm wafer. Nine or ten mask levels: n+ S/D, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation/pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab used 1:1 masks with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982.

##### Chrome-on-glass photomask plate `mb.cpu.mask.plate`

A 5x7 inch plate of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz coated with ~100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, then the exposed chromium etched away in hot sulfuric-perchromate or perchloric acid, washed, inspected, and defect-repaired.

###### Sputter target of chromium `mb.cpu.mask.chromium`

99.5% pure chromium cathode, vacuum-melted and rolled, sputtered with argon at ~1-2 kW onto the rotating plate inside a DC magnetron chamber. Chromium's high opacity in the deep-UV and its resistance to wet cleaning made it the universal mask absorber from the 1960s to the present.

###### Mask plate glass from melted quartz sand `mb.cpu.mask.glass`

Soda-lime float glass (most 1982 1:1 masks) or fused silica, melted from batched sand plus soda ash and lime in a continuous tank furnace and drawn into 1 mm plate, then annealed.

##### Pattern generator driving a mask exposure `mb.cpu.mask.plotter` _(medium)_

In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.

##### Photoresist for mask making `mb.cpu.mask.resist`

Positive resists of the era: Shipley AZ-1350 and AZ-1354 (which also served as the wafer resist for most process levels), Kodak KMR-8105, and Fuji HiP resist. Resist spun at ~3000 rpm to 0.5-1.5 um, soft-baked at 90-100 C, exposed in N2, developed in dilute alkaline developer.

##### Mask inspection and defect repair `mb.cpu.mask.inspection` _(medium)_

Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles (1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame) protected final production masks from dust; Commodore bought chips on wafers or in flatpacks and cut them at assembly instead, but many C64-era NORISTOWN parts were shipped in this way.

##### The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period `mb.cpu.mask.stepper` _(medium)_

Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.

#### 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack `mb.cpu.front-end` _(medium)_

A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.

##### 1. n+ source/dank pre-diffusion `mb.cpu.fe.nplus` _(medium)_

A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.

##### 2. LOCOS field oxide `mb.cpu.fe.locos`

The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.

##### 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric) `mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide`

After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

##### 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon `mb.cpu.fe.poly`

Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.

##### 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant `mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned`

With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

##### 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization `mb.cpu.fe.contacts`

Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.

##### 7. Passivation and pad opening `mb.cpu.fe.passivation` _(medium)_

The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.

##### Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop `mb.cpu.fe.photoresist`

Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.

##### Mask aligner: contact/proximity printing `mb.cpu.fe.aligner`

A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury lamp or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact (mask pressed straight down onto the resist) or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2.

##### Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces `mb.cpu.fe.furnace`

Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/dank drives.

##### Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer `mb.cpu.fe.deposition`

A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

##### Wet etch bench and plasma etcher `mb.cpu.fe.etcher` _(medium)_

Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.

##### Low-energy ion implanter `mb.cpu.fe.implanter` _(medium)_

A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.

##### Class 10 cleanroom bay with HEPA and FFU `mb.cpu.fe.cleanroom`

Wafer processing ran in a yellow-lit room with laminar-flow fan filter units (TAMCO, Flotronics) giving class 100 (ISO 5) work area over a class 1000 background, maintained at 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases came from a bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen distribution panel with stainless steel lines and mass-flow controllers.

###### Bulk high-purity nitrogen and hydrogen `mb.cpu.fe.nitrogen`

Liquid nitrogen trucked in and vaporised in a bulk tank; hydrogen by electrolysis of deionized water, or delivered in bulk; oxygen as a separate liquid tank. These gases flush furnaces, run LPCVD and implant hardware, and form a large part of the process cost.

#### Wafer probe (electrical die sort) `mb.cpu.probe`

Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.

##### Probe card: 40 needles on a printed board `mb.cpu.probe.card`

A fiberglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of 40 gold-plated probe needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. 1982 probe cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated tungsten or rhenium needles; automatic stepping probe stations (handling 200-1000 pads per die) were still a 1980s novelty for 40-pad parts.

#### Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw `mb.cpu.dicing`

The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

#### Die attach to the lead frame (gold-silicon eutectic) `mb.cpu.attach`

The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame pad and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond (Collberg, Balzer, or Kulicke & Soffa) raises the die and frame to about 400-450 C: the gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. This both makes the mechanical bond and gives the die a low-thermal-resistance path to the lead frame.

#### Gold wire wedge bonding `mb.cpu.bond`

A wire bonder (Orthomat, K&S 1470, or Balzer 4000) pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad to the frame (lead) and then an interconnect wire from pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than the ultrasonic ball bond used for aluminium. A single 6510 had about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 mm of 25 um gold each.

##### Bonding wire from refined gold `mb.cpu.bond.gold`

99.99% gold refined from ore by chlorination/electrolysis or cupellation, drawn through a die and a lubricant to 25 um. Roughly 0.3-1 m of wire per die.

###### Cyanide leach and activated-carbon recovery `mb.cpu.bond.gold.cyanide`

Gold concentrate is ground to a flotation product and leached in 0.02-0.05% NaCN at pH 10.5 with lime, oxidised by air: 4 Au + 8 NaCN + 2 H2O + O2 -> 4 Na[Au(CN)2] + 4 NaOH. The pregnant solution is passed over activated carbon, which adsorbs the aurocyanide; the carbon is stripped with hot cyanide or burned and the gold cupelled to 99.99% dore, then electrolytically refined.

#### 40-pin DIP lead frame, FeNi alloy or copper `mb.cpu.leadframe`

The die and its 40 leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi (C4-29) alloy in a thickness of 0.15-0.20 mm by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike, then gold for hermetic parts, then a matte tin or tin-lead surface for plastic parts. The frame is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and moulder.

##### FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy, vacuum-induction melted `mb.cpu.leadframe.feni` _(medium)_

The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy (C194 with 2.3% lead) and nickel were alternatives.

###### Electrolytic nickel from sulphide ore `mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel`

Nickel is won either by the Mond carbonyl refining loop (nickel sulfide concentrates are smelted, roasted and reduced to sponge) or by high-pressure acid leach of laterite. Then electrolytically refined to 99.8% cathode in a sulfate/chloride bath and rolled.

###### Pentlandite (Ni,Fe)9S8 ore concentrate `mb.cpu.leadframe.nickel-ore`

The world's nickel supply came overwhelmingly from sulphide ore - Sudbury, Ontario (Inco), the Norilsk-Talnakh massif (Norilnickel) and the Philippines (SLN). Ore at ~1.5-3% Ni is concentrated to 10-30% by flotation before smelting.

###### Low-carbon steel from iron ore `mb.cpu.leadframe.iron`

Electric arc or basic oxygen furnace steel from hematite ore (Lake Superior Mesabi, Carajás, Itabira) plus coke and limestone, with enough residual carbon kept very low so the frame does not contaminate the wire bonds.

#### Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy `mb.cpu.mold`

The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in a thermosetting epoxy molding compound: phenolic novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, plus a small amount of silicone release agent and catalyst. Typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes per cavity. Plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation.

#### Epoxy molding compound from phenolic resin and silica `mb.cpu.emc`

EMC starts from phenolic resin: phenol and formaldehyde condensed with an epoxy novolac. The resin is blended with angular ground silica (fired 0.5-3 um particles) to control shrinkage and thermal expansion, mixed with glass fibre in high-temperature grades, catalysed with a phenolic accelerator, and compounded on a two-roll mill under heat. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g.

##### Novolac epoxy resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin `mb.cpu.emc.phenolic`

Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac (phenol-formaldehyde) resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and NaOH to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of molding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene process oxidation of benzene (mostly from coal tar until the 1980s) or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

###### Benzene from the coke ovens `mb.cpu.emc.benzene`

Benzene was recovered from the light oil of the coke-oven battery that made coke for blast furnaces, and also made by catalytic reforming/dehydrogenation of naphtha. In 1982 it was overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative - the same coke-oven coke that fed the blast furnaces and (after calcining) the silicon furnaces.

###### Metallurgical coke for the blast furnace `mb.cpu.emc.coke`

Bituminous coal crushed and charged into a battery of coke ovens, heated to 1100-1250 C in the absence of air for 15-20 hours, then pushed out as coke and quenched with water. Coke is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace that makes the pig iron that makes the steel in the lead frame and the tin in the solder of the board.

###### Bituminous coal seam `mb.cpu.emc.coal`

A sedimentary seam mined by longwall or continuous miners. The coking-grade coals of the Appalachian basin (Clarion, Sewickley, Pittsburgh beds) were the premium feed in both the US and, exported, worldwide.

#### Trim, form, marking and final electrical test `mb.cpu.package`

After moulding, the leads are formed on a 8-16 station trim-and-form press (trimmed, bent to 0.6 inch pitch, flattened, and plated in a tin or tin-lead solder pot), the body is marked by a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with the part number, lot code and date code, and the part is inserted into a socket on a Teradyne or Fairchild automatic tester and run against a final test program.

#### Burn-in and final test `mb.cpu.burnin` _(medium)_

Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage (typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part) at 100-125 C for 24-168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in - the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.

#### MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road `mb.cpu.fab`

The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.

##### Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration `mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom`

Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

##### Electricity for the fab `mb.cpu.fab.power` _(medium)_

A device fab is an electricity sink, not a labour sink: 4-5 kWh per wafer per mask level for the furnaces and the aligners, plus a very large chilled-water load for the compressors and the wet benches. US industrial power in 1982 cost on the order of 5-7 cents per kWh, so electricity was a real fraction of the cost of a 6510.

##### In-house or commissioned mask shop `mb.cpu.fab.maskshop` _(low)_

A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.

##### Assembly and test lines in the same building `mb.cpu.fab.assembly` _(medium)_

Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.

#### Scribe-and-break or diamond-wheel dicing `mb.cpu.dice-tool`

A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

#### Hydraulic transfer moulding press `mb.cpu.mould-press`

A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and an encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: press close, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail. A 40-pin DIP cavity set produced dozens of parts per cycle.

#### From layout database to mask data `mb.cpu.mask.artwork` _(medium)_

The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database, and written to tape. A mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks, the die boundary and a grid-broken alignment structure, and produced the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. This data-reduction step - not the exposure - was where most mask errors were caught.

### Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM `mb.ram`

The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.ram.wafer` _(medium)_

A 4-inch boron-doped p-type CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed with a (100) primary flat. DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content (a higher oxygen precipitate density in the bulk) because the long trapped-charge lifetime helps refresh margin.

##### 9N electronic-grade polysilicon rod `mb.ram.polysilicon`

Polysilicon grown by the Siemens process: 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, giving a 200 mm diameter, 1 m long polycrystalline rod that is diced into CZ charge.

###### Trichlorosilane purification by rectification `mb.ram.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon + HCl at 300 C gives crude SiHCl3 plus boron and phosphorus trichlorides. Rectification in a batch or packed column on the 31.8 C boiling point takes it to 9N-11N, then it is stored in nickel or stainless bulk tanks.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%, from the arc furnace `mb.ram.msi`

Quartz plus petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to give grey lumps of 98-99% silicon containing a few hundred ppm of boron.

###### Submerged arc furnace, 200-400 kA `mb.ram.saf`

Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc keeps a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

###### Quartz lump, 5-30 mm, under 200 ppm Al and Fe `mb.ram.quartz`

Metallurgical-grade quartz crushed and screened from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2, mined `mb.ram.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand from a high-purity quartz deposit; acid-leached with HF and HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron before being shipped to the silicon plant.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) for the HF leach `mb.ram.fluorspar`

Acid-grade fluorspar, 97%+ CaF2, mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid to make the hydrofluoric acid that leaches quartz and etches oxide.

###### Fluorspar vein and stock ore `mb.ram.fluorspar-ore`

Hydrothermal and karst deposits worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and floated. The Xe-124 emission controversy of the mid-1980s was about elemental fluorine plants, not the mine.

##### CZ crystal pull `mb.ram.cz`

Polysilicon charge melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium; a (100) seed is dipped and withdrawn at 2-4 mm/min while rotating at 0.5-2 rpm, growing a 100 mm boule 1-1.5 m long. Boron trichloride sets the resistivity.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.ram.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.ram.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

###### Seed crystal and dopant gas `mb.ram.cz.seed`

A (100)-oriented 100 mm seed sliver cut from a previous ingot sets orientation; boron trichloride is dosed into the melt through a bubbler to set 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity; high-purity helium flows over the melt at 20-40 l/min to sweep away boron.

##### Sawing, lapping, wet chemical polish, clean `mb.ram.slice`

OD or ID diamond saw slicing to ~0.7 mm, double-sided lapping to 300 um with colloidal silica, then wet chemical polish in hot alkaline peroxide or HNO3/HF - CMP did not exist yet. Wafers are laser-scribed for the (100) primary flat and given a rounded edge in hot KOH, then megasonically cleaned in Piranha (H2SO4:H2O2, 120 C) and RCA SC-1.

#### The 1T1C memory cell and the 4164's three polysilicon levels `mb.ram.cell` _(medium)_

Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.

##### Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor `mb.ram.cell.doublepoly`

The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.

#### Single +5 V rail and the internal -5 V charge pump `mb.ram.vbb`

The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.

#### Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process `mb.ram.process`
