Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.

##### Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels `mb.ram.photolitho` _(medium)_

The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.

##### Alpha-particle and latch-up protection `mb.ram.protection`

DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.

#### 8-pin DIP package, die attach, bond, mould, test `mb.ram.package`

Dice are sawn apart, attached to an 8-pin lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, and wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder - typically 8 frame bonds plus 8-14 internal interconnect wires for the sense amps and cell array. Encapsulated in transfer-moulded silica-filled epoxy, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, socket-tested and optionally burned in.

##### Sintered chip cover over the die `mb.ram.package.cover` _(medium)_

On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.

#### 4164 photomask set `mb.ram.mask` _(medium)_

A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

##### 5x reticle: chrome on quartz `mb.ram.mask.reticle`

A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

###### Chromium sputtering target `mb.ram.mask.chrome-target`

99.5% pure chromium, vacuum-melted and rolled into a target, sputtered with argon at 1-2 kW in a DC magnetron chamber onto a rotating plate.

###### Chromite (FeCr2O4) ore concentrate `mb.ram.mask.chromium-ore`

Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex of South Africa, the Ural chromite deposits, or the Great Dyke of Zimbabwe - the entire industrial supply of chromium metal still traces to a handful of layered igneous intrusions.

##### 5x step-and-repeat aligner `mb.ram.mask.stepper`

An optical reduction stepper: a mercury-doped short-arc lamp, a 5x reduction lens, an x-y stage that steps the reticle across the wafer exposing one die field at a time, automatic mark-to-mark or die-to-die alignment with +-0.2 um repeatability, and a throughput of 30-60 die fields per minute. This was the tool that made 64K DRAM economics work, because one small reticle covered the whole die and one set-up covered many wafers.

##### Photoresist: AZ-1354 for the thick poly levels `mb.ram.mask.resist`

AZ-1354, a higher-solids positive resist used where a thicker film was needed (poly 2, aluminium) so the etch could go deep without thinning the resist. Spun at 3000-5000 rpm to 2-3 um, hard baked at 120 C, exposed through the reticle at 30-50 mJ/cm2, developed in TMAH. As with the CPU, the process ends in Piranha and RCA SC-1 cleans between every step.

#### 8-pin DIP: lead frame, bond, mould `mb.ram.assembly`

The 4164's assembly is the simplest IC assembly in the machine. The die goes face-up onto a gold-plated 8-pin lead frame tab with a gold-silicon eutectic bond at 400-450 C, 25 um gold wire makes eight frame bonds plus roughly a dozen internal wires for the sense-amp chain and the cell array, and the part is transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi. About 0.1-0.2 g of epoxy per part.

##### 8-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel `mb.ram.assembly.frame`

A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 8 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, with the bonding tab plated with a nickel strike followed by gold. Plastic-package frames get a tin or tin-lead plate over nickel so the leads solder; hermetic ceramic frames get a thicker gold plate.

##### 25 um gold bonding wire `mb.ram.assembly.gold`

0.5-1% palladium alloyed gold wire drawn to 25 um, spooled for the wedge bonder. A 4164 uses about 0.5 m; the VIC-II and SID use more.

###### Gold ore and cyanide refining `mb.ram.assembly.gold.ore`

Flotation concentrate leached in dilute sodium cyanide at pH 10.5, adsorbed on activated carbon, stripped and cupelled to dore, then electrolytically refined to 99.99% and drawn through a die with a phosphate lubricant.

##### Silica-filled epoxy molding compound `mb.ram.assembly.emc`

A phenolic novolac / epoxy novolac resin blended with 60-75% crushed silica filler and cured in a transfer press at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-mould-baked at 175 C. The low-alpha version used on many 4164s carried a specified alpha emission rate.

###### Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand `mb.ram.assembly.emc.silica`

The single largest mass ingredient in the package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is the reason a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.

#### Wafer sort and final test of the 4164 `mb.ram.sort` _(medium)_

Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.ram.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 4164 mask set printed on a 5x stepper, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: poly 2, bit line, metal. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.ram.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.ram.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.ram.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### RAS-only refresh and why the C64 counts it `mb.ram.refresh`

The 4164 has no refresh counter: the address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. The C64's 6510 does the counting in software - the KERNAL's refresh routine puts a 7-bit value into $D012 and clocks the CIA's A12 line every 7 machine cycles, so all eight chips are refreshed every 7 x 256 = 1792 cycles. That is why the KERNAL must be present for the machine to run, and why a 128-cycle-refresh 4164 (not a 256-cycle part) is mandatory.

### U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static) `mb.color-ram`

The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.

#### Why static rather than dynamic `mb.color-ram.why-static`

The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.color-ram.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed - the same substrate specification as the CPU and CIAs, and very possibly from the same lots, since a static RAM and a CPU need no exotic process.

##### 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process `mb.color-ram.polysilicon`

Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, cut into CZ charge pieces.

###### Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification `mb.color-ram.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.color-ram.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

###### Submerged arc furnace `mb.color-ram.saf`

Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-and-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc holds a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.color-ram.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached `mb.color-ram.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove boron. Also the source of the silica that goes into the package's epoxy and into the crystal puller's crucibles.

###### Semiconductor-grade quartz purification `mb.color-ram.quartz-leach`

Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible is acid-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 at 80-120 C and chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip boron, phosphorus, arsenic and alkali metals. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.

###### Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar `mb.color-ram.hf`

Finely ground acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. The same HF that leached the quartz later etched every thermal oxide in the process.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.color-ram.fluorspar`

Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity, mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits and flotation-beneficiated. Large deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching and no semiconductor-grade quartz anywhere in this tree.

##### CZ pull and wafer finishing `mb.color-ram.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped to 10-20 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (CMP did not exist in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.color-ram.crucible`

A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm inside diameter, holding the melt at 1420 C. Flame-fused around a rotating graphite mandrel from acid-leached quartz sand at ~2000 C, annealed, glazed inside and out, and scrapped after a handful of pulls.

#### The six-transistor NMOS static cell `mb.color-ram.cell`

Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.

##### The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor `mb.color-ram.cell.load` _(low)_

This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. I could not establish which the C64's 2114 used.

##### Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure `mb.color-ram.cell.access` _(medium)_

A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.

#### NMOS silicon-gate front end for the 2114 `mb.color-ram.process` _(medium)_

An NMOS process in the same family as the CPU: n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 then wet H2/O2 at 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, and 1-2 um aluminium with 0.5-1% Si sputtered and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG/nitride passivation. About 2-4 um minimum feature - a static RAM has no tight-pitch sense-amplifier chain to shrink, so it could run a coarser, older, cheaper process than the 6510.

#### Photolithography for the 2114 `mb.color-ram.litho`

AZ-1350 positive resist spun to about 1 um, soft baked at 90-100 C, aligned on a 1:1 Coburn contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner through a 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plate, developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard baked, stripped in hot sulfuric acid and megasonically cleaned before the next step.

##### The 2114 mask set `mb.color-ram.mask` _(medium)_

Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.

###### Chromite ore behind the mask absorber `mb.color-ram.chromite`

The chrome on every photomask in this tree starts as chromite (FeCr2O4) ore from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

#### How the VIC-II reads it during raster `mb.color-ram.vic-interface`

The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the 6-bit-per-channel RGB DAC and out through the 18-resistor palette on the mainboard. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.

#### 18-pin DIP package: frame, bond, mould, test `mb.color-ram.package`

Die attach on a gold-plated 18-pin lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

        - *40-pin DIP lead frame, FeNi alloy or copper* `mb.cpu.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Bonding wire from refined gold* `mb.cpu.bond.gold` *(seen above)*
        - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `mb.cpu.mold` *(seen above)*
        - *Epoxy molding compound from phenolic resin and silica* `mb.cpu.emc` *(seen above)*
#### Probe, sort and final test `mb.color-ram.test` _(medium)_

Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.

### 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL, 901225-01 character ROM `mb.roms`

The three mask-programmed NMOS ROMs on the C64 mainboard, all in 24-pin DIP: 901226-01 is the 8 KB (2364-compatible pinout) Commodore BASIC V2 interpreter at $A000; 901227-03 is the 8 KB KERNAL at $E000 (901227-01/-02 in earlier lots, and 901229-0x is the 1541 drive's KERNAL, not this one); 901225-01 is the 4 KB (2532-compatible) character generator ROM at U5. Mask ROMs are programmed by deleting or adding metal at one point in the flow, which means a whole extra mask set cut for each ROM revision.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for mask ROM `mb.roms.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. Mask ROMs ran the same NMOS front end as logic, and were often made on the same lots as the CPU.

##### 9N polysilicon charge `mb.roms.polysilicon`

Siemens-process polycrystalline silicon from 9N trichlorosilane reduced by pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

###### Trichlorosilane, rectified to 9N `mb.roms.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon chlorinated at 300 C with dry HCl, then fractionally distilled on the 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon from the submerged arc furnace `mb.roms.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to 98-99% silicon.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.roms.quartz`

Crushed and screened quartz of under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and acid-leached `mb.roms.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove boron.

###### Fluorspar concentrate for the HF leach `mb.roms.fluorspar`

97%+ CaF2 acid-grade fluorspar, mined and floated, converted to HF with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead retort at 200-250 C.

###### Elemental sulfur for the HF plant `mb.roms.sulfur`

Sulfur recovered from natural gas (Claus process, H2S + SO2 -> S + 2 H2O) or from sour crude, then burned to SO3 over V2O5 and absorbed to make the sulfuric acid used in the fluorspar retort.

##### CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean `mb.roms.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped to 10 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed with a ruby laser, OD or ID saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP existed), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.roms.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.roms.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

#### Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision `mb.roms.programming` _(medium)_

An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.

##### Thin-film alternatives: NiCr and Cr-SiO2 `mb.roms.ni-cr` _(medium)_

Some mask ROMs and PROMs of the era used a vacuum-deposited thin film as the memory element instead of a transistor array: nichrome (Ni80/Cr20) or chromium-silicon monoxide cermet resistor film, sputtered or co-evaporated to a sheet resistance of 25-200 ohm/sq, then laser- or sand-blast-programmed by burning gaps in the film. Commodore's ROMs were the ordinary transistor-array type; thin-film PROMs were more at home in TTL/PROM logic parts.

##### Bit-line sense amplifiers `mb.roms.sense` _(medium)_

A masked bit line is precharged high and then a dummy word is selected to develop a voltage across the bit line; a differential sense amplifier (a latch of four NMOS transistors plus a pair of cross-coupled load devices, exactly the same topology as the 6510's logic) amplifies the millivolt difference and latches it. The sense amps were the largest block in a mask ROM die - typically 10-15% of the area - because each needed a perfect match.

#### NMOS mask ROM front end `mb.roms.process`

The same silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU - n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium, PSG/nitride passivation - with one extra mask level for the ROM programming pattern. A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.

#### The ROM-only mask plate `mb.roms.mask` _(medium)_

Because the ROM pattern is a physical edit to the flow, Commodore held a separate chrome-on-glass plate for each ROM number. It was cut from the ROM's bit map by the same pattern generator used for the logic masks, inspected against the database, and stored in a mask library; 901226-01 and 901227-03 each required their own.

#### 24-pin DIP: attach, bond, mould, test `mb.roms.package`

Dice attached to a 24-pin gold-plated lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder (about 24 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires), transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked with the Commodore part number and date code, and socket-tested. In C64 assembly these were the only three chips soldered directly rather than in sockets.

##### 24-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel `mb.roms.package.frame`

A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 24 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, bonding tab plated nickel-then-gold, leads later tin-plated for soldering.

##### 25 um gold wire wedge bonding `mb.roms.package.wire`

About 24 pad-to-frame bonds plus a few internal wires, made on a wedge bonder because gold is soft; the wedge tool presses the wire flat. Ultrasonic energy and 300-400 C tool temperature.

##### Epoxy molding compound and quartz filler `mb.roms.package.emc`

Phenolic/epoxy novolac resin with 60-75% ground silica, transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-baked at 175 C.

###### Fused and ground silica from quartz sand `mb.roms.package.quartz-fill`

The 0.5-3 um angular silica that fills 60-75% of the moulding compound by weight, produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz.

#### Verifying every ROM bit `mb.roms.verify`

A mask ROM cannot be re-programmed, so its contents are verified twice. On the wafer, a 24-needle probe card runs a read-only pattern through the 8192 or 4096 addresses and sums the data; after assembly, the part goes into an automatic tester that reads the whole array and checks it against a resident signature and, for the C64's BASIC and KERNAL, the published checksum. Any failure meant a defective mask or a contamination particle, and the whole mask set had to be re-run.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.roms.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact printer with a 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plate, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: n+ field, LOCOS, poly, contact, metal, passivation. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.roms.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.roms.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.roms.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### ROM revisions are mask revisions `mb.roms.revisions`

Every fix to the C64's firmware cost a new mask set and a new wafer run. The BASIC ROM has exactly one version, 901226-01; the KERNAL went through 901227-01, -02 and -03, the last of which fixed a tape-loading bug and is what nearly every C64 shipped with; the character generator is 901225-01, with national variants 325018 (Swedish) and 325056 (Spanish C64C). A mask-ROM run also had to be large enough to fill the order, so a small revision could mean waiting weeks for wafers.

### 8562 VIC-II video chip, 40-pin DIP `mb.vic`

The C64's video, colour and sprite chip at U19, in a 40-pin DIP. The 8562 is the C64-specific part number for the NTSC VIC-II (the 6567/6569 are the Max Machine / PAL parts); it is an NMOS silicon-gate chip of the same generation as the 6510. The die contains the 40x25 text/bitmap video matrix, the 8 sprite (hardware sprite/clogger) engine, the colour-latch RAM interface, the 6-bit DAC colour outputs, the interrupt and border logic, the ~18 colour PAL palette resistors, and the 5-bit VIC-II colour registers. It reads VIC bank colour RAM through 8 pins and does no pixel-to-PAL conversion itself.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.vic.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, mirror polished and laser-scribed. The VIC-II is one of the largest CMOS/NMOS logic dies in the machine, so yield was lower and probe sorting mattered more.

##### 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process `mb.vic.polysilicon`

Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, cut into CZ charge pieces.

###### Trichlorosilane, rectified to 9N `mb.vic.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, then fractional distillation at 31.8 C boiling point to 9N-11N.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.vic.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.vic.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz from a pegmatite or quartzite vein, under 200 ppm Al and Fe.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached `mb.vic.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to strip aluminium, iron and boron.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.vic.fluorspar`

Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity, mined from hydrothermal veins and karst, converted with sulfuric acid to HF for the leach and for oxide etching.

###### Fluorspar vein ore `mb.vic.fluorspar-vein`

Vein and stock deposits of CaF2 worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and flotation-beneficiated.

##### CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean `mb.vic.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, and megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.vic.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.vic.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

#### NMOS front end for a large analog-plus-logic die `mb.vic.process` _(medium)_

The same silicon-gate NMOS sequence as the CPU, with extra care because the VIC-II mixes digital logic, a 6-bit DAC and analogue comparators on one die: 2 um minimum feature, ~400 A poly-oxide, LOCOS field oxide, self-aligned n+ source/drain, single 1-2 um aluminium layer, PSG plus plasma nitride passivation. The colour DAC outputs were open-source n-channel pull-downs that the external resistor ladder on the mainboard pulled up to +5 V.

#### The 18-resistor PAL palette on the mainboard `mb.vic.palette`

The VIC-II itself does not know what colour is 'red'. It emits six 4-bit-weighted analogue voltages per colour channel; a resistor ladder and a 74LS175 shift register on the C64 mainboard combine them with the border colour to synthesise the 16-entry NTSC palette and the 20-colour PAL palette. Those resistors are ordinary thick-film or wirewound parts and belong to the passives tree, but they are the physical interface between this die and a television.

#### 40-pin DIP assembly `mb.vic.package`

Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame by Au-Si eutectic at 400-450 C, 25 um gold wedge bonding (about 40 pad bonds plus internal busses for the colour and sprite routing), transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy, lead forming, dot-matrix marking, and automatic socket test. A ceramic version existed for industrial customers.

##### Ceramic DIP sintering, as the hermetic alternative `mb.vic.package.ceramic`

For hermetic parts the die went into a 96% alumina ceramic shell, sealed with a devitrifying glass frit in a belt furnace at ~850-950 C, and the metal flange was brazed or glass-sealed to the header. Ceramic was slower and costlier, and was used for the military/industrial grades; the C64's VIC-II was plastic.

#### VIC-II photomask set and 1:1 printing `mb.vic.mask` _(medium)_

The 8562's mask set was nine or ten levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, second diffusion, metal, ROM-programming (none here), passivation pad and the alignment/test levels. A 1982 small fab of this sort typically printed 1:1 on a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner with AZ-1350, using 1 mm chrome-on-glass plates about 5x7 inch. Overlay was held to +-0.5 um by a deliberate 'grid-broken' mask design: the layout broke the grid lines over active regions and added dummy structures so the stepper could align on a broken main grid rather than a continuous one.

##### Chrome-on-glass plate and its chromium target `mb.vic.mask.plate`

1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, photopatterned in positive resist, chrome etched away in hot perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected on a Zeiss comparison tool against the design database, and defect-repaired with a gallium or indium needle where a clear speck sat in a chrome line.

###### Chromite ore, the source of the mask chrome `mb.vic.mask.chromite`

Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and then to chromium metal for sputtering targets.

##### Shipley AZ-1350 photoresist `mb.vic.mask.resist`

The workhorse positive resist of the whole industry: a novolac phenol-formaldehyde resin with a photoactive quinone-diazoide group, dissolved in cellosolve/acetate solvents, spun to 1 um, soft baked at 90-100 C, exposed and developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. AZ-1354 (higher solids) was used for the aluminium and poly levels. Shipley was a Rohm and Haas business headquartered in Philadelphia, 30 km from the fab.

#### Probe, dice, attach and mould the VIC-II `mb.vic.dice`

The 8562 is one of the larger dies in the machine, so wafer sort in a Teradyne or Fairchild tester with a hand-drilled needle probe card mattered. Good dice are sawn apart, attached face-up to a gold-plated 40-pin lead frame with Au-Si eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder, transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy, formed, marked, and socket-tested.

##### Refined gold for the bonding wire `mb.vic.dice.gold`

99.99% gold refined from cyanide leach and cupellation, then electrolysed and drawn to 25 um. A VIC-II uses 60-100 bonds of it.

#### Wafer probe and pattern test of the 8562 `mb.vic.test` _(medium)_

The VIC-II is probed with a 40-needle card and a test program that exercises the character generator, the sprite pointers, the colour registers and the interrupt logic - and, on the analogue side, checks that all six colour outputs swing the full 0-5 V and that the 18-bit colour latches all decode. Assembled parts run the same program in a socket, often while a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester's video output.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.vic.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: n+ field, LOCOS, poly, self-aligned diffusion, contact, metal, passivation pad. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.vic.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.vic.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.vic.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### Die inspection and visual sort `mb.vic.die-inspect` _(medium)_

Before die attach the diced VIC-II dice were inspected under a stereomicroscope at 20-50x for pad damage, passivation cracks and contamination, and under dark-field illumination for particles. Because the VIC-II's colour outputs and the PAL raster timing were specified tightly, late-1980s and later C64As also shipped with a socketed VIC-II and hand-selected for stable raster; in 1982 the selection was done at final test.

### 6581 SID sound chip, 40-pin DIP `mb.sid`

The C64's sound generator at U18: three analogue subtractive-synthesis voices (two oscillators plus a noise source through a 12-bit DAC, one extra-noise-only channel for percussion), a ring modulator, a resonant multimode filter with a self-oscillating VCA, external-to-internal feedback volume routing, two pulse-width modulators and a hard sync. It is an NMOS hybrid - digital logic and poly counters driving an analogue poly on the same die - which is why it is noisy, why R4, R4AR, R5 and R6 differ, and why a 8580 (made on a newer process) sounds cleaner.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.sid.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed with a primary flat. Because the SID mixes a big analogue block with digital counters, the die is large and sensitive to oxide and substrate defects, so wafer sort did real work.

##### 9N polysilicon charge `mb.sid.polysilicon`

Silicon grown by the Siemens process: 9N trichlorosilane reduced with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

###### Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification `mb.sid.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus fall below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon from the arc furnace `mb.sid.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to 98-99% silicon with a few hundred ppm of boron.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz `mb.sid.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz lump under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined `mb.sid.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated to remove aluminium, iron and boron.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.sid.fluorspar`

97%+ acid-grade fluorspar, mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the HF used for leaching and oxide etching.

###### Fluorspar vein and stock deposit `mb.sid.fluorspar-ore`

Hydrothermal vein and karst deposits worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and floated to acid grade.

##### CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean `mb.sid.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under helium, pulled on a (100) seed, boron doped to ~10 ohm-cm. Boule ground and laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP yet), KOH edge-rounded, and megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.sid.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.sid.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

#### NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly `mb.sid.process` _(medium)_

The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.

##### Polysilicon load resistors `mb.sid.poly-res`

The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.

##### Probe test with audio characterisation `mb.sid.probe` _(medium)_

Wafer sort for the SID was as much a listening test as an electrical one: patterns stepped through the DACs and the filter and the DC output measured and sometimes listened to through a monitor speaker in the test head. Threshold voltages for the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.

#### External components the SID needs from the board `mb.sid.external`

The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 11 MHz colour clock derived from the VIC-II, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. Those are separate parts in the board and interconnect trees.

#### 40-pin DIP assembly `mb.sid.package`

Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonding with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder (roughly 40 pad bonds plus internal wiring for the analogue block), transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C / 700-1000 psi, lead forming to 0.6 inch pitch, marking and socket test. Some SIDs shipped with a ceramic (hermetic) package, which is where the 'SID in ceramic' collectors' market comes from.

##### SID photomask set `mb.sid.mask` _(medium)_

Nine or ten levels for the 6581: n+ field, LOCOS active area, base/well, contact, polysilicon (including the poly resistor pattern that is the DAC), second diffusion, metal, passivation pad, plus alignment. Printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plates, with the grid-broken alignment scheme. The analogue poly resistor pattern was itself a mask level, and trimming it by laser was an option some makers used.

###### Sputtered chromium for the mask plates `mb.sid.mask.chrome`

99.5% chromium, vacuum-melted, rolled and DC-magnetron sputtered with argon onto a rotating glass or quartz plate, giving a 5-8% transmission absorber at 100-150 nm.

###### Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate `mb.sid.mask.chromite`

Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to chromium metal.

###### Coburn 2400 contact printer / Micralign `mb.sid.mask.align`

1:1 mask printing: hard vacuum contact, or the Micralign's 100-500 um proximity gap which projected the image with a 5x optical system and so never touched the resist - the technology that removed the 'mask lifts off the wafer' failure mode that plagued pure contact printing.

##### Refined gold bonding wire `mb.sid.assembly.gold`

99.99% gold from cyanide leaching and electrolytic refining, drawn to 25 um with 0.5-1% palladium for strength. The SID, with roughly 60-80 bonds, consumed more of it than any other part in the machine.

###### Gold flotation concentrate `mb.sid.assembly.gold.ore`

Sulphide gold ore crushed, ground and floated; the concentrate is then cyanide leached, carbon-adsorbed, stripped and cupelled.

#### Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581 `mb.sid.test` _(medium)_

Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. Final test repeated it in a socket. This is why 6581 revisions are dated and marked (R4, R4AR, R5, R6) - each was a measured change to the analogue thresholds.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.sid.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: poly resistor/DAC pattern, metal, passivation. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.sid.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.sid.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.sid.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### SID revisions as an analogue-process story `mb.sid.revisions`

The 6581 shipped as R4 (1982), R4AR, R5 and R6. Each revision was a change to the analogue block - VCA threshold voltages, filter resonance scaling, DAC linearity - discovered by listening to the parts on probe. The 8580 (R4, 1984; R5 and R6, 1992) moved to a later NMOS process with a redesigned analogue section and a much larger die, and is universally regarded as cleaner and quieter. Nothing about the digital side changed enough to matter.

### Two 6526 CIA complex interface adapters `mb.cia`

CIA 1 at U17 and CIA 2 at U18 (PLA at U17 on some board revisions) provide the C64's two 8-bit parallel ports, the keyboard/joystick matrix scanning, the two 16-bit interval timers with one-shot/underflow interrupt, the shift register used for the serial (IEC) bus, and TOD (time-of-day) clocking derived from AC mains. Each 6526 is a 40-pin DIP NMOS part; CIA 1 sits at $D400 and reads port A from the VIC colour register file, while CIA 2 sits at $DC00 and drives the user port and serial bus.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.cia.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. The CIA is a modest-size die with a lot of analogue-adjacent timing circuitry, so it ran the same silicon-gate NMOS process as the rest of the logic.

##### 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process `mb.cia.polysilicon`

Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

###### Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification `mb.cia.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.cia.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.cia.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached `mb.cia.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove aluminium, iron and boron.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.cia.fluorspar`

97%+ acid-grade fluorspar mined and floated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the HF used for leaching and for etching the thermal oxide.

###### Fluorspar vein deposit `mb.cia.fluorspar-vein`

CaF2 vein and stock deposits mined by open pit and underground methods, crushed and flotation-beneficiated.

##### CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean `mb.cia.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.cia.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.cia.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

#### NMOS silicon-gate front end `mb.cia.process`

n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 then wet H2/O2 at ~1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon from silane at 800-850 C, self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant and 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium sputtered with 0.5-1% silicon and etched in hot H3PO4, then PSG plus nitride passivation. Ten mask levels, 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity printing with AZ-1350.

#### TOD clock and its mains-driven accuracy `mb.cia.tod`

The CIA's time-of-day clock is a 17-bit counter clocked from the serial pin, which the C64 mainboard drives from one side of the AC line through a 470 kohm resistor. The resulting clock is therefore a divided version of the mains frequency, trimmed per unit at final test by selecting a film capacitor. The timer counters themselves are static CMOS-style ripple counters, so they hold their count with the clock stopped - which is why a dead battery or a flat mains filter freezes the clock.

#### 40-pin DIP assembly `mb.cia.package`

Die attach by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C on a gold-plated lead frame, 25 um gold wedge bonding, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, lead forming, marking, socket test. Ceramic hermetic variants were also produced.

##### CIA photomask set `mb.cia.mask` _(medium)_

Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment levels - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from chrome-on-glass plates, using the grid-broken alignment scheme with dummy structures and stepper/diffusion checks. The two CIAs and the VIA were almost certainly the same process with three different mask sets.

###### Sputtered chromium mask absorber `mb.cia.mask.chrome`

100-150 nm of 99.5% chromium DC-magnetron sputtered with argon onto a rotating 1 mm glass or quartz plate.

###### Chromite ore concentrate `mb.cia.mask.chromite`

FeCr2O4 mined from the Bushveld Complex, Urals or Great Dyke and smelted to ferrochrome then chromium metal.

##### Gold bonding wire and lead frame plating `mb.cia.assembly.gold`

25 um gold wire wedge bonded to about 40 pads on a 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi lead frame plated nickel-then-gold; the finished leads get a tin or tin-lead plate so they solder into the machine's machined-pin sockets.

#### Wafer probe and final test of the 6526 `mb.cia.test` _(medium)_

Probe with a 40-needle card and a program that clocks both 16-bit timers against a reference, steps the serial shift register through a byte, checks the interrupt priority logic and the port handshake, and measures the TOD chain. Assembled parts repeat it in a socket. Because the TOD is clocked from the AC line, the accuracy test needed a calibrated frequency standard, not just a functional pass.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.cia.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: the same nine or ten levels as the rest of the CSG logic. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.cia.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.cia.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### The serial shift register and the IEC bus `mb.cia.serial`

The CIA's 8-bit shift register is what makes the Commodore serial bus work at all. Software sets a bit, shifts it out under CIA timer control with the handshake lines driving the ATN and CLK/CB lines, and reads bits back the same way; the VIC-II's serial output is decoded separately. This is a purely digital function built from ordinary NMOS flip-flops, but its timing jitter is the reason the KERNAL's serial routines are as delicate as they are.

### 6522 PPI/VIA, 40-pin DIP `mb.ppi`

The 6522 Versatile Interface Adapter at U15 on the C64 mainboard: two 8-bit parallel ports (the user port at $D420 and the cassette port at $D800), two 1-bit handshake lines, an 8-bit shift register for the cassette serial interface, two 16-bit timers with pulse output, four interrupt inputs and an I/O port with three latched control bits. It is the same 40-pin DIP silicon-gate NMOS part as the CIAs, from the same mask-family era and almost certainly the same process.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer `mb.ppi.wafer`

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. Identical substrate spec to the CIAs and the CPU - one fab, one process, many part numbers.

FeCr2O4 mined from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to chromium metal.

##### Gold bonding wire and lead frame `mb.ppi.assembly.gold`

25 um gold wire wedge bonded to about 40 pads on a 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi lead frame plated nickel-then-gold, then tin plated on the leads so the part drops into the C64's gold-plated machined-pin socket.

###### Gold concentrate, cyanide-leached `mb.ppi.assembly.gold.ore`

Flotation concentrate leached in dilute NaCN, adsorbed on activated carbon, stripped and cupelled to 99.99% dore for electrolytic refining and wire drawing.

#### Wafer probe and final test of the 6522 `mb.ppi.test` _(medium)_

Probe with a 40-needle card: both 16-bit timers clocked against a reference, the shift register stepped, both ports and the handshake lines cycled, and the interrupt inputs verified. Assembled parts repeat the program in a socket on the automatic tester, then go into the C64's machined-pin socket.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.ppi.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: the same nine or ten levels as the rest of the CSG logic. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.ppi.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.ppi.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.ppi.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### User port and cassette port wiring `mb.ppi.userport`

The 6522's two 8-bit ports are the C64's only general-purpose parallel I/O. Port A/B appear on the 12-way cartridge edge as the user port for printers, samplers and third-party cartridges, and as the cassette port on the mainboard. Both ports are quasi-bidirectional TTL with no bus contention protection beyond a weak pull-up, so driving them from two cards at once was a hardware error, not a negotiated one.

### U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS) `mb.pla`

The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.

#### What a PLA physically is `mb.pla.array`

Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.

#### Three ways to make a programmable array, 1982-84 `mb.pla.types`

A PLD or PLA is defined by how its links are made. (a) Mask-programmed: the links are decided in a photolithography mask and are present or absent as fabricated silicon; cheapest per unit at volume, but needs a unique mask set, a long lead time and a minimum order. (b) Fusible-link: every link exists as a real wire - typically nichrome or titanium - and a programmer blows selected links with a laser or a high-current pulse. Generic catalogue parts with a wide range of functions, user-programmable in seconds. (c) Antifuse: the links start as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide layer and a pulse converts the selected ones into high-resistance insulation. Commodore's 906114-01 is (a).

##### Mask-programmed route (this part) `mb.pla.mask-route`

The array is fabricated complete, with the links built into one of the lithography levels. There is no programming step at all: every 906114-01 off the line is already a working C64 address decoder. The cost sits entirely up front as non-recurring engineering - artwork, mask plates, mask fabrication and verification - and it is paid once per unique logic function.

##### Fusible-link route, for contrast `mb.pla.fuselink` _(medium)_

The 82S100 that gave the C64 PLA its name was originally marketed as a field-programmable bipolar array: its links were real chromium or nichrome fuses, and a laser programmer burned out the unwanted ones through the package's FE/NE pin. This is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and it is why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of different functions. Commodore could not use this route for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices, so they went to masks.

##### Antifuse route, for contrast `mb.pla.antifuse` _(medium)_

A link that starts conducting and is blown into an insulator. Fay's 1970 antifuse used a dielectric-coated metal; by 1982 the dominant versions were amorphous silicon and silicon dioxide films, written by a ~20-40 V pulse that punctured the film. Antifuses are tiny and need no laser, but they were slower to program and harder to test than blowing a metal fuse.

#### The fuse pattern is one more photomask `mb.pla.mask-programming`

This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.

##### Custom chrome-on-glass plate for the C64 address map `mb.pla.mask-plate` _(medium)_

A 1:1 chrome-on-glass or 5x quartz plate carrying the link pattern for the C64's memory map - ROM, RAM, I/O, colour RAM, cartridge and bank switching. Cut from the design database, inspected against it, defect-repaired, and stored in a mask library. One plate per unique function, like a custom printing plate.

###### Chromite ore for the mask absorber `mb.pla.chromite`

Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

#### PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads `mb.pla.vs-pal`

The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.

#### Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100 `mb.pla.provenance`

Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

#### The economics of one custom mask set `mb.pla.economics` _(medium)_

The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the 906114 `mb.pla.wafer` _(medium)_

A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. The NMOS PLA was made in-house at MOS Technology's Norristown plant, so this wafer almost certainly came out of the same furnace and the same process as the 6510 and the 6526 - which is the strongest evidence for the process family, even though no 906114-01 process manual has ever been published.

##### 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process `mb.pla.polysilicon`

Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

###### Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification `mb.pla.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.pla.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

###### Submerged arc furnace `mb.pla.saf`

Three graphite electrodes in a refractory shell maintain a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C; metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.pla.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached `mb.pla.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to strip aluminium, iron and boron.

###### Semiconductor-grade quartz purification `mb.pla.quartz-leach`

Hot HF/HNO3 leach to strip surface aluminium and iron, then chlorination at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to remove boron, phosphorus and arsenic. Yield from ordinary sand is a few percent.

###### Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar `mb.pla.hf`

Acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead retort at 200-250 C to make the HF that leached the quartz and etched the oxide.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.pla.fluorspar`

Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity mined from hydrothermal veins and karst and flotation-beneficiated, from deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa.

##### CZ pull and wafer finishing `mb.pla.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in this period), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.pla.crucible`

A thick-walled transparent silica cup flame-fused from acid-leached quartz sand around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed and glazed, then scrapped after a handful of pulls.

#### NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed) `mb.pla.process` _(low)_

The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. I am deliberately not asserting a specific figure for that line width, because no source states one for this part.

#### 28-pin 600 mil DIP package `mb.pla.package`

A wide-body package because the array needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation, marked with the part number and date code, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

        - *40-pin DIP lead frame, FeNi alloy or copper* `mb.cpu.leadframe` *(seen above)*
        - *Bonding wire from refined gold* `mb.cpu.bond.gold` *(seen above)*
        - *Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy* `mb.cpu.mold` *(seen above)*
        - *Epoxy molding compound from phenolic resin and silica* `mb.cpu.emc` *(seen above)*
#### Why it fails more than anything else in the machine `mb.pla.failures`

Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

#### Probe, truth-table test and final test `mb.pla.test`

A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.

### Discrete semiconductors on the board `mb.discretes` _(medium)_

The handful of non-IC semiconductors in the machine: small-signal NPN and PNP planar transistors (2N3904, 2N3906, 2N4124) for the serial/parallel port buffers, the colour-amplifier and video-driver stages and the cassette/joystick input switching; higher-voltage NPN power transistors (2N3055, 2N3792) in the power supply's regulator and short-circuit crowbar; rectifier, switching and zener diodes (1N4001, 1N4148, 1N47xx); one or two indicator LEDs; and a metal-oxide varistor across the AC input. Each of these was made in a bipolar or compound-semiconductor plant completely unrelated to the Norristown logic fab.

#### 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the discrete plant `mb.discretes.wafer` _(medium)_

A 4-inch p-type CZ wafer, 10-40 ohm-cm, mirror polished and laser-scribed. Bipolar discrete fabs used p-type CZ with a heavy oxygen content and generally a (100) or (111) orientation; many discrete lines of the era ran 75 mm wafers because they did not need fine geometry.

##### 9N polysilicon (same silicon, different plant) `mb.discretes.polysilicon`

Polycrystalline silicon grown by the Siemens process from 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C. Discrete makers bought the same electronic-grade silicon as logic fabs, usually from a merchant supplier.

###### Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification `mb.discretes.tcs`

Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `mb.discretes.msi`

Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

###### Metallurgical-grade quartz lump `mb.discretes.quartz`

Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

###### High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached `mb.discretes.quartz-sand`

Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated to remove boron.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate `mb.discretes.fluorspar`

97%+ acid-grade fluorspar mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the hydrofluoric acid used for the leach and for etching oxide.

###### Fluorspar vein deposit `mb.discretes.fluorspar-vein`

CaF2 vein and stock deposits mined by open pit and underground methods, crushed and floated to acid grade.

##### CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean `mb.discretes.cz`

Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium or argon, pulled on a (100) or (111) seed, boron doped to 10-40 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished, KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1. Discretes also went through a gettered or radiation-damage anneal to kill the silicon-germanium centres that degrade current gain.

###### Fused quartz CZ crucible `mb.discretes.wafer.crucible`

The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it.
