The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

###### Quartz sand for the crucible glass `mb.discretes.wafer.crucible-sand`

Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

#### Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process `mb.discretes.bjt`

The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.

#### TO-92 epoxy mould package `mb.discretes.bjt-package`

Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.

#### High-voltage power BJTs (2N3055, 2N3792) `mb.discretes.power-bjt`

The 2N3055 is a 15 A, 200-300 V NPN power transistor in a TO-3 metal can or a plastic TO-220, used as the series pass element in the C64's linear 5 V power supply. The 2N3792 is a 100 V, 0.5 A NPN used in the supply's short-circuit detection, driving an SCR crowbar. Both are triple-diffused or epitaxial-base-collector designs with large dies, thick aluminium (or nickel) metallization and often a molybdenum or copper heat spreader, die-attachable with a soft solder or silver brazing.

#### Rectifier, switching and zener diodes `mb.discretes.diodes`

Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.

#### Indicator LED (red/green/amber only) `mb.discretes.led`

The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

##### Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction `mb.discretes.led.epi`

A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.

##### Refined gallium `mb.discretes.led.gallium` _(medium)_

Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.

##### GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer `mb.discretes.led.substrate` _(medium)_

The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.

#### Zinc oxide varistor disc `mb.discretes.varistor` _(medium)_

A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.

##### Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate `mb.discretes.varistor.zinc` _(medium)_

Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.

###### Sphalerite (ZnS) ore concentrate `mb.discretes.varistor.sphalerite`

The world's zinc ore: a cubic sulphide mined underground or in big open pits, floated to 50-60% Zn. The Sierra de Orueba and MIDA deposits in China became dominant suppliers in exactly the period Commodore's supply chain depended on.

#### Black epoxy for the TO-92 shell `mb.discretes.to92-mould`

A discrete's package is 90% compound by mass: an epoxy or phenolic resin loaded with 60-70% silica and 0.5-2% carbon black for the black colour, injected at 150-180 C into a 3-cavity transfer tool and post-cured. A 2N3904 die is a fraction of a square millimetre inside roughly 0.1 g of this.

##### Silica filler from quartz sand `mb.discretes.to92-mould.silica`

Ground, angular silica of 0.5-3 um mean size produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz - the same material as the IC moulding compound filler.

#### Discretes lead frame: nickel, copper, tin plating `mb.discretes.leadframe`

A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.

##### Tin and tin-lead plating bath `mb.discretes.tin` _(medium)_

Tin plating of semiconductor leads was done chemically in an acid or alkaline stannate bath over a nickel underplate, later shifting to pure tin as the industry moved off lead. The tin itself comes from cassiterite (SnO2), mined in Indonesia, Malaysia and Bolivia.

###### Cassiterite (SnO2) concentrate `mb.discretes.cassiterite`

Heavy, high-density tin ore from alluvial and lode deposits; the Indonesian and Malaysian alluvial placers became the dominant supply in the 1980s and 1990s, with secondary output from Bolivia's Cerro Rico and Cornwall's abandoned tinfields.

#### Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes `mb.discretes.test`

Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.

#### Photolithography for this part `mb.discretes.litho`

Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact printer in the discrete plant (diffusion and epitaxial masks), expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: epitaxial n-layer, tub isolation, base window, emitter window, metallization. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

##### Positive photoresist chemistry `mb.discretes.litho.resist`

A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

##### Spin coater and hot-plate track `mb.discretes.litho.spinner`

A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

#### Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic `mb.discretes.clean`

A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.

#### Epitaxial growth reactor for the discrete plant `mb.discretes.epi`

After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.

##### Isolation diffusion and its moat `mb.discretes.isolation`

A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

### 74-series glue logic `mb.logic`

The eleven off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Nine are 74-series bipolar TTL in black epoxy DIP; three are CMOS; one is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.

#### 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8) `mb.logic.u8-7406` _(medium)_

Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.

##### How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL) `mb.logic.bipolar` _(medium)_

The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.

###### The junction-isolated bipolar flow `mb.logic.bipolar.process`

The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

###### p-type starting wafer `mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate`

A slice of p-type silicon, lightly doped so that it is a good insulator between transistor islands and does not leak much reverse current. Everything the tree contains - the transistors, the resistors, the isolation - sits on this one piece of crystal.

###### Where the silicon came from `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer`

No fab makes its own silicon. A logic fab in 1983 bought polished 75 mm or 100 mm wafers from a specialist supplier - Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo, Siltron, MEMC - who themselves bought metallurgical silicon, made it into trichlorosilane or silane, reduced that to polysilicon, pulled a monocrystalline boule by the Czochralski method, and sliced, lapped and polished it. This is the longest supply chain in the whole computer.

###### Metallurgical silicon from quartz and coke `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz`

The bottom of the silicon chain. Quartz - silicon dioxide, usually mined as high-purity quartzite - is mixed with coke and heated in a submerged-arc electric furnace at about 2000 C. The carbon reduces the oxide, and molten silicon collects at the bottom: metallurgical silicon, 98-99.5 percent pure. Every silicon wafer in the world begins here.

###### High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon) `metal.silica`

The refined element every chip in the machine is cut from. A 1982 Commodore 64 mainboard carried a handful of silicon dies and one 2 MHz quartz crystal, both traceable to this chain: quartzite or silica reduced to 98-99% metallurgical silicon, chlorinated to trichlorosilane, distilled to 9-nines, deposited as polysilicon, then pulled as a single Czochralski crystal. Note that the 6510 is NMOS, so the 1982 die uses ALUMINIUM gate metal and thermally grown field oxide, not a polysilicon gate; the polysilicon branch below is the industry feedstock route, which is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

###### Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N `metal.silica.polysilicon`

Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. IMPORTANT: the 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate. This branch is the industry feedstock route, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

###### Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods `metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition`

Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

###### Doped vs undoped polysilicon `metal.silica.polysilicon.doping` _(medium)_

Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.

###### Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod `metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking` _(medium)_

The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.

###### Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N `metal.silica.tcs`

Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

###### Fractional distillation of HSiCl3 `metal.silica.tcs.distillation`

Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.

###### Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C `metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination`

Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

###### Metallurgical silicon, 98-99% `metal.silica.mgsi`

The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

###### Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C `metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace`

A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.

###### Carbothermic carbon: petroleum coke and woodchips `metal.silica.reducer` _(medium)_

The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.

###### Calcined petroleum coke for silicon `metal.silica.petcoke` _(medium)_

Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.

###### High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2) `metal.quartzite`

A metamorphosed, recrystallised quartz sandstone that is quarried rather than deep-mined. The chemical silicon industry does not use beach sand at all - it uses very low iron, very low aluminium quartzite, because Al and Fe are the impurities that survive the entire chain into the crystal. Two regions have essentially all of it. Note this is a DIFFERENT rock from the industrial silica sand used for glass, foundry moulds and copper-smelter flux, which is a much more common material.

###### Quartzite quarry, ~100,000 t/year `metal.quartzite.quarry` _(medium)_

The Norwegian quartzite quarry is a bench mine in metamorphosed sandstone: drilling, blasting, a primary jaw crusher, and a sorting step where workers - and, later, optical sorters - remove the visibly iron-stained lumps by hand. The rock is then crushed, washed on a sluice or in a scrubber, dried and size-graded, because a single grain of iron left in the batch makes a bad day of the whole furnace.

###### Quartz sandstone protolith (metaquartzite) `metal.quartzite.rock`

The rock as a geologist would name it: a quartz-rich sandstone or siltstone, now a hard white metaquartzite of interlocking quartz grains with the bedding picked out by iron oxides. Some of the Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence. Either way the leaf of the silicon chain is a sedimentary or metamorphic rock exposed at the surface and dug out of a hillside.

###### Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling `metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle` _(medium)_

Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.

###### Hydrochloric acid (32-37%) `metal.hydrochloric-acid`

The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.

###### HCl synthesis and absorption `metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis`

Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

###### Czochralski monocrystalline ingot `metal.silica.czochralski`

Where the polysilicon chain ends and the semiconductor business begins. A 2 kg chunk is melted at 1420 C in a silica crucible over a seed crystal, and a slow pull at 0.5-2 mm/min with rotation grows a 75-150 mm boule. Every defect the 6510 die had in it - dislocations, oxygen precipitates, the dopant gradient along the length - was frozen in during this pull. Gas-phase-grown poly was cheaper and lower-defect than Czochralski poly in 1982, so the route below was standard.

###### Fused quartz growth crucible `metal.silica.czochralski.crucible` _(medium)_

The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.

###### Thermally grown silicon dioxide `metal.silica.field-oxide`

Gate oxide, field oxide and the photoresist mask oxides are not bought - they are grown. The wafer goes into a 1000-1150 C steam or dry-O2 furnace for an hour and a half and roughly a thousand angstroms of SiO2 comes off the silicon itself. So the machine's insulation is, chemically speaking, the same element as the chip, oxidised in place.

###### 2.048 MHz quartz clock crystal `metal.silica.quartz-crystal`

The C64's timing reference: an AT-cut quartz plate about 7.6 x 2.5 mm brazed between metal caps, resonating at 2.048 MHz. Quartz is the only material with a usable temperature-stable mechanical resonance that cheap. The plate itself is usually not natural rock - it is hydrothermally grown synthetic quartz in an autoclave of sodium hydroxide solution at about 400 C and 1.5 kbar.

###### Hydrothermal synthetic quartz `metal.silica.quartz-crystal.synthetic` _(medium)_

A seed of natural quartz hangs in aqueous NaOH in a steel autoclave at 380-450 C and 100-200 bar, and quartz grows on the seed at a few mm/day. The advantage over mined Brazilian rock is that the growth conditions are repeatable, so the Q and defect density of every boule match. Brazilian vein quartz was still used where natural material beat synthetic on Q.

###### Petroleum coke (the carbon reductant) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke`

The carbon that does the reducing. Petroleum coke is the heavy solid residue left from a refinery coker, essentially the same residuum that feeds the carbon-black furnace. It is mixed into the quartz charge as a reductant and, in the electric furnace, as a source of heat when it burns.

###### Crude oil (refinery residue) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.coke.crude`

The refinery that makes the coke is fed by crude oil. So the carbon that reduces quartz into silicon came, one step removed, from the same crude oil that made the epoxy, the resist solvents and the natural gas.

###### The submerged-arc electric furnace `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.furnace`

A steel shell lined with refractory, with three graphite electrodes plunging into a charge of crushed quartz and coke. An arc between the electrodes melts the mix; the carbon reduces the silicon dioxide and the carbon monoxide gas burns at the electrode tips, superheating the bath to about 2000 C. Molten silicon (99 percent pure) taps off the bottom. A single furnace makes tens of thousands of tonnes of metallurgical silicon a year.

###### High-purity quartzite (the ore of silicon dioxide) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.quartz.quartzite`

The silica must be unusually pure, because every impurity in the metallurgical silicon becomes a lifetime in the transistor. High-grade quartzite or vein quartz, low in iron and aluminium, is selected - from the Spruce Pine district in North Carolina, from Norway, from the Ural, from Brazil and China. It is crushed and reacted to make trichlorosilane, which is purified by careful redistillation before it ever becomes wafer silicon.

###### Polysilicon from the Siemens process `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon`

Metallurgical silicon is first reacted with hydrogen chloride at about 300 C to make trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), which is purified by fractional distillation. The purified trichlorosilane is then reduced with pure hydrogen at 1000-1150 C in a fluidised-bed reactor, and fine polycrystalline silicon ('polysilicon') grows on silicon seed particles. The Siemens process - the reaction invented at Siemens in 1954 - is how essentially all the world's polysilicon, and so all its silicon wafers, were made in 1983.

                  - *Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N* `metal.silica.tcs` *(seen above)*
###### Hydrochloric acid (for the trichlorosilane step) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrochloric`

Hydrochloric acid reacts with the metallurgical silicon to make the trichlorosilane gas. HCl was made from chlorine and hydrogen, or from brine, or bought as a bulk chemical. It is the same chlorine chemistry that makes the epoxy precursors and the resist solvents.

###### Chlorine gas `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrochloric.chlorine`

Chlorine for the hydrochlorination step, from the chlor-alkali cell on brine, with hydrogen from the same cell. The classic industrial pairing.

###### Brine `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrochloric.chlorine.brine`

Concentrated salt solution electrolysed to chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

###### Rock salt `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrochloric.chlorine.brine.salt`

Halite, mined or evaporated from seawater. Root of the chlorine chemistry underneath the silicon, the epoxy and the solvents.

###### Hydrogen for the reduction `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen`

High-purity hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane to silicon in the Siemens reactor. It was made largely by steam reforming of natural gas, with a final purification (molecular sieve and cryogenic adsorption) to get to the parts-per-billion impurity levels the polysilicon needed.

###### The hydrogen was mostly natural gas `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr`

By the 1980s the vast majority of the world's hydrogen for ammonia and for electronics was made by steam reforming natural gas - passing methane over a hot nickel catalyst with steam to give hydrogen and carbon monoxide, then shifting and scrubbing. This is the deepest tie in the whole tree: the natural gas that reduced the silicon came out of the same subsurface reservoir complex that the industry calls gas, and methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.

###### Methane (natural gas) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.methane`

CH4, the dominant component of natural gas, the simplest hydrocarbon. It was reacted with steam over a nickel reforming catalyst at 800-900 C: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2. A shift reactor then converts the carbon monoxide to more hydrogen. This hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane into pure silicon.

###### Natural gas (field) `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.methane.naturalgas`

Methane and light hydrocarbons drawn from a gas or oil field. This is the geological end of the chemistry: ancient buried organic matter, converted by heat and pressure over geological time into oil and natural gas, and now drawn out of the ground.

###### How natural gas formed `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.methane.naturalgas.form`

Buried ancient organic sediment, compressed and heated over millions of years by the weight of overburden, cracked into hydrocarbons. Methane is the lightest and most abundant product. This is the true root of the carbon in the computer: the natural gas that made the hydrogen that reduced the silicon that every transistor is built on.

###### The gas field `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.methane.naturalgas.form.field`

A reservoir of porous sandstone sealed under an impermeable cap, drilled vertically and produced through a christmas tree of valves, then gathered into a trunk pipeline system. This is where the chain physically ends: a hole in the ground in West Texas, the North Sea, the Dutch Groningen field or the Urengoy field in Siberia, with a gas treatment plant at the wellhead stripping out the hydrogen sulphide and the higher hydrocarbons that would poison a reforming catalyst a few thousand miles downstream.

###### Nickel reforming catalyst `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.catalyst`

The steam reformer is a bank of tubes packed with nickel on an alumina support. The nickel - from nickel ore - catalyses the methane-steam reaction at 800-900 C. A drop of this catalyst is one more place nickel enters the tree, alongside the NiCr resistor and the lead frame.

###### Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless `metal.nickel`

Nickel is small in mass and enormous in function. In a C64 it is the plating on the connector shells and the gold-plated edge connector fingers' underlayer, the constantan and nichrome of the thin-film resistors on the board, the Invar of the composite-video circuit's chroma delay, and the bulk of AISI 304 and 430 stainless in the audio jack and the shield cans. 1982 was the year nickel was in a price crisis - the 1982-83 LME collapse, following the Escondida-adjacent and the Sherritt expansions of the late 1970s, took nickel from about $4/lb in 1980 to under $1.30/lb by 1983.

###### Nickel laterite (garnierite ore) `metal.nickel.laterite`

A soft, earthy, red-brown clay-and-laterite ore, really a weathering product of ultramafic rock: olivine and pyroxene in a serpentinised peridotite are altered from scratch, and nickel substitutes for magnesium in the clay lattice, giving garnierite. There is no nickel mineral to concentrate; the whole ore body is the ore. The great deposits in 1982 were the Cuban Moa and Nicaro operations - where the ore was shipped to the United States and Japan for the nickel limit of the United States Defense Production Act of 1981 made government stockpiling a political event - the Philippines' Surigao and Bacojo operations, the New Caledonian laterite, and the Queensland laterite. Laterite is mined in the open pit in soft, wet ground with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline, and often leached in place.

###### Bucket-wheel excavator laterite mine `metal.nickel.laterite-mine` _(medium)_

The soft, wet, deeply weathered ore is the ideal bucket-wheel material. A walking or rail-mounted bucket-wheel excavator with a 20-40 m boom cuts the overburden and the ore bench itself, dropping it onto a belt conveyor, and the ore goes to a long washing and screening plant rather than to a crusher. The Philippine and Cuban operations had bucket-wheel excavators with booms over 50 m by the early 1980s. The ore arrives at the plant as a slurry, which is why the pressure leach of the 1980s was designed for a pumped pulp and not for a dry concentrate.

###### Serpentinised peridotite `metal.nickel.peridotite`

The leaf: an ultramafic igneous rock, mostly olivine, now largely converted to serpentine, that has been chemically weathered for tens of millions of years in a warm wet climate. The nickel is in the clay and in the limonite, not in a crystal. Cuba, New Caledonia and the Philippines all have large serpentinite bodies, and that is why the island arcs of the Pacific are the nickel map.

###### The laterite washing and screening plant `metal.nickel.ore-washing` _(medium)_

The laterite arrives from a bucket-wheel excavator as a slurry, and it goes through a log washer, a scrubber, a screen tower and a series of hydrocyclones, and the -0.5 mm fraction is rejected outright as low-grade clay. The coarse fraction is dewatered on a screen and stacked in a concrete bin. In the Cuban and Philippine operations the stacked ore was then leached in place on a pad, in the Queensland operations it was dried in a rotary dryer and shipped to a furnace. The whole plant exists because the ore is a soft, wet, variable, low-grade bulk material, and the plants are mostly about handling water.

###### Limonite and garnierite: the two nickel minerals `metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite`

The leaf of the nickel branch, and it is a mineral solution rather than a mineral. There is no nickel mineral in a laterite. Nickel substitutes for magnesium in the smectite and kaolinite clays - the mineral is garnierite, which is really a mixture - and it substitutes for iron in the goethite of the limonite, so a limonite laterite's nickel is spread through amorphous iron oxide at a few percent. The two grades of laterite that matter commercially are the high-iron limonite ore and the low-silica saprolite ore, and the difference between them is the grade of the nickel-bearing lattice, which is why the pressure leach was developed for one and not the other.

###### Drying the laterite for the furnace `metal.nickel.drying` _(medium)_

A laterite arrives at 30-45% moisture and the submerged arc furnace cannot take it wet, because the water costs more steam than the reaction releases. So the dewatered ore is dried in a rotary dryer or - in the Cuban and Philippine operations of the 1980s - in a suspension dryer with the hot flue gas, to below 1-2% moisture, and the drier's exhaust is the source of the dust and the fuel consumption that dominated the cost. Some plants solved the problem differently: the Queensland operations calcined and reduced the ore on the pad and then shipped a nickel oxide, which moved the water problem upstream to the leach.

###### Sherritt-Gordon ammonia leach and hydrogen reduction `metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon`

The process that unlocked the laterites in the 1970s and 1980s. The slurry is leached at atmospheric pressure with concentrated ammonia and oxygen at 50-70 C: nickel and copper form soluble ammine complexes while the iron precipitates as hematite. The pregnant liquor is heated in a pressure autoclave with hydrogen and more ammonia, and the nickel comes out of solution as a metal powder while the copper stays in solution as the ammine, so the two separate in one vessel. The powder is filtered, washed and dried in a rotary vacuum dryer. This is genuinely a 1980s technology - the first commercial laterite plant, at Browns River in Queensland, started in 1974 and Sherritt licensed the process to the Cubans and the Japanese in the second half of the decade.

###### The ammonia-hydrogen autoclave `metal.nickel.autoclave` _(medium)_

A 10-15 m long, 3-5 m diameter, titanium or 316L-lined pressure vessel in a 6-10 stage cascade. In each stage the liquor is contacted with hydrogen and stirred, and the nickel comes out onto the walls and the cooling surfaces. The whole chemistry depends on the fact that ammonia complexes nickel and copper so strongly that hydrogen alone cannot reduce them at atmospheric pressure; the autoclave gives the extra pressure to push the equilibrium over. Removing the ammonia and boiling the slurry then precipitates basic nickel carbonate, which is calcined to nickel oxide.

###### Nickel oxide (NiO) calcined from basic carbonate `metal.nickel.nickel-oxide` _(medium)_

The commercially traded intermediate. The pregnant solvent is stripped of ammonia and boiled, basic nickel carbonate NiCO3.2Ni(OH)2.4H2O drops out, it is filtered and washed, and it is calcined at 400-600 C to green-black nickel oxide at 99.0-99.5% Ni. In 1982 the overwhelming majority of nickel oxide went to ferronickel smelting; pure nickel oxide was a smaller but growing market for stainless steel and for plating.

###### Ferronickel: laterite plus iron ore in a submerged arc furnace `metal.ferronickel`

The dominant way nickel actually became metal in 1982. Dried laterite and quartzite are fed with coke into a large submerged arc furnace, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, running at 1350-1500 C. The laterite's iron is already present as hematite, so the whole charge reduces together and the product is not nickel metal but an alloy of about 60-75% Ni and 25-40% Fe, plus a slag of magnesium, silicon and aluminium oxides. The ferronickel is tapped and either refined in the same operation to pure nickel or - more commonly in the 1980s - sold straight to a stainless steel mill as a charge, which is why the whole ferronickel industry is really a stainless steel industry.

###### Nickel electrowinning from a pure sulphide circuit `metal.nickel.electrowinning` _(medium)_

Where the ore is sulphide rather than laterite, Sherritt's original ammonia-pressure process dissolves the concentrate in ammoniacal ammonium sulphate at 160-190 F (70-90 C) with oxygen, and then electrowins the nickel directly out of the pregnant liquor onto titanium cathodes in diaphragm cells at a very low voltage, about 0.5-1.0 V, because hydrogen evolution competes and the current efficiency is only 70-85%. This is the Sherritt-Gordon route as it was licensed in 1969-1972, and it is why the company is called after two towns in Manitoba. The cathodes are stripped, briquetted and remelted.

###### Nickel sulphide concentrate (Sudbury) `metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate`

The Sudbury basin of Ontario was the world's nickel capital and it is a genuinely strange deposit: an impact structure full of shock-melted, metal-rich breccia at the base of a 1.8 billion year old impact crater, with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and millerite NiS. The INCO operation mined both underground and, from 1962, from the open pit at the south end of the basin, and roasted the ore in fluidised beds to make 'fines' - a nickel-copper matte rather than a concentrate - before smelting. The tree therefore continues down through the Sudbury ore to a shocked sulphide breccia in an impact melt sheet, which is as geologically interesting an endpoint as this tree has.

###### Impact melt sheet at the base of the Sudbury crater `metal.nickel.impact-melt`

The leaf: a foot-thick to 20 m layer of rock melted and shock-altered by the impact, in which the nickel and copper sulphides were disseminated as droplets. It is a metamorphic and melt rock, not an igneous intrusion, and it is a band about 60 km long and 20 km wide across northern Ontario. The mining is ordinary room-and-pillar or open-pit on a sheet that lies only a few hundred metres below the Huronian cover.

###### Mond carbonyl refining (nickel from 99.9 to 99.999) `metal.nickel.mond`

Ludwig Mond's 1890s process, still used in the 1980s for the last nines. Nickel carbonyl Ni(CO)4 is formed at 50-60 C in a saturator, distilled off as a colourless liquid boiling at 43 C, and decomposed in a decomposer column at 200-230 C onto 99.99% nickel pellets. The trick is that the carbonyl of cobalt is much less volatile and iron forms a non-volatile carbonyl, so the distillation separates the three metals in one operation - the same volatility trick as the trichlorosilane column in the silicon branch. Cobalt is recovered from the residue as Co2(CO)8.

###### Cobalt recovered as dicobalt octacarbonyl `metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl` _(medium)_

The cobalt in the Mond residue is a genuine industrial source of cobalt: the residue is treated with copper at 200 C under hydrogen to reduce the cobalt and copper carbonyls, and then re-carbonylated to Co2(CO)8, which is filtered out and decomposed. In 1982 the two leading producers - INCO in Canada and OUTOKUMPU in Finland - between them controlled most of the world's cobalt from their nickel operations, and a period of low cobalt stocks in 1982-83 contributed to a real shortage.

###### Nickel carbonyl: the deadliest room in metals `metal.nickel.mond.safety` _(medium)_

Nickel tetracarbonyl is a colourless, volatile liquid that boils at 43 C and is lethal by inhalation at concentrations far below anything that can be smelled. A Mond refinery therefore runs on a rule that no one enters a carbonyl area without a respirator, that the vapour is continuously monitored at the floor and at breathing height, and that the whole plant is vented through a high-temperature incinerator that destroys the carbonyl before releasing it. The 1980s occupational-hygiene literature on nickel carbonyl is a case study in how a process can be kept running at all when the material is that toxic, and the number of fatal poisonings in nickel refineries over the century is a reminder that this is one of the most dangerous processes in the metals industry.

###### Electrolytic or cathode nickel, 99.9% `metal.nickel.ingot`

Nickel metal arrives at the user as a cathode or a briquette: 99.8% for ferronickel-grade stainless, 99.9% for stainless and for plating. For a plating line the metal arrives as matte or as a soluble anode, but in 1982 the majority of nickel plating anodes were still the insoluble carbon steel anode, with the nickel actually coming from the electrolyte as nickel sulphate made from nickel oxide. This is a deliberate convergence node: the laterite branch, the Mond branch, the plating branch and the stainless branch all meet here.

###### Nickel electroplating and the gold underplate `metal.nickel.electroplating`

The single most important metallurgical fact about nickel in a 1982 C64: gold plating does not sit on copper. It sits on a nickel underplate of 1-3 um, and the reason is electrochemistry - gold will not plate directly onto copper because the copper dissolves faster than the gold deposits, and a gold-copper diffusion couple makes a brittle, corrosion-prone joint. So the connector fingers and the IC leads get nickel and then a thin gold flash, or electroless nickel - a nickel-phosphorus deposit from a hypophosphite bath - followed by gold. The electroless route was standard in the semiconductor industry of the era and was how the die-attached gold on a hybrid IC was built.

###### AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel `metal.stainless.304`

The iron-chromium-nickel family, and a deliberate convergence point of three branches in this file. 304 is 18% chromium, 8% nickel, the balance iron - austenitic, non-magnetic, non-hardenable. 430 is 16-18% chromium with no nickel - ferritic, magnetic, and cheap. Both are made the way any steel is made: blast furnace for the iron, then a stainless steelmaking step that decarburises in an argon-oxygen decarburisation vessel, and the key is that the melt must not pick up more than about 0.05% carbon or the chromium goes into carbide and the metal loses its corrosion resistance. Stainless is the audio jack shell, the shield cans, some of the chassis and any fastener. Its cost is driven almost entirely by the chromium and the nickel, which is why the nickel price crash of 1982-83 directly cheapened stainless.

###### Cold rolling, bright annealing and finishing of stainless `metal.stainless.cold-work` _(medium)_

Stainless is rolled and formed by the same equipment as mild steel - a Sendimir mill, a continuous annealing line, a Timesaver - but the tooling is different, because austenitic stainless work-hardens violently and needs much more force, and because a bright anneal must be carried out in hydrogen or in a vacuum to avoid discolouration and to avoid needing a thick pickling. A 1982 bright annealing line used hydrogen at 1000-1100 C with dewpoint control, which is a very refined piece of metallurgy for a machine that cost $395.

###### Where a 1982 C64's stainless actually is `metal.stainless.jewel-audio` _(low)_

Not much: the outer shell of the composite or RCA connector, the shield cans over the analogue sections, some of the tuner and modulator housings, the hinge hardware, and any stainless fastener. In practice much of what looks like stainless in 1982 consumer electronics was nickel-chrome electroplated or tin-plated mild steel, because solid 304 in a thin stamping cost several times what a plating operation cost. The distinction matters and cannot be settled without the part.

###### The Siemens fluidised-bed reactor `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.reactor`

A steel vessel with a perforated plate, fluidised with purified hydrogen, into which trichlorosilane vapour is injected alongside seed silicon particles. On the hot (silicon-coated) walls the reaction deposits polycrystalline silicon as fine powder; the powder falls out the bottom. Twenty to thirty tonnes of polysilicon a year came out of one reactor in this era.

###### Czochralski growth of the single crystal `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz`

The polysilicon powder is melted with a dopant in a silica crucible at about 1420 C, just above the silicon melting point of 1414 C. A small seed crystal on a puller is dipped in and withdrawn at 1-3 mm/min, rotating. Silicon solidifies on the seed in the melt's lattice, producing a slowly tapering cylinder of near-perfect single crystal called a boule. Arsenic or phosphorus is added to set the wafer's conductivity type and resistivity.

###### The Czochralski puller `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.puller`

A tall crystal-growth machine: a graphite-heated crucible with a rotating seed shaft, a slurry of dopant, an argon atmosphere over the melt, and a diameter-control algorithm watching the melt's edge by laser/weight. It is the machine that turns dirty powder into the perfect single crystal every silicon chip in the world is cut from.

###### Argon `facility.argon`

Argon is not made; it is separated out. It is the third component of air and comes off the top of the ASU's nitrogen column, either as an argon-nitrogen mixture from a simple unit or as 99.99% pure from a dedicated argon column. Most 1980s plants bought it by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant.

###### Argon recovery column `facility.argon.argon-column`

A second, smaller column that separates the nitrogen-argon mixture from the top of the nitrogen column into pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops. Installed when the oxygen plant needed the argon value or the customer paid for it - usually in a semiconductor or welding-wire plant, not in a steelworks.

###### Where argon actually went in 1983 `facility.argon.uses`

TIG welding of the sheet metal and the transformer laminations, the inert blanket over the 1800 C silicon melt in the crystal puller, and - increasingly - argon sputter deposition of the aluminium interconnect in a fab.

###### The fused-silica crucible `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.crucible`

The melt is held in a crucible of fused quartz - amorphous silicon dioxide - because quartz melts above 1600 C and, crucially, because it introduces only oxygen and silicon, both harmless in the crystal, unlike a metal or nitride crucible. The crucible itself is made by flame-fusing pure silica in a hydrogen-oxygen flame, so even the vessel the silicon is melted in comes from the same quartz as the metallurgical silicon.

                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### The seed crystal `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.cz.seed`

A small, already-perfect single crystal - usually a few mm across and a few cm long - lowered into the melt to start the growth. Everything that follows inherits its lattice. The seed was itself cut from an earlier boule, so this is a lineage that goes back, crystal generation by crystal generation, to the first Ingot in 1950s.

###### Sawing the boule into wafers `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw`

The boule is ground to mark where each wafer will be, then an idling saw - a thin rotating diamond-impregnated steel blade - cuts it, losing up to a millimetre of silicon kerf per cut. A 100 mm boule gave roughly 300 wafers per metre of ingot. Wafers were then lapped flat and parallel, and finally polished mirror-bright.

###### Industrial diamond `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.saw.diamond`

The abrasive in the saw blade, the scribe and the CMP slurry. Synthesised from graphite under high pressure and temperature in a diamond press, or mined. Graphite itself is carbon, from coal or petroleum coke - another carbon branch off the crude.

###### Lapping and edge-rounding `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap`

The wafers are lapped against each other in a slurry to take the bow out of the sawn surface and make them parallel to within microns, then the sharp sawn edge is rounded off with a diamond wheel. The rounded edge is what stops the wafer cracking when it is chucked onto the probe stage and spun through the photolithography coater.

###### Lapping slurry `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.lap.slurry` _(medium)_

A slurry of loose diamond or alumina grit in water, to grind the wafer flat. The abrasive is the same industrial mineral as the blade.

###### Final polish `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polish`

A final, slow, chemically-assisted polish takes the lapped surface to a mirror finish, because every speck of damage left on the surface becomes a defect that kills transistors. A sacrificial thermal oxide is then grown on the polished surface and stripped, which anneals the last of the surface damage - the 'getter' that heals the crystal's outermost lattice layer.

###### 3-inch and 4-inch wafers in 1983 `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.sizes` _(medium)_

Standard wafer diameters in 1983 were 3 inches (75 mm) and 4 inches (100 mm); 5-inch (125 mm) was arriving at the leading-edge logic and memory lines. A 4-inch wafer holds roughly 1,500-3,000 of the small dies that a 14-pin logic part becomes, depending on die size and the edge exclusion the process could hold.

###### Die-per-wafer economics `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.diecount` _(medium)_

The economics of a merchant logic wafer rest entirely on this number: how many working dies of one part number come off a wafer. Multiply by yield, multiply by the cost of the wafer, divide by the dies, and you have the die cost - which for a 74LS gate is dominated not by the wafer but by testing, packaging and the fixed cost of the masks and the fab, amortised over millions of gates.

###### Epitaxial growth of the collector `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi`

The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.

###### The horizontal epitaxial reactor `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor`

A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.

              - *Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N* `metal.silica.tcs` *(seen above)*
###### Trichloroethylene-trichlorosilane vapour mix (not HCl) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.hcl`

The epitaxial gas box fed a mixture of silane or trichlorosilane in hydrogen, with dopant gas added for conductivity. Trichlorosilane is the workhorse chlorosilane of the period; silicon tetrachloride was the older, hotter source. The hydrogen carrier is dry and ultra-pure.

                - *Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N* `metal.silica.tcs` *(seen above)*
###### Phosphine (PH3) for the n-type epilayer `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine`

The dopant gas for the n-type collector and for the n+ isolation and emitter diffusions. A few parts per million of phosphine in the hydrogen carrier sets the resistivity. Phosphine itself is made by reacting phosphoric acid (from phosphate rock) or elemental phosphorus with hydrogen, or by burning phosphorus vapour.

###### Elemental phosphorus from phosphate rock `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.phosphorus`

White phosphorus was produced by carbothermic reduction of calcium phosphate (apatite) with coke and silica in an electric furnace, then condensed to a waxy solid. Most phosphine was made by reacting this phosphorus with hydrogen or by hydrolysing phosphorus trichloride made from it.

###### Phosphate rock (apatite) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.phosphorus.phosphate`

Calcium phosphate ore, mainly from Florida, Morocco, Senegal and China. Reduced in an electric furnace with coke and silica to make white phosphorus, which is the only practical high-purity source of the phosphorus dopant.

###### Arsine (AsH3) - the shallow-diffusion dopant `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine`

A very shallow-diffusing dopant, used where a junction must stop just below a thin gate oxide without drifting deeper in the subsequent hot steps. Arsenic replaced antimony for this job as the physics improved. Arcsine came from arsenic trioxide (from roasting arsenic-bearing ores) plus hydrogen.

###### Arsenic trioxide from ore roasting `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine.arsenic`

Arsenic occurs in some copper and lead ores as arsenide. Roasting the concentrate oxidises the arsenic to arsenic trioxide fume, which is captured and reduced to elemental arsenic, then combined with hydrogen to give arsine.

###### Growth of the field oxide `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation`

Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

###### The oxidation furnace `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furnace`

A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

###### Deionised steam for the furnace `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam`

Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange.

                - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Fused quartz tube and boat `mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quartz`

The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

                - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Collector-collector isolation `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation`

The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.

###### Diffusion into the window `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffusion`

The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

                - *Phosphine (PH3) for the n-type epilayer* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine` *(seen above)*
###### Guard rings around the islands `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guardring`

A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.

###### What a guard ring physically is `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guardring.how`

Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.

###### Dielectric isolation (the alternative, and Fairchild's route) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.dielectric` _(medium)_

Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.

                - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trench`

For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.

###### The base diffusion `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base`

A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

###### Boron as the p dopant `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron`

Boron came from a thin deposited glass or oxide doped with boron (B2O3, often as diborane gas) spun onto the wafer and driven in. It was the standard p-dopant for base diffusions throughout the era.

###### Diborane (B2H6) gas `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.diborane`

Boron hydride gas used as a diffusion or implantation source. It is pyrophoric and toxic, and shipped and handled in sealed steel cylinders under inert gas.

###### Borax / boron oxide source `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.borax` _(medium)_

For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a BN wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas.

###### The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter` _(medium)_

The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.

              - *Arsine (AsH3) - the shallow-diffusion dopant* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.arsine` *(seen above)*
###### The gold in the emitter `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold` _(medium)_

A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.

###### Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts `metal.gold`

A C64 contains perhaps 0.2-1 g of gold. It is the flash on the edge-connector fingers, the plating on the IC leads, the ball or wedge bond from the die pad to the package, and the contacts in the 'jewel' switch mechanisms. Gold is the only metal that does not tarnish and does not form an insulating oxide, which is the entire reason it is used where an electrical contact has to survive years untouched. All of that gold is refined to 99.99% from an ore averaging a few grams per tonne, and in 1982 essentially all of it came out of a cyanide leach.

###### Low-grade gold ore (0.5-5 g/t) `metal.gold.ore`

Gold at a few parts per million is not visible and not dense in a hand specimen - it is in the ore as discrete grains, often only microns across, or in tellurides. Most of it is in quartz veins, often with sulfides. The 1982 world had two completely different industries: the deep underground Witwatersrand, where a 15 cm face of reef at 10-40 g/t gave 100,000 tonnes a day through mills, and the Carlin trend and the Nevada heap leaches, where 0.5-2 g/t in oxide rock was stacked in 10 m heaps and leached in place. The heap leach was a genuine 1970s invention and by 1982 it had become a third of Nevada's production.

###### Heap leaching with cyanide, 10 m pads `metal.gold.heap-leach`

Run-of-mine ore, after a cyanide spray test, is crushed to a few centimetres and stacked in 100,000-tonne heaps on an impermeable pad. It is flooded with 0.02-0.05% NaCN solution, allowed to percolate for 30-60 days, and then drained and sprayed again. The pregnant solution is sent through a carbon bed and then an electrowinning cell. A heap-leach pad is a piece of civil engineering first and a chemical plant second: the entire economics depend on the liner holding and the pad draining properly, and the cyanide inventory on a large heap is the largest single cyanide hazard in mining. After the leach the cyanide is destroyed with lime and ferrous sulphate and the pad is detoxified before closure.

###### Sodium cyanide from natural gas `metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis`

Cyanide is an industrial chemical, not a mined material, and its feedstock is the same natural gas that makes hydrogen cyanide for acrylonitrile. The Andrussow process is the cheap one: natural gas plus ammonia plus oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at 900-1000 C gives hydrogen cyanide, which is absorbed in caustic to give sodium cyanide. So the cyanide that leaches the gold that plates the connector comes out of an ammonia-and-air reactor fed with methane.

###### Ammonia from natural gas or coal `metal.cyanide-precursor` _(medium)_

The leaf of this branch is natural gas and air. The methane goes into a reformer, the hydrogen and nitrogen out are Haber-Bosch'd at 400-500 C and 200-300 bar over a promoted iron catalyst to ammonia, and the ammonia goes into the Andrussow reactor. So the gold in the C64's edge connector traces, through cyanide, to a gas field and an air separation unit.

###### The Haber-Bosch iron catalyst from iron ore `metal.habers-catalyst` _(medium)_

The hydrogen in the cyanide comes from ammonia, and the ammonia's Haber-Bosch reaction runs over a promoted iron catalyst made from magnetite or from mill scale. So the cyanide that leaches the gold, and the chlorine that makes the hydrochloric acid, and the aluminium in the case all hang off an iron-ore-derived catalyst in a gas works. This is the last of the deliberate cross-branch loops in this file, and it is a real one: the Haber-Bosch catalyst is a 1980s version of the same magnetite that this tree mines for steel.

###### Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route `metal.magnetite`

The other main ore. Magnetite is magnetic, so it can be separated from a low-grade run of rock by magnetic separation, and that changes the economics of the whole business. The Mesabi taconite of Minnesota at 25-32% Fe is ground to 30-45 um and concentrated to 65-70% Fe pellets on a concentrator with a 3 m diameter separator. Krivoy Rog and the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly in the Soviet Union are magnetite districts at 55-65%, worked down to 100 m depths with sublevel stoping. The magnetite is also roasted in a fluidised bed to hematite before magnetic separation, or sintered and reduced.

###### Magnetic separation and the taconite concentrator `metal.magnetite.separators` _(medium)_

The separator is a rotating drum 1-2.5 m in diameter with a 4-10 pole magnet of 400-1,200 gauss at the drum surface, or a high-gradient can of ferrite pole pieces that achieves 10,000-20,000 gauss on the tips. Slurry flows past and the magnetic grains are held to the drum and carried around until they fall off the other side. With the magnetoferrite in the drum the recovery of a 30-45 um magnetite grain is above 95%. A taconite concentrator at 20-40 Mt a year is one of the largest single streams of water and solids in the world, and the tailings are a billion-tonne deposit in their own right.

###### Ferrite magnets in the separator `metal.magnetite.ferrite-magnets` _(medium)_

A short and important cross-link: the permanent magnet inside a magnetic separator is a ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite, sintered like the power ferrites but with a different composition and without the permeability requirement. So the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace contains ferrite magnets, and the ferrite branch of this file is the same powder metallurgy.

###### Deep underground magnetite mining `metal.magnetite.underground`

The Soviet iron ore industry - Krivoy Rog, the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, and the Khibiny - mined massive magnetite bodies at 300-1000 m with sublevel stoping, sublevel caving and room-and-pillar, on a scale with no real comparison anywhere else. The magnetite ore was magnetic enough that the mine was lit by the ore's own remanence in the early shafts. It is included to mark that the iron chain has two completely different mining geometries: a 300 m wide surface pit in Western Australia, and a 100 m thick tabular body a kilometre down in Ukraine.

###### Fluidised-bed roasting of magnetite concentrate `metal.magnetite.roasting` _(medium)_

The Krivoy Rog and Finnish magnetite concentrates were roasted before magnetic separation and before the blast furnace, because a magnetite concentrate that has been oxidised to hematite sinter is far easier to reduce - hematite is the reducible oxide, magnetite is not. A fluidised bed of concentrate with a magnetite-gangue composition can be held at 700-800 C indefinitely without sintering, and it is the only economical way to oxidise a hundred thousand tonnes of fine concentrate. The plant is a tall rectangular refractory-lined box with a bed of nozzles on the floor and water-cooled walls, and its throughput is enormous.

###### Oxide iron pellets and the direct reduction route `metal.magnetite.speciality` _(medium)_

A different branch of the same ore: magnetite concentrate is the only ore that can be reduced to sponge iron directly, without coke, by a hydrogen-nitrogen mixture at 1100-1200 C in a shaft furnace. That is the MIDOR and HYL processes, which by 1982 were the strategic reserve of the steel industry in the oil shock years - a few per cent of world steel but a hedge, and the reason a Soviet or Brazilian or Venezuelan integrated steelworks would spend a decade building an ore-based direct-reduction plant. It is also the only ore that can be shipped as a pellet and reduced at a distant site without smelting.

###### Witwatersrand underground gold mining `metal.gold.wits-mine`

The other end of the industry. A 15 cm to 3 m band of gold-bearing conglomerate called 'the reef' lies at 1000-6000 m below the Witwatersrand, and from 1886 to 1982 the industry sank shafts and drove long decline haulages and ventilation and cooling galleries into it. Ventilation was the limiting factor: rock at 3000 m is at 40-50 C because of the geothermal gradient and because the rock is 3-6 C warmer than surface, so a mine 4 km deep needed refrigeration and a shaft fan development that took hours to boost air through the raises. Each shift broke perhaps 30,000 tonnes of reef in the mine and treated 100,000 tonnes in the plant, so the metallurgy was crushing a very hard quartzite and recovering maybe 60-70% of a 10-40 g/t ore.

###### Witwatersrand gold reef conglomerate `metal.gold.reef`

The leaf: a 2.9 billion year old quartzite with rounded pebbles of quartz and jasper in a fine matrix - a fossil beach. The gold is in the matrix, as discrete grains a few microns across, and the deepest part of the deposit has the highest grade because it is the oldest and the most distal. It is one of the largest gold concentrations ever formed and it is a sediment.

###### The uraninite in the Witwatersrand reef `metal.gold.uraninite` _(medium)_

The gold reef is also the world's largest gold-uranium conglomerate, and the same reef that was being mined for gold was being mined for uranium by a separate set of shafts from the 1950s onwards. The uraninite is present as discrete grains on the carbon seams, and it recovers in the gold plant's gravity circuits and in the tailings retreatment plants. So the uranium in the C64's power supply - in a 1982 it might have been a South African or Canadian utility's grid, but the fuel cycle is the same one - began in the same bed as the gold on the edge connectors. It is the single best example in this tree of one layer of rock supplying two unrelated metals.

###### Cyanide leaching of gold ore at pH 10-11 `metal.gold.cyanide-leach`

The reaction is 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH, and it needs three things: cyanide, lime to hold the pH at 10-11 so the cyanide does not protonate into deadly hydrogen cyanide gas, and dissolved oxygen. The pulp - ground ore plus lime, at 25-50% solids by mass - is agitated in an aerated pachuca tank or a Dorr agitator for 12-48 hours. The design variables are all about cyanide consumption, most of which is not gold dissolving but the cyanide reacting with the copper, iron and zinc minerals in the ore. In 1982 the plant that won was the one that kept the concentration as low as possible and the oxygen pressure as high as possible, which is the lesson of the 1986 Carbonin/Small's Pouso Bello mine disaster in Brazil, where 5-6 tonnes of cyanide went into the environment through a tailings dam failure and poisoned a river.

###### Pachuca tank and the Dorr agitator `metal.gold.pachuca` _(medium)_

The 1982 standard leach vessel was either a Pachuca tank - a tall cylindrical tank with a cone at the bottom and a compressed-air rising pipe that boils the pulp like a carbonated drink - or a Dorr agitator, a vertical tank with a rotating central shaft and radial arms and baffles. A typical circuit was 4-8 tanks of 30-60 m diameter in series, 6 m deep, with the air line serving as both the agitator and the oxygen supply. Life before the mid-1980s the industry moved to Dorr thickeners and to the large rectangular Dorr-Oliver leach tanks.

###### Carbon-in-pulp and activated carbon adsorption `metal.gold.cip`

Gold is present in the pregnant solution as the cyanide complex at only about 1 mg/L, far too dilute to precipitate or to recover directly. The industry fix is adsorption onto activated carbon: the slurry after leaching goes through a bank of 4-8 tall columns of 1.5-3 mm coconut-shell carbon, which takes up the gold. In carbon-in-pulp the carbon is instead added directly to the leach tanks and separated by a static or centrifugal screen. The carbon is then stripped in a hot caustic solution - with a few parts in a million of cyanide and, from the late 1970s, acetonitrile, which is what makes the strip efficient - and the gold is electrowon off a lead or stainless cathode, or smelted.

###### Activated carbon from coconut shell `metal.activated-carbon` _(medium)_

The adsorbent is a botanical product, not a mineral: coconut or palm-kernel shell, or coal, carbonised at 500-900 C and steam-activated at 800-1000 C until the pore volume is about half the material's bulk volume. The pore structure is what holds the gold cyanide. So the carbon in the carbon-in-pulp column is a plantation or coal-mill product, and by the 1980s activated carbon was becoming an industrial commodity in its own right.

###### Hard coal and petroleum coke as activated carbon feed `metal.activated-carbon.coal` _(medium)_

By 1982 the industry was moving off coconut shell, which had become scarce and expensive as the plastics and activated-carbon markets grew, onto hard coal and - as the process matured - onto delayed petroleum coke, which has the right isotropic pore structure and essentially no ash. The activation is the same: carbonise, then blow steam at 800-1000 C to burn out the carbon and open the pores, giving a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. So the carbon in a carbon-in-pulp gold plant in the 1980s was often made from the same coke as the aluminium anode and the coke battery electrode, which is one of the more unexpected places this tree's carbon converges.

###### Steam activation at 800-1000 C `metal.steam-activation` _(medium)_

The step that makes charcoal into activated carbon. A bed of coke or coal is held at 800-1000 C while steam and carbon dioxide are passed over it, and the gas burns the carbon away, opening a pore structure with a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. The rate of the burn is the whole process: too fast and the structure collapses, too slow and the pores are too small to admit the gold cyanide complex. The gold is adsorbed as the ion-pair Au(CN)2- at the carbon surface, so the carbon's chemistry is an ion-exchange chemistry rather than a physical adsorption, which is why the carbon has to be chemically clean and why it has to be regenerated before its capacity falls too far.

###### Miller chlorination and the Aubure process `metal.gold.miller`

The refinery end. Gold doré - typically 90-95% gold with 5-10% silver - is fluxed with borax and litharge and blown with chlorine gas in an MRL (Mineral Resources Limited) chlorinator, heated by a propane torch, for 1-3 hours. The chlorine dissolves the gold as AuCl3 and the silver as AgCl, and the silver chloride precipitates as a crust. The gold is then stripped of the silver by the Aubure process - a hot parting - which reduces the silver chloride with wet wood chips and wet clay, a piece of technology that had not changed since the Middle Ages: the organic matter reduces the AgCl to metallic silver. What is left is gold at 99.5-99.9%, which is then electrorefined to 99.99% or cast directly into an anode.

###### Electrolytic refining of gold to 99.99% `metal.gold.electrorefining`

The Doré is cast into anodes and dissolved in an aqueous solution of gold chloride in hydrochloric acid at 50-60 C. The electrolyte is the Wohlwill process electrolyte, with a little silver nitrate added to make the silver chloride stay solid and drop out. Gold plates onto a pure gold or platinum cathode at 99.99% and the whole refinery runs at 2-5 V with a very high current efficiency. Every gold refinery in the world in 1982 used the Wohlwill process and it is essentially unchanged today.

###### Dore melting and the crucible `metal.gold.dore-melting` _(medium)_
