Before the gold can be chlorinated it has to be melted, and the doré - whatever mixture of gold and silver the refinery is holding - is melted with a little borax and litharge in a clay or graphite crucible to 1000-1200 C and poured into a dore ingot weighing 20-50 kg. The litharge is what makes the dore pour cleanly, because it fluxes the oxide skin; it also means a little lead comes along, which is harmless because the next step takes it out. The dore is weighed and assayed, and that assay is the number on which the refinery is paid for the month's production.

###### Refined gold anode, 99.99%, and the plated flash `metal.gold.ingot`

The gold that reaches the electronics industry is 99.99% minimum, as a rolled sheet or an anode, and it is used in three ways. Flash plating for connector fingers and IC leads: the gold is dissolved in a cyanide gold bath - typically a gold cyanide, potassium cyanide, gold hydroxide bath at 0.5-2 g/L gold - and deposited on the nickel underplate at 0.1-1 A/dm2 for a few seconds, giving 0.05-0.25 um. Wire bonding: 15-50 um pure gold wire, drawn through diamond dies like copper, is welded from the die pad to the package lead with a thermosonic bonder. And sputtering: thin film resistors and the gold metallisation on some hybrid ICs were gold, sputtered from a cathode.

###### Gold wire bonding of the die `metal.gold.wire-bonding`

Each die has to be electrically connected to the package. The 1982 method was wire bonding: a 25 um gold or aluminium wire is threaded through a ceramic or carbide capillary, the tip is melted by a discharge or by a heated work holder, and the first weld is made to the die's aluminium pad. The wire is then run out and the second weld is made to the package bond pad, and the wire is cut. A 40-pin chip has 80 of these welds per package, each under a milligram of gold, and the whole thing happens a thousand times a minute. Aluminium bonding wire was already displacing gold on most logic parts by 1982 for cost reasons, but gold remained the default for anything requiring a conductive epoxy or a eutectic die attach.

###### Gold-plated contacts: the edge connector and the switches `metal.gold.contact-jewel` _(medium)_

Two very different gold contacts in the C64. The 62-way edge connector at the rear has gold-flashed fingers - a 35 um copper-alloy finger with 0.1-0.5 um of gold and a nickel underplate, inserted in the board by a wipe in the card guides. The keyboard and the rocker switches use either gold-plated copper-alloy leaf springs or, in the better keys, solid silver or silver-alloy contacts. The gold flash on the edge connector is the only place where gold must survive thousands of insertions, and it does so because the nickel underplate stops the copper from diffusing into the gold and the gold itself never oxidises.

###### Polysilicon emitter (a later refinement) `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.polysilicon` _(medium)_

Instead of diffusing the emitter through a mask, a thin polysilicon film is deposited, doped with arsenic, patterned to define the emitter, and then pushed. The arsenic is confined by the polysilicon walls so the emitter comes out shallower and more uniform, and the emitter area - which sets the emitter resistance - is set by the same mask as the metal that contacts it. This self-aligned polysilicon emitter was one of the last big improvements to the classical bipolar process before CMOS took the business.

###### The Schottky clamp - the S in LS `mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky`

In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.

###### Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion `metal.aluminum`

Where the C64's aluminium comes from. Bauxite is dug, digested in caustic soda to alumina, and electrolysed in molten cryolite to 99.7% metal - about 13,000-17,000 kWh per tonne, the largest single industrial electricity draw anywhere in this tree. The ingot is then DC-cast to a rolling ingot and rolled down to 6-25 um foil for the electrolytic capacitors in the power supply, to sheet for the case and shield cans, and extruded for the heat sinks. Note that the capacitor foil and the plain foil are different jobs for the same rolling mill.

###### Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5% Al2O3 `metal.alumina`

A white, sandy, hygroscopic powder delivered to the smelter in railcars or 1-2 t bags. The contract is brutal: 99.5% Al2O3 minimum, loss on ignition below about 1%, total iron below 0.02%, because every gram of iron that reaches the cell ends up in the metal and the ingot stops being 99.7%. In 1982 this was a global commodity with about a dozen producers - Alcoa, Alcan, Kaiser, Norsk Hydro, Sumitomo, and the Australian and Jamaican national producers. This is the deliberate convergence point for the bauxite and the pot branch: both hang off it.

###### Bauxite (hydrated alumina ore) `metal.bauxite`

A soft, red-brown, pisolitic or clayey laterite, 45-60% Al2O3, still essentially the ore it was before anybody wanted it. Ore below about 180 C of gibbsite digest easily at low temperature and is called low-temperature bauxite; ore with diaspore and boehmite needs 240-280 C and is called high-temperature bauxite, which costs much more in steam. The three great districts in 1982 were Boke and Kindia in Guinea, the Weipa and Gove platforms in northern Australia, and the Clarendon and Saint Ann parishes in Jamaica.

###### Open-cast bauxite mine with dragline `metal.bauxite.mine`

Strip mining on a 10-20 m bench height, with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline stripping 10-50 m of overburden and then a bench of bauxite perhaps only 3-6 m thick. The dragline is the point: it digs the bauxite, swings and dumps it onto a ramp, and strips the next strip of cover, all in one machine. Loading is by conveyor, almost never by truck. The Weipa and Gove operations were built this way.

###### Lateritic bauxite profile `metal.bauxite.laterite`

The leaf: a 3-12 m pisolitic blanket of iron-stained bauxite nodules sitting on a Cretaceous or Tertiary lateritic surface above a kaolinitic clay. Guinea's deposits are the classic tropical pisolite; the Australian Weipa and Gove ores are flat-lying terrace deposits on Cretaceous sediments. Either way the rock outcrops at the surface and is dug, not tunnelled.

###### The kaolinite and gibbsite beneath the bauxite `metal.bauxite.kaolinite`

The leaf of the aluminium branch, and the reason the alumina process exists in the form it does. The economic bauxite is a 3-12 m blanket of iron-stained nodules sitting directly on kaolinite clay, and the kaolinite is the reactive silica that has to be neutralised by lime or washed out. Below that is the saprolite, the partly-weathered parent rock. So the aluminium in a C64 case began as an oxide that precipitated in a tropical weathering profile above a clay, on top of Cretaceous or Tertiary sediment, and the silica problem is a mineralogical fact about the same profile rather than an impurity someone failed to remove.

###### The creek and the pisolite `metal.bauxite.creek-wash` _(medium)_

The last leaf of the aluminium branch. In the Weipa and Gove deposits on the Cretaceous laterite surface, bauxite is dug in the wet season and the clay is washed out of it in a creek: a 200 m long, 30 m wide sluice excavated along the edge of the terrace, into which the bauxite is tipped and a stream of water is run, and the light clay washes away over a long distance while the pisolitic bauxite nodules, 5-50 mm and iron-stained, stay behind and are recovered by hand or by a mechanical rake. It is a 1980s technology on a Cretaceous rock surface in tropical Queensland, and it is the reason those deposits look the way they do.

###### The Cretaceous laterite surface `metal.laterite-terrace`

The leaf, geologically: a flat, deeply weathered surface on Cretaceous sandstone where a tropical lateritic profile has developed over tens of millions of years, with a bauxite horizon at the top, kaolinite below it, and the saprolite and fresh rock beneath. The flatness is the point - it is why the pits are cheap and the ore is shallow - and it is a direct consequence of the rock type and of the extraordinarily long, warm, wet chemical weathering that made it.

###### Bauxite crushing, washing and drying `metal.bauxite.beneficiation` _(medium)_

The Bayer plant does not want a 300 mm boulder and it certainly does not want the clay. The run-of-mine ore is crushed in a gyratory or a jaw crusher to 25-50 mm, and then - in the wet-grinding route that became standard for high-temperature bauxite - it is ground in a ball mill in a rod or a wet scrubber to a slurry, and that slurry is screened and washed to remove the clay, which is called 'desilication by attrition washing'. The under-0.5 mm clay is discarded as tailings, and it is often 15-30% of the mass. What goes into the digestor is a 40-50% solids slurry of 25-50 mm lumps with the reactive silica taken out, and the moisture matters because every kilo of water into the autoclave is a kilo of steam wasted.

###### Bayer process `metal.bayer`

A 110-year-old caustic-leach purification that every tonne of aluminium still goes through. Five steps: crush and wash, digest in caustic at pressure, clarify and throw away the red mud, cool and precipitate pure aluminium hydroxide, calcine to alumina. It works because the alumina in bauxite is amphoteric - it dissolves in hot caustic as sodium aluminate - while the iron and titanium oxides are not, and silica is neutralised by lime into a harmless calcium silicate.

###### Caustic digestion in autoclaves `metal.bayer.digestion`

Bauxite slurry and 150-300 g/L free caustic (as Na2O) are charged into stirred autoclaves and held at temperature for 30-90 minutes. The alumina dissolves as NaAl(OH)4; the iron oxide stays as a red slurry. Older low-temperature plants used a bank of horizontal autoclaves with indirect steam heating; high-temperature plants used vertical autoclaves. The pressure was only 5-15 bar because the vessel was not a modern high-pressure autoclave but a horizontal drum with a vapour space.

###### Reactive silica and the lime reaction `metal.bayer.desilication` _(medium)_

The killer impurity in bauxite is reactive silica - kaolinite clay and opal - which dissolves in the caustic and then reacts with aluminate to form a non-redissolving kaolinite-nepheline hydrate that permanently traps alumina. Two defences. In low-temperature digestion the clay is left undissolved by keeping the caustic concentration high. In high-temperature digestion the reactive silica dissolves, so lime is added and the silica is converted to hydrogrossite; the liquor is then given a short holding period during which the silica precipitates harmlessly. Every tonne of bauxite eats some caustic and some tens of kilos of lime that never come back.

###### Clarification and the red mud dam `metal.bayer.clarification`

The digested slurry is diluted with process water, cooled, and settled in a bank of gravity settlers with mechanical rakes; the red mud bottoms out and is pumped to the mud dam. A large plant produces 100-150 tonnes of red mud per tonne of alumina, which is why every alumina refinery has a mud dam engineered like a tailings facility.

###### Red mud (bauxite residue) `metal.red-mud`

A caustic, red, kaolin-rich sludge, typically 2.5-6 mol/L free NaOH, containing essentially all the iron, titanium and silica from the ore. A large refinery produces 100-150 tonnes of it per tonne of alumina. In 1982 the industry standard for handling it was to build a dam and pump it in; the search for a use was real academic work with no commercial outcome. Successful commercial red-mud use at scale did not arrive until the 2000s and later, so nothing in a 1982 C64 contains it.

###### Precipitation of Al(OH)3 from cooled liquor `metal.bayer.precipitation`

The clear caustic aluminate solution is cooled from 100-110 C to 60-80 C and seeded with a few grams per litre of finely ground aluminium hydroxide already in the plant. The seed grows into the supersaturated solution as a hexagonal-plate alumina trihydrate over 24-48 hours, and the mud is filtered and washed. Washing matters twice over: to remove the caustic that would otherwise attack the kiln, and to recover the soda. The mother liquor goes back to digestion, and this recycle loop is what makes the caustic consumption manageable at all.

###### Rotary vacuum filtration and counter-current washing `metal.bayer.filter` _(medium)_

The hydrate is filtered on a rotating vacuum drum with cloth- or paper-covered segments, then washed on a multi-stage counter-current filter. By the time the wash water reaches the pregnant liquor the caustic is essentially recovered, so the caustic circuit closes to better than 95%. This single piece of equipment is why alumina refining has the caustic efficiency it does.

###### Calcination of alumina trihydrate at 1000-1100 C `metal.bayer.calcination`

The hydrate goes into a rotary kiln or, more often by 1982, a fluidised-bed calciner, and at 1000-1100 C it gives off its water of crystallisation and recrystallises from gamma through theta to alpha alumina. Alpha alumina is the hard, insoluble, spark-resistant form that will dissolve in cryolite. The rotary kiln burns 400-600 kg of fuel oil or gas equivalent per tonne of alumina and emits a lot of carbon dioxide; the fluidised bed is more efficient and was being adopted through the 1980s.

###### Fluidised-bed calciner `metal.bayer.calciner`

Hot gas from a multi-flash evaporator is blown through a bed of alumina hydrate on a distributor of alloy nozzles, holding the bed fluid at 1000-1100 C by balancing gas throughput against feed rate. The bed fluidises like a boiling liquid and every grain sees the same temperature, which is exactly why the alpha alumina comes out with a tight particle-size distribution. The 1980s smelter-grade alumina market effectively standardised on this machine.

###### Primary aluminium ingot, 99.7% `metal.aluminum.ingot`

The metal itself, and the deliberate convergence point of the electrolysis branch and the rolling branch. Tapped from the pot every 24-48 hours, brought up to about 720 C, filtered to remove the entrained alumina and metal droplets, alloyed if the customer wants it, and cast. In 1982 the standard product was the 20-25 kg P1020 ingot, or the 500 kg or 1.5 t minimum-content ingot that newer smelters preferred, 99.70% minimum aluminium with iron and silicon the main impurities. Rolling ingots for the foil mills were a different shape entirely - see the foil branch.

###### Hall-Heroult electrolysis of alumina in cryolite `metal.hall-heroult`

The cell is a steel shell the size of a bathtub lined with carbon, containing 300-500 t of molten cryolite at 950-970 C. Alumina dissolves in the melt and is reduced at a carbon cathode; current passes through the anodes, where the oxygen from the alumina burns the carbon away and makes carbon dioxide. The metal pools on the floor and is tapped every day or two. A pot takes 3-6 V at 100-200 kA, which is why a 200,000 t/year smelter is also a 2-3 GW power station.

###### Carbon pot lining and the cathodic block `metal.hall-heroult.pot-lining`

The steel shell is lined first with refractory brick, then with a monolithic carbon lining about 400-600 mm thick made of calcined coke, graphite and hot pitch, rammed in place. A block lining of graphitised carbon blocks is better and was common in newer cells. The lining is deliberately cathodic: the aluminium that seeps into the pores becomes a cathode of itself, and when the cell is finally relined after 3-8 years the spent lining is leached for the metal it swallowed.

###### Alumina dredges and the alumina crust `metal.hall-heroult.alumina-dredge` _(medium)_

Alumina fed into the pot floats and solidifies into a chilled crust on the bath surface, which is far more stable than loose powder. Machines called dredges or skimmers break holes in this crust and feed alumina down them at a controlled rate; the classic 1980 design was the dual-feed with pneumatic runners. The holes are also where carbon dust from the anode is skimmed off. A floating crust is good for the pot but insulates the bath, so the balance between a thick stable crust and a cool cell is the operator's whole job.

###### Aluminium dross and the skimmings `metal.hall-heroult.dross` _(medium)_

Two or three tonnes of dross and sludge per pot per year: oxide, carbon, and aluminium that never reached the cathode. Because aluminium dross burns spectacularly it must be handled under cover, and the smelter had a dross furnace to burn out the aluminium and get it back. The recovered metal is dirty and low grade, and in 1982 it went straight back into the pot - a small but real recycling loop, since remelted aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy of primary metal.

###### Aluminium foil, 6-25 um, for capacitors `metal.aluminum.foil`

The C64's power supply is full of electrolytic capacitors, and every one of them is an aluminium foil sandwich: a thin cathode foil wound with a thicker anode foil and a paper separator soaked in electrolyte. Making 6 um foil is a genuinely hard rolling problem - at that gauge the metal is thinner than the oxide skin that forms on it, so the rolls and the housekeeping are the whole technology. This is a deliberate convergence node: the foil branch, the anode-foil etch branch and the rolling-mill branch all hang off it.

###### DC casting to a rolling ingot `metal.aluminum.dc-casting`

Molten aluminium at 700-750 C is poured into a steel mould that is being withdrawn by a hydraulic jack at a controlled few millimetres per second, so the metal freezes progressively behind a solidification front instead of all at once. The front is water-cooled and the emerging surface is squirted with a water mist to control its shape. This produces a big flat rectangular billet - typically 500-1000 mm wide, 600 mm thick, 5-25 t - with a fine equiaxed chill zone at the surface. Because it is a continuous process, a 1980s smelter and a modern one produce ingots of essentially identical shape.

###### Homogenising soak `metal.aluminum.homogenising` _(medium)_

A long hold in a gas- or electrically-heated pit furnace, typically 12-24 h at 450-600 C, whose only job is to let the alloying elements diffuse evenly. Without it a slab rolled on one edge behaves differently from the same slab rolled on the other and the foil tears. It also rounds the dendritic structure into equiaxed grains, which is what makes the achievable surface quality possible.

###### Hot rolling to 2-6 mm `metal.aluminum.hot-rolling`

The ingot is preheated to 300-400 C for wide slab or 450-550 C for narrower, thicker slab, and a reversing hot mill takes it down to 2-6 mm in one or two passes. Aluminium's rolling window is famously narrow - too cold and it tears at the edges, too hot and the ingot surface oxidises and scales - so a 1980s reversing hot mill had two or three stands and quite tight control. Scale is removed with hot descaling rolls, which presses a rolled-in oxide pattern into the surface that later helps the lubricant out of the pores.

###### Mill scale (iron-bearing aluminium oxide) `metal.aluminum.mill-scale` _(medium)_

Hot rolling oxidises the surface and the scale is knocked off by the descaling rolls. The chips that fall are a mix of alumina and iron oxides pulled in from the ingot surface, and they are the same material the ferroalloy and cement industries fought over - and, ground and magnetically separated, the raw iron oxide for soft ferrites. In 1982 most was dumped.

###### Cold rolling on a Sendimir high-roll mill `metal.aluminum.cold-rolling`

The 2-6 mm hot strip goes to a multi-high cold mill - a Sendimir 20-high or 24-high arrangement where a small work roll is backed by many intermediate rolls, giving the enormous rolling force needed at a small gap without a mill body the size of a building. The work rolls are hardened tool steel, 100-300 mm diameter, with a chasing finish that the operator keeps polished with emery and a lint-free cloth while the mill runs; at 6 um a single fingerprint is a visible defect. From 1980 onwards the Sendimir Z-High mill, which adds separate work-roll bending and flattening control, was the state of the art for aluminium foil width.

###### Aluminium rolling oil and the degreaser `metal.aluminum.rolling-oil` _(medium)_

Cold rolling of aluminium would tear without a lubricant: a water-in-oil emulsion or a neat mineral oil with fatty-acid esters, applied by nozzles at order 0.1-1 g/m2. The oil is what lets the gauge get down without the surface tearing, and it has to be removed afterwards - a few grams of oil left on capacitor foil ruin the capacitor, because the electrolyte chemistry and the oxide interface are that sensitive. Foil mills ran a dedicated degreasing line with naphtha or trichloroethane and a 200-300 C bake.

###### Fatty-acid esters from tallow and palm fat `metal.aluminum.rolling-oil.tallow` _(medium)_

The ester lubricants are made from animal or vegetable fats - tallow, palm, rapeseed - hydrolysed to fatty acids and re-esterified, on a paraffinic mineral base or a synthetic ester. This is the one place in the aluminium chain where biomass chemistry is genuinely load-bearing: an aluminium rolling lubricant is a soap-and-fatty-acid chemistry, not a petrochemical one. In 1982 tallow was still the dominant base; vegetable ester formulations grew through the 1990s.

###### Interstage and final annealing `metal.aluminum.foil-annealing` _(medium)_

Cold work leaves aluminium hard and full of stored energy, and a foil mill's rolls are too small to take that much reduction in one pass, so the strip is annealed between passes. A gas-fired or electric annealing furnace holds it at 200-400 C until the residual stress relaxes and the grains recrystallise. This is also where the rolling-direction texture that gives foil its foldability is reset, and where the elongated grain structure that capacitor foil later needs is created.

###### Foil slitting and rewinding `metal.aluminum.foil-slitting` _(medium)_

The 1-2 tonne coil of foil, 400-1300 mm wide, is slit into narrower coils for the capacitor maker and re-spooled. Slitter knives are tungsten-carbide or ceramic coated; a 6 um foil cut by a blunt knife simply tears. Slitting is also where a lot of the roll-to-roll handling difficulty lives, because a 6 um foil has almost no stiffness.

###### Etched anode foil for electrolytic capacitors `metal.aluminum.anode-foil` _(medium)_

The trick that made a decent electrolytic fit into an 8 mm diameter can. Plain anode foil etched in a hot acid bath grows an aluminium oxide/hydroxide layer over essentially the whole surface - up to about a hundred times the geometric area, and therefore a hundred times the capacitance per unit of volume. The 1980s etching chemistry was a chloride bath or, in the Japanese-dominated high-end market, a chlorate bath with acetic acid; the etch pits are then hardened with a phosphate or chromate formation treatment and the surface is impregnated with the electrolyte. This is a deliberate convergence node: the etch chemistry, the foil branch and the chromate chemistry of the plating branch all meet here.

###### The etch pit and the dielectric `metal.aluminum.foil-pore` _(low)_

The chloride ion eats its way into the foil along grain boundaries and leaves a field of round tunnels a few microns across. Oxidation inside those tunnels is what multiplies the area. The tunnels are then forced into a fixed geometry by a formation step that grows oxide in a controlled taper - the oxide at the mouth of the pit is the weakest point and it fails first if you get it wrong, which is why a 1982 capacitor that failed early usually failed as a short circuit and not as a leak.

###### Aluminium sheet: the case and the shields `metal.aluminum.sheet` _(medium)_

Two uses in a C64: the heat-sink and shield material, and the case itself. The Commodore breadbin case is an aluminium extrusion with a stove-enamel finish, and the internal shields and the modulator compartment are plain sheet. Cold-rolled 1050A or 3003 sheet at 0.3-1.5 mm goes into drawing and stamping; the anodising or powder coating is the plastics-and-paint agent's business, but the substrate starts here. Also the convergence point for the die-casting branch: a 1982 C64 has several kilograms of aluminium foundry alloy in its key plungers and the joystick and case-bracket castings.

###### Alloying to 3003, 6063 or A13 `metal.aluminum.blending` _(medium)_

The rolling mill is not a refinery. It melts primary ingot, remelted can scrap and dross recovery in a reverberatory or an induction furnace, adds the alloying elements as lumps of master alloy, degasses with a rotating argon lance to strip hydrogen, and skims the dross. Manganese for 3003, magnesium and silicon for 6063, silicon for the A13 casting alloy. So the C64's case metal is partly recycled metal, and its chemistry is set in a small furnace rather than a pot.

###### Aluminium extrusion: the case and the heat sinks `metal.aluminum.extrusion`

A hot billet is forced through a steel die by a ram at 420-500 C, at 20-100 MN of pressure, at several metres a second, and the profile that comes out is straight and, if the die is good, dimensionally within a fraction of a millimetre. The Commodore case is a complicated extrusion: the cooling fins, the rail and the case walls are all one profile, and the visible finish is a consequence of the die geometry. The rectifier and regulator heat sinks are separate small extrusions or machined blocks.

###### Hydraulic extrusion press, 500-2500 t `metal.aluminum.extrusion.press`

The industry standard was the 2300-2500 t class press with a 200-500 mm container, driven by a hydraulic intensifier that gave a hard step change in speed at the start of the stroke. A heated soak furnace beside the press holds the billets, a shear cuts them to length, and the runout bench stretches the profile while it is still hot. A C64 case would have been pressed at a Taiwanese or Hong Kong extrusion shop on a machine of exactly this size.

###### The soak furnace and the billet's temperature history `metal.aluminum.soak-furnace` _(medium)_

Billet quality is set before the press ever sees it. The billets are heated in a gas- or oil-fired pit furnace to 420-500 C and held for 3-24 hours so that the temperature is uniform through the section, because a billet with a hot core and a cold skin extrudes with a surface tear and a soft interior. The furnace is a 3-5 m long box with a hot zone and a transition zone, and the entire extrusion industry's reputation for inconsistent profiles is mostly the reputation of its furnaces. A C64's case extrusion depended on the profile being within a fraction of a millimetre, because it had to fit a plastic moulding and a painted finish.

###### Steel extrusion die and its forging `metal.aluminum.extrusion.die` _(medium)_

The die is a disc of hot-work tool steel with a cavity machined into it, and it has to be made before it can be used: drilled, rough-machined, heat-treated, then finish-machined and nitrided. A case profile takes a lot of steel and a lot of hours, which is why the extrusion industry is full of small specialist shops rather than a few giants. The same die steel family, SKD61 and H13, is the tooling steel of the plastics agent's injection-moulding branch.

###### The NiCr thin-film resistor level `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr` _(medium)_

A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. In a silicon-gate-era bipolar line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.

###### The nickel-chromium sputtering target `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target`

A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.

                - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome `metal.chromium`

Chromium does three separate jobs: it makes stainless steel stainless, it is the alloying element in the NiCr film resistors on the board, and as hexavalent chromium it is the hard chrome plating on switch contacts, the keyboard frame hinges and the RF shielding. The plating chemistry is the one with a body of regulation attached to it, and the ferrochrome industry is a South African monopoly that gave apartheid-era South Africa its nickname 'Chrome City'.

###### Chromite ore (FeCr2O4), 38-46% Cr2O3 `metal.chromite`

A hard, black, opaque spinel - FeO plus chromium oxide in a cubic lattice - that occurs not as veins but as layer after layer in the lower part of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group. It is unusually resistant to both chemical attack and heat, which is why chromite is also found in beach placer sands in Oregon and California, and it is effectively the only chromium ore of commercial scale. The Bushveld chromite pits run 200 m deep on a 1-6 m seam, which is one of the more extreme geometries in mining. This is a convergence node for the ferrochrome furnace, the AOD vessel and the chromium metal plant.

###### Layer-seam chromite open pit, 200 m deep `metal.chromite.mine`

The Bushveld chromite mines are among the deepest and most geometrically awkward open pits in the world. A 1-6 m chromitite layer is covered by 100-200 m of layered norite, and the pit must be advanced strip by strip along the seam, so the benches are narrow and the truck travels a long way for every tonne. The waste is platinum-group ore, so the chromite mines and the platinum mines are the same mines, and their combined revenue is what made the region what it is. The ore is crushed to about 100 mm and shipped to a smelter, sometimes 400 km away.

###### Layered norite of the Bushveld Complex `metal.chromite.layered`

The leaf: a 2 km thick layered mafic intrusion with a spectacularly regular magmatic stratification - a metre-scale layering of plagioclase and pyroxene laid down by a magma chamber over about a million years - with the chromite concentrating into a single thin seam at one horizon. It is the single most chromium-rich geological structure on Earth.

###### The Merensky Reef: the same layer as the chrome `metal.chromite.merensky`

Just below the chromitite seams of the Bushveld Complex lies a 0.4-1 m layer of pyroxenite carrying 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals - the Merensky Reef - and it is the reason the chromite is mined as it is. The waste from a chromite pit is a platinum ore, so the two industries are financially intertwined, and the chromite pits were dug by companies that made their real money on platinum. So a chrome-bearing steel for the key plungers of a computer came out of a pit whose main product was a catalyst for a chemical that is not in this tree at all.

###### Following a seam: the narrow-bench problem `metal.chromite.bench` _(medium)_

A normal open pit advances in benches 15 m high and 100-200 m wide, with haul roads on every bench. A chromite seam is 1-6 m thick, so the pit has to advance along the seam instead, and the benches are 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width and a haul road cut into the wall. The consequence is a bench width of a few tens of metres where a truck needs twenty, so the ore is either hauled a long way or handled by a shovel that strips the ore off the face and tips it down to a loading point on the bench floor. That is why the Bushveld pits look nothing like an iron ore pit even though they move similar tonnages, and it is a nice demonstration that mining cost is a function of geometry before it is a function of the rock.

###### High-carbon ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr `metal.ferrochrome`

Chromite ore and coke are charged into a submerged arc furnace at 1400-1600 C with a chromite self-fluxing slag, and the result is an alloy of 60-70% chromium, 1-3% silicon and 5-8% carbon. It consumes about 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome - a fifth of aluminium's energy per tonne but on a much smaller tonnage. In the 1980s the industry was the classic vertically integrated single-industry town: the chromite mine, the power station with its 400 MW supply contract, and the smelter were all owned by the same company in the same town. The 1982-85 US and European voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome were aimed squarely at the market power of one country, and it is why ferrochrome is one of the very few metals where the 1982 price environment is a real story.

###### The self-fluxing chromite slag `metal.ferrochrome.slag` _(medium)_

A ferrochrome furnace is self-fluxing, which means the ore's own silica is balanced by the ore's own magnesia and there is nothing to add - the chromite is 16% MgO and 20% SiO2 and the ratio of the two is already about right for a liquid slag at 1500 C. That is why the smelter does not need lime, and it is also why the ore is smelted as it is rather than being beneficiated: a ferrochrome plant is a furnace and a power station, and the beneficiation happens in the ore dressing only if the ore is too fine to charge.

###### The RF/DC sputterer `mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter`

A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

                - *Argon* `facility.argon` *(seen above)*
###### The contact window `mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact`

One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

###### Aluminium metallisation `mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal`

The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.

              - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
              - *Argon* `facility.argon` *(seen above)*
###### Sintering the metal into the contacts `mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter` _(medium)_

After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.

###### Nitrogen supply `facility.nitrogen`

The single largest bulk gas. Used for inerting storage tanks and vessels, blanketing, purging, and as the carrier gas in diffusion furnaces and plasma etchers. Small plants bought a few tonnes a month of liquid N2; a furnace-loaded fab wanted tens of tonnes a day and built its own ASU.

###### Atmospheric air `facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air`

78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, plus water and CO2. The single source of every bulk industrial gas. Delivered to an ASU intake through a windowless, acoustically baffled multi-bay intake so it arrived at a steady temperature, humidity and free of the dust that would plug a cryogenic plant.

###### Air intake stack `facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.intake` _(medium)_

A tall concrete or brick stack with louvres facing away from the prevailing wind, feeding a plenum and the air compressor. Intakes were sited so that no two of them - for air, for cooling water, for the coal yard - were close enough to contaminate each other.

###### Cryogenic air separation unit (ASU) `facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu`

Air is filtered, compressed in a large multi-stage compressor to about 6-7 bar, cooled against the cold product streams until it liquefies, then fractionally distilled in a low-temperature column to make oxygen and a nitrogen-argon mixture. A unit also making argon has a separate argon column fed from the top of the nitrogen column. Typical small unit: 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h of oxygen.

###### Cold box (plate-fin heat exchanger) `facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger`

A stack of aluminium brazed plate-fin exchangers, some 10-20 m tall, in which the compressed air is progressively cooled to -196 C by the outgoing oxygen and nitrogen. The heart of every ASU.

###### Fractionating columns `facility.nitrogen.asu-tower`

Insulated stainless-steel columns 5-10 m tall with trays or packing, holding the low-temperature distillation that separates oxygen (bottoms, warmer) from nitrogen and argon (top, colder). A common 1980s arrangement was a single low-temperature column producing oxygen plus a nitrogen-argon mixture, with a side argon column.

###### Expansion turbine (expander) `facility.nitrogen.expander`

A turbine in the cold box that recovers the enthalpy drop of the expanding nitrogen and uses it to generate power, offsetting part of the ASU's compression energy. Standard from the 1960s onward.

###### PSA / molecular-sieve nitrogen generator `facility.nitrogen.psa`

Pressure swing adsorption: compressed air is adsorbed on beds of zeolite molecular sieve at 7-10 bar, then dropped to near atmospheric and purged with a slice of product to release the nitrogen. Gave 90-99% nitrogen cheaply at small scale; the 1980s workhorse for factories of under a few hundred kW load.

###### Zeolite molecular sieve (synthetic) `facility.nitrogen.zeolite`

Crystalline hydrated aluminosilicate with a uniform 3-5 angstrom pore, made by hydrothermal crystallisation of bentonite, kaolin or synthetic gels. Uniform aperture size is what makes PSA possible - a zeolite with 3A pores excludes N2 and adsorbs only O2 and H2O; the 4A and 5A grades are used elsewhere in gas drying.

###### Membrane nitrogen generator `facility.nitrogen.membrane`

Hollow-fibre asymmetric polyimide or cellulose acetate membranes in a pressure vessel, 20-40 bar feed, with N2 diffusing through the wall faster than O2. Cheap, silent, no regeneration heat, and limited to about 90-95% nitrogen - which is fine for blanketing and not fine for a furnace. By 1983 membrane units were new and uncommon; they took the small-plant market from PSA in the 1990s.

###### Hollow-fibre polyimide membrane `facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide` _(medium)_

A thin-walled asymmetric fibre, about 0.1-0.2 micrometre wall, with a selectively permeable outer skin. Making a defect-free fibre over a 1 m length was, and is, the hard part.

###### Bulk cryogenic liquid storage `facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage`

A double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless tank on a skirt, with a vacuum-insulated transfer line (a double pipe with perlite or multilayer reflective insulation between) from the ASU or the delivery tanker. The tank is a pressure vessel rated to about 700-1000 kPa on the inner shell.

###### Tube trailer (bulk gas road delivery) `facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer`

A tractor-trailer carrying 30-40 high-pressure cylinders or a single multi-compartment tube bundle of 6,000-15,000 litres, delivering liquid nitrogen, oxygen or argon from a merchant plant. In 1983 this was how a factory without an on-site ASU got its gases; the driver's unload was a vent line that fogged the yard and alarmed the neighbours.

###### Passivation over the metal `mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation`

A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

###### The resulting 3-5 um geometry `mb.logic.bipolar.process.feature` _(medium)_

Put together, those four diffusions and the one resistor level put a transistor with a 0.5-1 um base and a 1-2 um emitter sitting inside an isolation island a few tens of micrometres across, wired with 3-5 um aluminium on a single level. That is the '3-5 um minimum feature' of the era's standard bipolar logic line. Compare the dynamic RAM on the same board, patterned at around 1-2 um with two or three aluminium levels and a polysilicon gate - that is where the money was, and that is why the DRAM cost more than the glue.

###### Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles `mb.logic.bipolar.litho`

A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.

###### The mask set `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks`

A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

###### The mask blank (soda-lime glass) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank`

A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.

                - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### The opaque chrome layer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome`

A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.

                - *Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome* `metal.chromium` *(seen above)*
###### The reticle (1:1 mask) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle` _(medium)_

A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.

###### The mask writer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer` _(medium)_

A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.

###### Spinning on the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat`

The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.

###### The coater/developer track `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner`

A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

###### Negative (image-reversing) resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.negative` _(medium)_

On a bipolar line in 1983, resist was still commonly negative: exposure cross-links the resist so it becomes insoluble in the developer, so the pattern left on the wafer after develop is the complement of the mask. This suits diffusion, where you want to open the mask where the oxide is. Positive resists, which behave the intuitive way, had taken over NMOS and CMOS from the late 1970s but lingered on bipolar.

                - *Photoresist chemistry* `chem.photoresist` *(seen above)*
###### Dehydration bake before the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration`

Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

###### The dehydration hot plate `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotplate`

A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.

###### Aligning the mask to the wafer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align`

The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.

###### The contact/proximity mask aligner `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer`

A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

###### The 1:1 projection stepper `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper`

A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

###### The mercury lamp `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp`

A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

###### Developing the image `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop`

The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows.

###### The alkaline developer `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az`

Aqueous alkali, traditionally potassium hydroxide or, from the late 1970s, tetramethylammonium hydroxide. It dissolves the unexposed novolac resin of a positive resist but leaves the exposed, cross-linked, imaged resin alone. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.

###### Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash`

The strong alkali in the developer, made by the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine alongside chlorine. It is the chemical that develops a positive photoresist.

###### Brine feed to the chlor-alkali cell `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.brine`

Concentrated sodium chloride solution, electrolysed to give sodium hydroxide (the alkali), hydrogen and chlorine gas. The same rock salt that makes the epoxy precursors makes the resist developer.

###### Rock salt (halite) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.az.potash.brine.salt`

The sodium chloride mined from halite or evaporated from brine. The root of both the chlorine chemistry and the sodium-hydroxide chemistry that strip, develop and etch the resist away.

###### Etching the oxide window `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch`

The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) - the ore of hydrofluoric acid `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite`

Hydrofluoric acid is made by treating fluorspar, calcium fluoride, with concentrated sulphuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C. Fluorspar is dug from hard-rock deposits, notably in Derbyshire and the Ilkley Moor field in England, Mexico, South Africa and China, and it is the single feedstock behind all the oxide etching in the entire semiconductor industry.

###### Limestone (CaCO3) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.fluorite.limestone`

The acid side of the HF process, and the source of the calcium sulfate byproduct. Limestone is quarried limestone, chemically calcium carbonate, and it is one of the most widely mined rocks on earth.

###### Stripping the resist `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip`

With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. The wafer goes into a hot organic solvent - historically xylene or trichloroethylene, later the piranha acid clean. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue that had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat.

###### Trichloroethylene solvent strip `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce` _(medium)_

A dense chlorinated solvent, 1,1,1-trichloroethane family, that dissolves the polymerised resist. Boiling in a hot bath it strips the wafer. It is a heavy, volatile, toxic chlorinated hydrocarbon made by chlorinating ethylene and destroying hydrogen chloride with chlorine - another chlorine branch of the tree.

###### Ethylene from the cracker `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylene`

The other half of the chlorinated-solvent chemistry. Ethylene came from the same steam cracker as the propylene that made the epoxy, from naphtha or from ethane off natural gas. The epoxy body of the package and the solvent that stripped the resist are siblings from one cracker.

###### Naphtha feed `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylene.naphtha`

The light hydrocarbon fraction of crude oil distillation, cracked to ethylene and propylene. Every chlorinated organic solvent and every epoxy in this tree comes from this one feed.

###### Crude oil `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.tce.ethylene.naphtha.crude`

The root hydrocarbon: the source of the resist solvents, the epoxy, the photoresist binders and the natural gas that made the hydrogen.

###### Piranha clean (H2SO4 + H2O2) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha`

A hot mix of concentrated sulphuric acid and hydrogen peroxide that oxidises organic residue to carbon dioxide and leaves a chemically clean, ion-free surface. Mixed in the fab at the wet bench, it is the standard clean before every photoresist coat and after every resist strip, and it is what made adhesion and ion control reliable.

###### Sulphuric acid from sulphur `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sulphuric` _(medium)_

Made by burning sulphur or hydrogen sulfide and absorbing in water. Sulphur itself came overwhelmingly from recovered petroleum - the sour crude 'sour gas' processing plants removed hydrogen sulfide from crude and Claus-processed it into elemental sulphur. So the acid that cleans the wafer also traces to crude oil.

###### Elemental sulphur (recovered) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sulphuric.sulphur` _(medium)_

Yellow solid recovered from hydrogen sulfide in oil and gas refining by the Claus process, or mined. Oxidised to sulphur dioxide and absorbed to make sulphuric acid.

###### Hydrogen sulfide from sour crude `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.piranha.sulphuric.sulphur.h2s` _(medium)_

The sour-smelling hydrogen sulfide stripped from oil and gas during refining, which is the raw feed for most of the world's manufactured sulphur.

###### The full cycle, counted `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.cycle`

One mask level's cycle, run eight times, with the non-lithography steps interleaved. Written out once: dehydrate, coat, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse, hard-bake, wet-etch, strip, clean - ten operations - then the furnace or the sputterer. Eight levels of ten is about eighty lithography-area operations, plus oxidation and diffusion pushes, plus metallisation, plus test. The brief's 'photolithography cycle count' for a 74LS chip is therefore roughly eight masks, ten steps each.

###### The photomask bay (Class 10 cleanroom) `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.bay`

Coating, exposing and developing happened in a 'yellow room' under filtered mercury light and then in a Class 10 (ISO 4) mini-environment with the aligners under hoods. Whole-body suits were only in the Class 100 (ISO 5) areas and the fab sub-fab; the mask bay and the diffusion bay were usually Class 1000 (ISO 6).

              - *Nitrogen supply* `facility.nitrogen` *(seen above)*
###### Electricity at the factory wall `facility.electricity`

The chain from the utility's service drop to the machine tool. This is the branch other subsystems should reference whenever they need 'mains power': the substation, the transformer, the low-voltage switchboard, the motor control centre, and finally the cord and plug.

###### Utility service and metering `facility.electricity.service`

A pad-mount or pole-mounted transformer on the utility side of the fence, with revenue metering and a fused cut-out. The customer owned everything downstream of the meter.

###### Customer substation `facility.electricity.substation`

Where a large factory bought at transmission or sub-transmission voltage: a fenced yard with the utility's metering, an incoming circuit breaker, a main transformer, a secondary switchgear line-up and the plant's own protection relays.

###### Distribution transformer `facility.electricity.transformer`

A laminated silicon-steel core with copper or aluminium windings on pressboard and paper insulation, immersed in mineral oil or Askarel. Oil-immersed units dominated until the 1980s-90s fire codes and the economics of dry-type began to change the picture in Europe and Japan.

###### Grain-oriented silicon steel (GOES) `facility.electricity.electrical-steel`

3.2% silicon steel rolled so its crystallographic grain lies parallel to the flux direction, giving a core loss an order of magnitude lower than hot-rolled steel. Made in a special continuous-annealing line. This is the same material used in the C64's switch-mode transformer and in every mains transformer in the world.

###### Grain-oriented steel rolling mill `facility.electricity.grain-oriented-mill` _(medium)_

Hot band rolled to 2 mm, cold rolled to 0.3 mm, decarburised in a hydrogen atmosphere and given a final magnetic anneal. Ends at the ore and the coke oven.

###### Transformer insulating oil `facility.electricity.insulating-oil`

Mineral oil (naphthenic or paraffinic), a by-product of vacuum distillation of crude. Also Askarel (PCB-filled chlorinated dielectric) in older units - a PCB source that explains part of the PCB contamination of the Hudson/Superfund sites.

###### Askarel (PCB-filled transformer dielectric) `facility.electricity.askarel` _(medium)_

A chlorinated biphenyl dielectric used from the 1930s until the 1980s ban. Ends at the chlorinated benzene/aromatics stream.

###### Chlorinated aromatic feedstock `facility.electricity.chlorobenzene` _(low)_

Chlorobenzene and biphenyl feedstock for the askarel blend, itself from the chlorination of benzene over a chloride catalyst. Ends at the aromatic hydrocarbon still.

###### Porcelain bushings and standoff insulators `facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing`

Glazed porcelain sheds, cemented with epoxy onto the winding ends, to bring the winding out to a terminal. These are the tall ribbed 'sheds' you see on any pole-top transformer.

###### Feldspar `facility.electricity.feldspar` _(medium)_

A potassium-sodium aluminosilicate used as a flux in porcelain and in the electrolytic alumina bath. Ends at the pegmatite quarry.

###### Low-voltage switchboard `facility.electricity.switchgear`

Air-circuit-breaker switchboards at 480/415 V, with bolted busbar, fuses/MCCBs per outgoing way and a transformer tap-selector. Most factory power for small machines was tapped off the board at 120/230 V through a plug.

###### Motor control centre `facility.electricity.mcc`

A vertical lineup of combination starters and contactors with a fused disconnect per motor, feeding the compressors, injection-moulding presses, conveyors and extract fans. The 1980s unit had no variable-frequency drives at all - speed control was a pole-changing or slip-ring motor.

###### AC contactors and overload relays `facility.electricity.contactors`

Silver-alloy contacts on a moulded phenolic base with a shading ring to stop contact chatter, plus a bimetal or electronic overload. The bimetal overload relay, unchanged since the 1920s, was the industrial motor's main protection.

###### Power factor correction capacitors `facility.electricity.power-factor`

Motor loads are inductive, so a big factory runs at 0.7-0.85 power factor and gets penalised by the utility. Banks of switched capacitor kVAr corrected it. A capacitor is the cheapest industrial electronics ever made - a polypropylene film between two aluminium foils.

###### Earthing grid and lightning protection `facility.electricity.earthing` _(medium)_

Copper rod or bare conductor bonded under the floor and up the steelwork, plus air terminals and down conductors to earth rods. In a fab with a raised floor, the earth grid and the electrostatic-dissipative floor were often the same conductor.

###### Busbar trunking and cable `facility.electricity.distribution-busbar`

Copper or aluminium busbar in an epoxy-impregnated sandwich ('busway') for high-current runs, and PVC/PVDF-insulated copper or aluminium cable in conduit or tray for the rest. Flexible conduit was still common above machine tools.

###### Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom`

The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.

###### The HEPA fan filter unit `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu`

A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

###### The wet bench `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench`

A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.

              - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Bulk process gases `mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.gas`

Nitrogen for purging tool chambers and for the sinter anneal, hydrogen for the metal anneal, and oxygen for oxidation and for ashing photoresist, all piped from a bulk gas farm outside the cleanroom. Dry, filtered nitrogen was also the blow-off gas for every wafer before it entered a hot tool.

              - *Nitrogen supply* `facility.nitrogen` *(seen above)*
###### The merchant logic fab that ran the process `mb.logic.bipolar.fab`

A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.

###### Oxidation and diffusion bay `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion`

The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Photomask bay `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baylitho`

Coaters, developers, aligners and the inspection stations, under Class 10 and Class 100 cleanroom. This was the largest bay by machine count and the largest by electricity draw after the cleanroom air.

              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Metallisation bay `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal`

The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.

              - *Argon* `facility.argon` *(seen above)*
              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers `mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities` _(medium)_

A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed. The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.

              - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
          - *Where the silicon came from* `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer` *(seen above)*
###### What happened to bipolar logic afterwards `mb.logic.bipolar.now`

The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches: high-voltage, high-current, precision-analog and microwave parts, where the bipolar transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat. The two families also merged into BiCMOS.

###### Where bipolar still survives `mb.logic.bipolar.now.bipolar-left`

Power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors. Bipolar transistors are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the very leading edge - the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not.

###### BiCMOS - bipolar and CMOS on one wafer `mb.logic.bipolar.now.bicmos` _(medium)_

A process that builds CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die: the CMOS for low power and density, the bipolar for high current drive on the outputs. It was used in some gate arrays and in the output stages of older CPUs, and it was abandoned once CMOS itself could drive high current enough. It is the process family that merged the two halves of this branch.

###### The 3-5 um feature, then and now `mb.logic.bipolar.now.scaling`

The 3-5 um minimum feature of this logic line is unrecognisably coarse today. Modern advanced logic runs at nanometre nodes with hundreds of millions of transistors per die, whereas a 74LS gate has of the order of a few dozen transistors in total. The geometry went from the thousands of transistors that fit on one 100 mm wafer of glue logic to the billions that now fit on one 300 mm wafer of a GPU. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the DIP pin spacing changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.

##### The black epoxy DIP `mb.logic.package`

Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history.

###### Why 0.1 inch and 0.3 inch `mb.logic.package.geometry`

The two dimensions that made the DIP work at all. The 0.100 in (2.54 mm) lead pitch was chosen so that a cheap single-row DIP socket, the same one used for the C64's own logic, could accept it. The 0.3 in (7.62 mm) row spacing was chosen so the body would just clear a 0.05 in hole-pad on 0.1 in centres and so a 14-pin part could be mounted on the older 0.6 in grid alongside the 40-pin parts. Wider bodies moved to 0.6 in rows.

###### 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch `mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch`

The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

###### 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants `mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing` _(medium)_

The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.

###### Nickel-iron lead frame `mb.logic.package.leadframe`

A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.

            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### The iron half of the lead frame alloy `mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron`

Most of a logic lead frame by weight is iron, not nickel. The nickel - typically 42 percent, a little over a fifth of the mass - is the expensive part that tunes the expansion coefficient; the iron is commodity steel and was bought on the open market.

###### Iron ore for the frame alloy `mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore`

The lead frame melt started life as steel, and the steel started life as ore. Two ores dominate: hematite (Fe2O3, the red ore) and magnetite (Fe3O4, the black ore). Both were shipped by rail and sea in bulk from the Lake Superior range, Mesabi and Labrador Trough, and the UK, and smelted in a blast furnace with coke and then converted.

###### Hematite (Fe2O3) `mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.hematite`

Iron in its fully oxidised state, typically 60-66 percent iron by mass, won by gravity concentration and magnetic washing of fine crushed ore. It was the dominant iron ore in world supply and the standard feed for a blast furnace.

###### Magnetite (Fe3O4) `mb.logic.package.leadframe.iron.ore.magnetite`

The magnetic iron ore, ~72 percent iron and strongly ferrimagnetic, which is why it can be separated from gangue by a magnetic separator instead of by gravity alone. Much magnetite in 1983 came from taconite pellets shipped from the Mesabi range, a sintered concentrate rather than a lump ore.

###### Progressive-die stamping of the frame `mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp`

The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.

###### The progressive die set `mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool`

A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.

###### Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel `mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating`

Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.

###### Tin plating bath `mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin`

A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux.

###### Cassiterite (SnO2) - the tin ore `mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.cassiterite`

Tin reached the plating tank as refined tin metal, made by carbothermic reduction of cassiterite, the tin oxide ore. In 1983 the world's tin supply came overwhelmingly from the Southeast Asian tin belt - Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand - and from Bolivia's Cerro Rico, and the price was famously volatile because the ore body was tiny in volume and the supply was political.

              - *Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts* `metal.gold` *(seen above)*
              - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing `metal.silver`

Silver is the most electrically conductive of any element, and it is used in a C64 where the contact has to carry current at low force: the contacts of the rocker switches and of many of the keyboard switches, the silver-bearing solder and brazing alloys for the heat sinks and chassis joints, the silver-filled epoxy and silver ink of the keyboard membrane, and the silver that comes out of the lead and copper refineries as a by-product. Most of the world's silver is mined as a by-product - of lead, of copper, of zinc - and only about a fifth comes from a primary silver mine.

###### Silver ore and the by-product sources `metal.silver.ore`

Silver behaves chemically like lead, so it substitutes for it in galena, and the world's most productive silver mines are really lead mines. The primary ores are native silver, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3 and stephanite Ag5SbS4 - the last two are why silver is also a lead-bysulphide metallurgy problem. The Cordillera Real of Potosi in Bolivia and Zacatecas in Mexico were the great producers, and Cobalt in Ontario is the historical outlier where silver was the target. Silver at 500-1000 g/t is a very good ore and at 5-50 g/t it is a credit.

###### The Zacatecas-Potosi silver vein mines `metal.silver.mine-mexican` _(medium)_

Mines like the Fresnillo, the Zacatecas and the San Luis Potosi: an underground operation on steeply dipping epithermal quartz veins carrying native silver, argentite and the antimony sulphides, worked in the Spanish colonial era by water-driven mills, mercury amalgamation and patio amalgamation, and by 1982 by mechanised narrow-vein mining and flotation. The Fresnillo mine is a silver mine that also happens to be the world's largest producer of antimony, which is a neat illustration of the interpenetration of these branches.

###### Mercury amalgamation of small silver operations `metal.silver.amalgamation`

Before cyanide, silver was recovered by amalgamating the crushed ore with mercury: 4Au + 8Hg -> 4AuHg4 and 4Ag + 4Hg -> 4Ag2Hg, then squeezing the amalgam in a heated press and retorting the sponge at 500-700 C to drive the mercury off and recover the metal. The process left 10-100 grams of mercury per tonne of ore behind in the tailings, and it is one of the largest anthropogenic mercury dispersals in history. In 1982 it was in decline in the large mines and still widespread in artisanal operations; in the small artisanal miners' union of Guanajuato it outlived the century.

###### Mercury: cinnabar from Idrija and Almaden `metal.mercury-source` _(medium)_

Amalgamation consumes mercury and does not give it back, so a silver mine that amalgamated needed a mercury supply. Cinnabar, HgS, the vermilion pigment mineral, came from Idrija in Slovenia - the largest mercury mine in the world for 500 years - and from Almaden in Spain, and from the New Idria and New Almaden mines in California. The leaf is a mercury deposit, which is itself a strange one: cinnabar forms in shallow hydrothermal systems, and the Spanish and Yugoslav mines are in exactly the kind of fractured carbonate and volcanic rocks that the precious-metal branches of this file have already been through.

###### The cinnabar vein `metal.cinnabar.bed`

The leaf: a scarlet vein of cinnabar in brecciated limestone, sometimes 10 m wide, worked by open pit and by fire-setting underground since Roman times. It is the only mercury ore that has ever mattered commercially, and it is a beautiful and rather grim example of a metal that exists in one mineral, in one setting, in a few places on Earth.

###### Silver mill: crushing, grinding and flotation `metal.silver.mill` _(medium)_

Ore at 300-1500 g/t is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground in a ball mill to 50-100 um, and floated with a xanthate or a thio compound collector at pH 8-10. Silver sulphides float with the lead and zinc sulphides they are intergrown with, so the circuit produces a bulk concentrate that the smelter treats as a lead concentrate. The recovery is 60-85% and the tailings are the reason the Zacatecas and Guanajuato districts look the way they do - a very large volume of finely ground rock in long, engineered tailings impoundments.

###### Concentrate to the lead smelter `metal.silver.concentrate-shipping`

A silver concentrate is not a product anybody wants to buy; it is a concentrate to ship to a lead smelter 500 km away, because the only economical way to separate silver from lead is the Parkes process, and that needs a lead smelter. So the silver chain leaves the mine, joins the lead chain inside a smelter that may be in a different country, and comes back out at 99.9%. This is the practical meaning of silver being a by-product metal, and it is why the silver price has so little to do with the silver mines.

###### Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead `metal.lead.blast-furnace`

A lead blast furnace looks like an iron blast furnace but is only 4-7 m tall, because lead reduces so easily. Self-fluxing sinter, coke and limestone are charged at the top; a blast of 200-350 C air is blown in at the hearth; the PbO is reduced to lead by CO at 1000-1100 C and the metal runs out. The sinter, coke and limestone charge comes down a shaft that is deliberately kept chilled so the metallic lead freezes before it goes further down - if it melted it would run into the tuyeres. Two outputs: crude lead bullion at 950-1050 C at the bottom, and a slag carrying off the iron and silica.

###### Crude lead bullion with silver and gold `metal.lead.bullion`

Tapped at 950-1050 C, the bullion is about 95-98% lead with 1-3% silver, a little gold, and copper, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. Silver at 1-3% is not a trace - it is often the difference between a viable mine and a marginal one, and the Parkes process that recovers it is the reason lead smelters have a refinery at all. By 1982 crude lead was increasingly sold as a low-grade bullion to the refinery and the smelter/ refinery was one continuous plant.

###### Parkes process: zinc drossing and desilverisation `metal.lead.parkes`

The genius step, invented in 1850 and still standard in 1982. The molten bullion is stirred with a few tenths of a percent of zinc, which has a much stronger chemical affinity for silver than lead does, so a zinc-silver intermetallic (AgZn2, Ag2Zn5) migrates to the zinc 'dross' floating on top.
