The dross is skimmed, and the now-silver-poor lead is treated again with fresh zinc until it is down to 10-30 g/t silver. The dross is then distilled in a retort: zinc boils at 907 C and is condensed, and the silver and gold stay behind, to be cupelled. The zinc is a sacrificial reagent and goes back into the alloy.

###### Betts process: electrolytic refining `metal.lead.betts` _(medium)_

The rival to the Parkes process, and the answer for the last fraction of a gram of bismuth. Anodes of impure lead are dissolved in a caustic soda solution containing sodium plumbite (Na2PbO3), and pure lead plates onto the cathode. The chemistry is unusual - the anode dissolves as plumbite and the deposit forms by the reaction of plumbite with metal, which is why the bath has to be kept in a narrow alkaline window. Cost is high, energy is high, so it was used only as a finishing step on top of the Parkes route, and in the 1980s it was being displaced by the Betterton-Krastchkow continuous drossing tower.

###### Vacuum degassing and the drossing tower `metal.lead.vacuum-degassing` _(medium)_

The modern version of both processes in one machine: a 6-10 m tall cylindrical steel vacuum vessel with an internal fractionating column. Molten lead is sprayed into the vacuum; the volatiles - hydrogen, oxygen, zinc, and the remaining silver on its way out - distil out and are fractionated, so the silver comes off as a separate metal rather than as a dross. It replaces two steps with one, cuts the labour, and gives 99.99% lead with under 5 g/t silver. It was the technology that spread through the lead industry in the 1980s, and it is a good marker for what was changing in smelting and what was not.

###### Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold `metal.lead.cupellation-lead`

The dross from the Parkes process is mixed with lead and flux and cast into a 30-50 kg charge, which is placed in a cupellation furnace at 1000-1150 C and blown with air. The lead oxidises to litharge, PbO, which melts at 888 C and is absorbed by the porous cupel, while the silver and gold do not oxidise and stay on the surface. When all the lead is gone the silver is 96-99% pure and the gold is 30-50% of it; the gold is then cupelled again, or electrorefined, to 99.9%. So every lead bullion makes a small pile of very pure silver - a deliberate convergence of the lead and silver branches.

###### Retorting the Parkes dross to recover the zinc `metal.lead.dross-smelting` _(medium)_

After the silver has been skimmed off as dross, the dross itself has to be processed, and it is done in a cast-iron retort: the dross is mixed with charcoal and a little limestone, charged into a retort at 800-950 C, and the zinc distils out - it boils at 907 C - into a condenser where it is collected as a crude zinc metal. The silver and gold stay in the retort. A dross retort holds 100-500 kg and takes 8-20 hours, and a refinery had six to a dozen of them. The recovered zinc is dirty and goes back into the next drossing cycle, which is why the Parkes process consumes no net zinc even though it uses some every time round.

###### The dross retort and its condenser `metal.lead.dross-retort` _(medium)_

A cast-iron or steel tube, 1.5-3 m long, charged at one end and heated in a coke-fired setting, with a condenser of iron pipes at the cool end into which the zinc vapour condenses and runs out as a crude metal. The retort has to be skimmed of oxide and it is a batch process, so a refinery ran a bank of them in shifts. It is an object that is essentially unchanged since the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest continuous processes in this file.

###### Hot drossing for copper comes first `metal.lead.copper-drossing` _(medium)_

Before the Parkes zinc drossing, the bullion is hot-drossed for copper. The blast-furnace bullion comes out at 950-1050 C holding copper, which is insoluble in lead at that temperature and forms a separate copper matte that floats on top; the refinery skims it off, cools it, and recovers the copper and its precious metals by further processing. It is the same physical principle as the zinc drossing - a metal that mixes preferentially with another - and it is done first because the copper dross would otherwise interfere with the silver dross.

###### Refined lead ingot, 99.99% `metal.lead.ingot`

Cast into 25 kg pigs or into 500 kg slabs. About two thirds of all the lead refined in the world was never made into a product in the refinery - it went straight into an alloy, most of it lead-acid battery plate and cable sheath. The solder industry took a small fraction, on the order of five to ten percent, and in 1982 that fraction was the entire basis of the electronics solder business. This is a deliberate convergence node: the blast furnace branch, the Parkes desilverisation branch and the solder branch all meet here.

                          - *Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold* `metal.lead.cupellation-lead` *(seen above)*
###### Silver refining to 99.9-99.99% `metal.silver.refining`

Most silver never gets a refinery of its own. It is separated inside the lead smelter and refinery, or the copper anode slime, and refined there. The copper route: the slime is dissolved in nitric acid or in an aqua-regia type circuit, silver precipitates as silver chloride which is then reduced with copper and melted, and gold is recovered separately. The lead route: the Parkes process and the cupellation furnace described in the lead branch deliver silver at 96-99%, and it is electrorefined in a small silver tankhouse with a silver anode and a silver cathode in a nitric acid or a copper nitrate electrolyte at 2-4 V. In 1982 perhaps 60% of the world's refined silver was made at a handful of silver refineries and the rest was by-product metal refined alongside lead and copper.

###### Silver ingot, 99.9%, and silver contact material `metal.silver.ingot` _(medium)_

A 99.9% ingot is the standard commodity grade, cast as 0.5-1 kg bars or as a 15-30 kg or 1000 troy ounce bar. For the contacts of the C64's switches and keys the relevant alloy is not pure silver but a silver-cadmium-oxide or silver-tin-oxide electrical contact material - a silver matrix with 5-15% of a refractory oxide that reduces the contact resistance rise caused by metal transfer, at the cost of a bit of conductivity. Silver-graphite is a related and very common sliding contact material: 50-95% silver in graphite, sintered and infiltrated, used where the contact has to rub.

###### Silver electrolysis and the doré loop `metal.silver.electrorefining` _(medium)_

The silver from the Parkes cupellation or from the anode slime is cast as anodes and dissolved in a nitric acid electrolyte with a little silver nitrate, at 2-4 V with a pure silver cathode. The electrolyte's job is to hold the silver as the nitrate while the gold and the base metals either stay in the anode mud or fall out as slime. A small refinery might have 20-40 cells and make 5-20 t a month. The silver cathode is then melted and cast, and the whole cycle - cupell, electrorefine, cast, cupell again - can run three times to get five nines.

###### Silver contact powder: Ag-SnO2 and Ag-graphite `metal.silver.contact-powder` _(medium)_

A switch contact is not silver metal. It is a powder metallurgy composite: 80-95% silver powder mixed with 5-15% of a refractory oxide - tin oxide, cadmium oxide or graphite - pressed at 200-400 MPa and sintered at 700-950 C. The oxide breaks up the silver grain boundaries and suppresses the metal transfer that otherwise builds up on a small, low-force contact, at the price of some conductivity. Silver-graphite is the same idea for sliding contacts, and silver-graphite in a rotary encoder or a potentiometer is the single most common use of silver powder in electronics.

###### Borax, litharge and the fire assay `metal.silver.borax-flux` _(medium)_

A refinery that also assays needs a cupellation furnace and a borax flux, because silver is assayed by cupellation: the sample is mixed with borax and litharge, cupelled, and the silver bead that is left is weighed. So the assay and the refining process are the same process, which is why a small refinery has a cupel furnace whether or not it refines. It is also why the assayer's skill and the refiner's skill are the same skill, and why the price of silver has always been set by a weighing scale on a furnace roof.

###### Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983) `mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4` _(medium)_

A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.

              - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
###### The separated, tested die `mb.logic.package.die`

Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

###### Scribing and dicing the wafer `mb.logic.package.die.scribe`

A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.

###### The glass over the aluminium `mb.logic.package.die.passivation`

After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.

###### Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not `mb.logic.package.die.hardtest` _(medium)_

A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.

###### Die attach, wire bond, moulding `mb.logic.package.assembly`

Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

###### Die attach to the frame paddle `mb.logic.package.assembly.attach`

The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.

              - *Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts* `metal.gold` *(seen above)*
              - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
###### Gold wire bonding `mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond`

A machine called a wedge bonder (or, for higher volume, a ball bonder) presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats on the other end at the pin. Each joint is an intermetallic wedge of aluminium-gold, cut with a pulled wire rather than cut. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.

              - *Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts* `metal.gold` *(seen above)*
###### The wedge bonder `mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonder`

A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

###### Transfer moulding the black epoxy body `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould`

A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 70-80 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out.

###### The transfer press `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press`

A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.

###### Epoxy moulding compound `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound`

A blend of roughly 15 percent resin system and 85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.

###### Epoxy cresol novolac resin `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin`

The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which came from propylene and chlorine, which came from salt and natural gas - so the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to crude oil.

###### Epichlorohydrin (1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane) `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin`

The bifunctional building block of every epoxy. Chlorohydrination of propylene (propene plus hypochlorous acid, with the propylene itself coming from the cracking of refinery hydrocarbons or of natural-gas liquids) gives 1,2-dichloropropane, and base dehydrochlorination closes the epoxide ring.

###### Propylene from the cracker `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.propylene`

Steam cracking of naphtha or of natural-gas-propane. Propylene is the second most produced organic chemical in the world and the cheapest epoxide feedstock, which is why epichlorohydrin was always made from it and never from anything else.

###### Naphtha (light petroleum fraction) `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.propylene.naphtha`

The low-boiling cut of crude oil distillation, roughly C5 to C11. Everything in the chain from the epoxy moulding compound through to the solder mask and the photoresist binder starts in this fraction, because it is the cheapest feedstock with the right carbon skeleton.

###### Crude oil `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.propylene.naphtha.crude`

The whole hydrocarbon trunk of the tree: the carbon in the package epoxy, the resist binder, the solder mask, the flex circuits and the petrol that moved it all.

###### Chlorine for the chlorohydrin step `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.chlorine`

Elemental chlorine from the chlor-alkali cell: brine electrolysed, producing chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen in one pass. The chlorine is reacted with water to make the hypochlorous acid, and the resulting dichloropropane is treated with caustic soda to open the epoxide.

###### Brine (concentrated sodium chloride) `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.chlorine.brine`

Saturated salt solution, the feed for every chlor-alkali plant. It is the base of the entire chlorinated organic chemistry that runs underneath plastics, solvents, refrigerants and the photoresist industry - including the acid used to strip a wafer's photoresist after it has been used.

###### Rock salt (halite) `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.resin.epichlorohydrin.chlorine.brine.salt`

Sodium chloride, mined or dissolved from halite deposits and then evaporated from seawater in salt pans. Almost all industrial chlorine and almost all industrial sodium hydroxide in the world in 1983 came from this one rock.

                - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Carbon black pigment `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.pigment` _(medium)_

About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.

###### Furnace black feedstock `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.pigment.soot` _(medium)_

Heavy petroleum residuum or natural gas fed to an air-cooled sooting furnace; the soot is scraped off water-cooled rotors and pelletised. It is chemically the same carbon black described in the resistor branch of this tree.

###### The mould cavity and ejector pins `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool`

A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.

###### Post-mould cure and stability bake `mb.logic.package.assembly.postmould`

Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature. Parts are therefore baked for hours at 175 C afterwards, which completes the cure and drives off the last of the residual stress. It was a batch operation: thousands of parts in a tray, hours in a oven, on a schedule that ran overnight.

###### Probe test before packaging `mb.logic.package.probe`

Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

###### The wafer probe station `mb.logic.package.probe.prober`

A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.

###### The probe card `mb.logic.package.probe.card`

A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.

###### The logic tester `mb.logic.package.probe.tester`

An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.

###### The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here) `mb.logic.package.ceramic`

For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.

###### Alumina ceramic body `mb.logic.package.ceramic.body`

A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.

###### Bauxite, the alumina ore `mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.bauxite`

Bauxite is the only commercial ore of aluminium, and alumina refined from it is both the ceramic used in ceramic packages and the feed for the aluminium metallisation on the die - two completely different routes to the same element, sitting a few centimetres apart on the same 74LS part.

###### Kovar lid and nickel seal ring `mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid`

For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

###### Glass frit sealing `mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal` _(medium)_

A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Marking the top of the package `mb.logic.package.marking`

Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.

###### Marking ink `mb.logic.package.marking.ink`

A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV or by laser ablation of the mould compound. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not.

###### Laser marking (emerging) `mb.logic.package.marking.laser` _(medium)_

A Q-switched Nd:YAG or CO2 laser ablating characters into the epoxy surface, or a carbon laser removing the top layer to expose an underlying white layer. Fimeless, indelible and fast, but in 1983 it was still a premium option used mostly for military marking.

#### 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25) `mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257`

Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14) `mb.logic.u14-74ls258`

The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15) `mb.logic.u15-74ls139` _(medium)_

Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26) `mb.logic.u26-74ls373`

Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27) `mb.logic.u27-74ls08` _(medium)_

Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29) `mb.logic.u29-74ls74` _(low)_

Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30) `mb.logic.u30-74ls193` _(low)_

A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.

        - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31) `mb.logic.u31-74ls629` _(medium)_

Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.

##### The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629 `mb.logic.cmos` _(medium)_

Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.

###### The twin-tub CMOS flow `mb.logic.cmos.process`

The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

###### p-type substrate (and the tub) `mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate`

The wafer is p-type, lightly doped. On top of it two wells are implanted: a deep n-well and a somewhat shallower p-well. The n-well holds every p-channel transistor; the p-well (or the substrate itself, on simpler parts) holds every n-channel transistor. Two tubs, two polarities, one chip - that is the 'twin tub'. The wells must be deep enough that they do not punch through into each other and short the two transistor types together.

              - *Where the silicon came from* `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer` *(seen above)*
###### n-well and p-well implants `mb.logic.cmos.process.wells`

Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

###### The medium-current ion implanter `mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter` _(medium)_

A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.

                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
              - *Boron as the p dopant* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron` *(seen above)*
              - *Phosphine (PH3) for the n-type epilayer* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine` *(seen above)*
###### LOCOS isolation `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos`

Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

###### The silicon nitride masking film `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride`

A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed.

                - *Silane chemistry* `chem.silane` *(seen above)*
###### Ammonia (NH3) `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammonia`

The nitrogen source for the nitride. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by the Haber-Bosch process: nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas, over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm. So the mask that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.

###### Nitrogen from the air `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammonia.nitrogen`

The other half of Haber-Bosch: air separated by cryogenic distillation or pressure-swing adsorption into nitrogen and oxygen. 78 percent of the atmosphere, liquefied at one atmosphere only at 77 K, which is why air separation plants are enormous cryogenic plants.

###### Air `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammonia.nitrogen.air`

78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, 1 percent argon and carbon dioxide. The raw material for every cubic metre of ammonia, and therefore of every silicon nitride masking film, in the world.

###### Hydrogen for the ammonia `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.ammonia.hydrogen`

Steam-reformed methane, exactly the hydrogen that reduces the trichlorosilane into polysilicon. Two branches of the same industrial gas meet here: one gas becomes silicon, the other becomes the mask that patterns it.

                    - *Methane (natural gas)* `mb.logic.bipolar.wafer.polysilicon.hydrogen.smr.methane` *(seen above)*
###### Hot phosphoric acid for the nitride strip `mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric` _(medium)_

Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it. The acid was made by burning phosphorus - itself from phosphate rock - in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.

                - *Elemental phosphorus from phosphate rock* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.phosphine.phosphorus` *(seen above)*
###### The gate oxide `mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide`

Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

###### The polysilicon gate `mb.logic.cmos.process.poly`

A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.

###### Silane (SiH4) as the polysilicon feed `mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.silane-source` _(medium)_

Silane decomposes on a hot surface at 700-850 C to lay down pure polycrystalline silicon. It is a cleaner and more controllable feed than trichlorosilane - no chlorine, no corrosive by-products - and by the early 1980s it was becoming the preferred source for polysilicon deposition in CMOS even though trichlorosilane still dominated for boule-grade silicon.

                - *Silane chemistry* `chem.silane` *(seen above)*
###### The self-aligned source and drain `mb.logic.cmos.process.sd`

With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.

###### The source/drain anneal `mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal` _(medium)_

After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.

              - *The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter` *(seen above)*
###### Contact and aluminium interconnect `mb.logic.cmos.process.contact`

The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.

              - *Aluminium metallisation* `mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal` *(seen above)*
              - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it `mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation` _(medium)_

An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.

###### Where a 4066 puts its resistors `mb.logic.cmos.process.thinfilm` _(low)_

The 4000-series CMOS parts rarely needed resistors at all - CMOS logic is naturally high impedance, so biasing resistors are sparse - but the 4066's on-resistance trimmer and some bias chains did use deposited polysilicon resistors at a value set by sheet resistance and length. Poly resistors are cheap to add because they are made at the same time as the gate, from the same film, at no extra mask.

###### The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive `mb.logic.cmos.litho` _(medium)_

A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.

###### Positive photoresist and the end of negative resist `mb.logic.cmos.litho.positive`

A positive resist is a novolac resin with a photosensitive protecting group. Exposure breaks the group off, the exposed resin becomes soluble in the alkaline developer, and the pattern on the wafer is the same polarity as the pattern on the mask - no mental inversion, no image reversal, and better control of linewidth on steps. Positive resists went from invention in the 1940s to default in the late 1970s; by 1983 they had won MOS and were displacing negative resist on bipolar. Within a decade negative resist was gone from production lines entirely.

              - *Photoresist chemistry* `chem.photoresist` *(seen above)*
              - *Developing the image* `mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop` *(seen above)*
###### What a CMOS transmission gate is made of `mb.logic.cmos.switch`

The 4066's four 'bilateral switches' are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS.

###### Where the CMOS parts were made `mb.logic.cmos.fab` _(low)_

The 4066 and MC4044 were Motorola and RCA parts, made in Motorola's own bipolar-compatible CMOS lines and in the Japanese and Southeast Asian fabs that had been built to supply them. By 1983 the merchant CMOS capacity was expanding fast and much of it was in Japan and Korea, where the cost of a CMOS line was falling faster than in the United States.

            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### What CMOS became `mb.logic.cmos.now`

The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed - shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS and finally gave way to fin-shaped gates; the gate material changed from polysilicon to metal; the number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen; the light source went from a mercury lamp to an argon fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.

###### Shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS `mb.logic.cmos.now.scaling`

The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer as geometries shrank. Shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide and a nitride liner, gives a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward. It is a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea described in the bipolar branch.

        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
#### CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044 `mb.logic.cmos-4000`

Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.

        - *The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629* `mb.logic.cmos` *(seen above)*
        - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
##### LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part `mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556`

Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.

#### Famous 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64 `mb.logic.not-on-this-board` _(medium)_

A warning about the part list. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 and 74LS181 look-ahead carry chips and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list.

      - *The black epoxy DIP* `mb.logic.package` *(seen above)*
      - *How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)* `mb.logic.bipolar` *(seen above)*
      - *The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629* `mb.logic.cmos` *(seen above)*
#### Where Commodore's logic chips came from `mb.logic.sourcing` _(medium)_

Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job.

##### The merchant logic vendors `mb.logic.sourcing.makers`

Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work.

###### Texas Instruments `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti` _(medium)_

The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.

###### Fairchild `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild` _(medium)_

The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.

###### National Semiconductor `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national` _(medium)_

A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.

###### Motorola and Signetics `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola` _(medium)_

Motorola was the dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts - the MC4044 and MC4066 on the C64 - and Signetics had been an important TTL second source. The two had been linked by a licensing and cross-supply arrangement since 1969, so both names turned up in the same catalogue.

###### Hitachi, Toshiba and the Japanese suppliers `mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan` _(low)_

By the mid-1980s Japanese and then Korean vendors had taken a large share of world logic volume, and they were undercutting American silicon hard. C64 boards are also found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's own bill of materials got cheaper every year of its life.

##### Commodore's own second sources: the 77xx house numbers `mb.logic.sourcing.second-source` _(medium)_

To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64.

##### How the chips physically arrived in 1983 `mb.logic.sourcing.distribution` _(medium)_

Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all.

###### Allocation and the queue `mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.allocation` _(medium)_

When demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed. A computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated, pro rata, and had to schedule its production around delivery dates rather than around its own. This is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make.

###### Authorised versus unauthorised: the 'pulls' `mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.pulls` _(medium)_

Parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled'. This could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or it could be diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference. The industry response in the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it.

###### Incoming inspection at the Commodore plant `mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.incoming` _(low)_

Every shipment of semiconductors was counted, and the number was checked against the bill of materials before the parts went anywhere near a board. Chips that did not match were quarantined. This is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected: the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.

#### What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost `mb.logic.economics` _(low)_

The whole point of the comparison: a 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors with a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price.

##### Bill of materials for one 74LS04 `mb.logic.economics.bill` _(low)_

An honest accounting of what is actually inside one of these chips, with the arithmetic shown so it can be checked.

###### Silicon: about 3 mg, not 3-5 um `mb.logic.economics.bill.silicon` _(medium)_

The figure usually quoted for a 74-series chip - '3-5 um of silicon' - is the depth of the active junctions, the epitaxial collector plus base plus emitter, which is what a device-physics description means by it. The wafer itself is a 300 um thick slice, and a 74LS04 die of roughly 1.5 by 2.4 mm weighs about 3 mg. So the chip that contains the logic is a few milligrams of crystal and a few hundred of package.

            - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Aluminium: order 10-30 mg on the die `mb.logic.economics.bill.aluminium` _(low)_

One single metallisation level about 1.0-1.5 um thick, covering maybe half the die. For a 3.6 mm2 die that is a few cubic millimetres of metal - on the order of 10 to 30 milligrams, not the 0.3 g sometimes quoted. The discrepancy matters because it is the difference between the aluminium in the chip and the aluminium that went through the fab's sputtering equipment to make every chip on every wafer.

            - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Gold: under a milligram `mb.logic.economics.bill.gold` _(low)_

Gold enters twice. About eighteen wire bonds of 0.5-1.0 mil gold wire on a DIP-14 work out at a few tenths of a milligram in total. The die attach preform of gold-silicon eutectic adds a fraction of a milligram more. Together, roughly half a milligram to a milligram of gold per finished chip - and the industry had been actively trying to get rid of it, because gold was one of the two most expensive materials in the package.

            - *Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts* `metal.gold` *(seen above)*
###### Nickel-chromium: a film, not a lump `mb.logic.economics.bill.nicr` _(low)_

The thin-film resistors are the only place nickel and chromium appear in the die itself. A thousand or so angstroms of film over a few percent of the die area works out to well under a milligram, so the NiCr is chemically trivial even though it is functionally essential - every pull-up and bias resistor in a 74LS chip is made of it.

            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
            - *Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome* `metal.chromium` *(seen above)*
###### Nickel: mostly in the lead frame, not the chip `mb.logic.economics.bill.nickel` _(low)_

The largest mass of nickel in the whole device is in the lead frame, a strip of 42 percent nickel iron about 0.2 mm thick weighing on the order of 100 mg for a DIP-14, plus the plating. The nickel that matters for supply-chain purposes is in that frame, not in the silicon.

            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### Epoxy moulding compound: the heaviest part `mb.logic.economics.bill.compound` _(medium)_

By mass the epoxy moulding compound is the largest single material in the chip - 0.3 to 0.6 g of silica-filled thermoset, of which about three quarters is fused silica. The die is a hundredth of the package's weight. That is the whole story of the 1983 IC in one comparison: 3 mg of clever silicon buried in 400 mg of dull polymer, so that the 3 mg could be handled, protected, and plugged into a socket.

            - *Epoxy moulding compound* `mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound` *(seen above)*
###### Total weight of a 74LS04 `mb.logic.economics.bill.total` _(low)_

Roughly half a gram. A thousand chips would weigh half a kilogram; a C64's eleven glue chips weigh about five grams between them. The tree is deep and the material branches multiply, but the object itself is tiny, light and almost entirely plastic.

##### How much human time, spread how thin `mb.logic.economics.labour` _(low)_

The brief's figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is the right order of magnitude and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention. It is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow: the ~60-100 front-end steps, most of which run unattended inside a tool cycle of minutes but each of which needs a cassette loaded, a recipe checked, a defect inspection and a wafer-count reconciliation. Front-end and back-end together put the figure in the low hundreds of person-minutes. The rest of the cost was in the fab: capital, cleanroom air, process engineering, and yield learning spread over years and shared across millions of gates.

###### Flow time versus touch time `mb.logic.economics.labour.flow` _(medium)_

The distinction that makes the whole estimate work. A batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, and almost all of that time is waiting - in a furnace, in a queue, in a cassette under a nitrogen purge. What costs money is not the waiting; it is the roughly twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention. Over a fortnight, that is a couple of hours, not a couple of weeks.

##### The price gap between the glue and the CPU `mb.logic.economics.price` _(low)_

The commercially important fact about the 74-series on the C64 is that it was nearly free. A commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned. The 6510 was a custom NMOS design on a finer process, and as a custom part on a custom mask set it cost several dollars and could not be shared with anyone. Which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue - and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.

###### Why merchant logic was cheaper per function `mb.logic.economics.price.glue` _(medium)_

A merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow which makes dozens of other part numbers. Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set Commodore did not pay for and a design Commodore did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count: one mask set, one customer, one buyer, and a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit.

### Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV) `mb.rf-modulator`

The box on the C64 mainboard that turns the VIC-II's separate luma and colour outputs plus the SID's audio into one RF carrier for a television's antenna socket. Commodore published it as schematic 251025 and 251696: a handful of Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, one trimmer capacitor and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack and a ten-way terminal strip on the edge of the board.

#### Video amplifier and clip network `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain`

Three small-signal transistors that take the VIC-II's pin 15 (sync + luminance) and pin 14 (colour), clip them with back-to-back diodes, and provide the two separate buffered outputs that go to the monitor connector as S-Video plus the summed composite that drives the RF section. Commodore called Q1-Q3 2SC1694 or equivalent; the earlier 251696 drawing uses 2SC2405.

##### 2SC1694 small-signal NPN `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor`

A TO-92 epoxy-potted silicon NPN with a 100-150 V collector rating, used as a common-emitter amplifier with a collector resistor and an unbypassed emitter resistor. The 2SC-prefix parts were the standard Japanese equivalents of the 2N series, and Commodore specified them as 'or equivalent'.

###### Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging`

The die is a small epitaxial NPN on a 100 mm P-type <111> wafer, sawn with a diamond blade, die-attached with a silver-glass preform, wire-bonded with 50 um aluminium and transfer-moulded in an epoxy-filled TO-92 tool at 150-175 C.

###### Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin `chem.epoxy`

DGEBA epoxy is made by hydrolyzing bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinating to close the epoxide ring. About 800,000-1,000,000 tonnes of epoxy resin were made in 1983, of which the largest single use was the glass-reinforced laminate for printed circuit boards. A C64 has epoxy in its board, in the transformer and coil potting of its power supply, in the die-attach of its chips, and in the adhesive that holds the SID's heatsink tab.

###### DGEBA (diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A) `chem.epoxy.dgeba`

The workhorse epoxy: bisphenol A condensed with two moles of epichlorohydrin, giving a resin with an epoxide group at each end of the molecule and epoxide number 172-190 equivalents per 100 g. It is a solid at room temperature (melting 4-12 C for the liquid grades) and it cures into a cross-linked network with anything that has active hydrogen or amino groups.

###### Epichlorohydrin `chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin`

1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane: the C3 building block. In 1983 most of the world's epichlorohydrin was made by the chlorohydrin route - propylene chlorohydrin from propylene plus hypochlorous acid, dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry - which is the same chlorohydrin chemistry that makes propylene oxide. It is a sensitiser and a carcinogen, and it is the reason the epoxy industry carried the same respiratory-protection regime as the propylene oxide plants.

###### Bisphenol A from cumene `chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a`

Two phenol molecules plus acetone, condensed over a strong acid to give 4,4'-isopropylidenediphenol, with the water stripped. In 1983 most BPA was made this way from the cumene process's phenol, and the rest from the older two-step route using bis(4-chlorophenyl) ketone. The 1980s were the period when BPA's endocrine activity was being investigated by accident, and when the epoxy industry began to substitute boron oxides and novolac epoxies to remove it from can linings and bottle resins.

###### Acetone as the BPA co-reactant `chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone`

The BPA reaction is where the case polymer meets the laminate resin: the phenol for BPA comes out of the cumene oxidation that also yields the acetone for the reaction, so the two halves of bisphenol A come from one reactor 20 km apart. The same bisphenol A went into the polycarbonate and the unsaturated polyester of the era.

###### Curing agents `chem.epoxy.hardeners`

An epoxy is useless until something cross-links it, and the curing agent decides the properties. Amines (aliphatic triethylenetetramine, cycloaliphatic diamines) give fast cures at room temperature and good mechanical properties; anhydrides give high-temperature cures and excellent electrical insulation, which is why the power supply's transformer potting and the chips' die attach were epoxy; and the phenols and novolacs give the flame-retardant laminates.

###### Amine cure and its problem `chem.epoxy.hardeners.amine-cure` _(medium)_

A primary or secondary amine adds to the strained epoxide ring, which is what starts the cure. The classic complaint of amine-cured epoxy is amine blush - a sticky, hygroscopic surface film from an atmospheric amine-carbon dioxide reaction with surface epoxy - and the reason the die-attach and potting processes of the 1980s used a controlled-amine epoxy with a controlled cure cycle rather than a general-purpose one.

###### 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS) `chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds` _(medium)_

The high-temperature laminate hardener: about 80 parts per 100 of DGEBA, cured at 180-200 C. DDS is made by sulphonating diphenyl sulphone, nitrating it to the dinitro compound and reducing the nitro groups - an aniline and chlorobenzene route for the aniline part. It is the hardener in the aerospace laminates and in the higher-temperature grades of FR-4, and it costs several times what the amine does.

###### 4,4'-Diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM/MDA) `chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd` _(medium)_

Made by condensing aniline with formaldehyde, it is the first-generation hardener: cheap, and it is the amine that showed up in the early carcinogenicity work on epoxies in the 1970s, which pushed the industry toward DDM's less toxic relatives. It is still in laminates and in the rubber industry as a vulcanisation accelerator.

###### Anhydride cure `chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride` _(medium)_

A cyclic anhydride (a methyl substituted tetrahydrophthalic or nadic anhydride) catalysed by an amine or a tertiary amine. The cure is slower and needs 150-200 C, but the network is very tight and the dielectric properties are excellent - which is why anhydride epoxy was the potting and the chip-attach system of the 1980s, where a chip sitting on a cured epoxy die attach with a controlled coefficient of thermal expansion was worth the cure temperature.

###### Branched and novolac epoxies `chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy` _(medium)_

Reacting DGEBA with a dihydroxy or trihydroxy compound - trimethylolpropane, bisphenol A again, or an epoxy cresol novolac - builds a molecule with more than two epoxide groups and higher functionality, which raises the glass transition temperature and lets a laminate hold a solder temperature. The epoxy novolac also carried the bromine: brominating the ring gives the flame-retardant epoxy that FR-4 used.

###### Brominated epoxy for FR-4 `chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy` _(medium)_

Tetrabromobisphenol A based epoxy, brominated to about 20-40% bromine, blended into the resin at 10-30% so the laminate meets UL 94 V-0. The bromine works by releasing hydrogen bromide in the flame and smothering it, and it works so well that the industry continued using it through the 1980s even as the first brominated flame retardant ban had already arrived. It is the epoxy in the C64's board.

###### Epoxy in a C64 `chem.epoxy.uses-c64` _(low)_

Four places. The board's laminate resin. The power supply's transformer bobbin and coil potting, and the mains filter capacitor's encapsulation. The die attach inside the VIC-II, the SID and the CPU packages, where the chip was bonded to a small ceramic or epoxy header with an epoxy that had to survive 180-260 C without delaminating. And the heatsink adhesive in the SID's tab, which in some designs was a two-part filled epoxy.

###### Semiconductor silicon, from quartz `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging.quartz`

Quartz (SiO2) is reduced with petroleum coke in an electric arc furnace at 1800-2000 C to 97-99% metallurgical silicon, upgraded by trichlorosilane disproportionation to 9-11N polycrystalline silicon, pulled as a Czochralski single crystal, sawn and polished. This is the shared root of every silicon device in the C64.

###### High-purity quartz `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging.quartz.quartz-ore`

Pegmatite and vein quartz, acid-leached and hydrothermally purified to 99.99% SiO2, is the only commercial source of semiconductor silicon. This is the leaf of the silicon branch.

###### Petroleum: light sour crude oil `chem.petroleum` _(medium)_

The dig-it-out endpoint of the whole petrochemical chain. Crude is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons from methane to asphaltenes, plus sulphur compounds, nitrogen compounds, resins, asphaltenes and trace metals. The grades that feed the 1980s steam crackers are light, low-sulphur: Arab Light at 35-36 degrees API and Brent Blend at 38-39 were the benchmarks of the era.

                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Electric arc furnace reduction of quartz `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging.quartz.quartz-ore.arc-furnace`

Quartz is mixed with petroleum coke and heated to 1800-2000 C by an electric arc furnace submerged in the charge. The carbon reduces SiO2 to silicon while the arc supplies the heat; the reaction is strongly endothermic and the furnace is the single biggest electricity consumer in the whole silicon chain.

                  - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Carbothermal slag `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging.quartz.quartz-ore.arc-furnace.slag`

The liquid residue from the arc furnace is calcium silicate, formed because limestone is deliberately added as a flux to keep the furnace from silting up. It is ground and sold as cement or as a road aggregate; a few hundred kg of slag per tonne of silicon is the main waste stream of the process.

                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Trichlorosilane and the Siemens process `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.sources`

The upgrade from 99% to 11N silicon is done in a fluidised-bed Siemens reactor: hydrogen reduces trichlorosilane vapour with the deposited silicon as the seed, at 1000-1150 C, growing rods of polycrystalline silicon at a few mm per minute. Trichlorosilane itself is made by chlorinating metallurgical silicon with hydrogen chloride at 250-350 C.

###### Polycrystalline silicon rod `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.sources.rod` _(medium)_

A 100-150 mm diameter, 1-2 m long rod of 11N silicon, sawn into ~250 mm slices by an inner-diameter or wire saw. In 1982 nearly all wafers were still sawn with an abrasive ID saw and then lapped, which is why wafers were 200-300 um thick before polishing took them to 250-300 um; the wafer laser was commercial but not universal.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
##### 1SS119 / MA151K clip diodes `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes`

Small-signal switching diodes, typically 50 mA class in a DO-35 glass can, wired back to back across the sync input. They conduct only on the tips of the sync pulses and the colour burst, which clips the signal to the amplitude a television's AGC expects and stops the modulator over-modulating.

#### Picture carrier oscillator `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator`

A Clapp or Colpitts oscillator built around Q4 (2SC1730, a VHF transistor with an f_T above 300 MHz) and a miniature RF transformer, with a capacitive divider setting the feedback ratio. Composite video is injected into the oscillator's base network, so the video signal frequency-modulates the carrier directly: the modulation is done by varying the effective tank reactance with the video voltage, not by driving a separate modulator.

##### 2SC1730 / 2SC2778 VHF transistor `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transistor` _(medium)_

A VHF small-signal NPN in TO-92, chosen because its unity-gain bandwidth is several times the 60 MHz operating frequency so the oscillator starts easily and stays linear, and because its output capacitance is low enough not to detune the tank.

          - *Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding* `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging` *(seen above)*
##### Channel and region switching `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-selection`

Three different ways of reaching the right channel appear across the revisions. The US 5-pin and 8-pin machines use a two-position H-L switch on the rear panel wired to change a component value in the oscillator tank or level network. Some later units bring a variable capacitor or a trimmer out to a dial so the user can tune to their local station. PAL machines use the UHF band, so their oscillator runs at several times the frequency of the NTSC one and the tank and output matching are different parts entirely.

###### Rocker switch `c64.mains.switch`

A mains switch in the line conductor, mounted in the case wall so the rocker is the only part exposed. It is a snap-action mechanism: a spring-loaded plunger forces a moving contact against a fixed one with a definite wiping motion as it passes through centre, which both makes the circuit and scrapes oxide off the contact faces.

###### Silver-alloy contacts and arc erosion `c64.mains.switch.contacts`

Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any metal and, unlike copper, its oxide is still conductive, so a silver contact keeps working even when it blackens. Contacts are riveted or welded to brass carriers so the spring force is set by the carrier rather than by the contact material. Every make operation evaporates a microscopic amount of metal as an arc; the contact is sized so that tens of thousands of makes erode it only slightly, and so that a failed contact fails open rather than welded shut.

              - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
###### Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts `metal.tin`

Tin is the metal that made electronics solderable. On a 1982 C64 board there are roughly 3,500 through-hole joints and most of them are joined with a lead-tin alloy, so there is a couple of hundred grams of tin per machine. Tin also does two other jobs in the machine: it is the coating on tin-plated steel (tinplate, though a home computer case is not canned food) and it is the facing on tin-plated copper-alloy switch and connector contacts, where it stops the copper from tarnishing and gives a low and stable contact resistance.

###### Cassiterite concentrate (SnO2) `metal.cassiterite`

Cassiterite is a very heavy, very hard, brown-to-black mineral - the specific gravity of 7 makes gravity separation unusually effective on it, which is why tin mining has always had a placer tradition. The concentrates bought by an smelter in 1982 came from four very different operations: alluvial and offshore dredging in Malaysia and Indonesia, hard-rock lodes in the Bolivian and Brazilian Precambrian shields, hard-rock in Cornwall and the Pan, and shallow residual deposits in Thailand and Nigeria. Concentrates assayed 40-80% Sn with arsenic, iron, tungsten and fluorine as the problem impurities - fluorine in particular is the reason the Bolivian smelter needed a roast.

###### Alluvial cassiterite gravel: dredging and panning `metal.cassiterite.alluvial`

Tin gravel is a beach or stream deposit: pebbles and clay with a few grams of cassiterite per tonne. The classical recovery is the sluice and the jig, where a stream of water over an inclined riffled box stratifies by density and the heavy mineral stays behind. The Kinta Valley in Perak, Malaysia, was dredged on an enormous scale from the 1900s through the 1980s by suction dredges working a 100 m wide alluvial fan at 30-100 m depth, pumping gravel through a 3-6 inch suction pipe to a floating washing plant and a jig. Off Thailand and Indonesia it was offshore and shallow-sea dredging. Gravel is essentially quarried from a sea floor.

###### Stanniferous alluvium and laterite `metal.cassiterite.gravel`

The leaf: unconsolidated stony clay and gravel of a valley floor or a coastal plain, with cassiterite grains scattered through it and concentrated at the base of gravel layers where the wave or the stream action is right. In Malaysia it is a young alluvial fan over limestone; in Bolivia it is not alluvial at all but a hard-rock lode in Ordovician slates and granites, which is why Bolivia's process chain is longer.

###### Cassiterite lode in the Bolivian and Cornwall tin belt `metal.cassiterite.lode`

For contrast: the tin lodes of the Cordillera Real in Bolivia and of the Cambrian granite cupolas in Cornwall are hydrothermal cassiterite in quartz veins and greisens, and they have to be blasted and milled. Bolivia's Oruro and La Paz districts still supply a fraction of world tin from ore averaging 0.3-1% Sn, with the famous manioc mill and the hydraulic concentrator. Cornwall's industry was by 1982 essentially finished - the last deep mine closed in 1984 - a hundred years after the smelter industry had been moved to the East.

###### Greisen and quartz vein `metal.cassiterite.greisen`

The leaf for the hard-rock route: a pneumatolytic alteration halo of topaz-bearing greisen and milky quartz with cassiterite disseminated through it, around a granite cupola. It is a rock, it is in a hillside, and it is drilled.

###### Topaz and the greisen alteration `metal.cassiterite.topaz` _(medium)_

The leaf, geologically: a pneumatolytic alteration halo around the granite cupola in which the feldspars are replaced by topaz (Al2SiO4F2) and quartz, and in the interstices sit the crystals of cassiterite, wolframite and native bismuth. The fluorine in the topaz is the whole reason the alteration happened - it is a fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluid - which is a satisfying way for the tin branch to close, because the same fluorine chemistry that greened the rocks is the fluorine chemistry that made the cryolite in the aluminium pot and the hydrofluoric acid for the silicon plant.

###### Tin smelting: reduction of SnO2 with carbon `metal.tin.smelting`

Cassiterite is one of the easiest oxide ores to reduce: SnO2 + C -> Sn + CO2 goes at only 1200-1400 C, far below copper or iron, because tin's oxides are unstable. The Malaysian and Indonesian smelters in 1982 were reverberatory or electric furnaces on 5-20 t capacity, fired with coke, charged with concentrate and about 15% limestone as a flux, and tapped a crude tin at 99.5-99.8% in maybe eight hours. The furnace is a long, narrow, brick-lined box with a step grate at the firebox end, so the charge moves gradually forward and meets rising temperatures - a reverberatory used for a purely solid-solid reaction, which is why tin smelting smells of SO2 only when the concentrate is sulphide.

###### Fluid-bed reduction of fine cassiterite (later invention) `metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor` _(medium)_

Worth noting as the direction the industry went in rather than as 1982 practice: the fine concentrates that a gravity circuit now produces reduce easily in a fluidised bed at 850-1000 C, which is a temperature no reverberatory furnace can hold at its hearth. This process is why the modern tin industry uses much less coke and produces much less CO. In 1982 essentially none of this existed.

###### Roasting of fluorine-bearing Bolivian concentrate `metal.tin.bolivian-roast` _(medium)_

Bolivian concentrates carry fluorine, which would carry through into the tin as a stubborn impurity. So they are roasted at 600-800 C before smelting to drive off the fluorine as HF and the arsenic as arsenic oxide, and the hot gas is scrubbed with lime to make calcium fluoride before release. That lime scrub is a genuine environmental control fitted in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is one of the reasons the smelters are the only tin plants with a scrubber.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) and hydrofluoric acid `metal.fluorspar`

Fluorine chemistry is unavoidable in aluminium and unavoidable in the tin smelter's gas scrub and in the tantalum digest. Fluorspar, the commonest natural fluoride, was mined mainly from Mexico's San Luis Potosi and Chihuahua districts and from South Africa's Transvaal, and about 90% of all fluorite went into aluminium electrolysis - as cryolite feed, as calcium fluoride in the bath, and as flux. Hydrofluoric acid is made from it, and HF is the reagent that turns silicon into trichlorosilane in the silicon branch, tantalum into K2TaF7 in the tantalum branch, and glass into etch gas in the plastics-and-glass branch - so this is one of the genuine convergence points of the whole tree. Note that the 1980s ozone worry about fluorocarbons does NOT apply here: this is the calcium salt, not a CFC.

###### Fluorite open-pit and underground mine `metal.fluorspar.mine` _(medium)_
