Fluorite fills the cavities and fracture zones of limestone, so it is mined either as a replacement body in a working limestone quarry or as a vein. Mexican fluorite was underground at Naica - where it grows the famous 12 m transparent crystals in a cave - and in open pits in Chihuahua. The South African deposits are in the carbonate sequences of the Transvaal Group, and the Chinese and Mongolian ones, which became dominant in the late 1980s, are in greisen and vein systems related to granite.

###### Fluorite vein in limestone `metal.fluorspar.vein`

The leaf: a purple, green or white vein of CaF2 a few centimetres to a few metres thick in a fractured carbonate host, in a limestone hill.

###### Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar `metal.hydrofluoric-acid`

The corrosive reagent. Fluorspar plus sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride in a kiln at 200-300 C; fluorspar plus concentrated sulfuric acid in a rotary kiln gives anhydrous HF directly, and the anhydrous route is what makes water-free fluorinations possible. HF is the reagent for silicon to trichlorosilane, tantalum to K2TaF7, glass etching, uranium hexafluoride, and the fluorochemical industry generally.

###### Charge preparation: drying, sieving, mixing `metal.tin.charge-prep` _(medium)_

Cassiterite concentrates are roasted if they carry fluorine or arsenic, dried to remove the 8-12% moisture, and sieved - because a reverberatory furnace with fine charge in it just makes dust. The charge is then mixed with the limestone flux and the coke, in the ratio that gives 15-20% flux and 15-25% reductant. Nothing about this is clever and everything about it is critical: an Indonesian smelter that got the coke ratio wrong lost a few percent of its tin into the slag, which at 3% is a third of its margin.

###### The tin smelter's slag and its tin loss `metal.tin.slag` _(medium)_

A tin smelter loses 1-3% of its tin into the slag, and the slag is a silicate of iron and silica with tin locked up in it. Recovering that tin is a separate business: the slag is crushed and re-smelted, or in Malaysia and Brazil it was re-smelted in a small furnace to recover the tin. A tin smelter therefore has a second, smaller smelter, and the discipline of a tin plant is judged by its recovery, which is why the industry published recovery figures with a seriousness that most primary metals do not.

###### Tin refining: liquation or electrolysis to 99.9% `metal.tin.refining`

Crude tin at 99.5-99.8% still carries iron, copper and arsenic, and the difference between 99.5% and 99.9% matters enormously for solder because iron is a solder poison and raises the liquidus. Two routes. Liquation, the old one, melts the crude tin at about 400 C: tin melts at 232 C, so the iron and copper stay solid and bottom out, and the clean tin is drawn off. Electrolysis, the modern one, uses a stannic chloride or a fluorostannate bath and gives 99.97-99.99%. Malaysia ran electrolysis; Bolivia's low-grade concentrate still used liquation.

###### Refined tin ingot or tin powder, 99.9-99.97% `metal.tin.ingot`

Shipped as a 25-50 kg or 250 kg ingot at 99.9-99.97%, or - for the electronics industry - atomised into a fine powder. This is the deliberate convergence point of the tin smelting branch and the solder branch: the solder manufacturer needs the ingot, and the solder-paste manufacturer needs the powder. Iron is the impurity that matters, because iron is a solder poison that wets badly and raises the liquidus.

###### Air atomisation of tin to powder `metal.tin.atomisation` _(medium)_

Molten tin at about 1150 C is poured into a launder and a high-pressure air jet at the bottom of a vertical stack sprays it into a fog of droplets that solidify on the way down. It is cheap, it works for metals that do not oxidise much, and it gives a bimodal powder. Under nitrogen it gives the fine, oxide-free powder that solder paste needs. Every particle in the can came out of a slot in a nozzle.

###### Tin plating of steel and of copper alloys `metal.tin.plating`

Tinplate - a 1.1-11.2 g/m2 tin coating on 0.15-0.3 mm of steel - is made by electrolytic tinning of a continuous steel strip on a horizontal passivating line: the strip is degreased, pickled in acid, tinned in a sulphate or fluoroborate bath, rinsed, and then either passivated in chromic acid (food can) or - through the 1980s - given an electrolytic chromate or tin-oxide passivation to stop the tin growing dendrites during storage. Food can was the dominant market by mass. A C64 uses tinplate only incidentally, in a switch body or a shield; tin plating of copper-alloy contacts uses a different chemistry altogether and is the node that matters for the machine.

###### Tin plating of copper-alloy contacts `metal.tin.contact-plating` _(medium)_

Not tinplate on steel, but tin on brass or phosphor bronze - the plating on the contacts of a C64 switch or a keyboard connector. The 1980s chemistry was an acid stannate or an alkaline stannate bath: SnSO4 with sulfuric acid, or sodium stannate with caustic soda and a puller such as sodium gluconate. Tin is on a connector contact because it forms a soft, low-resistance, non-tarnishing intermetallic with the copper. The reason it fails is the tin whisker - a single-crystal filament of tin that grows out of the plating under compressive stress in humid storage and can bridge a 0.1 mm gap. Tin whiskers were the reliability nemesis of exactly this kind of contact.

###### Copper and silver ores `c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver`

The moving and fixed blades are brass or phosphor bronze (copper with tin), and the contact faces are silver. Copper comes from sulphide concentrate and silver from argentiferous lead ores or from cyanide leaching of low-grade residues.

                - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
###### Lead: the other half of the solder `metal.lead`

Lead is the soft, low-melting, cheap half of the solder alloy, and it is the reason soldering works at all: pure tin wets copper badly and has no strength, and pure lead does not wet anything. Lead also has its own huge pre-electronics industrial life - storage batteries, cable sheath, pigment - and its 1982 smelting industry is the oldest continuous industrial process in the book. The C64 carries a couple of hundred grams of it, which is why the machine is the emblem of leaded-solder legislation.

###### Galena (PbS) concentrate `metal.galena`

Galena is cubic, bright grey when fresh and dull grey when oxidised, extremely heavy at 7.6 g/cm3, and it is one of the few common ores that a prospector could identify by eye. The great mining districts in 1982 were the Tri-State district of Missouri, Oklahoma and Kansas (which supplied most of the United States' lead and is a fossil limestone-hosted deposit), the Broken Hill and Mount Isa districts of Australia, Cerro de Pasco and Huancavelica in Peru, and the Iberian and Atlas belts. Concentrates assay 40-75% Pb and are always accompanied by enough silver and zinc to make a good deal of the mine's revenue.

###### Underground lead-zinc mine `metal.galena.mine`

The Tri-State district's galena bodies sit as veins and bedding replacements in Mississippian limestone only a few metres thick, and they were worked by room-and-pillar mining - essentially taking the limestone out and leaving the lead in place, because the ore grade at 3-6% Pb did not pay for selective mining. The mineral was hand-picked off the back of the working face and off the cars. This is a soft-rock, shallow, cheap mining operation, and its day had largely gone by 1982 as the deeper and lower-grade Missouri deposits took over.

###### Galenite replacement in carbonate rock `metal.galena.rock`

The leaf: galena crystals and veins in a fossiliferous limestone - literally the remains of a Carboniferous sea floor. The Tri-State district is one of the great fossil-mineral coincidences of industrial history: a lead-bearing limestone under a farm field.

###### Hand picking and gravity sorting `metal.galena.sorting` _(medium)_

The Tri-State district's ore was a 3-6% lead limestone that could not be selectively mined and could not be concentrated, so the technique was brute force: the rock was shot down, the lead-bearing rock was picked out of the face by hand by a face worker, and then the cars were run over a sorting table or a picking table where a sorter took out the visibly lead-coloured lumps from the limestone. In 1930 the Tri-State had about 15,000 sorters - a third of them children - and that is what made the district the largest lead producer on Earth. It is a labour technique rather than a machine, and it is a genuine leaf of the tree.

###### The sorting table `metal.galena.sorting-table` _(medium)_

A sloping table with a light on it and a raised lip, worked by two or three people, one on each side. Galena is bright and heavy and galena-bearing limestone is dark and light, so the visual contrast is real, and the sorter's job is to lift out the dark lumps at perhaps 2-4 tonnes per shift. It is the lowest-skill, lowest-pay, highest-volume job in the lead industry, and it is where a great many Missouri families started.

###### Roasting/sintering of galena to PbO `metal.lead.sintering`

The concentrate is roasted in a sinter plant: a travelling grate on which a 1-2 m bed of concentrate is ignited and slowly drawn through with the gas being pulled after the fire. The sulphide oxidises to lead(II) oxide: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. The point of sintering rather than fluidised-bed roasting is that the heat can be high and localised enough to sinter the fine particles into a coherent porous cake, which is exactly what the blast furnace needs to breathe. The sinter is 50-60% Pb and the SO2 - at 10-14% - goes to the acid plant, the same one the copper smelter uses.

###### Dwight-Lloyd sinter strand `metal.lead.sinter-plant`

A continuous chain of cast-iron pallets on an endless track about 1.2-1.5 m wide, with the ignition hood at the discharge end. Feed is a mix of concentrate, sinter returns, flux and coke spread to exactly 1-2 m - there is nothing clever about it and it works. The strand advances 1-2 m/min, the fire burns through the bed in about 20 minutes, and the hot sinter is broken off by a set of crusher jaws at the end and tipped into the blast furnace. One machine makes 200-400 t of sinter an hour and runs continuously for years.

###### Self-fluxing sinter mix `metal.lead.self-fluxing` _(medium)_

Sinter is not simply roasted concentrate. The mix is designed so the sintered cake is its own flux: the silica that comes with the concentrate is balanced with limestone so the blast furnace slag has a basicity near 1.5-2.0. Anything between about 1.0 and 2.0 works; outside that range the slag either freezes in the furnace or dissolves too much lead. The smelter's metallurgist is balancing silica, iron, calcium and lead every shift.

                  - *Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead* `metal.lead.blast-furnace` *(seen above)*
###### Silver refining from lead residues `c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.silver-refining`

Argentiferous lead concentrates are roasted and smelted, and the silver reports to the lead bullion, from which it is recovered by Parkes' process: the bullion is cooled so copper crystallises out and is skimmed, then zinc is added, which scavenges the silver and gold into a zinc crust that is skimmed off and distilled. The crude silver is cupelled and electrolytically refined to 99.9% or better.

                  - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
                  - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
###### Cupellation `c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.silver-refining.cupellation`

An ancient refining step that survives into the 1980s for precious metals: the metal is melted with a lead oxide flux and blown with air, which oxidises the lead and the base metals to litharge that floats off, while the silver and gold stay as metal. Agricola described it in the 16th century and it is still the standard way to remove base metal from silver dross.

                    - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Rocker actuator and case `c64.mains.switch.actuator`

The external rocker is moulded in a glass-filled thermoset or a self-extinguishing thermoplastic and clips over a phenolic or nylon body carrying the fixed contacts. The case must be rated for the insulation class and have the flammability rating appropriate to an appliance, and the actuator must not be able to be jammed in the on position.

###### ABS resin plant, and the C64 case `chem.abs`

Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene is not a copolymer but a polymer blend: a SAN matrix with a grafted polybutadiene rubber phase dispersed in it as 0.1-10 micron particles. Making it is four separate unit operations - make the rubber, graft styrene and acrylonitrile onto it, make the matrix, blend and pelletise - and then a fifth that most people forget, drying. The C64's case, its keyboard surround and the beige plastic of its keys are this material.

###### Graft copolymerisation: growing SAN on the rubber `chem.abs.grafting`

The heart of the process. 20-40 parts of a low-cis polybutadiene rubber dissolved in xylene or toluene is charged to a reactor, and styrene plus acrylonitrile is added at 60-80 C in the presence of a persulphate initiator, a chelating agent and a mercaptan chain transfer agent. The radicals abstract a hydrogen from the polybutadiene's 1,2-vinyl unit, creating a radical site on the rubber; styrene and acrylonitrile then copolymerise from that site, and SAN chains grow out of the rubber particle. Each particle therefore becomes a rubber core with a SAN shell.

###### The polybutadiene rubber phase `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase`

A low-cis (40-60% cis, therefore glassy rather than rubbery on its own) butyllithium-polymerised polybutadiene at 0.5-2% residual oil, with the whole chain ending in a couple of reactive sites. The low cis content is deliberate: a high-cis rubber dissolves in its own polymer at reactor temperature and the particle boundaries blur, whereas a low-cis rubber keeps a sharp core-shell particle that survives compounding.

###### Butadiene monomer for the rubber phase `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw`

99.0-99.7% butadiene from a cracker C4 extraction unit. The chain is why the C64's rubber phase is a petrochemical and not a natural rubber: the natural rubber alternative is cis-1,4-polyisoprene from latex, and the graft chemistry that works on polybutadiene's pendant vinyl group does not work on isoprene's chain.

###### Getting 99.7% butadiene out of the cracker's C4 `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction`

An ABS plant in 1983 did not make its own butadiene. It bought polymerisation-grade monomer, which meant the plant upstream had to extract butadiene from a C4 stream where it is one component among six, with a relative volatility from the alpha-olefins of about 1.01. That extraction unit is one of the largest distillation towers in the chemical industry, and its solvent is a forestry chemical or a pyrrolidone - so the rubber phase of a C64's case starts in a pine forest or a cracker, and the choice between them is thirty years old.

###### The extraction unit `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction.sounsby-unit`

Two columns, each 40-70 m tall: the first extracts butadiene and the butenes into the solvent, the second strips pure butadiene overhead and recycles the solvent. Capacity on a single unit in 1983 was 100,000-400,000 tonnes a year of C4, and the column's diameter was the throughput. It was also, incidentally, the largest single user of furfural or NMP in the world.

###### Furfural from pentosan (the forestry route) `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction.sounsby-unit.furfural-from-pentosan` _(medium)_

Furfural is made by treating a pentosan - hemicellulose, which is a fifth of the dry weight of a hardwood - with acid and steam. The classic sources are rice hulls, corn cobs and bagasse, the fibrous residue of sugar cane after the juice has been squeezed out. A C64's rubber phase, if the extractor ran on furfural, traces back through a cracker and an extractor to a sugarcane field. That is the least obviously petroleum thing in the machine.

###### NMP from butanone `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction.sounsby-unit.nmp-from-butanone` _(medium)_

The petrochemical route to N-methylpyrrolidone: butanone and ethylenediamine condensed to a cyclic amide, then methylated. Both reactants are cheap petrochemicals - butanone from acetone or from butanol, ethylenediamine from ethylene oxide or from 1,2-dichloroethane - so the same solvent molecule could be made from a cracker or bought from a forestry route. By the 1980s the chemical route had won, and NMP then went on to displace the chlorinated degreasers.

###### The methanol in the NMP `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction.sounsby-unit.nmp-from-butanone.methanol`

The last step of the NMP route is a methylation, and the methylating agent is methanol, which in 1983 was made from synthesis gas - from natural gas by steam reforming, or from coal, whichever the country had. So the degreaser that replaced the chlorinated solvents in the electronics plant was, three steps back, natural gas; and the plastic it was replacing in the very same plant was naphtha. Two feedstocks, one plant.

###### Methanol from synthesis gas `chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene-raw.cracker-c4-extraction.sounsby-unit.nmp-from-butanone.methanol.synthesis-gas`

CO plus hydrogen at 200-300 C and 50-100 bar over a copper-zinc-aluminium catalyst gives methanol. The hydrogen comes from a reformer - so from natural gas - and the carbon monoxide from the reformed methane, from coal gasification, or from coke oven gas depending on the country. By 1983 more than half the world's methanol was made from natural gas, which makes methanol a gas product that behaves like a liquid fuel, and is the reason the world's gas and coal markets met inside a single molecule.

###### How butadiene is polymerised `chem.butadiene.polymerisation`

Three chemistries, chosen for what you were making. Emulsion polymerisation gives cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and vinyl-1,2 structures mixed - a rubber but not a specific one. Anionic polymerisation with lithium butyllithium gives cis-1,4 selectively and controls chain ends. Coordination polymerisation with neodymium or titanium gives cis-1,4 with an extremely high cis content. The 4-vinyl group left on a cis-1,4 chain is the reactive site that grafting later exploits.

###### The four polybutadiene microstructures `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures` _(medium)_

cis-1,4 (the elastomer; the chain is flexible below its glass transition), trans-1,4 (the chain is regular and crystalline, so it is a plastic not a rubber), 1,2-vinyl (a pendant vinyl group, also rubbery but with a high glass transition because of the pendant group), and 3,4-vinyl (rare). The rubbery ones are cis-1,4 and 1,2; the ratio between them is set by temperature, catalyst and solvent, and it is why polybutadiene rubber has a glass transition near -100 C and is the most flexible of the common rubbers.

###### Controlling cis, trans and vinyl `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.microstructure-control` _(medium)_

The ratio of the four microstructures is not an accident; it is the dial the polymer chemist turns. Coordination catalysts with a rare earth or a titanium give cis-1,4 because the metal holds the growing chain in a specific geometry. Lithium butyllithium in a polar solvent gives more 1,2-vinyl; in a hydrocarbon it gives more cis-1,4. Temperature moves it again. And each structure has a different transition: cis-1,4 is the rubber, trans-1,4 crystallises into a hard plastic, and 1,2-vinyl is rubbery but with a pendant group that lifts its glass transition by about 20 C.

###### Lithium butyllithium polymerisation `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-catalyst`

The living anionic process: butyllithium in a hydrocarbon diluent (diesel oil or hexane) at 0-60 C, with the cis content set by solvent and temperature. Living means the chain end stays active, so the polymer can be chain-stopped with an electrophile - water, carbon dioxide, epoxide - and the whole molecule is a single block. This is the chemistry that makes the ABS graft rubber phase possible.

###### Butyllithium `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-catalyst.butyllithium`

A pyrophoric organolithium, always supplied as a 10-20% solution in hexane and never in bulk. In 1980s practice it was the initiator for the solution polymerisation of polybutadiene and for the SBR made by anionic polymerisation, and its manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane was a speciality chemical operation with a lot of solvent handling.

###### Neodymium-catalysed cis-polybutadiene `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-catalyst` _(medium)_

The high-cis technology of the 1980s: a neodymium (or lanthanide) compound with an alkylaluminium in a hydrocarbon diluent gives 97-99% cis-1,4, and because the cis content is so high the rubber does not need to be plasticised with oil. Linear low-cis polybutadiene was the growth product of the decade; the older lithium-process cis-PB at 90-95% was still the volume product in 1983.

###### Neodymium from bastnasite `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-catalyst.neodymium-source`

The high-cis polybutadiene catalyst needs a rare earth metal, and the rare earths come from bastnasite, a light-brown carbonatite ore mined in Mountain Pass, California, in Bayan Obo in China, and in Australia and India, concentrated and then separated by a long solvent-extraction cascade. The separation is the interesting part: fifteen chemically similar elements have to be separated one at a time by a solvent-extraction train, and the neodymium is the one that came into industrial demand in the 1980s for reasons nobody had predicted - a rubber catalyst.

###### Bastnasite ore `chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-catalyst.neodymium-source.bastnasite` _(medium)_

A light rare earth carbonate fluorosilicate, about 6-9% rare earth oxides, discovered in 1878 at Bastnas in Sweden and mined in quantity from 1949. It is the last dig-it-out node of the ABS branch's rubber phase: a C64's rubber comes from butadiene from a cracker, but the catalyst that gives that butadiene its cis content begins in a carbonatite dyke in California or in Inner Mongolia.

###### Potassium persulphate initiator `chem.abs.grafting.initiator` _(medium)_

K2S2O8 at 0.1-0.5 parts per 100 monomer, thermally decomposed in the aqueous-organic system at 60-80 C. The persulphate is deliberately an aqueous-phase initiator: it generates radicals in the aqueous phase, which is where the monomer droplets are, so grafting starts on the surface of the rubber particle rather than deep in the hydrocarbon phase.

###### Chelating agent `chem.abs.grafting.chelant` _(medium)_

A polycarboxylic acid or its salt - trisodium citrate, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt, or a polyacrylate - at 0.05-0.3 parts. It chelates the trace transition metals that would otherwise decompose the persulphate catalytically and produce a wild, uncontrolled radical rate. In the 1980s this was a standard part of the recipe and one of the few places where a detergent chemistry shows up inside a structural plastic.

###### Chain transfer agent (modifier) `chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent` _(medium)_

A mercaptan - typically a tertiary dodecyl mercaptan, or thioglycolic acid in some processes - at 0.2-1.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical, capping each SAN branch and setting the graft chain length. Too little transfer and the graft crosslinks into a gel that is insoluble and unprocessable; too much and the graft has too few grafts per rubber particle and the impact strength collapses.

###### Graft level and particle morphology `chem.abs.grafting.graft-level` _(medium)_

How many SAN chains are grafted onto each rubber molecule, and what shape the particle ends up. High-graft material (more than about 70% grafted) gives a small, uniform particle and the best impact strength; low-graft gives larger particles and lower impact. The morphology is either salt-like (a grafted particle with an elastomeric core and a rigid SAN shell) or sandwich-like (SAN core with a grafted skin), and the choice is set by how fast the graft shell precipitates.

###### Reaction medium: xylene and water `chem.abs.grafting.reaction-medium` _(medium)_

The rubber is dissolved in xylene (or toluene) and the monomer is emulsified in an aqueous phase containing the initiator, chelant and transfer agent. At the end the polymer is devolatilised at 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar to strip the xylene, which is the single biggest energy item in the plant - the solvent has a heat capacity of about 2 MJ/kg/K and there is one to two tonnes of it per tonne of polymer.

###### The SAN matrix `chem.abs.san-matrix`

The continuous phase: styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made separately by bulk, emulsion or suspension polymerisation. It has to be made separately because it has to be a continuous phase, not a grafted one. In 1983 a large ABS plant bought its SAN in, or made it on site in a bulk reactor and then devolatilised - the two-route choice is a plant's economics, not a chemistry question.

###### Styrene monomer `chem.abs.san-matrix.styrene-raw`

99.5%+ styrene with less than 100 ppm inhibitor, from a dehydrogenation unit. The inhibitor has to be removed or it stops the graft reaction dead, which is why the plant distils its own styrene or buys uninhibited grade.

###### Acrylonitrile monomer `chem.abs.san-matrix.acrylonitrile-raw`

99.5%+ acrylonitrile with less than 45 ppm of the stabiliser, from a SOVERE ammoxidation plant. Because acrylonitrile is acutely lethal through the skin, it arrived in the ABS plant in tankers and was handled in a closed system with an outside storage tank; the 1980s industry norm was glove boxes and an emergency shower at every sampling point.

###### Styrene-acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN) `chem.styrene.polymerisation.san` _(medium)_

Styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made in bulk at 130-180 C or in emulsion or suspension. The acrylonitrile raises the heat distortion temperature from about 100 C to about 110-120 C and cuts the solubility in aromatic solvents, which is what turns a commodity polystyrene into the structural plastic the SAN matrix of ABS is made of. SAN production in 1983 was of the order of 0.4-0.5 million tonnes a year.

###### SOVERE ammoxidation process `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere`

A mixture of propylene, ammonia, oxygen and steam is passed at 400-460 C and 15-25 bar (1.5-2.5 MPa) over a bismuth molybdate or antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst in a fixed-bed or fluidised-bed reactor. The reaction is a partial oxidation plus an ammonia substitution in one step: propylene + 1.5 NH3 + 0.75 O2 -> acrylonitrile + 2 H2O. Per tonne of acrylonitrile the plant consumes about 1.0-1.1 t of propylene, 0.22-0.30 t of ammonia (most of which is lost to N2 and to acetonitrile) and 1.0-1.3 t of air, and it makes 0.04-0.08 t of acetonitrile as the main by-product.

###### Fixed-bed or fluidised-bed ammoxidation reactor `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor` _(medium)_

The original SOVERE design was a series of fixed beds with salt bath or oil bath cooling, giving 90-93% conversion and 85-92% selectivity. The 1980s industry had largely moved to fluidised-bed or moving-bed designs, which were easier to heat and to strip of coke, at the cost of a lower selectivity (about 80-90%). A 1980s plant was a 100,000-250,000 tonne a year unit with a salt bath or a hot water reactor jacket and a lot of downstream distillation.

###### Heat removal from the ammoxidation `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-removal`

The ammoxidation gives out roughly 1,000 kJ per kilogram of acrylonitrile, and the reactor has to be taken out at a rate the metallurgy can live with. That is the single hardest engineering problem in the process, and it is why the original SOVERE design was a salt-bath reactor and why the later fluidised beds were better: the fluidised catalyst carries its own heat around, so the temperature is uniform and there is no hot spot to crack the catalyst.

###### Molten salt bath reactor `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-removal.salt-bath` _(medium)_

A tubular reactor immersed in a bath of a molten nitrate-nitrite salt (the working point is around 300-330 C), with the bed of catalyst on an inert support inside the tube. It is a beautiful heat-transfer arrangement and a nasty maintenance one: the salt is oxidising, the reactor is at 400-450 C inside, and a tube failure means salt into the process. By 1983 it was being replaced by the fluidised bed for exactly this reason.

###### The molten salt itself `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-removal.salt-bath.molten-salt` _(medium)_

A mixture of potassium nitrate, sodium nitrite and sometimes calcium nitrate, chosen for a melting point a little below the operating temperature and for a decomposition temperature a good deal above it. It is a beautiful heat-transfer medium and an oxidising one, and a small leak from the reactor puts hot nitrate into a hydrocarbon process - which is why the original SOVERE design was eventually superseded. The nitrate salts came from the same nitric acid that a fab's wet bench bought.

###### Ammoxidation catalyst `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst`

Three families existed. Bismuth molybdate on silica (Bi2Mo3O12 or Bi2(MoO4)3 on silica) was the original and still the industry standard for selectivity in fixed beds. Antimony oxide with phosphorus and boron oxides on a silica support (Sb2O3/P2O5/B2O3) was the workhorse of the fluidised-bed designs, cheaper and more active but a little less selective. Bismuth molybdate with vanadium and tungsten additives, and nickel or cobalt catalysts, were the newer directions.

###### Bismuth molybdate on silica `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismuth-molybdate`

The standard catalyst, chosen for its selectivity to acrylonitrile and its resistance to reduction by ammonia. The 1980s development targets were the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions and, later in the decade, the bismuth-molybdenum-phosphorus systems aimed at raising the acrylonitrile yield above 90%.

###### Antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antimony` _(medium)_

The fluidised-bed catalyst: a silica support promoted with phosphorus and boron oxides so that the phosphorus does not volatilise away at 450 C. It was less selective but far more active and far more mechanically robust than the bismuth catalyst, which matters in a fluidised bed.

###### Catalyst deactivation and promoters `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.deactivation` _(medium)_

Coking from the organic by-products and the loss of phosphorus are the two deactivation routes. A trace of a halide promoter (a few hundred ppm of hydrogen chloride or an alkyl chloride) was the standard answer: it suppressed the side reactions that made hydrogen cyanide, and its use is the reason the plant needed a chlorine supply of its own.

###### Making the ammoxidation catalyst `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catalyst-manufacture`

The ammoxidation catalyst is a shaped, robust porous solid, and making it is a small ceramics industry. A bismuth molybdate catalyst is prepared by impregnating precipitated bismuth molybdate or by sol-gel methods onto a silica support, then shaping it into 3-5 mm extrudates or spray-dried microspheres and calcining at 500-700 C. The support is silica gel, and silica gel is made from sand. That is the whole chain from a dune to a transistor's acrylonitrile in three steps.

###### Shaping and calcination `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catalyst-manufacture.extrusion` _(medium)_

The powder is extruded into trilobe or quadrilobe shapes - the lobes exist because a lobed extrudate has more external surface per unit volume than a cylinder, and more external surface means less diffusion limitation - then dried and calcined at 500-700 C. The calcination is what converts the oxide precursor into the active bismuth molybdate phase; too hot and the surface area collapses and the selectivity falls.

###### Silica gel support `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catalyst-manufacture.silica-support`

A porous amorphous silica of 300-700 m2/g surface area and a 6-20 nm pore diameter. The pore diameter matters twice over in this file: in the ammoxidation catalyst a small pore keeps the diene from cracking, and in the FCC catalyst a large pore lets the bulky alkylated intermediates in. The silica gel is made by hydrolysing a silicate solution and gelling it, and the silicate solution is made from silica sand.

###### Soda silica from sand `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catalyst-manufacture.silica-support.soda-silica`

Quartz sand is fused with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, which is dissolved in hot water to make the silicate solution, which is acidified to gel. This is the same soda-silica chain that gives the silica sol for the polysilicon ingot's crucibles and the quartz for the fused silica, and it is the industrial descendant of a two-thousand-year-old glassmaking reaction. It is the last dig-it-out node in this branch: sand.

###### By-products: acetonitrile, hydrogen cyanide, acrylic acid `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts` _(medium)_

Acetonitrile is the biggest by-product at 3-8% of the acrylonitrile and it had a real market - it went into solvent and into acrylonitrile copolymer fibres. Hydrogen cyanide was a small but lethal by-product, and its formation was the reason for the halide promoter. Acrylic acid came from the hydrolysis of a little of the acrylonitrile, and it was a nuisance in 1980s practice because it fouled the distillation train.

###### The hydrogen and oxygen side of the loop `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.hydrogen-oxygen` _(medium)_

A side reaction makes hydrogen: propylene plus ammonia plus oxygen makes propene imine, which cracks to acetonitrile and hydrogen, and the hydrogen is then burned to water with the oxygen. The 1980s development was to recover that hydrogen - it is a high-value gas and the plant bought hydrogen for the reactor - by separating the purge gas and feeding it to a hydrogen recovery unit. It is also why the net oxygen demand of the process is lower than the stoichiometry suggests.

###### Recovery and purification train `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation`

The reactor effluent is cooled and partly condensed, the unreacted propylene and ammonia are stripped and recycled, the acrylonitrile and acetonitrile are separated by distillation (acrylonitrile boiling 77 C, acetonitrile 81.6 C, which is a genuinely difficult separation and was the reason for the extractive or entrainer-assisted designs), and the acrylonitrile is finished to 99.9% with a stabiliser. In a plant where acrylonitrile boils at 77 C and is flammable from 3% in air, the distillation column was also the largest single gas hazard.

###### Acrylonitrile stabiliser `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.stabiliser` _(medium)_

A phenolic or amine stabiliser (a small percentage of a phenol such as hydroquinone, or a hindered amine) is added to prevent anionic polymerisation of the monomer in storage. Acrylonitrile has a third-order rate constant for anionic polymerisation that is high enough that a drum of uninhibited monomer left in a warm warehouse can polymerise from the bottom up, and this was a real and recurring accident.

###### Blending the graft into the matrix `chem.abs.blending`

The graft is mixed into the SAN at 25-50 parts graft per 100 parts SAN for a general purpose grade and up to 50-70 parts for a high-impact grade. That ratio - not the chemistry - is what a plastics buyer specifies: rubber content sets the impact strength, the heat distortion temperature and the price per kilogram.

###### Compounding and pelletising `chem.abs.pelletising`

The dry blend is melted in a twin-screw extruder at 230-260 C, the volatile xylene and the residual styrene are pulled out under vacuum, and the melt is cut into pellets. This is the operation that turns a powder into a product a moulding machine can eat, and it is where the ABS gets its second heat history - which is why the regrind content matters.

###### Twin-screw extruder `chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw` _(medium)_

Two intermeshing screws 50-90 mm in diameter at 10-30 rpm, length to diameter ratio 30-40:1, with an L/D feed zone, a melting zone, a vacuum vent and a second vent for the devolatilisation. In 1983 the counter-rotating or co-rotating twin screw was the standard compounding machine for ABS because it handles the powder blend, the pigment and the regrind in one pass; a 70 mm machine ran 500-2,000 kg/h.

###### Devolatilisation in the compounding line `chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.devolatilisation` _(medium)_

The xylene in the graft has to come out, and it comes out in the compounding extruder rather than in the reactor, because the reactor's melt is too viscous to devolatilise in a small unit. A falling-film or wiped-film vent at 240-260 C and 5-50 mbar with a steam ejector, or with a liquid ring pump for the high-boiling tail, is what turns a sticky powder blend into a pellet that does not smell of solvent. It is the single most expensive operation in the ABS plant per kilogram of resin.

###### Vacuum venting `chem.abs.pelletising.vacuum-vent` _(medium)_

A vent at 10-100 mbar with a steam ejector or a liquid ring pump, sized to remove the residual monomer and solvent. The residual styrene specification matters: a high-styrene ABS smells, and the monomer content of a 1980s pellet was typically under 500 ppm.

###### Die plate, water bath and rotary cutter `chem.abs.pelletising.cutter` _(medium)_

The melt is extruded through a die plate as a number of strands into a circulating water bath at 20-40 C, solidifies, is pulled by a first calender and chopped by a rotary knife mounted on the extruder die. The alternative is underwater pelletising, where the die is submerged and the pellets are cut in the water - fewer steps, no strands, and it was becoming the 1980s preference for a new line. Pellet size is 2-4 mm in both cases.

###### Static mixer in the melt line `chem.abs.pelletising.static-mixer` _(medium)_

A motionless packed element in the transfer pipe or the die adapter that blends the pigment and the regrind into the melt without shear. It matters because the impact property depends on the particle size distribution surviving, and every unnecessary shear element costs you 0.5-1 micron of particle size.

###### Drying `chem.abs.drying`

ABS is hygroscopic: its equilibrium moisture content is about 0.3-0.4% by weight, and a wet pellet in a mould produces a part with silver streaks on the surface, voids, and a lower impact strength than the design assumed. The moulding shop therefore dried the pellets at 80-90 C for 2-4 hours in a dehumidifying dryer before every moulding run. This is the step that separates a plastics engineer from a chemist and it is done with the pellets in a hopper with a 3A molecular sieve bed.

###### Molecular sieve desiccant `chem.abs.drying.desiccant` _(medium)_

A 3A or 4A zeolite in a heated bed at 200-350 C that adsorbs water to below 0.1% of its own weight, with a purge cycle on a hot air or nitrogen sweep. The same zeolite family as the cracker drier and the FCC catalyst, and in the 1980s this was the standard way every plastic was dried before moulding.

###### The 3A molecular sieve itself `chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-sieve`

The desiccant in the dryer is a synthetic zeolite with a 3 angstrom pore opening, which admits the water molecule (kinetic diameter about 2.65 angstrom) and excludes anything bigger. That single geometric fact is why a molecular sieve can dry a plastic to 200 ppm: it is a molecular filter, not an absorber. The zeolite is made by hydrothermal synthesis from an alumina gel, a silica source and an organic template at 150-200 C and autogenous pressure in an autoclave - and then the template is burned out of the pore at 500-550 C, which is what opens the pores.

###### Zeolite hydrothermal synthesis `chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-sieve.hydrothermal-synthesis`

Alumina, sodium silicate and sodium hydroxide are gelled together, seeded with a few crystals of the product zeolite as nuclei, and heated in an autoclave at 150-200 C for 24-96 hours. The nucleation and growth control is the whole art: it is why the crystal size distribution of a zeolite is a commercial specification, and why a 2-micron zeolite for a cracker drier costs more than a 50-micron one for a different job.

###### Binder and the shaped pellet `chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-sieve.binder` _(medium)_

A zeolite powder cannot go in a dryer bed: it will dust and it will fluidise. So the powder is formed into 2-4 mm extruded pellets with a clay and silica binder, and the binder is the part that stops the pellet from taking up water itself - a 4% clay binder will hold several weight percent of water and the bed's capacity is only about 20-22% of its own weight. The circle closes here: the drying equipment for the plastic is itself dried in a dryer.

###### Compounding additives `chem.abs.additives`

Colour and processing aids, dosed into the twin screw before the vacuum vent so that anything volatile is stripped there: 1-3% of a pigment masterbatch, 0.1-0.5% of an external lubricant (a metal stearate, usually zinc or calcium stearate or an EBS wax), and a UV stabiliser. The beige of the C64's case is a pigment on top of the natural colour of the polymer; the grey of a later model is a carbon black or a titanium dioxide blend.

###### Pigment masterbatch `chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch` _(medium)_

A pre-dispersed concentrate - typically titanium dioxide (rutile, for weather resistance), carbon black, ultramarine blue, phthalocyanine green, or an iron oxide - at 20-60% loading in an ABS or LDPE carrier, dosed at 1-3% into the compounding line. A masterbatch exists because a pigment dropped into a twin screw as a powder will not disperse, and undispersed pigment is visible as specks in the moulding.

###### Metal stearate release agent `chem.abs.additives.stearate` _(medium)_

Calcium stearate or zinc stearate, 0.1-0.5%, dosed to stop the ABS sticking to the screw and the die, and to help the mould release. The stearates come from stearic acid (from tallow or from a C18 fraction) neutralised with lime; the metal itself is the only heavy metal routinely added to a consumer plastic.

###### Regrind `chem.abs.regrind` _(medium)_

Runner, sprue and rejected mouldings are chopped and fed back. A 1980s injection moulder typically ran 5-10% regrind in the case and up to 20% in less critical parts, on the grounds that a second heat history costs some molecular weight and some impact strength. Commodore's own case moulding ran regrind; the amount is not documented and the C64's impact strength specification is a good indication of how much.

###### The ABS grade the C64 case used `chem.abs.grade` _(medium)_

A high-impact, general purpose injection moulding grade in the family of the low-cis, medium-graft commercial ABS sold as Cycolac 2800 or equivalent, with a notched Izod impact strength of 150-250 J/m and a moulding shrinkage of 0.4-0.7%. The UL 94 flammability rating would be HB or 2A: a home computer in a living room could not be in a 0.4 mm wall V-0 plastic, so the case had to be thicker than the V-0 rating allowed.

###### The Commodore 64 case, in ABS `chem.abs.c64-case` _(medium)_

About 350-400 g of ABS: a two-shot moulding, the beige or brown textured skin over the structural frame, with the moulding texture itself - a fine leather grain applied by the tool's EDM process - as the only decoration. Behind the front bezel there is a metal RF shield and a plastic shield can, and the vents are moulded through the wall. Everything visible on the outside of a C64, apart from the keycaps and the badge, is this one polymer.

###### The other polymers in and around a C64 `chem.abs.other-polymers`

A 1983 consumer electronic device used perhaps eight different engineering plastics and two rubbers. This branch traces each of them to its monomer, because they all come out of the same crackers, the same benzene and the same phenol. Each is a node with its own subtree; chem.pvc, chem.epoxy, chem.rubber, chem.polyester and chem.silicone are the ones other parts of this tree reference.

###### PVC: vinyl chloride and suspension polymerisation `chem.pvc`

About 3.5 million tonnes of PVC in 1983, of which maybe 5-8% was flexible and the rest rigid. Two-thirds of the monomer came from the oxychlorination of ethylene and the rest from acetylene and HCl. The C64 used it in the power cord's jacket and insulation, in the moulded cable accessories, and in the odd keycap or knob; the stability system matters because unstabilised PVC decomposes at 140 C.

###### Vinyl chloride monomer `chem.pvc.vcm`

C2H3Cl, boiling at -13.4 C, so it is a liquid only under pressure. It is a proven human carcinogen (angiosarcoma of the liver), it is flammable from 4-33% in air, and it is the reason the PVC industry of the 1980s had an unusual public health profile. In 1983 world VCM capacity was of the order of 9-10 million tonnes a year.

###### Acetylene plus HCl (the mercury route) `chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route`

Acetylene and anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute, at 15-25% conversion per pass with 90-95% selectivity. This is the route that ties PVC to natural gas, because acetylene is made from methane. It survives where there is no cracker - in Western Europe, in India, in China and in the Soviet Union - and where there is one, the oxychlorination route is cheaper.

###### Mercury in the PVC plant `chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury` _(medium)_

The mercury chloride catalyst is a genuine environmental liability. A 1980s European PVC plant was a mercury emitter at tens of kilograms a year, and by the mid-1980s both the German and the Dutch authorities were requiring either catalyst recovery or a switch to the oxychlorination route. The engineering answer, delivered in the 1980s, was a mercury recovery system on the reactor effluent that stripped the mercury into the hydrochloric acid stream and concentrated it to about 20%.

###### Acetylene to vinyl chloride `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride`

The reason the whole acetylene industry existed. Acetylene plus anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a 0.3-0.5% mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute gives vinyl chloride at 15-25% conversion per pass and 90-95% selectivity, the low conversion forced by the HCl ratio and by the fact that vinyl chloride is a vinylogous acrylate that polymerises readily.

###### Mercuric chloride catalyst `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride.mercury-catalyst` _(medium)_

Anhydrous HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and ethyne adds across it. The catalyst is a genuine environmental liability: mercury lost from a large acetylene plant was tens of kilograms a year, and by the 1980s both West Germany and the Netherlands were restricting mercury emission from chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride plants.

###### Oxychlorination of ethylene `chem.pvc.vcm.oxychlorination`

Ethylene, chlorine and hydrogen chloride over a copper(II) chloride catalyst at 150-250 C and 4-10 bar, giving VCM with 85-95% selectivity. The ratio of chlorine to HCl controls the dichlorethane versus vinyl chloride, so the plant can swing between making EDC for the chlorinated-solvent business and making VCM. By 1983 this was about two thirds of world VCM.

###### VCM storage and inhibition `chem.pvc.vcm.storage` _(medium)_

Bulk VCM in a refrigerated atmospheric tank at 10-15 C with a nitrogen blanket, or in a pressure vessel. It is inhibited against polymerisation with a phenolic or an organic peroxide, and it is kept below 50 C because vinyl chloride is a powerful inhibitor of its own polymerisation - a fact the industry discovered painfully, and which turned out to be a safety feature once understood.

###### PVC polymerisation `chem.pvc.polymerisation`

Suspension polymerisation in water with a suspending agent is about 65-70% of world PVC production: VCM is dispersed as 0.1-1 mm beads in water at 50-70 C and 6-12 bar for 5-10 hours to 70-85% conversion. Mass polymerisation gives a cleaner bead and no water to evaporate, and emulsion (paste) polymerisation is used for flexible and calendared products. The suspension process is essentially a stirred autoclave and the whole design problem is keeping the beads spherical and of a narrow size.

###### PVA suspending agent `chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent` _(medium)_

Partially hydrolysed polyvinyl alcohol at 0.5-2% of the water phase, with a second colloid stabilizer if needed. It is the same PVA chemistry as the suspension polystyrene suspending agent - one more appearance of a polymer from the vinyl acetate chain doing structural work in a different polymer's reactor.

###### Initiator and chain transfer `chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator` _(medium)_

Acyl peroxide or a persulphate at 0.05-0.5%, with a chain transfer agent (often chloroform, tetrachloromethane or an ester) to control molecular weight. The transfer agents are chlorinated for a reason: they also terminate the radicals that would otherwise go on to make chlorinated by-products, and the PVC industry has always been able to sell them.

###### Heat stabilisation, and the lead problem `chem.pvc.stabilisation`

PVC is unstable above about 140 C: the dehydrochlorination produces HCl, which catalyses more dehydrochlorination, which is why unstabilised PVC cannot be processed at all. The 1980s stabiliser systems were lead salts - dibasic lead phosphite, tribasic lead sulphate, lead stearate - which are excellent scavengers and which put lead into millions of tonnes of consumer product. Calcium-zinc systems based on stearates and organic co-stabilisers were the 1980s technology that began to displace them, and the reason is health regulation rather than performance.

###### Tribasic lead sulphate and lead phosphite `chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser` _(medium)_

The lead salts are cheap, opaque, and superb at scavenging HCl and chelating chlorine. The cost is that lead is a cumulative neurotoxin and PVC was, until recently, a major route of human lead exposure through pipes, and in 1983 the limits on lead in consumer products were tightening. The chemistry is basic: the metal salt of sulphuric or phosphorous acid, made by precipitating the oxide or sulphate onto a lead base.

###### Calcium-zinc stabilisers `chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn` _(medium)_

Calcium and zinc carboxylates (stearate, hydrostearate) with an organic co-stabiliser such as a beta-diketone or a polyol. Zinc carboxylates are the primary stabilisers and calcium carboxylates are the co-stabilisers that exchange zinc for calcium at the right moment. The 1980s engineering problem was matching the zinc-to-calcium ratio and the lubricant balance so the compound did not plate out on the extruder die, which is a real and stubborn processing problem rather than a trivial substitution.

###### Plasticisers `chem.pvc.plasticiser`

A flexible PVC is PVC with 30-60 parts per 100 of a liquid plasticiser, and the plasticiser is where most of the toxicology lived. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP, DOP) was the standard from the 1950s into the 1990s, made by esterifying phthalic anhydride with 2-ethylhexanol - itself from butyraldehyde or oxo synthesis of propylene and a C6 or C8 fraction. In 1983 there was no accepted evidence of harm at the levels in use, and the reappraisal came later.

###### Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate `chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp` _(medium)_

C8H17OOC-C6H4-COOC8H17, 391 g/mol, a colourless liquid with a very slight odour. About 200,000-250,000 tonnes of DEHP a year were made in 1983, most of it for PVC. The C8 alcohol comes from propylene and from ethylene via butyraldehyde, so a PVC cable jacket is a direct consumer of the cracker.

###### PVC in a C64 `chem.pvc.uses-c64` _(medium)_

The power cord: a two-core or three-core flexible PVC jacket, typically 1.5-3 mm of wall, with PVC insulation on the conductors and a PVC or PVC/rubber strain relief at the moulded connector. A C64 power cord is a couple of hundred grams of PVC. The keyboard keys and the side vents of the earlier cases were also often PVC or a PVC blend. A C64 whose power supply was the internal one had less of it, because the mains cable went to the brick.

                  - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
###### Polycarbonate `chem.polycarbonate`

Bisphenol A polycarbonate, made by the interfacial phosgene route from BPA and phosgene in dichloromethane, then melt polycondensed at 250-290 C. It is the transparent, tough, dimensionally stable engineering plastic of the 1980s, and in electronics it went into connector housings, terminal blocks, relay covers and the housings of the switchgear it replaced metal in. The C64 itself was not made of polycarbonate - the case was ABS - but the material surrounds the machine in the peripherals and in Commodore's later machines, and it shares the bisphenol A and the cumene chain with the epoxy and the polyester.

###### Interfacial phosgene route `chem.polycarbonate.phosgene-route`

Bisphenol A dissolved in aqueous caustic soda is reacted with phosgene in dichloromethane at 20-40 C with a tertiary amine catalyst. The product is a chloroformate-terminated oligomer that is then washed, and the oligomer is polymerised by melt condensation at 250-290 C under 0.1-1 mbar until the molecular weight is high enough. The plant has two halves - a wet interfacial reactor with a rotary film contactor and a dry finishing extruder - and the balance between them is the whole economics.

###### Phosgene `chem.polycarbonate.phosgene`

Carbonyl chloride, COCl2, made by oxidising carbon monoxide with chlorine over activated carbon at 100-150 C. It is acutely toxic, and it is one of the reasons the polycarbonate industry of the 1980s was moving toward the non-phosgene route based on bisphenol A carbonate and on the methylene chloride and pyridine route. The bisphenol A it consumes is the same bisphenol A as the epoxy, and the chlorine is the same chlorine.

###### Chlorine and carbon monoxide `chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine`

Chlorine from brine electrolysis plus carbon monoxide from a reformer or from coke. This is the point at which the chlor-alkali industry - which needs hydrogen to sell its chlorine, and therefore needs natural gas - touches the plastics industry through a molecule with two chlorine atoms and one oxygen.

###### Why it was chosen `chem.polycarbonate.properties`

Amorphous at 100-150% linear retention, glass transition near 145 C, tensile strength 60-70 MPa, and a notched Izod of 8-15 kJ/m2. It is the transparent tough polymer of the 1980s: sunglasses lenses, camera and instrument housings, the disc of a compact disc from 1982, and the dome of the keyboard on some machines. It was also the first engineering polymer to be explicitly targeted at the electronics market as a metal replacement.

###### Nylon 6 and nylon 6,6 `chem.polyamide`

The two polyamides that a 1980s machine used for its precision parts. Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, or nylon 6 from caprolactam which itself comes from phenol. Both are condensation polymers of a diamine and an acid or of a lactam, and both need the phenol-aromatic chain, so both are downstream of the same cracker benzene as the ABS.

###### Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and HMDA `chem.polyamide.nylon-66`

Adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine condense to nylon salt at 250-270 C and 10-20 bar in a batch or continuous process, then polymerise at 270-280 C under a small nitrogen pressure. Adipic acid in 1983 came mostly from the oxidation of cyclohexane or of a C4 route with nitric acid; hexamethylenediamine came from adiponitrile hydrogenation or from adipic acid plus ammonia.

###### Adiponitrile from butadiene `chem.polyamide.nylon-66.adiponitrile`

The 1980s route to nylon 6,6 feedstock: hydrocyanation of butadiene with hydrogen cyanide over a nickel catalyst, then hydrogenation of both nitriles. It made a cracker-based nylon 6,6 possible for the first time, and it is the reason hydrogen cyanide - the toxic gas of the acrylonitrile and methyl methacrylate chemistry - was on the books of a plastics company.

###### Nylon 6 from caprolactam `chem.polyamide.nylon-6`

Caprolactam is opened with water at 250-270 C in a hydrolysis-polymerisation reactor under 1-15 bar, giving a nylon 6 with a very narrow molecular weight distribution because the chemistry is a step growth from a single monomer. Nylon 6 is the form used where a low melt viscosity matters, and it was the standard for the textile filament and the carpet fibre trade.

###### Caprolactam from phenol `chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam`

Phenol hydrogenated to cyclohexanol, then dehydrogenated to cyclohexanone; cyclohexanone oximation to cyclohexanone oxime; the oxime rearranged with oleum (the Beckmann rearrangement, which expands the ring from six to seven members) to caprolactam, and the ammonium sulphate byproduct stripped and recycled. This is a five-step route from phenol and it is one of the longest petrochemical chains in the C64's ancestry.

###### Phenol to cyclohexanone `chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.phenol`

Phenol hydrogenated over a nickel or palladium catalyst at 120-180 C and 10-30 bar to cyclohexanol, which is dehydrogenated over copper at 250-300 C to cyclohexanone. The phenol comes from cumene, and cumene's propylene comes from the cracker, so nylon 6 is a third-generation descendant of the naphtha cracker.

###### Oleum and the Beckmann rearrangement `chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.oleum` _(medium)_

The rearrangement needs concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum, and it produces ammonium sulphate - typically 1.1-1.3 tonnes of ammonium sulphate per tonne of caprolactam, which has to be sold as fertiliser. It is the same sulphuric acid and the same fertiliser market that the Claus sulphur plant feeds. In 1983 the industry was moving to oleum-free rearrangements over solid acid or over a zeolite, precisely to lose that waste.

###### Polyesters: PET, PBT and unsaturated polyester `chem.polyester`

Three families that share the same two feedstocks - ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, and a terephthalic or maleic/fumaric acid. PET in 1983 was overwhelmingly a fibre and bottle business, PBT was the engineering thermoplastic, and unsaturated polyester was the resin of the glass-reinforced mouldings. In a 1983 electronic assembly, the polyester was the transformer bobbin insulation, the relay base, the film capacitors, and any glass-filled moulding.

###### PET from ethylene glycol and dimethyl terephthalate `chem.polyester.pet`

Dimethyl terephthalate plus ethylene glycol transesterified at 180-280 C over an antimony or titanium catalyst, then polycondensed at 270-290 C under 1-50 mbar. The bottleneck is the transesterification methanol coproduct, which is recovered and returned to the terephthalate plant, so the plant is a big methanol recovery column. The route through dimethyl terephthalate rather than terephthalic acid was chosen in the 1970s and 1980s because the acid route's oxidation step had the corrosion and the purity problems; by the late 1980s the acid route had caught up.

###### Para-xylene and terephthalic acid `chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid` _(medium)_

Para-xylene is separated from the C8 aromatics by adsorptive separation (UOP Parex, 4A zeolite) or by crystallisation, then oxidised with air over a cobalt-manganese-acetate catalyst at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar in acetic acid. The para isomer must be more than 99.5% pure because the meta and ortho isomers cannot be polymerised into a useful fibre.

###### Ethylene glycol side `chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol`

About 2.2 tonnes of ethylene glycol per tonne of PET resin, from the ethylene oxide hydration branch. The glycol is purified to 99.9% because the water it carries ends up as a hydrolysis chain terminator and it is the single largest cause of high-acid-value polyester.

###### PBT (polybutylene terephthalate) `chem.polyester.pbt` _(medium)_

Polymerised by transesterification then polycondensation like PET but with butanediol, giving a lower melting point (about 225 C against 260 C) and a faster crystallisation, which is why it is the engineering grade: it sets in a 5-10 mm wall in 5-10 seconds where PET needs a minute. It went into connectors, relay and transformer bobbin mouldings, and into the small gears and cams of the power supply mechanism.

###### Unsaturated polyester resin `chem.polyester.unsaturated`

Maleic anhydride plus propylene glycol condensed to about 1,000-2,000 molecular weight and dissolved in styrene; the crosslinker is styrene itself and the cure is a peroxide (usually methyl ethyl ketone peroxide) at 20-80 C. In the 1980s it was the resin of glass-reinforced moulding compound and of the cast reinforced parts - and it is the resin family most associated with the styrene emission complaints of boat building, which is the same styrene that the ABS matrix uses.

###### Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) `chem.silicone`

The only engineering polymer whose backbone is not carbon. Built from chlorosilanes made by the Rochow direct process - silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C - then hydrolyzed and condensed. In 1983 silicones were everywhere in electronics: as RTV sealing gaskets, as conformal coatings and encapsulants, as dielectric greases for the variable capacitors, and as the flexible key domes.

###### Rochow direct process `chem.silicone.rochow`

Metallurgical silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C gives dimethyldichlorosilane. The silicon comes from the quartz and coke reduction that the whole semiconductor industry depends on, so the silicone business and the chip business share an upstream - and share the same four-nines purity problem in their own way. The methyl chloride comes from the natural gas chlorination business, so the silicone plant and the semiconductor plant are both fed by chlorine and by methane.

###### Metallurgical silicon `chem.silicone.rochow.metallurgical-silicon`

98-99.5% silicon made in submerged arc furnaces from quartz and petroleum coke. The 1980s trade fed two very different industries: the ~100,000 tonne a year silicones and chlorosilanes trade, and the far smaller but far purer semiconductor-grade silicon trade, which used the same furnaces with nine-nines purification. Coke, silicon and chlorine are three inputs that appear in both branches of this tree.

###### Silicone rubber and fluids `chem.silicone.polymer`

The chlorosilane is hydrolyzed to a silanol and condensed with a silanol-terminated chain stopper, giving a silicone oil (low viscosity) or, with reinforcing silica and peroxide cure, a silicone rubber (elastomer). The 1980s mix in electronics was dominated by room-temperature-vulcanising silicone - a moisture-cured acetoxy or hydroxyl-terminated compound - because it cures in a fixture without heat, and by the fluorosilicone mould releases.

###### Conformal coating `chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating` _(medium)_

A 20-100 micron film of room-temperature-vulcanising silicone brushed or dipped over a populated board, cured in humid air, to keep water, dust, sulfur dioxide and salt off the conductors. In 1980s practice it was used on power supplies and on automotive electronics rather than on consumer boards, and the industry debate was whether a conformal coating is better than a conformal coating removed badly - the rework risk is the problem. The C64's mainboard is generally described as uncoated.

###### Conductive elastomer key domes `chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes` _(medium)_

A switch contact made of a silicone or neoprene elastomer filled with carbon black - or with metal-plated hollow glass spheres - so that the rubber itself conducts. When the dome is pressed it shorts to a printed conductor beneath; the dome's force curve (about 0.5-2 N operating, 8-12 mm travel) is the feel of the keyboard. The conductive filler is a petroleum carbon black or a silvered microsphere, and the elastomer is usually a peroxide-cured silicone or a neoprene, chosen for its fatigue life in millions of actuations.

###### Neoprene (polychloroprene) `chem.rubber.neoprene`

Chloroprene polymerised in emulsion at 40 C. It is oil-resistant, weather-resistant and flame-resistant, which makes it the rubber for gaskets, for the flexible jacket of a power cord, and for the cable's outer sheath when the cable is not PVC. It is made from acetylene and chlorine through vinylacetylene and dichloroacetylene - one more route that ends in acetylene, and therefore in natural gas.

###### Chloroprene from acetylene `chem.rubber.neoprene.chloroprene` _(medium)_

Acetylene dimerises to vinylacetylene, which chlorinates to 1,2-dichloro-2-butene; dehydrochlorination gives chloroprene, which polymerises in emulsion at 40 C to neoprene. The process is hazardous in a way that is instructive: chloroprene is a carcinogen and the dichloroacetylene intermediate is an extremely toxic pyrophoric gas, so the plant runs at low partial pressure with a fast quench.

###### Elastomers: natural rubber, neoprene, EPDM `chem.rubber`

Three rubbers for three different jobs in and around a 1983 machine: natural rubber for the feet and plinths and the moulded grips, neoprene for gaskets and the flexible cable jacket, and EPDM for the cable's weather-resistant insulation. The C64's case feet are elastomer pads stuck to the underside of the case, and they are the only rubber on the outside of the machine.

###### Natural rubber (cis-1,4-polyisoprene) `chem.rubber.natural` _(medium)_

Field latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis, coagulated, smoked and pressed into bales. In 1983 world production was of the order of 3.0-3.5 million tonnes a year, two thirds of it in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. It is cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a glass transition near -70 C, so it is the most resilient rubber at room temperature, and it needs vulcanisation with sulphur because the cis double bond is what makes it elastic.

###### Tapping and coagulation `chem.rubber.natural.tapping`

A quarter-spiral cut into the bark's tapping panel is made about every other day, and the latex is collected in a cup. Thirty per cent of a mature tree's latex can be taken without killing it over a 25-30 year tapping life. The latex is preserved with ammonia, coagulated by adding formic acid or acetic acid to bring it to the isoelectric point, pressed into sheets, and then smoke-dried.

###### Prevulcanised rubber and latex goods `chem.rubber.natural.prevulcanisation` _(medium)_

Before the 1930s the only way to make a rubber article was to vulcanise the whole thing in the mould. By the 1930s the industry could prevulcanise the compound in a mixer first - deliberately introducing some crosslink - so the compound was a flowable, uncured-on-the-surface material that could be shaped, then cured in the mould. That development is what made rubber mouldings mass-produced and is the direct ancestor of the ABS pellet.

###### Vulcanisation and the role of sulphur `chem.rubber.natural.vulcanisation`

Heated with sulphur and an accelerator (a thiuram or a sulphonamide), the cis double bonds get a short sulphur bridge between neighbouring chains: crosslinked, so the chains can no longer slide. The C64's case feet are a filled, carbon-black-reinforced natural or SBR compound cured in a mould at 140-170 C for 5-20 minutes. Elemental sulphur here came out of a Claus plant.

                    - *Neoprene (polychloroprene)* `chem.rubber.neoprene` *(seen above)*
###### EPDM `chem.rubber.epdm`

Ethylene copolymerised with a diene (norbornene or a cyclic diene), the diene content giving the vulcanisable double bonds. It has no unsaturation in the main chain, so it is ozone-resistant and will not crack in sunlight, which is why it replaced natural rubber in weather-exposed cable insulation and in the C64's power cord as the flexible jacket material of preference.

###### POM (acetal homopolymer and copolymer) `chem.pom`

Polyoxymethylene, made by polymerising formaldehyde - from the oxidation of methanol - either with an acetic anhydride chain transfer (giving the homopolymer, Delrin) or with a small amount of a diacetate comonomer (giving the Celcon-type copolymer). It is the 1980s precision engineering plastic: gears, cams, hinges, tolerance rings and the moving parts in a mechanism.

###### Formaldehyde from methanol `chem.pom.formaldehyde`

Methanol plus a controlled amount of oxygen over silver at 600-700 C, giving 25-35% formaldehyde in air (the Formox process), then concentrated to 60-70%. The methanol comes from synthesis gas, so this is a coal-or-gas-to-methanol-to-formaldehyde chain rather than a direct petroleum one - although in a 1980s plant the methanol would typically have been made from natural gas.

###### Formox partial oxidation `chem.pom.formaldehyde.methanol-oxidation`

CH3OH plus about 0.4 mol O2 per mol methanol over silver gauze at 600-700 C gives 25-35% formaldehyde with 90%+ selectivity. Silver is the only catalyst that works cleanly, and the reactor is a thousands-of-tubes packed bed. The oxygen is the whole control problem: too little and you get methyl formate, too much and you oxidise to carbon dioxide.

###### Acetal polymerisation `chem.pom.polymerisation` _(medium)_

The homopolymer route runs formaldehyde with acetic anhydride: the growing chain's hydroxyl end reacts with the anhydride to give an acetoxy end, which stops further polymerisation. The copolymer route instead uses formaldehyde with a 2-4% fraction of a methylol-substituted diacetate (methyl formal or a diacetate monomer) so that the chain stops at an inert C-O-C end. In both cases the polymer has to be stabilised with an antioxidant, because formaldehyde polymerisation reversibly gives back formaldehyde at temperature.

###### Where POM sat in a 1983 machine `chem.pom.uses` _(low)_

Small precision parts: the gear and cam of a fan, the hinges and catches, the insulator of a switch mechanism, the arm of a relay. In a 1983 home computer it was present in tens of grams at most, but it was there because nothing else moulded to a 0.05 mm tolerance with a low friction coefficient.

###### Phenolic and amino thermosets `chem.thermosets`

The two oldest synthetic plastics, still in a 1983 machine in the places where a thermoplastic will not do: phenolic for the switch and socket housings and the old-style bakelite knobs, and urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde for the white insulating parts, the plug bodies and the coil-formers. Both are condensation networks: once cured they do not melt, and they are made from phenol or from urea, which comes from the same cumene and ammonia chain as everything else in this file.

###### Phenolic resin (phenol-formaldehyde) `chem.thermosets.phenolic`

Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid (novolac, with hexamine as the curing agent) or under base (resol, self-curing). Bakelite, patented in 1907, was the first wholly synthetic plastic. In 1980s electronics it was in the switchgear, the relay covers and the phenolic laminate (paper or cotton cloth in phenolic resin) for the low-cost circuit boards and for the insulating barriers in a power supply.

###### The formaldehyde in a phenolic `chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde`

Methanol oxidised to formaldehyde over silver at 600-700 C. The same formaldehyde as the acetal plastics, from the same methanol, from the same synthesis gas. Phenolic resin and POM sitting a few hundred metres apart in a 1980s chemical park is not a coincidence; both are formaldehyde chemistry.

                        - *Formaldehyde from methanol* `chem.pom.formaldehyde` *(seen above)*
###### Hexamethylenetetramine (hexamine) `chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine` _(medium)_

Formaldehyde plus ammonia, and it does double duty: it is the curing agent for novolac phenolic and it is a slow accelerator and a decomposition source of formaldehyde in rubber compounds. It is one of the few molecules in this file that reaches into three unrelated chemistries.

###### Urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde `chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde`

Urea condensed with formaldehyde gives a thermoset used for the white insulation of plugs, sockets and coil formers, and melamine gives the tougher, heat-resistant version used for the panel fittings. Both are white, both are cheap, and both are moisture-sensitive, which is the defect that kept them out of anything structural. The urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide - the Haber-Bosch product - so this is a nitrogen branch rather than a hydrocarbon one.

###### Urea from ammonia and carbon dioxide `chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.ammonia`

2NH3 plus CO2 at 180-220 C and 15-25 bar gives ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea. Ammonia comes from the Haber-Bosch loop fed by steam-reformed natural gas, so the white plug body of a 1983 appliance is, four steps back, natural gas.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Glass-reinforced switch body `c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler`

Glass fibre is added to the switch body at 20-30% by weight and the compound is compression moulded. The glass reduces creepage and raises the distortion temperature, which is what keeps the moulding from softening near a hot transformer.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
              - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
###### UHF output stage for the PAL version `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-selection.uhf-output` _(medium)_

At 591 MHz a single transistor oscillator cannot drive a 75 ohm television input through a long lead, so the PAL modulators add a small tuned output stage and, in the later units, an output amplifier with its own bias network. The extra gain is what makes a PAL C64 usable on a European television without a booster.

###### RF output network and 75 ohm match `mb.rf-modulator.rf-output`

The picture carrier leaves the tank through a tap, is coupled out through a series capacitor, and is matched to the 75 ohm coax of the television's antenna input by a resistive network with a ferrite bead in the supply feed. Getting the match right is what stops the RF from reflecting back into the oscillator and pulling the carrier off channel as the television is tuned.

###### RCA phono socket `mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.rca-jack`

The US-style phono connector that carries the composite antenna signal. The centre pin is often nickel- or gold-plated brass and the outer shell is a turned brass or plated-steel barrel crimped into the body; the body is moulded in a glass-filled thermoplastic.

                - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
                - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
                - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
###### Ferrite bead choke `mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.supply-bead`

A small ferrite bead slipped onto the +B lead at the RF output stage so the supply current cannot feed RF back into the tank. The bead's impedance rises with frequency, so it is a good choke at 60 MHz while passing DC almost untouched.

###### Ferrite: transformer and choke cores `metal.ferrite`

The C64's power supply transformer, the filter chokes, the RF modulator coil and the ferrite beads on the board are all ceramic magnetic materials, not metal. A power ferrite is a spinel - either MnO.Fe2O3.ZnO or NiO.Fe2O3.ZnO - pressed as a powder and fired to 1200-1300 C, which is powder metallurgy in the truest sense: the magnetisation is not in the metal particles, it is in the magnetic domain walls of a ceramic. This is the branch where the metals tree stops being about metal and starts being about oxide chemistry, and the raw materials are iron oxide, manganese carbonate, zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

###### MnZn power ferrite for the switcher `metal.ferrite.mnzn`

The material of the C64's transformer core, the rectifier choke and the bulk filter chokes. Its job is to carry a large alternating flux at 15-65 kHz with as little loss and as little audible noise as possible, and that is a tight compromise: MnO raises the permeability and lowers the magnetostriction (which is what stops the transformer singing), ZnO raises the resistivity and pushes the Curie point up but lowers the saturation, and the two oxides partly cancel. A 1982 E-core for the C64's supply would be MnZn at roughly 0.2-0.35 W/cycle at 16 kHz and about 0.35 T saturation.

###### E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer `metal.ferrite.e-core` _(medium)_

The shape is dictated by the winding, and the 1982 supply for small switchers was a pair of E cores with a centre leg and a window, assembled 'E-E' or interleaved 'EI' so that the joint is staggered and the effective air gap is halved. The window has to fit the magnetising inductance and the wire; the cross-section is set by the core loss target. The same ferrite pressing produces E, EI, EE, U, toroid, drum and bobbin cores, and the shapes are made by different tools in the same press. The C64's transformer is one of the smallest: perhaps 25 mm across, 30-40 turns of 0.3 mm magnet wire on a bobbin, and a gap cut into the centre leg with a scraper to set the inductance.

###### Cutting the air gap in the centre leg `metal.ferrite.gap-scrape` _(medium)_

An ungapped ferrite E core has a very high inductance and would not regulate a switch-mode supply; the switcher's magnetising current would be wrong and the whole design fails. So the gap is made deliberately, and on a 1982 E core it was cut with a carbide-tipped scraper - literally a hand blade run along the face of the centre leg - to 0.2-1.0 mm. Cutting rather than inserting a gap material keeps the inductance high and spreads the gap's fringing over an area, and it does it with a machine a ferrite buyer can operate. The tolerance of that hand cut is what sets the inductance tolerance, and the whole thing is one of the more beautiful pieces of 1980s manufacturing: a blade and a number.

###### Filter chokes and the common-mode choke `metal.ferrite.choke` _(medium)_

The bulk filter chokes in a 1982 linear-supply C64 are 470 uH to a few millihenry with a current rating of 1-3 A, wound on an EE or a bobbin core of the same MnZn material. The switch-mode version instead has a common-mode choke: two windings on a single core, arranged so the two currents are equal and opposite, so the flux cancels and the choke does not need to store any energy - its only job is to present a high impedance to the common-mode noise on the mains lead.
