Both are the same pressed ceramic with a different winding.

###### Dopants: calcium, silicon, cobalt and the grain boundaries `metal.ferrite.dopants` _(medium)_

The last half percent of the ferrite recipe does most of the work. A small calcium and silicon addition forms a grain-boundary phase that makes the grain boundaries insulating and therefore suppresses eddy-current loss. Cobalt raises the anisotropy and the permeability at low field, which matters for a filter inductor. Lithium prevents wall-jumping in a high-coercivity ferrite. These additions are 0.1-2% each and they are why a power ferrite's chemistry is a trade secret and why the same nominal composition from two suppliers will not behave the same way.

###### NiZn ferrite for the RF and the beads `metal.ferrite.nizn`

The second family. Substituting nickel oxide for most of the manganese oxide raises the resistivity of the grain boundary by a factor of a hundred, so the eddy-current loss at high frequency collapses and NiZn is usable to about 100 MHz instead of 1 MHz. The price is a permeability of only 15-100 where MnZn gives a thousand, and a low saturation. In the C64 it is the RF modulator transformer and the video output circuitry, and off the board it is the small cylindrical bead slipped onto a wire to kill EMI. NiZn is pressed and sintered the same way; the only real differences are the raw material and the sintering atmosphere.

###### Ferrite bead: a small cylinder of NiZn or MnZn `metal.ferrite.bead`

A bead is just a pressed and fired ferrite with a hole through it, made on a bead press with a die that forms the cylinder in a few milliseconds. A 1982 board might carry a dozen: one on each supply line to the analogue section, one on the video line, one or two on the mains lead of the supply. The bead impedance is a rising curve with frequency, set entirely by the ferrite's complex permeability, and the bead's job is to convert a common-mode current into a small radiated field and a small conducted noise instead of a large one. The bead and the RF transformer are the same pressed powder.

###### The RF modulator coil `metal.ferrite.modulator` _(medium)_

The C64's TV modulator, which puts the composite video onto the RF of channel 3 or 4 so a television could display the machine, contains a small ferrite-loaded coil - a few turns of enamelled copper wire on a ferrite core or threaded through a ferrite bead. This is the one place in the machine where nickel-zinc ferrite is genuinely a radio-frequency component rather than a filter. The modulator itself and the television are the optics/television agents' business; the core is this branch's.

###### NiZn dopants: copper, cobalt and calcium `metal.ferrite.nizn.doping` _(medium)_

The NiZn family is doped with copper and cobalt to shape the grain-boundary physics, and with calcium to control the sintering. The NiZn product of the 1980s was deliberately split by composition into a high-permeability low-loss grade for transformers below 1 MHz and a very high-permeability grade for read heads and for antenna cores, and the difference between them was a fraction of a percent of dopant. It is a good example of a material in which the last tenth of a percent of the recipe is the difference between two products.

###### The nickel and cobalt raw materials for NiZn `metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source` _(low)_

The Ni-Zn family's nickel does not come as metal. It comes as nickel oxide, or as green nickel hydroxide precipitate from a laterite leach, and the cobalt comes either as cobalt metal or - much more cheaply, and this is the point - as a cobalt hydroxide carried out of the Sherritt-Gordon ammonia circuit as a precipitate, or as cobalt recovered from the spent nickel-catalyst streams. So the cobalt in a NiZn ferrite and the cobalt in a superalloy came out of the same nickel refinery, and that nickel refinery in 1982 was in the middle of a genuine cobalt supply crisis, which is a nice way for a ferrite material to be affected by a metals-market event.

                        - *Nickel oxide (NiO) calcined from basic carbonate* `metal.nickel.nickel-oxide` *(seen above)*
                        - *Cobalt recovered as dicobalt octacarbonyl* `metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl` *(seen above)*
###### Ferrite raw materials: the three oxides `metal.ferrite.raw-materials`

The three powders that get blended, and each one has its own industrial route. The iron oxide is either mill scale from the aluminium or the steel mill - washed, dried and milled, and the cheapest source - or a precipitated oxide made by acid leaching hematite. The manganese is manganese carbonate, a chemical precipitate from a manganese sulphate solution. The zinc is zinc oxide, made by roasting zinc ore or by burning zinc metal. The blend has to be accurate to about 0.2% in each component, because the magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to it, and by the 1980s the oxide suppliers were selling pre-blended 'master mixes' to the smaller ferrite makers precisely because the blending was the hard part.

###### Iron oxide from mill scale or from a precipitate `metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source` _(medium)_

The cheapest ferrite iron oxide is the mill scale from an aluminium rolling mill or a steel mill - but it comes as a mix of FeO, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 plus the alumina or silica the original metal carried, so it is milled and then passed over a strong magnetic separator to take out the magnetite, and the residue is calcined in air to convert all the iron to Fe2O3. The higher-purity route is to leach fine hematite in sulfuric acid and precipitate goethite or ferric hydroxide, wash it, and calcine it to a very pure Fe2O3 of 0.02% or less impurity - which is what the RF NiZn grades and the high-permeability grades need.

###### Manganese carbonate for the ferrite blend `metal.manganese-carbonate` _(medium)_

Not a mined material: a chemical precipitate. High-purity manganese sulphate solution is treated with sodium or ammonium carbonate at 60-90 C and pH 5-7, and manganese carbonate drops out as a pale pink powder. The iron must be kept out because MnCO3 with 1-2% iron pushes the ferrite's Curie temperature up and its permeability down. So the manganese chemistry of the ferromanganese branch in this file and the manganese chemistry of the ferrite branch share a plant but not a product, and a manganese mine does not touch either.

###### The mix house and the recipe book `metal.ferrite.mix-house` _(medium)_

The place where a ferrite formula is actually executed. A blend of perhaps 300 kg of oxide is weighed into a mixer - a ribbon blender or a ball mill - to 0.1 kg, sampled, analysed, and then the result is used to correct the next batch. The correction logic is where the manufacturer differs: some makers blend to the analysis and some blend to the recipe, and the argument between them is an old one. The mix house also holds the master recipes, and the confidentiality around them is a matter of pride rather than of deep mystery. A 1980s small ferrite factory had one mix house, one kiln line and one grinding room, and made a few hundred tonnes a year.

###### Ferrite powder metallurgy: blend to fire `metal.ferrite.manufacture`

Five steps, all of them inherited from the ceramic industry, none of them changed since the 1950s. Blend: the oxides are mixed wet in a ball mill or a vibrating mill to a few tenths of a percent. Calcine or pre-sinter: the blend is heated in air to about 900-1100 C, which drives off the moisture and the carbonate carbon dioxide and starts forming the spinel; the material comes out as a hard, sintered cake. Granulate: the cake is crushed and screened, and about 1-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or polyethylene binder is added with a little water so the powder will press. Press: a dry press - a 100-250 tonne hydraulic press - forms the shape at 100-200 MPa, with the tool steel die giving the final dimensions. Fire: the pressed part is sintered in air at 1200-1350 C, and the part shrinks about 1% linearly, which is why the die is made oversize and why every ferrite part in the world is ground afterwards. Finish: the fired part is ground on a double-disc or planetary grinder to final dimension, because the press cannot hold the tolerance.

###### Calcination and the spinel formation `metal.ferrite.calcination`

The chemical heart of the branch. Below the calcination temperature the blend is a mechanical mixture; by 900-1100 C the oxides have reacted and the cubic spinel lattice - which has three cation sites and eight for every 32 oxygen atoms - has formed, with the zinc on the tetrahedral sites, the manganese on the octahedral sites and the iron distributed across both. That distribution is why MnZn has a high permeability: Mn2+ and Fe2+ on opposing sublattices give an antiparallel but nearly equal spin arrangement, so the magnetisation can be tipped by a small field. It is an oxide chemistry result, and it is why a C64's transformer is ceramic and not iron.

###### Dry pressing in a tool steel die `metal.ferrite.pressing` _(medium)_

The pressed shape is the finished shape - an E, an EE, a toroid, a drum core - and the tool is a hardened steel die in a 100-250 tonne press. Ferrite presses in 1982 were 100-250 t, usually with a single or double action upper punch, and the cycle time for a small E core was 0.3-2 s. The part is pressed dry, which is why the powder has to be granulated first: free powder flows, granulated powder fills a die uniformly. The tooling is the same tool steel as an extrusion die, so the SKD61/H13 branch serves the ferrite industry too.

###### Firing at 1200-1300 C and the shrinkage `metal.ferrite.sintering`

The pressed part is fired on a belt or in a tunnel kiln in air, and in the last stage of the sintering it goes through the Curie temperature - about 200-250 C for MnZn - which is a magnetic transition, and above it the permeability of the material is irrelevant because it is paramagnetic. That is why a fire that goes too fast or spends too little time above the Curie point produces a core with poor low-frequency properties even though its density looks fine. During firing the part shrinks about 1% linearly, so a 20 mm E core comes out of a 20.2 mm die, and the finished dimension has to be set by grinding.

###### Grinding the fired part to size `metal.ferrite.grinding` _(medium)_

Because the fired part cannot be held to a useful dimension by pressing, it is lapped and ground. An E core is face-ground and the bore is ground; a toroid is OD and ID ground. In 1982 this was a double-disc or a planetary grinder with a diamond wheel, and it was expensive enough that a great many ferrite parts were still sold with a loose dimension tolerance and machined by the customer. The final steps are the coating: a thin epoxy or phenolic coat, or a dry lacquer coat and bake, which holds the core together, insulates it from the winding, and gives it a corrosion-resistant surface.

###### The firing schedule and the atmosphere control `metal.ferrite.quality` _(medium)_

The most closely guarded part of the whole ferrite industry is the firing curve: the ramp rate, the hold times, and the oxygen partial pressure through a 12-30 hour cycle. Too fast through the Curie point and the grain boundaries form in the wrong order and the core is lossy; too oxidising and Mn2+ becomes Mn3+ and the losses double; too reducing and the Fe becomes FeO and the permeability collapses. The kiln in 1982 was a tunnel kiln or a continuous belt with a controlled-atmosphere section and a dewpoint-controlled atmosphere, and the recipe was the plant's only real asset.

###### Hard and permanent ferrites (a note, not a C64 part) `metal.ferrite.hard` _(medium)_

Included because the same powder-magnetics plant makes them and because the raw-material branch is shared. A hard ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite - is sintered above its Curie point so the grains are aligned during cooling, and it is the permanent magnet in a magnetic recorder, a small motor or a magnetic separator. A C64 has no permanent magnet, but a floppy disk drive, a cassette mechanism or an electric screwdriver on the same production line does. Same presses, same kilns, same oxides - a different product from the same plant.

###### Strontium ferrite magnet `metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite` _(medium)_

SrFe12O19 pressed and fired like a power ferrite, then cooled through the Curie point in a magnetic field so the hexferrite grains line up. It is brittle, it is an oxide, and its key property is that it does not need any rare earth at all - which is exactly why barium and strontium ferrite are the standard cheap magnet, and why the two-share-the-mill argument makes this branch's economics obvious.

###### Strontium carbonate `metal.strontium-carbonate` _(medium)_

The only geologically interesting part: strontium is the rarest of the three alkaline-earth metals used in ferrites and ceramics, because it has no ore of its own that anyone uses. Strontium sulfate (celestine) is mined in Spain, Mexico and Iran, and almost all of it is converted to strontium carbonate. A C64 contains no strontium, so this is a dead end, but it is a real example of a mineral that exists only to make a ceramic.

###### Wet mixing and the ceramic ball mill `metal.ferrite.mixing` _(medium)_

The oxide blend is mixed wet in a rubber-lined ball mill or a vibrating mill, because water is the only way to get all three oxides into intimate contact within half a percent. A 1982 MnZn blend ran in a 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or in a ball mill with a few hundred kilos of zirconia or rubber-lined steel balls. The wet slip is then dried on a spray dryer or a rotary dryer to a granulated powder with the right moisture and the right particle size. The whole discipline of the ceramic industry is really about this step, and the blending tolerances of the finished core are set here.

###### Granulation and the binder `metal.ferrite.granulation` _(medium)_

Free powder flows; a pressed ferrite part needs the powder to fill the die uniformly, so the powder is granulated with 0.5-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or a PVA-polyethylene glycol binder and 8-12% water, on a spray granulator or a pan granulator, into 100-400 um granules. The granule has to survive being filled at a few grams per stroke and being pressed at 200 MPa, which is a tough mechanical requirement for a granule of ceramic powder.

###### Radio-frequency and rod ferrite `metal.ferrite.radio` _(low)_

A third shape family: ferrite rod and toroid for antenna and RF applications, pressed with an anisotropic die so the ferrite is oriented in the pressing direction. An isotropic pressed ferrite has half the usable permeability along the pressing axis as across it, because the pores are flattened; a ferrite maker who wants an antenna rod presses it in a die that aligns the grains. This is the ferrite in a portable radio's antenna, and it is the same powder as the transformer core, pressed in a different die.

###### The anisotropic pressing die `metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die` _(low)_

A ferrite pressed in an ordinary die has its pores flattened in the pressing direction, and flattened pores cut the permeability in that direction roughly in half - so a plain-pressed ferrite rod is a poor antenna core along its length. To avoid that, a rod core is pressed in a die with a fine central punch, so the powder is displaced radially and the pores and the grains align across the rod instead of along it. The same die idea is behind the toroid's oriented product and behind ferrite for read heads. It is a small piece of die engineering with a large effect, and it is why ferrite die makers were a specialist trade in the 1980s.

##### Oscillator coil and RF transformer `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-transformer` _(medium)_

A very small ferrite- or powdered-iron-cored coil wound on a 2-3 mm former with a tap, or a miniature two-winding transformer. The tapped winding gives both the feedback tap and an output tap, and the whole assembly sits within a few millimetres of the board's ground plane to keep the stray capacitance stable.

###### Radio-frequency ferrite core `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.tank-transformer.core-powder`

Nickel-zinc ferrite or iron powder, pressed or moulded into rings, cores or rods. NiZn is preferred above about 20 MHz because its resistivity is high enough that eddy-current loss does not swamp the circuit; MnZn is a low-frequency material and is the one used in the power transformer instead.

            - *Ferrite: transformer and choke cores* `metal.ferrite` *(seen above)*
            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain `metal.iron`

The bottom of the steel branch. Iron ore is dug, concentrated, reduced and never appears in a C64, and this branch exists so that the steel branch terminates in a mine rather than in an abstraction. The 1982 iron ore trade was dominated by three names: Mount Whaleback and the Pilbara in Western Australia, the Carajas and Quadrilatero Ferrifero in Brazil, and the Labrador Trough and the Mesabi range in North America. The ore is hematite, or magnetite, or both in a metamorphic banded iron formation - a rock that is 2 billion years old and was originally a chemical precipitate out of seawater.

###### Hematite (Fe2O3) and the Pilbara `metal.hematite`

Hematite is a steel-grey to red mineral that occurs as specular crystals, as kidney ore, and - the mass of the world's supply - as itabirite and hematite replacements in a banded iron formation. The Pilbara ore bodies in Western Australia are the richest hematite in the world at 62-66% Fe with almost no gangue, and the Brockman and Hamersley ranges were being mined at full rate by 1982. The ore ships from Port Hedland, where the ore handling and ship loaders are among the largest machines ever built.

###### Pilbara open-pit iron mine and the ore loader `metal.hematite.pilbara`

The Pilbara mines in 1982 were the mining engineering standard for the industry. A 15 m bench, 100-250 tonne haul trucks, 3-4 cubic metre shovels, and - this is the part everybody photographs - the huge travelling ore loaders that straddle the width of a haul truck and scoop up a 40-60 tonne load in one pass. The ore is crushed to 250 mm and conveyed up a 1.5 km incline to a stockyard, and then a 3-4 million tonne bulk carrier is loaded in about 20 hours at Port Hedland. One Pilbara mine shipped 40-100 Mt a year in the mid-1980s.

###### Banded iron formation: a chemical precipitate from seawater `metal.banded-iron-formation`

The leaf of the whole iron and steel branch, and one of the great ones. Around 2.0-1.8 billion years ago, the oceans contained dissolved ferrous iron and oxygen appeared in the atmosphere as a result of an earlier generation of photosynthetic organisms. Wherever the oxygen-rich surface water sank and met the anoxic iron-rich deep water, the iron oxidised and precipitated, as a jelly of iron oxide that settled as a chemical mud. It compacted into alternating silica and iron bands, and it is that banding which gives the rock its name and which makes the high-grade hematite ore bodies on the Hamersley Range the size they are. So the iron in a C64 chassis began, two billion years ago, as an oxide precipitating out of an ocean.

###### The silica and iron oxide banding `metal.bif-banding`

The leaf, described properly: a stack of alternating 1 mm to 10 m bands of chert (cryptocrystalline silica) and iron oxide, the whole thing metamorphosed, with the hematite in the oxidised upper part and magnetite in the reduced lower part and the P-rich band - the band that gives the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - where fossil bacteria oxidised the iron. Each band is a single depositional event or a group of them, and the ore-to-waste ratio of a Banded Iron Formation is often 1:2, so the pit that produces a tonne of iron ore has to move three tonnes of rock.

###### Crushing, screening and the lump/fines split `metal.hematite.crushing`

The ore is crushed in a gyratory and then on a screen, and the product is split three ways: lump ore above 6.3 mm that goes straight into the blast furnace, fines below 6.3 mm that must be sintered or pelletised, and a reject stream of the banded iron formation that is too low grade to smelt. The lump/fines split is a commercial decision rather than a metallurgical one: in 1982 the steelmakers wanted as much direct-shipping lump as possible because it avoided the sintering plant's capital and its fuel.

###### The ore stockyard and the ship loader `metal.hematite.stockyard`

Because the ships are 180,000-250,000 dwt and the mine's output is lumpy, the ore goes into a 1-2 million tonne stockyard with a stacker and a travelling shiploader. The shiploader is a 100 m long gantry on rails with a slewing chute that trims the ship's hold as it loads, so a 250,000 dwt vessel is filled flat without a bulker or a trimming machine. The whole Pilbara export chain - mine, conveyor, stockyard, loader, ship - was built to move one commodity in enormous tonnage at very low cost, and it is the reason Australian iron ore is the cheapest iron in the world.

              - *Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route* `metal.magnetite` *(seen above)*
##### Channel trimmer capacitor `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer` _(medium)_

The channel tuning element brought out to terminal 10 of the module: a small screw-adjusted trimmer, most often a ceramic or a mica trimmer in the 1-10 pF range. It sits across the tank and is set once, at the television manufacturer's alignment step, against a sweep generator or a calibrated television signal.

###### Multilayer ceramic capacitor `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer.multilayer-ceramic`

A stack of 20-50 alternating layers of barium titanate dielectric and internal nickel electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired at 1200-1350 C, then terminated in a fired-on silver or copper end-bump. This is the material of choice for small fixed RF capacitors because its self-resonance is high and its parasitics are tiny.

###### Barium titanate ceramic powder `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer.multilayer-ceramic.barium-titanate` _(medium)_

BaTiO3 is precipitated from barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, then doped and milled to sub-micron size. Barium carbonate comes from barite reduced with coke; titanium dioxide comes from ilmenite ore or from a chloride process fed on titanium ore and coke.

###### Barite ore (barytes) `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer.multilayer-ceramic.barium-titanate.barite`

A heavy white barium sulphate ore, mined chiefly as a drilling mud and as the feed for barium carbonate. This is the leaf of the barium chain.

                - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
###### Ilmenite and the chloride process `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer.multilayer-ceramic.barium-titanate.titanium-dioxide` _(medium)_

Titanium dioxide pigment is made either by sulphating ilmenite ore and calcining, or by chlorinating ilmenite with coke at 900 C and oxidising the TiCl4 in a flame to TiO2. Ilmenite is a beach or dune sand of FeTiO3, concentrated by gravity and magnetic separation.

###### Ilmenite sand `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-trimmer.multilayer-ceramic.barium-titanate.titanium-dioxide.ilmenite`

A black heavy mineral sand, essentially iron titanate, worked from beach placer deposits and from massive ore bodies. Dredged, concentrated and smelted to give titanium slag or chlorinated to give TiCl4. This is the leaf of the titanium chain.

                  - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
                  - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
##### MA57 tuning varactor diode `mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor` _(low)_

On the earlier 251696 drawing the tuning is done by D3, an MA57: a junction varactor whose capacitance falls as the reverse bias rises. Lifting the tuning out of the tank into a varactor keeps the temperature coefficient and the stray capacitance low. Later drawings use a mechanical trimmer in the same position.

          - *Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding* `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging` *(seen above)*
#### Audio intercarrier path `mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain`

A separate 4.5 MHz (NTSC) or 5.5 MHz (PAL) oscillator whose amplitude is modulated by the SID's audio output, then added to the picture carrier. Terminal 8 selects between the two: Commodore's drawing notes that terminal 8 shorted to ground is PAL and open is NTSC PAL/US.

##### FM modulator network `mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator`

The audio signal is fed to the intercarrier oscillator's base through a series resistor and a coupling capacitor, so the oscillator's amplitude follows the audio envelope. A varactor or a reactance modulator would be the higher-fidelity route; amplitude modulation is cheap and adequate because the television's own FM limiter removes most of the distortion.

###### SID audio amplifier transistor `mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.audio-amplifier` _(medium)_

On the C64 mainboard the SID's pin 27 output is amplified by Q2 before it reaches CN5 pin 3 and the modulator; the modulator's audio input then loads that amplifier. The stage is a common-emitter NPN with a bias divider and an emitter resistor, running from the CAN +5 V rail.

            - *2SC1694 small-signal NPN* `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor` *(seen above)*
##### Intercarrier selector terminal `mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier-selector`

A single link or jumper on terminal 8 that reconfigures the intercarrier oscillator between 4.5 and 5.5 MHz. It is the PAL/NTSC configuration link for the whole module, and it is why one board could serve both markets with a single part change.

      - *RF output network and 75 ohm match* `mb.rf-modulator.rf-output` *(seen above)*
#### Modulator supply and zener stabiliser `mb.rf-modulator.supply`

The modulator runs from the C64's ~9 V unregulated DC rail - the same rail that feeds the cassette motor - not from the clean 5 V. Q6 (2SC2120) buffers the feed and a zener with electrolytics sets the working voltage for the analog sections.

##### 8.2 V Zener diode `mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener` _(medium)_

A heavily doped PN junction reverse-biased into breakdown. The doping is so heavy that the depletion layer is only a few microns wide, which gives the device a very low capacitance and a fast, hard breakdown - ideal for a shunt regulator and for clamping.

          - *Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding* `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging` *(seen above)*
#### Encapsulated and hybrid module variants `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module` _(low)_

Some very early Commodore modulators and several third-party and Japanese-supplied variants were potted or epoxy-dipped modules rather than a bare board: the circuit is built on an alumina or ceramic substrate with deposited resistors, is trimmed and aligned, then covered in a clear or opaque epoxy that also acts as the environmental and RF seal.

##### Alumina substrate and its ceramic processing `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-substrate`

A thin, smooth, thermally conductive ceramic sheet. Alumina is made by calcining purified aluminium hydroxide, pressing or tape-casting it with an organic binder, sintering at 1500-1700 C, then lapping and laser-cutting the finished sheets to thickness. It is inert, dimensionally stable and easy to metallise.

          - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Magnesium oxide sintering aid `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-substrate.sintering-aid`

A few tenths of a percent of magnesium oxide is added to 96% alumina before sintering to stop the ceramic over-shrinking and to fire it at a lower temperature, which is what makes 96% alumina affordable for a hybrid substrate.

            - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Magnesite ore `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-substrate.sintering-aid.magnesite` _(medium)_

A magnesium carbonate rock mined in Austria, Spain, China and India, calcined at 1400-1700 C to magnesia. In the 1980s most ceramic-grade magnesia was calcined from seawater or from brine, but the rock remains the classic source.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
##### Thin-film and thick-film resistor networks `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-resistors`

A film of nickel-chromium is deposited by vacuum evaporation or sputtering onto the alumina, then patterned by photolithography and etching. Because the sheet resistance of the film is very uniform the as-deposited value is already within a few percent, so a trim brings it to its exact value.

          - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
          - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Ruthenium-oxide cermet paste `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-resistors.cermet`

The thick-film resistor material: finely divided ruthenium dioxide mixed with a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed through a 100-250 um mesh and fired on a belt furnace at 800-900 C. The glass binds conductor and semiconductor together, and the resistance is set largely by how much glass is in the paste.

###### Ruthenium, from anode slime `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-resistors.cermet.ruthenium`

Recovered commercially from the nickel-copper mattes of Sudbury-type nickel ores, where it concentrates in the anode slime. The slime is dissolved and the platinum-group metals separated by selective precipitation and solvent extraction.

###### Nickel matte and anode slime `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-resistors.cermet.ruthenium.slime`

Copper and nickel concentrates are smelted to a matte, converted to blister metal, then electrolytically refined in a copper or nickel tankhouse. Noble metals fall out of solution as an anode slime, which is filtered, dissolved in aqua regia and separated.

                - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
                - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
##### Epoxy encapsulant as RF seal `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-encapsulant`

A clear or opaque filled epoxy poured or transfer moulded over the finished substrate. In RF modules it does three jobs at once: it excludes moisture and contaminants, it holds the components against vibration, and - because it is a low-loss dielectric with a stable dielectric constant - it fixes the stray capacitance around the tank, which is what stops the carrier drifting with humidity. A conductive epoxy variant is used as a ground plane on the reverse of the substrate.

          - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
          - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
          - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
##### Gold-plated DIP lead frame `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame` _(medium)_

The substrate is attached to a lead frame by reflow or conductive epoxy, and the frame's pins are plated. Gold is used where the RF signal leaves the module, because a nickel or tin surface has poor conductivity at 60 MHz and tarnishes; in cheap modules only the signal pins are gold and the supply pins are tinned.

###### Gold and its ore `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.gold`

Gold is recovered by cyanide leaching of ore and tailings after gravity and flotation concentration, then adsorbed on activated carbon and electrowon or precipitated with zinc, and finally refined by electrolysis to 99.99%. This is the leaf of the gold chain.

###### Cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.gold.leach`

Crushed and agglomerated ore is soaked in dilute alkaline cyanide with aeration; gold dissolves as the dicyanoaurate complex and is adsorbed on activated carbon columns, stripped with hot caustic soda and zinc dust, smelted, and electrolytically refined.

              - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
###### Natural gas: the gas field `chem.natural-gas`

Methane, mostly: either the gas cap sitting on an oil reservoir or a gas-only field. In 1983 world gas production was roughly 2.9-3.0 trillion cubic metres a year, of which about 70% was still associated with oil and much of it was flared or burned at the wellhead. Gas matters to a C64 three ways: as acetylene for PVC and chlorinated solvents, as hydrogen for ammonia and hydrochloric acid, and as the fuel that moved the plastics.

###### What natural gas is `chem.natural-gas.composition`

A mixture, not a compound. A sour gas well may deliver methane with 2-10% ethane and propane, 1-8% C4, 1-20% hydrogen sulphide, 0.5-5% carbon dioxide and up to 15% nitrogen. Everything downstream - the pipelines, the dew point specification, the hydrogen plant - is set by those five impurities.

###### Methane `chem.natural-gas.composition.methane`

CH4, 80-98% of a dry gas, 39.8 MJ/m3 gross calorific value, -161.5 C boiling point. The single molecule most of this branch is about: because methane is hard to polymerise and hard to functionalise, the industry of the 1980s broke it into acetylene at extreme temperature or into hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, and those two products underwrote most of the polymer industry.

###### Ethane and propane (LPG) `chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-propane`

The C2 and C3 that make natural gas liquids, recovered as LPG at 1.5-8 bar in the field and as a debottlenecking liquid at the gas plant, then split for heating or fed to a cracker. LPG was the preferred cracker feedstock precisely because it is already light and needs no naphtha handling.

###### Propane as cracker feed `chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-propane.propane-cracker-feed` _(medium)_

A dedicated propane cracker needs far less steam dilution (20-40 mol% versus 200-400 mol% for naphtha) and so makes far less process gas per tonne of ethylene, but it makes relatively little co-product: the propylene and butenes streams shrink and the C4 stream effectively disappears. That single trade-off has moved cracker economics for forty years.

###### Nitrogen in natural gas `chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen` _(low)_

1-15% N2 in many fields. It is the impurity that most affects heating value, that forces the Wobbe index (a measure of interchangeability between gas supplies) onto a pipeline tariff, and that makes a gas which is 90% N2 unsaleable as town gas.

###### Hydrogen sulphide (sour gas) `chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s`

A lethal, corrosive, smelly component that must be taken to a few ppmv before the gas enters a steel pipeline, because H2S embrittles steel and attacks copper alloys. Sweetening it produces a concentrated acid gas stream whose H2S is the feedstock for the Claus sulphur plant in the refining branch.

###### Where the gas comes from `chem.natural-gas.sources`

Associated gas from the gas cap of an oil reservoir, and non-associated (gas-only) gas. The distinction matters industrially: associated gas was a by-product that had to be flared or reinjected until the late 1970s made it commercial, while gas-only fields carry the pipelines and the LNG trains.

###### Associated (oil-associated) gas `chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas`

Gas from the gas cap of an oil field, produced at roughly 50-150 m3 of gas per barrel of oil. Around 70% of world gas production was associated gas in 1983, and a large share was still flared: world flaring ran at the order of 100-130 billion m3 a year in the early 1980s, several million tonnes of hydrocarbons a year simply burned at the wellhead.

###### Flare and gas reinjection `chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.flare` _(medium)_

A flare tip burns whatever the oil plant cannot handle; in 1980s practice it was sized for peak oil rate, so routine gas-cap growth had to be reinjected into the reservoir or sold. Recovering associated gas was one of the clearest economic arguments for the gas-processing plants built in the Middle East and Nigeria in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

###### Non-associated (gas-only) field `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas`

A gas reservoir with no oil at the contact. The North Sea fields of the late 1970s - Frigg (1977), Heimdal, Sleipner, Troll (discovered 1979) - turned Europe from an import market into a gas market, and the Norwegian and British gas grids of the early 1980s were built around them. In the US the equivalent discovery was the tight and geopressured gas of the Anadarko and Rocky Mountain basins.

###### Discovering and drilling a gas field `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling`

Gas fields are found by the same seismic and drilled with the same rig as oil fields, but the completion differs: the log response that proves a gas column is high resistivity with low neutron density, and the well must be tested for absolute gas flow rather than liquid rate. Gas viscosity is about a hundred times lower than oil but its compressibility ten times higher, so the well responds to drawdown very differently.

###### Seismic over a gas prospect `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.seismic`

Gas sands are often visible before they are drilled: gas lowers the acoustic impedance of the rock, so the reflector dims and sometimes inverts (a bright spot). The amplitude anomaly is a well-known risk - it is also produced by a shale lens or by a tuning effect - which is why a 1980s exploration manager still had to drill to find out.

###### Drilling fluid for a gas well `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.drill-fluid`

Gas wells were drilled with the same bentonite mud as oil wells, with two differences: a low filter loss was mandatory because filtrate invasion had to be reversed before logging, and a gas-cut mud had to be controlled because entrained gas reduced hydrostatic pressure and made the well hard to control. The standard 1980s control was a mechanical gas trap plus defoamer.

###### Bentonite mud `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.drill-fluid.bentonite`

Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota, the same clay as the oilfield mud. In a gas well the requirement is a low solids count so the log response is not screened by a thick filter cake.

###### Casing and perforation for a gas well `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.casing-and-perforation`

Identical hardware to an oil well, different discipline: a gas well has to be tested to destruction of the casing and tubing if it is perforated below the point of no return, because the gas column is light and there is no fluid level to swallow a leak. High-strength casing and a cemented, pressure-tested completion were the rule.

###### Wellhead separation of gas `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.wellhead-separation`

A wellhead separator and a test separator drop the liquid out of the gas at 30-70 bar, then the gas goes to a knockout drum and to the gathering system. The liquid is the same crude or condensate as in the oil case; the gas is dried and sweetened at the plant, not at the wellhead.

###### Sweetening to pipeline specification `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.sweetening`

H2S and CO2 are removed with a 20-35 wt% alkanolamine in an absorber at 30-45 C and 20-70 bar, with the rich amine regenerated at 120-130 C and 1.5-2 bar in a reboiler. By the early 1980s the trend was to diethanolamine for economy and MDEA for lower heat duty and no carbamate degradation.

###### Alkanolamine `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.sweetening.amine` _(medium)_

Monoethanolamine (MEA, primary), diethanolamine (DEA, secondary), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA, tertiary). MDEA was the growth amine of the 1980s because it does not form carbamate with CO2, so its degradation and reboiler duty are lower; the penalty is a slower absorption rate and a lower equilibrium loading.

###### Dehydration to pipeline dew point `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.dehydration`

Gas must arrive at the pipeline dew point or the higher-pressure steps downstream condense water out and the line fills with liquid. By 1980s practice that meant a glycol unit (triethylene glycol at 80-95 wt% purity, contactor at 20-50 C and 40-70 bar, reboiler 120-140 C) and increasingly a 3A or 4A molecular sieve adsorption unit for the last kilogram of water per million standard cubic metres.

###### Triethylene glycol `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.dehydration.triethylene-glycol`

A heavy glycol made by reacting ethylene oxide with diethylene glycol; the standard dehydration absorbent because of its low vapour pressure at the contactor temperature. The 1980s trend was towards 95 wt% TEG purity, because glycol vapour carried upstream into a gas turbine or a carburettor was a real emission problem.

###### Gas reservoir `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.gas-reservoir`

Gas fills a porous sandstone or a fractured carbonate just as oil does, but with a lower density and a higher compressibility, so gas in place is quoted in trillions of standard cubic feet rather than billions of barrels. The largest gas fields in the world in the early 1980s were the giant Permian Basin fields (US), Urengoy and Yamburg in West Siberia, and Groningen (Netherlands, discovered 1959).

###### Gas in place `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.gas-reservoir.gas-in-place` _(medium)_

Trillions of standard cubic metres of gas in the pore space. The C64-scale fact: all the natural gas used worldwide in 1983 was of the order of 3,000 billion cubic metres a year, so one machine's plastics and energy are far below a thousandth of a cubic metre.

###### Unconventional gas (tight and coalbed) `chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.unconventional-gas` _(medium)_

The gas fields that had to be stimulated rather than merely completed: tight low-permeability sandstone and coalbed methane. The techniques are the oil branch's - massive hydraulic fracturing, and dewatering for coal seams - applied to rock that is not a reservoir in the classical sense. In 1983 tight gas was a real but small share of US supply and coalbed methane was still essentially an experiment in the Black Warrior basin.

###### Gas hydrate (a hazard, not yet a resource) `chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate` _(medium)_

Methane trapped as a clathrate of water, stable below about 20 C at surface pressure. Known since the 1930s and already recognised in the deep ocean and permafrost as a potentially enormous resource, but in the early 1980s it was a hazard - it plugged subsea pipelines and was one reason offshore gas lines carried inhibitors and heated risers - not a supply.

###### Gas processing and transport `chem.natural-gas.processing`

The plants that turn a wet, sour wellstream into a pipeline gas, a liquefied gas or a natural-gas-liquids fraction. A large 1980s gas plant handled 5-30 billion standard cubic feet a day; the North Sea, Gulf and Middle Eastern plants of that decade were among the largest chemical plants ever built.

###### Cryogenic separation (expander plant) `chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-separation`

The JT-expander process that became the industry standard for large gas plants in the 1980s: the gas is chilled by expansion through a turbine to -30 to -80 C and the resulting cold box distils methane from ethane and heavier. The plant cost is dominated by the aluminium cold boxes, which remain one of the largest single uses of aluminium in the world per tonne produced.

###### Cryogenic turboexpander `chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-separation.expander`

A radial or axial turbine in the cold box, handling 10,000-40,000 kW on a big plant, recovering 5-15% of the gas enthalpy and reaching -30 to -80 C. The expander train was the mechanical heart of the 1980s gas plant and its efficiency set the plant cost.

###### Aluminium cold box `chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-separation.cold-box`

A brazed plate-and-fin aluminium exchanger 10-30 m long, cryogenic to -80 C, containing dozens of channels. Aluminium-brazed cold boxes replaced copper wound exchangers in the 1970s and are one reason the gas plant business grew so fast in that decade.

###### Natural gas liquids recovery `chem.natural-gas.processing.ngl-recovery`

Ethane, propane, butane and pentane are stripped out of the gas and sold as NGL: ethane for crackers, propane and butane for LPG, C5+ for gasoline. A cryogenic plant recovers 90-99% of the methane but less of the heavy end, so the design trade is expander versus absorption. The NGL stream is the LPG that feeds the crackers in the ethylene branch.

###### LNG liquefaction `chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction`

Chilling gas to -162 C so it becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure, cutting volume about 600-fold for the same energy. In 1983 world LNG trade was roughly 55-70 billion m3 a year, about 2-3% of world gas production, on a network of roughly 60-70 liquefaction trains. The dominant cycles were the propane-precooled mixed refrigerant (9 stages, about 7-8% specific power) and the nitrogen expander cycle.

###### Mixed refrigerant cycle `chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.refrigerant` _(medium)_

Propane pre-cooling to -30 to -40 C, then an ethylene/ethane/propane mixture expanded through a series of exchangers to -120 C, then a nitrogen expander to -162 C. The hydrocarbons in the refrigerant are the same ones the petrochemical industry buys; the nitrogen expander cycle burns almost nothing but needs a lot of power and very large exchangers, which suited a plant with cheap power and no other outlet for its fuel gas.

###### LNG storage and regasification terminal `chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.terminal` _(low)_

A vacuum-insulated cylindrical tank of 20,000-160,000 m3 with a nickel-alloy inner tank over perlite insulation, plus a jetty for a 125,000-165,000 m3 carrier. Regasification burns about 0.3 tonnes of fuel gas per tonne of LNG, which is where the C64-scale fact becomes visible: the fuel burned to regasify enough LNG to make one machine's plastics is tens of grams.

###### LNG carrier `chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.carrier` _(low)_

A 70,000-125,000 m3 membrane or independent-tank ship with a re-liquefaction plant, because LNG boils off at 0.1-0.3% a day and the load has to be reliquefied in transit. The world LNG fleet in 1983 was of the order of 90-130 ships at $40-90 million each.

###### Gas pipeline `chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline`

Line pipe 0.6-1.4 m in diameter, API 5L grade X52-X70, laid by a lay barge or a trenching spread and internally coated with epoxy and polyethylene powder. Transmission lines run at 60-100 bar with compressors every 100-200 km. The 1980s were the years of the great gas transmission builds: the Central Asia-Centre system, the Norwegian and North Sea systems and the Trans-Med pipelines all date from this decade.

###### Subsea pipeline and riser `chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.subsea`

Concrete weight-coated line with a hot-water or electrical trace heater for hydrate prevention, and a wet-insulated riser with a buoyancy module for the first 100-300 m of water. Deepwater gas tiebacks of the 1980s established the standard development: subsea wellhead manifold, a dedicated line to a central platform, gas gathered ashore.

###### What the gas is for `chem.natural-gas.uses`

Three jobs in 1983: burn it, crack it, or reform it. Burning dominated volume; the petrochemical jobs - acetylene, hydrogen, ammonia - were small in tonnage but disproportionate in value, and they are the reason the polymer industry existed at all.

###### Acetylene from natural gas `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene`

The Reppe process, commercialised from 1959-1965: a mixture of roughly 6-8% methane with 30-38% air and 55-60% hydrogen is fired through a water-cooled burner at 1,200-1,800 C and quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds. The acetylene yield per pass is only 2-3% of the feed, so the process has to recycle a large stream, and the furnace consumes several GWh of electricity per tonne of acetylene. It survived because it made a C2 unit out of a C1 feed - the only route that can make vinyl chloride, and hence PVC, without cracking a barrel of naphtha.

###### Partial oxidation burner `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.partial-oxidation` _(medium)_

Methane is partially oxidised to CO and H2, which then combine to acetylene at flame temperature. The furnace runs at atmospheric to 2 bar with the flame held above the acetylene decomposition point; the burner is water-cooled because copper and steel both survive the flame while the mixture would otherwise decompose to soot. The process is violently sensitive to soot: any carbon in the gas feed poisons the burner.

###### Quench and acetylene recovery `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench` _(medium)_

The hot gas is quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds, then acetylene is absorbed selectively from the acetylene-hydrogen-methane-hydrogen-sulphide mixture by acetone at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar (about 2.2 volumes of acetylene per volume of solvent), stripped and the solvent recirculated. Recovered acetylene is 99.5-99.8% pure once hydrogen sulphide and water are removed.

###### The absorption and recovery train `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.absorption-train`

The acetylene is absorbed out of the cracked mixture in a solvent and taken off the top of the tower at high purity, which is the whole reason for doing the separation this way. Acetone's job is to hold acetylene - which at 20 C and 12 bar will dissolve to about 2.2 volumes of solvent per volume of acetylene - while letting the hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide straight through. The dark, dangerous part of this plant is not the chemistry but the acetylene itself: above 2 bar in the presence of a metal, acetylene will detonate into its own decomposition products, and the whole extraction plant is designed around never letting that happen.

###### Absorber and stripper `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.absorption-train.absorber`

A 20-40 tray absorber at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar with the acetone circulated, and a stripper that takes the pure acetylene overhead at 3-5 bar and the solvent off the bottom for recycle. The solvent must be regenerated at intervals because it accumulates the hydrogen sulphide and the water from the feed gas, and because the acetylene polymerises in it if it is left standing - the plant has a permanent low-temperature nitrogen blanketing problem.

###### Acetone as the selective solvent `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.absorption-train.absorber.acetone-solvent`

The choice of solvent is a compromise. Acetone has a high acetylene solubility and a low methane solubility and a manageable vapour pressure, and it is made from cumene on the same site, which is the practical reason it was chosen. It is also flammable and it is a reproductive toxin, which is a modern objection to a molecule the industry has used since 1945.

###### Drying and finishing the acetylene `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.absorption-train.acetylene-purification` _(medium)_

The last step before the acetylene goes to the vinyl chloride plant is a drying and finishing train: a molecular sieve or a chilled water wash to get the water under 10 ppm, a caustic or amine wash to take the last of the hydrogen sulphide, and a final distillation if the grade has to be 99.8%. Vinyl chloride does not tolerate water - it hydrolyses - so the last drying step before the HCl addition is not optional.

                    - *Acetylene to vinyl chloride* `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride` *(seen above)*
###### Acetylene to chlorinated solvents `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-trichloroethylene`

Chlorination of acetylene to tetrachloroethane followed by dehydrochlorination to trichloroethylene (1,1,2-TCE) was the original industrial route to the electronics degreaser and was still the route in much of the world in 1980. The acetylene-HCl chemistry is the same as the vinyl chloride chemistry; only the degree of chlorination differs.

###### Acetylene black `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.carbon-black`

Cracking acetylene at 1,200-1,400 C in a water-cooled steel retort and quenching in nitrogen gives a fine, high-surface-area carbon black, historically the standard channel black for rubber reinforcement and printing inks. Furnace black made from natural gas (CATB, from 1950) largely displaced it in tyres during the 1960s.

###### Chloromethanes and the semiconductor chain `chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.chloromethanes`

Acetylene plus chlorine gives tetrachloroethane and from it trichloroethylene and chloroform, while the same high-temperature HCl chemistry gives methyl chloride from methane - the starting material for the chlorosilane and semiconductor-grade silicon chain. Natural gas therefore reaches the C64's chips as well as its case, by a very indirect route.

###### Hydrogen by steam methane reforming `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen`

CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2 over nickel at 750-850 C and 20-30 bar, followed by the water-gas shift (iron oxide/chromia, 350-450 C) to raise the hydrogen fraction, then CO2 removal and cryogenic or PSA purification. A world-scale 1980s plant made 50-100 million m3 of hydrogen a day. Almost all of it went to ammonia; the rest to hydrotreating and to hydrochloric acid.

###### Nickel reforming catalyst `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-catalyst` _(medium)_

Nickel on alumina, or the older nickel-chromium used in the pre-1957 Topsoe SMR-180. By the 1980s the modern multi-bed reformer ran 25-40 tubes of 10-16 inch diameter at 30-50 bar, with an inlet temperature near 550 C and an outlet at 850-870 C, burning gas in a process furnace alongside the tubes.

###### Hydrogen to ammonia (Haber-Bosch) `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia`

N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 over promoted iron or ruthenium at 400-500 C and 150-250 bar, in a 1,000-2,500 tonne a day synthesis loop fed from a purge cascade. Ammonia is the single largest use of hydrogen, and it matters to the C64 in two places: the nitrogen for the polybutadiene and SAN polymerisations, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

###### Ammonia `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonia` _(medium)_

NH3: the feedstock for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation, for fertiliser, and for the electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide used to rinse and develop photoresist. World ammonia production in 1983 was of the order of 100-110 million tonnes a year.

###### Electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonium-hydroxide`

Aqueous ammonia at 20-29 wt% for semiconductor processing, made by sparging anhydrous ammonia into ultrapure water under a scrubbed laminar-flow hood. One of the handful of wet chemicals delivered to a fab in a fluoropolymer or electro-polished bottle rather than a tank.

###### Ammonia synthesis catalyst `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.catalyst`

The Haber-Bosch catalyst is promoted iron: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with potassium oxide and with alumina or calcium oxide. Ruthenium is better by an order of magnitude but was, in 1983, still a research curiosity as far as ammonia plants were concerned. The catalyst is made by melting magnetite with the promoters, granulating, and reducing it in situ with hydrogen, and a 1980s ammonia plant had a few hundred tonnes of it.

###### Magnetite from iron ore `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.catalyst.magnetite`

Fe3O4, the reduction product of hematite, and the raw material for the ammonia catalyst. It is also the mineral in the Claus catalyst's neighbourhood and in the polishing lapidary industry. A tonne of ammonia carries about 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron in its catalyst, and the catalyst is replaced every few years, so the ammonia business has a real, if modest, appetite for iron ore.

###### Hydrogen to hydrochloric acid `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrochloric-acid`

H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl at 250-400 C over an HCl synthesis catalyst, then absorption into demineralised water to 31-37%. This is the second largest industrial use of hydrogen and it is why the chlorine industry needs natural gas at all: without reforming hydrogen, chlor-alkali chlorine is very hard to sell. The HCl then feeds vinyl chloride, the chloromethanes and the chlorinated degreasers.

###### Hydrogen for hydrotreating `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrotreating`

The refinery's hydrogen - desulphurisation, hydrocracking, reforming - came from naphtha reformers and, as sour crudes grew, from dedicated gas reformers or hydrogen manufacturing units fed with refinery off-gas. In 1983 hydrogen was roughly 3-5% of refinery energy consumption and a genuine bottleneck.

###### Gas as fuel `chem.natural-gas.uses.fuel` _(medium)_

The largest single use of gas: heat, boilers, industrial furnaces and gas turbines. A 1980s gas turbine power station of 40-100 MW fired natural gas at 15-25 bar through a dual-fuel combustor; a plastics plant's furnace was gas-fired with 10-30% excess oxygen so its stack oxygen stayed high. Because gas burns cleanly, a gas-fired furnace could run a polyethylene line without the sulphur constraint of a fuel-oil furnace - one reason gas-based polymer plants grew up in the Gulf and in Western Europe.

###### Fertiliser ammonia `chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia` _(medium)_

About 80% of ammonia goes to fertiliser, a demand that sets the size of the hydrogen industry and therefore, indirectly, the amount of ammonia available for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The link to the C64 is indirect but real: the same ammonia plants that fertilised the fields also supplied the nitrogen that went into the case polymer.

##### Hybrid module assembly and transfer moulding `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly` _(medium)_

The die or chip components are bonded to the substrate, the lead frame is attached, and the whole assembly is transfer moulded in epoxy: a silicone-rubber mould loaded with epoxy powder is vibrated to pack it around the part, the encapsulant is pressed in, and it is cured at 150-175 C. This is the same process used for every integrated circuit in the machine.

          - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
          - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Attaching the substrate to the lead frame `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.lead-bond`

The substrate is aligned to the lead frame to within a few microns, given a thin coat of conductive epoxy - silver-filled epoxy is the usual choice because it cures at only 150-200 C - or a screen-printed solder paste is printed and reflowed, then the assembly is baked so the die attaches without stress. Silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and can debond with thermal cycling, which is the classic failure mode of a hybrid module.

            - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
            - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Silver-filled conductive epoxy `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.lead-bond.epoxy`

Epoxy resin loaded with 50-80% silver flakes. The flakes touch each other to form a percolating conductor while the epoxy gives mechanical strength and cures at a temperature the chip and substrate tolerate. Bulk resistivity is about 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm, two to three orders of magnitude worse than a metal, so it is used for bonding and for conductive fill, never for signal.

              - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
              - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
##### Chip inductor and chip capacitor `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passives` _(medium)_

In a hybrid RF module the high-value capacitors and the low-value inductors are not screen-printed but chip-bonded: a fired ceramic chip capacitor with metallised terminations is reflowed onto the substrate, and an inductor is a tiny spiral of metallised polyimide on a ceramic chip. The polyimide is photosensitised, plated, etched and diced, so the inductance is set by the artwork rather than by a winding machine.

###### Laser trimming of the film resistors `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passives.laser-trim` _(medium)_

A laser is pulsed at a deposited resistor while a bridge measures its value, cutting a slot in the film a few microns wide to raise the resistance by a controlled amount. Each pulse changes the value by a known increment and the bridge closes the loop, so a resistor can be trimmed to 0.1% or better in a fraction of a second. Before laser trimming was cheap, the same slot was cut by abrading with a sand jet under a bridge, which was slower and only got to about 5%.

            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
##### Substrate alignment and RF screening `mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment` _(medium)_

After assembly the module is screened: an RF sweep is injected at the output terminal and the response curve is checked against a mask. A damaged substrate, a lifted chip termination or a cracked lead frame shows up as a notch in the response, which is why a hybrid modulator's yield is dominated by the ceramic and the assembly rather than by the design.

          - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
#### Modulator part numbers and revisions `mb.rf-modulator.variants`

Commodore changed the modulator repeatedly and warned in the service manual that most modulators are different and the parts are not interchangeable between mainboards. Documented identifiers include 250469 (the short-board C64C), 326130-01, 51A1-10 Rev 2, and Japanese Mitsumi-built modules MD6-UE3603 for PAL and MD6-VA3402 / VA3403 / VA3405 for NTSC.

##### Mitsumi-built modules `mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi`

Mitsumi Electric was a major Japanese supplier of consumer-electronics subassemblies and shipped RF modulator modules to Commodore. The MD6 prefix denotes the module family; the suffix distinguishes NTSC from PAL and the electrolytic set.

###### The 1984 C64C video path `mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contrast` _(low)_

The later C64 boards do not simply carry a better modulator - they changed where the signal is encoded. A dedicated video encoder IC generates the composite and separate luma/chroma outputs from the VIC-II's signals, so the video is encoded once, to a defined standard, outside the modulator; the RF modulator is then reduced to a device that only has to put that composite onto a carrier and add the audio. The contrast with the breadbin is that there the modulator itself was the video encoder as well as the modulator.

###### Video encoder integrated circuit `mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contrast.encoder-ic` _(low)_

A mask-programmed device that takes the VIC-II's luminance and chrominance plus the synchronisation inputs and generates composite video and separate luma and chrominance outputs internally, using on-chip resistor-string DACs for the levels. Building the encoder alongside the VIC-II was what made the S-Video output clean enough to be worth using.

              - *Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding* `mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transistor.packaging` *(seen above)*
##### The 'toad' module nickname `mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad` _(low)_

Early Commodore modulators are sometimes described by hobbyists as a toad or a blob: the epoxy-covered module sits on the mainboard with its lead frame splayed out, and from the top it does look like an animal. The nickname is not a Commodore part name - it exists only in the collector community.

          - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
#### Why the RF picture was poor `mb.rf-modulator.quality`

The modulator is not the only reason the C64's television picture was soft and cross-talk-ridden, but it removes the last chance to recover quality: the VIC-II's own composite output already mixes luminance and chroma imperfectly, the television's 6 MHz vision channel is a narrow band-pass, the sound is on a separate subcarrier that leaks, and an analogue tuner adds its own noise. Every stage is lossy and they compound.

##### Two composite paths in one module `mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain`

Because the module has to keep working as a monitor passthrough, it carries two paths: the luma and colour signals are buffered straight through to CN5 so a monitor still gets an unmodified signal, while a separate summed composite is what drives the RF section. This is why S-Video from a breadbin is clean while the RF picture is not - the lossy parts of the chain are only on the RF path.

###### NTSC and PAL variants `mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain.ntsc-vs-pal` _(medium)_

The earlier 5-pin mainboard mixed sync, luminance and colour into composite on the board itself and fed that to the modulator, whereas the 8-pin boards pass luma and colour separately so the modulator can also provide S-Video. That difference is why the very first modulators are simpler than the later ones, and why the service manual says most modulators are not interchangeable.

#### Modulator manufacture, alignment and test `mb.rf-modulator.assembly` _(medium)_

A 1980s RF module was assembled by hand through a small number of components, soldered, then aligned: the channel trimmer is set against a television signal generator or a spectrum analyser, the intercarrier selector link is fitted for the market, the level network is checked on a video monitor, and the unit is burn-in tested with a television running.

##### Tin-lead solder and flux `mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder`

A 60/40 tin-lead alloy melts at around 190-215 C depending on composition, which is why it was the universal electronics solder of the era; the lead keeps the melting point low and wets the copper lead frames and the nickel-plated transistor legs. The flux is rosin or an organic acid, chemically inert but hygroscopic, so it had to be washed off or it caused resistive leakage in damp climates.

          - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
          - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
###### Rosin flux from pine `mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin`

Colophony, the sticky amber resin left when crude turpentine is distilled off pine resin, dissolved in isopropanol or in a blend of solvents to make the classic mild flux. It is non-corrosive but must be removed because it is hygroscopic and slightly conductive when damp.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
###### Crude turpentine and pine resin `mb.rf-modulator.assembly.solder.rosin.turpentine` _(medium)_

Distilling crude turpentine - a mixture of terpene hydrocarbons collected by tapping pine trees - leaves a viscous amber residue of rosin and pine gum. Natural rosin supply did not keep up with the 1980s electronics industry, so most flux rosin was actually tall oil rosin, a byproduct of pine kraft pulp production.

              - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
              - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
### C64 mains side: cord, plug, switch, fuse `c64.mains`

Everything between the wall socket and the transformer primary: the three-conductor line cord and its moulded plug, the rocker switch, the line fuse, the X-rated suppression capacitor and the protective-earth bonding. The brick's case is entirely plastic, so the earth conductor never bonds to an enclosure - it terminates on the interwinding screen inside the transformer, and that is the whole of the earthing arrangement.

#### Three-conductor line cord `c64.mains.line-cord`

A flexible cord with one heavier line conductor, one neutral and a green or green-and-yellow earth conductor, exiting the case through a clamp or grommet. The sheath is PVC in the 1980s rather than the older rubber; PVC is tougher, thinner and better suited to being moulded into the case.

##### PVC sheath compound `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath`

The sheath is not raw PVC resin but a plasticised compound: PVC resin mixed with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate or, from the mid-1970s onwards, with a polyester plasticiser as the industry moved away from phthalates. The resin itself is made by addition polymerisation of vinyl chloride.

###### Vinyl chloride monomer `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride`

Made by the oxychlorination of ethylene with oxygen and chlorine over a fluidised bed of copper(II) chloride at 180-220 C, or by the chlorination of acetylene. Vinyl chloride monomer is acutely toxic and carcinogenic, and its manufacture was one of the worst occupational hazards in the chemical industry until the 1970s-80s control campaigns.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
            - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Chlorine for oxychlorination `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride.chlorine`

Chlorine is made by electrolysing a brine of sodium chloride in a membrane, mercury or diaphragm cell. The membrane cell, introduced commercially in the 1970s, has no mercury and gives much purer caustic soda as a co-product; in 1982 the older diaphragm and mercury cells were still very widely used.

###### Brine, from halite `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride.chlorine.brine`

Saturated sodium chloride solution, made by dissolving mined rock salt in filtered water and purging the carbonate with hydrochloric acid. Rock salt is bedded halite, mined by room-and-pillar or solution mining. This is the leaf of the sodium-chloride chain.

###### Halite (rock salt) `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride.chlorine.brine.halite`

Evaporite deposits of sodium chloride, mined underground by room-and-pillar or dissolved and pumped as brine. It is dug, dissolved and chlorinated, and nothing more is done to it before it becomes the chlorine that makes the C64's plastics.

                  - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
                  - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Solution mining and brine clarification `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride.chlorine.brine.halite.solution-mining`

Two thirds of the world's salt is mined by dissolving the deposit in water: two wells are drilled into the salt, fresh water is injected into one and pumped from the other, and the brine is brought to the surface with the NaCl content raised to saturation by a settling stage. The insolubles are removed in settling tanks and the brine is filtered and acidified to kill the carbonate.

###### Salt dome geology `c64.mains.line-cord.pvc-sheath.vinyl-chloride.chlorine.brine.halite.solution-mining.earth` _(medium)_

Salt is one of the few minerals the body actively pushes up: buried evaporite deposits flow plastically and can breach the surface as salt domes or glaciers, so the seam follows the rock rather than sitting level. That plastic flow is what makes room-and-pillar mining possible at all - the roof deforms and closes behind the workings instead of collapsing.

                      - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
##### Stranded copper conductors `c64.mains.line-cord.stranded-copper`

Stranded rather than solid, because a cord is flexed at the strain relief and a solid conductor cracks there within a few years. Each strand is 0.15-0.20 mm bare copper wire; a 1.0 mm2 cord has roughly 30 strands.

          - *Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings* `metal.copper.wire` *(seen above)*
###### Wire drawing `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing`

A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

            - *Enamelled magnet wire for transformer windings* `metal.copper.wire` *(seen above)*
##### Strain relief clamp and grommet `c64.mains.line-cord.strain-relief` _(medium)_

A nylon or rubber bushing, or a two-screw clamp on a moulded boss, that stops the conductors being pulled out of their terminals. In a safety audit this is a named inspection point: the conductors must not be able to move more than a couple of millimetres, and no strand may be able to reach a terminal screw under tension.

          - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
#### Moulded mains plug `c64.mains.plug`

A two- or three-pole moulded plug permanently attached to the cord: in the North American build a polarised NEMA 1-15P with one blade rotated 180 degrees so it can only be inserted one way round; in most of Europe a CEE 7/16 Europlug with two round 4.0 mm pins. The body is a thermosetting or thermoplastic moulding with the cord entering through a separate bushing so the strain is not carried by the conductors.

##### Nickel-plated brass contacts `c64.mains.plug.nickel-plated-brass`

The blades are stamped from cartridge brass sheet and plated. Nickel under-plate plus a flash of nickel is the 1980s default for mains contacts because brass alone tarnishes and corrodes; silver plating was used where the contact had to carry more current or where the plug was screwed down, and silver-plated contacts remain the modern choice for high-current switchgear.

          - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
          - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
      - *Rocker switch* `c64.mains.switch` *(seen above)*
#### Primary fuse and thermal fuse `c64.mains.fuses`

Two serial protections on the mains side. The primary fuse is a small cartridge type rated at roughly 120 mA (115 V) or 200 mA (230 V), sized at about 125% of the running input current so the transformer draws its inrush without nuisance failure. The second, documented in the 251053-02, is a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary: a fusible alloy element that opens irreversibly if the transformer overheats.

##### Glass cartridge fuse `c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge`

A fuse element of pure tin or a tin alloy, historically a lead-antimony or tin-lead alloy, held between two metal end caps inside a glass tube. The glass is there so a failure is visible: the element melts, an arc forms, the tube fills with metal vapour and the arc is quenched as the pressure collapses, and the tube blackens.

          - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
          - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
###### Soda-lime tube glass `c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-glass`

The fuse tube is a drawn borosilicate or soda-lime glass tube, chosen because it is dimensionally stable, easy to seal and does not outgas. Glass tubing is made by melting the batch and drawing the softened gather between rollers, so the wall thickness and diameter stay within a few microns along the length.

###### Glass batch and silica sand `c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-glass.batch`

The batch is a few hundred kilograms of silica sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C. The silica sand, dug from high-silica deposits, is the leaf of the glass chain.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
              - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
              - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Regenerative furnace and cowper `c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-glass.batch.regenerator`

A glass furnace cannot simply burn gas, because glassmelting needs far more heat than combustion can deliver at that temperature. The answer is regeneration: a Cowper regenerator beside the furnace stores the heat of the exhaust in a refractory mass, then blows the air through it on the next firing. The two 1980s designs were the regenerative box furnace and the unit-regenerator furnace.

                - *Ferrite: transformer and choke cores* `metal.ferrite` *(seen above)*
###### Refractory lining and checker plates `c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-glass.batch.regenerator.refractory`

The furnace and regenerator are lined with refractory brick, and the regenerator's internal mass is a stack of checker plates of silica or chrome-magnesite. Refractory brick is made by pressing or hand-moulding a graded mineral aggregate with a clay binder and firing it in a tunnel or car kiln; the grading, not the chemistry, is what gives a lining its thermal-shock resistance.

                  - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
                  - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
                  - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
##### Ceramic wirewound fuse `c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound`

A slow-acting fuse for the high inrush of the reservoir capacitor: a length of resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin, shunted by a strip of fusible alloy that runs beside it. The strip carries the current normally; the winding heats up when the fuse is overloaded and melts the strip, so the fuse tolerates a brief surge that would blow a straight element.

          - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
          - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
          - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
          - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
##### Thermal fuse `c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse`

A one-shot temperature fuse: a fusible alloy link, often a fine wire of a low-melting alloy such as a bismuth-lead-tin-indium eutectic, bonded to the transformer or mounted in thermal contact with it. At its trip temperature - typically 100-130 C - the link melts and opens the circuit permanently. It cannot be reset, which is intentional: the fault that overheated the transformer is not allowed to be repeated.

###### Low-melting fusible alloy `c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy`

An eutectic or near-eutectic mixture chosen so that it melts sharply at one temperature.
