Each step loses yield, which is why an ore shortage shows up in capacitor prices months after the mining news.

###### Columbite-tantalite ore `mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.columbite-ore`

The tantalum-bearing ore, a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, mined both as placer gravels and as lode pegmatites. Concentrating it requires ore dressing by gravity and magnetic separation, because only a few per cent of the rock is Ta2O5. Historically the ore was concentrated from the Congo and Rwanda-Burundi, which is precisely why Western capacitor supply chains were politically and economically exposed in this period.

###### Dressing and concentration `mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.columbite-ore.beneficiation`

Columbite-tantalite is run through gravity, magnetic and electrostatic separation and then an acid-leach circuit to recover a concentrate of perhaps a few per cent Ta2O5. Because the ore is bulk low-grade rock, the mining and concentration stage - not the chemistry - is where most of the cost of a tantalum capacitor lives.

###### Alluvial and pegmatite placer workings `mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.columbite-ore.beneficiation.alluvial-placer`

Tantalum-bearing minerals are dense, so they concentrate naturally in stream and beach placers below any pegmatite outcrop. Much of the 1980s supply was won by artisanal and semi-industrial alluvial mining in the Kivu highlands, which is exactly why ore supply could be disrupted by regional politics rather than by mine closure.

##### Ceramic disc (monolithic disc) capacitor `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc` _(medium)_

A single fired barium-titanate disc with silver electrodes fired onto its two faces. Enormous capacitance for its size and very cheap, but microphonically noisy, temperature-drifty and physically large, with no self-cancelling inductance. On C64 boards of this era the small 0.1 uF parts were already largely the multilayer form.

###### Pressing, sintering and silver-firing `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sinter`

BaTiO3 powder is pressed into a disc, sintered at 1200-1300 C, then silver electrode paste is screen-printed onto each face and fired at 700-850 C so the silver is glass-bonded to the ceramic. Only two electrodes exist, so the part cannot cancel its own inductance - the structural reason a disc is useless at radio frequencies and a multilayer is not.

###### Disc press and sinter `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sinter.blade` _(medium)_

A mechanical or hydraulic press blanks the disc to a controlled thickness; the sinter then densifies it and fires on the silver electrodes.

###### Disc body material `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sinter.body` _(medium)_

The ceramic body of a high-K disc is a modified barium titanate with a glass phase, on an alumina or steatite base. The dielectric-strength figure of about 2.5 kV per micron of effective thickness is a design guideline for the ceramic, not for the finished part.

###### Steatite or alumina base `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sinter.body.base-ceramic` _(medium)_

Low-firing ceramic substrates, steatite (magnesium silicate) or alumina, onto which the high-K layer is applied. Steatite is cheap and fires low; alumina is tougher and better at heat.

###### Silica sand `mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sinter.body.base-ceramic.silica-sand`

Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

##### Film capacitors (polyester / polystyrene) `mb.passives.caps.film`

Film capacitors use a thin metallised plastic film as the dielectric. Non-polar, stable, and tolerant of voltage and temperature excursions. The C64 uses polyester (Melinex/PET) for coupling and decoupling in the analogue paths; polystyrene appears in the precision timing networks of the same era's equipment.

###### Vacuum-metallised polyester film `mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallisation`

PET pellets are extruded into a cast film, then stretched fast in two perpendicular directions to several times their original length, orienting the polymer chains. That gives a very thin, very uniform, high-tensile dielectric; then a sub-micron metal layer is vacuum-deposited on one or both faces and the metallised film is wound on a core. No separate foil is used - the electrode IS the deposited layer.

###### PET polymerisation `mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallisation.pet-polymerisation`

The film base is polyethylene terephthalate, made by condensing bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate - itself from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid - in a melt polymeriser at ~250-290 C under vacuum. The terephthalic acid came from paraxylene, which came from the aromatics fraction of a steam cracker or a catalytic reformer.

###### Paraxylene from a steam cracker `mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallisation.pet-polymerisation.paraxylene`

Paraxylene sits in the aromatics complex of a large refinery, separated from a mixed xylene fraction by fractional distillation and adsorption. It is the pivot molecule of the entire polyester industry: 1982 saw PET moving from bottle-grade into film, fibre and capacitor dielectric at once.

###### Polystyrene film capacitor `mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene` _(low)_

A polystyrene dielectric: exceptionally stable, very low dielectric absorption and low loss, historically the timing capacitor of choice for precision RC oscillators before polystyrene's poor mechanical behaviour pushed it into disfavour. Used in analogue equipment of the era, but not a significant part on the C64 mainboard.

###### Styrene polymerisation to polystyrene `mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styrene-polymerisation`

Free-radical or ionic polymerisation of styrene, in bulk suspension or emulsion, gives the amorphous thermoplastic. Unmodified polystyrene is brittle and has poor moisture resistance, which is precisely why metalised polystyrene was restricted to sealed precision parts and lost out to polypropylene.

###### Benzene from a steam cracker `mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styrene-polymerisation.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

###### Vacuum metallisation of PS film `mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metallisation` _(medium)_

The same vacuum-deposited aluminium electrode as on the polyester film, but on a more delicate substrate: polystyrene outgasses and embrittles under vacuum heat, so the film has to be baked and the deposition kept cool.

##### Mica capacitor `mb.passives.caps.mica` _(medium)_

A capacitor built from thin sheets of natural muscovite mica with vacuum-deposited aluminium or silver counter-electrodes. Superb temperature stability and high dielectric strength, too expensive and too fragile for general use, so mica was reserved for precision and high-voltage niches in equipment of the era.

###### Muscovite mica, heat-split into sheets `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite`

Natural muscovite is mined in large crystal books from pegmatites and delaminated by heating and cementing against a hot plate, so it splits along its perfect basal cleavage into micrometre-thick, optically flat sheets. The crystal's naturally layered atomic structure gives a very uniform, very thin, very stable dielectric when split this way.

###### Pegmatite host rock `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatite`

Mica books grow in the giant granitic pegmatites of the Precambrian shield - Minas Gerais in Brazil, Rajasthan in India, Madagascar, and in the United States the Appalachian and Spruce Pine districts of North Carolina. It is mined in situ and split, not manufactured.

###### Underground mica mining `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatite.mining` _(medium)_

Mica books are followed underground and extracted by hand; the deposit has to be worked selectively because the surrounding pegmatite has to stay intact. Brazilian, Indian and US districts all supply capacitor-grade mica.

###### Block and thin grading `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatite.grading` _(medium)_

Mica is traded in sizes: block for the thickest uses, thins for splitting, and capacitor mica is the thin and flexible sheet. Grading and splitting, not mining, account for most of the value in the material.

###### Heat-and-cement splitting and ruby splitting `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-splitting`

A mica book is mounted on a hot plate; a hot blade of mica is pressed onto it with a cement stick, which drives a wedge along the perfect basal cleavage and peels off a sheet a few microns thick. Repeated, it yields hundreds of optically flat sheets from one crystal, and it is the labour-intensive step that made mica capacitors expensive.

###### Hot knife and cement stick `mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-splitting.knife` _(medium)_

A heated mica blade driven by a cement stick along the cleavage plane. The blade has to be hot enough to part the sheets without charring the cement, and both blade and stick are specialist consumables of the splitting trade.

###### Vacuum-deposited counter-electrodes `mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation` _(medium)_

Aluminium or silver is evaporated or sputtered through a shadow-mask onto the mica sheets; sheets are stacked with a thin metallised layer between each, bonded under heat and pressure, and the stack is diced into individual capacitors.

###### Aluminium electrode evaporation `mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.aluminium-evaporation`

Aluminium is evaporated rather than sputtered because it is cheap and vapourises at a manageable temperature; it is then left unoxidised under vacuum. Silver electrodes were used where the highest capacitance per unit area was needed.

###### Alumina from bauxite `mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.aluminium-evaporation.alumina`

Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

###### Bauxite profile `mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.aluminium-evaporation.alumina.laterite`

A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

##### Trimmer and variable capacitors `mb.passives.caps.trim` _(medium)_

Small adjustable capacitors used to compensate or trim a circuit. On C64-family boards a trimmer capacitor sits in the crystal oscillator's load network, pulling the frequency exactly onto the NTSC or PAL colour subcarrier; later Commodore boards replaced the earlier adjustable resistor with this capacitor trim.

###### Air-gap / film trimmer capacitor `mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap` _(medium)_

Two sets of interdigitated metal plates with an adjustable overlap, separated by air or a thin film. Turning the screw changes the overlap and therefore the capacitance continuously, letting the factory trim the oscillator to the exact subcarrier frequency. The dielectric is air, which is why these parts are stable and non-drifting.

###### Stator and rotor plates `mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-plate`

The trimmer's rotor is a small disc of alumina ceramic, silver-metallised on one face through a spiral or interdigitated pattern. Turning the screw rotates the disc against a fixed plate, so the overlapping metallised area - and hence the capacitance - changes continuously.

###### Alumina rotor plate material `mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-plate.alumina`

The rotor disc is alumina, polished and metallised with a spiral or interdigitated silver pattern. Alumina is used because it is dimensionally stable, machinable to a fine finish and a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage.

###### Alumina from bauxite `mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-plate.alumina.alumina`

Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

###### Bauxite profile `mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-plate.alumina.alumina.laterite`

A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

##### Capacitor wrap, sleeving and marking `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking` _(medium)_

Not a separate component but the packaging shared across the capacitor families: dipped epoxy for ceramic disc and monolithic parts, printed PVC or polyester sleeving for film caps, cardboard or aluminium sleeves for electrolytics, and printed value/brand markings on all of them.

###### E dipped conformal coat `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-dip`

Ceramic and monolithic parts were dip-coated in epoxy or PVC after firing to seal the porous body and to carry the printed marking. A dipped part looks identical to a moulded one, which is why it is hard to tell from a photograph whether a given C64 ceramic is disc or monolithic.

###### Dip-coating line `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-dip.tank` _(medium)_

Parts on a wire rack are dipped in an epoxy or PVC solution and withdrawn so the coating tapers at both ends, leaving a characteristic tapered shoulder at the lead exit. A second dip gives the second shoulder.

###### Capacitor value marking ink `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink`

Values were printed on the sleeve or dipped coat in an oil-based or epoxy ink on an offset or screen coater. The two-digit and three-digit codes (104 for 100 nF, 104K5V) only became an industry standard in the 1970s.

###### Ink pigment `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pigment` _(medium)_

The value marking pigment is carbon black for dark parts and azo or phthalocyanine colour for bright ones, in a resin vehicle that will not be attacked by the board cleaning solvents.

###### Furnace black for the ink `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pigment.furnace-black`

The same petroleum-derived carbon black as in the resistor body and the rubber dome, ground fine enough to print.

###### Printed PVC sleeve on film caps `mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.pvc-sleeve` _(medium)_

Film capacitors arrived in a printed plastic sleeve printed with the value, the rating and the maker. Sleeve polymer is the same PVC family as the case and the cable jacket.

### Master clock crystal and oscillator `mb.crystal`

Y1, a hermetically sealed HC-49/U quartz crystal, plus the four glue-logic chips that turn it into the machine's entire timing reference: a colour subcarrier crystal oscillator, a PLL that quadruples it, a divider chain, and a phase/frequency detector that locks the dot clock to the colour clock. Every clock edge in a C64 descends from this one 11 mm metal can.

#### Y1 quartz crystal, HC-49/U `mb.crystal.y1` _(medium)_

A plano-convex quartz plate, 0.07 mm thick, with electrodes fired on its two faces, held on supports inside a small metal can filled with argon and sealed by a crimped, resistance-welded cap. The quartz is the oscillator's frequency-setting element: the whole machine's timing accuracy is the accuracy of one cut and lapped slice of Brazilian or synthetic silicon dioxide.

##### Natural rock crystal (Brazilian quartz) `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz` _(medium)_

Gem-quality clear quartz for crystal units came historically from the rock-crystal veins of Minas Gerais in Brazil, prized for natural faces that need no lapping and for the very low defect density that makes a low-phase-noise oscillator possible. By the early 1980s this was being displaced by hydrothermal synthetic quartz, which is chemically identical and far more uniform.

###### Quartz vein in pegmatite host `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.pegmatite-vein`

Clear quartz crystallises in the pockets and miarolitic cavities of granitic pegmatite, growing inward from the cavity walls until the void is filled - which is why Brazilian rock crystal comes out with flat crystal faces already in place. Mined by hand-scale underground workings and by washing decomposed pegmatite.

###### Granite pegmatite body `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.pegmatite-vein.granite`

A late-stage, volatile-rich, very coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock: quartz, K-feldspar, muscovite and tourmaline in crystals up to many centimetres across. Pegmatites are the pegmatite-parental source of both quartz and mica on this tree.

###### Pegmatite completion `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.pegmatite-vein.granite.pegmatite`

The last melt water of a granite intrusion concentrates volatiles into a very coarse, quartz-rich final stage. Rock crystal and mica are two products of the same geology, which is why both appear in this tree from the same kind of ground.

###### Hand mining of rock crystal `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.pegmatite-vein.hand-mining` _(medium)_

Brazilian rock crystal was worked in small underground operations following the vein, split out and sold as it was found. It was never a large-tonnage commodity, which is part of why synthetic quartz took over so decisively.

###### Hydrothermal synthetic quartz `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic`

Because natural quartz is limited and variable, industry moved to growing it: an autoclave is charged with silica (often crushed natural quartz) in a hot sodium-hydroxide solution and heated at around 400 C and 150 MPa. Quartz grows on seed crystals hung in the solution, growing the rough in days rather than geological time. This is the source of nearly all quartz crystal blanks made from about the mid-1970s onward.

###### Steel autoclave with seed crystals `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave`

A filled, sealed pressure vessel - usually Hastelloy or 17-4PH steel liner - held at high temperature and pressure so an alkaline solution dissolves silica from the feed and re-deposits it on zoned seed crystals. Temperature gradients create the supersaturation that drives growth; the growth zones themselves are what later become the tuned crystal's resonators.

###### Alkali solvent `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave.caustic`

The growth solution is hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide, which dissolves silica at the elevated temperature while quartz re-deposits on the seeds. The alkali is made from chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine - so the crystal ultimately touches rock salt as well as quartz sand.

###### Rock salt / brine `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave.caustic.rock-salt`

Halite, mined or solution-mined, and the source of the chlorine and sodium that make the caustic soda that seeds the quartz growth. A surprising number of industrial processes begin at a salt mine.

###### Seed crystals and zoning `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.autoclave.seed`

Growth happens on thin zoned seed plates hung in the vessel, and the growth itself develops the acoustic zoning structure that later becomes the crystal's resonators. This is why synthetic quartz, not natural quartz, is what nearly every 1982 crystal was grown from.

###### Quartz sand / crushed quartz feed `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.silica-feed` _(medium)_

The silica feedstock for the autoclave is cleaned quartz sand or lumps of milky quartz. Natural quartz sand is a common beach and dune sand: essentially SiO2, left behind as quartz survives weathering while everything else dissolves and washes away.

###### Quartz sand, SiO2 `mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.silica-feed.quartz-sand`

The most abundant framework silicate in continental crust. Weathering destroys feldspar and ferromagnesian minerals and leaves a residue of quartz grains, which are worked by screening and magnetic separation into glass sand, foundry sand and ceramic-grade sand.

##### Sawing, lapping and X-ray orienting the blank `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation`

Rough crystal is sawn into blanks, then the cut face is lapped to about 0.15 mm and X-ray diffracted to find its crystallographic orientation. Orientation is everything: only an AT-cut at the right angle gives the flat temperature curve a frequency-stable oscillator needs.

###### X-ray orientation and AT-cut angle selection `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.xray-orienting`

A synthetic rough is indexed by X-ray diffraction so its Z axis and X axis are known, then sawn at a chosen angle to the X axis (the 'AT-cut'). The mid-1980s standard for general-purpose oscillators was about 35 degrees; this angle is chosen because it lands the resonance on a flat, temperature-insensitive point in the quartz stiffness-temperature curve.

###### Lapping and double-lap polishing `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping`

The cut blank is lapped on rotating cast-iron plates with progressively finer abrasives (aluminium oxide, then colloidal silica) down to about 0.15 mm, then double-lapped against a second plate to remove bow and damage left by the saw. Crystal blanks for a 1982 oscillator were lapped on plates run by lapidary and lapping shops, not in the same plant that makes the finished crystal.

###### Final lapping abrasive `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.colloidal-silica` _(medium)_

The last lapping stage uses a colloidal silica slurry, which polishes rather than cuts. Colloidal silica is precipitated from a dilute sodium silicate solution, itself made from silica sand and sodium carbonate.

###### Silica sand for the sodium silicate `mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.colloidal-silica.silica-sand`

Quartz sand fused with sodium carbonate makes the water glass that the colloidal silica is precipitated from.

##### Grinding the lens shape `mb.crystal.y1.grinding` _(medium)_

The face is bevelled and the outline ground so the finished blank is a lens or plano-convex dome rather than a flat slab. The convexity is deliberate: it makes the crystal's resonant frequency less sensitive to surface damage and to where the mounting points press on it.

###### Mounting and soldering of the crystal `mb.crystal.y1.supports` _(medium)_

The four HC-49 leads are formed to a right angle and soldered onto the board in a wave-solder pass. The crystal's case sits at the board's natural mechanical frequency well below the circuit's operating frequency, which is deliberate: an HC-49 body has several overtone resonances that would otherwise produce spurious oscillator modes.

###### Formed leads `mb.crystal.y1.supports.lead-form` _(medium)_

The four flat HC-49 leads are bent to a right angle and trimmed, then soldered onto the board. The case is deliberately stood off the board so air can move around it, because the case's own overtone resonances must sit well below the operating frequency.

###### Diamond grinding wheel `mb.crystal.y1.grinding.diamond-wheel` _(medium)_

A resin-bonded diamond wheel, used wet, that bevels the plate edge and cuts the lens curvature. In 1982 diamond abrasive was largely synthetic, made from graphite under a shock wave; natural diamond was reserved for dressing the wheels.

###### Graphite precursor of synthetic diamond `mb.crystal.y1.grinding.diamond-wheel.graphite` _(medium)_

Explosion-wave synthesis of diamond is fed with graphite, itself made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C in an Acheson furnace. So even the abrasive that cuts the crystal descends from petroleum coke.

###### Frequency grinding `mb.crystal.y1.grinding.centre-frequency`

The final grinding is done with the plate already oscillating in a test jig: the grinder watches the frequency change as material is removed and stops at the target. This is why a crystal can be hit to within a few hertz before it is even put into its can.

##### Metal electrodes on the blank faces `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes` _(medium)_

Chromium is evaporated or sputtered onto both faces as an adhesion layer, then gold or silver is deposited over it as the conductive electrode, through a shadow mask that defines the electrode area. Chromium-gold is the classic 1980s crystal electrode stack: Cr to bond, Au to conduct.

###### Chromium adhesion layer `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium`

Chromium is evaporated as the adhesion layer because bare quartz will not hold gold by van der Waals forces alone. Chromium wets both the quartz surface and the gold film, and it is itself a hard, chemically inert metal.

###### Chromium (chromite) for the adhesion layer `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.ore`

The chromium in a crystal electrode is a small mass but it is ordinary metallurgical chromium, and chromite ore from the Bushveld Complex is the source.

###### Gold electrode film `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film`

Gold evaporated through a shadow mask to give the electrode its final geometry and conductivity. The mask pattern fixes the electrode area, which together with the plate thickness is what sets the crystal capacitance.

###### Evaporation shadow mask `mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.mask` _(medium)_

A thin metal mask placed above the rotating blank during evaporation so the electrode pattern is defined. The mask is made from a drawn stainless or nickel strip, chemically etched to the electrode shape.

##### Cutting the plate and vacuum baking `mb.crystal.y1.cutting`

The plated blank is cut with a diamond wheel into individual resonator plates, then the plates are vacuum-baked at around 400 C to drive off adsorbed moisture and contaminants. That vacuum bake is what removes the piezoelectric pyroelectric drift and the 'dope' effect - the stress-induced frequency shift as a crystal heats - and it is why a crystal that has been opened is never a good crystal.

###### Diamond dicing saw `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.dicing-saw`

A thin resin-bonded diamond wheel, ~0.03-0.05 mm thick, cutting the plated blank into resonators. The wheel has to be extremely thin and extremely flat to avoid chipping a 0.07 mm plate.

###### Cleaning between steps `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom`

Every step from lapping onward is done washed and clean: a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate changes the frequency. Crystal preparation is one of the few wet, cold, dirty-looking processes in electronics.

###### Deionised rinse water `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionised-water`

Every crystal process rinse uses deionised water, because a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. City water is nowhere good enough.

###### Ion-exchange resin `mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionised-water.ion-exchange`

A cation and an anion resin pair in two columns, regenerated with acid and alkali, removes the dissolved ions. The resin is a cross-linked polystyrene with sulfonic or quaternary ammonium groups.

##### HC-49/U case: crimp, weld and argon fill `mb.crystal.y1.case` _(medium)_

The plate sits on a pair of wire supports in a crimped and welded nickel can, filled with argon or krypton at a few kPa. The can is drawn from nickel-plated steel or brass, and its small welded lid is what makes the unit hermetic - the reason a 1982 crystal does not drift as the humidity of an attic changes.

###### Nickel can stock `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can` _(medium)_

HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel is used because it matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.

###### Drawn can stock `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock`

The HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from thin nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool, then the crimped collar is rolled and the lid welded on. Both operations happen before the plate goes in - the can is made empty and loaded later.

###### Welded lid and crimped collar `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld`

The lid is spot-welded or resistance-welded to the collar in an atmosphere of dry hydrogen or forming gas, which keeps the internal oxide clean and lets the fill gas stay inert. Hermeticity is what makes a forty-year-old crystal hold its frequency.

###### Forming gas for welding `mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas` _(medium)_

A mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen used as a cover during the lid weld. Hydrogen also diffuses any internal oxide onto the getters, which is why a well-made can can have a getter mirror at the bottom after opening.

###### Argon or krypton fill gas `mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill`

The can is filled with a chemically inert gas before welding. Argon is preferred because it does not react with the electrode and cannot outgas; krypton was used where a slightly more hermetic atmosphere was wanted. The gas also damps acoustic vibration in the plate.

###### Cryogenic air separation `mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.cryogenic-distillation`

Argon and krypton are separated from liquefied air by fractional distillation at around 90 K in a double-column distiller. Every quartz crystal can on earth is filled with gas that was once part of the atmosphere, separated cryogenically.

###### Spring-wire supports `mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire`

Two short wires spot-welded to the plate's major faces at the nodal points. Because quartz is piezoelectric, mechanically stressing it shifts its resonant frequency, so the supports must sit where the strain of the vibrating mode is smallest - the whole reason the plate is bevelled and domed.

###### Gold or nickel support wire `mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire` _(medium)_

Fine wire, 0.1-0.2 mm, spot-welded to the plate electrodes. Gold is preferred where maximum Q is needed; nickel is the cost-driven choice for the volume 1982 HC-49.

#### Oscillator and PLL circuitry `mb.crystal.oscillator`

The crystal is only the frequency reference. Turning it into the machine's clocks takes a 74LS629 dual VCO crystal oscillator, a Motorola MC4044 phase/frequency detector, a 74LS193 divider, and a 74LS74 flip-flop, with R27 or a trimmer capacitor setting the exact pull.

##### Pierce oscillator and load capacitors `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce`

The crystal acts as a negative-resistance element in a Pierce oscillator with a small load capacitor at its CL, and the drive level set by a series resistor. The load capacitors and the trim element together decide the frequency pull range; this is why the crystal's specified CL (typically about 30 pF in an HC-49/U) has to be matched by the board.

###### Load capacitors and stray capacitance `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.load-capacitor`

The Pierce oscillator's frequency is set by the crystal's CL, the load capacitors and the transistor's input capacitance all in series. At 14 MHz with a few tens of picofarads involved, a 0.5 mm of stray copper changes the trim range - which is why the C64 needed an adjustable element here rather than a fixed capacitor.

###### Load capacitor type and value `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.load-capacitor.type`

A small ceramic part, chosen with a tight tolerance because its value enters the oscillator directly. On the C64 this is where the C0G-grade ceramic timing caps are used, and where the trim element sits.

###### Alumina from bauxite `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.load-capacitor.type.alumina`

Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

###### Bauxite profile `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.load-capacitor.type.alumina.laterite`

A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

###### Oscillator startup and drive level `mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.startup-noise` _(medium)_

The oscillator is a high-gain positive-feedback amplifier at all frequencies until the crystal's impedance peaks at the design frequency. The circuit is designed to start on noise and settle; a badly driven crystal never settles, which is the classic symptom of a crystal with a cracked plate.

##### PLL: MC4044 into the 74LS629 VCO `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll`

The 74LS629's second oscillator is a voltage-controlled oscillator. The MC4044 phase/frequency detector compares a divided colour clock against the VIC-II's phase-0 clock and returns a DC control voltage on pin 8, which the 74LS629's frequency-control pin steers. That is the whole of the C64's PLL: a crystal oscillator for the exact subcarrier, and a tracking VCO four times faster, locked to it, for the pixel clock.

###### Why a trim is required at all `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.trim-range`

The NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and an untrimmed crystal and oscillator would wander far more than that over temperature and supply. The trim element (R27 on breadbin boards, a capacitive trim later) lets the whole PLL be pulled onto the exact frequency at the factory and then holds it there.

###### PAL and NTSC crystals `mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.pal-variant`

The PAL machine uses a 17.734475 MHz crystal (four times the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier) in the same circuit, and the 74LS193 divider is switched to divide by nine instead of seven. Later C64B/C boards moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC, dropping the discrete VCO.

    - *Front and rear I/O connectors* `c64.connector-jacks` *(seen above)*
### Lead-tin solder and every joint it makes on the board `mb.solder`

The metallurgical spine of the whole machine. Every joint on the C64 mainboard is made with 63/37 tin-lead alloy activated by rosin flux: about 600 in one pass through a wave-soldering machine, the rest by hand afterwards on the connectors, fuse clips and wire jumpers.

#### 63/37 tin-lead eutectic `mb.solder.alloy`

A true eutectic: solid below 183 deg C, liquid above it, no pasty region in between. That sharpness is what lets a drag-soldered joint finish setting the instant it leaves the wave, and it is why the wave pot and the pad finish are the same alloy.

##### Tin, 63 % of the alloy `mb.solder.alloy.tin` _(medium)_

Tin does the actual joining: it reacts with the copper in the pad to form the intermetallic that holds the joint, and it flows first and wets the joint, which is why a good joint is shiny where the tin pooled.

##### Lead, 37 % of the alloy `mb.solder.alloy.lead` _(medium)_

Lead lowers the melting point, widens the working window and suppresses tin whisker growth. It is also soft, creeps, and is a cumulative poison that nobody in a 1983 electronics factory thought about.

##### Antimony and silver additions `mb.solder.alloy.additives` _(low)_

A little antimony hardens the alloy and slows the tin pest; silver is used in higher-temperature solders to slow pad dissolution. General-purpose wave bar in 1983 was usually plain 63/37.

        - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
        - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
#### Cast solder bar and the dross it makes `mb.solder.bar` _(medium)_

Solder arrives at the plant as roughly 0.5-1 kg bars and is dropped into the wave machine's pot. As tin dissolves copper from every pad that passes through the wave, the pot chemistry drifts and a grey oxide sludge called dross accumulates on the surface, which has to be skimmed off or the wave itself is contaminated.

        - *63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste* `metal.solder` *(seen above)*
#### Solder wire with a rosin core `mb.solder.wire` _(medium)_

For joints the wave cannot reach, the line uses 0.5-0.8 mm wire with a rosin flux core extruded down the middle. About a quarter of the wire by weight is flux; as the solder melts the flux boils off ahead of it, cleaning the joint just before the tin arrives.

##### Drawing the wire from the bar `mb.solder.wire.draw` _(medium)_

Cast bar is hot-worked and cold-drawn through a series of dies to a fine round or rectangular section, with the flux core fed into the tube just before the final pass. The dies are carbide, because tin-lead is abrasive and destroys steel tooling quickly.

###### Carbide drawing die `mb.solder.wire.draw.die` _(medium)_

A tungsten-carbide insert in a steel holder. Carbide is used throughout the solder shop and the board shop, from wire drawing dies to the wave pot's skimmer blade, because nothing softer survives contact with molten tin.

###### Tungsten and cobalt in the carbide `mb.solder.wire.draw.tungsten` _(medium)_

Tungsten comes from wolframite and scheelite concentrates, cobalt from cobalt ore. Both are mined metals, and both are chosen here for one reason only: they do not wear away in molten tin.

###### Tungsten ore (wolframite) `mb.solder.wire.draw.ore` _(medium)_

Heavy, dark ore worked for its tungsten content, usually concentrated from alluvial and vein deposits before conversion to ammonium paratungstate and then to the metal.

###### Wolframite ore body `mb.solder.wire.draw.ore.body` _(medium)_

A vein or alluvial concentration of iron-manganese tungstate, mined by stope or by hydraulic gravel washing and concentrated before the conversion plant. Diggable rock, at the very bottom of a chain that exists only because a die must survive molten tin.

##### Rosin flux core `mb.solder.wire.core`

Sticky pine resin dissolved in alcohol with a mild organic-acid activator. Rosin is not corrosive, and at wave temperature it burns off cleanly, but what is left behind is a sticky, mildly acidic film that has to be cleaned off the board. Its whole job is to displace the oxide film on the copper in the few milliseconds before the solder touches it.

###### Colophony (rosin) from pine `mb.solder.wire.core.colophony` _(medium)_

The sticky amber resin tapped from living pine and, in modern supply, distilled from pine stumps. Dissolved in alcohol it is the flux; it is non-corrosive and, crucially, only slightly conductive, which is what keeps a rosin-fluxed board from slowly corroding itself.

###### Pine stumps and resin `mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.stumps` _(medium)_

Stumps left by logging are chipped and steam-distilled to recover the resin, which is why pine-resin supply for electronics solder is a forestry business and not an agriculture one.

###### Abietic acid in the rosin `mb.solder.wire.core.colophony.acid` _(medium)_

The organic acid that gives rosin its mild acidity and its ability to dissolve metal oxides. It is also what makes the residue on an uncleaned board slowly corrosive, which is the whole argument for cleaning after soldering.

###### Flux activator (halide-free) `mb.solder.wire.core.activator` _(medium)_

A small addition of organic acid, chosen to be aggressive against copper oxide but free of ionic halides. An ionic chloride in a flux does a better job of the chemistry and then quietly destroys the board with corrosion under the mask years later, so the halide-free requirement is a deliberate long-term trade.

###### Pine rosin (colophony) `chem.rosin` _(medium)_

The sticky amber solid left when turpentine is distilled out of pine resin. Most rosin is made from pine stumps - the resinous wood left behind when a tree is cut for pulp - by destructive distillation: the stump is chipped, heated in a still to about 150-200 C, turpentine and pine oil come over, and the residue is the rosin, which is then graded by colour and by softening point. About 700,000-800,000 tonnes of rosin were made in the early 1980s, mostly in China, the United States and Brazil.

###### Stump distillation and grading `chem.rosin.distillation`

Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps. The stump is chipped into 5-10 cm pieces, charged to a still, and heated; turpentine comes over first and is condensed and separated by distillation into alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and dipentene, and then pine oil and a heavy residue come over, and what is left in the pot is the crude rosin. The rosin is then graded - by colour (X, WW, WW, W) and by softening point (batter 75 C, fir 80 C, Norway 85 C, I 90 C, P 110 C, S 120 C) - and the Y grade, at about 165 C softening point and clear, is the one the flux core needs because it has almost no crystallisation and it does not go brittle.

###### Chipping and the still `chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping` _(medium)_

A whole-tree distillery burns about 1.5-2.5 tonnes of dry pine stumps per tonne of rosin plus its turpentine, and yields about 5-8% rosin, 3-4% turpentine and 1-2% pine oil by mass of dry wood. The stumps come from pine killed by beetle attack, from pine cut for pulp, and from the thinning of a plantation - so the rosin business is downstream of a forestry, and specifically of a beetle, in a way that is often overlooked when the flux is described as a petrochemical.

###### Retort and the batch cycle `chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.retort-and-still` _(medium)_

The classic stump still is a cast-iron or steel retort holding one to two tonnes of chipped wood, charged, closed, and fired with the turpentine vapour going to a condenser and the rosin staying in the pot. A cycle takes 12-20 hours and the still is charged by hand - which is why the business has barely changed since the 1850s in its mechanics while every other part of the 1980s chemical industry has been rebuilt twice. The 1980s changes were in the condenser and in the chip size, not in the process.

###### Rosin grading `chem.rosin.distillation.rosin-grade` _(medium)_

Colour by optical comparison against a reference chip, softening point by the ring-and-ball method, and acid value by titration. The flux maker's specification is colour and softening point; the abietic acid content follows from them. A rosin that is too yellow discolours the solder joint and shows through a white silkscreen, and a rosin that is too soft runs off the core during the wave.

#### Wave-soldering machine `mb.solder.wave` _(medium)_

A conveyorised machine that drags the underside of the board through a standing wave of molten solder. Components are all inserted from the top so they point the same way, and the wave only ever touches leads and pads. It is why a 1983 line could put hundreds of sound joints on a board for the price of the solder.

##### Welded machine frame and shell `mb.solder.wave.frame` _(medium)_

The pot, tunnel and conveyor sit in a welded steel frame that also carries the fume hood and the flux plumbing. It is a heavy, deliberately boring object: the machine is bought for its repeatability, not its elegance.

###### Structural steel sections `mb.solder.wave.frame.steel` _(medium)_

Mild steel angle and section from the arc or induction furnace. The mass of the frame is what keeps the wave flat while the pot runs.

###### Steel from iron ore and coke `mb.solder.wave.frame.iron` _(medium)_

Pig iron made in a blast furnace, refined in a basic oxygen furnace. The same ore, coke and limestone as the laminate press platen and the insertion machine bedplate.

###### Iron ore and metallurgical coke `mb.solder.wave.frame.iron.ore` _(medium)_

Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal. The two materials that make every steel machine on this floor, from the wave machine to the drill press.

##### Solder pot and wave former `mb.solder.wave.pot` _(medium)_

A stainless or cast-iron pot holding tens to hundreds of kg of molten solder at roughly 250 deg C. Inside, a pump or a tilted paddle throws solder up against a forming dam, which spills over as a smooth standing wave. The pot is lined or plated because molten tin attacks iron.

###### Pot lining and dross skimmer `mb.solder.wave.pot.lining` _(medium)_

Dross collects as a floating raft that is dragged off the surface by a skimmer bar. Skipping this is the classic way to put oxide particles into every joint on the line, and it is why the skimmer is on the machine and not optional.

###### Stainless steel pot wall `mb.solder.wave.pot.wall` _(medium)_

The pot is stainless or plated cast iron, chosen because molten tin dissolves iron at 250 deg C. A bare iron pot would be eaten away in weeks, taking the wave geometry with it. This is the material decision that makes a wave machine a five-year purchase instead of a consumable.

###### Nickel in the stainless steel `mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel` _(medium)_

Nickel is the component that makes stainless steel stainless: it forms a self-repairing chromium-oxide surface film that survives molten tin and most acids. The same nickel is the underplate beneath the gold on the board's edge contacts and the element in the burn-in oven's heating alloy.

###### Nickel ore `mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.ore` _(medium)_

Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite, smelted and refined to metal.

###### Laterite or sulphide ore body `mb.solder.wave.pot.wall.nickel.body` _(medium)_

A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter. The last rock in a chain that began as the lining of a solder pot.

##### Drag-free twin-wave design `mb.solder.wave.dragfree` _(medium)_

A single long wave exerts a strong forward drag on the board, which tears fine-pitch parts sideways and is the mechanical reason wave soldering lost to through-hole reflow. A twin-wave machine uses a main wave plus a smaller, faster secondary wave, or a double-peak former, that cuts the drag while still filling holes. Any serious 1983 machine had some version of this.

##### Preheat tunnel `mb.solder.wave.preheat` _(medium)_

An oven before the wave that brings the whole board to roughly 120 deg C so the thermal shock of hitting 250 deg C solder is spread out. It also drives off moisture, which would otherwise spit solder out of the holes as the board hits the wave.

###### Recirculating hot-air preheat `mb.solder.wave.preheat.air` _(medium)_

Preheating is by moving air or radiant tubes, with the zone held below the solder melting point so nothing melts early. Too little preheat gives thermally shocked joints; too much dries the resin and lifts pads off the laminate.

            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
##### Flux foamer `mb.solder.wave.foam` _(medium)_

Just before the wave, a bank of porous stone immersed in rosin flux bubbles air through it and lays a thin, even, pre-activated film on the board's underside. Foaming gives uniform coverage a spray or brush never does, and it is where the smell of boiling pine on a board line comes from.

###### Sintered porous stone `mb.solder.wave.foam.stone` _(medium)_

A sintered polyethylene or polyurethane stone whose pore size is chosen to bubble air finely through the flux. It clogs with crystallised flux and has to be soaked out on a schedule.

##### Conveyor chain and fixtures `mb.solder.wave.conveyor` _(medium)_

A stainless or phenolic chain carries boards through the machine, held by their edge in fixtures spaced along the chain. Chain pitch and fixture design, not the pump, set the real throughput. The fixtures were often the board's own edge, which is one reason board edge quality was a production concern.

##### Nitrogen blanket over the pot `mb.solder.wave.nitrogen` _(medium)_

Many machines piped nitrogen over the solder surface to keep the oxide skin thin and stop dross forming. It also stops the skin from insulating the pot from the wave, which makes the wave itself erratic.

          - *Nitrogen supply* `facility.nitrogen` *(seen above)*
##### Cooling zone `mb.solder.wave.cooling` _(medium)_

After the wave, boards sit in moving hot air before leaving the machine. Hot air rather than cold, because chilling a freshly soldered joint around a large thermal-mass lead is how you get a cracked solder fillet.

##### Spares pot and solder return `mb.solder.wave.spares` _(medium)_

A small pot under the wave catches solder running off the ends, which is then returned to the main pot. Recycling saves tin and, more importantly, stops the pot chemistry from drifting toward copper contamination.

#### The wave-soldering profile `mb.solder.profile` _(medium)_

The machine is set by five numbers together: pot temperature, conveyor speed, preheat temperature, preheat time, and flux concentration. Get them wrong in a specific way and you get a specific, diagnosable defect.

##### Why preheat sets joint quality `mb.solder.profile.thermal` _(medium)_

A joint cools from 250 deg C to 183 deg C in about a second. If the board and the lead start cold, the joint solidifies from the outside inward and you get the dull, grainy, poorly wetted fillet a line inspector rejects. Starting at 120 deg C lets the alloy flow properly before it freezes, which is the entire point of the preheat tunnel.

##### Heavy leads set the slowest joint `mb.solder.profile.thermalmass` _(medium)_

Large thermal-mass leads, such as the big axial electrolytic or the tabbed regulator, heat far more slowly than the solder around them. The line compensates by running the conveyor slowly enough that the solder stays molten until the lead is hot, which in turn slows every board on the machine.

#### What the joint is actually made of `mb.solder.reliability`

Solder does not merely sit on a pad, it reacts with it. Within seconds of contact, tin and copper fuse at the surface into a hard intermetallic, which grows over time and eventually turns brittle and cracks. That is the origin of solder fatigue, and it explains why a leaded joint is forgiving and a lead-free one is not.

##### Copper-tin intermetallic growth `mb.solder.reliability.intermetallic` _(medium)_

Cu6Sn5 forms at the pad surface and is the actual metallurgical bond holding the joint. It is hard and brittle, and its growth is limited by diffusion through itself, which is why higher-temperature solders containing silver or gold exist: to slow the reaction at the pad.

##### Named defects and what causes them `mb.solder.reliability.defects` _(medium)_

Dull grainy joints mean a dirty pad or too little preheat. Dry joints and unfilled holes mean a hole too tight for the lead or a wave too slow. Solder balls and spatter mean moisture in the board. Bridging between fine pads means too much flux, a pot too hot, or a wave too shallow. Blowholes in the joint mean damp.

#### Hand soldering on the line `mb.solder.hand` _(medium)_

Soldering iron, solder wire and pliers on a bench under a smoke extraction arm. Used for the connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers, the big electrolytics and every joint the inspector rejected. A small minority of joints, but where the line rejects come from too.

##### Soldering iron and tip `mb.solder.hand.iron` _(medium)_

A nichrome or cartridge heater in a barrel with a replaceable copper tip. The tip has to be kept tinned; a dry tip oxidises and then stops transferring heat at all, which is the real reason beginners conclude solder will not melt on a joint.

##### Copper tip material `mb.solder.hand.tip` _(medium)_

Oxygen-free copper for heat transfer, sometimes plated. Copper dissolves into molten tin if left sitting in the pot, so tips were changed once they had thinned noticeably.

##### Fume extraction `mb.solder.hand.extraction` _(medium)_

An arm or hood over the bench draws off the flux smoke. The smoke is resin vapour, not tin vapour, but it is unpleasant and it is the reason every solder bench in 1983 had a hood over it.

        - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
#### Connectors, fuse clips and heavy joints `mb.solder.selective` _(medium)_

The parts that cannot simply be taken through the wave in the usual way: the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers and the large electrolytics. These were soldered by hand, sometimes with a second iron used as a heat sink, and sometimes with a small solder pot.

##### Soldering with the connector already fitted `mb.solder.selective.tack` _(medium)_

The board-mount connectors on the C64 mainboard are right-angle types with solder tails projecting out of the back of the shell. They were soldered from the underside with the shell already in place, which means a short working time and a hot iron in a cramped space.

##### Bridging between connector pins `mb.solder.selective.bridge` _(medium)_

A D-sub or DIN connector has pins close enough that molten solder wicks along a pin and jumps the gap to the next pad, and inside a shell the bridge cannot be seen happening. The countermeasures in 1983 were flux plus a steady iron, then a probe and rework iron to break the bridge.

##### Two-iron technique for heavy joints `mb.solder.selective.heat` _(medium)_

One iron on the joint and one on the lead keeps the lead at temperature while the solder melts, so the solder actually wets the lead instead of freezing a cold slug around it. Slower per joint, but the only way to get a sound joint onto a big thermal-mass part.

### Populating, cleaning and finishing the C64 mainboard `mb.assembly`

What happens between the bare board and the tested machine. Components are inserted, a few hand-fitted wires and jumpers are added, the board is soldered, cleaned, shielded and screwed into the case. On this board the whole operation is through-hole and hand-and-machine insertion: there is no surface-mount reflow anywhere in the C64 mainboard assembly.

#### Component insertion `mb.assembly.insertion` _(medium)_

Every part goes into the board from the top. Because there are no vias and no bottom-side components, the whole machine is one-sided: one operator can see every joint from the solder side and there is no second-side insertion operation at all.

##### Insertion pitch set for the machine `mb.assembly.insertion.layout`

Component spacing on this board was dictated by the insertion machine rather than by the circuit designer, which is exactly the argument Commodore had with its Japanese plant and lost. The same board could not be hand-inserted efficiently and machine-inserted efficiently at once.

##### Insertion engine and its cycle time `mb.assembly.insertion.engine` _(medium)_

A machine with a magazine per part type picks a part, leads it to the right hole and pushes it in, typically in 0.3-0.6 s per component. On a board of about 90 parts that is roughly half a minute of machine time, which is why insertion engines paid for themselves on volume this high.

###### Machine frame and bedplate `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.frame` _(medium)_

A cast-iron or welded steel bed with a linear axis and a vertical insertion head. The bedplate's flatness is the limit on how accurately a lead can be placed in a hole.

###### Cast iron machine base `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.iron` _(medium)_

Grey cast iron, machined flat. The same material and the same blast-furnace iron ore as the laminate press platen; machine tool bases have been cast iron for a century for the same reason.

###### Blast-furnace iron ore `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.ironore` _(medium)_

Hematite or magnetite reduced with coke in a blast furnace. The industrial floor under this whole subsystem is iron ore and metallurgical coke.

###### Iron ore body `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.orebody` _(medium)_

A concentration of iron oxides, mined open pit or underground, crushed, concentrated and sintered before the furnace.

###### Metallurgical coke `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coke` _(medium)_

Baked coal, the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace and the source of its carbon monoxide.

###### Coal seam `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.coalseam` _(medium)_

Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. Diggable rock.

###### Part magazines and vibratory feed `mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines` _(medium)_

Radial magazines shake components down a track to a pick head. Cut, formed axial leads are the hardest part to feed; resistors and capacitors with wide leads feed easily.

##### Insertion fixture and board handling `mb.assembly.insertion.fixture` _(medium)_

The board is held in a jig with locating pins while components go in, and the same family of jig carries the board through the wave and into test. Every fixture on the line solves the same problem: the board has to land in exactly one position, every time.

###### Fixture steel plate `mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.steel` _(medium)_

Machined mild steel with hardened locating pins. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

##### Manual insertion and bench work `mb.assembly.insertion.manual` _(medium)_

Everything the machine could not do: the fuse clips, the connectors, the small-signal parts in awkward places, the wire jumpers. Operators sat at the line with a board in a fixture and worked down a traveler's list of parts.

#### Axial and radial lead forming `mb.assembly.leadforming` _(medium)_

Axial parts are cut to length and formed to a right angle or left-right offsets so they drop into a fixed hole pitch. Radial parts are spread to the lead spacing of the board. The forms are set in the machine and are a real cost: a wrong form is a board that will not insert.

#### DIP sockets as the C64's serviceability choice `mb.assembly.sockets` _(medium)_

This is the single most underappreciated decision on the board. The C64 sockets its integrated circuits rather than soldering them directly. It means any chip can be swapped in the field, and it means the number of joints roughly doubles, because each socket has two contacts per pin on each side.

#### Resistors and the resistor networks `mb.assembly.resistors` _(medium)_

The board is full of small carbon-film resistors, some laid down as axial parts and some consolidated into resistor networks to save board area. The C64 is a good example of the 1980s trend toward integrating discrete resistors into single packages.

##### Resistor networks and hybrid packs `mb.assembly.resistors.networks` _(low)_

Several resistors in one small package with a common connection, replacing a handful of separate parts and their board area. The C64's data-line resistors are a good example of the era's move toward integration.

##### Carbon-film resistor element `mb.assembly.resistors.film` _(medium)_

A thin ceramic substrate coated with a semiconducting carbon film, trimmed to value. The resistor is the most numerous single part on the whole board.

#### Wire jumpers and configuration links `mb.assembly.jumpers` _(medium)_

Because the board has no vias, the few places where a connection must cross between the two copper layers with no component to do it are bridged with a short tinned copper wire, hand-fitted into two holes and hand-soldered. These are the E1 and E2 links on the 250407 layout.

##### Tinned single-core jumper wire `mb.assembly.jumpers.wire` _(medium)_

A short length of fine tinned copper wire, cut and formed to the two holes, fitted and soldered by hand. It is the mechanical ancestor of the jumper link on every later board.

#### Connector and ribbon soldering `mb.assembly.connector` _(medium)_

The edge-connector slots, the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips and the keyboard ribbon interface are all fitted and soldered by hand, because a conveyorised wave cannot hold them. This is a long bench task and a common source of rejects.

#### Reflow and surface-mount: not on this board `mb.assembly.reflow`

It is worth being explicit that the C64 mainboard has no surface-mount parts and no reflow step. Everything is through-hole, everything is either waved or hand-soldered. Reflow ovens were already known in 1983 but were used for flat-pack IC packages and for the small daughterboards, not for the main logic board.

##### The RF modulator as a separate daughterboard `mb.assembly.reflow.note` _(low)_

The C64's analogue RF modulator is a small separate board, not part of the main logic board, and in early machines it sits on the mainboard. Its construction and any SMT content belong to that module, not to this through-hole assembly.

#### Cleaning after soldering `mb.assembly.cleaning` _(medium)_

Rosin flux leaves a sticky, slightly conductive film. The board is washed, historically in a solvent or detergent wash, sometimes with a little ultrasonic, then dried. The film matters: rosin is hygroscopic and mildly acidic, and in humid climates it slowly corrodes the board.

##### Ethanol `chem.ethanol`

C2H6O, boiling 78.4 C. In 1980s electronics it was a solvent and a cleaning fluid for a few specialist applications, and it was the fuel additive competing with MTBE for the octane that lead had given up. Chemically it can be made either by hydrating ethylene over phosphoric acid at 300 C and 60-70 bar, or by fermenting sugar. Both routes existed in 1983; the fermentation route made most of the world's ethanol in that decade because it was cheaper.

###### Ethylene hydration (the synthetic route) `chem.ethanol.ethylene-hydration`

Ethylene plus steam over phosphoric acid on silica at 280-330 C and 60-70 bar gives 4-6% ethanol per pass, so the off-gas is recycled. The selectivity limit is thermodynamic: the reaction is an equilibrium, and the industry spent decades on better catalysts and on pervaporation and extractive distillation to get around it.

###### Fermentation route (the biomass route) `chem.ethanol.fermentation`

Sugar from cane, beet or starch fermented by yeast at 30-35 C for two to three days, then rectified to 95% or dehydrated to absolute. In 1983 this made most of the world's fuel ethanol and it is the one large ethanol supply in the tree that does not begin with crude oil. It is also the honest boundary of this subsystem: a C64's plastics begin in petroleum, but a C64's fuel ethanol begins in a field.

        - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
#### Conformal coating `mb.assembly.conformal`

A thin insulating coating over the assembled board to keep moisture and contaminants off the copper. The C64 mainboard was not conformally coated.

#### EMI shield bonding `mb.assembly.shield` _(medium)_

The metal shield around the video and audio circuitry is bonded to the board's ground so that the enclosure is actually part of the ground return. Without a real bond the shield picks up the very signals it is there to contain.

##### Shield lug and solder bond `mb.assembly.shield.lug` _(medium)_

A small tab on the shield is soldered to a ground pad or held by a screw into a plated hole, giving the enclosure a low-impedance path to the board's ground pour.

##### The VIC-II heat-sink tab `mb.assembly.shield.tab`

A metal tab welded inside the shield lid pressed against the top of the video chip package, so the shield doubled as a heat sink for the chip that dissipated about 1.5 W. This was a deliberate design fix for a real heat problem, not a later addition.

#### Board-level rework and repair `mb.assembly.repair` _(medium)_

Bad joints are reworked on the line: the joint is reflowed with an iron, the part is replaced, and a full set of consumable tips is kept to do it. Commodore's own engineering position was famously to ship rather than to hold back, which shows up here as rework being a normal, high-volume operation rather than an exception.

#### Volume and yield reality of the line `mb.assembly.volume` _(low)_

Commodore sold on the order of two million C64s a year at the 1983-84 peak, on a production cost that started near 130 dollars and fell as volume rose. Every board here was one of millions per year through the same line. Boards were made in Hong Kong, and in the first year of production at Kentron in Japan, which is where the 1982-83 units came from.

### Factory test of the C64 mainboard and machine `mb.test` _(medium)_

How a populated C64 board was proved working before it left the factory. Electrical test on the bare board, then a functional test that boots the machine from a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port and checks it against a monitor and a test cradle, then burn-in, then final test and packing. The practice was mostly manual, and Commodore's own engineers admitted it was thinner than it should have been.

#### In-circuit electrical test `mb.test.ict` _(medium)_

A bare populated board is checked electrically before it is ever plugged into a machine. The point is to catch a missing component, a shorted pad or a broken trace while it is still trivially fixable.

##### Bed-of-nails fixture `mb.test.ict.nails` _(medium)_

The board is pressed down onto a fixture whose probes touch every node of interest, so the tester can measure each net without a probe being placed by hand. On a board with no vias and only DIP footprints, the fixture is comparatively simple to design and to wire.

###### Spring probe pins `mb.test.ict.nails.spring` _(medium)_

Small hardened probes on a sprung wire that survive repeated thousands of insertions. The fixture pinout has to be cut specifically for the board artwork, which is why fixtures were an expensive per-part-number investment.

###### Probe wire `mb.test.ict.nails.spring.wire` _(medium)_

Fine gold-plated or beryllium-copper wire drawn to a small diameter and formed into a sprung pin. Beryllium copper is used because it takes a permanent set and keeps its spring force after millions of cycles.

###### Copper (and beryllium) in the probe `mb.test.ict.nails.spring.copper` _(medium)_

The probe wire is copper alloy, drawing on the same copper supply as the board foil itself and the wave-solder pot. Copper is traced from cathode to concentrate by the metals subsystem.

##### Continuity, resistance and short detection `mb.test.ict.measure` _(medium)_

The tester looks for opens in the artwork and for shorts between nets that should be isolated, and on some fixtures measures absolute values. On a simple two-layer board with no vias, continuity checking is very nearly the whole job.

##### Component-presence and seating check `mb.test.ict.presence` _(medium)_

Checking that the right part is in the right place is a distinct and important test on a board with thirty sockets and a hundred passive parts. A missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the single most common fault on any 1980s logic board.

##### The tester itself `mb.test.ict.tester` _(medium)_

A rack of switching electronics driving the fixture, with a go or no-go readout and a reject bin. It is ordinary 1980s digital test equipment: a small computer, a relay matrix and a display, all built from the same logic families the C64 itself uses.

#### Functional test with a test ROM `mb.test.functional`

The populated board is mounted in a test cradle with a power supply and a monitor, and the machine proves itself by running a diagnostic program from the cartridge port. This exercises the real boot path: CPU, ROM, RAM, character ROM, VIC, SID and the I/O chips, all in the configuration they will ship in.

##### Diagnostic and dead-test ROM `mb.test.functional.rom`

A small EPROM in a cartridge shell which, on power-up, prints a screenful of named tests and runs each one, reporting RAM, ROM and video faults by pattern rather than by instrument. The operator's job is to look at the picture and read the verdict.

##### Test cradle `mb.test.functional.cradle` _(medium)_

A jig that holds the board, presents a regulated 5 V and 12 V, routes the video and audio outputs to a monitor and speaker, and presents the cartridge and edge connectors. Several cradles were usually in line so inspectors could work in parallel.

###### Cradle body and fixture plate `mb.test.functional.cradle.frame` _(medium)_

A machined plate with locating pins that hold the board in exactly one position, mounted on a steel frame with the electronics below. Every fixture on the line has this same problem: the board has to land in the same place every time, and the pins are what guarantee it.

###### Fixture steel `mb.test.functional.cradle.steel` _(medium)_

Mild steel plate, machined and hardened at the locating pins so they do not wear out of tolerance. The same blast-furnace iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

###### Iron ore and coke `mb.test.functional.cradle.ore` _(medium)_

Hematite or magnetite ore with coking coal, the two materials that make every steel jig on the line.

###### Coal seam `mb.test.functional.cradle.coalseam` _(medium)_

Bituminous coal mined from a seam, crushed and carbonised in coke ovens. A dug rock.

###### Test power supply `mb.test.functional.cradle.psu` _(medium)_

A regulated supply with a current limit so a shorted board does not destroy it. The C64's 5 V and 12 V came from its external supply, so the factory had to prove both the board and that supply; testing the PSU itself belongs to the power branch of this tree.

##### Keyboard and ribbon test `mb.test.functional.keyboard` _(medium)_

Because the keyboard connects to the mainboard through a soldered ribbon on this design, the functional test has to cover that joint: every key is checked, which is a simultaneous test of the connector, the ribbon, the keyboard matrix and the CPU's scanning routine.

#### CRT display test `mb.test.video`

The machine's own composite video output is fed to a test monitor and the inspector reads the picture. Nothing instruments this: the pass criterion is that the picture is correct, which means the human being in the loop is doing the measuring.

##### Test monitor `mb.test.video.monitor` _(medium)_

A small composite monochrome monitor, or a colour television, used as the reference picture. Each is a cathode-ray tube: drawn glass envelope, phosphor coating, deflection yoke and a high-voltage supply.

###### Shadow mask `mb.test.video.monitor.mask` _(medium)_

A perforated steel sheet just behind the phosphor screen that makes each phosphor dot land on its own gun. It is made from Invar, a nickel-iron alloy whose thermal expansion is almost zero, so the mask does not move as the tube warms up.

###### Invar (nickel-iron) `mb.test.video.monitor.mask.invar` _(medium)_

About 36 % nickel in iron, notable for expanding almost not at all between 0 and 200 deg C. Nickel comes from sulphide ore or laterite, iron from iron ore.

#### Burn-in `mb.test.burnin` _(medium)_

Finished machines are powered up under load, often at elevated temperature, for an extended period. This was originally to weed out infant-mortality failures in the custom chips, which is exactly where the C64's problems were, and it is why there had to be a diagnostic ROM that could run unattended.

##### Burn-in oven or rack `mb.test.burnin.oven` _(medium)_

A room or cabinet holding powered machines on racks, warmed to speed up failure. Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is, which is why burn-in exists at all.

###### Heating element (nichrome) `mb.test.burnin.oven.element` _(medium)_

The resistance wire in the oven heater, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists oxidation at red heat.

###### Nickel `mb.test.burnin.oven.nickel` _(medium)_

The main constituent of the heating alloy, and also the underplate under the gold on the board's edge contacts. Nickel comes from sulphide ore, and later heavily from laterite.

###### Nickel ore (sulphide or laterite) `mb.test.burnin.oven.ore` _(medium)_

Pentlandite in nickel sulphide ore, or limonite in laterite. Smelted, refined and electrolytically won to metal. Diggable rock.

###### Laterite or sulphide ore body `mb.test.burnin.oven.mine` _(medium)_

A weathered or igneous concentration of nickel minerals, mined by open pit or underground and concentrated before the smelter.

###### Chromium `mb.test.burnin.oven.chrome` _(medium)_

The second constituent of nichrome, from chromite ore. It is also the wear-resist plating on cutting tools and a constituent of the stainless steel used all over this factory.

###### Chromite ore `mb.test.burnin.oven.chromite` _(medium)_

Iron chromium oxide, smelted to ferrochrome. Diggable rock.

###### Burn-in rack `mb.test.burnin.oven.rack` _(medium)_

A steel frame carrying a shelf of machines, with ventilation so the heat is actually reaching them. Racks were moved in and out of the oven on a schedule, which is a large amount of manual handling for what looks like a passive wait.

##### Unattended running `mb.test.burnin.attended` _(medium)_

The diagnostic ROM is left to run so a machine that fails on its own gives a visible failure, freeing the line from one operator per machine. This is why the dead-test ROM's pattern output mattered as much as its pass or fail verdict.

#### Final test and packing `mb.test.final` _(medium)_

A last pass over the complete machine in its case: keyboard, control ports, serial port and a final power-on. Surviving machines are packed with the cord and the manual for shipment.

##### Control and serial port check `mb.test.final.ports` _(medium)_

The two control ports and the serial port are exercised with known-good peripherals or loopback plugs. These are the connectors most often left untested on a line that was under pressure, and it is where the documented field failures of this era cluster.

##### Packing for shipment `mb.test.final.pack` _(medium)_

The machine, cord and manual go into a carton, typically corrugated board with a printed outer. The packaging branch has its own industrial chemistry; this node marks only where the tested board leaves the factory.

### Phototooling: how C64 copper artwork became an etched board `mb.photo`

The chain that turns a board database into a resist image. The 250407 artwork is number 251137. It was drawn on a design workstation, reduced to aperture-table plot files, plotted onto photographic film at a jobbing house, developed, checked on a test coupon, and used as the mask that prints the board's dry-film resist before etching.

#### The board database on the design system `mb.photo.design` _(medium)_

In 1983 the layout lived on the CAD vendor's own workstation, not in a modern repository. Traces, pads, components and drill data were edited on the machine and periodically written out as plot files on tape or floppy. Copying it to the jobbing house was a physical act of transporting magnetic media.

##### CAD workstation `mb.photo.design.workstation` _(medium)_

A dedicated 16-bit microcomputer or small minicomputer with its own storage, a high-resolution monochrome display, and often a pen plotter and a digitizer on the desk. The digitizer mattered as much as the plotter: designers drew and revised artwork on mylar overlays and digitised the changes back into the database.

###### Monochrome CRT display `mb.photo.design.workstation.display` _(medium)_

A high-resolution green or white phosphor CRT on which the layout was examined trace by trace. The glass envelope, the phosphor coating and the shadow mask are all thin-film processes on a drawn glass bulb.

###### CRT envelope glass `mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glass` _(medium)_

The bulb is soda-lime glass formed on a glass lathe from the same kind of batch as the reinforcing cloth: silica sand plus limestone plus alkali. A design workstation's screen is a small consumer item, but it is the terminal through which every copper trace of the board was examined.

###### Silica sand in the display glass `mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glass.sand` _(medium)_

The main glass former in the CRT envelope, from the same washed and purified sand used for glass fibre. The glass chain of this tree has two exits to the same rock: reinforcing cloth and display glass.

###### Quartz sand deposit `mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glass.rock` _(medium)_

Unconsolidated or friable sandstone worked for its sand. A dug mineral, and one of the few things in the whole phototooling chain that is not a petroleum product.

###### Plot-file storage media `mb.photo.design.workstation.storage` _(medium)_

Plot files and library data were written to nine-track tape, then to 8-inch floppy disks. The magnetic oxide on a thin polymer backing is the physical carrier the jobbing house receives, and a lost tape meant the whole panel waited.

##### Backannotation from a drawn overlay `mb.photo.design.backannotation` _(medium)_

The designer taped mylar over the plotted printout, drew routing changes with a special pen, and passed the overlay through a digitizer that read the new lines and apertures back into the database. Slow, physical, and fiddly, and the reason routing history on boards of this era reads the way it does.

#### Data reduction and CAM `mb.photo.cam` _(medium)_

The database is converted into per-layer plot files. This is where a net becomes copper, a component pin becomes a pad, and the drill hits are separated out. Errors here are replicated across a whole panel, which is why the step is done once, carefully, for hundreds of boards.

##### Netlist to routed copper `mb.photo.cam.netlist` _(medium)_

Connectivity becomes tracks per layer. On this two-layer board the routing problem is comparatively simple because there is no plane layer, but the ground return still has to be poured around the routing, and it is that pour which carries most of the finished board's signal integrity.

##### Aperture table `mb.photo.cam.apertures`

Every distinct pad shape and track width is assigned an aperture in a table the plotter reads, so a 1.0 mm round pad and a 0.3 mm track are drawn as repeated simple shapes rather than as free curves. This aperture-table idea is the direct ancestor of the Gerber format, still the universal interchange format for board artwork today.

##### Drill file separation `mb.photo.cam.drill` _(medium)_

The drill programme is split out from the copper data. On this board that is easy and low-risk because there are no vias, so the drill file is only component holes, mounting holes and the connector slots. A via-heavy board of the same era is where plot data and drill data were most often confused, and the result was a hole in the wrong place.

##### Design rule checks `mb.photo.cam.checks` _(medium)_

Automated checks for minimum track width, minimum spacing, pad-to-pad clearance and annular ring. On a board with no vias the annular-ring check has almost nothing to check, but spacing between fine pads on the IC footprints still matters.

#### Photoplotting the artwork film `mb.photo.plotter` _(medium)_

The plot files drive a photoplotter that draws the copper artwork onto a transparent film. In 1983 these machines lived at the fabricator, not the design office, and were the company's most valuable single asset.

##### Electrostatic plotter `mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic`

The dominant plotting technology of the era. A fine wire or shaped electrode is stepped across the film under computer control and a corona discharge exposes the emulsion wherever copper is wanted. Flatbed machines laid a film flat and exposed quickly, which is why they became the standard for two-sided work.

##### Artwork film stock `mb.photo.plotter.film` _(medium)_

A high-contrast, dimensionally stable photographic film that the plotter exposes and the shop develops into a finished mask. It must hold its geometry over a store door and be opaque where there is copper. The polymer base is the same class of polyester as the dry-film photoresist carrier.

###### Polyester film base (PET) `mb.photo.plotter.film.base` _(medium)_

The dimensionally stable base the emulsion is coated on, made from polyethylene terephthalate. It is the reason a 1983 plotter film does not stretch and shift during handling, and it is the same polymer family as the photoresist carrier used on the board itself.

###### Ethylene glycol `mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg` _(medium)_

One of the two feedstocks of PET, made by oxidising ethylene derived from ethylene. Ethylene comes from steam cracking of naphtha.

###### Ethylene `mb.photo.plotter.film.base.eg.ethylene` _(medium)_
