The two-carbon olefin from a steam cracker, parent of polyethylene and, with glycol, of polyester film.

###### Naphtha `mb.photo.plotter.film.base.naphtha` _(medium)_

The liquid petroleum fraction that is steam-cracked to make ethylene.

###### Crude oil `mb.photo.plotter.film.base.crude` _(medium)_

The hydrocarbon mixture from a reservoir, fractionated and cracked into the aromatics and olefins that make the film, the resist, the ink and the machine tools of this entire tree.

###### Petroleum reservoir `mb.photo.plotter.film.base.reservoir` _(medium)_

Porous rock holding crude under pressure, produced through steel casing into a gathering system. This is the bottom of the whole tree: everything on this branch that is not mineral is a refined version of this.

          - *Photoresist chemistry* `chem.photoresist` *(seen above)*
##### Pen plotter (older, slower) `mb.photo.plotter.pen` _(medium)_

A carriage carrying a light-sensitive pen draws the artwork directly on film or mylar. Simple and reliable, but slow, with real line-width variation, so it was being displaced by the electrostatic plotter through the early 1980s and by the laser plotter later.

##### Laser plotter (arriving) `mb.photo.plotter.laser` _(medium)_

An argon-ion or, later, a diode laser writes the film or the photoresist directly. Sharper than corona discharge and faster, but in 1983 it was still being adopted and the electrostatic plotter was not yet history.

#### Developing and fixing the film `mb.photo.develop` _(medium)_

The exposed film is developed, fixed, washed and dried before it can serve as a mask. The chemistry is ordinary silver-halide photographic processing, run as a short line of tanks.

##### Photographic developer (hydroquinone) `mb.photo.develop.developer` _(medium)_

The film emulsion is silver halide; hydroquinone reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, giving the opaque image that will block the resist. The reducing agent is itself an aromatic chemical made from benzene, so the mask chemistry is a petroleum chain like everything else in this branch.

###### Benzene-derived intermediates `mb.photo.develop.developer.aromatic` _(medium)_

Hydroquinone is made by dihydroxylating benzene. Benzene comes from the heavy naphtha fraction of crude oil, so the developer that draws the copper pattern is two refinery steps from crude.

###### Heavy naphtha `mb.photo.develop.developer.naphtha` _(medium)_

A mid-boiling petroleum fraction, solvent-extracted for benzene.

###### Crude oil `mb.photo.develop.developer.crude` _(medium)_

The unrefined petroleum the naphtha is cut from.

###### Petroleum reservoir `mb.photo.develop.developer.reservoir` _(medium)_

The sedimentary rock that holds it.

##### Fixer (ammonium thiosulfate) `mb.photo.develop.fixer` _(medium)_

The unexposed silver halide is dissolved away and the image made light-stable, so the film can be handled, stored and re-exposed without latent-image changes.

#### Rephotography, the master, and the coupon `mb.photo.rephoto`

The plotted working film is rephotographed onto a higher-quality film to get a sharper, dimensionally stable master. Before a whole panel is committed, a test coupon is exposed and etched with every line width the panel uses, and the widths are measured. This is how a shop proves its process still holds tolerance.

##### The artwork master `mb.photo.rephoto.master` _(medium)_

The film treated as the authoritative copy of the design, stored flat and handled by the edges. It is the board's master record, and losing it means paying for the panel again.

#### Printing the artwork onto the resist `mb.photo.mask` _(medium)_

The artwork film is laid against the exposed dry-film resist on the board and exposed in the vacuum frame. Where the film is clear, the resist hardens and resists the etch; where it is opaque, the resist stays soft and the copper beneath is etched away. This is the moment the phototooling chain finally touches the board, and every solder joint on the finished machine is located by this exposure.

##### Two-sided registration `mb.photo.mask.registration`

The hard part of a two-sided board. The second side's artwork has to land on the copper to within a fraction of a millimetre, using alignment pins and a register mark. On this board it matters mainly for the mounting holes and the connector slots; on a via-heavy board it is what decides whether every barrel lands on its own pad.

#### Panelising the order `mb.photo.panel` _(medium)_

The board is one part out of a panel of identical boards nested in a sheet large enough for the process equipment. The panel gets tooling holes for registration and for the drill, and the boards are separated later. This is where the layout cost of an order is amortised, and why a two-layer panel in 1983 could hold a surprising number of boards.

##### Tooling and mouse-bite tabs `mb.photo.panel.mousebites` _(medium)_

The nested boards are held by small perforated tabs, broken out by hand or by a router after the panel is finished. The tabs leave a characteristic rough edge on the board outline, which is visible on a 1983 board if you look at it.

## Commodore 64 external 'brick' power supply `c64.psu`

A sealed black ABS box roughly 150 x 100 x 60 mm that sits under the C64 and converts wall mains into 5 V DC for the logic plus unfiltered ~9 V AC for the cassette motor, the RF modulator, the VIC-II's CAN +5 V rail, the SID's +12 V doubler and the 50/60 Hz time-of-day clock. It is a linear supply: an iron-core transformer, two rectifier diodes, one 4700 uF electrolytic, one three-terminal 5 V regulator and a folded aluminium heatsink, all buried under a minty-green epoxy pour from 1983 on.

### Mains transformer, 40-46 VA `c64.psu.transformer`

The whole of the supply's energy conversion. One primary on 117 V mains, a centre-tapped ~18 V secondary feeding the 5 V regulator, and a separate ~9 V winding feeding straight out to the C64. The two secondaries are galvanically isolated from each other as well as from the primary - that isolation is what lets the C64 tie their grounds together only at the rectifier.

#### E-I laminated silicon-steel core `c64.psu.transformer.core`

A stack of punched E and I laminations with interleaved joints, taped along the yoke edges with a single wrap of masking or Kapton tape. For a 40 VA unit at 60 Hz the stack is maybe 25-35 mm tall in 0.35-0.5 mm plate, and it is clamped hard enough that the laminations must be isolated from each other by the oxide scale left on the punched edges.

##### Punched E and I lamination `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination`

One E and one I punched from a strip of grain-oriented electrical steel by a high-speed progression press, roughly 200-600 strokes per minute. The die is a hardened tool-steel stamping die with a compound profile; the strip is fed on a roll and the interlamination burr left by the punch is small enough not to short adjacent plates.

###### High-speed stamping press `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punch`

A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.

###### Hardened tool-steel stamping die `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punch.die` _(medium)_

Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.

###### Grain-oriented electrical steel (Hi-B) `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes`

Steel whose crystal grains are aligned so the easy magnetisation axis runs along the sheet. Magn permeability along the grain is several times higher than across it, so a transformer built from oriented steel needs roughly half the core cross-section of one built from hot-rolled plate. It is made by cold rolling to 0.35 mm, then annealing in a stream of hydrogen at 1100-1200 C, which lets the austenite grains rearrange into the aligned 'Goss' texture.

###### Cold rolling to 0.35 mm `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.coldroll`

A reversing four-high cold mill takes hot strip down through several annealing and rolling passes to 0.35 mm, with the rolling direction being the future flux direction. Reduction ratios above 20:1 in the final pass are what set the grain elongation.

###### Magnetic anneal in hydrogen `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.maganneal`

Coils of 0.35 mm strip are annealed for 20-40 hours at 1100-1200 C in a stream of high-purity hydrogen at dew points below -60 C. Hydrogen both removes oxygen that would pin grain boundaries and, on cooling through the Curie point at about 770 C in the field-free furnace, lets the austenite transform into oversized aligned grains.

###### High-purity hydrogen `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.maganneal.hydrogen`

Made in the 1980s by steam methane reforming of natural gas followed by pressure-swing adsorption and a cryogenic final purification to 99.999%. It was the standard controlled-atmosphere gas for grain-oriented electrical steel because it neither oxidises nor carburises the surface.

                - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Upstream: ore to hot-rolled sheet `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream`

The chain that makes the steel the laminations are punched from, from hematite ore through sinter, blast furnace, basic oxygen furnace, continuous casting, hot rolling, descaling and a primary base anneal, before the cold rolling and magnetic anneal that make it 'oriented'.

###### Iron ore concentrate, ~62-66% Fe `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.ore`

Run-of-mine hematite and magnetite is crushed and either shipped as lump ore to a blast furnace or upgraded to sinter/pellet. Commodore's steel chain in 1982 was almost entirely sinter-based: the ore was blended with coke and limestone, sintered on a Dwight-Stewart travelling grate into 5-6 cm porous sinter, and charged hot.

###### Limestone flux `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.ore.limestone`

Calcite crushed to 3-6 mm and used both as sinter flux and as the blast-furnace flux that combines with silica to form a fluid slag. It is mined quarried and used essentially as dug.

                  - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Limestone quarrying and calcination `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.ore.limestone.calcination`

High-grade calcite is extracted by drilling and blasting, then crushed in two stages to 3-6 mm for the sinter mix and to 25-75 mm for the furnace burden. Only a small fraction is calcined; the bulk goes to the sinter mix as a flux, and the remainder goes down the furnace to become the fluid lime slag. Calcination itself, CaCO3 to CaO plus CO2, happens in the sinter mix and in the coke ovens.

                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
                    - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Metallurgical coke `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.ore.coke`

Metallurgical coke is made in 1980s batteries or coke ovens by carbonising coking coal at 1000-1100 C in the absence of air; later plants added petroleum coke to the blend. It is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace.

                  - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
###### Blast furnace and hot metal `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.blastfurnace`

A 300-1000 m3 shaft furnace charges sinter, coke and limestone in a burden; preheated blast at 900-1200 C burns coke to CO, and the burden descends against the ascending gas, being reduced from Fe2O3 through Fe3O4 to Fe. The furnace runs continuously for years, tapping iron at 1450-1550 C every few hours.

                - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Cowper stoves and the blast `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.blastfurnace.stove`

The 900-1200 C blast is not heated directly: cleaned top gas from the furnace is burned in a refractory-lined Cowper stove, a tall cylindrical regenerator roughly 8-10 m across, and the 300-500 C exit gas is recovered in a gas-cleaning plant of cyclones and scrubbers. A furnace has three or four stoves, each on a 20-40 minute cycle.

###### Silica-alumina refractory brick `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.blastfurnace.stove.refractory`

Stove and furnace linings are fired silica brick or aluminous firebrick, made from carefully graded silica sand or bauxite blended with a clay binder and fired in a tunnel kiln. Getting the grain size distribution right matters more than the chemistry: a graded pack gives a lining that survives thermal shock without spalling.

                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
                    - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Tapping the hot metal `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.blastfurnace.tapping`

Every three to four hours the drill is run through the tap hole and the hot metal runs into torpedo ladle cars holding 100-300 t. Skulls of solidified iron must be broken out afterwards with castings, which is why a blast furnace has a cast-house full of mud guns and running bars. The slag, lower in density, is skimmed off the top of the ladle.

###### Hot metal desulphurisation `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.blastfurnace.tapping.desulphurisation` _(medium)_

Electrical-steel heats need sulphur below about 0.01% because sulphur embrittles steel. In the 1980s this was done either in the ladle with basic slag stirrer agitation or by injecting lime and aluminium powder with a lance under pressure of compressed air.

                    - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
                    - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.bof`

Hot metal is charged with scrap and lime into a tilting vessel and a water-cooled lance blows oxygen for 15-25 minutes. The carbon content is adjusted to whatever the rolling mill needs - around 0.05-0.1% for the electrical-steel grades - and the heat is tapped at about 1600 C.

###### Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel `metal.steel`

Steel is the machine's frame, its shields, its fasteners and its tooling, and in mass it dominates everything else in the C64. The route is: iron ore plus coke plus limestone into a blast furnace for hot metal; hot metal plus oxygen plus scrap into a steelmaking vessel; steel through a continuous caster into a slab; slab through a hot mill and a cold mill into sheet. Then three specialties matter for this tree: grain-oriented electrical steel for the power supply transformer, stainless for the jack and the shields, and hardened tool steel for the injection moulding dies and the extrusion dies.

###### Blast furnace hot metal, 4.3% C `metal.iron.hot-metal`

A 25-30 m tall, 8-11 m wide stack, charged at the top with sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and limestone, and blown at the bottom through 3-4 tuyeres with 1000-1300 C blast at a pressure of 2-4 bar. The iron oxide is reduced in stages on the way down - hematite to magnetite at 400-600 C, magnetite to wüstite at 700-900 C, wüstite to iron below 1000 C - and the carbon goes out as CO. The iron arrives at the hearth as a liquid at about 1450-1550 C, containing 3.5-4.5% carbon, 0.3-1% silicon, 0.1-0.2% manganese, 0.05-0.1% phosphorus and about 0.5% sulphur, and it is tapped every 4-6 hours. The slag floats on top and is tapped separately. A 1982 furnace made 5,000-15,000 t of hot metal a day on 3,000-4,500 m3 of volume and consumed about 400,000 m3 of blast a minute.

###### The burden: sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke, flux `metal.iron.burden`

The furnace eats a precisely weighed blend, batched in 1-3 t bins and dumped in a rotating order around the bell-less throat so the burden descends evenly. Sinter is 55-65% Fe and 8-12% gangue; pellets are 62-66% Fe and are nearly always the majority of the iron-bearing burden in a modern furnace because they are uniform and permeable; lump ore is 45-60% Fe and is in retreat. The blend is sized and ground so it is permeable enough for the gas to reach the burden and rigid enough not to collapse into the raceways.

###### Sintering the fine ore on a travelling grate `metal.sinter`

Fine iron ore cannot be charged into a blast furnace - it would be blown away or it would pack. So it is sintered: mixed with 8-12% returning sinter fines, 5-7% coke and 10-20% lime, moistened to 6-8%, spread in a 0.7-1.0 m bed on a travelling grate, and ignited. At 1200-1400 C the bed self-fuses into a porous 100-150 mm cake. A modern sinter strand produces 3,000-6,000 t of sinter an hour and consumes about 1 GJ of fuel per tonne. It is the same machine as the lead sinter and the manganese sinter, and it emits a great deal of dust.

###### Coke breeze: the sinter fuel `metal.coke-breeze`

The 3-10 mm fraction of coke, screened out at the coke plant, that would be too small for the blast furnace. A steelworks' sinter plant is therefore a consumer of its own coke plant's fines - a neat example of an internal recycling loop in the iron and carbon chain that closes from the coke oven's quench, through the sinter plant, back into the blast furnace's burn.

###### Pelletising the concentrate on a disc or a pelletiser `metal.pellet`

Very fine concentrate - under 45 um - is mixed with 5-8% bentonite binder and 0.5-1% limestone, moistened, and fed to a rotating disc pelletiser or a drum pelletiser where 3-10 mm green pellets are rolled up by capillary action. The green pellets are then fired on a travelling grate at 1200-1350 C in an oxidising atmosphere, which sinters the surface, gives the pellet its compressive strength and, if the furnace is properly controlled, magnetises it - the hematite becomes magnetite, which means the pellet can itself be recovered magnetically, and its reduction in the blast furnace is faster. Pelletising is what made the 1970s and 1980s post-and-tensile steel possible and it is the reason Brazil and Canada have a modern steel industry at all.

###### Bentonite binder from a clay pit `metal.bentonite` _(medium)_

A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.

###### The furnace stack, throat and bustle pipe `metal.iron.burden-shaft`

The 20-30 m stack is lined with 1,000-2,000 mm of refractory and carries the burden down through a rotating throat seal into a stock column. The burden rests on a 'ledge' in the wall where the gas changes from upward to horizontal flow - the place every blast furnace operator watches, because if the burden descends too fast the gas gets through and the furnace races. At the bottom, the bustle pipe wraps the furnace and delivers the blast through the tuyeres, with the hot blast stoves - Cowper stoves, 8-12 per furnace, each 8-12 m tall - heating the air to 1000-1300 C on the gas from the previous cycle. A 1982 furnace is a machine about 25 m tall and 9 m wide with a 3,500 m3 working volume, and it holds about 100 tonnes of burden in flight at any moment.

###### Copper stave hearth cooling `metal.iron.copper-cooler`

The stave coolers that protect the hearth from 1500 C molten iron are made of copper or copper alloy with a water passage cast into them, because copper conducts heat far better than cast iron. They are a copper industry product, and they are one of the more elegant cross-links in this tree: the blast furnace cannot survive without a copper casting technology. On a modern furnace the stave is cast as a composite with a cast-iron backing and a copper water-cooled front, and about 400-900 staves are fitted.

###### Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking `metal.steel.bof`

Hot metal is charged into a 40-60 t vessel - a pear-shaped converter with a refractory lining - together with about 20-30% scrap, and then a lance lowered into the bath on a boom blows 99.5% oxygen at 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h for 15-25 minutes. Three things happen at once: the carbon burns, the silicon and phosphorus oxidise, and the carbon monoxide boils the bath. The phosphorus removal is the reason the process is called basic: the lining is doloma, calcined dolomite, and the phosphorus ends up as calcium phosphate in the slag, which is why BOF slag is a genuine phosphorus fertiliser. The chemistry is violent and self-accelerating - the bath heats itself to about 1600 C from the oxidation reactions alone, so no fuel is added at all.

###### Choosing the steelmaking vessel in 1982 `metal.steel.vessel-choice`

Three vessels made the world's steel in 1982 and only one of them was winning. A short parent node so the basic oxygen furnace, the dying open hearth and the scrap-based electric arc furnace sit side by side instead of inside one another.

###### The open hearth furnace, in decline `metal.steel.open-hearth`

A 200-500 t rectangular basin of refractory with a hearth at 1300-1400 C, in which pig iron and scrap were melted while fuel gas or oil was burned above them and air was blown across the surface. It was dominant in 1920-1960 and it took 6-10 hours for a heat, produced a lot of nitrogen (so it could not easily make low-carbon steel) and consumed a lot of fuel. In 1982 it was a historical footnote in most of the world, still running in India, in Japan at a few works, and in a handful of Eastern European plants. It is included because it is the process the industry left, and because the heat-transfer engineering of the open hearth was the same furnace that the BOF was designed to eliminate.

###### Electric arc furnace on scrap `metal.steel.eaf`

The other route, and the one that was growing fastest in the 1980s. Three carbon electrodes are lowered into a 30-100 t shell furnace and an arc struck, melting scrap with 600-1,500 A at 30-50 V - a physically brutal heat transfer that lets a small furnace melt steel quickly. In 1982 the units were mostly the smaller, older 'three-phase' EAFs of 30-50 t; the 100 t+ DC furnace that transformed the industry came at the end of the decade. The EAF makes about 20% of US steel and rather less of world steel, and it is the route that makes the recycling loop of car scrap back into new sheet possible.

###### Carbon electrodes from needle coke and pitch `metal.carbon-electrode`

The EAF, the submerged arc furnaces of the ferroalloy industries, the aluminium pot anodes and the large carbon blocks of the blast furnace all consume the same two materials: calcined petroleum coke or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as a binder. An electrode is milled green - coke, pitch and sometimes a sulphur or metal additive - extruded, and baked at 800-1200 C in a graphitising furnace to above 2500 C. The 1980s problem was exactly the nickel crisis showing up here: the EAF plants had no electrodes of their own in Japan, and when the 1979-80 nickel spike also hit electrode prices, Japanese steelmakers found that making steel required nickel, in the electrodes. UHP electrodes and the shift to larger electrode sizes was the industry response.

###### Ladle treatment, degassing and the steel's last chemistry `metal.steel.ladle` _(medium)_

In 1982 the most important development in steelmaking was not the furnace but the ladle. A 1980s steel ladle is a 100-200 t vessel on a rotating turret, and it is where three things happen in sequence. Secondary metallurgy: argon is stirred in to homogenise the temperature and composition and to flush hydrogen and nitrogen. Desulphurisation: calcium or a calcium-bearing reagent is added and stirred, taking the sulphur out as calcium sulphide in a basic slag. Deoxidation and inclusion control: aluminium is added as the last deoxidiser, and in a bottom-pour ladle the whole ladle is streamed through a nozzle to collect the inclusions in the nozzle. This is the technology that made clean, low-inclusion, low-carbon steel a reproducible product, and it is why modern sheet steel for tinplate and for deep drawing exists at all.

###### Continuous casting of steel slab `metal.steel.caster`

Steel is not poured into moulds one heat at a time; it is cast continuously. Liquid steel at 1600 C is fed from a tundish through a nozzle into a water-cooled copper mould 1-2.5 m long, where the shell freezes in seconds. The strand then passes through a series of spray headers that remove the rest of the heat, and finally through a torch-cut or a flying shear, and is coiled. The whole point is yield: continuous casting replaced ingot casting in the 1980s across the industry, and a modern continuous caster turns out better than 95% of its steel while ingot casting threw away the 10-20% of each ingot that was the crop - the ends, the segregation, and the shrinkage void. The C64's steel exists because of this machine.

###### The copper mould wall `metal.steel.mould-wall` _(medium)_

The copper alloy plate - phosphor bronze in most designs - that does the single hardest job in the whole of steelmaking, withdrawing heat from 1600 C steel at a rate that makes a millimetre of metal freeze in a second, and doing it hundreds of thousands of times. The plates are thin, 5-30 mm, and are cooled internally by high-pressure water, and they are plated and re-ground as they wear. Their thermal-fatigue cracking is the plant's central maintenance problem, and every crack means a slab defect that a tinplate maker will find on the inspection line.

###### Hot and cold rolled sheet steel `metal.steel.sheet`

The slab goes to a reversing hot rolling mill at 1150-1250 C - first through a roughing stand, then a rail mill or a continuous mill - and comes out as strip 2-12 mm wide. Then the cold mill, a Sendimir or a multi-high cluster mill with a Sendzimir Z-High line upgrade, takes it to 0.2-0.5 mm, with the rolling oil and the annealing line in between. Annealing in a hydrogen or hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere gives the recrystallised, equiaxed grain structure that makes a stamping possible. Cold-rolled sheet at 0.3-1 mm is the C64's case panel, the shield cans, the brackets and the heat-spreader, and the tinplate branch below is the same mill with a different end.

###### Steel rolling oil: emulsion and hydraulic oil `metal.rolling-oil` _(medium)_

Hot rolling of steel uses water emulsion; cold rolling uses a neat oil or a water-in-oil emulsion, chemically similar to the aluminium rolling lubricant but with a much higher base oil viscosity and a lot of boundary additives. So the C64's steel mill and its aluminium mill are the same kind of lubricant plant, and both are quietly downstream of crude oil.

###### Paraffinic base oil from crude `metal.rolling-oil.petroleum` _(medium)_

The leaf of this sub-branch: a refinery vacuum distillate fraction, hydrotreated and dewaxed. It is the same crude that makes the plastics, and the energy agent owns the refinery; this node exists so the metals tree has a real bottom for its lubricant.

###### Annealing, tempering and the sheet properties `metal.steel.heat-treatment` _(medium)_

Cold-rolled low-carbon steel is hard and full of internal stress, so it is annealed in a continuous line - a few seconds to a few minutes at 700-850 C in a hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere - to recrystallise it into soft equiaxed grain, and then, if it is going to be drawn rather than stamped, given a temper mill pass to raise the yield point by 50-150 MPa. The temper mill is a roll that puts in a deliberate rolling reduction that the temper roll locks in as a dislocation structure the anneal will not remove. The 1982 temper mill was a three-high Sendimir with a work-roll diameter of about 300 mm, and it is the reason a can and a deep-drawing panel are different products from the same mill.

###### Pickling, oiling and the surface specification `metal.steel.surface` _(medium)_

Cold-rolled sheet is covered in mill scale and must be pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to remove it, or the next operation cannot stick to it. Then it is oiled or lacquered so it does not rust in storage. On the 1980s tinplate line the acid was hydrochloric, which put a genuinely dangerous hydrogen into the atmosphere, and the 1982 line ran its pickling tanks under a hood with an acid fume scrubber using sodium carbonate - which is another place the sodium chain of this file enters. The surface specification is a contract: roughness, cleanliness, and oil film weight in grams per square metre.

###### Tinplate: the tin-coated steel sheet `metal.tinplate`

Tinplate is 0.15-0.3 mm of low-carbon steel with 1.1-11.2 g/m2 of tin on both sides, made on a continuous electrolytic line at 4-8 m/s. The strip is degreased and pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, rinsed, then tinned in a stannous sulphate bath with a fluoroborate additive, rinsed, and either given a food-can passivation in chromic acid or - in the electronics and tinplate trade - an electrolytic passivation in a chromate or tin-oxide bath. A C64 uses a few square metres of tinplate a year at most, in switch bodies and shields, but tinplate is worth a node because it is the one place where tin and steel and electrochemistry all meet, and because the chromate passivation is the same chemistry as the zinc chromate passivation in the plating branch.

###### The tinning line: greening, tinning, soaking `metal.tinplate.tin-pots` _(medium)_

The line has four electrolytic tanks in series - a 'greening' or pretreat tank to strip the last oxide, two or more tinning tanks with soluble tin anodes, and a 'soaking' tank to heal any bare spots. The strip runs through as a ribbon, and the tin is applied at a controlled thickness by the current and by how long the strip spends in the stannate bath. The mechanical complexity is in the handling: a 0.2 mm ribbon travelling at 6 m/s has to be threaded, cleaned and welded end to end several times a shift.

###### Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) `metal.electrical-steel`

The C64's power supply transformer is the one place where the metal of the machine is deliberately not stainless or mild steel. Grain-oriented electrical steel is a 3.2% silicon low-carbon steel whose grains have been given a preferred orientation - the classic route is a 700-1000 C anneal in hydrogen in a field or, in the modern continuous process, a high-temperature final anneal with a bias field - so that the flux runs along the grain and the core losses and the magnetostriction both fall. The 1982 transformer in a C64 used M4 to M6 grade GOES, somewhere around 0.3-0.5 mm thick, wound as E-E laminations. Without the silicon the core would saturate, the transformer would be too big, and the whole switching supply would not fit. Silicon steel is therefore not a speciality of this tree - it is load-bearing.

###### E-E laminations and the stamping `metal.electrical-steel.lamination`

The 0.3 mm strip is blanked and stamped into E and I shapes - or, in a cheaper 1982 supply, into E-E pairs and then stacked and interlocked - on a 400-800 tonne mechanical or hydraulic press with a compound die that does the whole lamination stack in one stroke. The stamping is heavily lubricated and the edges are deburred and then given a magnetic insulation treatment: a thin epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an 'insulation coating' of an inorganic glassy film, applied so that the laminations do not short-circuit each other. The core of the C64's transformer is about 30-60 stamped laminations, and the number is set by the stack height and the available die.

###### Silicon added to the steel `metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source`

How does 3% silicon get into sheet steel at all? Ferrosilicon is added to the ladle, or - in the parent process - the ore is smelted with silica and coke in a submerged arc furnace to give 45-75% Si ferroalloy, and that alloy is added to the steel in the ladle or in the EAF. So the silicon steel branch intersects the ferrosilicon furnace, which is a carbon-reduction electric furnace just like the ferromanganese and ferrochrome furnaces in this tree, and which ultimately runs on the same metallurgical silicon and quartzite chain as the semiconductors. One of the more satisfying loops in the tree.

###### Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace `metal.ferrosilicon`

Ferrosilicon at 45-75% silicon is made in a submerged arc furnace very like the one that makes metallurgical silicon, but with more coke and a much higher silica ratio in the slag: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO, with the silicon going into the ferroalloy instead of condensing as dust. The largest producers make it in 60-100 MVA three-electrode furnaces, and the furnace is a genuinely different beast from the silicon one - the slag is liquid and the electrode has to tap through it. So the electrical-steel transformer in a C64 and the quartzite in a silicon plant converge at two different kinds of arc furnace.

                      - *High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2)* `metal.quartzite` *(seen above)*
###### Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent `metal.coke`

Coke is the black, porous, 90% carbon solid that makes the blast furnace possible, and it is also the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, manganese, ferrochrome and ferrosilicon furnaces. A tonne of coke is roughly 70% of the fuel and 30% of the reductant in a blast furnace charge, and nothing works without it. By 1982 the coke oven was a mature and much-diagnosed industry: the air pollution from coking, and the fact that a coke oven is the largest single source of coal tar and benzene in the industrial world, were the reasons the Clean Air Act of 1970 and its amendments hit coal and coke first.

###### Coking coal, caking and prime coking blends `metal.coking-coal`

Not any coal: a blend of coals that fuse and solidify into a coherent cellular cake when heated. The caking power comes from the vitrinite, and the best coking coal is a low-volatile, medium-bituminous coal that goes plastic around 350-450 C. The 1982 sources were the Appalachian basin (the US steel industry ran on Appalachian coal shipped up the Great Lakes and the Mississippi), the Ruhr, the Donbass, the Kuzbass, the Bowen Basin in Queensland, and the Gondwana coals of India, which are so low in caking power that India had to import coking coal to make coke for its own steel - a good illustration of how coal rank, not just coal carbon, is the relevant property.

###### Longwall coal mine at 300-1000 m `metal.coal-mine`

A coking coal mine in 1982 was almost always a mechanised longwall: a shearer cuts a 1.5-3 m thick seam across the face, the roof is allowed to collapse, the coal is loaded onto a pan chain conveyor and a main belt carries it to a preparation plant and up the shaft. The seam is a few metres thick, so the mine is a thin dark ribbon of coal a kilometre wide. Pennsylvania, the Ruhr and the Kuzbass are the three great coking coal provinces, and they are the geological reason those three places have both the coke ovens and the blast furnaces - the coal is too bulky to ship, so the steel industry grows where the coal is.

###### Bituminous coal seam (Middle and Lower Kittanning) `metal.coking-coal.seam`

The leaf: a 2-3 m band of bright, banded, caking bituminous coal lying within a cyclothemic sequence of sandstone, shale and fireclay - the same sequence that holds the Pennsylvanian iron ore, coal and limestone together in the Appalachian basin, and the reason Pittsburgh is the steel capital of America. The Kittanning and the Freeport seams were the premium coking coals; the coal is Carboniferous, about 320 million years old, and it was deposited in a swamp.

###### Coal preparation: crushing, washing, blending `metal.coal-preparation`

Run-of-mine coking coal is crushed to under 50 mm and washed, because the ash that matters is the mineral matter - clay bands and pyritic nodules - that can be taken off by a dense-media wash at about 1.4-1.6 specific gravity. The washed coal then goes to a blending yard, because a coke oven wants a consistent blend and no single seam is consistent. Blending is done by a stacker-reclaimer in a yard, and the recipe is a metallurgical decision that is still made on the basis of the dilatation and the sulphur.

###### The wash plant tailings and the creek `metal.coal-tailings` _(medium)_

The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures - the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people - were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.

###### The valley fill and the contour mine `metal.valley-fill` _(medium)_

The deep end of coal preparation's waste problem. In a contour mine the seam outcrops along a hillside, the coal is taken off along the contour and the overburden is pushed into the valley below, so the terrain ends up as a stream of grey waste from the highwall to the toe. It is cheap mining - no stripping, no trucks - and it is the reason the Appalachian coalfield has a hundred kilometres of dead grey creeks. In 1982 the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 required the mine to backfill and revegetate, with a bond per tonne, and that is the direct ancestor of the reclamation practices that the rest of the extractive industries adopted later.

###### The wash plant tailings and the creek `metal.coal.tailings` _(medium)_

The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures - the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people - were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.

###### Coking in a battery of by-product ovens `metal.coke.oven`

Two hundred and fifty horizontal chambers, 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide and 3.5-5 m high, arranged in a brick battery 40-100 m long, heated in the flues between them by coke oven gas and reheated to 1100-1300 C. A charging car pushes 20-30 tonnes of crushed coal through a hopper into each chamber in about 30 seconds; the chambers are then sealed, and 16-20 hours later the doors are opened and the red-hot coke is pushed out by a pusher machine onto a quenching car. That cycle, 16-24 hours, is the heartbeat of the plant and it never stops. In the meantime the gas coming off the coal - the raw coal gas, typically 15-20% hydrogen, 20-25% methane, 15-20% CO, 5% CO2, 20-30% nitrogen - has been drawn off, cooled, and cleaned of tar and ammonia.

###### Coke quenching: wet and dry `metal.coke.quenching`

The coke comes out of the oven at 1000-1100 C and must be cooled fast or it will keep burning. Wet quenching sprays it with 3-4 m of water in a 30-60 s tower; the water flashes to steam, the coke is cooled to about 200 C and comes out wet with 3-8% moisture, which the blast furnace operator hates. Dry quenching pushes the coke into a sealed horizontal chamber and cools it with nitrogen or recirculated coke-oven gas. In 1982 nearly every coke plant in the world was wet, and the change to dry came later, mostly driven by the same air-pollution regulation that hit the oven itself.

###### Quenching, the coke breeze and the drain `metal.coke.quench-blow` _(medium)_

Quenching has three products, not one: the coke, the water with the fine carbon in it, and the coke breeze - the 3-10 mm fraction that the blast furnace cannot use because it would be blown through the burden. Breeze is worth something: a coke plant sells it for sinter-plant fuel, for foundry moulding sand, and in 1982 increasingly for the electrode and anode pitch trade as a cheap carbon filler. So the coke oven's smallest product feeds three of the other branches in this file, and the water carries 1-3 kg of suspended carbon per tonne of coke quenched.

###### Coke oven gas and its by-products `metal.coke.gas`

The gas is the profit centre as well as the fuel. After cooling it goes through a primary cooler and a benzol washer, which strips out benzene, toluene and xylenes; then a saturator removes tar and ammonia; then a Quinolining or electrostatic precipitator removes the last of the dust. What is left is coke oven gas, which is burnt in the battery flues to supply exactly the heat the ovens need - the plant is roughly self-sufficient - and the surplus goes to the steelworks as fuel and to a chemical works as a benzene and ammonia feedstock. Crude benzene from the benzol washer is one of the most valuable by-products in the plant, and it is where the aromatic chemistry of the plastics agent's chain starts.

###### Crude benzene from the coke oven `metal.benzene`

A 1982 coke oven produced a very large fraction of the world's synthetic benzene, and benzene was the root of the styrene-polystyrene, phenol-formaldehyde and epoxy industries - so this node is where the coal branch and the plastics branch join. The benzol was drawn out of the oven gas with a wash oil, and the wash oil was then steam-stripped. It is a dense, sweet-smelling, carcinogenic liquid and it is a document about the chemical industry that produced nylon, epoxy resin, phenol formaldehyde resin, styrene, and polyurethane precursors all at once.

###### The quench tower and the coke push `metal.coke.quench-tower` _(medium)_

The physical heart of the battery: a tall steel tower with spray nozzles fed by a 300 mm main, a receiving pan, and a surge hopper from which a 2-3 m pusher car pushes the cooled coke onto a belt. Behind it stands the battery, bricked with about 20,000 refractory bricks per oven chamber in the modern design and castable in the older one, all of which has to survive 1300 C cycling every twenty hours forever. The doors are the coke-side door on top and the charging door below, and the charging machinery is driven by a single large winch.

###### Coal tar and pitch: the binder under everything `metal.coke.tar-pitch`

The tar that comes off a coke oven condenses as a dense black liquid, and it is the source of three of the most important carbonaceous materials in this file. Distilled, it gives crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and pitch - the binder in the carbon anode, the coke-battery electrode, the extrusion die lubricant and the aluminium pot lining. A tonne of coke gives roughly 30-50 kg of crude tar, and a tonne of that tar gives a few tens of kilos of soft pitch. So the coke oven is upstream of the aluminium pot, the coke battery and the graphite electrode, and the carbon-anode branch of this file is not an independent industry at all - it is the coke oven's tar still.

###### Soft pitch and hard pitch `metal.soft-pitch` _(medium)_

Pitch is classified by softening point: soft pitch around 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard pitch above 110 C. The carbon anode wants a medium-to-hard pitch for the extrusion binder; the pot lining wants a softer grade that can be rammed hot. Pitch is also a dense, black, aromatic, carcinogenic material that has to be kept hot at every stage, so the anode plants had their own pitch melting and storage tanks. It is one of the dirtiest materials in the metals tree and one of the least replaceable.

###### Crude coal tar and creosote `metal.coke.tar` _(medium)_

The tar is separated into a light fraction (benzol wash oil and crude benzene), a middle fraction of heavy oils used as a coking-plant quench medium and a wood preservative, and a heavy pitch fraction. Creosote as a wood preservative is a genuinely large market and it is the same molecule family as the pentachlorophenol and the coal-tar pitch that the board and case coatings used. So the coke branch of this tree touches the plastics, the coatings and the timber-preservation branches as well as the metals one.

###### Pitch as an anode binder: the full loop `metal.pitch.from-pitch`

Putting the carbon branch together as one loop. Coal is distilled for rosin and turpentine on one side and for tar and pitch on the other; the pitch becomes the binder in the carbon anode, which becomes aluminium; the coke from the same oven becomes the fuel for the silica reduction that becomes the metallurgical silicon that becomes the polysilicon; the coke breeze becomes the sinter plant's fuel; and the benzene becomes the styrene and the phenol and the epoxy resin. One oven on a 1982 coking plant therefore feeds at least six branches of this tree, and it is the single most connected node in the file after the quartzite.

###### Carbon anode for the Hall-Heroult cell `metal.carbon.anode`

Calcined petroleum coke at 90-95% carbon, ground to 1-20 mm, mixed with 25-30% of crushed and baked coke returns and 25-30% coal-tar pitch as the binder, extruded through a die with a threaded stud on the end, and roasted at 1000-1100 C for 20-30 hours. The point of roasting rather than baking is to drive the volatiles out before the anode goes into the cell, because an anode that gases in the pot poisons the metal. Consumption is 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium, and the anode is consumed continuously - which is what makes aluminium smelting a carbon business as much as an electrochemical one.

                              - *Crude benzene from the coke oven* `metal.benzene` *(seen above)*
                              - *Soft pitch and hard pitch* `metal.soft-pitch` *(seen above)*
###### The battery, its flue and the chimney `metal.coke.battery`

A coke battery is a long brick building - 50-100 ovens in a row, 40-60 m long, with a 60-70 m chimney at one end and a quenching tower at the other. Between every pair of ovens is a heating flue, so there are twice as many flues as ovens, and the gas from the ovens is burned in those flues and the hot gas is then drawn up the chimney. The chimney is the tall thing on the coke works skyline, and it is there for the combustion products, not for a draft. A battery is a piece of 1880s engineering that has been continuously rebuilt ever since and is essentially the same machine today.

###### The cold-strip push and the bench `metal.coke.cold-strip` _(medium)_

The hottest, ugliest machine in the coking plant: a horizontal bar on a chain, 3-5 m long, permanently red, that pushes red coke out of the chambers onto the collecting bench. Its life is measured in weeks and its water-cooling is the operator's main concern. Everyone who worked on a battery in the 1980s had a job that was hot enough to need its own PPE rotation, which is the reason the whole industry has a 'coke oven man' occupational category and a very specific set of burn scars.

###### Continuous casting and the Goss texture formation `metal.electrical-steel.casting` _(medium)_

Electrical steel is continuously cast, hot rolled, and then given the two anneals that make it grain-oriented. The first, at 800-1100 C, is an ordinary recrystallisation anneal in wet hydrogen; the second, at 1100-1200 C, is the orientation anneal, in which the steel is held just below the Curie point in a magnetic field aligned with the rolling direction so the alpha-iron grains with their [110] axis along the field grow preferentially. The second anneal takes a week or more in a hydrogen atmosphere, which is why GOES costs three or four times what mild sheet costs and why a C64's transformer was one of the most expensive parts in it.

                  - *AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel* `metal.stainless.304` *(seen above)*
###### Tool steel: SKD61 / H13 / D2, the moulds and dies `metal.die-steel`

The C64's case, the keycaps, the key plungers and the disk-drive and modulator housings were all made in injection-moulding dies, and every one of those dies and every aluminium extrusion die was cut from tool steel. SKD61 in Japan and H13 in the US and DIN X40CrMoV51 in Europe are the same alloy: 5% chromium, 5% molybdenum, 1% vanadium, 0.4% carbon, air-hardening to about 50-54 HRC. It is made in a small vacuum arc or vacuum induction furnace, forged, annealed, and then given three heat treatments - austenitising at 1000-1050 C, air cooling, and double tempering at 500-550 C - before it goes near the machine. A single C64 case die weighs 1-4 tonnes and cost tens of thousands of dollars, and it is the reason the tool steel branch is in this file at all.

###### Molybdenum: a tool steel alloying element `metal.molybdenum` _(medium)_

Molybdenum is in the tool steel, in the stainless and in the hydrodesulphurisation catalyst, so it belongs in this tree, but its own branch is short because in 1982 almost no molybdenum came from a molybdenum mine: about half came from the molybdenite recovered as a by-product of the porphyry copper concentrators, where it is a few hundred ppm of the concentrate and reports to a separate flotation circuit, and the other half came as molybdic oxide from roasting. The ore is molybdenite, MoS2, in the Climax and Henderson porphyry in Colorado and in the Bingham Canyon concentrate. The leaf is a porphyry or a granite vein.

###### Molybdenite in a porphyry `metal.molybdenite`

Soft, greasy, platy flakes of MoS2 in the quartz and feldspar of a granitic porphyry, associated with the copper minerals of the Climax and Henderson molybdenum operations or with the Bingham copper concentrate. The leaf is the same porphyry intrusion the copper branch ends in, which is a genuine shared endpoint.

###### Scheelite and wolframite: the limestone vein alternative `metal.molybdenum.scheelite` _(low)_

Almost all molybdenum came from porphyry copper, but there is a second source: the molybdenite that sits in the tungsten skarn and vein deposits - the Climax and Henderson molybdenum orebodies in Colorado were actually a Colorado Clueca-type porphyry with a molybdenum-bearing skarn. The relevant geology is that molybdenum and tungsten share the hydrothermal vein environment, and scheelite (CaWO4) and molybdenite (MoS2) are sometimes intergrown in the same greisen. So the molybdenum in a C64's injection-moulding die could in principle have come out of the same vein as a tungsten electrode - which is the point the brief made when it said no tungsten in a 1982 C64, and this is where that fact becomes interesting: the tungsten was there, in the same rock, but it went into other industries.

###### Vanadium: a small alloying element `metal.vanadium` _(medium)_

Included only because tool steel and the AOD of stainless steel both use it, and because the source is genuinely unusual. Most vanadium came from vanadiferous titanomagnetite - a magnetite containing 1-6% vanadium - which was a problem in the iron ore of the Panzhihua district in China and in the U.S. and Canadian Mesabi ranges until somebody worked out how to separate it. By 1982 the US route was slag processing: the titanomagnetite went into a blast furnace or an oxygen converter, and the vanadium reported to the slag, and the slag was ground and reprocessed. The other source is spent petroleum catalyst, which by the late 1980s was a genuine and growing vanadium source. Both of those are consequences of processes elsewhere in this tree.

###### Vanadiferous titanomagnetite `metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite`

The leaf: a magnetite with the iron partly replaced by titanium and vanadium, occurring as an iron ore in itself. At Panzhihua it is a magnetite-ilmenite ore in a vanadium-bearing magnetite gabbro; in the Mesabi it was a nuisance component of the taconite. Either way it is an iron ore, and the vanadium is a consequence of somebody mining iron.

###### Vacuum melting and the purity of tool steel `metal.die-steel.vacuum` _(medium)_

A tool steel that contains a hundred parts per million of sulphur will embrittle, and one with two hundred ppm of oxygen will pit. So the melt for a die is made in a vacuum induction or a vacuum arc furnace rather than in an air-melted crucible, and the ingot is remelted by the VAR or the EB process - electron beam - which gives a fine equiaxed grain with no inclusions and no segregation. The vacuum arc furnace is a modified version of the vacuum-arc remelting process that the titanium industry invented, and by 1982 the extrusion die industry and the mould industry both bought them.

###### Continuous cast slab and hot rolling `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.castroll`

The molten steel is cast continuously into a 200-300 mm slab through a water-cooled mould with electromagnetic stirring, then hot rolled on a reversing mill straight down to 2-4 mm. The surface is descaled with high-pressure water or a mill scale breaker, and the strip is coiled.

                - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Base anneal `c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.goes.upstream.baseanneal`

Hot-rolled low-carbon steel is coiled and annealed in a bell or stack furnace at 650-800 C, then pickled in dilute hydrochloric acid to remove mill scale and, if it is to become oriented steel, cold rolled and given the hydrogen magnetic anneal described above.

##### Core stack assembly and clamping `c64.psu.transformer.core.stack`

E and I plates are stacked in alternating layers with the joints staggered so no section of the stack has an unbroken air gap, then clamped end to end by angle plates and bolts or by rivets through the yoke. The joints are the dominant core loss, so the assembler has to keep the interleaving sequence right by hand.

###### Clamp bolts and angle plates `c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.clamp-hardware` _(medium)_

Mild steel angle plates bolted across the yokes, or two long tie bolts through the core legs, with the axial clamp force chosen so the interlaminar pressure is roughly 3-10 kg/mm2 - enough to stop the stack buzzing at 50 Hz, not so much that the punched edges crack.

            - *Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel* `metal.steel` *(seen above)*
##### MnZn ferrite E-core alternative `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative` _(medium)_

Later Commodore bricks and the C64C/Plus4 supplies switched to a pressed manganese-zinc ferrite core. Ferrite has much higher resistivity than silicon steel so it can be used as a solid moulded shape with no lamination joints, giving lower core loss at 60 Hz and a much lighter assembly - at several times the material cost, and with a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill.

          - *Ferrite: transformer and choke cores* `metal.ferrite` *(seen above)*
###### MnZn ferrite powder blend `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.powder`

A pre-mixed powder of iron oxide, manganese oxide and zinc oxide, ball-milled to a few microns. Zinc raises the resistivity and pushes the useful frequency band up; manganese lowers the magnetostriction and kills the 50 Hz mechanical buzz that would otherwise be audible inside the C64.

###### Manganese ore and oxide `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.powder.manganese-ore` _(medium)_

South African 'Highveld' or Gabon Gabon-type manganite is roasted and reduced to manganese oxide, then used as the fluxing component of the blend. Manganese is what gives MnZn its low magnetostriction.

###### Ore roasting `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.powder.manganese-ore.roasting` _(medium)_

MnO2 ore is roasted in a fluid-bed or shaft furnace at 700-1000 C, driving off moisture and converting the higher oxides, then the product is leached or carbon-reduced.

###### Zinc concentrate `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.powder.zinc-ore` _(medium)_

Sphalerite flotation concentrate from a zinc mine, roasted to zinc oxide then reduced in an Imperial Smelting furnace or electrolytically to zinc metal or zinc oxide. The oxide goes straight into the ferrite blend.

###### Iron oxide base `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.powder.iron-oxide` _(medium)_

High-purity ferric oxide, made by roasting hematite ore or by precipitating iron hydroxide from pickling acid, is the majority component of the blend.

###### Dry pressing and sintering the E-core `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.press-sinter`

The powder is mixed with 1-3% PVA or PVA/PVP binder plus a lubricant, granulated, uniaxially dry pressed in a steel die to the E shape, then fired in a continuous tunnel kiln in air or oxygen. Sintering closes the pores and the core shrinks several percent, so the tooling is deliberately oversize and the part is ground to final dimensions afterwards.

###### PVA granulation binder `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.press-sinter.binder`

Polyvinyl alcohol, made by hydrolyzing polyvinyl acetate (or by polymerising vinyl acetate) in water, gives the pressed blank enough green strength to be handled without crumbling. The organic burns out completely during the firing, which is why the finished ferrite has an open pore structure.

###### Vinyl acetate monomer `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.press-sinter.binder.vinyl-acetate`

Made by addition of acetic acid to ethylene in the presence of a palladium catalyst at 150-200 C and 10-60 bar; the acetic acid comes from methanol carbonylation of carbon monoxide. Vinyl acetate is the monomer for PVA, polyvinyl acetate and polyvinyl chloride.

                - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
                - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Sintered core grinding `c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative.press-sinter.grinding` _(medium)_

The sintered E is diamond or carbide-wheel ground on the mating faces and the outer leg so the stack closes properly. The 1980s alternative to this was a lapped or as-pressed core, which is why cheap cores had audible air gaps.

#### Enamelled copper winding `c64.psu.transformer.winding`

The primary, the 18 V centre-tapped secondary and the 9 V output secondary are wound in layers on a moulded bobbin, with a few hundred turns of 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper wire. Layer insulation between each pass and interleaved padding between the primary and the secondaries carry the 1000-1500 V RMS of the mains.

##### Enamelled magnet wire `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire`

Bare copper rod drawn down to 0.25-0.4 mm through a series of tungsten-carbide or diamond dies, then coated in two or more passes of a thermosetting enamel - typically polyester-imide (Grade 2 / THEIC) - and baked to cure it. Each coat adds roughly 5-10 um, so a double-grade wire has 25-40% more copper per given window area than bare wire.

          - *Wire drawing* `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing` *(seen above)*
###### Polyester-imide enamel coating `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel`

The wire runs continuously through a die-casting oven where a 25-30% solids solution of the modified polyester-imide resin in cresol/xylene is applied, then through a 350-450 C curing oven, and through the same pair again for a second coat. The thermal cure crosslinks the resin to a hard film that resists varnish, oil and coolant.

###### Polyester-imide resin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.resin`

The workhorse magnet-wire enamel of the 1980s. The base is a polycondensation of dimethyl terephthalate (or trimellitic anhydride) with polyols; the imide is introduced with a polyamide of trimellitic anhydride and a diamine such as ethylenediamine, which is what raises the class to H (180 C).

###### Trimellitic anhydride feedstock `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.resin.trimellitic-anhydride` _(medium)_

The 1980s industrial route to trimellitic anhydride was liquid-phase air oxidation of pseudocumene (1,2,4-trimethylbenzene), which is itself a product of the catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction of petroleum naphtha. The 1980s chemistry is what makes this enamel a petroleum-derived product rather than a coal-tar one.

                - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
                - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Copper feedstock `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.copper-feedstock`

Wire rod copper begins as blister copper from a copper smelter-flour mill, which begins as copper sulphide concentrate.

###### Copper concentrate (chalcopyrite) `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.copper-feedstock.concentrate`

Froth flotation of a porphyry copper ore, typically 20-40% Cu. The concentrate is smelted in a flash furnace to a 50-70% copper matte, converted in a converter to blister copper at 1250-1300 C, and cast.

###### Porphyry copper ore `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.copper-feedstock.ore`

The run-of-mine ore is a heavily disseminated sulphide system in an igneous intrusion. It is mined by open pit or block caving, crushed, and ground in SAG and ball mills to about 50-70% passing 100 microns so that the collector can float the sulphides.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
              - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Froth flotation `c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.copper-feedstock.ore.flotation`

The ground ore is mixed with reagents - a xanthate collector, a frother such as pine oil or MIBC, and a depressant for iron sulphides - and air is blown through a bank of cells. The sulphide particles adhere to the rising bubbles and are carried off as froth, while the gangue falls to the bottom. Recovery on a porphyry concentrate in the 1980s was 80-90% with a concentrate grade of 20-40% copper.

                - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
                - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
##### Moulded nylon bobbin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin`

A spool-shaped coil former in glass-filled or unfilled nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, with cheek flanges that locate it on the core leg and a continuous slot that keeps the layer insulation in place. Bobbins were (and still are) a Miles-Platts product line, which fits the 'MP' mark found on this transformer.

###### Nylon 6 (polycaprolactam) `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.nylon`

The older and cheaper of the two bobbins materials. Kaprolactam is made by the Beckmann rearrangement of cyclohexanone, which itself comes from the catalytic air oxidation of cyclohexane, which comes from benzene hydrogenation, which comes from toluene or from a naphtha cracker.

###### Benzene from petroleum `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.nylon.benzene`

The 1980s route to benzene was catalytic reforming of naphtha (a C6-C8 fraction of crude) over platinum on alumina at 450-520 C, which aromatises the naphthenes and paraffins; benzene is then separated by extractive distillation with sulfolane or n-heptane. A minority came from coal-tar benzene well into the 1980s.

              - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Injection moulding the bobbin `c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.moulding`

Nylon is hygroscopic so the pellets are dried at 80 C for 4-8 h before moulding, then injection moulded at 240-280 C into a multi-cavity tool with hot runners and a mould temperature of 60-90 C. The mould cavity is polished because a flash of loose fibre on the winding slot would be a turn-coat defect.

##### Layer and interwinding insulation `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation`

Crepe paper or glass-cloth tape between winding layers, a wide kraft or composite tape wrap between the primary and the secondaries, and in the potted builds strips of polyimide (Kapton) film around the whole winding. The 1983-84 bricks visibly used masking tape on the core yoke edges and something like Kapton over the coil to keep the epoxy pour off the windings.

###### Crepe paper insulation `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper`

A lightly crinkled, unbleached kraft paper that stretches to follow the winding contour without bunching. Made on a Fourdrinier machine from a dilute suspension of long-fibre softwood pulp.

###### Mechanical wood pulp `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper.pulp`

Softwood (spruce/fir) is debarked, chipped, steamed and refined in a disc or refiner mill; the long fibres are ideal for electrical insulation paper because they give high dielectric strength and mechanical strength in the thin sheet.

###### Process water and whitewater `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper.pulp.water`

Paper machines consume enormous volumes of water: several tonnes per tonne of pulp, treated at the mill with alum, rosin and starch, then clarified in a primary settling basin and recirculated.

                - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Softwood pulp `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.crepe-paper.pulp.softwood`

The species matters as much as the process: long-fibre softwood pulp from spruce, fir or pine gives the dielectric strength and tear resistance that electrical insulation paper needs, while hardwood pulp from birch or aspen gives opacity and printability and is used in the thinner papers. Softwood is bought as chips or as market pulp.

                - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
###### Glass-cloth insulation tape `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.glass-cloth`

Woven E-glass yarn cloth, ~0.1 mm thick, silane-sized for adhesion, wound in the last layer before the outer tape. Glass has no moisture absorption and much higher dielectric strength than paper, which is why the safety-approved design puts it nearest the primary.

###### E-glass fibre from molten glass `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.glass-cloth.fibre`

A sand/coke/limestone batch is melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C, drawn into bushings, and attenuated with air and water jets into 3-20 um filaments, then sized with silane and a PVA size. The filaments are gathered into rovings, then woven on a rapier loom into cloth.

              - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
              - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
              - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Polyimide (Kapton) film `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.kapton`

A 12-25 um amber polyimide film used as the barrier between the coil and the epoxy pour and, in later builds, as the layer insulation. Its value is that it does not soften, dissolve or outgas in a hot epoxy cure.

###### Pyromellitic dianhydride monomer `c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.kapton.pyromellitic-dianhydride`

The diacid anhydride half of Kapton is made by air oxidation of pseudocumene to trimellitic acid and then dehydrating it - a petroleum-aromatics chain. The diamine half is 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine, both aromatics intermediates.

              - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
        - *Interwinding earth screen* `c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen` *(seen above)*
##### Layer winding on a coil winder `c64.psu.transformer.winding.process`

A single-spindle or two-spindle coil winder turns the bobbin while traversing the wire, and the operator lays interleaved insulation between each layer with a slow-moving 'paper feeder'. Bobbin layers are counter-wound to flatten the coil, and the leads are brought out through the bobbin flange and dressed so they cannot chafe on the core.

###### Lead termination and crimped flag terminals `c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.lead-termination` _(medium)_

The winding leads are soldered or, in the 1983-84 bricks, soldered directly to the transformer's own pins; the line cord and interwinding conductors terminate in tin-plated brass crimp flags. Under the epoxy pour the crimps are the weak link - they can anneal and let go - and the PVC of the line cord is visibly browned right at the pin.

            - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
##### Polyester varnish impregnation and oven cure `c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation`

The finished assembly is vacuum impregnated with a thermosetting polyester or epoxy varnish so the winding becomes a solid block and cannot move at 50 Hz. Viscous impregnating varnishes were standard by the early 1980s; the alternative is dip-and-bake in an epoxy or a polyurethane.

###### Impregnating varnish `c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.varnish`

A low-viscosity, high-solids unsaturated polyester resin dissolved in styrene, with an organic peroxide cure catalyst. It cures by crosslinking rather than by solvent loss, so it shrinks very little and fills completely.

###### Styrene monomer `c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.varnish.styrene`

Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene, which is made by alkylating benzene with ethylene. Again a petroleum-aromatics chain.

              - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
#### Transformer pin terminal board `c64.psu.transformer.pinboard`

A row of brass pins on a small phenolic or nylon board carrying the primary, the interwinding earth, and all the secondary taps. The rectifier diodes and fuses in the 1983-84 bricks are soldered straight onto these pins, which is why the schematic 'terminals' that appear in a teardown are the transformer's own pins rather than a separate board.

##### Phenolic laminate board `c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic`

Paper or cotton-linen web impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin under heat and pressure. Cheap, dimensionally stable and self-extinguishing, which is why it was the default material for transformer terminal boards and fuseholders.

###### Phenol-formaldehyde resin `c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic.resin`

Condensation polymerisation of phenol with formaldehyde, catalysed by acid or base, typically 6-9 phenol to 1 formaldehyde. Phenol itself was made in the 1980s by cumene hydroperoxide cleavage from the cumene/propylene-aromatics complex, so this too is a co-product of petroleum refining.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
#### Transformer final test `c64.psu.transformer.test`

Every wound transformer is tested before it is potted or assembled: a 1500-2500 V AC dielectric withstand between primary and all secondaries, an insulation-resistance check, turns-ratio and phasing checks between the taps, and a loaded run at nominal line voltage to check regulation and temperature rise. A transformer that passes can still be potted badly, which is exactly what Commodore did.

### Rectifier diodes, 400GI / 1N5400 `c64.psu.rectifier`

Two or four stud-less axial rectifier diodes convert the 18 V centre-tapped secondary into pulsating DC. The 902503-02 uses two General Electric 400GI silicon rectifiers in a full-wave centre-tapped configuration, which saves the two extra dice of a bridge; other builds use four 1N5400s or a moulded bridge. The diodes are soldered directly onto the transformer pins.

#### Axial rectifier diode `c64.psu.rectifier.diode`

A single silicon junction in an axial package with a formed lead, cathode band marked with a stripe. Inside: a die a few hundred microns across with a heavy anode metallisation, a glass passivation, and epoxy or a voidless glass body filled with silicone stress-relief gel to survive the power cycling.

##### Silicon rectifier die `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die`

A 100-150 mm wafer ground to a die typically 2 x 2 x 0.3 mm, with a diffused N-type cathode and metallised anode. The same Czochralski silicon as the VIC-II and the 6510; the detailed wafer process belongs to the silicon branch of this tree.

###### Silicon metal from quartz `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die.silicon-feedstock`

The only starting point is high-purity quartz. Coke and quartz are carbothermically reduced in an arc furnace at 1800-2000 C to 97-99% metallurgical-grade silicon, then upgraded in a bed-type fluidised reactor to 9-11N (99.9999999%) polycrystalline silicon by trichlorosilane disproportionation or silane decomposition, which is the material pulled into a single Czochralski crystal, sawn into wafers, and polished.

###### High-purity quartz (SiO2) `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die.silicon-feedstock.quartz`

Quartz is dug from pegmatite or high-purity veins, crushed and acid-leached, then hydrothermally or flame fused to remove the last few ppm of aluminium, boron and iron. The semiconductor industry needs 99.99%+ SiO2 as the feed to the arc furnace.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
###### Die attach, wire bond and axial encapsulation `c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging`

The die is die-attached to the anode lead with silver-loaded glass or a soft solder, one or two aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the cathode metallisation to the cathode lead, then the whole assembly is transfer-moulded or cast in an epoxy body filled with silicone gel to relieve the thermal cycle between the glass and the leads.

            - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
##### Moulded bridge rectifier alternative `c64.psu.rectifier.bridge-alternative`

Some builds and most replacement supplies use a packaged bridge: four dice mounted on a common ceramic or moulded body with the terminals formed into the four corners. Commodore's own choice of two discrete diodes over a bridge saved two dice and one package, at the cost of a centre tap on the transformer.

### 5 V linear voltage regulator `c64.psu.regulator`

The pass element that turns roughly 8-10 V of pulsating DC into 5.00 V. Three different implementations appear in C64 bricks inside two years, and the choice of which one determines how much heat has to be removed. At full load the drop across the pass device is 3-5 V at 1.5 A, so 4.5-7.5 W has to go into the heatsink - which is why these supplies run hot and why the electrolytics above them cook.

#### 7805-class three-pin regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-7805`

The simplest form: a monolithic regulator containing the reference, error amplifier, current limit and the pass transistor, in a TO-220 or TO-3P-like plastic body with a tab bolted to the heatsink. In the 251053-02 brick it is a three-legged part with rectangular legs, screwed straight into the folded aluminium plate under a blob of epoxy.

#### Sanken SI-3052P integrated regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p`

The regulator in the later 902503-02, which many hobbyists misidentify as a transistor because it is moulded in a TO-3P-looking package. It is a 5 V / 2 A linear regulator with an internal error amplifier and a foldback current limit that kicks in at about 2.4 A. The datasheet explicitly warns that the output must not be raised by inserting a resistor in the ground pin - and Commodore inserted a 300 Ohm resistor in the ground pin anyway, to make up for the drop in the output cable.

##### Output stability capacitor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.stability-cap`

A small electrolytic or tantalum directly across the regulator's input and output pins. The datasheet requires it for loop stability; a 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum appears on some 902503-02 builds and the 3-83 version has the holes for it but does not populate it, which suggests it was a late cost change.

#### Discrete 2N3055 / 2N3792 series-pass regulator `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete` _(medium)_

The earliest 'repairable' silver-label brick used a discrete design: an NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can bolted to a heatsink as the series pass, a smaller driver transistor, a zener or low-current regulator as the reference, wirewound resistors in the emitter and base for current limiting, and a thermal shutdown in contact with the heatsink. It is the arrangement the 902503-02's monolithic regulator replaced.

##### 2N3055 / 2N3792 power NPN `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn`

A triple-diffused planar NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can: a bolted metal header with an isolation disc, the die brazed or soldered to the header, one or two emitter bonds, and a hermetic can with a glass-sealed pin feedthrough. The 2N3055 is grossly oversized for a 1.5 A load (15 A, 60 V, 115 W dissipation capability), which is exactly why it was chosen: it could not fail thermally even when the circuit was badly designed.

###### Triple-diffused planar process `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.triple-diffusion`

Three sequential dopings - collector-base, base-emitter, and a deep collector-emitter - through a photolithographically masked oxide. The heavy collector-emitter diffusion carries the load current while the shallow, tightly controlled base-emitter diffusion sets the gain and the breakdown voltage. This is the process that made 15 A transistors possible at all.

###### Die attach and hermetic TO-3 sealing `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.die-attach`

The die is brazed to the header in a hydrogen atmosphere at 700-800 C with an active-metal braze, or soldered with a 50Pb-50Sn or AuSn preform at 220-300 C; the header is then nickel-plated. The can is crimped or cold-welded onto the header with an annular glass or ceramic feedthrough insulator; mica or a thin mica-fibre washer goes between the can and the heatsink to isolate the collector while conducting heat.

            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
            - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Emitter wire bonds `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-npn.wire-bond`

Two to four 100-200 um aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the emitter metallisation to the emitter lead to carry the full emitter current; the collector current flows through the die's back contact straight into the header. Ultrasonic wedge bonding at 50-250 g per wire was the universal method - ball bonding was for fine-pitch.

            - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
