##### Driver / error-amplifier transistor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.driver` _(medium)_

A small-signal NPN whose job is to supply the ~0.7 V of base drive plus the feedback signal the pass transistor needs. In a 1982 discrete supply this is typically a TO-92 part with hFE around 100-400, or one half of a matched pair. Its collector dissipation is small but its junction temperature is close to the pass transistor's, so it shares the same heatsink metal.

##### Voltage reference `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.reference` _(medium)_

In a 1982 discrete supply the reference is either a 5.1-6.2 V zener diode biased from a constant-current source, or a low-current three-terminal regulator such as a TL431 or a small 7805 in a TO-92 used purely as a reference. The zener route needs a stable bias current; the temperature coefficient of an ordinary zener is poor, which shows up as output drift with case temperature.

          - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
##### Emitter ballast resistors `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitter-ballast` _(medium)_

One to three wirewound resistors in series with the pass transistor's emitter. Their purpose is to develop a signal proportional to output current for current limiting and to force a standing current through the pass transistor so its hFE and therefore the loop gain do not collapse at light load. Wirewound rather than film because the dissipation is fractional watts but the temperature rise has to stay small.

###### Manganin wire `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitter-ballast.manganin-wire`

A copper-manganese-nickel alloy (typically 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni) whose resistivity barely changes with temperature. A spiral-wound wirewound resistor is made by winding manganin or constantan wire onto a ceramic or plastic former and baking it under high tension so the winding stress-relaxes and stays against the form.

            - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
            - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
##### Thermal shutdown `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.thermal-shutdown` _(medium)_

A temperature-sensitive element in contact with the heatsink - a thermistor or a bimetallic thermal switch - that shorts or removes the driver bias when the sink passes roughly 90-110 C, so the supply folds back rather than destroying itself. Commodore's bricks more often relied on a thermal fuse in the primary and on the epoxy pot for heat retention, which is the root of their reputation.

###### NTC thermistor `c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.thermal-shutdown.thermistor`

A bead or disc of semiconducting metal oxide whose resistance falls steeply with temperature (10 kOhm at 25 C, ~1 kOhm at 100 C for the standard 10K curve). Glued or bolted to the heatsink and shunting the driver bias, it gives a soft, non-resetting protection that must cool before it re-conducts.

            - *Ferrite: transformer and choke cores* `metal.ferrite` *(seen above)*
#### Bolting the regulator to the heatsink `c64.psu.regulator.mounting`

The regulator tab or TO-3 can is bolted to the folded aluminium plate with a thin layer of thermal compound - in 1982 typically a zinc-oxide paste in a silicone or hydrocarbon base, or sometimes simply a piece of thin copper foil. The thermal interface matters more than the compound brand: dry metal-to-metal contact is roughly ten times worse than a properly filled joint.

### Folded aluminium heatsink `c64.psu.heatsink`

A thin aluminium plate folded into a U so that one leg clamps under the case and the other presents an area against the regulator. There are no fins: the design relies on the natural convection of a brick sitting under a desk. It is the reason the case runs at 60-70 C and the epoxy never fully cools.

#### Sheet folding and tapping `c64.psu.heatsink.forming`

Strip or sheet is blanked, then folded on a press brake to a U; the mounting hole is punched or drilled and tapped with a thread-forming tap. Aluminium's low modulus means the fold must be given a generous inside radius or the sheet tears, and the tapped hole must be at least 1.5 diameters from the bend.

#### Aluminium sheet and its ore `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock`

Commercial-purity aluminium sheet is made from an electrolytic ingot of 99.0-99.7% aluminium, which is refined from alumina dissolved in cryolite.

##### Smelter-grade alumina `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.alumina`

Aluminium oxide obtained by the Bayer process from bauxite. The ore is crushed, digested in hot caustic soda under pressure, the insoluble red mud is separated by settling, and alumina is precipitated from the clarified sodium aluminate by cooling and seeding, then calcined at 1000-1100 C.

###### Bauxite `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.alumina.bauxite`

The aluminium ore, 30-60% Al2O3 with up to 50% Fe2O3 and SiO2, dug from tropical laterite and bauxite terraces. This is the leaf of the aluminium chain.

###### Bauxite mining and washing `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.alumina.bauxite.mining`

Bauxite is dug from shallow open pits in tropical laterite caps, typically only 5-20 m of overburden, then crushed and washed. The Bayer process is defeated by high silica, so the ore is beneficiated: scrubbed and screened to remove the clay, and often upgraded by gravity separation. The waste is red mud - a thick alkaline sludge held in ponds.

###### Laterite and bauxite geology `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.alumina.bauxite.mining.laterite`

Bauxite is not a mineral but a rock: a residual soil that forms when tropical weathering leaches silica and alkalis out of aluminous parent rock, leaving the insoluble alumina and iron behind as hard concretions. That is why bauxite only forms within about 30 degrees of the equator and why the deposits sit as blankets on old erosion surfaces rather than as veins.

                - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
                - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
###### Caustic soda for digestion `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.alumina.caustic`

The Bayer process reagent, made by the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine. It is recovered from the red-mud wash liquor and recycled, so a 1980s alumina plant consumed a few hundred kg of net Na2O per tonne of alumina.

            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
            - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
##### Hall-Heroult electrolysis `c64.psu.heatsink.aluminium-stock.electrolysis`

Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite at 950-970 C and electrolytically reduced; molten aluminium collects on the carbon-lined cathode and is tapped every one or two days. A modern pot consumes 13,000-15,000 kWh per tonne of aluminium, essentially all of it as thermal/electrical energy from a dedicated power station.

          - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
          - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
#### Anodising or painting the heatsink `c64.psu.heatsink.finish`

A black anodised or painted surface raises the emissivity enough to improve radiation heat transfer a little, but on a folded sheet with no fins the benefit is marginal. Anodising is a sulphuric or chromic acid bath at 20 C with a few volts across the part, growing a thin aluminium oxide film.

### 4700 uF 16 V aluminium electrolytic `c64.psu.bulk-cap`

The single reservoir capacitor on the rectifier output. It is the part that has killed the most C64s: as the electrolyte dries out the ripple current is no longer smoothed, the series regulator loses headroom and starts pumping 100/120 Hz ripple onto the 5 V rail, and eventually the cap leaks current into the regulator's ground reference and pushes the output up past 5.5 V. Replacements are still sold as the C64 'fix' four decades later.

#### Aluminium anode foil `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil`

The anode is a 12-20 um aluminium foil that has been chemically etched in a hot chlorate or permanganate bath to roughen the surface into a high-area sponge. Because capacitance is proportional to real surface area, the etch multiplies the effective area by 30-100x and is the entire reason a 4700 uF part fits in a 25 mm can.

##### Rolling aluminium foil to 12-20 um `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.rolling`

Cast rolling ingot is hot rolled to a few mm in a reversing mill, then cold rolled in a Sendzimir or 20-high mill to 0.05 mm and finally foil rolled to 12-20 um. Foil rolling is done dry or with a light kerosene/paraffin lubricant, and the last pass determines the tensile strength and the pinholes - a pinhole becomes a short, which is why foil is rolled in the tightest gauges last.

          - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
##### Chemical etching of the anode foil `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching`

The foil is threaded continuously through an etch tank at 70-80 C. Sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid, or potassium permanganate, dissolves aluminium faster where the surface is already rough, so the etch runs away into a deep microscopic pore structure rather than eating away uniformly. The etched foil is rinsed, dried and cut to length.

###### Potassium permanganate etchant `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.permanganate`

An alkaline potassium permanganate bath oxidises the aluminium surface; the loose MnO2 sludge is removed by brushing or a nitric acid dip. The alternative chlorate chemistry was being phased out for safety and environmental reasons through the 1980s because chlorate/dioxide is toxic.

            - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
##### Electrolytic formation of the anode oxide `c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation`

The wound wet cell is energised from a DC source at a voltage ramped up to the rated working voltage. At the anode the aluminium oxidises to a dense amorphous alumina film only a few nanometres thick - the dielectric. Raising the voltage thickens the film; raising the temperature thickens it faster but also lets it dissolve, which is why forming is done hot and forming voltage is always lower than the operating voltage.

      - *Electrolytic electrolyte* `c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte` *(seen above)*
#### Cell separator `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator`

A porous dielectric sheet between the anode and the cathode foil, keeping them apart without shorting. Low-voltage parts in 1980-82 used cellulose (paper) separators, which is the direct cause of the decades-later failure: paper is hygroscopic and absorbs electrolyte, and the carbonisation of that paper when leakage current rises shorts the cell.

##### Polypropylene separator `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene`

The 1980s onwards replacement for paper. Made by extruding isotactic polypropylene from propylene obtained in a steam cracker, then stretching and/or solvent extraction to make a microporous film. It does not absorb electrolyte and does not carbonise into a short when it overheats.

###### Propylene from the steam cracker `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.propylene`

Propane and butane from natural-gas liquids or from crude fractionation are steam cracked at 800-900 C with a residence time of under a second to give a propylene-rich C3 stream, which is then purified by selective hydrogenation or distillation. Polypropylene and acrylonitrile both start here.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
            - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
##### Cellulose paper separator `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose`

A thin kraft paper sheet, ~10-20 um, made on a Fourdrinier or a twin-wire machine. Absorbs electrolyte and swells; on ageing it chars and shorts. This is why a decades-old electrolytic usually fails suddenly and violently rather than just drifting.

###### Cellulose from wood hydrolysis `c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.hydrolysis`

The cellulose is made by the soda or kraft process: wood chips are cooked at 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide, the lignin is washed out with the caustic liquor and burned for heat, and the remaining cellulose is bleached with chlorine or hypochlorite. A paper-grade mill in 1982 recovered well over a tonne of black liquor as fuel per tonne of pulp.

            - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
#### Winding and impregnating the cell `c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding`

The anode foil (etched) and the cathode (bare aluminium foil, or the can itself in later types) are separated by the separator and wound on a mandrel into a compact roll, the leads are brought out, and the roll is impregnated under vacuum with the electrolyte so the pores fill completely. Air left in the roll is the single biggest cause of high ESR.

### Tantalum and small electrolytic capacitors `c64.psu.aux-caps`

Secondary filtering: a 0.22 uF 35 V tantalum and a 47 uF 10 V electrolytic on the 5 V output for stability and for the load transients the VIC-II produces when it banks memory. The tantalum is polar and fails short, so it is the more dramatic failure of the pair.

#### Sintered tantalum bead capacitor `c64.psu.aux-caps.tantalum`

A porous sintered tantalum pellet, pressed from tantalum powder and sintered at 1200-2000 C under vacuum, dipped in manganese dioxide as the solid electrolyte, then coated with a conductive polymer or resin and epoxy for protection. Extremely high capacitance per unit volume and no liquid electrolyte to dry out, but it fails short and can burn.

##### Tantalum and its ore `c64.psu.aux-caps.tantalum.ore`

Tantalum columbite ore (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 is mined from pegmatites in Australia, Brazil and Zaire, converted to potassium tantalofluoride K2TaF7 by caustic fusion and acid digestion, then reduced to tantalum powder with potassium as the reductant. The metal is then capacitor-grade: electron-beam or vacuum refined, and only the small crystal grains are used.

###### Potassium reduction of K2TaF7 `c64.psu.aux-caps.tantalum.ore.reduction`

Calcium or potassium reduction of the double fluoride at 700-900 C under vacuum, in batches of a few hundred kilos. This is a batch chemical reduction, not a smelting process, which is why capacitor-grade tantalum was expensive and rare relative to aluminium.

###### Columbite-tantalite in pegmatite `c64.psu.aux-caps.tantalum.ore.pegmatite`

The ore is a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, chemically almost identical niobium and tantalum oxides, and it concentrates in the last stages of pegmatite crystallisation. Because tantalum and niobium are so hard to separate, the industry uses fractional re-crystallisation of the fluoride: K2TaF7 and K2NbF7 have different solubilities, so repeated precipitation progressively enriches the tantalum.

            - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
### Small regulator PCB, 'PNE-5' `c64.psu.board`

A single-sided glass-epoxy board about 40 x 30 mm carrying the regulator, the two electrolytics, the tantalum and two resistors, with the identification 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the earlier build and no marking at all on the later one. It is held in place only by the epoxy that floods the whole case, which is why de-potting usually breaks it.

#### FR-4 glass-epoxy laminate `c64.psu.board.fr4`

Woven E-glass impregnated with brominated epoxy resin and heat-cured into a sheet. By the early 1980s FR-4 had displaced the older phenolic paper laminate (FR-2) for anything that needed dimensional stability or a higher Tg.

        - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
        - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
        - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
        - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
##### Copper-clad laminate pressing `c64.psu.board.fr4.prepreg`

Glass fabric is woven to a controlled thickness, impregnated with brominated epoxy in a treater, and partially cured into a B-stage prepreg. The prepreg sheets and copper foil are then stacked - typically two or four copper layers for a two-sided or four-sided board - and pressed between platens at 160-200 C and 1-3 MPa, which completes the cure and bonds the foil to the laminate. The board is then drilled, the holes plated through with copper, and the pattern etched.

          - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
          - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
          - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
### Epoxy potting pour `c64.psu.potting`

From mid-1983 Commodore filled the case with a two-part epoxy so the whole assembly became one solid block: transformer, board, fuses, leads, the lot, in a minty-green or cool-grey mass. It made the unit tamper-proof and un-serviceable, and it turned out to be the primary cause of failure because the heat of the linear regulator could no longer escape.

      - *Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin* `chem.epoxy` *(seen above)*
#### Two-part epoxy chemistry `c64.psu.potting.chemistry`

A diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A liquid resin, crosslinked with a polyamine or anhydride hardener. In an unfilled pour the potted block is a poor thermal conductor (0.2-0.4 W/m.K), so it acts as a thermal blanket around its own contents; filled versions with silica or alumina flour conduct 1-3 W/m.K and would not have had this problem.

##### Epichlorohydrin feedstock `c64.psu.potting.chemistry.epichlorohydrin`

The other half of the bisphenol-A epoxy molecule. In the 1980s it was made by chlorination of propylene to propylene dichloride, then dehydrochlorination to allyl chloride, then addition of hypochlorous acid (from chlorine and water) to give epichlorohydrin. Both propylene and chlorine are basic chemicals.

          - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
##### Bisphenol A from phenol and acetone `c64.psu.potting.chemistry.bisphenol-a`

Two moles of phenol condensed with one mole of acetone in the presence of an acid catalyst give bisphenol A. Both phenol (from cumene oxidation) and acetone (from the cumene process, or from propylene via isopropanol) are petroleum-aromatics or -ketone co-products, so the epoxy is a petroleum-derived plastic.

          - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
### Black ABS enclosure `c64.psu.case`

A two-half injection-moulded case in black ABS, ~150 x 100 x 60 mm, with a tongue-and-groove seam, ribbing on the sides for stiffness, four case screws and one larger screw holding the cable clamp. On the potted builds the seam is a line of epoxy. Some units have the rating text moulded into the plastic; others have it printed on the underside and on a metallised label.

      - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
#### UL 94 flammability test `c64.psu.case.flammability-test`

A 125 x 13 x 13 mm bar of the plastic is held 10 mm above a burner. For the HB rating it must not burn faster than 1 mm/s over the first 100 mm. For V-2 the flame must extinguish within 30 s and the glowing material within 60 s; V-0 requires extinction within 10/30 s. Natural ABS is normally HB; flame-retardant ABS grades exist but were not used here.

#### Case screws `c64.psu.case.screws`

Cross-recessed pan-head self-tapping screws into moulded bosses in the plastic, and in a mains appliance they must be short enough that they cannot reach the primary wiring - a specific check in the safety audit.

        - *Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel* `metal.steel` *(seen above)*
### 6-pin DIN output connector `c64.psu.connector`

A moulded round DIN socket on the case face carrying the two 5 V conductors, the two 9 V AC conductors and, in the six-pin version, the second 9 V AC leg. Later builds reduced it to four pins. The C64's mainboard has the mating plug, and the two ends of the 5 V pair are deliberately larger-diameter so the plug cannot be inserted backwards.

#### Connector nylon shell and brass pins `c64.psu.connector.nylon-shell`

The shell is moulded from a glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF) with a chamfered keyway that defines the pin polarisation; the pins are brass, often nickel-plated for wear, and are a press-fit or riveted into the shell. The 5 V pins are larger so that the plug is keyed by power, not by numbering.

        - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
        - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
### Power indicator LED `c64.psu.power-led` _(low)_

Not present on every brick. Where fitted it is a 3 mm red LED in a small nylon bezel, fed from the 5 V rail through a 330 Ohm to 1 kOhm resistor so that the constant ~7 mA is well inside the LED's safe operating current, and the resistor - not the LED - is what limits the current when the rail is at 5.4 V.

      - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
### Rating label and moulded markings `c64.psu.nameplate`

The safety-critical data: input volts and frequency, VA input, 5 V DC watts, 9 V AC VA, the approval marks and the warning text. On the 3-83 build the text is moulded into the case; on the 13-83 it is printed on the underside, duplicated on a top label and given a date on a metallised sticker. Every approval scheme requires this data to be legible without opening the unit.

#### Metallised polyester label `c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label`

A 25 um metallised polyester film printed with one or two hit spot colours and applied with an acrylic adhesive. Metallised polyester is used because it is tear-resistant, solvent-resistant and survives the polyester solvents in the potting epoxy, unlike paper.

##### Metallised BOPP film `c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp`

Biaxially oriented polypropylene film, stretched in both directions so the molecules line up to give high tensile strength and tear resistance in any direction, then vacuum-metallised with aluminium. The printing inks are solvent-based dyes and pigment pastes that are dried and overlaminated.

          - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
          - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
###### Biaxial orientation `c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp.orientation`

A cast polypropylene or cast polyethylene film is stretched in the machine direction, cooled, then stretched again in the transverse direction and heat-set. The two stretching steps line the polymer chains up in both directions, so the film has high tensile strength and tear resistance whatever the pull direction - which is exactly why a torn BOPP label ends in a straight line rather than a ragged one.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
            - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
### Brick assembly and final test `c64.psu.assembly`

The order of operations is visible in the potted builds: the transformer is soldered to by the diodes and fuses at its own pins, the small board is populated, the LED and connector are fitted, the assembly is dropped into the case, epoxy is poured, the halves are screwed together, and the finished unit is then hi-pot tested, earth-continuity tested and burned in on load. Testing after potting is what lets a potted brick be safe and unrepairable at the same time.

      - *Hi-pot dielectric withstand test* `c64.psu.assembly.hipot` *(seen above)*
#### Protective-earth continuity test `c64.psu.assembly.earth-continuity`

A low current (typically 25-50 A for a Class I product, but only a few amps here) is passed from the earth pin of the line cord to the earth tab on the transformer, and the resistance must be below ~0.1 ohm. In this all-plastic brick the earth stops at the transformer, so the test is a continuity check on one bond, not on a case.

#### Load burn-in and temperature rise `c64.psu.assembly.burnin`

Every unit is run at rated load - a resistive or electronic load drawing 1.5 A from the 5 V rail plus a load on the 9 V AC - for 2-8 hours while case temperature and output voltage are logged. This is the test that finds the dry solder joints and thermal-runaway designs that a 30 second hi-pot never will. Hobbyists have independently rediscovered it: stress the brick for hours, with thermal cycling, before trusting it on a C64.

      - *UL 478 / IEC 65 listing* `c64.psu.assembly.approval` *(seen above)*
  - *C64 mains side: cord, plug, switch, fuse* `c64.mains` *(seen above)*
## Supplied cables: RF lead, A/V lead, mains cord `c64.cables`

Three cables shipped with or sold alongside a breadbin C64. The RF cable carries the modulator's VHF output from the machine's phono socket to a television's aerial input, so it is a 75-ohm coaxial. The A/V lead carries luma, chroma, composite and audio to a monitor through an 8-pin DIN. The mains cord is a two- or three-core PVC-jacketed cord with a moulded plug that feeds the external power supply.

### RF cable (phono plug to TV plug) `c64.cables.rf-cable`

A 75-ohm coaxial lead. Its job is to get a 1 MHz video signal, sitting on a VHF carrier, into a television's analogue aerial input without picking up half the room on the way. Impedance matching and a decent screen are what keep the picture from ghosting.

#### 75-ohm coaxial cable `c64.cables.rf-cable.coax` _(medium)_

Centre conductor, dielectric, braid screen, PVC jacket. The braid is what does the shielding; the jacket is only there to survive being dragged under a TV cabinet for twenty years.

##### Centre conductor (copper, or copper-clad steel) `c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor`

The signal-carrying core. Consumer coax uses solid bare copper or, to save money, copper-clad steel. At RF frequencies a CCS core is perfectly adequate for a metre of cable.

###### Copper wire rod and drawing `c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire`

Copper cathodes are melted, cast into wire rod, then drawn through a series of dies to the finished diameter. A cable plant buys rod and draws it in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.

##### Dielectric (polyethylene or PTFE) `c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric`

The insulating foam between conductor and braid. Polyethylene is the volume material for consumer coax, often gas-injected or foam-injected to lower the dielectric constant and hold 75 ohm with a bigger centre conductor. PTFE (Teflon) is the low-loss, low-noise alternative used where a very clean signal or a tight bend radius matters.

###### Cable extrusion line `c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion`

A vertical or horizontal line where conductor is drawn through a die, dielectric tube is extruded or foamed around it, braid is laid on from a rotating carrier, and the jacket is extruded and cooled in a trough. Cable extrusion is one of the few polymer processes that is genuinely continuous and high-speed.

###### Braided screen (tinned copper) `c64.cables.rf-cable.braid`

A flat bundle of tinned copper wires woven over the dielectric by a braiding machine, usually with a second pass to push coverage from ~70% toward 90%. Tinning reduces oxidation and makes the braid easier to terminate.

###### Low-density polyethylene (the volume dielectric) `c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe`

The bulk of consumer coax dielectric is LDPE made by high-pressure or low-pressure polymerisation of ethylene. LDPE is branched and low-density, which is exactly what you want here: the branching lowers the dielectric constant so the coaxial geometry lands on 75 ohm with a reasonable centre-conductor size.

###### LDPE polymerisation of ethylene `c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe-polymerisation`

Ethylene is polymerised either at high pressure (1000-3000 bar, 200-300 C, initiated by peroxides) or at low pressure with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (20-40 bar, 70-110 C). Cable plants typically run high-pressure LDPE because it extrudes cleanly and fast; low-pressure LLDPE is the modern preference for some uses.

###### Ziegler-Natta catalyst (TiCl4 + alkylaluminium) `c64.cables.rf-cable.zn-catalyst`

The low-pressure catalyst: titanium tetrachloride supported on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl co-catalyst. It polymerises ethylene in a stereoregular way and gives the higher-density grades.

###### Titanium tetrachloride `c64.cables.rf-cable.titanium-tetrachloride`

Made by chlorinating titanium metal or a titanium-bearing slag at 400-900 C in carbon or fluidised bed. The metal itself is made by the Kroll process: rutile or ilmenite is chlorinated to TiCl4, which is reduced with magnesium metal.

###### Rutile / ilmenite feedstock for titanium metal `c64.cables.rf-cable.rutile-feedstock`

The same titanium ores that make the white pigment in the case, here reduced to sponge titanium and then chlorinated for the polymerisation catalyst. One ore, two very different products.

###### Aluminium alkyl co-catalyst `c64.cables.rf-cable.aluminium-alkyl` _(medium)_

Aluminium triethyl or aluminium diethyl, made by reacting aluminium with the corresponding alkyl chloride. It is what activates the titanium and controls the polymer's branching.

###### Polymerisation-grade ethylene purity `c64.cables.rf-cable.purity-ethylene`

Cable-grade polyethylene needs a very clean monomer: oxygen, water, sulphur and acetylene all poison or degrade the polymer. Ethylene from the cracker is therefore purified to 99.9%+ by distillation, molecular sieves and catalyst scrubbing before it reaches a reactor.

##### Outer jacket (PVC) `c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket`

A lead-compounded PVC jacket, usually flexible grade with a plasticiser so the cable stays bendable. The jacket has nothing to do with the signal; its job is abrasion and handling.

###### Plasticiser in flexible PVC `c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser`

Cable PVC is not rigid: it is compounded with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate (DOP) or trimellitates, dropped into an extruder at 5-10% and mixed before extrusion. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle.

#### Moulded phono plug and TV plug `c64.cables.rf-cable.plug`

Both ends are moulded: a phono (RCA) plug with a nickel-plated centre pin in a moulded barrel at the C64 end, and a television coaxial plug at the other. The pin is plated rather than bare so it survives being shoved in and out of the TV a thousand times.

##### Nickel plating of the pin `c64.cables.rf-cable.plating`

Electrolytic nickel plating on a brass pin, giving a hard, corrosion-resistant, non-tarnishing surface. Nickel is the classic choice for connector contacts because its contact resistance stays low and it does not corrode in a socket.

##### Brass pin stock `c64.cables.rf-cable.brass`

Free-cutting brass (typically leaded brass) machined or cold-formed into the pin and barrel. Brass is the standard connector material because it machines well, springs enough to take a wipe, and does not rust.

#### Strain-relief boot `c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief`

A moulded rubber or PVC boot at each cable end where it enters the plug body, taking the bending load so the conductor does not fatigue at the termination. Cheap to add, and the difference between a lead that survives ten years and one that breaks at the root.

#### Cable assembly and test `c64.cables.rf-cable.assembly`

Cables are made by cutting, stripping, crimping or soldering the conductor into the plug, moulding or snapping the plug body on, and testing. A continuity and insulation-resistance check, often on an automatic line tester, catches the faults before the lead reaches the box.

### A/V cable to a 1701/1702 monitor `c64.cables.av-cable`

A monitor lead carrying luma, chroma, composite video, audio in and out, and +5V/ground, in an 8-pin DIN connector at each end. It was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

#### DIN connector and cable `c64.cables.av-cable.din`

A moulded DIN plug with a metal shell and a screw-on or clip-on backshell that clamps the cable and provides strain relief. The shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, and the interior is filled with a phenolic or thermoplastic insert holding the female contacts.

#### Cable conductors and insulation `c64.cables.av-cable.wires`

Stranded tinned copper conductors with PVC insulation, colour-coded to the DIN pinout. Shielded or twisted pairs for the audio lines to keep the 1 MHz clock out of the speaker.

### Mains power cord `c64.cables.power-cord`

A detachable mains lead for the external power supply: two or three PVC-insulated copper conductors in a moulded outer jacket, with a moulded mains plug at one end and a moulded figure-8 or IEC connector at the other. In Europe it is a two-pin contour plug; in North America a three-pin NEMA plug, often polarised.

#### Stranded copper conductors `c64.cables.power-cord.conductors`

Fine-strand flexible copper, made by bunching many small wires in a roving machine and twisting them. Flexible stranding is what lets a mains lead bend without breaking the strands.

#### PVC insulation extruded onto the conductors `c64.cables.power-cord.insulation`

Each conductor is passed through a die in an extrusion line and coated with a rigid or semi-rigid PVC at a few hundred volts' worth of insulation. Extrusion is continuous and the colour is added by pigment masterbatch.

#### Outer jacket `c64.cables.power-cord.jacket`

A second extrusion over the assembled, twisted conductors. The conductors are first twisted together on a planetary twister so the cord resists unwinding, then jacketed.

#### Moulded mains plug `c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug`

A plug with a thermoplastic cord body wrapped around the cable entry to take the bending strain, and two or three brass prongs riveted or crimped in. The cord body is the part that actually fails: the plug is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.

##### Brass prongs `c64.cables.power-cord.brass-prongs`

Blanked, formed and plated brass strip. Brass is used rather than steel because it must not spark and must not corrode; the plating gives the dull, non-tarnishing surface a moulded plug has.

##### Cord body / strain-relief grip `c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body`

Moulded in PVC or polypropylene and over-moulded onto the jacket. It is deliberately flexible so the cable can swivel, which is also why a moulded cord body eventually tears at its root after years of being yanked out of a wall socket by the wire.

### TV switch box (optional accessory) `c64.cables.switch-box` _(medium)_

Commodore part 904778-01, an external box that let the C64's RF output share a television aerial socket with an actual antenna, switching between them. It is an accessory rather than a cable, but it is in the same moulded-plastic-and-coax family and shares the cable supply chain.

## Retail packaging: printed box, foam, polybag, manual `c64.packaging` _(medium)_

A breadbin C64 shipped in a corrugated board box printed lithographically with Commodore's rainbow graphics, with the machine cradled in two moulded polystyrene end blocks and wrapped in a polyethylene bag, plus the user's manual and a warranty card. Boxes went to a corrugated master carton on a timber skid for shipping to warehouses.

### Retail corrugated box `c64.packaging.retail-box`

A regular slotted container or a tuck-end box in B-flute corrugated board, printed on a sheet-fed or web offset press in up to four or six colours plus a rainbow gradient, then creased, cut and glued. It is a commodity: the board is a mill product and the printing is a printshop product, not a Commodore product.

#### Corrugated board (liner + medium) `c64.packaging.box-board`

Two kraft liners glued to a fluted medium. In 1982 a consumer-electronics box was usually C-flute or B-flute single wall, made from semichemical or recycled kraft; the flute is what gives the box its edge crush strength for a couple of Newtons of stacking force.

##### Kraft liner (topside and underside) `c64.packaging.kraft-liner`

Unbleached paper made from long-fibre softwood pulp, typically 120-200 gsm. Its brown colour is the kraft process itself: the pulp is brown before it reaches the paper machine, because the kraft cook keeps the lignin.

###### Kraft pulp `c64.packaging.kraft-pulp`

Wood chips are steamed, cooked in a kraft digester with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide, washed, and bleached only lightly. The brown colour is retained kraft lignin, which is why kraft paper is brown and recycling it is easy.

###### Wood chips from sawmill waste `c64.packaging.wood-chips`

Roundwood is debarked and chipped into 20-30 mm chips in a disc chipper, ready for the digester. The chips are the whole reason the paper mill sits next to a forest: you cannot make paper without wood fibre.

###### Roundwood logs `c64.packaging.log`

Trunk sections felled and delimbed, usually conifer in northern Europe and North America. Softwood is preferred for kraft because its long fibres give paper strength; hardwoods go into hardwood kraft or into mechanical pulp.

###### Planted softwood stand `c64.packaging.forest-stand`

Managed conifer plantations (spruce, pine, or southern pine) felled on a rotation and replanted. This is where the fibre chain ends: a box is wood, and the wood is a tree that was grown, cut and chipped.

###### Kraft cooking (digestion) `c64.packaging.digestion`

Chips are cooked in a spherical or continuous digester with white liquor (sodium hydroxide + sodium sulfide + sodium carbonate) at 160-180 C. The alkali dissolves the lignin; the sulfide keeps the dissolved lignin in solution so the fibres do not darken.

###### Caustic soda for the digester `c64.packaging.sodium-hydroxide`

The same chlor-alkali caustic that makes VCM and soaps comes to the paper mill, typically as a 50% solution in tank cars.

###### Brown (kraft) grade versus bleached `c64.packaging.kraft-process`

Unbleached kraft keeps its brown colour and is the cheapest strong liner. A bleached or semi-bleached top liner costs more and is used where the print needs a white background. Commodore's boxes are brown board with printing on top, so the brown liner is exactly right.

###### Fourdrinier paper machine `c64.packaging.paper-machine`

The pulp is diluted to a few tenths of a percent solids and laid as a continuous web on a moving wire mesh, squeezed, dried over felt-covered heated cylinders, calendered, and wound onto reels. This machine is where a tree becomes a sheet.

##### Fluted medium (recycled) `c64.packaging.corrugated-medium`

The wavy centre of the board is usually made from 100% recycled paper, because the flute does not need virgin-fibre strength. Old corrugated boxes are collected, pulped (the recycled / OCF route), and run onto a corrugating machine.

###### Recovered paper (OCC / mixed waste) `c64.packaging.wastepaper`

Collected corrugated and box board, baled, repulped in a hydrapulper and screened. The deinking stage is needed for printed waste; unprinted OCC is repulped as it is. The fibre in a C64 box's fluted medium is therefore almost certainly several previous boxes.

###### Repulping and deinking `c64.packaging.deinking`

Bales are dropped into a hydrapulper, torn up into fibre, screened, and deinked with a flotation cell and surfactant to remove printing inks. A high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered in exactly this way.

###### Corrugating and sheet making `c64.packaging.corrugating`

Medium paper is corrugated between two rotating fluted rolls with heat and starch glue, then glued to liners; the sheet is cut and creased. The board then goes to the box plant for slotting, folding and gluing.

##### Starch corrugating adhesive `c64.packaging.starch-adhesive`

The glue holding the flutes and the liners is a corn- or tapioca-starch dextrin, cooked on the corrugator and applied hot. It is the standard adhesive in corrugated board and the reason the board is not a fire hazard in the way solvent glues would be.

###### Corn (maize) starch `c64.packaging.corn-starch`

Starch is wet-milled from maize: the kernels are steeped in warm water to soften the germ, ground, and the starch is separated by gravity or centrifugally and dried. Every corrugated box is glued with a plant, not a petrochemical.

###### Maize crop `c64.packaging.maize`

A cereal grain grown in enormous tonnages in the US corn belt and in Europe, China and Brazil; the harvested cobs are shelled and the kernels go to wet milling. This is the agricultural end of the adhesive chain.

#### Box printing (offset litho) and the rainbow graphics `c64.packaging.box-printing`

The printed sheet is run on an offset litho press - sheet-fed for short runs, web-fed for long runs - in a small number of process colours, with the Commodore rainbow reproduced as a multi-stop gradient. The board is then cut, creased and glued.

##### Offset lithographic printing `c64.packaging.offset-litho`

The image is on a flat plate, wetted with dampening solution so the image areas reject ink, and printed by a rubber blanket onto paper. Litho gives fine detail and consistent colour on uncoated board, at the cost of a plate-making step per colour.

###### Lithographic printing plate `c64.packaging.litho-plate`

A thin aluminium or copper plate, grained and treated, with a photopolymer or metal-image layer carrying the separations. The classic long-run offset plate is an aluminium sheet electro-grained and anodised; short runs use photopolymer plates directly.

###### Offset printing ink `c64.packaging.litho-ink`

A pigment dispersed in a drying-oil-based vehicle (linseed/soy alkyd) with resin, wax and a drier. Water-based offset inks became the norm for corrugated in the 1990s; oil-based inks were standard in 1982.

###### Alkyd / drying-oil ink vehicle `c64.packaging.ink-resin`

Built from vegetable oil (linseed or soybean) fatty acids condensed with a polyol and a phthalic or maleic anhydride, then crosslinked by oxidative polymerisation on the press. So the ink vehicle on the box traces back to a phthalic anhydride plant, the same chemistry as the pigment in the case.

###### Soy or linseed oil (ink vehicle base) `c64.packaging.soy-oil`

A vegetable oil pressed from a crop. It oxidises (dries) on the printed sheet, which is what 'drying ink' means. In 1982 soybean oil was becoming the preferred ink vehicle because of the 1970s linseed-oil shortages.

###### Ink pigments (organic and inorganic) `c64.packaging.ink-pigment`

In 1982 most packaging colourants were still inorganic: iron oxides, chrome yellow, ultramarine. The bright synthetic organic pigments (phthalocyanines, azo yellows) were used for the saturated rainbow, and the titanium dioxide white for the light areas.

###### Offset press (sheet-fed or web) `c64.packaging.litho-press`

A printing press: plate cylinders, blanket cylinders, inking units, and either a sheet feed with a delivery stacker or a web unwind and rewind with a folder. For a corrugated box liner, the press is the capital equipment a converter owns.

##### Rainbow gradient (duotone / multi-stop blend) `c64.packaging.rainbow-gradient` _(medium)_

Commodore's rainbow on the box and the case logo is a set of graded colour bands. On a flexo or litho box it is made either with a multi-colour duotone (the two separations overprinted at varying screen densities) or, on later short runs, printed with a spray/airbrush unit. This is where a printing shop makes one-off artwork effects cheaply.

##### Varnish / water-based coating `c64.packaging.varnishing` _(medium)_

A thin scuff-resistant coating over the printed board, applied on the press or in-line. It stops the rainbow rubbing off in the warehouse. Modern converters would use a water-based or UV-cure acrylic; 1982 used a solvent or water-based acryl.

#### Slotting, creasing, folding and gluing `c64.packaging.box-converting`

The printed board goes through a slotter-creater which cuts the slots, scores the creases and trims the blanks; the blanks are then folded on a folder-gluer, which applies a hot starch or PVA glue to the tab and forms the box. It is a fast, near-fully-automated process.

#### Parts tray for the loose items `c64.packaging.parts-tray` _(low)_

Inside the box, below or beside the machine, the power cord, the A/V lead and the paperwork were either tied together in the foam or held in a separate moulded tray. Where a tray was used it was expanded polystyrene or, on later runs, a folded pulp tray.

### Moulded polystyrene end blocks `c64.packaging.foam-caps` _(medium)_

Two white expanded-polystyrene blocks that cradle the ends of the machine so the case cannot be crushed in the box and cannot slide. They are moulded to the machine's outline in a steam-heated block mould, then cut down to size.

#### Expanded polystyrene (EPS) `c64.packaging.eps`

Small beads of polystyrene, each already blown up with a chlorinated blowing agent, are heated and expanded again in a mould so the beads fuse into a solid block shaped to the part. The polymer is the same styrene copolymer chemistry as the ABS and the SAN; only the physical form is different.

##### EPS beads (expanded in a bead expander) `c64.packaging.eps-beads`

Styrene is suspension-polymerised in water to small beads, then a chlorinated blowing agent is dissolved into them under pressure; on heating the agent flashes and expands each bead from ~0.5-1 mm to 2-6 mm, and the beads are chilled and sieved by size.

###### Chlorinated blowing agent (CFC-11 / dichloromethane) `c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent`

Trichlorofluoromethane, or methylene chloride in the European trade. Both are excellent blowing agents: low boiling point, no flammability risk in the bead, and chemically inert enough to survive the polymerisation. They are also chlorinated, which is the whole problem — they destroy stratospheric ozone, so they were phased out of packaging foam through the 1990s and replaced by pentane and by butane.

##### Bead expansion (bead expander) `c64.packaging.eps-expansion`

Beads are fed into a steam-heated expander where they expand, are held at temperature to sinter them into a cake, and are then cooled and dried in a silo. The expander is the machine that sets the final foam density.

##### Block moulding in a steam-heated mould `c64.packaging.eps-moulding`

Beads are blown into a heated aluminium mould and the steam expands them to fill it; the mould is then cooled and the block ejected. A block mould makes a slab that is later cut on a band saw or hot wire into the end blocks. The mould is a heat exchanger - the steam lines run through it.

### Polyethylene sleeve over the machine `c64.packaging.polybag`

A plain polyethylene bag over the boxed machine, to stop the moulded case and the printed manual from rubbing and to keep dust out during transit. It is a low-cost LDPE sleeve, blown as a tube on the same film-blowing line used for all commodity packaging film.

#### Film blowing and bag making `c64.packaging.film-blowing`

LDPE pellets are blown as a thin tube through a die and a bubble, cooled in an air ring, collapsed and wound; the tube is then cut and heat-sealed into a bag. Film blowing is high-volume and very cheap - the bag is cents, not dollars.

### User's manual (fold-in-fold booklet) `c64.packaging.manual`

The Commodore 64 user's manual - part 320974 in the service-manual parts list - is a cheap but well-made fold-in-fold booklet: a single sheet of coated wood-pulp paper printed in colour on both sides, folded twice with a 16-page section glued in the middle. It is the same construction as a road atlas, which is how a large amount of operating documentation was printed in 1982.

#### Coated printing paper `c64.packaging.manual.paper`

Wood-pulp paper filled and coated with clay (kaolin) and a binder, then calendered, so the ink sits on the surface and the colours are bright and sharp. It is the same stock as a supermarket leaflet.

#### Colour offset printing of the manual `c64.packaging.manual.printing`

Sheet-fed offset litho in four colours (CMYK), plus spot colours for the Commodore rainbow and the red 'RESTORE' key highlights. The manual's diagrams and BASIC listings were set in hot-metal or phototypeset, then printed from plates.

#### Fold-in-fold bindery `c64.packaging.manual.bindery`

A long sheet is printed with the page imposition for a 16-page booklet, folded twice with a plate, and a 16-page section is glued into the middle crease. The result is a bound booklet that opens flat and costs almost nothing to assemble - it is pure paper engineering.

#### Letterpress covers (regional variants) `c64.packaging.manual.letterpress` _(low)_

Some Commodore manuals and the box artwork of this period were printed letterpress from metal type on a platen or cylinder press rather than litho, and some C64 documentation was printed that way. Where a manual was letterpressed, the type impression is visible on the reverse and the cover has that slightly embossed, absorbent-paper look.

### Warranty and registration card `c64.packaging.warranty-card`

A small printed card with the warranty terms and a serial-number registration slip. It is the same litho process as the manual on a heavier board stock, and it is the only part of the package with a legal function.

### Shipping master carton and skid `c64.packaging.master-carton`

Retail boxes were packed into corrugated master cartons, several to a carton, and banded on a timber skid for palletised shipping from the Hong Kong or Taiwan assembly plant to a regional warehouse. Skids - not euro-pallets - were the norm for export shipping of this period.

#### Timber skid `c64.packaging.skids`

A wooden skid: three or more bearers with a top deck, or a bare skid with the cartons loaded straight onto it. Skids are made from rough-sawn softwood offcuts, which is why they are the cheapest way to make a heavy load forkable.

##### Rough-sawn softwood `c64.packaging.timber`

Kiln-dried or green softwood, band-sawn to bearers and deckboards. The sawmill waste that cannot be pulped into paper - knots, ends, slabs - is exactly what a skid is made of, which is a neat closure of the wood chain.

#### Strapping (steel or polypropylene) `c64.packaging.strapping`

Steel band with a stamped seal, or the polypropylene strapping that had largely displaced it by the 1980s because it does not rust, does not cut the carton and is lighter to ship back as waste.

#### Master-carton board `c64.packaging.carton-board`

Heavier double-wall corrugated, usually a recycled medium and recycled liners, with the shipping marks stencilled or flexo-printed rather than litho-printed.

### Final pack-out and pack-out line `c64.packaging.packaging-line`

At the end of the case-moulding and assembly plant, machines are bagged, placed in the foam blocks, dropped into the printed box with the manual and card, and the box is closed and labelled. This was semi-automatic and was the labour-heavy step that determined where a home computer was finally assembled.

## Also required to use it `c64.peripherals`

A C64 shipped as a box with no screen, no way to save a program, and no way to enter one. In 1983 the machine was useless without a television set, a cassette recorder, and a joystick — arguably all three were part of 'a computer' in the way the question was meant.

### What you plug into it `peripheral`

A C64 shipped with no screen. It drove a television set through an RF modulator, saved to a cassette deck through the 1541 drive, and took input from a joystick. These three are arguably part of 'a full computer' in 1983.

#### Why a television set was mandatory `peripheral.why-rf` _(medium)_

The VIC-II chip outputs a 1 MHz-ish analogue composite signal on its own pin: luma, blanking and a colour subcarrier, but no RF. In 1982 there was no agreed analogue video standard between a computer and a monitor, no DE-15 or VGA, and no DVI. Commodore's answer was a small RF modulator, a printed board with one video modulator oscillator and a VHF converter, whose output was injected into the aerial socket of an ordinary television. The TV then had to be tuned to channel 3 (61.75 MHz in the US) or channel 4, and the picture was in colour only if the TV had a colour decoder for that subcarrier frequency.

##### The -60 dB that nobody mentions `peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm` _(low)_

A broadcast TV station transmitted tens of kilowatts; a C64 modulator put out about a milliwatt. The set had to be tuned by hand, and reception quality was a function of the modulator's output impedance matching the aerial input. Anyone who ever moved the TV or unplugged the aerial lead knows how marginal this was.

##### What replaced it `peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison` _(medium)_

Commodore's own 1702 monitor took a composite luma-and-blank input over a 5-pin DIN, and in 1985-86 Commodore adopted the DE-9 connector used by the C128's RGBI monitors, which carried separate red, green and blue analogue signals on pins 5, 6, 7 with no modulation at all. There was still no standard, which is why the C128 ended up with a proprietary DIN-8 video connector rather than a DE-15.

#### Domestic colour television set, 13 inch NTSC `peripheral.tv`

A 1982-84 US domestic set: 12.5 or 13 inch diagonal, 525-line NTSC, 60 Hz field rate, all-signal-in-a-can. It was the only display a C64 owner was likely to have, and the C64 looked terrible on it: no separate chrominance bandwidth, a modulated sound carrier that carried the computer's audio, and a colour subcarrier at a frequency the TV's chroma band had to be tuned to.

##### The picture tube (CRT) `peripheral.tv.crt`

A vacuum envelope of two pieces of glass welded together: a flat-ish panel carrying the phosphor screen inside its face, and a flanged funnel tapering to a cylindrical neck that carries the electron gun. The panel-to-funnel joint is sealed with a lead-oxide frit fired in a belt kiln. Inside the tube, electrons leave a hot cathode, are focused and accelerated to about 25 kV, steered magnetically across the panel, and slam into phosphor grains through a steel mask.

###### Faceplate panel and funnel, borosilicate glass `peripheral.tv.crt.panel` _(medium)_

The tube is made of two glass parts that must expand at the same rate or the tube shatters at the seal. The funnel is a leaded or unlead borosilicate; the panel is a flatter, alkali-free glass with a much lower thermal expansion coefficient. Their junction is a strip of lead borosilicate frit, printed onto both parts and fired, which melts at a temperature low enough that the base glass does not slump.

###### Funnel glass batch, melted at 1400 degrees C `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass` _(medium)_

Funnel glass is a borosilicate with low alkali, formulated so that its thermal expansion matches the panel. The batch is silica sand, boric acid, soda ash, limestone and a little red lead or litharge as a fining agent, melted for tens of hours in a regenerative gas-fired tank furnace and then drawn into tubing.

###### Quartz sand (SiO2) for the glass batch `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.silica`

Silica sand, over 99% SiO2, dredged or quarried and washed, is the largest single ingredient of a glass batch by weight. Glass-grade sand has to be low in iron (which green-tints the glass) and low in alumina variation. It is not chemically refined, which is unusual for an optical material: it is washed and sieved.

###### Dredge or quarry `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.silica.dredge`

A dragline or bucket-line dredge lifts sand from a dune or river bed; it is washed, sized and dried. No chemistry at all: the purity of a television's glass came out of the ground and was protected from contamination by handling it dry.

###### Boric acid, from colemanite ore `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.borax` _(medium)_

Borates lower the glass's expansion coefficient and its melting point, which is exactly what a funnel that must survive a 25 kV implosion needs. Most borax for the western hemisphere came from borate ores in southern California and from Turkey.

###### Colemanite and borate ore `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.borax.ore` _(medium)_

A calcium borate mineral, often in veins with gypsum and limestone, crushed and digested in acid to give boric acid which is then crystallised out as sodium tetraborate.

###### Lead borosilicate frit seal (about 24% PbO) `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit`

The seal that makes a television tube possible. A paste of lead oxide, silica, boric oxide and alkali is screen-printed as a thick band onto the panel rim and the funnel rim, fired to devitrify, and then the two parts are brought together in a continuous belt kiln where the frit softens and fuses. Lead does three jobs: it drops the sealing temperature far below the point where the base glass would slump, it can be tuned to match the expansion of either glass, and its high atomic number soaks up the bremsstrahlung X-rays that 25 kV of beam current unavoidably produces inside the tube.

###### Lead oxide, PbO, from galena concentrate `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo`

The lead in the frit started as galena, PbS, roasted in air to a PbO litharge cake, then smelted. Nothing about this is exotic: it is the same 1900s Parkesine process that made lead-acid battery plates, refined to the point where the oxide is pure white and free of the bismuth and antimony that would grey it.

###### Roasting, sintering, blast furnace and cast refining `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-smelt` _(medium)_

The whole lead chain in one furnace hall. Concentrate is roasted in a fluid-bed roaster to litharge, PbO, with the SO2 sent to a contact plant for sulphuric acid; the litharge is mixed with sinter, coke and limestone and charged to a blast furnace that produces crude lead at about 1250 degrees C and 1100-1250 degrees C of shaft temperature. The crude is drossed and electrolytically refined to 99.99% Pb, then converted back to pure white PbO for the frit. The economics were dominated by the acid plant and by how much silver the Parkesine dross carried.

###### Galena (PbS) concentrate, 60-80% Pb `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-smelt.galena`

Galena is cubic and dense at 7.6 g/cm3, which is why it separates from gangue so cleanly in froth flotation or a heavy-media washer. A lead-zinc mine's flotation plant produces three products: lead concentrate, zinc concentrate and a copper concentrate, and the economics of a 1982 lead plant stood or fell on the price of the sulphuric acid made from the roast's SO2.

###### Underground lead-zinc mine and concentrator `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-smelt.galena.mine` _(medium)_

Sulphide ores are heavy and low-grade, so they are mined underground and milled rather than scraped off a hillside. The rock is broken, ground to a few tens of microns in a ball mill and floated; the concentrate is trucked or rail-loaded a thousand kilometres to a smelter. In 1982 the American lead belt along the Mississippi and the Mexican states of Chihuahua and Sonora were the sources for the North American television trade.

###### Lead-zinc sulphide ore in the ground `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.pbo.roast-smelt.galena.mine.ore` _(medium)_

Galena and sphalerite intergrown in limestone and dolomite, deposited from hydrothermal fluids in Palaeozoic sediments. The whole industry of this branch's lead and zinc hangs off a few stratabound orebodies in Missouri, Broken Hill, Sullivan, the Upper Mississippi valley and northern Mexico.

###### Frit paste and screen-printing of the seal `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit.ink` _(medium)_

Frit is mixed into a paste with a water-soluble or organic vehicle, printed through a fine mesh screen onto the rim of the panel and the flange of the funnel, then dried and fired to devitrify. The printed band has to be dimensionally exact: too narrow and it will not seal, too wide and it costs lead.

###### Belt kiln and vacuum leak test `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln` _(low)_

Panel and funnel enter a continuous refractory belt kiln, aligned by a jig, and travel through the firing zone where the frit melts. The seal is judged by how far the heated frit bulges past its own edge. The tube is then helium leak tested before it ever goes near the vacuum pumps.

###### Panel glass, alkali-free `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass` _(medium)_

The panel is not the same glass as the funnel. It is alkali-free borosilicate with an expansion coefficient about a third lower than the funnel, so that when the panel is pressed against a mould during cooling it develops exactly the curvature the shadow mask geometry needs and stays there. Alkali is kept out because sodium and potassium diffuse and react with the phosphor layer on the inside face.

###### Alkali-free batch: silica, alumina, boron `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batch` _(medium)_

Where the funnel batch leaned on lead and alkali for its expansion match, the panel batch deliberately excluded sodium and potassium and got its properties from silica, alumina and boric oxide plus a small amount of barium to suppress solarisation under the phosphor firing. It is the same silica sand as the funnel, but a batch designed to be unfriendly to sodium.

###### Alumina for the panel batch `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batch.alumina` _(medium)_

Refractory-grade alumina from bauxite, the same Bayer-process alumina chain as the CRT's aluminium foil. It raises the panel glass's viscosity and its thermal shock resistance, which matters because a tube has to survive being handled and shipped while cold.

###### 4N aluminium foil from bauxite `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.bauxite`

99.99% four-nines aluminium, 0.1-0.15 mm foil. Bauxite is digested in hot sodium hydroxide to sodium aluminate, seeded to precipitate aluminium hydroxide, calcined to alumina, then reduced in a Hall-Heroult cell by carbon at about 1000 degrees C and cast.

###### Lateritic bauxite open pit `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.bauxite.mine` _(medium)_

A tropical, laterite-capped pit mined a few metres of high-grade ore and left the silica behind. The Bayer process is essentially a selective alkaline attack: bauxite dissolves, silica does not, and the residue (red mud) is pumped out as waste.

###### P22 phosphor screen, blue/green/red `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor` _(medium)_

The inside face of the panel carries a printed tri-colour phosphor: blue zinc sulphide doped with silver, green zinc sulphide doped with gold, and a red phosphor around 610 nm, arranged as a dot triad maybe 0.6-0.8 mm pitch behind the shadow mask. The whole layer is only about 25-40 microns thick wet and shrinks to 15-25 microns fired, then gets a mirror of aluminium vapour on top so the electron beam that misses the phosphor is absorbed instead of lighting the room.

###### Internal screen print through a nylon mesh `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print` _(medium)_

Three slurries are laid down in turn: red, then green, then blue, each through a fine nylon mesh onto the inside of the panel, each registered to the last to a few tens of microns. The mesh, not a photo-emulsion, defines the dots. A photographic stencil fixes the screen area and the black border.

###### Three-roll mill `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.mill` _(medium)_

The phosphor slurry is refined on a three-roll (three-mill) gap mill: the rollers set a gap of a few microns and shear the agglomerates down so that the particle size distribution is tight. Screen printing needs a narrow size distribution or the dots print with a rough edge and the resolution falls off.

###### Glass frit binder in the phosphor slurry `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.print.frit` _(medium)_

Without a glassy binder the phosphor dust would wipe off the panel at the first wipe. A low-melting glass frit, finely ground, is mixed into the slurry at 10-30% by weight and melts during the firing step to fuse the phosphor grains into a solid, adherent, moisture-resistant layer.

###### Firing at 430-450 degrees C `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.fire` _(medium)_

The printed panel goes into a conveyor oven. The organic vehicle decomposes and burns off completely, which is why the tunnel has to be exhausted, and the glass frit flows and wets the phosphor grains. Under-400 degrees leaves carbon in the layer; over 460 starts to attack the phosphor and shift the colour.

###### Vapour-deposited aluminium black layer `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium`

The single most important trick in a CRT. Without it, ambient light reflecting off the phosphor coating would lift the black level and the picture would look grey in a lit room. Aluminium is evaporated at better than 1e-4 mbar onto the phosphor; it is a mirror that passes 25 kV electrons but reflects visible light, so emitted light passes through while room light is bounced back out through the glass. Afterwards a thin dust-protection layer of a silicate or organosilicon compound is vapour-deposited on top of the aluminium, because bare aluminium under 25 kV slowly forms aluminium oxide.

              - *4N aluminium foil from bauxite* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.bauxite` *(seen above)*
###### Zinc sulphide from sphalerite concentrate `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns` _(medium)_

Zinc sulphide is the host crystal for all three P22 phosphors. It came from sphalerite, the zinc-iron sulphide ore, roasted in air to ZnO with the sulphur captured as SO2 for sulphuric acid. The ZnO was then converted back to high-purity ZnS, either by reacting with H2S or by reducing with hydrogen and re-sulphurising, because phosphor-grade sulphide has to be free of the iron and manganese that quench the emission.

###### Sphalerite concentrate, 50-60% Zn `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.sphalerite`

The world's zinc was a by-product of lead and copper mining: sphalerite is so closely associated with galena that the two are separated only by froth flotation. The concentrate came from underground or open-pit zinc-lead mines, and the roast's SO2 was the reason those mines mattered, because it was the cheapest industrial source of sulphuric acid for the fertiliser industry.

###### Electrolytic zinc from the roasted ZnO `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.sphalerite.electrolytic-zinc` _(medium)_

After roasting, the ZnO was leached in sulphuric acid to zinc sulphate and electrowon on aluminium cathodes at about 99.995% purity. The zinc was then either shipped as metal, or reduced to high-purity oxide and converted back to sulphide with H2S for phosphor use. The electrowinning cell and the smelter were the two ends of the same 1982 zinc plant.

###### Sulphur dioxide to sulphuric acid `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2`

The roaster's off-gas is cleaned, converted to SO3 on a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at about 450 degrees C and absorbed in 98% acid in a double-contact plant. It is the reason a 1982 zinc smelter had an acid plant as large as the roaster.

###### Sulphur feed, from sour natural gas `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfur` _(medium)_

Where a smelter did not have its own roast gas, elemental sulphur was produced from hydrogen sulphide in sour crude oil or sour natural gas, or by the Claus process. The sulphur then burned to make the SO2 the contact plant needed.

###### The Claus process for elemental sulphur `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.so2.sulfur.claus` _(medium)_

Where a zinc smelter had more roast gas than its contact plant could take, hydrogen sulphide was burned to make elemental sulphur in a Claus unit: two thermal reactors at 250-450 degrees C and a catalytic reactor over alumina at about 350 degrees C. The sulphur then went to a new roaster, which is why sour gas fields and zinc smelters were economically linked.

###### Natural gas, mostly methane `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.acrylonitrile.ammonia.gas`

Methane trapped in sedimentary rock, usually alongside the oil. It is the second leaf of this branch, alongside crude oil. Beyond feeding ammonia for the plastics in the cabinet, natural gas was the fuel for the tank furnaces that melted the television's own glass and the recovery ovens of every plating line in the supply chain.

###### Silver activator, from argentite `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver` _(medium)_

The blue ZnS is activated by silver at a fraction of a percent, supplied as silver nitrate. Silver itself came from argentite and from the anode slimes that accumulate in electrolytic copper refining, which is where most of the world's silver of the era was actually recovered.

###### Gold activator, from gold ore `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.gold` _(medium)_

The green ZnS:Au needs a discrete gold level about 0.1% down. The gold came from cyanide leaching of refractory ore and from the anode slimes of copper refining, refined by the Wohlwill process to 99.99% and dissolved in aqua regia.

###### Copper activator, from chalcopyrite `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.copper` _(medium)_

Copper, usually added as copper oxide, deepens the green and creates the donor level that the blue's co-activator needs. It came from copper concentrate, smelted and electrorefined to 99.99% copper and converted to CuO.

###### Europium (or calcium sulphide) for the red `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium` _(low)_

The 1980s red was the least settled of the three. CaS:Eu and Eu-doped ZnS were both in service; CaS:Eu has the better red chromaticity but is hygroscopic and needs protection from moisture. The europium came from bastnasite, a light rare-earth carbonate, cracked with acid and solvent-extracted to 99.9% europium oxide.

###### Shadow mask and aperture grille `peripheral.tv.crt.mask` _(medium)_

Without something to stop every beam landing on every phosphor, a CRT would be a monochrome tube with three faint colour washes. The shadow mask is a curved steel foil perforated with about 25,000 slots; the electron beam is steered so each of the three guns aims through the correct hole. The alternative is the aperture grille, two combs of tensioned vertical wires with no foil at all.

###### Cold-reduced low-carbon steel strip `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel` _(medium)_

Low-carbon sheet with very little residual stress, because a mask that warped would break the geometry. It comes off the hot strip mill, is cold-reduced to 0.1-0.2 mm in a reversing mill, annealed in a hydrogen or nitrogen atmosphere, and slit.

###### Blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf`

Sintered iron ore, coke and limestone are charged to a blast furnace at 1500-1600 degrees C. Hot metal comes out at about 4% carbon, is blown in a BOF to 0.05-0.1%, and is continuously cast into slabs that go to the hot strip mill.

###### Hematite and magnetite iron ore `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.ore`

Fe2O3 (hematite) and Fe3O4 (magnetite) are the two commercial ores. Hematite ships from the Pilbara and the Mesabi range as 62-66% Fe fines; magnetite ships as pellets from the Labrador Trough and as taconite concentrate from the Mesabi. Neither is chemically purified: the blast furnace does the chemistry.

###### Coke from coking coal `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.coke`

Metallurgical coke is made by destructive distillation of bituminous coal at about 1100-1200 degrees C in a battery of coke ovens. It supplies both the heat and the carbon for the reduction of iron oxide. Bituminous coal is the one fossil fuel in this chain that was not petroleum.

###### Photoetch of the slots `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.etch` _(medium)_

The flat sheet is cleaned, coated with photoresist, exposed through a master plate that defines every slot, developed, and etched. Ferric chloride is the etchant of the period for steel. After etching the sheet is washed, stress-relieved by heating, then pressed into a spherical section on a matched former, and the round holes open into slots as it bends.

###### Aperture grille (Trinitron-type) `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.grille` _(medium)_

The alternative to a foil: two combs of vertical wires under tension, typically nickel-chrome plated steel wire, at a 0.5-0.6 mm pitch. Because the mask is vertical wires only, the beam can strike them from any horizontal position, which gives the Trinitron its famous vertically sharp picture and lets the two outer guns share a defocus. Two thin damper wires keep the combs from ringing.

###### Electron gun, three guns `peripheral.tv.crt.gun`

Three parallel electron guns in one pinch, one per phosphor, each with a hot cathode, a control grid, a screen grid, a focus grid and an anode. In a 13 inch set of 1982 they were usually separate but adjacent, converging at the screen; the convergence magnets on the neck bent them into line and the electrostatic or magnetic focus brought the three spot sizes down to about 0.5-1.0 mm at the panel.

###### Oxide-coated cathode, Ba-Sr-Ca on nickel-chromium `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode` _(medium)_

A cup-shaped nickel-chromium alloy base, sprayed with barium, strontium and calcium carbonates fired to oxides, with a caesium or platinum-tantalum dispenser. The oxides are a thermionic emitter: work function about 2 eV against 4.5 eV for tungsten, which is why a cathode runs at 750-850 degrees C while a tungsten filament runs at 2500.

###### Nickel-chromium cathode base, and the barium source `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr` _(medium)_

The base metal is a nickel-chromium alloy because it does not react with the oxide and does not outgas badly in vacuum; the barium, strontium and calcium came from barium carbonate and strontium carbonate, both alkaline-earth salts. This is the same barium and strontium as the ferrite magnet in a loudspeaker and the barium getter in the neck, so one barite and strontinite mining chain served three parts of the same set.

###### Barite ore for the barium carbonate `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.barite` _(medium)_

Barium carbonate is made from barite (BaSO4), the same ore that is reduced to barium metal for the CRT getter and sintered into a speaker magnet. Barite is mined both as a vein fill (underground) and as a residual beach placer (open pit).

###### Converges on the nickel chain `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.cathode.nio-cr.nickel` _(medium)_

The same electrorefined 99.0-99.2% nickel cathode that went into the CRT grid foils and the permalloy head cores went into the cathode cup, where it had to be free of hydrogen because the cathode is heated in vacuum for thousands of hours.

###### Nickel sheet for the grid foil `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.nickel` _(medium)_

99%+ nickel, rolled to 0.02-0.1 mm, chosen because it has no gas to give up in vacuum and it does not sputter. Electroformed nickel was the higher-grade route. Nickel itself is refined from sulphide ore concentrate, usually laterite-derived or from pentlandite in Sudbury-type nickel iron sulphide.

###### Tungsten heater filament `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater`

A hair-fine tungsten wire folded into a flat zig-zag under the cathode cup and buried in its oxides. Typical wire 0.04-0.08 mm diameter, 60-150 mm long, running at 6.3 V. It is the only hot tungsten in the gun and by far the largest source of tube failure.

###### Tungsten wire from wolframite concentrate `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite` _(medium)_

Tungsten does not exist as a pure ore anywhere. Wolframite (Fe,Mn)WO4 and scheelite CaWO4 are decomposed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate to sodium tungstate, then to APT (ammonium paratungstate), then to tungsten trioxide reduced with hydrogen at 800-1000 degrees C to a fine powder, which is doped with potassium and drawn.

###### Tungsten mine and concentrator `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.wolframite.mine` _(medium)_

Wolframite is dense and refractory, so the ore is mined, crushed and gravity-concentrated or floated to a 60-70% WO3 concentrate. Because the ore is often a by-product of a tin or molybdenum mine, tungsten supply followed the fortunes of tin mining, and the price spiked hard whenever the tin market wobbled.

###### Scheelite (CaWO4) ore `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite` _(medium)_

The calcium tungstate ore, usually from scheelite skarn or from the Climax and Pine Creek molybdenum-tungsten porphyries. It decomposes in sodium carbonate or caustic, and its tungsten content is often a fraction of a percent of the rock, so the mill has to be big and the recovery obsessive.

###### Soda decomposition to sodium tungstate `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.decomp` _(medium)_

Scheelite has to be opened chemically because it is calcium tungstate and calcium is hard to leach. The ore is crushed and cooked with soda ash or caustic soda at about 900-1000 degrees C, converting it to sodium tungstate in solution; the calcium stays behind as calcium carbonate and the liquor is filtered. From sodium tungstate the APT intermediate is precipitated with ammonium chloride.

###### Soda ash from trona or salt `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.heater.scheelite.decomp.soda-ash` _(medium)_

The caustic in the scheelite and wolframite decompositions. In the 1980s most of the world's soda ash was made from trona (a sodium carbonate-bicarbonate double salt) in Wyoming by roasting and leaching, with the Solvay process from salt and limestone filling the rest. Both are diggings.

###### Rock salt, NaCl, for the chlorine `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.salt`

Salt was either mined from bedded evaporite (rock salt) or pumped as brine and evaporated in the sun (the Gulf Coast and the Cheshire salt towns). Electrolysis of the brine or of a saturated salt solution gives chlorine and sodium hydroxide, and the chlorine went into PVC jackets, into the chlorinated solvents used to clean printed circuit boards, and into the chloromethane blowing agent for cable foam.

###### Focus and screen grids, nickel sheet `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids` _(medium)_

The grid stack is a set of thin nickel foils laser-welded or spot-welded into a unit: G1 the Wehnelt and video modulator, G2 the screen grid at a few hundred volts, G3 the focus grid at 5-20% of the anode voltage, and the anode block itself in graphite or aluminium with a ceramic or mica spacer stack. Every surface is blackened.

              - *Nickel sheet for the grid foil* `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.nickel` *(seen above)*
###### Kovar, the Fe-Ni-Co lead-in glass match `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar` _(medium)_

A 29% Ni, 17% Co, 53% Fe alloy whose expansion matches a lead borosilicate glass. It is how the anode lead and the stem get sealed into the glass funnel without cracking the tube wall, and it is the same idea as the frit seal but metal instead of glass.

###### The iron and nickel behind Kovar `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar.inputs` _(medium)_

Kovar is 53% iron, 29% nickel and 17% cobalt, so it draws on the iron ore of the blast furnace, the nickel of the electrolytic refinery and the cobalt of the laterite or the Congo copper belt. Cobalt was a genuinely scarce metal in 1982 and set the price of the alloy.

                  - *Nickel sheet for the grid foil* `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.nickel` *(seen above)*
                  - *Hematite and magnetite iron ore* `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.ore` *(seen above)*
