###### Carbon blacking of the anode `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening` _(medium)_

The anode block and the inside of the funnel near the neck are flame-blacked with a sooty acetylene flame so that any stray electrons are absorbed rather than bouncing around the tube. Carbon black, the same pigment as in the cabinet and in a car's tyres, does the job here.

###### Carbon black, from petroleum coke `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.carbon-black`

Made by the oil method: heavy residual petroleum oil or the green oil from the cracker is sprayed into a hot gas flame at 1200-1900 degrees C, quenched, and the soot agglomerates are pelletised. Carbon black goes into tyres, into black cabinet pigment, into conductive paint and into the inside of the CRT.

###### Heavy petroleum oil (residual fuel oil) `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.carbon-black.oil`

The bottom of the barrel: what is left of crude oil after the refinery has taken the light fractions. A carbon black plant buys it on a fuel-oil price, so carbon black cost tracks crude directly.

###### Static focus coil on the neck `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.focus-coil` _(low)_

On the cheaper sets the three guns were focused by one small coil slipped over the neck outside the vacuum envelope, adjustable from the back of the set. Sets without static focus simply ran the focus grid at a fixed voltage and adjusted focus only for the corners with a convergence adjustment in the yoke.

###### Deflection yoke and deflection coils `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke`

A bell-shaped ferrite or powdered-iron core clamped on the tube neck carrying two orthogonal saddle windings. The horizontal winding is driven by the line output stage and sits in series with the flyback, so the scan current is the same current that steps up to 25 kV. The vertical winding is in the collector of the vertical output stage and carries a sawtooth at 60 Hz.

###### MnZn ferrite or powdered iron core `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core` _(medium)_

The yoke has to carry a 15 kHz sawtooth of several amps and not heat up, so the core is a high-permeability ferrite or a bonded powdered iron (ferrite dust in a phenolic or rubber binder), pressed and sintered. Ferrite is MnO with ZnO added to raise the saturation flux; powdered iron (Ferralium-type alloys) was used where saturation beat loss mattered.

###### Manganese oxide and manganese ore `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.core.manganese` _(medium)_

Most manganese ore went to steelmaking, but a small fraction of high-purity electrolytic manganese dioxide went into ferrite. The ore is a sedimentary or lateritic material and the metallurgical chain runs ore to manganous sulphate to electrowinning.

###### Enamelled copper winding, single harness `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding` _(medium)_

Copper wire, 0.2-0.4 mm, enamel-insulated and wound onto a bobbin with the horizontal coils outside and the vertical coils inside, then immersed in epoxy or polyurethane varnish to lock the winding rigidly. The hum-cancelling trick on the read head of a cassette deck has an ancestor here: the horizontal coils are arranged so their fields oppose.

###### Copper wire from chalcopyrite concentrate `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.copper`

A copper wire factory buys blister copper at 99.5% from a smelter, electrorefines it to 99.99% cathode, casts it into a wire-rod, then hot draws and cold draws. Enamelling is a coating of polyurethane or polyesterimide over polyester or a phenolic base, applied in a multiple-pass oven and then tested by a high-frequency spark test.

###### Chalcopyrite concentrate, 20-30% Cu `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.copper.ore`

CuFeS2, the dominant copper ore, concentrated to 20-30% by froth flotation and roasted and smelted. A 1982 colour TV contained on the order of a kilogram of copper: in the yoke, the line output transformer, the speaker voice coil, the field coils, the signal wiring and the mains lead. In 1982 about half the world's mined copper came from porphyry deposits in Chile and the US.

###### Glass-filled nylon bobbin `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin` _(medium)_

Yoke bobbins and coil formers were glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF30) because the winding runs hot and phenolic would crack. Nylon 6,6 comes from adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine, both from petroleum.

###### Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.nylon` _(medium)_

Adipic acid is made by oxidising a cyclohexanol/cyclohexanone mixture (KA oil) which itself is made by hydrogenating benzene; hexamethylenediamine comes from adiponitrile, made by hydrodimerisation of acrylonitrile. Both routes start from benzene, so nylon is a great-grandchild of crude oil.

###### KA oil: cyclohexanol from benzene `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.nylon.ka-oil` _(medium)_

Benzene is hydrogenated to cyclohexane (nickel or platinum catalyst, 150-220 degrees C, 15-30 bar), a fraction of it oxidised to a KA oil, then hydrogenated to cyclohexanol, then oxidised to adipic acid with nitric acid on a cobalt-catalyst process.

###### Benzene, from a catalytic reformer `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.nylon.ka-oil.benzene`

Benzene for chemicals was made by hydrodealkylating toluene or by extracting it from reformate, never by cracking straight to benzene, because the ring is hard to build. Reformate is a high-octane blend of naphtha from the refinery.

###### Conicity and geometry correction magnets `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry` _(medium)_

A 13 inch set with a 90 degree deflection had visible pincushion and barrel distortion. Correction was partly mechanical: a pair of small magnets on the neck that tilted the field to change the deflection centre, a static C-core for pincushion, and inside the flyback a 'geometry' winding that shapes the scan current. The customer-facing result was a V-hold, H-hold, width, height, linearity and convergence control on the back of the chassis, and on a cheap set a bright-line adjustment they could get wrong.

###### Alnico and samarium-cobalt correction magnets `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.geometry.magnets` _(medium)_

The small magnets that set the deflection centre and the geometry of a 1982 set were usually Alnico, an iron-aluminium-nickel alloy, or a small ferrite. Samarium-cobalt was the high-performance alternative but was too expensive and too new for a domestic set; it became standard in the small deflection magnets of the 1990s. Samarium is a rare earth, and the rare earths came from bastnasite.

                - *Europium (or calcium sulphide) for the red* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.europium` *(seen above)*
###### EHT / line output transformer (flyback) `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback`

The flyback does three jobs at once: it steps the 120 V B+ up to 20-25 kV for the anode, it develops the high flyback pulse that the line output transistor uses to make its collector current fall fast, and it carries auxiliary windings that supply the 12-25 V the gun heater, the tuner motor, the oscillator and the horizontal oscillator circuits need. In 1982 it was an open-frame transformer on a laminated or ferrite core, wrapped in epoxy and varnished, mounted on the chassis next to the tube neck with several hundred volts between it and everything else.

###### Ferrite E-I or C core `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.core` _(medium)_

An open-frame core of MnZn ferrite or powdered iron with a gapped section. The gap is deliberate: the flyback has to store a lot of field energy and be reset every line. The core is wound on a bobbin, then potted in epoxy so the 15 kHz and 25 kV windings cannot move.

###### Silicon EHT rectifier diode `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier` _(medium)_

A single high-voltage silicon diode, or a small stack of them, rated 3-10 kV reverse and 1-5 mA forward, potted in silicone rubber or epoxy so the 25 kV does not arc. The cathode end of the HV winding goes to the rectifier and the anode to the tube's anode terminal. A set with a failing EHT rectifier was a common and unpleasant repair.

###### High-purity silicon from quartz `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.silicon`

The EHT rectifier needed silicon of 200-1000 ohm cm with very low oxygen, because the junction had to hold 25 kV without leakage or breakdown. High-purity silicon is made by reducing trichlorosilane or silane, in the trichlorosilane route, from metallurgical silicon, which itself is made in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and coke.

###### Quartz (high-purity SiO2) for the arc furnace `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.hv-rectifier.silicon.quartz`

Metal-grade quartz, not glass sand. The furnace needs the silicon dioxide to be chemically clean enough that the reduction goes to 98-99% silicon in one pass. Quarried rock is crushed and purified by acid leaching to quartz, then reduced with coke in a submerged arc furnace where the arc itself is the furnace's only heat source.

###### Anode terminal: the lead burned through the funnel wall `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead`

The EHT gets into the tube through a metal button, usually a nickel or Kovar cup, sealed into the funnel wall with a glass frit and then fired. Above that terminal sits a silicone-rubber-covered anode cap that had to survive being touched with a screwdriver in a live set. A rubber anode cap failing was a genuine fire and electrocution hazard, and the safety information people remember about 1970s-80s TVs comes from exactly this part.

###### The glass-to-metal seal materials `peripheral.tv.crt.flyback.anode-lead.seal` _(medium)_

The anode button was a nickel or Kovar cup frit-sealed into the funnel wall, and the external cap was moulded silicone rubber. The seal frit was the same lead borosilicate as the panel seal, which is why the button had to be fired at the same 430-460 degrees C in the same continuous kiln as the tube.

                - *Lead borosilicate frit seal (about 24% PbO)* `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.frit` *(seen above)*
                - *Kovar, the Fe-Ni-Co lead-in glass match* `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.grids.kovar` *(seen above)*
###### Implosion protection and the safety faceplate `peripheral.tv.crt.implosion` _(medium)_

A colour TV tube holds about 0.5-1.5 tonnes per square metre of glass at a quarter atmosphere, and shatters into shards that will cut. Three defences: a laminate or thicker-than-necessary faceplate whose edges are the thickest part, a mask retaining ring that holds the faceplate to the frame rather than letting it come out, and a wraparound rim so the panel cannot pop forward. Cheap sets used less glass; expensive and safe sets used a tempered or laminated panel and, from the late 1970s, an implosion protection plate bonded to the front.

###### Evacuation, getter flash and exhaust tip `peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum` _(medium)_

The tube is evacuated on a manifold to better than 1e-6 mbar with a backing line of mechanical and diffusion pumps, tested with a spark-gap or ion gauge. Then the exhaust tip, a small tubulation drawn on the end of the funnel with a tantalum or aluminium-alloy cap welded over it, is opened with a glass break or an RF induction heater. The get, a flash of barium-titanium-palladium inside the neck, absorbs any remaining gas and then fixes a mirror-like barium film on the tube wall. The tip is then crushed flat and sealed.

###### Barium getter, from barite ore `peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.barium` _(medium)_

The getter is a thin foil strip of barium, titanium and palladium powder bonded with a glass frit in a nickel tube. When RF-heated it explodes in a burst of vacuum, sprays barium across the neck, and the barium burns and sticks to the glass as a mirror film. That film is the biggest vapour getter in the tube and turns residual gas into metal. Barium metal was made by reducing barite (BaSO4) with carbon or aluminium.

###### Tantalum exhaust tip, from coltan `peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.tantalum` _(medium)_

The exhaust tip cap has to be sealed by welding without oxidising and has to be gas-tight at 10^-7 mbar. Tantalum was chosen because it is refractory and forms its own oxide. It is also the material behind every solid-state tantalum capacitor, which is why a small 1980s television contributed a gram of coltan to a supply chain that later became a political problem.

###### Aluminium coating on the funnel wall `peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al` _(medium)_

A separate aluminium mirror, vapour-deposited on the inside of the funnel behind the gun, intended to bounce stray light back towards the phosphor and raise light output. It is distinct from the phosphor back layer, which is where the black level comes from. Modern practice replaced it with a black internal coating on the neck to absorb stray light instead, and moved efficiency to the phosphor and to tinted faceplate glass.

###### The aluminium foil that goes in the evaporator `peripheral.tv.crt.vacuum.rear-al.foil` _(medium)_

The same 0.1-0.15 mm four-nines aluminium foil used for the phosphor black layer, pinched to a wire in the evaporator and flashed off in the same pump run. One roll of 4N foil fed both the mirror behind the phosphor and the mirror behind the gun.

                - *4N aluminium foil from bauxite* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.bauxite` *(seen above)*
##### RF tuner, VHF and UHF `peripheral.tv.tuner`

The front end. In 1982 the US TV band was VHF channels 2-13 (55-220 MHz) and UHF 14-83 (470-890 MHz), and most sets had either a combined tuner or two side-by-side ones behind a single dial. A high-quality set used a rotary switch with a chain of interlocking contacts; a cheap one used a varactor diode and a small motor, or a continuous mechanical tuning with a motor and a rotor. Whatever the mechanism, the output was always the same: a fixed 45 MHz intermediate frequency.

###### VHF gangs: RF amplifier and mixer coils `peripheral.tv.tuner.vhf` _(medium)_

Two tuned circuits on ferrite cores: an RF amplifier and a mixer, both switched through a gang so they track. The coils are a few turns of enamelled copper on ferrite slug cores; the switch has a rotor with printed or wound inductors that tap through the band, and an AFC or motor to pull it into lock.

###### UHF tuner with varactor diode `peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf` _(medium)_

At 500-800 MHz a lumped LC circuit is hopeless, so the UHF tuner used a coaxial cavity or a stripline distributed resonator made of folded sheet metal, with a silicon varactor diode as the tuning element. Reverse-biasing the diode changed its junction capacitance from tens to a few picofarads, which moved the resonance across the band. A small DC motor rotated the cavity to track, or a servo pushed a varactor.

###### Varactor diode, silicon planar junction `peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.varactor` _(medium)_

A reverse-biased silicon pn junction used as a voltage-variable capacitor. At zero bias the depletion layer is thin and the capacitance is at its maximum; raising the reverse voltage widens the depletion layer and drops the capacitance. The diode is a small pill or a leaded axial part soldered into the cavity wall, and the DC bias arrives through a high-value resistor from the tuner supply.

###### Cavity resonator, brass or nickel-plated steel `peripheral.tv.tuner.uhf.cavity` _(medium)_

The UHF resonant circuit is a piece of metal: folded sheet or machined brass forming a half-wavelength line, with the shunt capacitance of the varactor at the open end and a tap for the transistor. This is one of the few places in a television where the RF circuit is metal rather than a PCB, because at 800 MHz a printed board would radiate. Brass came from zinc and copper ores.

###### RF amplifier and mixer `peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end`

A low-noise bipolar or MOSFET amplifier at the antenna frequency, then a mixer down to 45 MHz. In 1982 the RF device was often a silicon planar MOSFET (dual-gate, for the UHF) or a wideband bipolar. The whole RF section lived in a die-cast or stamped zinc-plated steel can to keep it away from the switching supply and the line output.

###### SAW filter at 45 MHz `peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw`

By the early 1980s a SAW (surface acoustic wave) filter had largely replaced the LC or ceramic filter in the IF path. Two interdigital transducers on a piezoelectric crystal launch and pick up an acoustic wave along the surface; the finger pattern is designed to pass the wanted band and reject the adjacent channel, sound and colour carriers. It gave a picture with no intermodulation and no cross modulation between the picture, colour and sound carriers.

###### Lithium niobate wafer from spodumene `peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithium` _(medium)_

The acoustic medium. Spodumene (LiAlSi2O6) ore is beneficiated and converted to lithium carbonate by sulphuric acid roasting; the carbonate is reacted with niobium pentoxide from pyrochlore (columbite-tantalite) tantalum residue in a lithium hydroxide or carbonate flux at 1000-1200 degrees C to grow Czochralski crystals of LiNbO3, which are sliced and polished to a 0.25-1 mm wafer. In 1982 much of the world's LiNbO3 came from Japanese and Chinese plants, with the tantalum industry as the source of the columbite residue.

###### Spodumene pegmatite ore `peripheral.tv.tuner.front-end.saw.lithium.spodumene` _(medium)_

A lithium aluminium silicate, 6.0-7.0% Li2O, that occurs in granitic pegmatites and is mined in enormous tonnages because a lithium battery plant in 1982 needed thousands of tonnes a year. Roasting with sulphuric acid turns it into lithium sulphate, and the impurity that everyone fights is iron.

###### Die-cast zinc or stamped steel RF can `peripheral.tv.tuner.can` _(medium)_

The tuner and front end were a sealed metal can soldered to the main board. On a cheap set it was a stamped zinc-plated steel can; on a good one a die-cast zinc or aluminium can with a machined seam. Zinc plating comes from zinc electroplating baths, so it is the same zinc industry as the galvanised chassis.

###### Zinc electroplate on the RF can `peripheral.tv.tuner.can.zinc` _(medium)_

The stamped steel RF can was plated in a zinc sulphate or zinc chloride bath with an aluminium or steel anode, then often given a chromate passivation. Zinc plating is cheap corrosion protection and it is the same zinc industry as the CRT phosphor and the die-cast tuner body.

              - *Sphalerite concentrate, 50-60% Zn* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.sphalerite` *(seen above)*
###### Dial cord and pulley gear train `peripheral.tv.tuner.dial-cord`

The channel knob turned a pulley that wound a braided cord onto another pulley geared to the tuner rotor. It was a real mechanical system that stretched, slipped and broke, and it is the reason every vintage-TV owner has a drawer of spare dial cords. The cord was a braided polyester or nylon sheath over a cotton core.

##### The chassis: video, sync, line output, audio `peripheral.tv.chassis`

The electronics of the set. By 1982 this was a single-sided or double-sided printed circuit board carrying a mix of discrete transistors, a handful of silicon integrated circuits (the video amplifier, the chroma, the vertical, the audio), a rotary switch bank and about forty electrolytic and film capacitors. The board sat in a zinc-plated steel chassis with a perforated steel cover, and the flyback sat beside it throwing both heat and electromagnetic noise.

###### FR-4 epoxy-glass printed circuit board `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb`

Glass-reinforced epoxy laminate with a copper foil laminated to each side and printed photolithographically. The glass fibre is the reason FR-4 has a low, controlled thermal expansion; the epoxy binds it. It is drilled, plated through with copper, mask-printed and silkscreened.

###### E-glass fibre from silica sand `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.glass` _(medium)_

The reinforcement is a textile of drawn glass filament: silica sand is melted in a bushing at 1400 degrees C, drawn to a fibre a few microns across, and woven into cloth. It is the same silica as the tank window glass, run through a different furnace.

###### The silica the E-glass comes from `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.glass.sand` _(medium)_

E-glass cloth is drawn from the same quartz sand as the television's own faceplate glass, at a slightly different composition with a little boron and calcium to lower the softening point of the fine filament. One silica mining and glass-melting industry supplied the picture tube, the circuit board and the yarn on the speaker cone.

                - *Quartz sand (SiO2) for the glass batch* `peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.silica` *(seen above)*
###### Epoxy resin from bisphenol A `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.epoxy` _(medium)_

The resin that glues the glass in FR-4 is an epoxy, made from bisphenol A (itself from two mols of phenol and acetone) and epichlorohydrin. It cures by cross-linking rather than by condensation, which is what gives FR-4 its low shrinkage and high heat resistance.

###### Bisphenol A from phenol and acetone `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.epoxy.bpa` _(medium)_

Phenol comes from benzene sulphonation or cumene oxidation; acetone comes from cumene or from propylene oxide. Bisphenol A is the condensation of two phenols with one acetone under acid, and by the late 1980s this single molecule would become the centre of a long-running regulatory argument about plastics and hormone disruption.

###### Electrolytic copper foil, 35 micrometres `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.copper-foil`

The copper that becomes every trace on the board. Electrolytic copper foil is deposited on a rotating drum cathode from a copper sulphate bath, then treated with a nodularisation pass so the reverse side bonds to the epoxy. It is the same copper as the yoke wire, one step earlier in the chain.

###### Solder mask and silkscreen legend `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.mask`

After etching, the whole board is flooded with a green or brown epoxy solder mask, and only the pads are left open. Then white legend ink is silkscreened through a fine mesh for the reference designators. The mask material is itself an epoxy, and the legend ink is a screen-printable ink with a solvent carrier, one of the few places in a television where an ink is cured rather than melted.

###### HASL: tin-lead solder on the pads `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating` _(medium)_

The board was dipped or dragged through a molten bath of 60/40 tin-lead, which left a solder film on the pads and bridged the copper under the mask. Immersion tin plating or gold-flash were also used, but a television of 1982 was overwhelmingly hot-tin-dipped. Tin from cassiterite, lead from galena, both of which are already in this tree.

###### Tin from cassiterite (SnO2) `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating.cassiterite` _(medium)_

Cassiterite is a heavy mineral at 7 g/cm3, so it concentrates by gravity or by froth flotation with an amine collector. It is carbothermically smelted with carbon or coke at 1200-1300 degrees C to crude tin, refined by liquation and electrolysis to 99.9% tin. Tin was also the metal plating on the inside of food cans, which is why the same ore supplied the solder and the can.

###### Video chain: IF, detector, video amp, colour `peripheral.tv.chassis.video`

The 45 MHz IF is amplified, limited, then detected: the video signal rides on the picture carrier at 45.75 MHz, the colour subcarrier sits 3.58 MHz below it as a sideband, and the sound carrier sits 9 MHz above at 54.75 MHz. The synchronous detector recovers the baseband video; a PLL multiplies the recovered 3.58 MHz subcarrier up and phase-shifts it 90 degrees to drive the two demodulators; the result is U and V, added back to luminance to give R, G and B, which drive the gun cathodes.

###### Silicon integrated circuit, 4-micron NMOS `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic` _(medium)_

The video, chroma and audio functions in a 1982 set were often one or two chips of 40 to 80 pins, made on a 4-5 micron NMOS or bipolar process. The die is a slice of 99.99% silicon, oxidised, photolithographically patterned through eight to ten mask steps, and packaged in epoxy or ceramic. Purity, oxide quality and aluminium interconnect over a polysilicon gate is the whole story of the 4-micron generation.

###### Silicon wafer, P-type, 99.99% `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die`

The same trichlorosilane and Siemens process as the EHT rectifier gave the wafer, then it was doped p-type with boron to build a pn substrate and n-epitaxy grown on top for the bipolar transistors. A 4-micron process of 1982 was a 100 or 125 mm wafer. Note the silicon itself came from the same quartz-to-metal-to-trichlorosilane chain documented under the EHT rectifier; the difference here is the epitaxy and the oxide.

###### Discrete IF, driver and video transistors `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors` _(medium)_

Most transistors in a 1982 set were discrete: a high-gain IF transistor, the video driver, the video output transistors, the horizontal oscillator and driver, the vertical output, the audio output, and the horizontal output. Each is a tiny die, 10-40 transistors, wire-bonded to a plastic or metal can. Metal-can transistors (TO-18) were still common in the IF and video stages where heat and shielding mattered.

###### The transistor die and its package `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.transistors.die` _(medium)_

A small-signal NPN transistor is a few hundred square microns of silicon, aluminium metallised, mounted on a header and sealed in epoxy or metal. The die itself is a slice of the same 99.99% wafer as the video IC, cut with a diamond-impregnated wheel and diced on a saw.

                - *Silicon wafer, P-type, 99.99%* `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die` *(seen above)*
###### Automatic gain control `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.agc` _(medium)_

The AGC samples the DC level off the video detector and feeds a reverse bias back to the first two IF stages, holding the picture bright whether the aerial is good or the C64 modulator is a milliwatt away from nothing. This was the one part of a TV that genuinely cared about the C64 signal, because a C64 was a much weaker source than a broadcast station and the AGC had to find a way to open up. A key-operated AGC defeat, or a 'manual gain' switch, was a modification for fringe-area reception.

###### Horizontal line output stage, 15,734 Hz `peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out`

The heart of the set's power and geometry. The line oscillator runs at 15,734 Hz; the driver and the output transistor switch the flyback primary, so the collector current rises linearly during scan and then collapses in the flyback retrace. The flyback uses that collapse to develop a high-voltage pulse, rectified to the EHT. The same transformer runs back through the damper to create a 200-250 V pump rail for the video output stage. In 1982 this was usually a discrete silicon EFT (a triple-diffused or a high-voltage epitaxial transistor) because a single silicon transistor could not safely switch a 900 V collector at 15.7 kHz.

###### Line oscillator and AFC `peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.oscillator`

A free-running LC oscillator locked to the incoming video by a sync separator and an automatic frequency control loop. When the set was fed a C64 signal it was free-running off the internal oscillator and being pulled by the modulator's sync; it could not lock to a broadcast, so it did not drift. Most of the visible misbehaviour of a C64 on a TV (rolling, tearing, drifting) came from this loop or from the modulator's own sync, not from the computer.

###### Line choke or choke-and-flyback combination `peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.choke` _(medium)_

Some sets had a separate choke, some combined the choke with the flyback into one transformer. The choke carries the DC component of the line current and presents a high impedance to the 15.7 kHz pulse. It was an iron-powder or ferrite part with a thousand volts across it and was a common failure.

###### EHT rectifier and capacitor `peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hvt` _(medium)_

After the flyback, a single silicon rectifier at 25 kV. On larger sets a doubler or tripler with plastic film capacitors at 2-5 kV each was used. The current was tiny (1-2 mA) so the capacitors were small in value but enormous in voltage rating, and their failure mode was spectacular and occasionally violent.

###### High-voltage film capacitor `peripheral.tv.chassis.line-out.hv-caps` _(medium)_

A metallised polypropylene or polystyrene film capacitor rated at kilovolts. The film is stretched polypropylene, metallised with a thin aluminium or zinc layer, wound, and the whole thing impregnated and potted. Zinc metallising was cheap and equivalent to aluminium for small values; aluminium became standard for reliability.

###### Vertical output stage, 60 Hz `peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical`

The vertical sweep at 60 Hz. The oscillator ran at twice the line rate and a count-down circuit divided by two, a design that keeps the vertical locked to the horizontal. The output stage amplified a small ramp and drove the vertical yoke, with a small electrolytic capacitor across the coil to correct the crosstalk that coupling into the horizontal yoke produced. A IC did most of this, with one or two power transistors at the output.

###### Vertical IC `peripheral.tv.chassis.vertical.ic` _(medium)_

A single IC contained the oscillator, the count-down divider, the ramp generator and the driver, needing only two or three external transistors. It was one of the first large consumer uses of a mixed-analogue IC that made a television much easier to build, and it is the reason a 1982 TV was a single-board affair.

###### Audio: 4.5 MHz intercarrier to a speaker `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio`

The sound carrier is taken off the same IF strip at 54.75 MHz, recovered at 4.5 MHz above the video, limited and FM-demodulated, then amplified. The 4.5 MHz intercarrier was chosen so the sound did not interfere with the video and to let the sound survive a picture cut-off (the 'intercarrier' idea). Amplified to a few watts into an 8 ohm speaker, or about 2 W per speaker into two 8 ohm speakers in parallel. The C64's audio came out of this amplifier, which is why it was loud, thin and slightly buzzy.

###### Sound traps and SAW `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.traps`

The 4.5 MHz intercarrier has to be lifted out of the video baseband without disturbing the 3.58 MHz colour subcarrier, so a trap or SAW filter at 4.5 MHz ran between the video detector and the audio detector. A ceramic or SAW trap on 4.5 MHz was a very visible part in a 1982 set.

###### Audio output amplifier `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp` _(medium)_

An integrated amplifier (a few watts, a single 8-14 pin IC) or a discrete predriver plus two complementary power transistors pushing 5-20 W peak into 8 ohms from a 115 V rail. The output stage ran in class B or class AB, and the bias and the idle current were the main design problem.

###### The output power transistor `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.amp.power-device` _(medium)_

The device that actually pushed the current into the speaker: an NPN/PNP complementary pair on a thick die in a TO-3 or plastic power package, bolted to the chassis as its own heatsink. From 1990s multisilicon dice replaced the single-crystal die, but a 1982 set had one transistor per output channel.

                - *Silicon wafer, P-type, 99.99%* `peripheral.tv.chassis.video.ic.die` *(seen above)*
###### Volume potentiometer, carbon track `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot`

A rotary carbon track pot, typically 10 kohm or 100 kohm logarithmic (audio taper), spliced into the audio line. The track is a carbon film printed or sprayed on a phenolic or ceramic substrate; the wiper is a sprung brass or copper blade. This is the same technology as the volume control in a pocket radio, and the carbon comes from petroleum coke exactly as the CRT blackening does.

###### Carbon track from petroleum coke `peripheral.tv.chassis.audio.volume-pot.carbon` _(medium)_

A mix of graphite and carbon black in a resin or ceramic binder, screen-printed onto the substrate and fired. Carbon track pots were cheap, noisy and prone to wear, and a 'crackle' as the volume control was turned was a common household complaint. Cermet (metal oxide) track came in for better pots, and the two technologies coexisted for decades.

###### Power supply: mains transformer and reservoir `peripheral.tv.chassis.power`

Most 1982 sets were linear: a hot-chassis or a cold-chassis series/parallel mains transformer stepping 117 V down to about 110 V AC, a diode bridge rectifier, and a big electrolytic reservoir at 120 V feeding the line output. The main electrolytic was the largest, hottest component on the board and usually the first thing to dry out. A minority used a small switchmode supply for the logic rails with a flyback of its own.

###### Mains transformer, E-I silicon steel `peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer`

A laminated core of thin silicon steel (about 0.35 mm) stamped into E and I shapes and stacked, with copper windings on bobbins, potted in epoxy or wrapped in tape and varnished. The laminations were needed because mains hum would otherwise magnetostrict the core; the 1982 design was exactly the design from the 1930s.

###### Aluminium electrolytic reservoir, 200 microfarad 160 V `peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir`

The reservoir is a wound aluminium foil anode with an oxide film formed on it, an aluminium cathode can, and a paper or synthetic-fibre separator soaked in electrolyte (an ammonium borate or an aluminium chloride solution in glycol). Formed at a few hundred volts, it hums and it leaks, and in a hot chassis it did the most to kill itself.

###### Etched high-purity aluminium foil `peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir.al-foil` _(medium)_

The anode foil is 99.99% aluminium, electrochemically roughened in a chloride bath so the effective surface area is tens of times the geometric area, allowing a 200 microfarad, 160 V capacitor to fit in a 25 mm can. It converges on the same four-nines aluminium chain as the CRT's aluminium foil.

###### Mains rectifier bridge `peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge`

Four silicon diodes in a moulded bridge package, rated at a few amps and 100-200 V. Cheap sets rectified with two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer instead. The bridge was usually on the chassis edge with the heatsink tab or in free air.

##### Loudspeaker, 8 ohm, 3-4 inch `peripheral.tv.speaker`

An 8 ohm speaker of about 3.5-4 inch diameter on a small set: a paper pulp cone, a pressed steel or plastic basket, a copper voice coil on a former, and a ferrite magnet. It was screwed to a baffle in the cabinet with the back magnet projecting into whatever space was left, which is why small speakers of the period often had a shallow magnet or a rear vent.

###### Paper pulp cone `peripheral.tv.speaker.cone`

The cone is a paper pulp: refined wood fibre pressed wet into a shaped blank and dried, giving a light, stiff, cheap diaphragm. It is essentially the same material as a paper bag, which is why it creases if you poke it. A small set used a paper cone; a later or better one a woven or moulded polypropylene cone.

###### Pressed steel basket `peripheral.tv.speaker.basket` _(medium)_

The cone is glued to a stamped steel basket that holds the magnet and the voice coil in register. It came off the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, with the same iron ore behind it.

###### Cold-reduced low-carbon steel for the basket `peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.steel` _(medium)_

The basket was stamped or drawn from the same low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, because it needed stiffness at low cost. The whole speaker weighed less than a kilogram and used perhaps 200 g of steel.

              - *Cold-reduced low-carbon steel strip* `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel` *(seen above)*
###### Ferrite magnet `peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet` _(medium)_

A ring or cup magnet of barium or strontium ferrite, sintered and magnetised across the gap. Barium ferrite needed barium carbonate, which is why barite mining also fed speakers. Ferrite, not Alnico, was the standard by 1982 because it was cheap and had a higher coercivity.

###### Copper voice coil on a former `peripheral.tv.speaker.voice-coil` _(medium)_

Two layers of enamelled copper wire, about 40-60 turns, wound on a paper or aluminium former and centred in the magnet gap. It is a minute amount of copper, on the order of a gram, and it sits in a gap of under a millimetre.

##### Cabinet and front bezel `peripheral.tv.cabinet`

The outside of the set: a moulded plastics shell wrapped around the chassis and the tube, with a wood-grain print or a real veneer. A 1982 13 inch set was typically an injection-moulded ABS or ABS/polycarbonate cabinet, textured, with the front bezel carrying the speaker grille, the control knobs and the brand badge. Larger and older-style sets had a wood-veneered or wood-framed cabinet; the very cheapest had a printed paper laminate over a steel or plastic shell.

###### ABS resin `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs`

Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix with polybutadiene rubber grafted on. The acrylonitrile gives chemical and heat resistance, the butadiene gives toughness and impact strength, and the styrene gives the surface gloss and the rigidity. A television cabinet was usually ABS with a flame retardant, or a polycarbonate-ABS blend for the parts around the tube.

###### Styrene and SAN matrix `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene` _(medium)_

Styrene comes from ethylbenzene, which comes from benzene by alkylation with ethylene and then is dehydrogenated. Benzene is itself from a refinery reformer, so a plastics cabinet is a great-grandchild of crude oil three steps away.

###### Benzene from catalytic reforming `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbons for the chemical industry came out of the refinery, not out of the well. Naphtha was reformed over platinum at 450-520 degrees C to rearrange straight-chain paraffins into aromatics, benzene among them, which were then extracted with a solvent such as sulfolane or diethylene glycol.

###### Naphtha fraction from crude oil `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene.naphtha`

The light, colourless fraction of crude, roughly 30 to 200 degrees C boiling, separated in an atmospheric or vacuum distillation column. Naphtha was the feedstock for essentially all of the aromatic chemicals and, in the cracker, for all of the alkenes. A 1982 television drew on crude oil at least six times over: the cabinet, the tape, the case, the connectors, the solder and the black.

###### Atmospheric and vacuum distillation `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene.naphtha.distillation`

Crude is heated to about 350-400 degrees C and fractionated in a tall column, the top of which gives naphtha, the middle kerosene and diesel, and the bottom residue. The residue is then vacuum-distilled at 30-50 mmHg to lift the heavy gas oil. Almost every synthetic organic chemical in the electronics supply chain starts at the top of one of these columns.

###### Crude oil, the leaf of this tree `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene.naphtha.crude`

A mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons, asphaltic and paraffinic, plus sulphur, nitrogen and metals, drawn from sedimentary basins where ancient organic matter was buried and cooked. Everything organic in a 1982 electronics chain - plastics, solder flux, black paint, solvents, lubricants, insulation, the fibre in the speaker cone - starts here. This is a leaf: you can buy it or pump it out of the ground.

###### The well that fills the distillation column `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene.naphtha.crude.ofshore` _(medium)_

By 1982 most of the light crude the electronics industry bought came from offshore fields in the North Sea, the Gulf of Mexico and the Arabian Gulf, produced from steel jackets or concrete gravity structures, and from onshore fields with water or steam injection to hold up the pressure. A single barrel is about 159 litres and a large field produced millions of barrels a day.

###### 1,3-butadiene from the steam cracker `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.butadiene` _(medium)_

The rubbery part of ABS. It is not made from natural rubber but by cracking butane or the C4 fraction of a naphtha cracker, and by 1982 the biggest source was the co-product gas of a large steam cracker, which is why ABS prices tracked ethylene capacity.

###### Acrylonitrile, and the ammonia it needs `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.acrylonitrile` _(medium)_

Acrylonitrile was made by the Sohio process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen over a bismuth-antimony catalyst at about 450 degrees C to give acrylonitrile and water. The ammonia came from steam reforming natural gas, so the plastics chain and the gas chain converge here.

###### Ammonia from natural gas, steam reforming `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.acrylonitrile.ammonia`

Natural gas is mostly methane. It is mixed with steam, desulphurised, and passed over a nickel catalyst at 700-900 degrees C to give hydrogen and carbon monoxide; a second reformer shifts the carbon monoxide with more steam to give hydrogen and carbon dioxide. Nitrogen from a second air reformer is mixed back in, and the whole mixture is compressed and taken through a synthesis loop at 200-300 degrees C and 150-300 bar to give ammonia.

                - *Natural gas, mostly methane* `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.acrylonitrile.ammonia.gas` *(seen above)*
###### Pigment: titanium dioxide and carbon black `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.pigment` _(medium)_

A beige or brown cabinet was pigmented. The workhorse was titanium dioxide, rutile grade, a white pigment made from ilmenite or from ore plus a chloride process; the black or dark brown was carbon black. A woodgrain was printed, not pigmented.

###### Titanium dioxide from ilmenite ore `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.pigment.ilmenite` _(medium)_

Ilmenite (FeTiO3) was smelted with coke in a fluid bed or an electric furnace to give titanium slag, then chlorinated with chlorine and carbon to give TiCl4, which was oxidised in a flame at 900-1500 degrees C to rutile pigment. It went into the cabinet, into white paint and into the paper the instructions were printed on.

###### Injection moulding of the cabinet `peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding`

ABS pellets were dried, melted at 230-260 degrees C, injected into a nickel-chromium plated steel mould at 1000-2000 bar, held under pressure to pack, cooled on a water circuit and ejected. The cabinet was a single moulding with the speaker grille, the bezel ledges, the screw bosses and the airflow slots all integral; the front bezel was often a separate moulding in a different colour. A 13 inch set's mould ran 10,000 to a few hundred thousand shots.

###### P20 pre-hardened tool steel `peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.tool-steel`

The mould is made from a pre-hardened alloy steel, typically 0.38% carbon with chromium, molybdenum and nickel, supplied at about 30-35 HRC so it needs no final heat treatment and can be ground and polished to a texture. The plating is electroless nickel, 3-8 microns, then polished, then a hard chrome or a fine texture etch for the leather grain.

###### Wood veneer or woodgrain laminate `peripheral.tv.cabinet.wood` _(medium)_

A console or a large set of the early 1980s was often a real cabinet: a wood frame veneered with walnut, mahogany or teak, sometimes over particle board. The cheaper route was a printed polyester or melamine laminate, several sheets laminated and printed with a photographic woodgrain. A 13 inch portable used moulded ABS with the grain embossed into the mould texture and painted.

###### Case screws and brackets `peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws` _(medium)_

The chassis was fastened into the cabinet with self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, and the back was held with a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. The brackets that carried the tube and the board were zinc-plated sheet steel.

###### Zinc plating on the case screws `peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-plating` _(medium)_

Self-tapping screws into plastic bosses and a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. Zinc plating is the cheapest corrosion protection for a small steel part and it came off the same zinc chain as everything else in this branch.

              - *Sphalerite concentrate, 50-60% Zn* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.sphalerite` *(seen above)*
###### Brand badge and control knobs `peripheral.tv.cabinet.badge` _(medium)_

The logo badge was an embossed or plated plastic medallion, and the knobs were moulded ABS or phenolic on a zinc or aluminium die-cast core with a moulded pointer. On a cheap set the badge was printed; on a good one it was a plated plastic insert.

##### Front controls: pots, switches, dial `peripheral.tv.controls`

Brightness, contrast, colour, tint, volume and the channel selector, plus a fine-tuning and a V-hold behind the cabinet. The pots are carbon track or cermet; the switches are an AC line switch and often a rotary band switch or push-buttons for the a/v functions.

###### Phenolic resin for the pot bodies `peripheral.tv.controls.phenolic` _(medium)_

Phenolic (Bakelite) moulded in a compression press at 150-180 degrees C, using phenol and formaldehyde. Phenol came from cumene oxidation or benzene sulphonation, so it is petroleum; formaldehyde came from methanol, which came from natural gas. Phenolic was used because it would not soften near a hot chassis.

###### AC line switch and interlock `peripheral.tv.controls.switch` _(medium)_

A rotary or push-pull mains switch on the front panel, often interlocked so that a set with a back cover off could not be switched on (the 'interlock' on a portable). The switch contacts were silver-plated brass, and the whole switch was a snap-action mechanism in a phenolic body.

###### Silver-plated switch contacts `peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver` _(medium)_

Mains switch and rotary tuner contacts were silver-plated brass or copper, because silver has the highest conductivity of any metal and does not oxidise. Silver plating was applied from a cyanide or an acid bath, and the silver itself came overwhelmingly from the anode slimes of copper refining.

              - *Silver activator, from argentite* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver` *(seen above)*
###### VHF dial and channel drum `peripheral.tv.controls.vhf-dial` _(medium)_

The channel numbers were on a printed drum or card behind a window, or on a flat dial plate, driven by the cord from the knob. The UHF channels 14-83 needed a drum or a fan-shaped card because there were 70 of them, which is why UHF dials of the period were a distinctive piece of mechanical design.

##### Aerial input and antenna lead `peripheral.tv.aerial`

The 75 ohm coaxial aerial socket at the back, the twin-lead alternative for indoor aerials, and the telescopic whip on a portable. The C64 was plugged into that socket, in parallel with whatever aerial the set had. The socket was either a threaded F-type, or a cheaper bayonet or push-on type in Europe.

###### F-type coaxial connector `peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector` _(medium)_

A threaded, quarter-turn connector for 75 ohm coax, usually brass with a nickel or cadmium plate and a dielectric insert of PTFE or polyethylene. Brass is copper-zinc, so this little part pulls from both the copper and the zinc industry; the zinc can also be the zinc plated steel shell.

###### Brass from copper and zinc `peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.brass` _(medium)_

Brass is melted from cathode copper and zinc ingot, roughly 60/40 for free-cutting brass, and cast or extruded into fittings. The zinc came from sphalerite and the copper from chalcopyrite, both already in this branch.

###### Coaxial or twin-lead antenna lead `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax` _(medium)_

RG-59 or RG-6 coax: a copper or tinned copper braid, a polyethylene or PTFE dielectric, and a solid copper centre conductor. RG-59 is 52 ohm and was what an indoor or a bench lead of the era was. The alternative was 300 ohm flat twin-lead, which matched indoor dipoles and did not need coax. The polyethylene in the coax came from ethylene, which came from the cracker, which came from naphtha and from crude.

###### Polyethylene from ethylene, and the salt that made the chlorine `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene` _(medium)_

Polyethylene is polymerised from ethylene, which comes from a steam cracker on naphtha. Where the chlorination route was used (for PVC or for the chloromethane that goes into the foam blowing), the chlorine came from salt electrolysis. Both the polymer and the chlorine are therefore descendants of crude oil and of halite, and both branches meet in the cable jacket.

              - *Rock salt, NaCl, for the chlorine* `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.salt` *(seen above)*
###### Telescopic whip antenna `peripheral.tv.aerial.whip` _(medium)_

On a portable set, a telescopic whip: a chrome-plated steel rod in a plastic base, with a ball joint for the angle. It was a whip antenna for VHF, and on UHF-only portables it was a loop inside the cabinet.

###### Chrome plating on the whip rod `peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating` _(medium)_

A telescopic rod plated in hard chrome over nickel, in several decorative layers so it could be extended and retracted thousands of times without wearing through. The chrome came from chromite ore, the same ore that made the chromium dioxide in a Type II cassette tape.

###### Chromite ore, FeCr2O4 `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.chromite`

Chromite is the only economic chromium ore, a spinel of iron and chromium oxide at 45-50% Cr2O3, mined from the Bushveld Complex and from layered intrusions. It was smelted to ferrochrome, the alloy in stainless steel, and the same ore fed the pigment chemistry.

##### Mains lead, filter and fuse `peripheral.tv.mains`

A 1982 set had a two or three core mains lead, an entrapment and bypass capacitor for radio interference, and one or two fuses. The mains filter is the reason a television did not buzz on an AM radio, and the reason the plastic of a 1980s set smelled faintly of phenolic. The fuse was a small glass or ceramic cartridge with a wire or a metal link.

###### Mains cord, PVC jacket over stranded copper `peripheral.tv.mains.cord` _(medium)_

A flexible cord of 16 or 18 AWG stranded copper inside a PVC or rubber jacket, moulded on to the plug and to the set's inlet. The set's inlet on a 1982 television was not an IEC C13 appliance coupler (that became common on computers and later sets); most were a hard-wired rubber or vinyl cord straight into the chassis, with a moulded two-pin or three-pin plug at the wall end. A detachable cord on a set was unusual until the mid 1980s.

###### Mains suppression: X capacitor and common-mode choke `peripheral.tv.mains.filter` _(medium)_

A high-voltage capacitor across line and neutral (the X capacitor) plus a ferrite-beaded choke in series, to keep the set's switching noise out of the radio. In a 1982 set this was often a paper or film capacitor at 0.01 microfarad rated for mains transients; the modern purple or orange epoxy-drop X capacitor of the 1990s had not appeared, though a metallised film in a plastic case was used. The choke was a few turns on a ferrite or powdered-iron core.

###### Metallised polypropylene mains capacitor `peripheral.tv.mains.filter.metallised-film` _(medium)_

A polypropylene or polystyrene film, vacuum-metallised with a thin aluminium layer on both faces, wound and potted in epoxy. It was the capacitor of choice across the line because a self-healing metallisation would recover from a mains transient rather than failing short. Polystyrene was also used for its stability and low microphonics.

###### Fuse and buss fuse `peripheral.tv.mains.fuse` _(medium)_

A 3-4 amp buss fuse in the mains lead holder on sets with a detachable cord, or an internal fuse on the line. The fuse element was a low-melting alloy or a silver wire in a glass cartridge.

###### Glass cartridge and silver fuse wire `peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material` _(medium)_

A small glass or ceramic cartridge containing a link of silver or of a fusible alloy such as a lead-bismuth-tin eutectic, in a sand or chalk packing that quenched the arc when the link melted. The glass was soda-lime, drawn as a tube and sealed with an end cap.

              - *Silver activator, from argentite* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver` *(seen above)*
#### Datasette and cassette `peripheral.cassette`

A C64 with no drive could not save. Commodore's answer was a 1530 or 1541 disk-shaped drive that took ordinary compact cassettes and wrote them with a magnetic head at 9,600 baud, plus a spool of tape that was mostly polyester film and mostly iron oxide. Saving a 1541 program to tape was a two minute operation of real-time winding, and the alignment problems of a 1541 were a running joke precisely because a cassette had no feedback.

##### The 1541 disk drive `peripheral.cassette.deck`

A disk-shaped grey box with a slot on top, containing a stepper motor, a capstan flywheel, a read/write head on a load arm, and a small circuit board with a 6502 CPU, a 6522 interface chip and a mask-programmed logic array. It reads and writes the same standard compact cassette as a music cassette deck, which is why Commodore's error messages included CLOAD and why a music cassette recorder could in principle play a C64 tape.

###### 6502 CPU, 6522 PIA and M50174 PLA `peripheral.cassette.deck.logic` _(medium)_

The 1541's electronics are almost identical in content to the C64's, which is not a coincidence: Commodore reused its own chips. A 6502 runs the operating system and the serial protocol; a 6522 versatile interface adapter talks to the tape, drives the stepper and reads the serial bus to the C64; and a mask-programmed logic array, the M50174, handles the address decode and the stepper phase sequencing so the CPU does not have to bit-bang them.

###### The silicon this logic is made from `peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon` _(medium)_

The 6502, the 6522 and the PLA were all made on 1980-era processes: a 3-5 micron NMOS or bipolar line, or a custom bipolar array. The wafer was the same trichlorosilane-to-polysilicon-to-epitaxy chain already traced under the television's video IC, and the die was diced, wire-bonded and epoxy-moulded.

###### Epoxy mould compound, silica-filled `peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.mould-compound` _(medium)_

The black or off-white plastic that a chip is set in. It is an epoxy novolac resin filled to about 70% with ground fused silica, with a cure promoter and a mould release. The silica filler is what stops the encapsulant from shrinking and cracking the die during cure, and it comes from the same kind of sand as the glass batch.

###### Gold bonding wire from the anode slimes `peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire` _(medium)_

The 6502 was a 40-pin DIP with gold or tinned copper wires ball-bonded or wedge-bonded from the die pads to the lead frame. Gold came almost entirely from the anode slimes of copper electrolytic refining, and a modest 40-pin DIP of the period had a few milligrams of it.

###### Hybrid stepping motor `peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper` _(medium)_

A hybrid stepping motor: a permanent-magnet rotor with fine teeth running between two toothed stator poles, with coils on the poles. Two phases driven in sequence step the rotor a fraction of a degree at a time. This is how the 1541 knew where the tape was, and the motor's own inertia is why a 1541 could not skip forward as fast as it could seek.

###### Toothed stator laminations of silicon steel `peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.stator` _(medium)_

The stator is a stack of thin silicon steel laminations with fine teeth, each pole carrying a bobbin of magnet wire. The laminations are punched from the same 0.35 mm silicon steel as the television's mains transformer, but the teeth are punched to a pitch of well under a millimetre, which is the reason a hybrid stepper has far more rotor teeth than its stator poles.

###### Sintered ferrite permanent magnet rotor `peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor` _(medium)_

The rotor is a ferrite or Alnico magnet with fine teeth machined or ground onto its circumference, magnetised radially or axially. A ferrite magnet is barium or strontium ferrite, the same material as a speaker magnet; a stepper rotor is a small ring of it.

###### End bells, bushings and the mounting bracket `peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing` _(low)_

The motor is held between two stamped steel end bells with bronze or sintered bronze bushings for the shafts (or plastic bushings on a cheap drive), and mounted on a steel bracket riveted or screwed into the deck. The whole assembly sat on a die-cast or folded steel chassis plate.

###### End bell steel and sintered bronze bushings `peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.materials` _(medium)_

The stamped steel end bells came off the same low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the speaker basket. The bushings were sintered bronze, a copper-tin alloy made by pressing bronze powder and sintering it in a reducing atmosphere so it had a connected pore structure that held oil. Copper and tin both feature elsewhere in this branch.

                - *Cold-reduced low-carbon steel strip* `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel` *(seen above)*
                - *Tin from cassiterite (SnO2)* `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating.cassiterite` *(seen above)*
###### Tape transport: capstan, pinch roller, worm reduction `peripheral.cassette.deck.transport` _(medium)_

The cassette slid in and the tape was pressed against a capstan on the drive by a rubber pinch roller, at 4.76 cm/s. The capstan was on a flywheel turned by the stepper motor through a worm reduction, which also let the motor's back-driving put the capstan in the right phase. The same motor rotation drove a cam that loaded the head against the tape. There was no tachometer, no position sensor and no closed loop: the drive simply counted steps and hoped.

###### Pinch roller and rubber `peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.pinch-roller` _(medium)_

A small roller of black nitrile or butyl rubber on a moulded plastic or nylon hub, on a bent spring steel arm. The rubber had to grip the capstan and the tape without slipping and without depositing rubber onto the tape, and a dried-out pinch roller was the single most common cause of a 1541 failing to read a tape it had just written.

###### Worm and worm-wheel reduction `peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.worm` _(medium)_

The stepper's rotation was reduced by a worm on the motor shaft running in a nylon or brass wheel on the capstan shaft. A worm gear is quiet and gives a high ratio in a small space and is self-locking, which is exactly what is wanted: when the power was off the capstan could not back-drive. The wheel was usually a moulded nylon or acetal wheel with a brass insert.

###### Read/write head, gap about 1 micrometre `peripheral.cassette.deck.head` _(medium)_

A miniature magnetic recording head, essentially the same object as the one in a cassette deck but smaller and more carefully shielded. A ferrite or permalloy core with a laser-cut gap of about a micrometre, a figure-eight winding of lacquered copper to cancel hum from the drive's own motor, a mumetal shield can around the front, and a printed circuit board carrying the preamplifier right at the head to keep the signal short.

###### Permalloy or ferrite core `peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core` _(medium)_

The gap has to be made with both faces flat and parallel to a micron or so across a couple of millimetres, which ferrite does well by lapping and permalloy does well by etching. A high-permeability nickel-iron alloy, permalloy, gives the inductance needed for the playback winding; the mu-metal shield can around the front suppresses external fields.

###### Lacquered copper wire, figure-eight `peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding`

The winding was a fine enamelled (lacquered) copper wire, typically 40 AWG, a few hundred to a couple of thousand turns, wound so that it sits astride the gap with two halves that see the drive motor's stray field in opposite directions. The hum-cancelling figure-eight was the reason a 1541 did not pick up the buzz of its own motor. The lacquer itself is the same polyurethane-imide over a polyester base as a television yoke winding.

              - *Copper wire from chalcopyrite concentrate* `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.copper` *(seen above)*
###### The 1541 circuit board `peripheral.cassette.deck.board`

A single FR-4 board with the CPU, the PIA, the PLA, a handful of logic gates, the head preamplifier, the stepper driver transistors, and the power regulators. It was a through-hole board in 1982, socketed for the CPU and the PIA so they could be replaced, and hand- or wave-soldered.

###### Laminate, foil and solder on the 1541 board `peripheral.cassette.deck.board.materials` _(medium)_

The same FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate, 35 micron copper foil, epoxy solder mask and tin-lead solder as the television's board. The entire electronics industry of 1982 ran on one laminate supplier chain and one solder alloy, and a 1541 board and a TV board were made on the same sort of line.

              - *FR-4 epoxy-glass printed circuit board* `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb` *(seen above)*
              - *HASL: tin-lead solder on the pads* `peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb.plating` *(seen above)*
###### Power supply: 5 V and 12 V from the C64 `peripheral.cassette.deck.psu` _(medium)_

The 1541 has no mains input. It gets 5 V and about 12 V DC from the C64 through the six-pin cassette port, and regulates them locally: the 12 V feeds the motor and the head bias, the 5 V feeds the logic, and a linear regulator or a discrete dropper makes the 5 V from a higher rail on some models. There was a fuse and a reverse-polarity protection diode because the port was known to be a point of user error.

###### The regulator and its electrolytics `peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.chain` _(medium)_

The 1541 regulated the 9-12 V rail down to 5 V with a small linear regulator or a discrete zener-transmitter, and used a handful of aluminium electrolytics to ripple-filter it. Both are the same parts as the television reservoir: etched four-nines aluminium foil in a wound foil anode, with a fibre separator and a chloride or borate electrolyte.

              - *Aluminium electrolytic reservoir, 200 microfarad 160 V* `peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir` *(seen above)*
###### The 1541 plastic case `peripheral.cassette.deck.case`

A grey ABS clamshell, disc-shaped, about 40 cm across and 9 cm deep, moulded in two halves with the lid carrying the Commodore logo badge and the slot for the cassette. The material is the same ABS as a television cabinet, from the same styrene-butadiene-acrylonitrile chemistry.

###### Converges on the ABS resin chain `peripheral.cassette.deck.case.abs-chain`

The 1541's case is the same acrylonitrile butadiene styrene as a 1982 television cabinet, made from styrene, butadiene and acrylonitrile, each a descendant of crude oil. The chain is documented under peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.

              - *ABS resin* `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs` *(seen above)*
###### Activity LED `peripheral.cassette.deck.led`

A small red LED on the front of the drive, lit while the motor was running or the head was active. It was a gallium arsenide or gallium phosphide die in a 2.5 mm epoxy lens, running at about 2-10 mA from the 5 V rail through a resistor. The LED itself was 1980s technology; the indicator lamps on earlier drives had been incandescent bulbs or neon.

###### Gallium arsenide from gallium in the Bayer liquor `peripheral.cassette.deck.led.gallium` _(medium)_

A red or amber LED of the period was gallium phosphide or gallium arsenide phosphide on a gallium arsenide substrate. Gallium is not mined on its own: it is recovered as a minor by-product from the Bayer liquor when bauxite is digested in caustic soda, because gallium is amphoteric and dissolves with the alumina. By 1982 gallium was becoming strategically important precisely because of this concentration in the aluminium industry.

              - *4N aluminium foil from bauxite* `peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.aluminium.bauxite` *(seen above)*
###### The nine-pin serial link to the C64 `peripheral.cassette.deck.link`

The 1541 connected to the C64 by a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable carrying the serial bus, which is how the drive knew there was a computer and the computer knew there was a drive. This is the peripheral-plug branch's territory and is cross-referenced there rather than duplicated.

###### Nine-pin serial link to the drive `peripheral.plug.serial-link`

The 1541 was not daisy-chained through the cassette port; it plugged into the C64's second serial port through a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable. That separate port is how the computer knew a disk drive was present at all: there was no other way for the 1541 to announce itself except by talking on this line, and the drive type was auto-detected from what it said.

##### The cassette tape itself `peripheral.cassette.tape`

A compact cassette is a 3.81 mm wide strip of polyester film 12 microns thick, coated on one side with about one to two microns of acicular iron oxide pigment in a binder, and wound onto hubs inside a plastic shell. The C64 wrote 9,600 baud onto it, which at 4.76 cm/s works out to a flux transition every 200 to 300 microseconds, near the limit of what a standard-bias cassette could resolve. Almost everything in it is either crude oil or iron ore.

###### Polyester (PET) film base `peripheral.cassette.tape.film` _(medium)_

The base is 9-12 microns of polyethylene terephthalate, extruded as a biaxially oriented film. The path to PET runs from crude oil through naphtha to paraxylene, then through dimethyl terephthalate, which is condensed with ethylene glycol into the polyester. It is the same chemistry as a soda bottle, just 20 microns thinner and stretched hard, which is why it is dimensionally stable enough to run past a 1 micron head gap.

###### Para-xylene from naphtha reforming `peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene` _(medium)_

Para-xylene is the key intermediate to PET. It is produced by catalytic reforming of naphtha, then by selective adsorption (UOP Parex, a molecular sieve that picks out the para isomer from the mixed xylenes) because only the para isomer is useful and it is a minority of the xylene mixture. It is then oxidised to terephthalic acid or esterified to DMT.

###### Converges on the naphtha fraction `peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene.naphtha`

The same naphtha fraction of crude oil that feeds the styrene and the ethylene in the television cabinet branch. One barrel of crude is the ultimate ancestor of both the plastics cabinet and the polyester tape base.

                - *Naphtha fraction from crude oil* `peripheral.tv.cabinet.abs.styrene.benzene.naphtha` *(seen above)*
###### Acicular iron oxide pigment `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide` _(medium)_

The magnetic pigment is acicular gamma-iron(III) oxide, gamma-Fe2O3: needle-shaped crystals about 0.3 microns long by 0.08 microns across by 0.01 thick, an aspect ratio of about 3 to 5. It is precipitated from an iron(II) salt by oxidising with air while a surfactant is present, and the surfactant is what forces the crystals to grow as needles instead of spheres. That morphology is the whole reason a cassette can hold what it holds: the long axis lines up with the tape's direction of travel and the short axis resists it.

###### Iron from ore or scrap, leached to a ferrous salt `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron` _(medium)_

Tape pigment iron did not need to be virgin: it was often made from ferrous scrap, mill scale or ore, dissolved in hydrochloric or sulphuric acid to ferrous chloride or ferrous sulphate, then precipitated and oxidised. The ore route, when it was used, was the same hematite or magnetite that goes to a blast furnace, digested in acid rather than reduced in a furnace.

###### Converges on the iron ore `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.ore`

Hematite and magnetite concentrate, the same feed to every blast furnace in the tree, here dissolved in acid instead of reduced with coke. One grade of ore fed both the steel of a shadow mask and the oxide on a cassette, by two completely different routes.

                - *Hematite and magnetite iron ore* `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.ore` *(seen above)*
###### The surfactant that makes needles `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactant` _(medium)_

Crystal habit is controlled by what is adsorbed on the growing face. The pigment industry used a fatty acid or an alkylbenzene sulphonate, or in the classic process a hydrolysed protein or a polyol, adsorbed on the iron oxide as it precipitated so that growth was fastest along one axis. Without it the pigment came out spherical and a cassette tape of the same thickness held a fraction of the data.

###### Chromium dioxide (Type II pigment) `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium` _(medium)_

For high-bias Type II tape, chromium dioxide (CrO2): acicular, 20-50 nm, higher coercivity and higher signal-to-noise than ferrite. It is made by oxidising chromic chloride in the presence of a surfactant under pressure and heat, and was patented and controlled tightly by its Japanese inventors. Chromium came from chromite ore, which is mostly in South Africa and the Soviet bloc.

              - *Chromite ore, FeCr2O4* `peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.chromite` *(seen above)*
###### The dispersion: pigment, binder, dispersant `peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion` _(medium)_

The pigment was not coated as a powder. It was dispersed in a binder so that the needles separate and stay separated, and then magnetically oriented on the film. A typical binder was a cellulose lacquer, an acrylic or polyurethane, dissolved in a solvent such as toluene, xylene or methyl ethyl ketone; in the 1970s and early 1980s there was also a water-based polyurethane dispersion. The dispersant was a surfactant or a phosphate ester that wets the oxide surface so the needles do not clump back together.

###### Three-roll mixing and milling `peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.mixing` _(medium)_

The pigment and the binder were combined and then refined on a three-roll mill or a sand mill, working the agglomerates apart until the dispersion was smooth. The dispersion quality set the noise floor of the finished tape, because a clump of pigment is a defect that scatters the recording.

###### Coating line: doctor blade, orientation field, cure ovens `peripheral.cassette.tape.coating` _(medium)_

A web of polyester film, a metre or more wide, unwinds and passes under a coating station where the magnetic dispersion is laid down in one or two passes by a doctor blade or a gravure roll, a few microns thick. It passes between magnets that align the acicular particles along the length of the film, then into an oven at 60-100 degrees C to drive off the solvent and cure the binder. A backing-coat station then applies the carbon-black anti-smear layer, and the whole web is slit to width.

###### Backing coat: carbon black for the leader and anti-smear `peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing` _(medium)_

On the back of the magnetic coating was a sub-micron layer of extra pigment and carbon black. It did two things: it gave the visible leader tape (the clear or white strip at the start of a cassette) its colour and its opacity so a deck could find it, and it suppressed print-through, where a signal on one layer of the wound tape magnetises the layer next to it and comes back as a ghost. Carbon black, again, from petroleum coke.

###### Converges on the carbon black chain `peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.carbon`

The same oil-blackened soot from heavy petroleum oil that blackens the CRT anode, colours the television cabinet and gives a resistor its track. A cassette, a television and a computer shared one pigment supply chain.

                - *Carbon black, from petroleum coke* `peripheral.tv.crt.gun.blackening.carbon-black` *(seen above)*
###### Toluene and xylene from naphtha `peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.solvent` _(medium)_

The aromatic solvents that carried the binder. Toluene was made by hydrodealkylating the benzene from the reformer or by methylating benzene with methanol; xylene came straight off the reformer as part of the aromatics cut. Both are naphtha descendants.

###### Cassette shell and hubs `peripheral.cassette.tape.shell`

The compact cassette case: two thin polystyrene or ABS shells, each with a hub, so that the tape is enclosed in a rigid 100 x 64 x 12 mm box with five windows on one edge for the head, capstan and the pressure pad, two hub windows, and the write-protect notches. The hubs were glass-filled nylon or moulded ABS with the six drive slots, running on the two hub spindles.

###### Shell material: polystyrene or ABS `peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs` _(medium)_

A cassette shell is thin and needs to hold a dimension, so it was moulded from general-purpose polystyrene (cheap, brittle, easy to mould) or from ABS for a stiffer shell. Audio tapes were conventionally clear or smoke polystyrene or ABS; computer and C64 tapes were frequently the same shells, since nothing about the shell distinguished them.

###### Hub, glass-filled nylon `peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.hub` _(low)_

The reel hub runs on the shell's spindle and drives the tape through a wind process. It had to be dimensionally stable and dimensionally tight so the tape wound at a given radius came off at the right tension. It was glass-filled nylon or ABS, with the six drive slots on the inside face for the winding spindle.

###### Converges on the nylon chain `peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.hub.nylon`

Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, both from benzene and acrylonitrile, both from crude oil. The hub, the yoke bobbin and a 1980s radio knob were all nylon.

                - *Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid* `peripheral.tv.crt.yoke.winding.bobbin.nylon` *(seen above)*
###### Pressure pad and felt `peripheral.cassette.tape.pad` _(medium)_

A small pad of felt or synthetic non-woven on a stainless steel leaf spring, mounted in a plastic carrier inside the shell behind the head window. Its job was to press the tape gently against the head so the head could read and write reliably, and to press the tape against the shell's ribs to select the C-1 to C-5 path. The felt was the one consumable part of a cassette; it shed debris into the head gap and a worn pad was a classic cause of a 1541 failing.

###### Felt and the stainless spring `peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials` _(medium)_

The pad was wool felt or a bonded polyester fibre web about a millimetre thick, glued to a stainless steel leaf spring in a plastic carrier. Wool felt is carded wool fibre matted and pressed; the spring was a 300-series stainless, so the iron came from the blast furnace and the chromium from chromite, the same chromite as the chrome plating on a telescopic antenna.

              - *Hematite and magnetite iron ore* `peripheral.tv.crt.mask.steel.bf.ore` *(seen above)*
              - *Chrome plating on the whip rod* `peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating` *(seen above)*
###### Slitting to 1/8 inch `peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting`

The coating line made a web a metre or more wide; it was then slit into 3.81 mm strips with rotary knives, tens of kilovolts of static keeping the thin film from clinging to the rollers. The slit tape was wound onto master reels, then onto cassette reels by a winding line that also cut it to length (45 m per side for a C-60), formed the leader, and inserted the hub.

###### The polyester film that is slit `peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.film` _(medium)_

The web being slit is 9-12 micron biaxially oriented PET, made from dimethyl terephthalate condensed with ethylene glycol. The whole chain from crude oil to a 90 metre C-60 is the same petrochemical chain that made a television cabinet and a ribbon cable.

              - *Para-xylene from naphtha reforming* `peripheral.cassette.tape.film.paraxylene` *(seen above)*
#### The connectors that carry the signal `peripheral.plug`

Three connectors that made a C64 usable rather than just powered: the aerial socket the RF modulator hijacked, the nine-pin link to the 1541, and the 34-conductor ribbon on the back that opened the machine up. This branch is deliberately short. The mains plug and the C64's own power inlet belong to another agent's branch.

##### The aerial socket, hijacked `peripheral.plug.rf`

The 75 ohm coaxial socket on the back of the television. The C64's modulator lead was a short 75 ohm coax with an F-type plug that went into it in parallel with the set's aerial. Because the modulator was a weak source, the lead had to be a good 75 ohm match and the set's aerial input had to be isolated or the local signal would back-feed.

###### Converges on the coaxial antenna lead `peripheral.plug.rf.cable`

The copper braid, the copper centre conductor, the polyethylene dielectric and the PVC jacket are all documented under peripheral.tv.aerial.coax. The F-type connector's brass and nickel plating are under peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.

            - *Coaxial or twin-lead antenna lead* `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax` *(seen above)*
            - *F-type coaxial connector* `peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector` *(seen above)*
        - *Nine-pin serial link to the drive* `peripheral.plug.serial-link` *(seen above)*
##### The 34-conductor user port ribbon `peripheral.plug.userport` _(medium)_

On the back of the C64, a 34-conductor edge connector on a card, which brought out the 6510's eight data lines, twelve address lines, the read and write strobes, the IRQ and NMI lines, the serial and parallel ports, and the 5 V and ground. It was the machine's expansion door, and it was how a disk interface, a printer interface, a sampler or an EPROM programmer reached the CPU. The cable was a flat ribbon with a mylar or tinned-copper conductor, a foil shield and a PVC or polyester jacket.

###### PVC jacket and polyester film from crude oil `peripheral.plug.userport.pvc` _(medium)_

The ribbon's jacket is PVC (from ethylene and salt-derived chlorine) and its insulation between conductors is polyester film (from the same PET chain as the cassette tape base). Both are grandchildren of crude oil, and both are the same two chemistries already traced elsewhere in this tree.

###### Converges on the salt for chlorine `peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.salt`

The chlorine in the PVC came from the electrolysis of brine or rock salt, the same sodium-chloride electrolysis that fed the chlorinated solvents used to clean printed circuit boards. The chain is documented under peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.salt.

              - *Rock salt, NaCl, for the chlorine* `peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.salt` *(seen above)*
###### Card-edge and D-sub connectors `peripheral.plug.userport.connectors` _(medium)_

The connectors were gold-plated or nickel-plated brass and copper contacts in a thermoplastic (usually glass-filled nylon or a phenolic) insulator, crimped or soldered to the ribbon. A D-sub has a metal shell (often tinned steel or nickel-plated brass) that both shields the connection and provides the mechanical polarisation that stops anyone plugging it in backwards.

##### The six-pin cassette port `peripheral.plug.cassette-port` _(medium)_
