The connector that carries both the audio to a tape recorder and the power to a 1541. It is a 6-pin connector, carrying read, write, sense, motor, 5 V and the 9-12 V motor rail. Commodore's own cable turned it into a DIN-style socket that plugged into a consumer cassette recorder, so a C64 could save to a music deck. The same port carried the power for the 1541, which is why a 1541 has no power socket of its own.

### Joystick controller `c64.joystick`

The self-centring 4-way joystick Commodore bundled with the C64 and sold with most of its software: a moulded gate plate held neutral by four springs, four miniature microswitches underneath it, a steel shaft with a ball top, a plastic knob, and a coiled cable to one of the DE-9 control ports. Five moving electrical contacts and one mechanical centring mechanism, in a shell of black ABS.

#### 4-way direction gate `c64.joystick.gate`

A cross-shaped sliding gate that physically interlocks so only one of the four directions can be closed at a time - the same gating trick as a keyboard's 3-key rollover prevention. The gate rides on four ribs and is held centred by four springs, so it is self-centring and has no detented 'gate 2' half-way position.

##### Centring springs `c64.joystick.gate.spring`

Four small compression or torsion springs push the gate back to neutral from every direction. They are the part that wears out: once the springs weaken, the stick stays pushed, which is the most common repair on a vintage joystick and the reason 'joystick centering' appears in every retro repair guide.

###### Spring wire for the centring springs `c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire`

Drawn music-wire or stainless spring wire, coiled and closed. Centring springs are the cheapest consumable in the whole joystick and the one that is always replaced rather than repaired.

###### Iron ore for the spring wire `c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.iron-ore`

The same ore-to-bar-to-wire chain as every other steel spring on the machine.

###### Why springs are the failure point `c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement`

Gate springs carry the whole centring duty and are cycled by every direction press. Once one is weakened the stick sits off-centre and the machine reads a direction the user is not pressing - the most common single joystick fault of the era.

##### Bushing and friction washer `c64.joystick.gate.friction` _(medium)_

The shaft is supported by a plastic bushing or a nylon washer in the chassis, and a felt or fibre friction pad under the gate sets the feel. Friction pads compress and shed debris with age, which is the second classic cause of a stiff or drifting stick.

###### Nylon bushing in the chassis `c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing` _(medium)_

A moulded nylon bushing in the ABS chassis that the steel shaft runs in. Nylon is used because it is self-lubricating and will not gall the shaft; a metal bushing would seize onto the shaft as it rimes.

###### Nylon resin for the bushing `c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.resin` _(medium)_

A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. Nylon-6-6 from caprolactam, the same polymer as the microswitch case.

###### Caprolactam `c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.resin.caprolactam`

The caprolactam-to-nylon-6-6 chain. The joystick contains nylon in its bushing, its microswitch cases and its knob overmould.

###### Benzene from a steam cracker `c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.resin.caprolactam.benzene`

Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

###### Friction pad `c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad` _(medium)_

A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.

###### Wool felt `c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool` _(medium)_

Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.

#### Four miniature microswitches `c64.joystick.microswitches`

Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

##### Sprung leaf and contact-plating detail `c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves`

Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.

###### Gold plating of the microswitch leaf `c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-plating`

The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.

###### Brass leaf metal `c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-plating.leaf-metal`

Phosphor bronze or brass strip, stamped and formed into a bowed leaf. Copper alloy from mined ore, as everywhere else in this file.

##### Switch case polymer `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case` _(medium)_

A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.

###### Glass-filled nylon case `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.nylon`

A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.

###### Nylon-6-6 resin `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.nylon.nylon-6-6`

Caprolactam polymerisation - the same chain as the switch body and the keycap legend. A single C64 contains nylon in its switch housings, its joystick bushings and its microswitch cases.

###### Through-hole mounting and solder lugs `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.solder-lugs`

The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.

###### Joystick switch board `c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.solder-lugs.board` _(medium)_

A small printed board inside the joystick carries the four microswitches and drops the switch pins to the cable. It is a two-layer FR-4 board with the same glass-epoxy laminate and copper foil as the keyboard board.

#### Steel shaft and ball top `c64.joystick.shaft`

A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.

##### Cold-drawn steel bar `c64.joystick.shaft.steel`

Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed.

###### Iron ore (limonite / hematite) `c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore`

The steel shaft begins as iron ore. The bulk of world steel in 1982 was made in a blast furnace from sintered hematite-magnetite pellets/coke, refined to steel in a basic oxygen furnace. Rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.

###### Pelletising and blast furnace `c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet`

Concentrate is pelletised and fired with limestone and coke, charged with the coke burden, and reduced to pig iron. The coke is what makes it economically possible, and it is where the energy density that lets a steel part cost less than a plastic one comes from.

###### Metallurgical coke `c64.joystick.shaft.steel.iron-ore.pellet.coke`

Coking coal heated in coke ovens to drive off the volatile matter, leaving a porous carbon fuel that is also the reducing agent. Mined coal, and the reason a 1982 steel plant sits next to a coking battery.

#### ABS knob and top button `c64.joystick.knob` _(medium)_

The moulded handle on the top of the shaft. On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.

##### ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene) `c64.joystick.knob.abs`

The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.

###### Glass or mineral filler and the TiO2 whitener `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler` _(medium)_

The knob's black colour is a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS. Where a lighter colour was wanted the pigment was titanium dioxide, a white pigment made from ilmenite, and it is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.

###### Pigment dispersion in the ABS `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion` _(medium)_

The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.

###### Titanium dioxide whitener `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion.tio2` _(medium)_

Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.

###### Alumina from bauxite `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion.tio2.alumina`

Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

###### Bauxite profile `c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dispersion.tio2.alumina.laterite`

A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

###### Injection moulding of the knob `c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding`

The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.

###### Knob mould tool `c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool` _(medium)_

A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.

###### Iron ore `c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.iron-ore`

Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

###### Fire button on shaft and knob `c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button` _(medium)_

On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.

#### Coiled cable and DE-9 plug `c64.joystick.cable` _(medium)_

A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.

##### DE-9 male plug contacts `c64.joystick.cable.plug`

Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.

###### Cable assembly and strain relief `c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly`

The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.

###### Stranded conductor `c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor` _(medium)_

Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.

###### Tinning of the conductor `c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinning` _(medium)_

The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.

## Finishing and bundled extras `c64.extras`

Branches that hang off the machine rather than being part of it: how legends and colours were printed onto plastic, how one keyboard key becomes a bit, and the joystick that shipped in the box in some markets.

### Decoration: legends, logos and metallised inks on plastic `c64.decor`

Getting colour and type onto moulded plastic in 1982 meant printing it, not moulding colour into it. Commodore used two-colour pad printing for the keycap legends and the rainbow badge, screen printing where a flat surface allowed it, metallised flake ink for the shiny logo bars, and - in later production - two-shot moulding and painted or lacquered surfaces. Each process has its own pad, ink, screen and cure chemistry.

#### Pad printing (tampo printing) `c64.decor.pad-printing`

The workhorse process. A soft silicone rubber pad is pressed onto a flat metal cliche carrying the image in wet ink, picks the ink up on its raised relief, then deforms against the curved or crowned plastic part and transfers the image. One pad, one colour, one station; two stations give the two-colour keycap legends.

##### Two-colour pad printing press `c64.decor.pad-print.machine`

A small cast frame with a plate table, an ink cup or doctor blade, a silicone pad on a shuttle head, and part fixtures on a rotating or indexing table. Each colour station is one table position with its own pad.

##### Silicone rubber printing pad `c64.decor.pad-print.pad`

A soft, solvent-resistant, low-surface-energy pad - almost always silicone rubber - cut or cast with the relief to pick up and transfer the image. It is the consumable that has to be replaced every few thousand impressions, and pad choice (hardness, hardness-to-image ratio) is the operator's main variable.

###### Two-part silicone pad compound `c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound`

A polydimethylsiloxane casting system cured at room temperature with a tin catalyst or an addition-cure platinum system. Pads are cast in a mould against the plate image so the relief matches exactly.

##### Cliche (the printing plate) and its electrotype `c64.decor.pad-print.cliche`

The image is held in a flat copper or nickel electrotype, or a photopolymer plate, sunk into a plate table and flooded with ink. The traditional route is a photograph on a copper plate, which is electroplated up to 0.5-1 mm and then hand- or machine-polished back to leave only the image proud - the electrotype.

###### Photopolymer plate `c64.decor.pad-print.photopolymer`

A photosensitive polymer film laminated to a steel backing, exposed through a film negative, washed out to leave the image in relief, and cured. It replaced the electrotype for short runs because it needs no electroplating step.

###### Copper electrotyping of the plate `c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating`

The sensitised copper plate is electroplated in an acid copper bath to build a thick deposit on the image, then the surface is ground and polished back so only the image stands proud. It is an old, slow process, but it gives an image hard enough to print millions of impressions.

##### Pad-printing ink (solvent or UV) `c64.decor.pad-print.ink`

A free-flowing, low-viscosity ink that will transfer off a soft pad and then dry on a plastic part. In 1982 most pad inks were solvent-based (glycol ether / xylene / ester solvent with an alkyd or acrylic resin and a pigment); UV-curing pad inks existed and were gaining ground, and were faster but needed a lamp.

###### Ink binder resin (alkyd or acrylic) `c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin` _(medium)_

The film-forming part of the ink: an alkyd built from drying-oil fatty acids and a polyacid (the same chemistry as the printing ink vehicle on the box), or an acrylic copolymer. It is chosen for adhesion to ABS, which is notoriously hard to print on without a surface treatment.

###### Legend and logo pigments `c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment`

The legend white is almost always titanium dioxide in an alkyd binder; the rainbow logo uses a set of saturated organic pigments - phthalocyanine blue, quinacridone magenta, azo yellow - and sometimes a metallised flake for the bright bars.

###### Ink solvent (glycol ether / ester blend) `c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent` _(medium)_

The volatile carrier that gives pad ink its low viscosity. Common 1980s pad-ink solvents were propylene glycol ethers, dibutyl phthalate or xylene blends. It flashes off the pad quickly enough to give a sharp print and slowly enough that the impression can be placed.

###### Propylene oxide (for the glycol ether solvent) `c64.decor.propyloxide`

Made by the chlorohydrin route (propylene + chlorine + water, then caustic dehydrochlorination) or the older hydroperoxide route (propylene + hydroperoxide, then a base-catalysed rearrangement). It is what turns propylene into propylene glycol ethers and acetates, the commonest 1980s pad-ink and screen-ink solvent.

###### UV curing of ink `c64.decor.uv-curing`

A mercury or metal-halide lamp floods the printed part in under a second and the photo-initiator in the ink polymerises it in place. It was the big printing-technology change of the late 1970s and early 1980s: instant cure, no solvent, no oven, and a harder, more abrasion-resistant print.

#### Screen printing `c64.decor.screen-printing`

Silk screening through a mesh, used on Commodore parts where the surface is flat enough: printed panels, keycap sets on flat-topped caps, cartridge labels and some case markings. It cannot print the grain-textured bezel reliably, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case.

##### Screen mesh (nylon monofilament or stainless wire) `c64.decor.screen-print.mesh`

A woven mesh stretched and glued to an aluminium frame. Nylon is used where solvent or epoxy inks would attack a wire screen; stainless wire is used where long life under abrasive inks matters. Both are woven from a drawn filament or wire on a loom.

##### Screen emulsion (PVA or diazo) `c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion`

The photosensitive coating that becomes the stencil. Diazo emulsions, standard in 1982, are washed out with water after exposure; PVA emulsion requires a separate exposure through the base and is more solvent-resistant. The stencil is exposed through a film positive and then washed.

##### Squeegee blade `c64.decor.screen-print.squeegee`

A rubber or neoprene blade in a wooden or aluminium holder that forces ink through the stencil and wipes the surface. The durometer of the blade is the operator's variable: hard for fine detail, soft for heavy coverage.

###### Neoprene squeegee rubber `c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene`

Polychloroprene, chosen because it resists the solvents in screen ink and wears well. It is the same chloroprene rubber used for cable jackets and gaskets, again pointing back to the C4 cracker cut.

##### Screen-printing ink (one-part epoxy) `c64.decor.screen-print.ink` _(medium)_

A one-component epoxy or polyester ink with a latent hardener, screen-printed through the stencil and then heat-cured. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels and keycap overlays used.

#### Metallised and pearlescent ink `c64.decor.metallised`

The shiny bars in the Commodore rainbow logo and the metallic trim on some panels are metallised ink: pigment-grade aluminium flake, or vacuum-metallised polyester film, suspended in a binder and printed, then optionally burnished to align the flakes flat so they reflect.

##### Atomised aluminium flake `c64.decor.metallised.flake`

Molten aluminium is atomised with air into 5-15 um flakes, which are then washed, sifted by size and coated with an oxidation-inhibiting lacquer so they do not go grey. The same basic process makes the aluminium in the EMI shield, only at a different scale.

##### Binder for metallised ink (acrylic or alkyd) `c64.decor.metallised.binders` _(medium)_

A drying ink binder that holds the flakes flat and lets them reflect. Formulated so the flake lies parallel to the surface; this is what produces the flat metallic look rather than a sparkly one.

##### Burnishing (or calendering) the flake `c64.decor.metallised.burnish` _(medium)_

Passing the printed part between heated polished rollers flattens the flakes into the surface so they mirror rather than scatter. Burnished metallic ink on a moulded part looks like a metal panel - which is precisely the intent of a rainbow badge.

##### Hot foil stamping (alternative to flake ink) `c64.decor.hot-stamping` _(medium)_

A heated metal foil is pressed onto the plastic with a type plate and the image transfers. On rigid ABS this needs a rougher surface or a soft stamping die, which is why flake ink beat foil stamping on a textured case - but foil stamping was used on smooth panels and on some packaging.

#### Two-shot / in-mould decoration `c64.decor.two-shot` _(medium)_

Deciding not to print at all and moulding the colour or the decoration in: a second shot in a second colour, or an in-mould printed film or transfer placed in the tool before the shot. Both existed in 1982 but were expensive, and neither is used on the breadbin case - the colour there is pigment in the resin.

#### Spray lacquer and paint (used on accessories, not the case) `c64.decor.paint` _(medium)_

Spray-applied lacquer over plastic - used on joystick housings, on some panels and on plastic accessory parts - was an acrylic or nitrocellulose lacquer, sprayed in a ventilated booth and stoved at 60-80 C. It is how a plastic part gets a uniform, slightly textured finish that hides mould flow marks.

##### Spray lacquer (acrylic or nitrocellulose) `c64.decor.paint.lacquer` _(medium)_

A solvent-borne film former with pigment, sprayed and baked. Nitrocellulose was standard for consumer plastic coatings in 1982; 2K polyurethane and water-borne acrylic were the better performers but more expensive and better suited to metal.

##### Cure oven (batch, gas-fired) `c64.decor.paint.cure-oven`

A batch oven with gas burners and forced circulation, holding 60-80 C for 20-30 minutes to flash off the solvent and crosslink the lacquer. The gas burners are the only fossil fuel on the decorating line.

#### Keycap legend overlays and printed inserts `c64.decor.overlay` _(low)_

An alternative to printing the cap is to bond a printed film or a moulded insert onto or into the cap. Commodore keycaps are printed, not overlaid, but the technique was in use on contemporary keyboards and appears on some Commodore accessories and on the memory-expansion modules. Recorded here for completeness with low confidence for the C64 specifically.

#### Decoration inspection (100% look) `c64.decor.inspection` _(medium)_

Printed parts are checked for legibility, registration and offset before they go into the machine. On a two-colour legend, a shift by half a character width is a reject, so this is a genuinely tight tolerance - and one of the reasons legends look so consistent on surviving machines.

#### Prepress: artwork to printing film and plate `c64.decor.prepress`

Every legend and every logo started as artwork, which in 1982 was mechanically or photographically composed, then copied onto film by a process camera, and the film was used to expose a plate. Text was set in hot metal or phototype, and the Commodore rainbow artwork was assembled from painted separations by hand.

##### Ortho photographic film (negative) `c64.decor.prepress.film`

The black-and-white film that carries the image to the plate. It is a cellulose or polyester film coated with a silver-halide emulsion; exposed in a process camera or a contact frame, then developed and fixed in a chemical line.

###### Film base (cellulose triacetate or polyester) `c64.decor.prepress.film-base`

A flexible transparent film on which the emulsion is cast. Cellulose triacetate was the standard photographic film base, made from acetic anhydride and cellulose; polyester (PET) film base became common later for its dimensional stability.

###### Acetic acid / acetic anhydride for film base `c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid`

Made by catalytic oxidation of ethanol, or by the carbonylation of methanol. Methanol comes from synthesis gas, which comes from natural-gas reforming.

###### Cellulose (for triacetate) `c64.decor.prepress.cellulose` _(medium)_

Dissolved from wood pulp and regenerated into fibre. The film route is a small, high-purity use of cellulose compared with paper, but it is the same feedstock: a tree.

###### Silver halide emulsion `c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide`

Silver bromide or silver iodide crystals suspended in gelatin. The silver comes from silver ore, and most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.

###### Silver (recovered from ore and refinery residue) `c64.decor.prepress.silver` _(medium)_

Silver metal recovered from argentite and galena ores, and from the anode slimes of electrolytic copper refining. It is refined to photographic purity by cupellation and electrolytic refining.

###### Galena (lead sulfide ore) and silver-bearing concentrates `c64.decor.prepress.lead-ore`

Galena is the dominant lead ore and almost always carries silver as argentite or as silver dissolved in the galena lattice. It is mined, concentrated by flotation, and reduced in a blast furnace or sinter plant.

###### Cupellation of lead bullion `c64.decor.prepress.cupellation`

Lead bullion is oxidised in a cupellation furnace; the litharge formed is absorbed back into the bath and the noble metal - silver and gold - floats as dross on top. The silver is then refined electrolytically to photographic purity.

###### Electrolytic refining of silver `c64.decor.prepress.silver-electrolysis`

Crude silver from the cupellation hearth is dissolved in nitric acid and electrolytically refined: silver anodes, silver-nitrate electrolyte, pure silver cathodes. The result is 99.99% silver - the purity photographic chemistry needs for its emulsion.

###### Silver nitrate `c64.decor.prepress.silver-nitrate`

Made by dissolving silver in hot nitric acid. Silver nitrate is the classic photographic salt: reacting it with halide in gelatin is what makes the silver-halide grains in a film or paper negative.

###### Nitric acid (Ostwald process) `c64.decor.prepress.nitric-acid`

Ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-950 C, to nitrogen dioxide, and absorbed in water to give nitric acid. The ammonia comes from natural gas via steam reforming and Haber-Bosch synthesis.

### Keyboard matrix switches and domes `c64.keyboard-switches`

How one keystroke on a C64 becomes a 1 in memory: 63 rubber domes on a rigid printed circuit board, scanned by CIA #1 as an 8 x 8 matrix. The domes are carbon-loaded rubber pills that short two plated pads when a keycap's plunger drives them closed, and the scanned result is simply a pair of row and column lines being connected.

#### 8 x 8 keyboard matrix `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix`

Eight column lines snake around the board and eight row lines snake around the other way, each pair of crossing traces forming one key. Pressing a key connects its column to its row; the firmware walks the matrix by writing a pattern to CIA #1's port A and reading port B. Because one row line can touch eight different columns, a single conducting bridge is the entire 'switch'.

##### Rigid keyboard PCB with plated pads `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb` _(medium)_

A glass-epoxy laminate board, drilled and plated through in the usual way, carrying the matrix traces as copper and terminating each key position in a pair of plated pads. On the breadbin keyboard the pads are plated metal; on the earlier VIC-20-derived boards they were bare copper, and bare copper oxidises into a high-resistance film - the reason those keyboards need periodic cleaning and later ones generally do not.

###### Electrodeposited copper foil `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-foil`

The matrix traces are copper, deposited on the laminate by an electroplating line using acid copper sulphate solution and an insoluble anode. The same copper foil process as the mainboard, at a much thinner gauge.

###### Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-foil.chalcopyrite`

The dominant copper ore, mined underground in porphyry and skarn deposits and in open pits. Copper was electrorefined to cathode and rolled into foil long before it was ever plated onto a board; the board industry simply bought the foil that the copper industry already made.

###### Plating of the key pads `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-plating` _(medium)_

The exposed pads are plated - gold over nickel on later keyboards - so the carbon contact of the rubber dome has a low-resistance, non-oxidising surface to bridge onto. Where the plating is absent or has worn through, the bare copper oxidises and the key needs cleaning.

###### Gold for the pad flash `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-plating.gold` _(medium)_

A thin gold flash over nickel on the key pads. Gold does not oxidise, so the dome keeps making contact for decades; where the flash is thin or gone, the key stops working until cleaned.

##### Glass-epoxy laminate (FR-4) `c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-epoxy`

Woven glass-fibre cloth impregnated with epoxy and pressed into a sheet. The standard printed-circuit laminate since the 1960s, replacing the older phenolic paper board. The keyboard board is a trivial two-layer FR-4 part, but it goes through the same copper foil lamination and hole-drilling lines as a mainboard.

###### Woven E-glass cloth `c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-cloth`

Silica glass is melted and drawn into fine filaments a few microns across, woven into a cloth and woven again into a fine gauze. This cloth is the reinforcement in every FR-4 board in the world.

###### Silica batch from silica sand `c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-cloth.silica-batch`

The glass batch is made from silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes. The sand is dredged or quarried, and it is the same quartz sand that fed the hydrothermal quartz reactors.

###### Glass batch formulation `c64.keyboard-switches.keyboard-glass-cloth.silica-batch.batch` _(medium)_

Silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes, and a little salt as a catalyst, melted at ~1400-1600 C. The same batch chemistry as container glass, only drawn rather than floated.

###### Epoxy resin of the laminate `c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin`

The epoxy that binds the glass cloth is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both of which are petrochemical. A two-layer keyboard PCB is thus a woven silica sheet glued with a fossil-derived resin and clad in copper.

###### Epichlorohydrin `c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlorohydrin`

One of the two building blocks of epoxy resin, made by chlorinating propylene with hypochlorous acid. Epoxy is used on the keyboard laminate, on the capacitor bungs, on the tantalum seals and on the connector overmoulds - one of the most widespread materials on the whole machine.

###### Crude oil `c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.epichlorohydrin.crude-oil`

The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

#### Carbon-loaded rubber domes `c64.keyboard-switches.domes`

Each key position has a small moulded rubber pill, domed upwards, whose underside carries a conductive carbon-loaded contact that bridges two pads when the dome is crushed. Because carbon is loaded into the rubber as a filler rather than plated on, the dome is its own contact - it wears slightly with use and it is the consumable part of the switch.

##### Carbon-filled elastomer compound `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition`

Carbon black is compounded into the elastomer at a few tens of per cent by weight. The particles form a percolation network so the dome conducts along its own bulk, and the higher the loading the lower the resistance - but too much loading makes the dome brittle. This is the same black powder that goes into resistor films and pot tracks.

###### Silicone or neoprene elastomer `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.elastomer` _(medium)_

The dome body. Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) was favoured for its high compression set and wide temperature range; neoprene (polychloroprene) for oil and abrasion resistance. Both are thermoset elastomers, vulcanised in the mould rather than injection-moulded as thermoplastics, which is why they are compression-moulded sheet.

###### Silicone dome compound `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.elastomer.silicone` _(medium)_

Silicone rubber is built on a silicon-oxygen backbone and is filled with reinforcing silica. It stays elastic over a wide temperature range and does not take up much oil, which is why a silicone dome does not swell and seize.

###### Silica sand `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.elastomer.silicone.silica-sand`

Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

###### Carbon black filler (petroleum-derived) `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.carbon-black`

The same furnace-black feedstock used in the resistors, compounded into the elastomer. The dome's conductivity and its wear rate are both set by the grade and loading of this powder.

###### Grade selection for the dome `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.carbon-black.grade` _(medium)_

A high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, so a dome can be made conductive with less filler and stay soft. The grade choice is the difference between a responsive key and a stiff one.

##### Compression moulding of the dome sheet `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding` _(medium)_

The domes are moulded as a continuous sheet on a heated platen press: uncured compound is placed in a multi-cavity tool, pressed, cured, and the sheet released as one piece with every key's dome attached. Domes therefore arrive as a single printed-circuit-sized rubber sheet that has to be aligned to the pads by hand.

###### Heated platen press `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.platen-press` _(medium)_

A hydraulic flat-bed press with heated platens holds a multi-cavity dome tool against the compound long enough to cure the elastomer. Small presses of this type did the whole dome sheet for a keyboard in one shot.

###### Steel dome tool `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.tool` _(medium)_

A machined or spark-eroded steel tool with one hemispherical cavity per key. It has to be replaced as the dome geometry is re-specified, and its surface finish is what the dome's mating face is polished against.

###### Spark-erosion machining of the dome cavity `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.tool.spark-erosion`

A fine copper electrode is brought within micrometres of the workpiece in a dielectric bath and pulses of a few microseconds melt a microscopic crater per pulse. Spark erosion is how a one-micron hemispherical cavity gets cut in hardened tool steel without any mechanical stress on the surface.

###### Graphite tool electrode `c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.tool.spark-erosion.graphite-electrode` _(medium)_

Graphite is the standard spark-erosion electrode: it is conductive, machinable to a fine tip, and wears slowly by re-graphitising. Machined graphite is made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C.

#### Keycap and plunger mechanism `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap`

A double-shot moulded keycap on a cross-shaped plastic stem. The stem sits in a plunger barrel and carries either a coil spring back up (the common later C64 keycap) or, on the earliest VIC-20-derived keyboards, nothing at all - those rely purely on the rubber dome for their return and feel markedly sluggish.

##### ABS keycap polymer `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs`

Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix rubberised with polybutadiene. It is tough, dimensionally stable, chemically scratch-resistant and - crucially for legends - it takes paint and plating well. Almost every C64 keycap is ABS or ABS/PC.

###### Polybutadiene rubber phase `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadiene`

The elastic phase that makes ABS impact-resistant, made by polymerising butadiene derived from refinery butadiene, which itself comes from steam cracking propylene. This is the hydrocarbon tree: propylene to butadiene to the rubber in the keycap's grip surface.

###### Butadiene monomer `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadiene.butadiene`

The rubber phase of ABS is made from butadiene, produced by steam cracking of refinery butane or by dehydrogenating butenes. It is the same butadiene the synthetic-rubber industry used.

###### Crude oil `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadiene.crude-oil`

The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

###### Styrene monomer `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene`

Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene, itself made by alkylating benzene with ethylene from steam cracking. Styrene is the rigid phase of the copolymer; benzene is ultimately a refinery product of crude oil or of pyrolitic gasoline from steam crackers.

###### Ethylbenzene to styrene `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.ethylbenzene`

Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, then dehydrogenated to styrene over a promoted iron oxide catalyst.

###### Naphtha `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.styrene.ethylbenzene.naphtha`

The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

###### Acrylonitrile monomer `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylonitrile`

The acrylonitrile monomer is made by the Sohlo process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen are passed over a bismuth-antimony or bismuth-molybdenum catalyst to give acrylonitrile selectively. Propylene itself comes from steam cracking of naphtha, so the keycap of a C64 is roughly one and a half hydrocarbon molecules away from crude oil.

###### Bismuth-antimony catalyst `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylonitrile.bismuth-catalyst` _(medium)_

The ammoxidation catalyst is a bismuth molybdate or bismuth-antimony promoted silica. Bismuth came from bismuthinite, a comparatively rare ore worked chiefly in Bolivia and China, and it was a real bottleneck for acrylonitrile capacity in the 1980s.

##### Double-shot moulding of the legend `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot` _(medium)_

The keycap is injection-moulded twice: once in the base colour, then a second shot of a second colour is injected into a slightly larger cavity, covering everything except the legend characters, which were left as uncoated islands of the first shot. This gives a legend that cannot wear off - the reason a forty-year-old C64 keycap still reads.

###### Second-shot colour `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.legend-colour` _(medium)_

The outer shot is pigmented with an organic or inorganic colourant at high loading. Brown, red, orange and grey legends - the four C64 keycap colours - are all achievable with pigmented ABS; the moulding must be run at a high enough pressure that the two shots fuse rather than delaminate.

###### Colourant in the second shot `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.legend-colour.pigment` _(medium)_

The second-shot colour is a pigment dispersed in the ABS matrix at high loading. Organic pigments give brighter colours and are more expensive; inorganic iron oxides give the earthier browns and reds.

###### Iron oxide pigments `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.legend-colour.pigment.iron-oxide` _(medium)_

Synthetic iron oxides, made by oxidising iron scrap, were the standard browns, reds and blacks of the period and are still used. They begin at iron ore and end up in the keycap.

###### Iron ore `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.legend-colour.pigment.iron-oxide.iron-ore`

Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

###### Co-moulding cycle `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.cycle`

Both shots are moulded in one press cycle using a hot-runner or a runnerless hot manifold so the second colour is injected onto the first while the first is still hot enough to bond. That is what makes the legend wear-proof rather than a coat of paint.

##### Coil return spring `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring` _(medium)_

A small stainless or music-wire spring inside the plunger barrel returning the key to its rest position and setting the initial (pre-dome) force. Without it the user bottoms out on the dome itself, which is why the earliest keyboards feel hard and inconsistent.

###### Music wire (patented steel) `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.music-wire` _(medium)_

A high-carbon steel wire, patented and drawn to a fine diameter, with a very high tensile strength - which is what lets a millimetre-thick coil inside a keycap return thousands of times without taking a set.

###### Iron ore for spring steel `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.music-wire.iron-ore`

The same hematite/magnetite chain as the joystick shaft. Almost all ferrous stock in 1982 was basic-oxygen-furnace steel from imported ore.

###### Spring coiling machine `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil-winder`

A cam-controlled coiler winds a coil spring from wire, sets its free length and closes the ends, tens of thousands per hour. Every keycap plunger spring on the keyboard was made on a machine of this type.

###### Tool steel cam and dies `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil-winder.steel` _(medium)_

The coiler tool is hardened tool steel, and the coiler is a Camweld or similar automatic machine. Ferrous tooling, so iron ore again.

###### Iron ore `c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil-winder.steel.iron-ore`

Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

#### SHIFT LOCK and RESTORE, the two off-matrix keys `c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock`

Two of the 63 keys are not in the scanned matrix. SHIFT LOCK is wired to the same line as LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot distinguish it and simply sees a latched shift. RESTORE is wired directly to the 6510's NMI line, so pressing it halts the CPU without any firmware involvement at all - a hardware reset, not a key.

##### Latching dome for SHIFT LOCK `c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latching-dome`

A dome that latches: pressing it collapses it and it stays collapsed, requiring a second, firmer press (or a press on a neighbouring key) to release. Mechanically it is a deformation of the rubber dome itself rather than a separate switch, which is why no space in the matrix is spent on it.

###### Bistable dome geometry `c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latching-dome.bistable` _(medium)_

The latching dome works because the rubber is shaped so that under a light press it collapses past the rubber's own elastic limit and stays collapsed. It is a mechanical latch, not an electrical one, which is why the firmware has no idea a separate key exists.

##### Wiring to the LSHIFT line `c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.wiring`

SHIFT LOCK is simply wired in parallel with LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot tell the two apart: pressing SHIFT LOCK just holds the shift bit down. Restore is on a completely different wire, straight to the 6510 NMI pin.

#### Flat ribbon cable to the mainboard `c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon`

A flat multi-conductor ribbon leaves the keyboard board, loops through the case, and terminates at the pin header on the front-left edge of the mainboard. The ribbon is crimped into an insulation-displacement connector on the keyboard end in later designs, and soldered directly to the header on the mainboard end.

##### PET/PVC flat flexible cable `c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film`

Parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film layers with a PVC jacket. The jacket and the film are all hydrocarbon polymers, so this cable is chemically the same family as the switch housings and the case.

###### PVC jacket `c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc`

The ribbon's outer jacket is extruded PVC, the cheapest flexible insulation available. Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from salt - rock salt mined or solution-mined - while the ethylene comes from a steam cracker. So the ribbon cable ends at both rock salt and crude oil.

###### Vinyl chloride monomer `c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vinyl-chloride`

Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine over a promoted catalyst. The ethylene comes from a steam cracker and the chlorine from brine electrolysis - so the ribbon jacket touches both an oil field and a salt field.

###### Naphtha `c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.vinyl-chloride.naphtha`

The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

    - *Joystick controller* `c64.joystick` *(seen above)*
## Where every branch terminates `c64.bottoms-out`

Everything above ends in one of three trunks: refined metals, petrochemicals, and the utilities and factories that supply both. Most component subtrees inline their own copy of the relevant chain — a capacitor really does carry its own aluminium, and an ABS case really does carry its own acrylonitrile — so these are the canonical, deepest versions of those same chains, kept together so you can read one end to end.

### Metals, ores and industrial minerals `metal`

Every mineral stream behind a 1982 Commodore 64: the quartzite that becomes silicon, the bauxite and cryolite that becomes aluminium foil, the porphyry copper that becomes PCB track and transformer magnet wire, the tin and lead that become 63/37 solder, the iron ore and coke that become the steel chassis and the transformer laminations, and the specialty metals - gold, silver, nickel, tantalum, zinc, chromium, manganese, cobalt - that end up plating contacts, filling ceramic capacitors and setting the sinter point of every solder joint. Each branch runs from the finished metal down to the quarry, the open pit, the evaporite bed or the seabed.

      - *High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)* `metal.silica` *(seen above)*
#### Sodium compounds: caustic soda and soda ash `metal.sodium`

Sodium is not in the machine as a metal, but the C64 could not exist without it: caustic soda dissolves bauxite to make alumina, and the same chlor-alkali industry that makes the caustic soda also makes the chlorine and hydrogen that become the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Behind both sits a bed of rock salt or a bucket of evaporite from a solar salt pan.

##### Caustic soda (NaOH), 50% solution `metal.caustic-soda`

Two entirely different consumers in this tree. The Bayer process digestion liquor, where a caustic grade tanker holds roughly 300-400 t of 50% solution and a refinery's caustic and steam costs dominate its operating cost. And the chlor-alkali industry, where the same product comes out of the same cell as the chlorine and hydrogen that make the hydrochloric acid for the silicon plant. Cost accounting in aluminium is dominated by caustic and steam; every tonne of caustic lost to red mud is recovered by lime in the causticisation circuit or bought.

###### Chlor-alkali electrolytic cell `metal.chlor-alkali`

2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. In 1982 almost all of it was a diaphragm cell or a mercury cell. The diaphragm cell - an asbestos-cloth cathode separator - gave low-purity caustic loaded with salt and was steadily displaced through the late 1970s and 1980s by the membrane cell, which delivers 50% NaOH essentially free of salt. Mercury cell caustic went to a short finishing step, causticisation with sodium carbonate, to strip the last mercury; the Hooker Chemical conversion of its Niagara Falls works to membrane in 1984 is the emblematic date.

###### Chlorine gas (Cl2) `metal.chlorine`

A pale yellow-green gas denser than air, made in the chlor-alkali plant and piped or tanker-shipped to the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit. Around 1982 much of it went to solvent makers and to water treatment as chlorinated organics; only a fraction ever reached a silicon plant, and silicon-grade chlorine must be bone dry, because water plus trichlorosilane gives hydrochloric acid and hexasiloxane gel that plugs the fluidised bed.

###### Electrolysis hydrogen from the chlor-alkali cathode `metal.hydrogen` _(medium)_

The wet hydrogen off the cathode goes to acid synthesis, and in a silicon plant it also goes to the Siemens reactor as the carrier that carries trichlorosilane to the rod and strips the chlorine off. The purification train is a caustic scrubber, then a drying tower, and the carbon monoxide has to be taken below a few ppm or the polysilicon comes out with carbon in it. The same hydrogen, purified a stage further, is what a stainless bright-annealing line uses.

###### The diaphragm cell and the asbestos problem `metal.chlor-alkali.digram-cell`

The 1980s chlor-alkali cell was a rectangular steel box, 2-3 m long, with an anode compartment of brine and a cathode compartment of water separated by an asbestos cloth diaphragm deposited on a wire gauze. The diaphragm was cheap, durable and effective, and it was the reason the world's chlor-alkali industry had a mesothelioma problem. The cell voltage was low, 3.0-3.5 V, and the caustic carried 10-15 g/L of salt because the diaphragm let chloride through. The Hooker Chemical conversion at Niagara Falls in 1984 to a membrane cell was the moment the asbestos diaphragm began to disappear from the industry.

###### Dechlorination and the brine circuit `metal.chlor-alkali.dechlorination` _(medium)_

The brine leaving a cell still has hypochlorite in it, because chlorine dissolves in the caustic. It is treated with sodium sulphite and then acidified, the brine is re-saturated with salt and re-purified on a soda ash and barium carbonate cycle, and it goes back to the cell. So a chlor-alkali plant also consumes sodium carbonate and barium carbonate - the latter being, note, the barium carbonate from the barium branch of this file. The barium carbonate is there to remove the sulphate from the brine as barium sulphate, which is filtered off and, until the 1980s, dumped.

###### Ceramic-grade barium carbonate `metal.barium-carbonate`

A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

###### Calcining barium carbonate to a reactive powder `metal.barium-carbonate.calcination` _(medium)_

The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.

###### Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade `metal.barium-carbonate.contamination` _(medium)_

The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.

###### Rock salt and solar salt brine `metal.salt-brine`

Salt for a chlor-alkali plant arrives either as mined halite from a salt operation or as brine evaporated from seawater. Solar evaporation was the cheap route for a plant on a hot, dry coast - Israel's Dead Sea and Atlantic coast, California's San Francisco Bay, the Gulf of Mexico - while inland plants in the saltbelt of Michigan, Ohio, New York and Ontario bought mined rock salt from underground, which is also where the bromine came from.

###### Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt `metal.salt-rock`

Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.

###### Halite evaporite: the rock `metal.salt-evaporite`

The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

###### Solar salt evaporation pond `metal.salt-solar-pan` _(medium)_

A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.

##### Soda ash (Na2CO3) by the Solvay process `metal.soda-ash`

Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

###### Ammonia-soda carbonation tower `metal.soda-ash.ammonia` _(medium)_

A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.

###### Coal/coke ammonia from the gasworks `metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source` _(medium)_

In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

###### The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower `metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln`

The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.

###### Limestone (CaCO3) quarry `metal.limestone`

High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.

###### Carbonate platform limestone `metal.limestone.bed`

The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.

###### Limestone quarry and crushing plant `metal.limestone.quarry`

A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.

###### Recovery of the salt from the brine `metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery` _(medium)_

The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.

#### Lime (CaO) and calcium `metal.lime`

Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone; limestone is quarried rock.

##### Lime in the Bayer circuit `metal.lime.bayer-uses` _(medium)_

Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently - the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.

###### Causticisation: the lime goes round the loop `metal.lime.causticisation` _(medium)_

The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.

            - *Limestone quarry and crushing plant* `metal.limestone.quarry` *(seen above)*
###### Pre-desilication by attrition washing `metal.lime.pre-desilication` _(medium)_

By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings - and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.

##### Limestone and lime as blast furnace flux `metal.lime.blast-flux` _(medium)_

The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.

##### Lime as etch regeneration and neutralisation `metal.lime.pcb-etch` _(medium)_

At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride, CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath - which is where a lot of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed. Lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; this node exists only because the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

##### Lime as a metallurgical slag flux `metal.lime.scavenger` _(medium)_

Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.

##### Shaft and rotary lime kilns `metal.lime.kiln`

Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln - a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom - makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product; the rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

###### The counter-current shaft kiln `metal.lime.shaft-kiln` _(medium)_

Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.

###### Slaking: quicklime to hydrated lime `metal.lime.slaking`

CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

###### Lime in Portland cement `metal.lime.cement`

By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch - limestone, kiln, CaO - and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

              - *Limestone (CaCO3) quarry* `metal.limestone` *(seen above)*
###### The lime kiln gas and its CO2 `metal.lime.kiln-gas` _(medium)_

A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and - much later - the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.

###### The rotary kiln and the preheater `metal.lime.rotary-kiln` _(medium)_

A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln - the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt - but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.

###### Overburnt lime and the clinker problem `metal.lime.kiln-clinker` _(medium)_

If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.

#### Potassium chloride (KCl) for tantalum reduction `metal.potassium`

Not a C64 component - potassium never appears in the machine - but it is a mandatory reagent in the tantalum branch, because the metal is won as a fluoride salt and reduced with metal, not from an oxide. Potassium also divides tantalum from niobium in the fluoride chemistry. It is included so the tantalum branch reaches a real, mined leaf instead of stopping at an implied reagent.

##### Sylvinite (KCl + NaCl) `metal.sylvinite`

The ore of the Devonian Prairie Evaporite in Saskatchewan, mined underground at 800-1100 m by potash shafts where the ground is artificially frozen so the salt stays put, or by solution mining in Ontario. Run of mine is about 8-14% K2O; it is beneficiated by flotation or hot leaching and sold as muriate of potash.

###### Potash evaporite bed `metal.potash.evaporite`

The leaf: a buried evaporite sea - sylvinite interbedded with halite, carnallite and mudstone, formed by the same evaporation of a restricted sea that made the salt used in chlor-alkali. The Colville and Hatchet lakes area of Saskatchewan sits over one of the largest.

###### Artificial ground freezing in the potash shaft `metal.sylvinite.freezing`

The Saskatchewan potash ore is 800-1100 m down in a bed that is 30-40 C and gassy, and it is a weak, water-bearing shale-like rock that would flow into the shaft. The solution since 1967 has been to freeze it: brine is circul through freeze pipes in the shaft and the decline for two to three years before sinking, turning the ground into a self-supporting frozen plug of ice and salt. It works, and it is one of the more unusual pieces of mining engineering anywhere - and it is the reason the Saskatchewan potash industry looks the way it does.

###### Potash flotation and hot leaching `metal.sylvinite.beneficiation` _(medium)_

Run-of-mine sylvinite is about 12% K2O with a lot of NaCl and clay. Beneficiation is by flotation of the sylvinite in a saturated KCl-brine solution (because sylvinite is barely soluble while halite is much more so, so the brine selectively wets the sylvinite), or by hot leaching at 85-100 C which dissolves the potassium chloride and leaves the salt. For the tantalum industry the relevant product is not potash at all - it is the KCl that goes into the K2TaF7 precipitation.

###### Muriate of potash and the tailings `metal.potash-product` _(medium)_

The product is 60-95% KCl, bagged or bulk, and the waste is a slurry of NaCl and clay that goes into a tailings pond impoundment. Two points of interest for this tree: the potassium chloride that ends up in a potassium fluoride bath for the tantalum reduction is bought from this industry, and the tailings pond is a genuinely large hole in the ground - the Belle Plaine potash mine near Esterhazy had a tailings pile that became, by the 1980s, a place people went to watch birds. So a fertilizer industry byproduct is where the tantalum industry gets its potassium.

###### The potash rail link `metal.potash.stockyard` _(medium)_

Saskatchewan potash moved to world markets by unit train - a dedicated train of a hundred or more hopper wagons - to Vancouver, Prince Albert or Minneapolis, and then by ship from Vancouver or by barge and lake freighter to Chicago. So the potassium in a 1982 tantalum capacitor travelled down a potash shaft, through a washer and a flotation plant, into a bulk railcar, onto a ship, and into a plastics extruder. It is the most ordinary logistics chain in the tree and it is the shortest path from a geological process to a metal part.

###### Solution mining of potash `metal.sylvinite.solution-mining` _(medium)_

Where the potash seam is deeply buried and thin - as at Thames, Ontario - the shaft is not worth sinking. Instead two horizontal wells are drilled into the seam, one to inject hot water and one to draw the resulting brine, and the potash is recovered from the brine by evaporation. Two wells can produce a million tonnes a year. It is a solution-mining technique borrowed from the salt industry and it works because sylvinite dissolves in hot water while the clay it sits in does not.

###### The injection and recovery well pair `metal.solution-mining.well` _(medium)_

Solution mining is two wells and a plant. A cemented well is drilled horizontally into the potash seam and a casing is set with a perforated liner; hot water at 80-90 C is injected at a pressure of a few hundred psi, the seam is about 1-3 m thick and dissolves over a 30-200 m horizontal section, and a second well 500 m away draws the brine back. The well field is fracked between the wells to connect the fracture, and the plant evaporates the brine in a multiple-effect evaporator. It is a genuine engineering oddity - a mine with no mine - and it works because potash dissolves in hot brine and clay does not.

##### KCl as the tantalum and fluoride flux `metal.potassium.flux` _(medium)_

The only reason potassium is in this tree. Potassium chloride is added to the tantalum fluoride solution to precipitate K2TaF7, and potassium fluoride is used as a flux in some silicon and aluminium processes. Both are bought from the potash industry as a commodity, in tonnes. So a handful of grams of tantalum in a C64's capacitors required a few grams of potassium chloride, which required a shaft in Saskatchewan or a pond on the Dead Sea, which required a bed of evaporite. It is the shortest branch in this file and the funniest, because it starts with an ocean drying up.

      - *Primary aluminium: ingot, foil, sheet, extrusion* `metal.aluminum` *(seen above)*
      - *Copper: track, winding wire, foil, contacts* `metal.copper` *(seen above)*
      - *Tin: solder alloy, tin plate, contacts* `metal.tin` *(seen above)*
      - *Lead: the other half of the solder* `metal.lead` *(seen above)*
      - *63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste* `metal.solder` *(seen above)*
#### Zinc: die-cast alloy, plating, brass, varistor `metal.zinc`

Zinc is the fourth non-ferrous metal and the most recycled one. In a 1982 C64 it appears as a die-cast zinc alloy for the case-mounted parts and the key plungers, as a plating on steel for EMI shields and chassis fasteners, as brass (copper-zinc) for the bus-bar and connector bodies, and as zinc oxide in the varistor that clamps the supply spikes off the mains input. The smelting industry in 1982 was in the middle of its biggest change in a century: the roast-leach-electrowin zinc-iron plant was replacing the horizontal retort furnace.

##### Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate, 50-60% Zn `metal.sphalerite`

Sphalerite is one of the few ores that is not visually recognisable: it is a black to honey-brown cubic crystal whose colour depends on the iron substituting in the lattice, so the industry grades it in grades of iron - a 4% iron concentrate looks black and a 12% iron concentrate looks ruby red-brown. Concentration is by flotation with an amine or xanthate collector. The great districts were the Red Dog and the Sullivan mine in British Columbia, Broken Hill, the Cerro Rico of Potosi, the Rammelsberg of Goslar, and the Appalachian and Midwestern US zinc districts such as the Bartlesville and the Tennessee mines.

###### Underground zinc-lead mine `metal.sphalerite.mine`

The Red Dog and Sullivan type deposit: a massive sulphide body in a sedimentary basin, mined underground from a ramp or a shaft, with the ore hoisted in a friction hoist or a skip, and the mill right at the portal. Broken Hill's Broken Hill Proprietary was the other archetype, an open pit above a very large primary orebody that was mined for sixty years. Where the zinc and lead are in separate veins, gravity and flotation split them: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 do separate well on a dense-medium separator.

###### Massive sulphide in a sedimentary basin `metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide`

The leaf: a lens-shaped body of fine-grained sulphide - sphalerite, galena, pyrite, with chalcopyrite and arsenopyrite - conformable with the bedding of a marine shale or carbonate, and sitting at a specific stratigraphic horizon. The Red Dog deposit is exactly this: a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin. The ore is not in a vein you can see from the surface; it is a stratigraphic layer you have to know is there.

###### Zinc concentrator: differential flotation `metal.sphalerite.mill` _(medium)_

The ore is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground to 50-100 um in a ball or autogenous mill, and floated in stages. The classic circuit is differential: copper and lead sulphides are floated first with a stronger collector and a higher pH, and then the sphalerite is floated from the tailings with a weaker collector at a lower pH, with copper sulphate added as an activator because sphalerite does not float on its own. That gives a 50-60% Zn concentrate at 85-92% recovery. The Red Dog and Sullivan concentrators were among the largest in the world and are the reason those two mines could be mines at all.

###### Dense-media separation of galena from sphalerite `metal.sphalerite.dms` _(medium)_

Galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 are separable on a shaking table or, much faster, in a dense-medium separator using a ferrosilicon or magnetite suspension at a cut density of about 3.0-3.5. The lead concentrate and the zinc concentrate are thereby split before flotation, which lets the flotation plant be small. Dense-medium separation of a polymetallic ore is one of the great quiet successes of twentieth-century mineral processing.

###### The dense-medium medium: ferrosilicon from silica `metal.dms.fe-silicon` _(medium)_

The liquid in a dense-medium separator is ferrosilicon - an alloy of iron and silicon made in exactly the submerged arc furnace described in the electrical-steel and metallurgical-silicon branches of this file. So a 1982 concentrator that separated galena from sphalerite by density was running a slurry of metallurgical silicon, and the silicon branch of this tree reaches a zinc concentrator as well as a power transformer. Silicon really does end up everywhere: 60-90% of all ferrosilicon production goes into the steel and aluminium branches, but the rest goes into heavy-media separation, and it is the sharpest possible illustration of why a tree like this has cross-links.

                  - *Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace* `metal.ferrosilicon` *(seen above)*
###### The host basin and its caprock `metal.sphalerite.host`

The final leaf of the zinc chain is not a rock but a structure: a sedimentary basin with a metal-bearing horizon in it. The Red Dog deposit is a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin on the Tukarakka Peninsula; Broken Hill is a metamorphosed, deformed massive sulphide in a sequence of Proterozoic metasediments. In both cases the orebody sits at a specific stratigraphic level, and the mine is a series of ramps and stopes chasing a bedding-parallel body a few metres thick. So the zinc in a C64's die-cast key plunger came out of a bed that happens to lie a kilometre beneath a river delta.

##### Roasting of sphalerite to zinc oxide `metal.zinc.roasting`

The concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed or on a sinter strand, 850-1000 C, with the result 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. The 1980s plant that grew out of this is the roaster-sinter plant, in which the hot ZnO and Fe2O3 sinter together into a porous 'dead roast sinter' that is a much better feed for an acid leach than a fine powder. The SO2 at 8-12% goes to the acid plant. This roasting step is where a zinc smelter became a sulfuric acid producer of the same order as a copper smelter, and where the sinter plant's dust catch and its dewpoint control - keep the gas above about 150 C or the zinc and lead fume plasters the plant - became a real engineering discipline.

###### Fluidised-bed roaster `metal.zinc.roaster` _(medium)_
