Concentrate is fed into a bed of 1-3 m of the roast itself on a distributor of tuyeres, held at 850-950 C by the fluidising air, and the bed overflows continuously into a hot cyclone and then a sintering conveyor where the last 100-150 C of roast and the sintering happen together. The whole thing was invented at the Balotelawezwa plant in South Africa and Canadian Calumet in the 1960s and was standard new-plant practice by 1982. An older plant would instead have used a multiple-hearth roaster or a sinter strand and produced a fine, un-sintered ZnO.

###### Fume capture: cadmium and lead from the roaster gas `metal.zinc.fume-catch` _(medium)_

The roaster gas carries a fine zinc oxide fume and, in the vapour phase, the cadmium and the lead. Economically the cadmium is the point: the fume goes to a baghouse, and the cadmium is recovered in a separate cadmium plant. The lead in the same gas is a nuisance and an occupational hazard, and in 1982 the zinc plants of North America were beginning to worry about it for exactly the reason they would later worry about it in the environmental context. The dust is one of the more awkward solid wastes in metallurgy because it is both valuable and toxic.

###### Copper-cadmium residue to the cadmium plant `metal.cadmium-residue` _(medium)_

A 1980s cadmium plant roasted the residue in a retort at 600-800 C: the cadmium volatilised off (it boils at 767 C) and was condensed in a condenser, giving 99.9% cadmium metal, while the copper stayed behind. This is the only major industrial source of cadmium, and it is a zinc by-product. It matters here only as a consequence of zinc refining; a C64 has no cadmium.

###### Zinc oxide sinter: the smelter's intermediate `metal.zinc.oxide` _(medium)_

The dead-roast sinter is the actual feed to the leach circuit, and its specification is a compromise between the roast and the leach. It wants to be as completely roasted as possible so that the zinc is all in the oxide, but it also wants to be porous enough for the sulphuric acid to reach it, which is what the sintering stage of the roaster-sinter plant is for. Between 5 and 10% of the zinc stays locked up in the silicate matrix and is lost in the leach residue, which is the second big reason a zinc plant's recovery is not higher than it is.

##### Acid leach and purification of the zinc sulphate solution `metal.zinc.leach-purify`

The dead-roast sinter is leached in spent electrolyte diluted with water, at pH about 4.5 and 40-60 C, in a series of leaching tanks. Then the solution must be purified, because almost every impurity that reaches the cell either consumes current or plates out on the cathode as a short circuit. Iron is removed by air oxidising the pH up to 5.2 so it precipitates as jarosite or goethite - a step that consumes zinc as well and is where most of the zinc plants' zinc loss is. Then copper, cadmium and cobalt are removed by adding zinc dust, which by cementation throws those metals out of solution. Chloride is kept down by jarosite precipitation. Every one of these is a chemistry rather than a metallurgy, and every one of them costs zinc.

###### Zinc dust for cementation `metal.zinc.dust` _(medium)_

The purification step uses zinc metal itself, atomised from a small kettle, as the reagent that throws out copper, cadmium and cobalt. The cemented metals - a black sludge heavy with copper and cadmium - is filtered off and shipped to a cadmium refinery, which is where the world's cadmium came from in 1982. So the zinc plant's purification residue is a cadmium ore in all but name.

            - *Copper-cadmium residue to the cadmium plant* `metal.cadmium-residue` *(seen above)*
###### Jarosite residue and the zinc it costs `metal.zinc.jarosite-residue` _(medium)_

The iron precipitation step that makes the zinc plant's chemistry work is also its biggest single loss. Oxidising the iron out at pH 5.2 throws down jarosite or goethite, and both of them carry zinc in their lattice - typically 4-10% Zn. At 1-3 tonnes of residue per tonne of zinc made, and 5-10% of the contained zinc never recovered, the iron removal step is where a zinc plant loses a million dollars a year. It is also a waste stream: acidic, iron-rich, and in the 1980s dumped in a lined pond. This is the residue the modern jarosite and goethite processes are designed to shrink.

###### Air oxidation and the jarosite goethite process `metal.zinc.iron-removal` _(medium)_

The purification chemistry in one process. The leach liquor's pH is raised with limestone and the iron is oxidised with air in a bank of aeration tanks at 90-100 C. Whether the precipitate is jarosite (the older route, at pH 5.2 with sodium sulphate added, at 90-100 C over 10-20 hours) or goethite (the newer route, at 80-95 C with less retention time) decides how much zinc the residue holds and how much sulphate the plant makes. Every zinc plant in 1982 had made a choice between these two, and the choice is the single biggest determinant of its cost.

##### Electrowinning of zinc on aluminium cathodes `metal.zinc.electrowinning`

Zinc is one of the few metals won by electrolysis out of an aqueous solution at industrial scale. The reason is that zinc is more negative than hydrogen and would just deposit hydrogen from water if it were not for the high hydrogen overvoltage on aluminium; each cathode is an aluminium plate of 1-2 m2 and 10-25 mm thick, and the scraper at the top of the cycle knocks off a 5-25 kg slab. The slabs are melted in a small induction furnace and cast into 25 kg ingots at 99.995%. The energy is 3,000-3,500 kWh per tonne of zinc - high, but the purity and the by-product recovery make the route worth it for ores that cannot be smelted. This is the convergence point of the roast, leach, purification and ingot branches.

###### Lead-silver anode in the tankhouse `metal.zinc.anode-mb`

The insoluble anode is a lead alloy - 99% Pb with 0.5-1% Ag, cast as 10-40 mm thick plates - which works because when it does corrode slowly, the lead dioxide layer that forms is a perfectly good anode surface. Silver is added because it slows the corrosion. So the zinc tankhouse is structurally a lead operation: it consumes lead anodes at a rate of a few kilograms per tonne of zinc, which is one of the more elegant hidden cross-links between the lead and zinc branches in this file.

###### The single-deck electrolysis cell `metal.zinc.electrowinning-cell` _(medium)_

The 1980s zinc tankhouse cell was a plain open-top concrete or rubber-lined steel box, 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, with an aluminium cathode every 15-25 mm and a lead anode between them. The electrolyte is fed in at one end and pulled out at the other; the plates go in, run for 24-72 hours, come out, get scraped, and go to the melting furnace. A modern plant with 300,000-400,000 m2 of cathode area is a building the size of a football pitch. This is one of the least mechanised and most manually-intensive electrolysis plants in the industry, because the plate handling has never lent itself to automation.

###### Stripping the slabs and the melting furnace `metal.zinc.stripping` _(medium)_

At the end of the cycle each cathode is lifted out, tipped against a steel plate that shears the zinc slab off, and the slabs are charged to a 100-500 kg induction furnace. The furnace has to be held at 450-470 C and under a cover flux because zinc oxidises readily and every gram of oxide is a loss. Two refinements came in during the 1980s: induction furnaces with better stirring and better control, and the move to a single large furnace rather than a fleet of small ones, which cut the oxide loss and the labour.

      - *Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless* `metal.nickel` *(seen above)*
#### Manganese: the steel deoxidiser `metal.manganese`

Manganese has no visible place in a C64, but without it the steel the case and the shielding are made from would have inclusions and blowholes in it. Almost all manganese ore is used to make ferromanganese, which is added to the steelmaking furnace as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser and as an alloying element. It is a branch included because the steel branch cannot honestly stop without it.

##### Pyrolusite and manganiferous ore, 25-50% Mn `metal.manganese.ore`

Manganese ore is almost never a clean manganese mineral. The Groote Eylandt and South African supergene ores are a hard, black, sooty mass of MnO2 cryptocrystalline material - wad and psilomelane - interbedded with iron formation. Grade is 25-50% Mn, and low-grade ore needs beneficiation: the South African ores were washed and jigged to reject the iron, and Groote Eylandt is washed in a scrubber and on a sluice. Silica and phosphorus are the two impurities that destroy value. This is a convergence node: the ferromanganese furnace, the ferrite branch's manganese carbonate and the steel deoxidiser all hang off it.

###### Supergene manganese mining in the Kalahari `metal.manganese.laterite-mine` _(medium)_

The Transvaal and the northern Cape were the world's largest producers in 1982 by a wide margin, and the operation was surface mining on a 5-20 m ore layer over a 100 m thick band of black manganese-bearing sandstone. Drag hoists, belt conveyors, and a scrubber-and-jig beneficiation plant, then a sinter belt. The ore is a black, hard, siliceous rock and it is dug out of a 30 m face.

###### Scrubber, sluice and jig beneficiation `metal.manganese.washing-plant` _(medium)_

Groote Eylandt and the South African operations do not smelt the raw lump: they wash it. The ore is dumped on a heap, a high-pressure water monitor scrubs off the fines and the clay, and the coarse goes over a sluice and a jig where the density difference between the manganese minerals (4.5-5.1) and the iron formation (5.0-5.3 but with a very different mineralogy) and the waste gangue separates the product. That is why a 30% Mn ore can make a 40% Mn product at low cost: the operation is a placer operation with a shovel in it.

###### The oxide and carbonate phases of the ore `metal.manganese.oxide-phase`

The leaf of the manganese branch's rock: the manganese in a supergene ore is not one mineral but four. Pyrolusite MnO2 is the black, soft, fibrous one; psilomelane is a barium-bearing cryptocrystalline mixture; braunite Mn2O3 is the hard brown one; and rhodochrosite MnCO3 is the pink carbonate in the primary zone. The refractory braunite is the one the smelter hates, because it takes three times the reductant and gives a high slag. Which phase a shipment is made of determines whether it goes to a ferromanganese furnace or to a chemical plant, and the assay is a chemical analysis, not a visual test.

###### Abyssal manganese nodule dredge `metal.manganese.nodule`

The other, entirely different source: polymetallic nodules lying in thousands of square kilometres of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and the Peru Basin at 4,000-6,000 m depth, containing 30% Mn, 2% Ni, 1% Cu and 25% Fe. Collecting them means a 10,000-tonne ship dragging a pipe across the seabed for 20,000 hours a year. It was never commercial in 1982 - technology trials were running but no mine was producing - and the incentive that eventually made it real was nickel, not manganese. This node is here because the 1980s seabed mining industry was built by exactly the people looking at the ore as a nickel resource, and by 1982 the C64's nickel supply chain and this geological curiosity were the same corporate conversation.

###### Manganese oxide concretions on pelagic clay `metal.manganese.nodule-rock`

The leaf: millimetre-to-centimetre potato-shaped concretions of Mn-Fe oxide lying unattached in a soft abyssal red clay. The metal has precipitated out of seawater around a nucleus, slowly, over millions of years. It is the most extraordinary leaf in this tree: the manganese in a C64's steel is, in principle, available from the floor of an ocean.

###### The abyssal red clay beneath the nodules `metal.abyssal-clay` _(medium)_

The true bottom of the manganese branch: a soft, red, pelagic clay that covers the abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m and that took the better part of 100 million years to accumulate, one centimetre at a time. The nodules sit on top of it. So the deepest leaf in this tree is a handful of dark potatoes on a carpet of red mud at the bottom of the Pacific, and the entire industrial-manganese question of whether to mine it is a question about that carpet.

###### The 1970s technology trials and the industry that funded them `metal.manganese.nodule-tech` _(low)_

By 1982 seabed nodule mining was a real programme with real money behind it, and the money is the interesting part. The incentive was not manganese - the grades were assumed recoverable but nobody had proved it at scale. The incentive was nickel and cobalt, because the strategic metal studies of the 1970s and early 1980s concluded that the West had too little nickel and too little cobalt and that the seabed was the answer. The trials - the French Nodule, the American DOMES and NOAA work, the Japanese and the German programmes - put a collector on the bottom and brought up tonnages. Nothing commercial resulted before the 2000s, largely on legal grounds, but the 1982 assessment was optimistic, and that is a genuine piece of the 1982 story rather than hindsight.

###### The hydraulic collector head `metal.collector` _(low)_

The machine the whole idea rests on: a manifold of suction nozzles, 10-30 m across, towed along the seabed at 1-3 knots, that lifts the nodules into a riser pipe and up to a ship 4,000-6,000 m above. The 1970s trials worked at the point where the ocean is deepest to learn whether nodules survive being lifted - the attrition of the nodules on the way up turned out to be a genuine engineering problem - and the riserless concepts that would have solved it were still on paper. It is a beautiful illustration of how much of deep-sea mining is really a fluid mechanics problem.

##### High-carbon ferromanganese, Mn 65-80%, C 6-8% `metal.ferromanganese`

Made in a submerged arc furnace, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, at 1400-1600 C with the electrode tips submerged in the slag. The charge is sintered manganese ore, coke, limestone and often a good deal of iron ore, because the aim is an alloy of about 70% manganese at 6-8% carbon, and manganese is expensive enough that the industry buys more ore than stoichiometry requires in order to reach the assay. The manganese comes out as a carbide, Mn7C3, not as the metal, which is why the alloy has a carbon content at all. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: high-carbon ferromanganese is 6-8% C, not 13-15%; medium-carbon is 1-4% and low-carbon is under 0.5%, so 13-15% is not a real grade.

###### Sintering the manganese ore `metal.manganese.sintering` _(medium)_

Manganese ore is very fine and very friable, so it cannot be blown into a submerged arc furnace as a powder; it is sintered first, on a travelling grate exactly like the lead sinter, to make a 30-50 mm porous cake. The sinter belt at a manganese works is a zinc-works sinter plant or a lead-works sinter plant wearing different clothes, which makes it a nice example of a single machine serving three of the branches in this file.

###### Deoxidation and desulphurisation in the steel ladle `metal.manganese.deoxidiser`

Where the alloy is actually used. During tapping, ferromanganese is added to the steel. Manganese has a higher oxygen affinity than iron, so it combines with the dissolved oxygen to form MnO inclusions - which is the point: the oxygen is now safely tied up in an oxide the steelmaker can float out instead of being trapped as a gas bubble or an oxide stringer. Manganese also lowers the sulphur by forming MnS. The cost is that every kilo of manganese added becomes an inclusion unless the steel is properly deoxidised and the slag properly cleaned, which is why the amount is carefully calculated and why clean, low-inclusion steel is a specific technical achievement.

###### Aluminium and silicon deoxidation `metal.manganese.melt-deoxidation` _(medium)_

The last step in the ladle is the one that actually decides the steel's quality. Manganese ties up the bulk of the dissolved oxygen as MnO inclusions, and then a calculated addition of aluminium - 0.5-2 kg per tonne - ties up the rest as Al2O3. Those inclusions have to go, and in a well-run plant they are floated out in the ladle or removed later by degassing and filtering. Manganese is what makes the aluminium deoxidation work: without manganese in solution, aluminium would oxidise preferentially as Al2O3 straight out of the bath and never reach the steel.

###### Removing the inclusions: degassing and filtration `metal.manganese.inclusion-removal` _(medium)_

A modern low-sulphur steel has few MnS inclusions but a lot of fine Al2O3, and that is a different problem: fine alumina does not float out, so it has to be filtered. A 1980s plate mill that wanted clean, formable sheet for deep drawing or for tinplating ran a ladle through a vacuum degasser to flush hydrogen and nitrogen and then through a ceramic foam filter in the ladle, or poured through a tundish filter. This is the technology that made the C64's chassis panel and the tinplate base material reproducible rather than lucky.

###### The submerged arc furnace and its refractory `metal.manganese.furnace-lining` _(medium)_

A ferromanganese furnace is 25-100 MVA with three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m in diameter, and the difference from a silicon furnace is the slag: the ferromanganese process makes a large volume of a liquid, low-basicity slag, so the furnace is a slag vessel with an electrode in it. The shell is steel with a refractory lining of magnesite or magnesite-carbon, and the lining is eroded by the slag at 1500 C faster than in a silicon furnace. Carbon pastes, electrode paste made of the same coke-and-pitch as the aluminium anode, are rammed into holes in the roof around each electrode. So a ferromanganese plant is a coke-and-pitch shop as much as a manganese shop, which is the same convergence as the ferrochrome and ferrosilicon branches.

###### Graphite and carbon electrodes `metal.graphite.electrode`

The EAF electrodes, the submerged arc furnace electrodes of the ferrosilicon, ferrochrome and ferromanganese industries, the aluminium pot anodes, the silicon furnace electrodes and the large carbon blocks of a blast furnace hearth all consume the same two feedstocks: calcined petroleum or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as the binder. A 'graphite' electrode is green-milled from petroleum coke, extruded, and baked above 2500 C; a 'carbon' electrode stops at 800-1200 C. Pitch coke dominates for the graphite grades because it gives the higher density and the lower ash.

###### The electricity contract behind a ferroalloy furnace `metal.manganese.smelter-electricity` _(medium)_

A 100 MVA submerged arc furnace draws about 80-90 MW continuously and cannot be stopped without destroying the furnace. So it needs a long-term supply contract and, in most cases, its own generating plant or a dedicated hydro or coal share. In the 1980s several ferroalloy industries - Norway's ferrochrome and ferrosilicon, South Africa's ferrochrome, Norway and Quebec's ferrosilicon - were built around cheap hydropower, and the industry's geography is essentially a map of where the cheap electricity was. It is the same fact as the aluminium smelter's, and the reason the same two or three countries dominated both.

##### Charging the ferromanganese into the ladle `metal.manganese.ladle-charging` _(medium)_

A ladle of steel is a bad place to drop a lump of ferromanganese, because the lump floats, the reaction is violent and the steel is left with unreacted alloy inclusions. So the FeMn is added in sized lumps and, increasingly in the 1980s, in cored wire - a steel tube filled with powdered ferromanganese and flux, fed into the ladle on a lance and dissolved by the passage of the steel through it. Cored-wire charging was a genuine 1980s development in secondary metallurgy and it improved the yield of the manganese, because it puts the metal into the steel rather than onto it.

      - *Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome* `metal.chromium` *(seen above)*
      - *Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts* `metal.gold` *(seen above)*
      - *Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing* `metal.silver` *(seen above)*
#### Tantalum powder for electrolytic capacitors `metal.tantalum`

A 1982 C64 has a handful of tantalum capacitors on the mainboard, in the analogue filter section, and tantalum beads in small packages. Each one is a sintered porous tantalum anode with a tantalum oxide dielectric and a solid manganese dioxide or a liquid electrolyte. The tantalum metal is won from columbite-tantalite, a refractory oxide ore, through a hydrofluoric-acid digestion that is one of the most corrosive industrial processes in existence. In 1982-83 there was a real tantalum supply crisis - the Congo and Brazil supply, the Botswana and Zimbabwe expansions, the US stockpile, and a price that doubled - and it is the one place in this tree where a commodity shock from a mining country touched a home computer.

##### Columbite-tantalite concentrate `metal.columbite`

A hard, black, sub-conchoidal mineral - (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 - that in practice is never a pure species but a solid solution, and that is the whole problem of the tantalum industry: tantalum and niobium are chemically almost identical and always occur together, with the tantalum content ranging from a few percent to more than 50% of the total. The separation is the entire industry. The main 1982 sources were the Greenbushes and Wodgina pegmatites in Western Australia, the Cat Creek and Oarkopper operations in Brazil, and the columbite-tantalite concentrates from the Congo, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Tantalum-bearing tin slags from Malaysia and Brazil were a secondary source.

###### Pegmatite open pit with sluicing `metal.columbite.mine` _(medium)_

The tantalum ore is in a pegmatite dyke, a very coarse-grained granite intrusion, and the extraction in the small operations is almost artisanal: the dyke is blasted, the rock is crushed and hand-sorted, and the heavy tantalum minerals are concentrated on a sluice or a jig. The Greenbushes operation, at the time one of the largest, mined a 3 km pegmatite by open pit with a 200,000 t/year plant. So the tantalum in a 1982 C64's capacitors very plausibly came out of an Australian open cut in a pegmatite, hand-sorted and sluiced.

###### Granitic pegmatite dyke `metal.columbite.pegmatite`

The leaf: a coarse-grained, quartz-feldspar-mica rock so coarse that individual crystals are centimetres across, with the tantalum-bearing minerals in small pockets of rare-metal enrichment. Pegmatites are the last-crystallising fraction of a granite magma, so they are the natural home of every incompatible element - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, rare earths. There is no more apt end point for the tantalum chain than a dyke of crystals bigger than your fist.

###### The crystals and the rare-metal pockets `metal.pegmatite-crystals`

The leaf of the tantalum branch. A pegmatite is the last thing a granite magma crystallises, and because it is water-rich and volatile-rich it can hold elements that have no business being in a granite at all - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, tin, the rare earths - at hundreds of times their normal concentration. Those elements concentrate in the last pockets to crystallise, and a pocket 30 cm across can hold a few kilos of coltan worth more than the whole pegmatite around it. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor came out of small pockets in a last-stage granite pocket, hand-sorted out of a rock whose crystals are bigger than your fist, in a pegmatite that is less than 0.1% tantalum.

###### Coltan concentrator: gravity, magnet and electrostatic `metal.columbite.concentrator` _(medium)_

The coltan upgrade in a small operation is a classic three-stage gravity and magnetic plant: a shaking table or a jig throws away the quartz and mica, a magnetic separator takes off the magnetite and ilmenite, and a second gravity stage with a dense-medium separator makes a 20-30% Ta2O5 concentrate from a 0.05-0.1% pegmatite. Electrostatic separation takes out the zircon. The mass yield is under 1%, so the concentrator's job is mostly to throw away 99.5% of the rock, which is why a coltan operation is a small, cheap, labour-intensive plant sitting next to the pit rather than a large mill.

###### The coltan tailings and the river below `metal.columbite.tailings` _(low)_

A coltan concentrator throws away over 99% of the mass it treats, and in the artisanal operations of the 1970s and 1980s that was put into the creek bed without any attempt at settling, and the creek carried it away. The ecological consequence of that was small compared to what followed - the coltan rush of 2000-2008 - but the mining itself was the problem and the tantalum industry spent most of the 1980s designing a better process and a better tailings facility precisely because it was planning for exactly the kind of scrutiny it eventually got. A node whose importance is only visible in hindsight.

##### Hydrofluoric acid digestion at 100-200 C `metal.tantalum.hf-digest`

The concentrate is digested in a mixture of hydrofluoric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid at 100-200 C in a Teflon-lined or Monel vessel with a condenser to keep the HF in the loop. Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 both dissolve as pentafluorides, while iron, tin, thorium and most of the rare earths stay as insoluble fluorides or oxides and are filtered off. Thorium in particular is a problem: it is a radioactive alpha emitter that comes with the coltan and has to be separated and disposed of carefully. The mixed HF/HNO3/HCl digestion was the industry standard for decades; the Bayer process digest, using anhydrous HF with calcium fluoride at 150-200 C, arrived later.

          - *Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar* `metal.hydrofluoric-acid` *(seen above)*
###### Thorium in the coltan: a radioactive by-product `metal.tantalum.thorium` _(medium)_

Columbite-tantalite carries thorium and uranium in solid solution, typically 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2, and because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths it follows them through the whole fluoride circuit and reports with the rare-earth product. It is an alpha emitter, so the refinery's thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, and in 1982 the disposal arrangements in most producing countries were informal. The leaf is a radioactive waste site, which is a legitimate if slightly grim terminus for a branch of the metals tree.

###### Monazite, the thorium and rare-earth carrier `metal.tantalum.monazite` _(medium)_

Monazite, (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4, is a heavy placer mineral from the same beach sands as the ilmenite and the rutile - the Kerala and Queensland and Cape Breton sands. It is the world's main thorium source and, after a very difficult separation, a rare-earth source. In the tantalum circuit monazite is an impurity that has to be filtered off the fluoride solution. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor, the titanium dioxide in its casing, and the thorium residue all come out of the same Queensland beach sand.

###### The heavy-mineral beach and its dredge `metal.monazite.beach`

The leaf of the tantalum branch's by-product chain: a beach on the east coast of Queensland or on the Malabar coast of Kerala where the wave has concentrated ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite and xenotime into a dark, 1-10% heavy-mineral band a metre or two thick in the sand. It is worked by a suction dredge on a barge that pumps the sand onto a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnetic separator and an electrostatic separator. Everything in this file that is 'derived from a beach sand' - the titanium dioxide, the coltan, the thorium, the rare earths, the zircon - came out of a band like this one.

###### The fluoride digestion vessel `metal.tantalum.digest-vessel` _(medium)_

The digestor is the most aggressively corrosive piece of equipment in the metals tree. Anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 100-200 C attacks glass, attacks most metals, and attacks concrete; so the vessel is Monel, nickel, or Teflon-lined, with the condenser and the piping also in Monel, and there is a continuous fluoride leak problem because HF is off-gassing from a boiling slurry. The industry answer through the 1980s was the Monel plant, with a steam stripping system to recover the HF and a caustic scrubber on the vent, and it was the single largest reason the industry needed a process chemist rather than a metallurgist.

###### Monel: nickel with copper `metal.nickel-monel` _(medium)_

The alloy that made the fluorine chemistry of the 1980s possible: 60-70% nickel with 30% copper, and sometimes molybdenum, made in the same vacuum-melted, cast-and-rolled route as any nickel alloy. Monel resists hydrofluoric acid better than almost anything because the nickel fluoride film that forms is protective while aluminium fluoride and steel fluoride are not. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor was separated in a vessel made of a nickel alloy that came out of the nickel branch of this same file, and the aluminium capacitor in the power supply is made with an acid that would destroy it.

##### Separation of tantalum from niobium: K2TaF7 `metal.tantalum.separation`

From the fluoride solution the tantalum is selectively precipitated as potassium heptafluorotantalate, K2TaF7, by adding potassium chloride and hydrofluoric acid at 70-90 C - and this is the step that separates it from niobium, because K2TaF7 is far less soluble than K2NbF7. The K2TaF7 crystals are filtered, washed and dried. Then the metal is won from it in one of two ways. The potassium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with liquid potassium metal, or with sodium, at 700-800 C, giving a coarse tantalum powder. The aluminium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with aluminium in an induction furnace, and the charge is self-separating by particle size - the tantalum comes out as the finer powder and the aluminium-fluoride slag on top. The capacitor industry wanted the sodium-reduction powder specifically, because it could be made much finer.

###### Tantalum powder for the anode `metal.tantalum.powder`

The anode of a tantalum capacitor is a pressed and sintered tantalum pellet of porous sintered tantalum powder, sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, then anodised - electrolytically grown Ta2O5 - to a formation voltage of about 2-4 times the working voltage. The dielectric is the anodised oxide itself, which is why a tantalum capacitor is a bipolar electrolytic part with no liquid. The powder must be pure and must be milled and classified so the particle size is right for the pellet's porosity: a sintered pellet has to have a tortuous pore path, or it will short.

###### Recycling the potassium and fluorine `metal.tantalum.kcl-cycle` _(low)_

The potassium in K2TaF7 and the fluorine in it both come back. The mother liquor from the precipitation is evaporated and the potassium is recycled, and the fluoride is recovered from the aluminium fluoride slag in the metal reduction by hydrolysing it to fluoride and re-fluorinating. A modern tantalum plant's fluorine and potassium consumption is a small fraction of its theoretical requirement because of this loop, and the 1980s plants were learning it. It is a small detail that says something about how tight the tantalum business economics were - and the answer is that they were tight enough to make the 1982-83 supply crisis severe.

      - *Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent* `metal.coke` *(seen above)*
      - *Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel* `metal.steel` *(seen above)*
      - *Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain* `metal.iron` *(seen above)*
      - *Ferrite: transformer and choke cores* `metal.ferrite` *(seen above)*
#### Barium titanate: the ceramic capacitor dielectric `metal.barium`

The disk and multilayer ceramic capacitors on a 1982 C64 mainboard are barium titanate - BaTiO3 - and barium titanate is an industrial material made from barite, the same heavy white mineral that makes the drilling mud. The chain is barite to barium sulphide to barium carbonate to barium titanate, and then a 1000-1400 C calcination and a ceramic pressing. It is the most complete oxide-mineral chain in this file: a sulphate ore, a carbothermal reduction, a carbonate, a perovskite, and a dielectric constant of several thousand.

##### Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98% `metal.barite`

Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

###### Barite vein and replacement mine `metal.barite.mine` _(medium)_

Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.

###### Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue `metal.barite.rock`

The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

###### Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system `metal.barite.mud-system` _(medium)_

A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.

              - *Bentonite binder from a clay pit* `metal.bentonite` *(seen above)*
              - *Lime (CaO) and calcium* `metal.lime` *(seen above)*
###### Drilling grade barite and its mud `metal.barite.drilling-mud` _(medium)_

The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.

##### Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate `metal.barite.reduction`

The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

          - *Ceramic-grade barium carbonate* `metal.barium-carbonate` *(seen above)*
###### Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation `metal.hydrogen-sulfide` _(medium)_

The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.

##### Barium titanate BaTiO3, calcined at 1100-1350 C `metal.barium.titanate`

The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

###### Titanium dioxide from rutile sand `metal.titanium-dioxide`

The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

###### Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge `metal.ilmenite-sand`

The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

###### The ceramic capacitor and its dielectric classes `metal.barium-titanate-capacitor` _(medium)_

The finished use. A 1982 C64 mainboard carries perhaps 30-60 ceramic capacitors, mostly small discs and a few multilayer blocks. The disc is a pressed or cast barium titanate body, sintered at 1250-1350 C, silver-coated on both faces and fired to make the electrodes, and dipped in an epoxy or phenolic encapsulant. The multilayer capacitor stacks hundreds of microns-thick dielectric layers with internal nickel or palladium electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired - a technology that was genuinely new in 1982 and was the reason a 10 nF 50 V part started to fit in a 1.6 mm-tall package. The dielectric classes are named by their temperature coefficient: X7R and Z5U for the general-purpose 1980s parts, Y5V for the high-capacitance low-stability ones.

###### Grading barium titanate into the dielectric classes `metal.dielectric-grading` _(medium)_

The same powder cannot make a Y5V capacitor and an X7R one. Y5V is made from a fine, uniform, high-surface-area powder near the Curie point, where the dielectric constant is enormous and wildly temperature-dependent - a huge capacitance that changes by a factor of five over the working range. X7R is made from a coarser powder with barium zirconate or barium strontium titanate added, which flattens the temperature curve at the cost of the peak. So the capacitor 'class' is really a powder specification, and the class marking on the part is a statement about the ball mill that ground it.

###### The internal electrode metal and the reducing atmosphere `metal.dielectric-grading.mlc` _(medium)_

A multilayer capacitor's internal electrode is nickel or palladium, printed as a paste and co-fired with the ceramic. That will not work in air - the ceramic would reduce and become a lossy semiconductor - so the whole stack is fired in a low-oxygen atmosphere at 1200-1350 C in hydrogen or in a nitrogen-hydrogen mix, and then re-oxidised afterwards so the barium titanate goes back to being an insulator. The oxygen partial pressure is controlled to a few millibars. It is the most metallurgically demanding step in the whole electronics supply chain that nobody ever sees, and it is a barium carbonate problem.

### Petrochemicals and process chemistry `chem`

Everything on the C64 that began as crude oil or natural gas: the polymers of the case and the keyboard, the solvents of the assembly plant, the wet chemicals and photoresists of the silicon fab, the laminate resin and flux of the board, and the fuels that moved all of it. Traces roughly a tonne of hydrocarbons per kilogram of plastic back to a barrel of light sour crude.

#### Crude oil: finding it, drilling it, lifting it `chem.crude`

The upstream end of the chain. Seismic surveys pick a structure, a rig drills a 5-7 km hole through rock, casing and cement line the hole, the well is completed and perforated into the reservoir, then often artificially stimulated. An 8 kg C64 case corresponds to only 1-3 litres of crude oil, but that crude was found under 5-10 km of overburden using a drilling rig that cost tens of millions of dollars.

##### Petroleum exploration `chem.crude.exploration`

Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well. In 1980s practice this was reflection seismology over regional grids, closed by wildcat drilling. Cost per barrel discovered had fallen from tens of dollars to roughly $2-8 by the early 1980s.

###### Reflection seismic survey `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey`

A surface source sends a pressure wave down through the rock section; reflectors return it to hydrophones and the travel times are stacked into a two-dimensional depth section. Seismic is a time-domain method: it maps reflectivity contrasts (sandstone/shale, gas-sand amplitude dimming) and gives no direct information about fluid type.

###### Seismic vibrator truck `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vibrator`

A truck-mounted hydraulic vibrator sweeps 10-80 Hz into the ground under hold-and-hold conditions; on land it replaced explosive shot holes because it gave repeatable, higher-energy sources with no shothole cleanup. Regionally a 1,000-2,000 m shotpoint spacing was normal in 1980s 2-D work.

###### Airgun and marine seismic source `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.airgun-array`

Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel. Compressed air from compressor trucks on deck; a single 1980s 3-D crew vessel carried up to four sources.

###### Dynamite shothole source `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.explosive-shot`

Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot. Cheap per shot but slow, noisy and it polluted a producing field's drill cuttings.

###### Seismic shot-hole explosive ammunition `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.explosive-shot.ammo-case`

Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation. This is a one-off consumable of a survey, not part of any C64 material.

###### Marine seismic streamer and hydrophone cable `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.streamer-cable`

A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups; it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry line whose integrity was the limiting factor on data quality. Hydrophone elements used piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-5) discs coupled to silicone oil in a pressure-compensated housing.

###### PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.streamer-cable.pzt-element`

Lead zirconate titanate ceramic discs, typically 25-50 mm diameter, epoxied onto a diaphragm and back-electrode in a silicone-oil-filled housing; sensitivity about -190 dB re 1 V/uPa in the 10-60 Hz band. Silicone oil here is one of the petrochemical elastomers/fluids, unrelated to the case material.

###### Seismic geophone array `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array`

On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried. In 1980s 2-D the fold of coverage (usually 6-fold to 24-fold) was chosen by geophone group interval and source spacing, not by 3-D binning.

###### Moving-coil geophone `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array.geophone`

A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across; coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity. A second coil acts as a position feedback for the servo. Cost per channel in the early 1980s was several hundred to a few thousand dollars.

###### Geophone takeout cable and junction box `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.geophone-array.takeout-cable`

Polythene-insulated multi-pair takeout cable to a junction box, then a line-trap and telemetry radio link to the recording truck. Cable insulation here is polyethylene from the same steam-cracking chain as the C64's power cord jacket.

###### Seismic recording system `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.recording-truck`

Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-compatible cartridges. The whole array recorded simultaneously; it was common for the record to be demultiplexed and copied to a computer tape for onshore stacking.

###### Seismic data processing (CDP stack) `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.data-processing`

Common-midpoint stacking, normal-moveout correction via velocity analysis, deconvolution, migration and depth conversion, run on a mainframe or minicomputer. 1980s emphasis was on multiple suppression and on 2-D and early 3-D (a 3-D survey over one field cost $1-3 million per acre-foot).

###### Discovery test and hydrocarbon indication `chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.discovery-test`

A log response indicating oil or gas in a sandstone (high resistivity, low neutron density, gas effect on the seismic) is a test, not a discovery. A discovery required a producing well; industry experience was that one test in eight to one in thirty was commercial.

###### Exploration (wildcat) well `chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well`

The first hole into a prospect. Cheap success-failure logging with mud logging and core, drilled to the deepest prognosis rather than the shallowest pay. Exploration wells in the early 1980s averaged about 3,000-5,000 m of hole and took 30-90 days offshore.

###### Wildcat cost and success statistics `chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.wildcat-cost` _(medium)_

A North Sea or Gulf of Mexico wildcat cost $3-20 million in the early 1980s; the historical industry success rate was about 1 in 10 wells dry, 1 in 15 total wildcats a commercial discovery, and about 1 in 8 wildcats found non-commercial hydrocarbons. Exploration cost per barrel discovered was roughly $2-8.

###### Reserve estimation `chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate` _(medium)_

Volumetric and material-balance estimates, presented to a board and to governments as proved, probable and possible reserves. Rules of thumb: recovery factor 15-35% of oil-in-place for a sandstone reservoir, higher (35-60%) for a fractured carbonate. Reserve booking was and remains a commercial and legal judgement, not a measurement.

###### Oil-in-place calculation `chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.oil-in-place`

H = pore volume x saturation x (1 - water saturation) x formation volume factor B_o. B_o for a light crude at reservoir temperature can be 1.1-1.3, so reservoir barrels convert to stock-tank barrels at a meaningful ratio; the calculation is sensitive to saturation, which is the least measurable input.

###### Reserve uncertainty and contingency `chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.uncertainty` _(medium)_

Undiscovered reserves behind existing fields were treated as of similar magnitude to proved reserves. The industry view of world ultimately-recoverable oil in 1983 was around 1,500-2,000 billion stock-tank barrels, versus about 700 billion produced or proved.

###### Mud logging and cuttings examination `chem.crude.exploration.mud-logging`

A mud-logging unit beside the rig sampled cuttings and gas continuously, with a hot-wire or infrared hydrocarbon detector on the gas line. It found the shows that decided whether to run a full log suite, and in 1980s practice a mud-logging unit was manned for 24 hours a day on a producing-field well.

##### The reservoir: where the oil sits `chem.crude.reservoir`

Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water. This is the physical thing that the whole upstream industry is trying to reach.

###### Sedimentary basin `chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin`

A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed; the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it takes 1-100 million years of that history. By 1983 the world's producing basins were a few hundred in number, with the Middle East and the Gulf of Mexico dominating reserves.

###### Source rock and kerogen `chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock`

Organic-rich marine shale. Type I and type II kerogen give oil; type III, humic and mainly terrestrial, gives gas. Maturation is measured by vitrinite reflectance, with the oil window at roughly 0.6-1.3% Ro and the gas window above about 1.3%.

###### Thermal cracking of kerogen in the source rock `chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.kerogen-thermal-crack`

At 60-160 C kerogen breaks down into oil, and at higher rank into wet gas and dry gas; the same thermal-cracking chemistry, far slower and without a catalyst, that a steam cracker performs in seconds. Laboratory kinetics (Messelbrock-type compilation) were fitted to these systems from the 1960s.

###### Migration up the carrier bed `chem.crude.reservoir.migration`

Oil squeezed out of the source rock moves updip along a permeable sandstone or through a fault until it is trapped. Buoyancy of about 0.2-0.4 API gravity per 1,000 ft drives it; the seal is an impermeable shale or an evaporite whose capillary entry pressure sets the column height.

###### Geological trap `chem.crude.reservoir.trap`

Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap. The Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia, discovered in 1948, remained the largest oil field on earth for decades, holding some 100+ billion stock-tank barrels in a stacked series of Arabian carbonate reservoirs.

###### Reservoir rock: sandstone and carbonate `chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock`

Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone; carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity. Around 60% of world oil reserves and 80% of world gas reserves were in carbonate rock, most of it fractured Arab-type in the Middle East.

###### Marine carbonate (Arab-type) reservoir `chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.marine-carbonate`

Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline and high water cut. Saudi production was essentially all of this rock type in 1983.

###### Oil column in the pore space `chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column`

An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume. That gap, plus the reservoir rock and the seal, is why recovery factors are 15-35% and why hydraulic fracturing and acidising exist.

###### Oil in place `chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-place`

The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor. Multiply it by the C64 scale: the entire world shipped about 200,000 Commodore 64s in 1983, so the machine is a rounding error on a single wellhead's hourly output.

            - *Petroleum: light sour crude oil* `chem.petroleum` *(seen above)*
###### Asphaltenes and resins `chem.petroleum.asphaltene`

The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude. Roughly 2-20% of crude, soluble in the light ends and precipitated by heptane in the standard n-heptane asphaltene test. Asphaltenes are the coke precursors in every thermal cracker, coker and reformer, and their content is what decides whether a crude makes a good or bad feedstock.

##### The drilling rig `chem.crude.rig`

Rotary drilling: the drill string is rotated from the surface, the bit mills a hole, mud circulates to carry cuttings out and to control formation pressure. Offshore this is a jack-up, a semisubmersible or a drillship; onshore it is a land rig with a derrick. 1980s rigs reached 6,000-7,500 m total depth on routine programs.

###### Rotary drilling `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling`

A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit. Weight-on-bit and torque are the two variables the driller steers with; the drilling engineer watches torque and bit exponent while the driller watches penetration rate.

###### Drill string `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstring`

Drill pipe, drill collars and a bit, threaded or coupled API 5-1/2 in and 6-5/8 in in the 1980s, with 3-1/2 in drill collar subs. Length is a queue of 5,000-7,000 m of 5 in pipe plus 200-400 m of collars; the string must be strong enough for tensile load at the maximum string weight yet remain within the derrick.

###### Mud circulation system `chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-system`

Active and reserve pits, the pump, the surface mixing hopper (mud pit) and the flowline over the shaker. 1980s volumes for a single rig were 400-1,500 m3 of active mud with 150-400 m3 of reserve, and the pit room needed chemical dosing, dilution and waste disposal for one well's worth of chemically treated clay.

###### Drilling mud (drilling fluid) `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud`

A thixotropic clay-water or oil-water emulsion that removes cuttings, lubricates and cools the bit, carries hydraulic pressure to the formation, and crucially gels to hold formation pressure when the pumps stop. In practice it was a chemically engineered suspension with four control jobs: viscosity at the bit, gel strength in the hole, filtrate control to stop the formation claying off, and compatibility with the formation.

###### Bentonite (montmorillonite clay) `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite`

Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota; the single most important mud component. It gives the thixotropy: at rest a high gel strength to suspend cuttings, under shear it drops to low viscosity so the bit can cut. Drilling-grade bentonite is API 13/14 with a viscosity of 30+ s/qt and a low montmorillonite ratio.

###### Montmorillonite and the bentonite bed `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.montmorillonite`

Sodium montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite: two tetrahedral silica sheets sandwiching an octahedral aluminium sheet, with the negative layer charge balanced by exchangeable sodium. Between the layers is water, and that water is why the clay swells, gels and gives the mud its thixotropy. The drilling grade comes from the Cretaceous Bentonite bed of Wyoming and South Dakota, a marine sediment about 65-72 million years old that is a calcium montmorillonite until it is mined and soda-ashed to the sodium form.

###### Soda ash conversion to sodium bentonite `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.montmorillonite.soda-ash`

The pit clay is a calcium montmorillonite and has to be converted. The clay is blunged with water, treated with sodium carbonate so that the exchangeable calcium is replaced by sodium, and then dried and milled. That step is what turns a geological curiosity into an industrial material, and it is also the step that makes the drilling specification possible, because the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not.

###### The clay pit `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.montmorillonite.soda-ash.clay-pit`

A 10-20 m thick bentonite bed, opened up and worked as an open pit or a shallow underground mine, in a landscape that looks like a lunar plain because the clay is grey-white when fresh and weathers to a pale crust. It is the last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's drilling chain, and it is the point at which a machine that will one day hold a C64's case first touches something that came out of the ground with no hydrocarbons in it at all.

###### Barite (barium sulphate) weighting agent `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite`

Almost all the weight in a mud: API-grade barite at 4.28 g/cm3 (42.8 ppg) added to a base mud of about 1.03-1.2. Barite is also the standard drilling weighting because it is nearly insoluble in water. The same mineral appears as filler in the plastics and cable branches of this file, via chem.barium-sulfate.

###### Chrome/lime mud (invert emulsion) `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lime-mud` _(medium)_

The classic high-temperature mud: a water-in-oil (invert) emulsion with oil as the continuous phase, bentonite in the aqueous phase, and calcium carbonate and a lime (Ca(OH)2) emulsion. Chrome/lime muds were standard to about 120-150 C but they fail in a cement job because the calcium in cement breaks the emulsion, so a salt-water mud or a chrome-free lime mud had to be switched in first.

###### Oil-based (diesel) mud `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mud`

Diesel or mineral oil as the continuous phase with water as the dispersed phase, organophilic clay (amine-treated montmorillonite) for viscosity. Chosen for high-temperature deep wells and for formations where water filtrate would swell clay. Its environmental reputation in the Gulf in the 1980s was poor, and it had to be stabilised with organophilic bentonite and lime.

###### Mixed-weight additive (iron ore + barite) `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix` _(medium)_

Where barite was unavailable or too expensive, ground iron ore was blended in as a second weighting agent. It attacks steel components by corrosion and needs a passivation layer of lime or sulphide film, but it saved cost in a tight barite market.

###### Mud rheology and filtration control `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.rheology-control` _(medium)_

Funnel viscosity, plastic viscosity, yield point and the PV/YP ratio (a rule of thumb required PV/YP <= 3 for good hole cleaning at the pump), plus low-pressure filtration rate (Baroid/API filtration test) to limit the mud filtrate that causes formation damage and differential sticking.

###### Chelants, biocides and defoamers `chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-biocide` _(medium)_

The 1980s mud chemist's standard additive cabinet: phosphate and polyphosphate sequestrants for calcium, lignosulphonate and polyacrylamide viscosifiers, benzyl alcohol defoamer, and glutaraldehyde or formaldehyde-based biocides against sulphate-reducing bacteria, which produce hydrogen sulphide and sour the cuttings.

###### Drill bits `chem.crude.rig.bit`

The cutting tool at the bottom of the string. In 1980s practice a soft-formation bit was a sealed journal bearing with a cone of natural diamond, a medium bit a sealed or unsealed mud turbine with tungsten-carbide nose buttons, and a hard rock bit a milled-steel body with tungsten-carbide inserts on the three cones.

###### Tungsten carbide cutters and buttons `chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide` _(medium)_

WC-Co cemented carbide: 6-12% cobalt binder, 900-1,600 HV, pressed and sintered in a vacuum furnace then brazed onto the cone or into a milled-steel body. Cemented-carbide rock-bit consumption was the largest single use of tungsten carbide in the world in the 1980s, comparable to carbide tooling.

###### Natural diamond (soft-formation bit) `chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond`

Gem-quality or bort diamond in a matrix of tungsten and cobalt sintered into a cone. Natural diamond bits dominate soft sandstone and were the standard drag-bit insert in 1980s drilling; synthetic (polycrystalline) diamond began to displace them in abrasive sandstone late in the decade.

###### PDC (polycrystalline diamond compact) bit `chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit`

The emerging bit of the early 1980s: sintered diamond compact cutters brazed to a steel body with no cones and no bearings, turning rather than grinding. PDC began as a hard-rock bit, spread into soft rock in the mid-1980s and largely replaced roller cones in soft formations by the early 1990s. In 1983 it was perhaps 10-20% of the market.

###### Polycrystalline diamond compact cutter `chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter` _(medium)_

Diamond powder sintered at 5,000-6,000 bar and 1,400-1,600 C with a cobalt metal catalyst from the diamond-graphite phase boundary. Over a 1980s field life a soft-formation PDC cutter could cut tens of kilometres of sandstone; hard-rock PDC arrived later with tungsten-carbide substrates and domed cutters.

###### Casing and cementing `chem.crude.rig.casing-cement`

Steel casing is run to isolate the hole and to carry the pressure; cement is pumped between casing and formation (and sometimes inside the casing) to seal the annulus. Without a good cement job the whole completion leaks and stimulation injects into the wrong zone. Cementing is one of the few oilfield jobs that is nearly a repeatability disaster: 10-30% of wells take a cement squeeze.

###### API Class G oilwell cement `chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g` _(medium)_

Portland-type cement with 40-60 wt% Class G sulphate-resisting blend, gypsum for set control, silica flour as a retarder for the thickening time, and additives for fluid-loss control. Mixed on location with water and spacers at 1.7-2.0 g/cm3 and pumped at 30-90 bbl/min.

###### Cement dispersants and additives `chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant` _(low)_

Sulfonated naphthalene formaldehyde condensates (BNS) or sulfonated formaldehyde melamine (SFM) to keep the slurry workable at low water; and bentonite as an extender. Early 1980s practice was to optimise with laboratory thickening-time tests before the job, because a primary cement job cost $0.2-1 million.

###### Casing string and cement sheath `chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.casing-string`

Conductor, surface, intermediate and production casing, each cemented across its shoe. The C64-scale point: even a modest producing well consumes tens to hundreds of tonnes of cement and hundreds of metres of steel, dwarfing the machine it ultimately supplies.

###### Rig types and their 1980s cost `chem.crude.rig.rig-types` _(low)_

Jack-up rigs (4-6 legs, 60-90 m water-depth limit) and fixed derricks onshore; semisubmersibles (700-1,000 m, self-propelled, expensive); drillships (ice-strengthened, for deep water and harsh climates). Costs in the early 1980s: onshore rig $1-3 million, jack-up $20-45 million, drillship $30-70 million, semisubmersible $60-120 million. Offshore dayrates in 1983 ran $25,000-60,000 a day.

###### Well control: BOP, diverter and kill `chem.crude.rig.pressure-control`

The blowout preventer stack (annular preventer plus 3-5 ram preventers) and the choke manifold above the wellhead, rated 5,000-15,000 psi. Before the 1970s and 1980s safety emphasis, the classic profile was a vertical string, overbalanced mud and a diverter; 1980s practice added the above-the-bit diverter packoff for kick tolerance.

###### Core drilling and coring `chem.crude.rig.core-drilling`

Diamond core barrels cut 1-4 in core in a special drilling string, giving the reservoir rock, its porosity, its saturation and its capillary properties undamaged. A cored well is the most expensive way to get reservoir data, so it was used on 1-3 wells out of 20 and almost always on the discovery well.

###### Diamond core barrel `chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.core-barrel`

A steel or aluminium tube with a diamond-set reaming shell and a core lifter, run on the bottom hole assembly at low RPM (20-100) and low weight. Carbit tungsten-carbide bits dominated abrasive sandstone, PCD for softer beds, and set diamond for carbonate.

##### Well completion `chem.crude.well-completion`

Turning a drilled hole into a producing well: set production casing, cement to the pay, run and perforate the tubing, pack the annulus, and install a tree. This is where the reservoir is deliberately connected to the borehole for the first time.

###### Perforation `chem.crude.well-completion.perforation`

Shaped charges fired down the casing to punch 1-3 cm holes through steel, cement and formation in one shot, linking pay zone to borehole. A 1980s completion might be 4-6 perforations per metre of pay; perforation is done in stages so only the best footage is shot.

###### Shaped-charge perforator `chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.shaped-charge` _(medium)_

A copper or steel cone lined with a high explosive (RDX/HMX or HMX-wax, 5-30 g per shot in the 1980s) with a steel or ceramic liner; the detonated cone forms a copper or tungsten-alloy jet at 8-10 km/s which drills the hole. Charges were fired on a wireline in a gun barrel or in a TCP (tubing conveyed perforator).

###### Entry hole into the pay zone `chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.entry-hole`

The first connection to the reservoir is itself a jet-perforated hole in cement, and it is the smallest diameter in the whole production system: a few millimetres through which the entire well's flow must pass. That single fact justifies the next node in the tree.

###### Packer and completion hardware `chem.crude.well-completion.packer`

An elastomer-sealed packer run and set in the casing to isolate zones and provide a seat for the tubing hanger. In 1980s completions this was single- or dual-packer tubing with sliding sleeves or selective stimulation, increasingly mechanical rather than hydraulic.

###### Packer elastomer (nitrile / HNBR) `chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elastomer`

A nitrile (acrylonitrile-butadiene) or HNBR element that swells or mechanically expands to grip the casing. Nitrile is the same chemistry as chem.nitrile-rubber in the polymer branch: acrylonitrile copolymerised with butadiene.

###### Christmas tree (wellhead assembly) `chem.crude.well-completion.christmas-tree`

The valve stack on top of the casing: casing spool, tubing spool, master valve, wing valves with gauges, and the flowline tee off the wing. Every stream the well ever produces has to pass through this steel gatework, which is why it is the most pressure-rated cluster of parts in the business.

###### Production logging and well testing `chem.crude.well-completion.production-logging`

Spinner and turbine flowmeters, noise logs, temperature logs and a well test with a multi-hour rate and pressure buildup. The 1980s production log also included an EST (emission spectral tool) for tracer detection in injection wells.

##### Well stimulation: fracturing and acidising `chem.crude.stimulation`

Almost no reservoir delivers its whole potential through a millimetre perforation. Stimulation makes the rock permeable by fracture or by dissolving the rock; it is one of the biggest single levers on oil and gas supply and it consumes enormous volumes of water, sand and, for acidising, corrosive acid.

###### Hydraulic fracturing `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing`

A water-based or gel fluid pumped down the casing into the pay, then into the perforations at 40-100 bbl/min and up to 6,000-10,000 psi surface pressure to part the rock; a proppant is carried in to hold the fracture open when pressure is released. Born in 1947 (experiments) and industrialised in the late 1950s (Massive Hydraulic Fracturing, 1961-1965), by the 1980s it was routine on low-permeability gas reservoirs and increasingly common on oil wells. A big 1980s job used 10,000-100,000 bbl of fluid and 500-2,000 tonnes of sand.

###### Fracturing fluid and gel `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.frac-fluid` _(medium)_

Water plus a viscosity builder (hydroxyethyl cellulose in water, or a hydrocarbon gel), often crosslinked with borate or an organometallic zirconium/titanium chelate to hold the proppant in suspension at high temperature. Waterfracs (no crosslinker, friction-reducer only) took a large share of the market by the mid-1980s because they were cheaper and left less residue.

###### Proppant sand `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.proppant` _(medium)_

Sized, round, silica sand or resin-coated sand, typically 20/40 or 30/50 mesh (0.4-0.6 mm), graded to carry a hundred thousand tonnes a year in a region. Ottawa River and Illinois Basin sands were the standard, with regional sources in Texas and Arkansas. It was a heavy, low-value, high-bulk freight commodity.

###### Fracturing sand and its plant `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.proppant.sand-processing`

The proppant is a silica sand that has been sieved, washed, resin-coated and graded, and the plant that does it is a small mineral processing operation that exists in the Permian basin because the proppant has to be nearby. The oilfield sands of the Permian have a problem that glass sands do not: a weak grain crushes under the closure stress of a hydraulic fracture, so the 1980s industry coated a fraction of the proppant with a phenolic resin to make it stronger.

###### Resin-coated proppant `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.proppant.sand-processing.resin-coating` _(medium)_

A fraction (5-30% in the late 1980s) of the sand is coated with a cured phenolic or furfural resin so that it does not embed into the formation when the fracture closes. The consequence for the industry was a new solid waste: sand that cannot be reused, because it has been used once and coated once. That is the same shift - from a mineral commodity to a consumable - that the chlorinated solvents made in the electronics plant.

###### Frac sand mine `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.proppant.sand-processing.sand-mine`

A sand quarry that happens to contain almost pure silica in a dune, worked at 1,000-10,000 tonnes a day. The last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's stimulation chain, and a reminder that a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral supply chain: the water, the sand and the chemicals are all mining and manufacturing, and only the pressure is petroleum engineering.

###### Fracturing pumping equipment `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.frac-equipment`

Blender trucks, sand trucks and a high-pressure pump unit (one pumping unit at 25,000 psi), laid out in a yard over the rig. A 1980s job mobilised 10-40 trucks and 100-200 people, and it was the largest single water consumer in the oilfield outside steam flooding.

###### Fracture geometry and conductivity `chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fracturing.fracture-geometry` _(medium)_

A propped fracture's job is conductivity x length. The first fractures were vertical and planar (d = 2h for radial, reservoir height-limited), so 1980s design moved toward multiple parallel fractures per zone; conductive fracture area had to be raised by resin-coated proppant (1980s) or by larger grains, because proppant embedment in soft rock closed fractures within months.

###### Matrix acidising and fracture acidising `chem.crude.stimulation.acidising`

Hydrochloric or hydrofluoric acid injected to dissolve or acid-fracture the rock, typically 15-28% HCl in sandstone and HF-containing mud acid in carbonate. Sandstone acidising only reached the late 1970s as a standard service; carbonate mud-acid fracturing with a 12% HCl-3% HF system had become the standard carbonate treatment by the mid-1980s.

###### Mud acid (HCl + HF) `chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-acid` _(medium)_

Hydrochloric acid to dissolve carbonate, with 1-3 wt% HF to attack the clay in sandstone and 2-5 wt% HF in carbonate muds. The reason for mud acid was a reserve shift: by the early 1980s mudstone was around 80% of world oil reserves, and mudstone cannot be treated with pure HCl because of its clay reactivity. Acid is pumped downhole in steel or titanium coils, with corrosion inhibitors (amines, thiourea) and a surfactant.

              - *Hydrogen to hydrochloric acid* `chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-hydrochloric-acid` *(seen above)*
###### Hydrofluoric acid `chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid`

The silicon etchant. HF dissolves silicon dioxide, and it does so fast, cleanly and without leaving a residue - which is why it is the single most important wet chemical in a silicon fab and also the one that produces the most fatalities. Anhydrous HF is made from fluorspar (CaF2) with sulphuric acid at 200-250 C, and the aqueous grades are made from that.

###### Fluorspar (fluorite, CaF2) `chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.fluorspar`

A mineral mined in Mexico, South Africa, China and elsewhere, and a genuinely strategic material: the entire fluorine chemistry of a semiconductor fab - the HF etch, the fluorocarbon plasma etch gases, the fluoropolymer bottles and the O-rings - descends from this rock. It is the one raw material in the whole tree that is neither a petroleum nor a metal nor a silicate.

###### Buffered oxide etch (BOE) `chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.buffered-hf`

Hydrofluoric acid diluted to 0.5-5% and buffered with ammonium acetate or acetic acid to hold the pH at 4-6. The buffer is not cosmetic: it stabilises the etch rate by controlling the reaction's HF2- concentration, and it stops the etch from accelerating as the acid is consumed. Buffered HF is used for the native oxide strip, for the field oxide etch, for the contact and via etch, and - importantly - for the removal of the hardened, plasma-exposed photoresist, because an unhardened resist would just dissolve in the acid.

###### Hydrofluoric acid safety `chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid.hazard`

HF penetrates skin and travels down the nerve sheaths, causing deep burns and systemic hypocalcaemia with cardiac arrest, often hours after the exposure. The 1980s response was calcium gluconate gel at every sink, a mandatory buddy system for handling above 5%, and the practice of handling dilute HF in a PTFE or polypropylene carrier rather than in glass. It is the most dangerous liquid in a semiconductor fab and the reason a fab's wet bench is a room with a raised floor and its own ventilation.

###### Acid corrosion inhibitor `chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-acid.corrosion-inhibitor`

Hydrofluoric acid at 12% and hydrochloric acid at 12%, pumped down a steel coil, will remove a hundredth of an inch of steel a day. The inhibitors - a long-chain amine, thiourea, an acetylenic alcohol - adsorb on the steel and cut the corrosion rate by several orders of magnitude without touching the rock. It is a thin grey film of chemistry doing the work, and it is the reason mud-acid jobs of the 1980s could be pumped downhole at all.

###### Acid-resistant tubing `chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-acid.corrosion-inhibitor.tubing` _(medium)_

Coiled tubing and the acid lines were, by the mid-1980s, routinely nickel alloy - a nickel-molybdenum alloy such as Alloy C-276 or a titanium grade - rather than carbon steel, because the inhibitor was never perfect and the steel was never quite good enough. Nickel alloys and titanium both come out of a metallurgical chain that this file does not own; the reason they are here is that the acid chemistry forced them there.

###### Acid pumping and coiled tubing `chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.acid-pumping` _(medium)_

Acid was bullheaded down casing or, by the mid-1980s, coiled-tubed into the perforation tunnels; continuous coiled tubing for acid and sand work was itself a growth industry in the 1980s. Placement mattered more than chemistry: because HF precipitates calcium fluoride, a 1.2-1.5 m of HCl preflush was always pumped first to keep Ca out of the rock.

###### Steam stimulation `chem.crude.stimulation.thermal-stimulation` _(low)_

On heavy oil and tar sands, steam at 250-350 C injected into the formation to lower viscosity, followed by soak and production. In 1983 this was a Cold Lake and Athabasca-scale proposition; the C64-scale point is the water and fuel: a single steam cycle consumed several tonnes of water and roughly 0.5-1 barrel of 60% FO-2 fuel oil per tonne of steam.

##### Wellhead and terminal separation `chem.crude.separation`

The wellstream arrives at 15-100 bar and 60-100 C as an oil/gas/water froth. It is separated in stages: test separator, stock tanks, heaters and desalters, gas-oil separator, and finally a train of electrostatic and coalescing vessels that make a storable crude. Field separation is where the crude assay is determined and where the oil is counted.

###### Test separator `chem.crude.separation.test-separator`

The first vessel, sized 1-5% of the field's liquid capacity, where the wellstream is bled at 25-70 bar to a stable pressure and temperature. Its records are the raw data for reservoir performance, gas-oil ratio and oil assay. A field with 100,000 bbl/d of oil needed a test separator of a few hundred bbl.

###### Three-phase separator and stock tanks `chem.crude.separation.three-phase`

A horizontal or vertical vessel at 2-10 bar with a mechanical or electrostatic coalescing section that separates oil, gas and water, then atmospheric storage tanks that settle the remaining water and sediment. Stock tank bottoms and the settled water carry the production's salt and heavy ends, and their disposal was the field's environmental problem in the 1980s.

###### Demulsifier chemistry `chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demulsifier` _(medium)_
