Nonylphenol- or alcohol-based surfactants dosed at 5-50 ppm to break the oil-water emulsion; in the 1980s a growing share of demulsifiers were polyalkoxyamine and polyglycol ethers. A stable water-in-oil emulsion (chocolate mousse) could hold 20-50% water into the crude and was the single largest quality loss on a wet field.

###### Heater-treater and desalter `chem.crude.separation.heater-treater`

A crude preheater to 150-200 C followed by a settler and then a desalter, where the crude is washed with recycled water to strip salts. Needed because sour Middle East crudes carry 1-3 wt% dissolved salts, and because naphthenic acids plus water at 200 C will corrode the hot exchanger on the way to the refinery. A crude desalter separates maybe 90-95% of the salt in one stage.

###### Electrostatic coalescer (electrogravitational) `chem.crude.separation.electrostatic` _(low)_

Charged droplets are attracted into the water phase, collapsing the emulsion in seconds instead of hours. Small pipeline electrocoalescers were introduced in the mid-1980s for crude pretreatment, cutting the demulsifier dose; they were used in 1980s practice wherever the crude conductivity allowed (hence electrogravitational not electrocoalescing for most crudes).

###### Oil-water coalescer `chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalescer` _(medium)_

A packed or membrane device that lets separated water droplets out of the crude without carrying oil. Produced-water disposal in 1983 was to a pit or a treatment plant; the offshore discharge limit under the 1983 amendments to the US Clean Water Act required 42 ppm oil and no visible sheen, which is why coalescers and hydrocyclones appeared on offshore platforms.

##### Crude assay `chem.crude.assay`

The certificate that turns crude into a priced commodity: density and API gravity, sulphur, metals, pour point, carbon residue, and a simulated distillation curve. Assay decided which refinery gets which crude and, ultimately, which chemicals are made from it.

###### Density and API gravity (ASTM D1298/D287) `chem.crude.assay.api-gravity` _(medium)_

Specific gravity at 60/60 F measured in a pycnometer, converted to API gravity by 141.5/SG - 131.5. Light crude means a low API number. This single number set the transport economics: a tanker mile costs the same whether it carries 35 or 40 API crude.

###### Sulphur content (ASTM D1266) `chem.crude.assay.sulfur` _(medium)_

Total sulphur by bomb combustion with an oxyhydrogen burner and infrared detection. 0.5% S is a rough dividing line between sweet and sour crude. The 1980s pattern of increasing sourness (Arabian and Mexican crudes) was the single most important driver of the rise in demand for desulphurisation and for recovered Claus sulphur.

###### Simulated distillation (ASTM D2887) `chem.crude.assay.simulated-distillation`

A GC method that fakes a slow fractionation, giving a boiling curve from the C7 fraction to the 538 C end point. The naphtha cut, the gas-oil cut and the vacuum residue are all defined by this curve, so this assay is the direct ancestor of the distillation scheme in the refining branch.

###### Conradson carbon residue and metals `chem.crude.assay.conradson` _(medium)_

Coking value and the vanadium/nickel/iron trace metals that poison catalytic cracking catalysts. Nickel and vanadium at 1-20 ppm are a hard constraint on FCC feed; sour crudes with high metals were thus discounted for refinery use relative to their heating value.

###### Pour point, cloud point and viscosity `chem.crude.assay.properties`

The cold-flow properties of the residue and the crude. A Middle East crude at 4 deg C in the North Sea was, in 1980s practice, handled by heating the tanks or by blending with a pour-point depressant copolymer; that is a real recurring cost on North Sea production.

##### One Commodore 64's share of the wellhead `chem.crude.c64-fraction` _(medium)_

The plastic mass of a C64 is about 350-400 g of ABS in the case plus 100-200 g in the keys, and ABS comes from roughly 2 kg of crude oil per kilogram of polymer. Add the energy to make it, the fuel to ship it and the polymer's own energy in the burning, and one machine corresponds to roughly 1-3 litres of crude oil - about one minute of production on a small Arabian field, and undetectable in the world oil balance. This node is the reminder that the whole upstream industry exists to supply a mass flow, not a concept.

      - *Natural gas: the gas field* `chem.natural-gas` *(seen above)*
#### Refining: turning crude into fuels and feedstocks `chem.refining`

Atmospheric and vacuum distillation to cut crude into fractions, then conversion and upgrading processes to make the specific products industry wants. For the C64 the interesting products are not the fuels but the naphtha that gets steam-cracked to ethylene, the benzene for styrene, the LPG for crackers, and the elemental sulphur recovered from hydrogen sulphide. In 1983 world refining capacity was roughly 65-70 million barrels a day, about 30% above demand, and the industry was running at 65-75% utilisation.

##### The refining industry in 1983 `chem.refining.scale` _(medium)_

Around 750-850 refineries existed worldwide, of which more than 300 were in the United States alone (US capacity about 19 million bbl/d). The largest refining regions in 1983 were the US Gulf Coast, the US Midwest, Western Europe (Rotterdam, Antwerp, Fos-sur-Mer), the Caribbean (USVI, Curaçao), Japan and Singapore, and the Middle East (Ras Tanura, Ruwais, Kuwait). About 3-5% of the crude throughput was burned as refinery fuel gas.

##### Atmospheric distillation `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation`

Fractional distillation of crude at atmospheric pressure in a 35-50 m fractionating tower, separating a barrel of crude into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, and a 700 F residue. It is the first process every molecule of the polymer industry passes through, and it is where the difference between a 30 and a 40 degree API crude turns into a 200 versus 260 dollar a tonne cracker feedstock.

###### Crude preheat train `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.crude-preheat`

A train of shell-and-tube exchangers that takes crude from ambient to 220-300 C by recovering heat from every hot stream in the refinery, then the fired heater takes it the rest of the way to 350-370 C. Preheating was the classic refinery heat-integration project: a crude preheat train alone recovers tens of megawatts and pays for itself in fuel.

###### Fired crude heater `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.crude-preheat.crude-heater` _(medium)_

A radiant box furnace with 150-400 coils of cast alloy or wrought-alloy tube (Cr-Mo, 5 in outside diameter, 0.3 m apart), firing gas at 30-80 MW. Tube metallurgy matters: the coil sees a 30-40 C metal temperature above the oil temperature, and the 1980s move to coiled tubing and to higher radiant efficiency cut fuel use several percent.

###### Fouling and how the preheat train was kept clean `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.crude-preheat.exchanger-cleaning` _(medium)_

A crude preheat train is a hundred shell-and-tube exchangers in series, and everything in the refinery that is hotter than crude is a source of fouling for one of them: coker bottoms gas, FCC slurry oil, diesel bottoms, hot water. Fouling costs pressure drop and fuel, and the 1980s counter-measures were crude preheat exchangers designed with a deliberately large shell-side velocity, online cleaning with a pigging system, and - in a few cases - a fouling monitor using a differential pressure transmitter on one exchanger as a leading indicator.

###### Fractionating tower `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower`

A 35-50 m column with 40-50 trays, at about 1.1-1.5 bar overhead and 2.5-3 bar at the bottom, condensing a vapour-liquid staircase in which each tray separates hydrocarbons by boiling range. A large atmospheric tower is a pressure vessel of 100-200 tonnes, and it is still the cheapest separation device ever built per tonne of product.

###### Distillation trays `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.trays` _(medium)_

Valve, sieve, bubble-cap or proprietary proprietary-type trays at 0.4-0.6 m spacing. In 1980s practice a new refinery would install valve or sieve trays, and an old one would often be kept and given a new tray-packing section on the vacuum side.

###### Tray efficiency and reflux `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.tray-efficiency` _(medium)_

A modern valve tray is 70-90% efficient against an ideal stage, and the tower needs enough reflux (a few percent of the feed, recirculated as a liquid stream) to wet the trays. Cutting reflux to save furnace duty is the classic operating trade, and it costs separation; the 1970s energy crisis pushed the industry toward heat integration and then toward better internals instead of more energy.

###### Reboilers and side strippers `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.reboiler`

A fired or steam reboiler supplies the vapour to the bottom of the tower, and side strippers remove the light ends from the kerosene and gas-oil draws so the side columns are not loaded with vapour. Kerosene is stripped with a few hundred kPa of steam; diesel often went straight to the bottom because the vacuum column handled its light ends.

###### Overhead condenser and gas recovery `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.overhead`

The naphtha overhead is condensed in a shell-and-tube condenser with a reflux drum, and the non-condensable gas (methane, ethane, hydrogen, H2S) goes off to the fuel gas header. In 1980s practice the gas was usually simply burned, although the recovery unit for ethane and propane (an absorber) was standard in complex refineries because it paid for itself.

###### Off-gas recovery unit `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.overhead.gas-recovery`

An absorber (propane) or a deethaniser-absorber column recovers 60-90% of the ethane and propane from the fuel gas before it is burnt. The recovered propane and butane become LPG, the same stream that feeds the crackers in the ethylene branch.

###### Cut points and the product slate `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.cut-points`

The fractions a refinery aims for, by boiling range: naphtha (C5 to about 200 F end point, roughly 30-40% of crude), kerosene/jet (200-300 F, 8-15%), gas oil (300-700 F, 20-30%), and the atmospheric residue (700 F plus, 25-40%). Naphtha is the fraction that matters to this tree: it is the steam-cracker feedstock, and its exact end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker will run at 800 or 850 C.

###### Naphtha hydrotreating before the cracker `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.naphtha-hydrotreating`

The cracker feedstock was almost never straight-run naphtha. It was hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% total sulphur (often 0.05-0.3 wt%) and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen, because sulphur poisons the reforming and cracking catalysts and nitrogen poisons the polymerisation catalysts downstream. Naphtha hydrotreating is the first place refinery chemistry meets polymer chemistry.

###### Cobalt-molybdenum / nickel-molybdenum catalyst `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.naphtha-hydrotreating.cobalt-molybdenum` _(medium)_

Sulphided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo on alumina in a fixed bed at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar hydrogen, with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 200-1,000. Lumping several reactors in series gave 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur naphtha; a naphtha cracker in 1980s practice wanted 0.5 wt% S or less.

###### Sour water stripper `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.fractionating-tower.naphtha-hydrotreating.sour-water`

The hydrogenating reactors make water and ammonia, and the separator water carries dissolved H2S and NH3. A stripper removes them, otherwise the recycled hydrogen carries ammonia into the cracker, where ammonia poisons the polymerisation catalysts and shows up as a colour defect in the polymer.

###### Overhead corrosion control `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.corrosion-control` _(low)_

The naphtha overhead is where refinery corrosion happens: water condenses out of the vapour, dissolves HCl from the brine that came with the crude, and dissolves H2S to make very aggressive sulphuric acid. By 1980s practice this was attacked with an overhead neutraliser - ammonia or an amine - injected to the overhead condenser plus a wash-water draw, and with alloy upgrade in the worst services. The naphthenic acids in Arabian crudes added a second, hot-side corrosion problem in the vacuum column.

###### Vacuum distillation `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.vacuum-column`

A second column at 25-50 mmHg absolute (740-760 mmHg vacuum) that distils the 700 F plus residue down to a vacuum gas oil and a vacuum residue of 2-5% of the crude, without cracking it. Lowering the pressure raises the boiling points' relative spacing so heavy molecules can be distilled instead of decomposed, and the vacuum is made by steam ejectors or by a barometric leg.

###### Steam ejectors and vacuum `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.vacuum-column.ejectors` _(medium)_

Three-stage steam ejectors holding 25-50 mmHg, using 10-25 t of steam per hour for a mid-size unit. Ejectors are simple but they cost a lot of steam; by the 1980s mechanical vacuum pumps (rotary or liquid-ring, with a surface condenser) were being installed to save that steam, and most plants still had ejectors as backup.

###### Flash zone and thermal cracking side reactions `chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.vacuum-column.flash-zone`

Below about 350 C the residue starts to crack rather than distil, so the vacuum column flash zone runs at 340-370 C and the vacuum gas oil contains some cracked material. Side reactions make coke and acids, which is why vacuum columns need wash sections, anti-fouling coatings and a coke limit in the feed.

##### Converting the vacuum residue `chem.refining.vacuum-residue-processing`

The 2-5% of crude that will not distil is the hardest material in the refinery. It must be converted - into coke, into gasoline, or into distillate - or it is sold as fuel oil. This is where the refinery's biggest single units and its biggest capital decisions sit.

###### Delayed coking `chem.refining.delayed-coking`

Vacuum residue is heated to 350-400 C and held in large coke drums for 12-24 hours, during which it cracks to 15-25% petroleum coke while the vapours are continuously drawn off and fractionated. Delayed coking was the dominant residue conversion process of the 1960s and remained so through the 1980s, handling maybe 40-50% of vacuum residue in a complex refinery, largely because it makes the anode-grade coke the aluminium industry needs.

###### Coke drum `chem.refining.delayed-coking.coke-drum` _(medium)_

A 6-11 m diameter vessel 20-35 m tall holding 100-400 tonnes of coke per cycle, switched in parallel with a fractionator overhead. Switching a drum is the highest-risk operation in a refinery: the drum is water-quenched and de-coked with a full-diameter drill and coke cutter while the neighbouring drum runs at temperature.

###### Calcined petroleum coke `chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-coke`

Green coke is calcined at 1,250-1,350 C in a rotary kiln or a fluid-bed calciner to make calcined coke for carbon anodes. Needle coke, with low sulphur, low metals and low volatile matter, is the anode grade; sponge coke is the fuel grade. The aluminium smelting industry consumes a few million tonnes a year of anode coke, which is the economic reason delayed coking survived the fuel-oil era.

###### Coke sulphur and metals specification `chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-coke.sulphur-content` _(medium)_

Anode coke must be under about 1.5-2 wt% sulphur, because sulphur burns off during electrolysis and eats the carbon lining and the anode plant. Vanadium, at over 200-300 ppm, is worse still because vanadium carbide is abrasive on the anode. A sour crude therefore yields fuel-grade coke while a light sweet crude yields anode coke - which is why the biggest cokers stand next to the biggest sweet crude streams.

###### The anode plant that consumes the coke `chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-coke.anode-plant`

The reason a refinery bothered with delayed coking at all: an aluminium smelter's carbon anode is made from calcined petroleum coke, petroleum coke pitch and a petroleum coke binder, and the anode plant is a 200,000 tonne a year market for a product that is otherwise a waste. Green coke is crushed, blended with calcined coke and pitch, extruded at 100-140 C, and baked at 1,000-1,100 C for hours in a ring furnace. The whole coking complex - the delayed coker, the calciner, the coke handling and the anode plant - is one market chain with one customer.

###### Green anode and the ring furnace `chem.refining.delayed-coking.calcined-coke.anode-plant.ring-furnace` _(medium)_

Anodes are baked at 1,000-1,100 C for up to 30 hours in a ring or shaft furnace on a car of green anode, under a forced hydrocarbon flame. The carbon comes out as calcined coke; the volatiles come out as a burner gas that heats the calciner. It is a carbon plant, not an aluminium plant, until the anode is dropped into the pot.

###### Green coke `chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke`

The unreformed coke straight out of the drum: 85-92 wt% carbon, 8-15% volatiles, with all the feed's sulphur and metals still in it. Green coke is the intermediate between the coker drum and the calciner, and it is also what the plastics industry noticed in the 1980s: green coke is a needle-coke precursor, and it is the reason carbon fibre of aerospace grade became possible after the large-scale-carbon-fibre work of the late 1960s.

###### Fluid catalytic cracking `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking`

Vacuum gas oil is contacted with a zeolite catalyst at 500-530 C and 1-3 bar in a riser, cracked into gasoline, light ends and coke, and the catalyst is continuously regenerated in a fluidised-bed regenerator at 650-750 C. FCC was the largest refinery process by capacity in the early 1980s - a large unit processing 40,000-100,000 bbl/d - and the source of most of the world's leaded-free gasoline blending components and of the propylene that fed the older chemical crackers.

###### Riser and regenerator `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.riser` _(medium)_

The riser reactor is a vertical pipe 10-20 m long with the catalyst and feed entering at the bottom; the cyclone separators strip entrained catalyst back; the regenerator burns the coke off the catalyst with air. A 1980s unit's two-stage regeneration was the standard answer to how to get more heat into the reactor while cutting carbon monoxide from the stack.

###### FCC zeolite catalyst `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst`

A synthetic zeolite (USY, made by dealuminating Y zeolite) dispersed in a silica-alumina or silica matrix, rare-earth exchanged by lanthanum and neodymium. The zeolite gives shape-selective acid sites; the matrix gives attrition resistance and heat capacity. This is the same family of materials as the zeolites that would crack naphtha for styrene a decade later.

###### Silica-alumina matrix `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst.silica-alumina` _(medium)_

Amorphous silica-alumina, precipitated from sodium silicate and aluminium sulphate and caustic-gelled, then spray dried as 40-90 micron microspheres. The matrix is what gives the catalyst its attrition resistance and its heat capacity; it also carries a good part of the cracking, because the matrix surface area is large and the zeolite is expensive.

###### ZSM-5 octane additive `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst.zsm-5` _(medium)_

A small-pore zeolite (mordenite framework, 10-membered rings) blended at 3-15% into the USY catalyst to crack the C7-C10 straight chains that were killing octane after the lead phase-down. This is the direct ancestor of the propylene and isobutylene it also made: ZSM-5 selectively shapes the products towards C3 and C4 olefins.

###### Catalyst additives and contaminant tolerance `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst.catalyst-additives` _(medium)_

Vanadium and nickel in the feed deposit as mobile vanadates and nickels that destroy zeolite acid sites and accelerate dehydrogenation, so passivation additives (aluminium monohydride slurry, antimony compounds) were standard by the 1980s. Gasoline desulphurisation additives appeared later, at the end of the decade.

###### Making the FCC zeolite `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst.zeolite-manufacture`

A synthetic zeolite is not mined; it is crystallised. The reagents are an alumina source, a silica source, an alkali and a template, and the product is a 3-5 micron crystal of a lattice so regular that it was named after the mineral zeolite. The FCC catalyst's lattice is what makes it a shape-selective acid, and the same recipe with a different template and a different silica-to-alumina ratio gives the MFI zeolite of the styrene alkylation and the 3A sieve of the cracker drier. One family of chemistry, four jobs, and about a tenth of a tonne of catalyst per year for every 10,000 bbl/d of FCC capacity.

###### Hydrothermal crystallisation and the dealuminated Y `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.zeolite-catalyst.zeolite-manufacture.crystallisation` _(medium)_

The Y zeolite is grown from an aluminosilicate gel at 100-200 C with a seed, and then dealuminated to raise its silica-to-alumina ratio - by acid leaching, by chlorination with HCl or ammonium persulphate, or thermally with steam. Dealumination is what turns the dealer's USY into the ultrastable Y that became the standard cracking component, and it is also the step that makes the zeolite's acid site density lower and its selectivity higher. The dealumination agents are, note, the same mineral and base chemistry as the wet bench: hydrochloric acid and ammonium hydroxide.

###### Cracked gasoline and the propylene route `chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.cracked-gasoline`

FCC gasoline is high in olefins, aromatics and isoparaffins, with an octane number well above the reformer's, and it is the blending component that let the industry drop lead. Its propylene stream - 2-4% of FCC feed - fed the old chemical industry: by 1983 propylene from FCC and from crackers together supplied roughly half the world's propylene, and the older propylene splitter process existed precisely to make more of it.

###### Hydrocracking `chem.refining.hydrocracking` _(medium)_

A fixed or trickle-bed catalytic process at 350-450 C and 80-200 bar of hydrogen that cracks heavy oils and hydrogenates the fragments in one step, giving 70-90% diesel yield with almost no sulphur. By the early 1980s hydrocracking had been converted from coal-liquefaction-derived catalysts to the cobalt-molybdenum and nickel-molybdenum on alumina and silica-alumina form, and it was the process that allowed a refinery to make diesel rather than fuel oil.

##### Hydrotreating and desulphurisation `chem.refining.hydrotreating`

The refinery's chemistry of taking things out: sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals, plus saturation. It is the answer to sour crude, and it is the process that made Arab Light and Mexican crudes usable in 1980s refineries. It also produces the acid gas from which elemental sulphur is recovered.

###### Naphtha hydrodesulphurisation `chem.refining.hydrotreating.naphtha-hdt`

300-400 C, 20-50 bar hydrogen, cobalt-molybdenum on alumina, to 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur. This is the pretreatment that makes a crude usable in a cracker; see the naphtha node under the fractionating tower.

###### Diesel hydrodesulphurisation `chem.refining.hydrotreating.diesel-hdt` _(medium)_

300-400 C and 30-80 bar hydrogen over Co-Mo/Ni-Mo to take the sulphur in the gas oil down to 0.1-0.3 wt%, with a 0.05 wt% deep-desulphurisation variant developed in the late 1970s for the emerging 1990s fuel specifications. In 1983 the pressure on refineries to build these units was rising because of the US 1990 diesel sulphur rules and Europe's equivalent, and because every barrel desulphurised is a barrel of fuel oil turned into saleable middle distillate.

###### Jet kero hydrotreating `chem.refining.hydrotreating.kero-hdt` _(medium)_

Aviation turbine fuel must be under 3 wt% sulphur (later 0.3-0.5 wt%), free of water, and made to a smoke point and a thermal stability specification, because the fuel goes through a turbine at 800-1,000 C with water condensing in the fuel-oil nozzles. The kero hydrotreater is a 300-400 C, 30-50 bar hydrogen unit with a naphthenic acid problem of its own.

###### Acid gas to the Claus unit `chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas`

Every hydrotreater and every amine unit makes an acid gas of mostly H2S with some CO2. In 1983 that stream was worth real money: recovering its sulphur turns a disposal liability into a product, and about 80-90% of world sulphur production was elemental sulphur recovered this way.

###### Amine scrubbing of the acid gas `chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.amine-scrubbing`

A 20-35 wt% MEA or DEA absorber removes H2S and CO2 from the hydrogen recycle gas, and the rich amine is stripped in a 120-130 C reboiler. The amine itself is degraded by the oxygen in the gas and by hydrocarbons, and the resulting amine/oil/water effluent was one of the refinery's worst waste streams in 1980s practice.

###### Claus process: recovering elemental sulphur `chem.refining.claus`

Three-quarters of a mole of oxygen is used to burn a third of the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur dioxide, then the two react over an alumina catalyst to make sulphur and water: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. The Claus unit turns the refinery's or gas plant's worst stream into a saleable commodity, and its output is the elemental sulphur that the whole 1980s chemical industry - rubber vulcanisation, fungicides, sulphuric acid - depended on. The Canadian oil sands' sulphur problem and the Arabian gas sweetening builds both exist because of this unit.

###### Claus furnace `chem.refining.claus.furnace` _(medium)_

A refractory-lined furnace at 250-400 C where a third of the H2S is burned with oxygen or air. The burn has to be kept on the rich side: too much oxygen and the H2S is oxidised all the way to SO2, which wastes the sulphur; too little and soot forms and plugs the catalyst.

###### Claus catalyst (activated alumina) `chem.refining.claus.catalyst` _(medium)_

High-surface-area alumina, sometimes promoted with titanium, in two or three fixed beds at 200-350 C with interstage reheating. Because the reaction is exothermic and reversible, a multi-bed converter with controlled quench keeps the equilibrium favourable; a single-bed converter cannot get above about 80% overall recovery.

###### Claus alumina catalyst and its support `chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-catalyst`

The catalyst is not a mystery material: it is activated alumina, and the alumina is refined from bauxite. A Claus unit's catalyst life is measured in years and its loss rate is what sets the unit's sulphur recovery, so a good 1980s unit used a promoted, high-surface-area alumina with a shape (extrudate or cylindrical) chosen to hold surface area at 300-400 C.

###### Bauxite `chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-catalyst.bauxite`

An aluminium oxide hydroxide rock, 30-60% Al2O3, which is the only ore worth mining for aluminium. The Claus catalyst is therefore a dig-it-out node too, just a different one from the oil and the sand: a bauxite mine in Guinea or Australia, or a later low-grade Australian deposit, feeds a refinery's sulphur recovery.

###### Bayer process `chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-catalyst.bayer-process`

Bauxite digested in hot caustic soda at 150-250 C and 3-5 MPa, the alumina dissolved as sodium aluminate, the iron and silicon left behind as a red mud, and the alumina precipitated as aluminium hydroxide and calcined at 1,000-1,200 C to give the alumina. The caustic is recovered, the water is recycled, and the red mud is a waste stream of 1-2 tonnes per tonne of alumina - the well-known environmental problem of the alumina industry. The Claus unit's catalyst is the last stage of this process, run by a completely different industry.

###### Elemental sulphur (brimstone) `chem.sulfur` _(medium)_

Bright yellow solid sulphur, one of the four commodities - alongside crude, natural gas and coal - that a 1980s chemical plant could buy. It is used in vulcanisation, in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (which is then used to make titanium dioxide, fertiliser and phosphates), in 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid herbicides, and in the elemental sulphur vulcanisation of rubber. World sulphur production in 1983 was of the order of 8-10 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it recovered from H2S by Claus.

        - *Claus process: recovering elemental sulphur* `chem.refining.claus` *(seen above)*
##### Catalytic reforming and the aromatics complex `chem.refining.catalytic-reforming`

Reforming naphtha over platinum at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar converts paraffins and naphthenes into aromatics, releasing about 0.2-0.3 tonnes of hydrogen per tonne of feed and upgrading the octane number. It is where the world's benzene comes from, and therefore where the styrene in the C64's ABS comes from.

###### Platforming (UOP, 1943) `chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platforming` _(medium)_

The process that made the aromatised gasoline era possible: naphtha (C5 to about 220 C) over 0.3-0.4 wt% platinum and rhenium on chlorided alumina, at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 5-6. Rhenium was the key 1970s development: it let the platinum loading drop and the operating severity rise, so a unit could make 100-120 octane unleaded without coke trouble.

###### Platinum-rhenium on chlorided alumina `chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platinum-catalyst` _(medium)_

Platinum crystallites of about 1 nm on gamma-alumina promoted with chlorine to keep the metal and the acid function in balance. Platinum is one of the most expensive catalysts in the plant, so catalyst regeneration and platinum recovery are real economics: the platinum in a 1980s reformer was worth tens of thousands of dollars, and the catalyst was shipped off site for reclamation.

###### Aromatics complex (benzene, toluene, xylene) `chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.aromatics-complex` _(medium)_

The benzene plant: extract the C6 aromatics from the reformer effluent, separate benzene, toluene and the C8 isomers, and hydrogenate the xylenes back to benzene because a tonne of xylene is worth less than a tonne of benzene. Around 1983 the benzene yield from a reformer run for octane was only 2-5% of the feed, so a refinery that wanted aromatics ran a dedicated naphtha aromatics complex in parallel with its octane unit.

###### Spent catalyst and platinum recovery `chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platinum-recovery` _(medium)_

Deactivated catalyst is shipped out and the platinum, rhenium and gallium recovered by chlorination, aqua regia dissolution and solvent extraction. This closed loop was one of the better examples of industrial metal recycling in the 1980s and it is also where the refinery's radioactive coke (from the feed's radium) had to be disposed of.

##### Isomerisation and octane boosting `chem.refining.isomerisation`

The C5 and C6 straight-chain paraffins in naphtha have terrible octane numbers; isomerising them to the branched isomers does something about that with almost no yield loss. This is the cheap half of the unleaded-gasoline story; MTBE and alkylate were the expensive half.

###### C5/C6 isomerisation `chem.refining.isomerisation.c5-c6` _(medium)_

300-180 C over platinum on chlorided alumina (a 1960s process) or, from 1980s, a zeolite (molecular sieve) isomerisation unit running at 250-350 C with an aromatics-rich recycle. Yield was 98-99% and the octane gain about 8-12 numbers, which sounds trivial until it is multiplied by a million barrels a day.

###### MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether) `chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe`

Methanol plus isobutylene over an acidic ion-exchange resin (Amberlyst, sulphonic acid polystyrene, about 100 C, 5-10 bar), giving a 100+ octane component. MTBE was the big gasoline technology story of the late 1970s and early 1980s in the United States, and its feedstock - isobutylene - came from the crackers and the FCC, which is the direct petrochemical link: the same C4 that becomes butadiene rubber becomes the octane booster in American petrol.

###### Ion-exchange resin catalyst `chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exchange-resin` _(medium)_

A macroporous or gel-type sulphonic-acid polystyrene resin, the same chemistry as the ion exchange resins used in water treatment. MTBE resins had to be replaced every 10,000-20,000 hours in the 1980s as they aged.

###### Alkylate (isooctane by HF alkylation) `chem.refining.isomerisation.alkylate` _(medium)_

Isobutane plus isobutylene or propylene over anhydrous HF at 20-40 C, or over solid acid, giving the premium aviation and premium gasoline blending component. HF alkylation was a large and dangerous business in 1980s practice: a cloud of HF is dense, water-soluble and causes deep burns, so alkylation units had their own HF storage and a dedicated water curtain.

##### Lead phase-down and the unleaded problem `chem.refining.octane`

Tetraethyl lead was phased out of most industrialised markets between 1978 and 1985 as catalytic converters spread. The lead phase-down is the single most consequential fuel specification change of the decade and it is the reason MTBE, alkylate, isomerate and the ZSM-5 additive were all developed on that timescale.

###### Tetraethyl lead `chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead`

Pb(C2H5)4 blended at a few grams per litre, discovered in 1921 and the cheapest octane technology for fifty years. It was the cheapest route to octane and the most expensive in externalities: it destroyed the lead and phosphorus catalysts that were the whole point of the catalytic converter. Teledyne and DuPont stopped adding it to road fuel in most markets by 1985.

###### Unleaded blending and the octane shortfall `chem.refining.octane.unleaded-blending` _(medium)_

Without lead the refiner needed 3-8 octane numbers from somewhere. In 1983 the US was short and the industry solved it with MTBE, ZSM-5 and alkylate; Europe, with the smaller and cleaner European car fleet, was much less short, which is why MTBE uptake was overwhelmingly American.

##### Refinery products and by-products `chem.refining.products`

Fuels, lubricants, waxes, coke and sulphur. For this tree the interesting list is short: naphtha to the crackers, benzene to styrene, LPG to crackers, propylene and butylene to the older chemical plants, and sulphur to rubber and to sulphuric acid.

###### Lubricant base oils `chem.refining.products.lubricants` _(low)_

Distillate fractions solvent-extracted (2,700-5,000 Ns at 100 C) and hydrofinished, or in the 1980s increasingly hydroisomerised. The C64 link is not the lubricant in the gearbox but the fact that the same hydrofinishing catalysts and the same additive chemistry (zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, made from phosphorus pentasulphide) appear in the machine's grease and in the rubber and plastic stabilisers.

###### Petroleum waxes and slack wax `chem.refining.products.waxes` _(medium)_

Waxy distillate from solvent deasphalting, deoiled on a centrifuge train to give hard, medium and soft paraffin wax and microcrystalline wax. Slack wax goes into paper, board and packaging film; the microcrystalline waxes are the petroleum fraction that was blended into the first generation of hot-melt adhesives.

###### Fuel oil `chem.refining.products.fuel-oil` _(low)_

The bottom of the barrel: a 1-3% sulphur residue sold to power stations and ships. After 1973, and especially after the 1980s tanker accidents, the political life of fuel oil in Europe and the US got hard, and the refinery's answer was more conversion. In 1983 fuel oil still took about 25-30% of world refinery production.

##### Refinery to polymer: the handover `chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks`

Three handovers matter. Naphtha plus steam into a cracker gives ethylene and propylene. C4 from the same cracker gives butadiene and isobutylene. Reformer naphtha into the aromatics complex gives benzene, which with ethylene gives styrene. This node is the place where the fuel industry stops and the polymer industry starts, and it is the join that makes a C64 physically possible.

###### Naphtha to ethylene `chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha-to-ethylene`

The handover. Naphtha plus steam at 800-900 C over a cast alloy coil, giving 25-35% ethylene by weight with propylene, butenes and a benzene-rich C9+ residue. Roughly 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983 was naphtha-based, with the rest ethane and propane; the Gulf Coast and the Far East were naphtha and the Texas Gulf was liquid-fuelled ethane.

###### Steam dilution and coke suppression `chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha-to-ethylene.steam-dilution` _(medium)_

Steam does two jobs in the cracker: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so the cracking goes towards smaller molecules and away from carbon, and it carries heat into the coil. Naphtha crackers of the 1980s ran 200-400 mol% steam per mole of hydrocarbon, and the coil deposited coke at 0.05-0.2 wt% of the feed before it had to be decoked.

###### Naphtha feedstock `chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha`

A C5 to 200-220 F hydrocarbon cut, hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% sulphur and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen. Beyond its hydrocarbon content what matters is the coniocarbon and the asphaltene content: those are what coke the coil. The naphtha from an Arabian light crude is comparatively clean, which is one reason Gulf crackers could run at a lower steam dilution than a naphtha cracker fed with heavy California naphtha.

###### C4 to butadiene `chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.c4-to-buta-diene`

The cracker produces a C4 stream of 1-butene, cis- and trans-2-butene and isobutylene; extracting the butadiene out of it is a second plant (see chem.butadiene.sounsby). The isobutylene left behind goes to MTBE or alkylate; the 1- and 2-butenes left behind go to butene hydroformylation for plasticisers, or are put back into the cracker.

###### Benzene to styrene `chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.benzene-to-styrene`

Benzene from the aromatics complex is alkylated with ethylene in the presence of excess benzene (to suppress diethylbenzene) to give ethylbenzene, which is dehydrogenated. Both steps are the styrene branch.

#### Ethylene: steam cracking and the polymers of it `chem.ethylene`

Steam cracking naphtha at 800-900 C over cast alloy coils is the largest single chemical reaction in the world by tonnage. World ethylene capacity in 1983 was about 27-30 million tonnes a year, and roughly half of it went into polyethylene and the rest into ethylene oxide, styrene and solvents. Every polyethylene cable sheath, every styrene monomer and every polyester fibre in a C64 starts in a coiled coil furnace.

##### The ethylene industry in 1983 `chem.ethylene.scale` _(medium)_

About 27-30 Mt/yr of world ethylene capacity in 1983, of which the United States held roughly 19 Mt (about two thirds) and Western Europe about 8 Mt, with the Gulf Coast of the US, the Rhine-Ruhr, Antwerp, the Suez Gulf and the Japanese and Korean coasts as the clusters. A 1980s cracker cost $150-400 million and took three to five years to build.

##### Cracker feedstock `chem.ethylene.feedstock`

Naphtha was 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983, ethane and propane 20-30%. The choice is regional and historical: US Gulf crackers run on ethane piped from the Gulf's gas fields because the ethane price under a gas contract made it unbeatable; European and Japanese crackers run on naphtha because they had no ethane to hand. A naphtha cracker is the one that makes propylene and butadiene as well as ethylene, which is why the older chemical industry grew up on it.

          - *Naphtha feedstock* `chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha` *(seen above)*
###### Ethane feedstock `chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane` _(medium)_

Ethane cracks cleanly with little coke and needs almost no steam dilution, so an ethane cracker is cheaper to run and its ethylene yield (50-55%) is much higher. But it makes almost no propylene and no butadiene, so a pure ethane cracker has to buy its co-products. The 1980s US Gulf argument about ethane versus naphtha was really an argument about whether propylene and butadiene were worth more than the extra ethylene.

            - *Ethane and propane (LPG)* `chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-propane` *(seen above)*
###### Gas oil feedstock (the third choice) `chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil` _(medium)_

The heavier option, chosen when naphtha and gas oil were both dear: a 300-700 F cut cracked harder to get ethylene, coking heavily, and yielding the most propylene of the three. Gas oil cracking existed in the Middle East and in Japan through the 1970s and mostly disappeared in the 1980s because its cost per tonne of ethylene was the worst of the three.

##### Steam cracking `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking`

A hydrocarbon feed mixed with steam is brought to 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second in a serpentine coil inside a radiant furnace, at 1-3 bar. The chemistry is brutal free-radical chain cracking: the large molecules fall apart into smaller ones and a large hydrogen-rich tail gas. What decides the plant is how fast the coil can be taken to temperature without coking it, and how fast it can be cooled again.

###### Cracker furnace and radiant section `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace`

A refractory-lined box 20-40 m long with 40-80 coiled coils hung side by side, each coil 30-80 m of 4 in (100 mm) cast tube in ten passes of 10-20 m. The fire is gas- or oil-fired at 30-50 MW per furnace, and the radiant duty is the whole point: roughly 70% of the process heat has to arrive by radiation because convection through the gas is too slow to get the coil to 850 C in half a second.

###### Cracker coil metallurgy `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coiled-coil` _(medium)_

The coil is cast alloy, not steel: 25Cr-35Ni (Incoloy 800, 800H, 802) or the HP-modified 35Cr-45Ni alloys of the 1980s. The radiant fire gas is oxidising and its metal skin runs 30-50 C above the process temperature, so at 850 C process the skin is 880-900 C; a carbon steel coil crept and failed. Incoloy 800 became the industry standard, and its nickel content is one reason a cracker is so expensive.

###### Ceramic (CHA) coil coating `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epoxy-coating` _(low)_

Cracking alumina or silicon carbide coated onto the coil inside the furnace. The industry spent the 1970s and early 1980s trying to reduce coil metal temperature by 50-100 C; silicon carbide coatings (the CHA process, from Combustion Heat Exchanger) were the commercially successful route and let a furnace run hotter for the same metal temperature, which is worth several percent of ethylene yield.

###### Steam dilution and coke suppression `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.steam-dilution`

Steam does two jobs: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so radical recombination makes smaller molecules rather than carbon, and it is the heat carrier. Naphtha crackers of the 1980s ran 200-400 mol% steam per mole of hydrocarbon, and the hydrocarbon partial pressure at the coil outlet was 0.3-0.8 bar. The trade is explicit: more steam means less coke and less ethylene, less steam means more coking and a shorter cycle.

###### Coke and decoking `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking`

Coke builds up on the coil, which insulates it, raises the skin temperature and finally blocks the tube. 1980s practice was to shut the furnace and decoke in place by burning the coke out with steam and air (off-line decoking), taking several hours and costing several thousand dollars a cycle; a shift to shorter, more frequent on-line decokes came later with the high-performance coils. The coke itself is a fine, hard, low-metal material that has to be disposed of.

###### Cracker coke `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.coke` _(medium)_

A granular, high-carbon, low-hydrogen solid with vanadium and nickel that came out of the feed. It is a nuisance rather than a product in the 1980s - the FCC coke market was far bigger and the cracker coke was dirty - and a large cracker made a few hundred to a few thousand tonnes a year of it.

###### Cracked-gas expander turbine `chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.expander` _(medium)_

The cracked gas at 800-900 C is not simply cooled; in the 1980s it was let down through a turboexpander that recovered most of the sensible heat as work, doing the job of the quench exchanger. The expander recovered 10-20% of the cracking energy and was one of the reasons the energy crisis of the 1970s produced a generation of much more efficient crackers.

##### Quenching and acetylene control `chem.ethylene.quench`

The cracked gas leaves the coil at 800-900 C and has to come down to under 40 C in a second or two before anything can be separated, or the reactor metallurgy melts. The choice of quench is a real fork in the road: a gas quench to 350-400 C followed by selective hydrogenation, or a direct spray quench to under 40 C.

###### Gas quench to 350-400 C `chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench`

The cracked gas is quenched with recycled process gas rather than directly with liquid, stopping at 350-400 C. This keeps the gas hot enough that the acetylene survives, so the acetylene can be destroyed deliberately afterwards in a selective hydrogenation reactor (palladium on alumina at 130-180 C, 10-30 bar hydrogen) rather than being allowed to polymerise into gums in the cooler. Ethylene purity of 99.9%+ with acetylene under 5 ppm is the target.

###### Acetylene selective hydrogenation `chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.selective-hydrogenation` _(medium)_

Pd on alumina at 130-180 C and 10-30 bar of hydrogen converts acetylene to ethylene (and some to ethane) with high selectivity. It is the standard ethylene finishing step of the 1980s and it is why palladium was one of the few precious metals in a cracker: the catalyst was typically a few tonnes of 0.5-2% Pd, and the hydrogen partial pressure had to be controlled tightly because too much hydrogen makes ethane and costs ethylene yield.

###### Spray quench to under 40 C `chem.ethylene.quench.spray-quench` _(medium)_

Liquid hydrocarbon or quench oil is sprayed straight into the cracked gas. It is simple and it is cheap and it puts the gas into the quench oil circuit immediately, but it cannot be combined with selective hydrogenation because the acetylene has already polymerised in the cooler. In 1980s practice a naphtha cracker could run either way; the gas quench became standard on the big units where acetylene had to be controlled.

###### Decanter and quench oil circuit `chem.ethylene.quench.decanter`

The condensed liquid is settled and decanted, separating the heavy C9+ tar from the gasoline and C4 streams. The heavy fraction - about 5-10% of the cracker feed - was the benzene, toluene and xylenes rich C9+ cut in the 1980s, and it was the aromatics feed for the styrene plants and the solvent plants.

##### Ethylene purification `chem.ethylene.purification`

Before the ethylene can be polymerised it has to be dry and essentially free of oxygen and carbon dioxide, because both water and oxygen poison a radical or coordination polymerisation catalyst irreversibly. A cracker therefore had a molecular sieve drier taking water to under 1 ppm and a CO2/CO removal stage.

###### Molecular sieve drying `chem.ethylene.purification.drying`

A 3A or 4A zeolite molecular sieve in beds switched in parallel, taking the water to below 1 ppmv. The zeolite is the same material family as the FCC catalyst and the styrene alkylation catalyst - a good illustration that one piece of chemistry (a synthetic zeolite) runs through the whole tree.

###### Oxygen and CO2 removal `chem.ethylene.purification.oxygen-removal` _(medium)_

Oxygen under 1 ppm and CO2 under 5 ppm, by an amine or a solid bed. CO2 is the dangerous one: it poisons the coordination catalysts and it reacts with the organoaluminium cocatalyst of a Ziegler-Natta polymerisation to give carbon dioxide polymers and aluminium alkoxides.

##### Ethylene oxide `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide`

The oxidation of ethylene over silver at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar, in which every eighth or tenth ethylene molecule is burned to carbon dioxide and water instead of being oxidised. It was about 1.5-2.5 million tonnes a year in 1983, most of it going to ethylene glycol for polyester and to surfactants, and it is one of the most hazardous large-scale chemical processes in existence.

###### Air-oxidation process (the industrial one) `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidation`

Ethylene and air over silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina in a multi-tubular reactor at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar. Per-pass conversion is only 10-15% and the selectivity to ethylene oxide is 80-90%, so the unreacted ethylene is recycled with the inert diluent. The alternative process - the chlorohydrin route, ethylene plus hypochlorous acid to chloroethanol to oxide - was still running in the United States in the early 1980s but had been almost entirely displaced by air oxidation elsewhere.

###### Silver on alpha-alumina catalyst `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidation.silver-catalyst`

10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, promoted by chlorine. Silver is the only catalyst that works: it is the only metal that both activates oxygen and lets ethylene through, and the geometry matters as much as the chemistry, because the low surface area keeps the pore diameter small enough to suppress the combustion pathway. Catalyst life is 2-5 years and the silver is recovered at the end of it.

###### Chlorohydrin route (superseded) `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidation.chlorohydrin` _(medium)_

Ethylene chlorinated in water to ethylene chlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry to ethylene oxide. It was the original process and it made a chlorinated calcium salt waste for every tonne of product, which is why it did not survive outside the United States. It is the classic example of a process displaced not by yield but by waste.

###### Ethylene oxide safety `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety` _(medium)_

Ethylene oxide boils at 10.7 C, so it is a liquid only just below ambient and a gas in a warm tank; its flammable range in air is 3-80% by volume and its ignition energy is about 0.06 millijoule. It is acutely toxic, it polymerises without catalyst into a runaway, and it is kept in equilibrium by a trace of tertiary butyl alcohol or hydrochlorinated hydrocarbon inhibitor. In 1980s practice the industry standard was a fixed tank or a pressure vessel with an inert blanket, nitrogen purging and a quench section that could handle a deflagration.

###### Ethylene oxide to ethylene glycol `chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.to-glycol` _(medium)_

One tonne of ethylene glycol needs about 3.5 tonnes of ethylene oxide at 100% selectivity. The world ethylene glycol capacity was around 4-5 million tonnes a year in 1983, and the big consumers were polyester fibre and film and polyethylene terephthalate.

##### Ethylene glycol and the glycols `chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol`

Monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and triethylene glycol, made by hydration of ethylene oxide in a 1:1 to 1:20 mole ratio of oxide to water, with the ratio chosen to steer the product distribution towards the wanted glycol. In 1980s practice monoethylene glycol was about half the output and went into polyester, antifreeze and diester coolant, and diethylene glycol went into antifreeze and into the unsaturated polyester resins of the same family as the C64's case resin.

###### Catalytic hydration (the older process) `chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.catalytic-hydration`

Ethylene oxide over phosphoric acid on silica at 200-220 C and 60-70 bar, with about 20% ethylene glycol recycled as diluent to suppress the ether side products. Selectivity to monoethylene glycol is 85-90%, and the whole plant's economics depend on keeping that selectivity, because the diethylene glycol and the dioxane by-product have to be sold at a discount.

###### Direct oxidation-hydratation `chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.direct-oxidation` _(medium)_

The Shell process, commercialised in 1965: ethylene, oxygen and water are converted in one step over a supported silver-phosphorus-tungsten catalyst, avoiding the separate oxide intermediate. It gives a higher MEG yield and less waste water but needs very pure oxygen and is harder to control; both routes were still running side by side in 1983.

###### Glycol finishing by vacuum distillation `chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-distillation`

Water is removed in a multi-column vacuum system because the glycols boil at 197, 245 and 285 C and water outranks them everywhere; a set of vacuum columns at 30-100 mbar separates mono-, di- and triethylene glycol and recovers the unreacted oxide. This is one of the clearest cases in the whole tree where the separation, not the chemistry, is the expensive part.

##### Polyethylene `chem.ethylene.polyethylene`

The largest use of ethylene: about 12-14 million tonnes of polyethylene were made in 1983, split roughly between low-density (free radical, high pressure) and high-density (coordination catalysis, low pressure). The C64-scale uses are the power cord's insulation and jacket, the moulded cable accessories, and the keyboard membrane's insulation.

###### LDPE: free-radical high-pressure process `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe`

Ethylene is polymerised at 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar in a jacketed or tubular reactor with a peroxide initiator, in the liquid phase (below about 280 C) or the gas phase (above it). The density of 0.91-0.93 comes entirely from chain branching: the very high pressure creates radicals on the growing chain, the chain folds, and the branches that stop it crystallising. In 1983 the process was mature to the point of being a cost exercise, and it still made most of the world polyethylene.

###### Peroxide initiator `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiator`

Di-tert-butyl peroxide, or in the autoclave process a mixture of di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate. The initiator decomposes at temperature to give the two tert-butoxy radicals that start the chain, and the choice of half-life at operating temperature sets the run length.

###### Autoclave versus tubular reactor `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.autoclave` _(medium)_

The autoclave process (Union Carbide, 1930s) stirred the gas-phase reaction; the tubular process (Sons, 1950s) had plug flow with injection quills and much better temperature control. By the 1980s the tubular reactor was the standard large unit because it gave a narrower molecular weight distribution and better ethylene conversion, and because the autoclave's bulk polymer needed devolatilising.

###### HDPE: coordination catalysis at low pressure `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe`

Ethylene at 20-60 bar and 150-260 C over a transition-metal catalyst gives linear polyethylene with almost no long-chain branching, so it crystallises tightly and has a density of 0.94-0.97. Because the polymer comes out of the reactor as a powder or a slurry rather than a melt, HDPE in 1983 was made in a slurry loop or a gas-phase fluidised bed and then converted by extrusion.

###### Phillips chromium oxide process `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.phillips`

Chromium oxide on silica at 20-40 bar and 150-200 C in a slurry (diluent) loop reactor. The Phillips process dates from 1952 and is the reason the 1980s plastics plant looked the way it did: the diluent recovery section was the biggest energy consumer on the site, and the catalyst was a supported chromium oxide whose active site nobody fully understood.

###### Ziegler-Natta polymerisation `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta`

Titanium tetrachloride or titanium dichloride with an aluminium alkyl (triethylaluminium or diethylaluminium chloride) at 50-100 bar and 50-80 C in a hydrocarbon diluent. Ziegler was the 1953 discovery that started the whole low-pressure polyethylene industry; by the 1960s it had become Ziegler-Natta by supporting the titanium on magnesium chloride, which gave the multiplicity of active sites and therefore the control of molecular weight distribution that made high-density pipe grades possible.

###### Titanium-magnesium chloride catalyst `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta.titanium-catalyst`

TiCl4 supported on finely divided MgCl2, activated with an aluminium alkyl. The MgCl2 support is the whole trick: it generates about a hundred active titanium sites per gram of catalyst with a range of stereospecificity, and that is what turned HDPE from a family of blends into a graded set of grades.

###### Titanium tetrachloride and the sponge route `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta.titanium-catalyst.tetrachloride`

The titanium tetrachloride of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is made from titanium ore - rutile or ilmenite - by chlorinating it with coke and chlorine at 900-1,000 C, then distilling the TiCl4 out at 136 C. Titanium metal comes back by reducing the tetrachloride with magnesium (the Hunter process, which is the Kroll process in reverse) and distilling the magnesium chloride off. So the most important catalyst in the low-pressure polyethylene business is made in a plant that looks exactly like the zirconium and hafnium plants of the nuclear industry, because they all make volatile tetrachlorides.

###### Carbochlorination of rutile `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta.titanium-catalyst.tetrachloride.carbochlorination`

Rutile or ilmenite plus coke plus chlorine at 900-1,000 C gives TiCl4 with iron chloride and vanadium chloride impurities that have to be removed by distillation. The metallurgy is the reason a titanium-bearing sand exists at all: it is an oxide in a rock, and making a volatile chloride is the cheapest way to get a pure element out of an oxide. It is the same trick the silicon business uses in reverse, with methyl chloride instead of chlorine.

###### Magnesium reduction to titanium sponge `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta.titanium-catalyst.tetrachloride.magnesium-reduction`

TiCl4 plus magnesium at 800-900 C under argon in a sealed can, then vacuum distillation of the magnesium chloride at 1,000 C leaves a porous titanium sponge. The titanium sponge is then argon-melted and turned into the mill product. It is an expensive route to an element used in a catalyst at one per cent, which is why the catalyst industry never made the titanium - it bought the tetrachloride.

###### Triethylaluminium `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-natta.aluminium-alkyl`

The cocatalyst. It alkylates the titanium and reduces Ti(IV) to Ti(III), and it scavenges the water and oxygen that would kill the catalyst. It is pyrophoric, and the 1980s industry response to that fact was the standard practice of diluting it to 5-10% in a hydrocarbon before it ever left the cylinder.

###### Gas-phase polymerisation `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.gas-phase` _(medium)_

Union Carbide's Unipoly process: ethylene polymerised as a gas in a fluidised bed at 20-30 bar and 70-100 C with the catalyst dispersed on a support. No diluent to recover, no slurry to centrifuge, and by the early 1980s it was the technology for new large plants - it is exactly the same fluidised-bed machinery the ethylene and polyethylene industries shared with the catalyst makers.

###### Linear low density polyethylene `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe` _(medium)_

Copolymers of ethylene with a small amount of alpha-olefin - 1-butene or 1-octene - which gives a linear chain with short branches: low density with high stiffness. LLDPE was the fastest-growing polyethylene family of the 1980s (about 10-15% of PE production by 1983 and climbing), and the switch from 1-butene to 1-octene was a change in the crackers' product slate rather than in the polymer plant.

###### Metallocene catalysis (emerging) `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.metallocene`

A single-site catalyst: one sandwich compound with a zirconium atom between two cyclopentadienyl rings, activated with methylaluminoxane. Discovered in the early 1980s (Kaminsky and Sinn, 1980), it was not yet an industrial process in 1983, but it was the obvious next step because it gives a narrow molecular weight distribution and predictable comonomer placement. The full industrial arrival of metallocene polyethylene was in the 1990s.

###### Polyethylene additives `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives`

Antioxidants (hindered phenols such as BHT, and phosphites), stabilisers, and pigment. The antioxidant is the reason a polyethylene cable in a C64's power supply does not go brittle: a radical from the mains or from a metal ion attacks the chain and causes scission or cross-linking, and a phenol traps it.

###### BHT (2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol) `chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht`

The workhorse antioxidant, dosed at 0.05-0.2 wt%. It is made by alkylating para-cresol with isobutylene over a solid acid or an aluminium chloride catalyst, and it was also in the C64's power supply as a capacitor-filling fluid (as the antioxidant of the impregnant).

##### Where the C64's ethylene ends up `chem.ethylene.uses-c64` _(low)_

Concretely: the styrene monomer for the ABS case and the SAN matrix, the ethylene oxide route to ethylene glycol for anything polyester in the power supply, the polyethylene in the power cord's insulation and in the moulded cable accessories, and the C2 in the vinyl chloride monomer for the PVC jacket and for the keyboard's keycaps in the less common grades. A C64's ethylene demand is a few tens of grams.

          - *ABS resin plant, and the C64 case* `chem.abs` *(seen above)*
          - *PVC: vinyl chloride and suspension polymerisation* `chem.pvc` *(seen above)*
          - *Polyesters: PET, PBT and unsaturated polyester* `chem.polyester` *(seen above)*
#### Propylene and its derivatives `chem.propylene`

Propylene is the C3 that the cracker makes whether you wanted it or not, and for two decades the propylene splitter process existed purely to turn that unwanted C3 into more of it. By 1983 most propylene came from the cracker and from FCC, and it went into polypropylene, propylene oxide, cumene for phenol and bisphenol A, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

##### Where propylene comes from `chem.propylene.sources`

Three sources, in order of size in 1983: the steam cracker (roughly 40-45% of world propylene supply), catalytic cracking (roughly 30-35%), and dedicated processes. A naphtha cracker makes propylene at about 15% of its hydrocarbon product, so a cracker and a propylene splitter were bolted together in the 1960s to turn the whole C3 stream into pure propylene; by the 1980s the splitter had mostly been bypassed because the C3 could just be purified.

###### Cracker C3 stream `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3` _(medium)_

The propylene and propane that distil out of the cracker's quench separator. Naphtha crackers make roughly 0.15 t of propylene per tonne of feed, which on a 500,000 t/yr cracker is about 75,000 t/yr of propylene - more than a small polypropylene plant needs.

###### C3 recovery and the propylene column `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery`

How the propylene actually leaves the cracker. The C3 and C4 streams are separated in a deethaniser, then the propane and propylene go to a propylene splitter column where the propylene is taken overhead. Before that column, the stream is caustic washed to remove the carbonyls and the oxygenates; in the 1980s this was an option rather than an obligation, and the plants that skipped it were the plants whose polymerisation catalyst was drinking acetone.

###### Caustic wash `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.caustic-wash` _(medium)_

A 10-20% sodium hydroxide wash column that neutralises the acidic oxygenates - propanal, acetone, propionic acid, and the phenol and cresols from the C9+ - that the cracker makes. The spent caustic is a refinery effluent problem: it is a phenolic wastewater with a high chemical oxygen demand, and in the 1980s it was often incinerated on the site.

###### Chlor-alkali (brine electrolysis) `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.caustic-wash.chlor-alkali`

Salt water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 60-90 C and 3-4 V DC to give chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. It is the source of every chlorine molecule in this file - the PVC monomer, the epichlorohydrin, the chlorinated solvents, the hypochlorous acid of the propylene chlorohydrin, the phosgene of the polycarbonate, and the trichlorosilane precursor chain of the silicones - and the source of the caustic and the acid that made the phenol-formaldehyde and the ester plasticisers. It is the largest single tonnage of chemistry that a 1983 computer sits on top of, indirectly.

###### Membrane cell `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.caustic-wash.chlor-alkali.membrane-cell` _(medium)_

The cell type that replaced the mercury cell through the 1980s: a perfluorosulfonate membrane separating the anode and cathode, giving chlorine at 99.5%+ without the mercury the older cell had to manage. The conversion of the world's chlor-alkali from mercury to membrane was one of the largest and fastest industrial changeovers of the decade, and it was driven by mercury emissions - the same environmental logic that removed mercury from the PVC acetylene process.

###### Brine (salt) `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.caustic-wash.chlor-alkali.brine`

A saturated sodium chloride solution, made from a salt mine or a solar evaporation pond, purified to remove calcium and magnesium because they foul the membrane and foul the diaphragm. Salt is the one raw material in this branch that is dug out of the ground rather than taken from a refinery, and it is the true end of the chlorine chain.

###### The propylene splitter column `chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.propylene-column` _(medium)_

A 50-70 tray column 50-70 m tall that separates the propylene overhead from the propane that has to be recycled back to the furnace. Propylene and propane have a relative volatility of about 1.1, so this is a distillation with a reflux ratio of 15-25 and a lot of energy; the 1980s development was a packed or tray hybrid with a side stripper and a low-pressure-drop design, because the column's cost is its energy consumption.

###### Propylene splitter (the older dedicated unit) `chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitter` _(medium)_

A dedicated thermal cracker that re-cracked propane and the cracker's propylene-rich C3 stream at 500-600 C to make more propylene, at 15-25% selectivity, with a big furnace and a bad energy balance. It was the standard propylene route of the 1960s, it was still running in 1983 in a few places, and it was generally obsolete by the mid-1980s because the selectivity was hopeless and the cracker had become the cheaper source.

###### Depolymerisation of polypropylene `chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation` _(low)_

Reheated polypropylene was fed back to a reactor to recover the propylene it was made from. This was developed as a recycling route in the early 1970s when the word recycle meant something and it survived as a niche process for decades, mostly because the chemical plant could not discharge a plastic waste stream.

###### Isoprene from C5 `chem.propylene.sources.c5-isoprene` _(medium)_

The other half of the cracker C5 problem. Isoprene was isolated from the FCC C5 stream or synthesised from isobutylene and formaldehyde until synthetic isoprene replaced it in the 1980s. Natural rubber was never seriously displaced - isoprene's polymerisation gives cis-1,4-polyisoprene only with a stereospecific catalyst, and cis-1,4-polyisoprene is a poor substitute for the natural article.

##### Propylene purification `chem.propylene.separation` _(medium)_

The propylene has to be at 99.5-99.9% with less than 10-20 ppm of carbonyl compounds, because propanal and acetone stop an ionic polymerisation dead. In 1980s practice the purified propylene was made by distillation plus an alkaline wash, and by the later 1980s by hydrazine or hydrazone treatment which converts the carbonyls into something removable.

##### Polypropylene `chem.propylene.polymerisation`

About 7 million tonnes of polypropylene in 1983, the fastest-growing major plastic. It needs a stereospecific catalyst to be anything but glue: isotactic polypropylene is crystalline and rigid, atactic is a sticky amorphous gum, syndiotactic is a curiosity in the 1980s. The 1980s advances were the high-yield supported catalyst and, on the way in, gas-phase and slurry-loop reactors.

###### Stereospecific titanium catalyst `chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospecific-catalyst` _(low)_

Titanium trichloride or titanium tetrachloride on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl, refined in the 1970s and 1980s to give activities high enough that no catalyst removal was needed. The MgCl2-supported catalyst with an internal donor (a phthalate or a diether) was the technical development that made modern polypropylene economics work, and the diether donors were commercialised around 1980-83.

###### Slurry loop, gas phase and slurry reactor `chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-slurry` _(medium)_

The 1980s reactor competition: the slurry loop (heptane diluent, polymer as a slurry, then solvent recovery and devolatilising), the loop slurry with 30-50% solids, and the gas-phase fluidised bed with no solvent at all. The gas-phase process was the 1980s newcomer and its whole commercial case was the elimination of the solvent recovery section.

##### Propylene oxide `chem.propylene.propylene-oxide`

Propylene epoxidised, then made into propylene glycol, polyether polyols for polyurethane foam, and propylene chlorohydrin. World production was of the order of 0.7-0.9 million tonnes in 1983. Because the epoxidation of propylene was historically done with hypochlorous acid, a chlorinated by-product stream came with it, and that is why 1,2-dichloropropane and the flame retardants derived from it were part of the same business.

###### Chlorohydrin route `chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohydrin`

Propylene plus hypochlorous acid gives 1-chloro-2-propanol (about 90%) and 2-chloro-1-propanol (about 10%); the mixture is dehydrochlorinated with a lime or caustic slurry to propylene oxide and the chlorides are recycled as chlorine. The 10% isomer is the problem: it goes on to make propylene chlorohydrin and then the toxic 1,2-dichloropropane, so the plant had a dedicated caustic hydrolysis section for it.

###### 1-chloro-2-propanol `chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohydrin.propanol` _(medium)_

The intermediate whose dehydrochlorination is propylene oxide. It is mildly toxic, it is the reason propylene oxide workers were exposed to a chlorinated alcohol, and it is the direct chemical relative of propylene chlorohydrin, the skin sensitiser that caused occupational dermatitis in the plastics industry before closed systems became normal.

###### 1,2-dichloropropane `chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohydrin.dichloropropane` _(medium)_

The unwanted isomer stream, made when propylene chlorohydrin is treated with excess caustic. It is a solvent and a flame-retardant intermediate, and it is toxic to the liver and kidney. In the 1980s the industry reduced its production by selling propylene oxide as a propylene glycol monomethyl ether ether or by shifting to the hydrogen peroxide route, both of which avoid the chloride.

###### Hydrogen peroxide epoxidation `chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-peroxide` _(medium)_

Propylene plus hydrogen peroxide over a titanium-on-silica catalyst at 40-80 C and 1-10 bar, with the propylene chlorohydrin recycled as the phase-transfer catalyst. It makes no chloride, it is nearly quantitative, and it depends on a cheap supply of hydrogen peroxide - which in 1983 was the reason the anthraquinone peroxide plant and the propylene oxide plant sat next to each other in a few integrated sites.

##### Chlorinated flame retardants from propylene `chem.propylene.flame-retardants`

Polymers and elastomers for electronics and furniture were made to burn slowly by chlorinating a paraffinic or a phosphate ester. Chlorinated paraffins, and the phosphorus esters derived from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride, went into the flame-retardant grades of ABS, polypropylene and polyurethane foam that a consumer electronics company would specify for enclosures but not for a home computer.

###### Chlorinated paraffin `chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorinated-paraffin` _(medium)_

Paraffins chlorinated to 40-70% chlorine, used as a secondary flame retardant and, in the 1970s, as a plasticiser for PVC. It is a cheap and effective flame retardant and a persistent environmental contaminant, which is why the 1980s trend in electronics housings was towards phosphorus systems and towards thin walls that did not need as much of it.

###### Tris(2,3-dichloropropyl) phosphate `chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp` _(medium)_

The organophosphate flame retardant made from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride. It is an effective flame retardant for ABS, rigid polyurethane foam and polyester resins, and its precursor, tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate, is the classic story of a flame retardant that was banned in the United States in the 1970s after it caused animal tumours. That ban is the single clearest link between a 1960s consumer polymer and a 1990s regulation.

##### Cumene route to phenol and acetone `chem.propylene.cumene`

Benzene plus propylene gives cumene; cumene plus oxygen gives cumene hydroperoxide; the hydroperoxide is cleaved with acid to give phenol and acetone. About a million tonnes a year of phenol in 1983 came out of this route, and phenol went to bisphenol A (and therefore to the C64's epoxy laminate resin), to phenol-formaldehyde plastics, and to caprolactam. Acetone came out of the other end of the same reaction, which is why acetone supply in the 1980s was really cumene capacity in disguise.

###### Cumene alkylation `chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation`

Benzene with excess benzene over phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar in an adiabatic bed, or over a solid acid. The large excess of benzene (3-5 mol per mol of propylene) is deliberate: it suppresses the diethylbenzene and triisopropylbenzene by-products and stops the reactor polymerising the propylbenzene.

###### Phosphoric acid on silica `chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phosphoric-acid-catalyst`

The classic cumene alkylation catalyst is orthophosphoric acid on a silica carrier: the acid is absorbed into the silica's pore structure and the pore structure holds it there, and the catalyst's whole life is the slow loss of that acid to the reactor walls. The 1980s industry answer was a solid acid and a moving-bed or slurry reactor; the answer that arrived later was a zeolite. Three catalysts for one reaction in fifty years, and the C64's epoxy resin is downstream of all three.

###### Silica carrier (the same silica as the cracker drier) `chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phosphoric-acid-catalyst.silica-carrier`

A silica gel of 200-400 m2/g surface area, and a strong family resemblance to the 3A molecular sieve's carrier and to the FCC catalyst's matrix and to the ammoxidation catalyst's support. One amorphous silica, made from sand by the soda-silica route, appears in this file as a support four different times, and it is the petrochemical branch's quietest link to a mineral.

###### Cumene oxidation to the hydroperoxide `chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation`

Cumene with air at 120-140 C, either with a hydroperoxide initiator or with a cobalt or manganese catalyst, gives cumene hydroperoxide at 20-40 wt%. This is a liquid-phase autoxidation, and it has the classic autoxidation hazard: the reaction is exothermic, it runs away above 150 C, and the product is a shock-sensitive organic peroxide.

###### Acid cleavage to phenol and acetone `chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage`

The cumene hydroperoxide is cleaved with sulphuric acid (or with a zeolite in later plants) at 50-80 C, giving phenol and acetone with 85-95% selectivity. The 1980s safety concern was the rearrangement of the cumene hydroperoxide to the phenol and acetone, which is violently exothermic: a small holdup upstream of the cleavage reactor would flash-boil, and the famous 1979 and 1985 phenol plant incidents are what the modern design rules are written around.

###### Phenol `chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol` _(medium)_

The molecule that goes into bisphenol A for epoxy, into phenol-formaldehyde for the phenolic plastics of switches and sockets, and into caprolactam for nylon 6. 1983 world phenol production was of the order of 3.5-4 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it from cumene.

###### Acetone `chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone`

The co-product of the cumene process and, from 1960s, a major product in its own right from the acetone cyanohydrin process. Acetone was the electronics plant's solvent of choice for degreasing and photoresist stripping in 1980s practice, and it is also the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the bisphenol A plus chloroform route to epoxy.

#### Acrylonitrile and the ammoxidation `chem.acrylonitrile`

The SOVERE process - SOx-free reductive ammoxidation - oxidises propylene with ammonia and air in one step to acrylonitrile. It was invented at Standard Oil of Ohio and licensed worldwide from 1960-1965, and by 1983 essentially all the world's roughly 1.2-1.5 million tonnes a year of acrylonitrile was made by it. Acrylonitrile is the most dangerous liquid in a polymer plant: it is acutely lethal by skin absorption, flammable at 3-20% in air, and boils at 77 C.

        - *SOVERE ammoxidation process* `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere` *(seen above)*
##### Acrylonitrile hazard `chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.safety` _(low)_

Acrylonitrile inhibits cytochrome oxidase and causes methemoglobinemia; it is absorbed through intact skin, which is why a 1980s acrylonitrile plant used gloves, face shields and shower-and-eyewash stations at every sampling point, and why the recommended limits fell through the 1980s. The 1980s occupational limits in force were around 10 ppm as an 8-hour time-weighted average in the United States, with much lower values adopted by later committees. There is no safe long-term exposure and the whole industry of the period treated it as an acute poison.

##### The older nitric acid route `chem.acrylonitrile.hno3-route` _(medium)_

Propylene nitrated with 15-20% nitric acid at 30-60 C and 2-5 bar to a mixture of 1- and 2-nitropropane, the 1-nitropropane converted with a dialkyl amine to a propylhydroxylamine, then dehydrated to acrylonitrile. It was a 30-50% route with a heavy nitrate waste stream and a very large plant, and by 1983 it existed only in a few older Soviet and Eastern European plants. It is the standard example of how completely a single-step oxidation can displace a three-step one.

##### Downstream acrylonitrile `chem.acrylonitrile.downstream`
