RMA fluxes were specified with a halide content under 0.05% because halides are what makes a flux corrosive and what makes a circuit hiss. The C64's board was very likely assembled with a halide-bearing flux and cleaned afterwards.

          - *Pine rosin (colophony)* `chem.rosin` *(seen above)*
###### Flux activator `chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activator`

Rosin alone is a weak flux. The activator is what makes the flux work, and it is also what makes the residue corrosive, so the whole specification of a flux is a trade: enough acid to remove the oxide, not enough ion to eat the board. The 1980s activators were carboxylic acids (stearic acid, abietic acid itself, succinic acid and its anhydride), fatty acid salts such as the zinc and amine stearates, and - in the older RMA grades - amine hydrochlorides, which is where the halide came from.

###### Amine halide activator (the halide source) `chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activator.amine-halide` _(medium)_

A triethanolamine or an alkylamine neutralised with a mineral acid, giving a halide ion in the flux. It is the reason a halide flux is corrosive if the residue is left on, and it is the reason the halide-free no-clean flux of the mid-1980s removed them rather than replacing them: the halide was never functional, it was just the most convenient way to get an acid and an amine together. The MIL-F-14161 halide-free standard of the late 1970s is what the industry measured against.

###### Balancing a halide activator `chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activator.amine-halide.neutralisation` _(medium)_

The whole trick of a halide flux is the neutralisation: enough amine to dissolve the resin and enough mineral acid to supply the fluxing acidity and the halide ion, and not so much of either that the residue eats the board. In practice a formulation is a matter of parts per million of chloride, and the measurement is an ion chromatography titration of an extracted sample rather than anything the flux maker could see. It is the least visible quality control in electronics and it is the one that decides whether a board passes its bias test.

###### The flux base and its solvent `chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-flux-base` _(medium)_

A liquid flux is rosin, activator and solvent, and the solvent is what makes it a liquid. Through the 1980s the solder wire's core was a rope of activated rosin flux in an alcohol or glycol ether solvent (isopropyl alcohol, or a glycol ether), and the core was drawn into a wire of solder by a wire-drawing machine. The active rosin in the core had to be clean enough to be drawn: any acid-value drift or gum would tear the wire.

###### Drawing the flux core into the wire `chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-flux-base.core-extrusion` _(medium)_

A solder wire is a core-drawing operation: a rope of activated flux is drawn together with a tube of solder alloy through successive dies until the wire is 0.3-0.8 mm across and the flux core is 0.1-0.3 mm. It constrains the flux chemistry severely - the flux has to be viscous enough not to run out of the die and fluid enough to fill the core - and it is why a 63/37 wire with a 0.2 mm core held about 1% of its mass in flux. One C64 has a few tens of joints and therefore a few grams of wire.

##### 60/40 tin-lead solder `chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy`

The eutectic at 183 C, which is why a wave-solder bath sat at 250-260 C and a hand iron at 300-350 C: 70-80 C of superheat above the melting point, which keeps the bath molten at the top and fluxes the joint as it passes through. In 1983 about 60-70% of the world's solder was 60/40 tin-lead for electronics; the alloy is cheap, it has a low melting point, and its oxide comes off in a flux. The 40% lead was the subject of the entire lead-free soldering programme of the 1980s and 1990s, and the lead itself came out of a flotation concentrator, not out of a refinery.

###### Where the tin came from `chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-source`

The tin in a 60/40 solder was smelted from cassiterite, the tin ore, and cassiterite is one of the rarer tin deposits in the world: Bolivia's placer and vein cassiterite, the Cornish tin belt, the Nigerian and the Indonesian deposits, and the alluvial cassiterite of Malaysia and Thailand. In 1983 the world mined something like 25,000-30,000 tonnes of tin a year - a small metal market by volume and a strategically awkward one, because the electronics industry's solder demand is a large fraction of it.

###### Cassiterite (SnO2) `chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-source.cassiterite`

Tin oxide, 78.8% tin by mass, the principal tin ore. Recovered from placer deposits by panning and gravity concentration and from hard-rock veins by flotation, then smelted or reduced to tin. The C64-scale observation is the interesting one: a single soldered joint holds a few milligrams of tin, and there are a hundred and fifty million of them, so the tin industry exists in part because of solder joints.

##### The intermetallic that actually joins `chem.solder-chemicals.intermetallic`

A solder joint is not tin-lead metal. On the copper side, copper and tin interdiffuse to make Cu6Sn5 and then Cu3Sn, and the joint's strength is in the intermetallic layer, not in the alloy. Two consequences: the intermetallic grows at service temperature until it embrittles the joint, and copper dissolves fast enough in a 260 C bath to put a bare copper lead into the solder pot within minutes - which is why the lead was flow-boned (plated with tin) before it ever entered the wave machine.

##### Halide-free no-clean flux `chem.solder-chemicals.no-clean` _(medium)_

The technology change that arrived in the middle and late 1980s: a flux with no halide at all, based on organic acids and esters rather than on amine hydrochlorides, and with an ionic residue mild enough that the board did not have to be washed. It solved the wash-water problem and it created a reliability problem, because the residue was left on the board and the industry spent a decade arguing about whether it was ionic enough to matter. The C64 predates it; Commodore's successors did not.

##### Board cleaning after soldering `chem.solder-chemicals.cleaning` _(medium)_

The flux residue had to come off, and the 1980s answer was either an organic solvent (1,1,1-trichloroethane, or isopropanol after 1983, or a mixture) or an aqueous detergent wash. The solvent was the same molecule as the degreaser, and its replacement by isopropanol is one of the cleanest single substitutions in the file: the board plant's solvent went from a chlorinated hydrocarbon to a propylene oxidation product in about two years, for regulatory and cost reasons rather than performance ones.

          - *Isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol)* `chem.isopropanol` *(seen above)*
##### The thermal profile is the process `chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile` _(medium)_

The reason the soldering chemistry is mostly temperature management: a through-hole joint sees 250-260 C for one to three seconds in the wave, which is enough to make the intermetallic and not enough to damage the flux or the laminate; a surface-mount joint sees a 220-245 C peak for 30-120 seconds in a reflow oven or a hot plate. Over-temperature grows the intermetallic and dulls the joint; under-temperature makes a cold solder joint that fails in service. Every one of these numbers is a chemical property, because the eutectic is a chemical fact.

###### Wave soldering `chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wave-soldering`

A through-hole board is soldered by passing it through a standing wave of molten solder at 250-260 C under a layer of flux, and the specific energy of the solder wave is what wets the joint and leaves the surface behind it clean. The 1980s wave machine had a two or three wave pot, a preheat tunnel, a flux station and a drying tunnel, and it consumed a surprising amount of both flux and deoxidised solder.

###### Dross `chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.wave-soldering.dross` _(low)_

The oxide skimmed off the surface of the solder pot: tin oxide and lead oxide, a few tenths of a per cent of the metal every shift. It was a real loss and a real fire risk, and the 1980s industry answer was a combination of the deoxidised (oxygen-free) wave and the automatic skimmer. The dross was returned to the refiner as a low-grade solder.

### Foundries, factories, utilities and logistics `industry`

The plant and the plumbing behind the Commodore 64: who made the chips, who assembled the box, what burned to light the lights, where the water came from, where the waste went, and how many hands and hours it took. A C64 is an artefact of eleven industries, not one.

#### Industrial electricity supply (1983) `facility.power`

The electricity that ran every press, oven, wave-solder machine, conveyor and test rig. In 1983 the world's grids were coal, oil, gas and hydro - not the gas-turbine-dominated grids of today - and industrial customers bought it on a two-part tariff with a demand charge.

##### The 1983 generating mix `facility.power.generation`

Coal, oil, gas and hydro carried the whole industrial world in 1983. In Taiwan, the grid that powered the subcontractors' factories was still mostly oil (58.8% of supply in 1980) with coal at 17.1% and hydro at 13.9%; by 1990 coal had taken over at 38.4% and oil had fallen to 25.6%. Korea and Hong Kong had almost no indigenous fuel at all.

###### Coal-fired steam power plant `facility.power.coal-plant`

The workhorse baseload of the 1980s. Coal from a mine or a rail/barge unloading dock is crushed, pulverised to talcum fineness, blown into a furnace with preheated air, burned under a boiler, and the resulting steam drives a turbine-generator. Net efficiency typically 33-38% thermal to electricity on a unit built in the 1960s-70s.

###### Steam coal (run-of-mine to sized) `facility.coal`

The fuel. Bituminous coal, 20-35 GJ/t, 0.5-3% sulphur, bought on the international steam coal market or delivered by rail from the field. Its ash and sulphur content set the flue-gas desulphuriser and the bottom-ash grinder bill.

###### Coal mine `facility.coal.mine` _(medium)_

In 1983 the relevant supply was room-and-pillar underground mining in the Appalachian basin (Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky) for the US East Coast grid, and open-pit truck-and-shovel or bucket-wheel in the Powder River Basin, Silesia, the Ruhr, the Bowen Basin and the Witbank coalfield.

###### Longwall face `facility.coal.longwall`

A mechanised shearer cuts a 2-3 m slice across the panel; the roof is allowed to cave into the goaf and the coal flows to a shearer loader. High recovery, high output, and a lot of subsidence.

###### Bituminous coal seam in sedimentary rock `facility.coal.seam`

The raw input, full stop. In the northern Appalachian basin the commercial coal is in the middle and upper Pennsylvanian (Conemaugh, Monongahela, Kittanning, Freeport) formations - Carboniferous, roughly 300 million years old, laid down in swamp forests and buried under Pennsylvanian sediment.

###### Room-and-pillar mining `facility.coal.room-pillar`

Still the dominant method for Appalachian metallurgical and steam coal: rooms driven to the pillar, pillars left behind to hold the roof. Cheap but leaves 30-50% of the seam underground.

###### Seam between shale and sandstone beds `facility.coal.room-pillar-seam`

The same Carboniferous coal-bearing sequence as the longwall face, mined from a shaft or slope rather than a portal. Ends at the rock in the ground.

###### Open-cut coal mine `facility.coal.opencut`

Overburden stripped by dragline or shovel, coal ripped by bulldozer, loaded into 100-tonne rear-dump trucks. Dominant in the Powder River Basin, the Ruhr, Limburg, New South Wales and Limpopo.

###### Overburden strip of shale and clay `facility.coal.overburden-strip` _(medium)_

Burden stripped in benches to reach the coal seam - often 10-60 m of rock and dirt per metre of coal in the Powder River Basin. The overburden itself becomes a backfill and a landfill-pond liner.

###### Coal preparation plant `facility.coal.prep-plant`

Crushed, screened, washed and dried at the mine mouth. 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones; the resulting 2-inch x 0 coal with 8-12% moisture is what a boiler of that era was designed to burn.

###### Dense-medium coal washing `facility.coal.washing` _(medium)_

Raw coal is floated on a magnetite/water slurry of specific gravity ~1.35; the light coal floats, the ash-rich shale sinks. This is where the mountaintop-removal debate's 'coal refuse' piles come from.

###### Magnetite sand for dense-medium fluid `facility.coal.magnetite` _(medium)_

Fe3O4, a natural iron oxide sand used as the density medium because it is dense, cheap, recoverable magnetically and chemically inert.

###### Magnetite ore body `facility.coal.magnetite-ore` _(medium)_

Typically mined from a lake-shore or igneous deposit and concentrated by flotation. Ends at the ore body in the ground.

###### Thermal drying of coal `facility.coal.moisture` _(medium)_

Screen-deck dryers or flash dryers bring the fuel down to about 8-12% moisture. A wetter coal burns slower, raises stack temperature and can quench a boiler screen tube.

###### Coal receiving and stockyard `facility.power.coal-plant.receiving` _(medium)_

Unload from rail unit trains or self-unloading barges into a yard. In the 1980s the East Coast plants were fed by unit trains; Japan's and Korea's coal came by Panamax and post-Panamax bulker.

###### Coal pulveriser (mill) `facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser`

A ball or roller mill grinds run-of-mine coal to a powder with at least 70% through 200 mesh (75 micrometres) so that it will burn in suspension. This was the technology that made the 1950s-80s boiler possible at all.

###### Hot-air fan and primary air `facility.power.coal-plant.fan` _(medium)_

A fan supplies the 60-80% of combustion air that dries and suspends the powder in the furnace and the remainder that sweeps it out between the boiler tube banks.

###### Boiler furnace and combustion `facility.power.coal-plant.furnace`

A refractory- and water-wall-lined firebox. Coal and preheated air enter at the burners, burn at 1300-1600 C, and give up radiation to the water walls lining the furnace walls.

###### Ljungstrom / regenerative air preheater `facility.power.air-preheater` _(medium)_

The flue gas gives up its heat to the incoming combustion air through a slow-rotating bank of corrugated steel plates - exhaust gas at ~300 C, air at ~300 C. This alone recovered several percent of the coal's energy.

###### Wet flue-gas desulphuriser (scrubber) `facility.power.coal-plant.scrubber` _(medium)_

Required in the US from about 1978 onward once new-source performance standards took effect. Slaked lime or limestone slurry absorbs SO2 to calcium sulphite, which is then forced-oxidised to gypsum; the stack gas is reheated so the plume still rises.

###### Limestone (calcium carbonate) slurry `facility.power.limestone`

Crushed and slaked to calcium hydroxide for wet scrubbing, or used directly in dry/semi-dry scrubbers. Ends at the quarry.

###### Limestone quarry `facility.power.limestone-quarry`

A bench quarry in Ordovician-Silurian carbonate rock, crushed on site. Ends at the rock in the ground.

###### Water-tube boiler and evaporator `facility.power.coal-plant.boiler`

Drum-type water-tube boiler, typically 300-900 MW, drum at ~15 MPa and 340-370 C. Feedwater circulates through downcomers and up risers around a flame path several hundred passes long; saturated steam leaves the drum to be superheated.

###### Economiser `facility.power.coal-plant.economiser` _(medium)_

A bank of finned tubes in the flue gas path that preheats feedwater from ~120 C to the saturation temperature, using the last 8-10% of the flue-gas heat. Standard since the 1930s, near-universal by 1980.

###### Bottom ash and fly ash handling `facility.power.coal-plant.ash-handling` _(medium)_

Ash from the boiler hoppers was quenched, then either dewatered and trucked to a landfill or put wet into a hopper and pumped as slurry. Fly ash was collected in electrostatic precipitators or baghouses and trucked dry or ponded.

###### Superheater and reheater `facility.power.coal-plant.superheater`

Superheaters raise saturated steam to 540-565 C by hanging banks of tube bundles in the radiant and convective pass; reheaters do the same again to the steam coming back out of the high-pressure turbine. Higher steam temperature is the single biggest lever on plant thermal efficiency.

###### Steam turbine `facility.power.coal-plant.turbine`

A multistage expansion turbine: high-pressure, intermediate-pressure and low-pressure sections, the last with the long bladed rotor of a wet-steam half-pressure machine. Exhaust goes to the condenser at about 0.05 bar. Steam rate for a 1980s unit was roughly 9-11 MJ/kWh.

###### Surface condenser `facility.power.coal-plant.condenser`

Thousands of stainless-steel tubes with condensing exhaust steam outside and cooling water inside. The condensate is the plant's own feedwater; cleanliness here directly sets boiler-tube life.

###### Nickel-alloy rotor and casing steel `facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel` _(medium)_

For a 540 C steam turbine the high-pressure rotor needed 0.5-0.8% Cr-Mo-V steel and the last stages austenitic stainless; the whole thing was forged, normalised, stress-relieved and then creep-rupture proof-tested.

###### Iron ore (hematite/magnetite) `facility.power.iron-ore`

The blast-furnace feed. Mesabi Range hematite in the US Lake Superior district, or imported Brazilian pellets/ore.

###### Iron ore open pit (Mesabi) `facility.power.iron-ore-pit`

Taconite and hematite are dug by 15-tonne payload shovels and hauled in 90-tonne trucks from a strip 60 m deep. Ends at the orebody.

###### Metallurgical coke `facility.power.coke`

Bituminous coal coked in batteries of 30-45 ovens to make the fuel and the reductant for the blast furnace. Ends at the coking plant.

###### High-Bituminous coking coal seam `facility.power.coking-coal-seam` _(medium)_

A very specific subset of bituminous coal - the seam that swells and fuses in the coke oven, distinct from the steam coal the power station burns. The Pennsylvania/Kentucky/West Virginia 'High Bituminous' field.

###### Generator (turbo-alternator) `facility.power.coal-plant.generator`

The turbine shaft turns a 2- or 4-pole alternator at 3000/3600 rpm. A 500 MVA water-cooled unit is about 12 m long and 6 m wide. Output was 13.8 kV or 21 kV - far too low to transmit, hence the step-up transformer next door.

###### Generator step-up transformer (GSU) `facility.power.coal-plant.stepup-transformer`

A single-phase or three-phase bank of 240-500 kV oil-filled transformers that takes 21 kV from the alternator to the transmission line. This is the piece of iron that makes the whole grid possible, and it is why every power station has a lumpy, oil-filled, bunded yard next door.

###### Switchyard and circuit breakers `facility.power.coal-plant.switchyard`

Outdoor busbars, disconnectors, dead-tank and live-tank oil circuit breakers and surge arresters, on a steel lattice gantry. The step-up point where the plant connects to the transmission network.

###### Hydroelectric power plant `facility.power.hydro-plant`

Genuinely important for the 1980s Far East: Taiwan took 13.9% of its supply from hydro in 1980 and 24.5% by 1990 (Sun Moon Lake, Tachia, Feitsui, Wujie), and Taiwan's run-of-river stations are exactly the kind of small plant Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors drew from. Elsewhere hydro was the cheap baseload of Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Canada.

###### Concrete penstock and headrace tunnel `facility.power.hydro-plant.penstock` _(medium)_

A 3-6 m diameter steel or concrete conduit carrying water from the intake at head to the turbine, usually several hundred metres and dropping 50-300 m of head.

###### Rockfill dam and riprap `facility.power.rockfill` _(medium)_

Dams of the era were built of quarried rock tipped into the river and compacted, faced with concrete or asphaltic membrane. Ends at the quarry face.

###### Aggregate and riprap quarry `facility.power.aggregate-quarry`

Granite/gneiss quarried, crushed and screened for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material. Ends at the rock in the hillside.

###### Portland cement `facility.power.cement-portland`

Limestone plus clay, fired in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, ground with gypsum. The universal structural binder of the 1980s industrial plant: dams, cooling towers, substation foundations, effluent tanks, the fab's raised floor.

###### Rotary cement kiln `facility.power.cement-kiln`

A 60-150 m inclined steel tube rotating 1-2 rpm, burning coal or oil at 1450 C to drive off CO2 and drive the reaction forward. Ends at the limestone and clay pits.

###### Francis turbine `facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine`

The standard medium-head machine: water enters the spiral casing, turns a runner on a vertical or horizontal shaft at 100-750 rpm, and exits into the draft tube.

###### Tailrace and reservoir `facility.power.hydro-plant.tailrace`

Where the water goes back to the river - and, downstream of the dam, the river itself is the raw water intake for the industrial park that the dam's power attracted.

###### The river itself `facility.power.river`

A glacial or monsoonal river carrying suspended sediment, hardness and organic colour. This is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water in this tree.

###### Oil-fired steam power plant `facility.power.oil-plant`

The 1980s default in much of Asia and the Middle East, and the reason Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. Residual fuel oil and fuel oil burned in a boiler instead of coal - cheaper to handle, dirtier, and dead on arrival once the 1979 oil shock and OPEC reset prices.

###### Crude petroleum and fuel oil `facility.oil`

The liquid fuel of the whole industrial world in 1983. Kuwait and Saudi Arabian Light for the Far East, plus North Sea Brent and US domestic crude for Europe and the US East Coast.

###### Oil and gas well `facility.oil.well`

A rotary or cable-tool hole completed into sandstone or carbonate. In 1983 the Far East's oil was largely onshore (Gawair in Kuwait, Ghawar-equivalent fields) with growing offshore production.

###### Sandstone or carbonate oil reservoir `facility.oil.reservoir`

Porous sedimentary rock (typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate) saturated with oil under pressure. This is where the story actually ends for oil.

###### Refinery `facility.oil.refinery`

Atmospheric and vacuum distillation plus hydrotreating to make fuel oil and, in a complex refinery, the naphtha feed for the hydrogen and ethylene crackers. Ali Qaido in Kuwait (1945) or Amuay in Venezuela (1962) typified the scale.

###### LPG (propane/butane) `facility.oil.lpg` _(medium)_

The liquid the Hong Kong and Japanese industrial estates burned for process heat and factory heating, and the feedstock for the 1980s alkylation route to isobutylene. Ends at the well or the refinery.

###### Oil-fired boiler `facility.power.oil-plant.boiler`

Same water-tube boiler as the coal plant, but with oil burners instead of a pulveriser and an induced-draft fan sized for the lower flue-gas volume. Two to four boilers typically share one stack.

###### Tall chimney `facility.power.oil-plant.stack`

A 150-250 m concrete or steel chimney to get the plume above the inversion layer and disperse sulphur dioxide over a large area. Not a pollution control device - a dilution device.

###### Gas-fired power plant `facility.power.gas-plant`

Two different things share this name. For the 1983 industrial economy the honest answer is that almost none of the grid came from natural gas - gas turbines ran mainly for peak load, standby and cogeneration. Taiwan's first LNG cargo arrived in 1983 and natural gas did not become a grid fuel until the 1990s.

###### Gas turbine `facility.power.gas-plant.turbine`

A compressor, a combustor at 1400-1600 C and a turbine in a single shaft or two. Open-cycle efficiency only 25-35% in 1983 - the poor number that made gas peakers expensive until combined cycle became standard in the 1990s.

###### Natural gas `facility.power.natural-gas`

Methane with ethane and propane, delivered by pipeline or (from 1983 in Taiwan and Japan) as LNG. Western Europe's gas was North Sea and Groningen; the US grid burned domestic Appalachian, Texas and Louisiana gas.

###### North Sea gas field `facility.power.natural-gas.northsea`

Permian Zechstein gas reservoirs beneath the southern North Sea - the source that made Netherlands and UK power stations coal-light in the 1970s and 80s. The gas arrives at the platform's own gas turbines over a 30-40 km undersea pipeline.

###### LNG cargo `facility.power.natural-gas.lng` _(medium)_

Liquefied at -162 C in one of the big North African/Middle East trains and shipped in a 125,000 m3 membrane or Moss-type tanker. Taiwan's first LNG landed at Kaohsiung in 1983 from Algeria.

###### LNG liquefaction train `facility.power.natural-gas.liquefier` _(medium)_

A cascade of propane and mixed-refrigerant heat exchangers that chill the gas to -162 C. The 'missing link' for helium also hangs off this kind of plant.

###### Appalachian / Gulf Coast gas `facility.power.natural-gas.us-domestic` _(medium)_

In the US - which is where the Commodore fab and the assembly lines in Pennsylvania and California were - electricity generation burned natural gas mostly on the Gulf Coast and in Texas, plus Appalachian gas in Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia.

###### Nuclear power plant `facility.power.nuclear-plant`

Not a 'coal/oil/gas/hydro' machine, but it was 10.2% of Taiwan's electricity in 1980 - the first reactor at Chinshan came on line in 1978, followed by Chinshan 2 (1979), Chinshan 3, Feitsui and Lungmen. Any 1983 power bill in northern Taiwan could legitimately be traced to a uranium fuel rod.

###### Uranium fuel `facility.power.uranium` _(medium)_

Uranium concentrate converted to UF6 and enriched from natural 0.71% U-235 to 2.5-3.5%, then fabricated into ceramic UO2 pellets 8 mm across, sintered, ground to length, clad in zircaloy and made into a fuel assembly. In 1983 the US HEU was being phased down and the world's enrichment market was switching to centrifuge cascades.

###### Uranium ore (U3O8) `facility.power.uranium-ore` _(medium)_

Graded and leached in the 1970s-80s, largely from the Colorado Plateau (Uravan) and New Mexico, plus Namibia and Canada. Ends at the orebody.

###### Vanadiferous uraninite ore `facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore` _(medium)_

The US Colorado Plateau ore was processed mainly for vanadium with uranium as a by-product, in mills that roasted the ore with salt and soda ash and leached it with chlorine.

###### Transmission and distribution network `facility.power.grid` _(medium)_

High-voltage transmission from the plant's switchyard to the city, then medium-voltage distribution to the industrial park, then the service drop to the customer. This is the piece almost nobody thinks about: roughly 8% of generated electricity is lost in transmission and distribution before it reaches the meter.

###### Overhead transmission line `facility.power.grid.line`

Steel lattice towers or wooden H-poles carrying three phases on aluminium conductor, with shield wires and porcelain or glass suspension insulators. The thermal rating of the conductor, not the voltage, is the limit.

###### Aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR) `facility.power.acsr-conductor` _(medium)_

Aluminium strands around a steel core for tensile strength, twisted and stranded on the line. Ends at an aluminium smelter fed by alumina.

###### Bauxite -> alumina (Bayer process) `facility.power.alumina-bauxite`

Aluminium exists as bauxite ore -> alumina -> aluminium. The Bayer process leaches alumina from bauxite with hot caustic soda under pressure, then precipitates aluminium hydroxide. 4 tonnes bauxite give 2 t alumina give 1 t aluminium.

###### Bauxite mine `facility.power.bauxite-mine`

Residual laterite capping on old limestone terrain, stripped by shovel and truck or by cable-sbucket wheel excavator. Ends at the bauxite body.

###### Porcelain suspension insulator `facility.power.insulator-porcelain`

Glazed (glassy) or unglazed (ceramic) insulator strings, 10-20 discs to hold a 230-500 kV line up in the air. Replaced later by composite polymer strings, which is why the classic transmission silhouette disappeared after 1990.

###### Kaolin (china clay) `facility.power.kaolin`

A white kaolinite clay from a kaolin pit, washed and beneficiated for the ceramic and paper trades. Ends at the clay pit.

###### Utility substation `facility.power.grid.substation`

Transformer bays, circuit breakers, buswork and the control house that steps transmission voltage down to the 11-34.5 kV distribution level. Utility substations outnumbered the plants; a 1980s industrial park typically had one primary substation feeding a ring of unit substation transformers.

###### Medium-voltage distribution feeder `facility.power.grid.distribution` _(medium)_

Overhead or underground 11-13.8 kV feeders with reclosers, sectionalisers and fuses. Underground feeders were standard in the new Hong Kong industrial estates and in Japanese and Korean industrial parks; overhead was normal in the US outside cities.

        - *Electricity at the factory wall* `facility.electricity` *(seen above)*
##### The industrial electricity tariff (1983) `facility.power.tariff`

Industrial customers never paid a simple price per kWh. The tariff was two-part: an energy charge per kWh plus a demand charge per kW of measured maximum demand over a 15 or 30 minute interval. The demand charge rewarded flat load and punished a factory that ran its ovens and its wave-solder line together. Tariff classes ('medium general service', 'large power and light') were negotiated against contract demand and often a five-year commitment.

#### Industrial steam plant `facility.steam`

Process steam for soldering, cleaning, degreasing, autoclaving and heating the building. Most industrial steam plants of 1983 were coal- or oil-fired package/field-assembled water-tube boilers, often with their own turbo-alternator so that the site exported some of its own electricity.

##### The boiler house `facility.steam.boiler-house`

A tall, heavily built single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, the boilers in a row, coal bunkers or an oil day tank alongside, and the chimney outside. Even in 1983 it was the tallest building on most industrial sites.

###### Fuel handling and bunker `facility.steam.fuel-handling` _(medium)_

A conveyor, a hopper and a boiler feed screw, or an oil tank and a pump skid. Manual barrow-and-shovel coal handling was still normal at plants below about 10 t/h.

##### Water-tube boiler `facility.steam.boiler`

Two-drum or three-drum evaporators with a superheater. Industrial boilers of 4-20 t/h fired coal at about 6-9 bar saturated, directly into the plant's heating and process network. Economisers and feedwater heaters recovered heat; blowdown controlled the dissolved solids.

###### Industrial boiler fuel `facility.steam.fuel`

Anthracite, bituminous coal, fuel oil or - very commonly in Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan - coal briquettes pressed from imported anthracite fines in a ring-die or pillow press.

###### Coal briquette (hongsha / pressed coal) `facility.steam.briquette`

Binderless or starch-bound anthracite fines pressed at 200 bar into egg-shaped briquettes about 100 g each, fired on a grate. Hong Kong's thermal power and much of its industrial boiler load ran on exactly this fuel.

###### Anthracite fines `facility.steam.anthracite` _(medium)_

Hard, high-carbon coal, largely imported to the Far East from South Wales, Vietnam and China. Ends at the anthracite seam.

###### Blowdown and demineralised make-up `facility.steam.blowdown`

A fraction of boiler water is blown down to keep total dissolved solids and alkalinity inside limits; the make-up has to be soft or demineralised or the cycles of concentration collapse. Blowdown is sent to a flash tank for heat recovery and then to the cooling-water basin.

###### Safety valves and drum level control `facility.steam.safety-valves` _(medium)_

Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator on the drum, and the refractory-lined sight-glass port that operators actually looked at. A steam plant is a place where the concrete is usually older than the manager.

##### Industrial turbo-alternator `facility.steam.turbo-alternator` _(medium)_

Where a plant burned coal continuously it made sense to take steam past 300 C and put it through a small turbine to make some of its own electricity. A 2-6 MW pass turbine driving a 480 V alternator, exporting a few hundred kW and buying back the rest at peak rates, was a standard arrangement in Taiwan, Korea and Britain.

###### Speed governor and overspeed trip `facility.steam.turbine-governor` _(medium)_

A flyball or hydraulic governor on the turbine shaft plus a mechanical overspeed trip and, in larger sets, a turbine protective device that tripped the generator breaker. The overspeed trip was the last line of defence against a runaway.

##### Steam header and distribution `facility.steam.header`

A large-diameter steel pipe - 300-800 mm - with flanged or socket-welded branches to each user, insulation lagged in magnesium-block or calcium-silicate, and a trap at every low point. Steam was distributed at constant pressure from a header rather than generated at each machine.

###### Steam pipe insulation `facility.steam.insulation`

Moulded magnesium-block sections, calcium silicate or, on hot surfaces, an asbestos-based rope and canvas wrap. Asbestos lagging was utterly routine on a 1980s steam line and is the reason so many power and chemical plants have mesothelioma claims decades later.

###### Asbestos (chrysotile) mineral `facility.steam.asbestos`

Fibrous magnesium silicate mined from open pits and shafts in Quebec, South Africa, Italy and the Soviet Union, and spun, carded and woven into rope, cloth and board. This is the single most under-acknowledged raw material in any 1980s industrial plant.

###### Asbestos mine and mill `facility.steam.asbestos-mine`

A serpentinite or chrysotile orebody worked by open pit or underground, then crushed, graded and carded. Ends at the serpentinite rock in the ground.

##### Condensate return `facility.steam.condensate-return`

Steam traps in every steam-consuming process returned hot condensate to the hotwell. Recovering it saved both fuel and water-treatment chemical, and the copper condensate pipework of a 1980s plant was a continuous, weeping mess of unions and gaskets.

###### Steam trap `facility.steam.trap`

A thermostatic (bimetallic or liquid-expansion) or mechanical bucket trap with a strainer upstream. Failed-open traps cost fuel; failed-closed traps flooded the plant. Every steam system of the era leaked at a few percent of its steam load, largely from these.

##### Boiler feedwater treatment `facility.steam.feedwater-treatment`

Two chemistries: lime-soda softening for the low-pressure plant, and ion-exchange demineralisation for anything above about 20 bar. By 1983 the whole industry standard was sodium-cycle cation plus strong-base anion demineralisation with a mixed-bed polish.

###### Lime-soda softening `facility.steam.lime-soda`

Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 and soda ash Na2CO3 are dosed into a hot reaction basin, converting the scale-forming calcium and magnesium hardness into calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide sludge, which settles in a clarifier. This is the classic 1900-1960 process, still running at small industrial plants in 1983. Produces a lot of sludge.

###### Slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) `facility.steam.lime`

Quicklime CaO burnt in a vertical or flash calciner to 1000 C, then hydrated. Ends at the limestone quarry.

###### Limestone (CaCO3) `facility.steam.limestone`

Carboniferous and Permian limestone, crushed to 20-40 mm for the kiln. Ends at the quarry face.

###### Soda ash (sodium carbonate) `facility.steam.soda-ash` _(medium)_

Solvay or Leblanc-process sodium carbonate for the lime-soda process. Ends at salt and limestone.

###### Calcium carbonate / magnesium hydroxide sludge `facility.steam.hardness-sludge`

The lumpy waste from lime-soda softening, pumped to a thickener and then to a drying bed or trucked to landfill wet. This is the sludge that fills the lagoons around old steel and chemical works.

###### Ion-exchange demineralisation `facility.steam.demineralisation`

A cation exchanger in the sodium form swaps Ca/Mg for Na; a strongly basic anion exchanger then swaps the bicarbonate/sulphate/chloride anions for OH; CO2 is degassed between the two beds; the effluent is then polished in a mixed bed to sodium chloride equivalent of a few tens of ppb. Resin is regenerated with 10-20% caustic and 6-12% hydrochloric or sulphuric acid.

###### Ion-exchange resin (polystyrene-DVB) `facility.steam.ion-resin`

A gel-type cation resin (sulfonic acid groups) or an anion resin (quaternary ammonium groups) on a cross-linked polystyrene-divinylbenzene bead. Beads of 0.3-1.0 mm, sieved into size fractions so the fine resin could be kept out of the top of the bed.

###### Styrene monomer `facility.steam.styrene`

Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene or by cracking benzene, both from the aromatic fraction of an oil refinery. A C8H8 molecule - the same feedstock family as the styrene in the ABS case of the C64.

###### Divinylbenzene crosslinker `facility.steam.divinylbenzene`

A small fraction of a C10H10 comonomer added to the styrene so the bead does not dissolve in the caustic used for regeneration. This crosslinking is what makes the resin insoluble and gives it its capacity.

###### CO2 degasser `facility.steam.co2-degas`

A packed or bubble column that strips dissolved carbon dioxide from the water between the cation and anion beds. Skipping it overloaded the anion resin with carbonic acid and shortened its life.

###### Brine regeneration and waste `facility.steam.brine-regen` _(medium)_

Regeneration blew a large slug of acidic or alkaline brine once or twice a day, which had to go somewhere. In 1983 the answer was usually a lined lagoon, a settling pond and then a discharge permit.

      - *Water for a factory* `facility.water` *(seen above)*
#### Industrial gas supply `facility.gases`

The bulk gases a 1980s electronics plant bought by the tanker load: nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen, plus the specialty gases. Supplied either by an on-site air separation unit, an on-site PSA/membrane/electrolyser, or delivered as liquid from a merchant producer in a road tanker.

        - *Nitrogen supply* `facility.nitrogen` *(seen above)*
##### Oxygen supply `facility.gases.oxygen`

Supplied as liquid oxygen from a merchant AS U or from the site unit. Used for the oxy-acetylene flame of the mechanical and maintenance shops, the gas-shielded welding of the metal frames, and increasingly for the oxygen plasma strip in a fab.

###### Oxy-acetylene flame for tool and frame welding `facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene`

Oxygen plus a locally generated acetylene from calcium carbide (in the Far East, imported cylinder acetylene was common). This is the flame that welded every sheet-metal chassis, rack and jig in the factory.

###### Acetylene cylinder `facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder`

Dissolved acetylene at 15 bar in a porous monolithic mass (calcium carbide + acetone), in a steel shell. Calcium carbide came from the electric arc furnace carbide plant, i.e. ultimately from coal coke and quicklime.

        - *Argon* `facility.argon` *(seen above)*
##### Helium `facility.helium`

In 1983 helium was a genuinely scarce, genuinely odd commodity. Most of the world's supply came from a handful of natural-gas fractionation plants in Texas, Wyoming, Kansas and New Mexico, which extracted the 0.0005-0.005% helium in the gas as a crude 50-75% mixture. The rest came from four dedicated underground helium fields - the hug gas of Amarillo, Texas, and the Dixon and Harley fields in Kansas. Cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s.

###### Cryogenic helium separation from natural gas `facility.helium.cryo-separation`

The gas is chilled to -190 C through a train of plate-fin heat exchangers; helium, having the second-lowest boiling point, stays in the vapour phase and is drawn off from the top of the cold box as a crude 50-75% helium stream. Then purified by cryogenic adsorption, catalytic dehydrogenation of the residual hydrogen and activated-carbon adsorption of the nitrogen.

###### Activated carbon helium purification `facility.helium.activated-carbon-adsorber`

The last step: nitrogen is adsorbed on a char bed at 77 K to give 99.995% (5N) or 99.9999% (6N) helium. The same activated-carbon adsorption principle as the water-treatment carbon, run at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

###### Liquid helium dewar (4.2 K) `facility.helium.liquid-helium`

A double-walled stainless vessel with a superinsulating vacuum jacket, holding 4.2 K liquid helium for a cryostat or a superconducting magnet. Expensive, evaporating at about 0.5-1% a day, and topped up by truck in a dewar that looked like a scaled-down rocket stage.

###### Hug gas from an underground helium reservoir `facility.helium.hug-gas`

The Permian Basin of west Texas and the southwest Kansas gas fields hold helium that never migrated out of the crust, trapped under impermeable salt and anhydrite since geological time. These are drilled specifically for helium, at tiny volumes - Amarillo field production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year even in its peak.

###### The 1980s helium shortage `facility.helium.supply-constraint` _(medium)_

US Bureau of Mines and then BLM administered the supply; the Cliffside field ran out in the mid-1970s and production was rationed, so helium became genuinely rationed and expensive for laboratories and for leak testing. This is a real constraint on the 1980s helium supply chain, not a later phenomenon.

##### Hydrogen `facility.gases.hydrogen`

Three routes in 1983: (a) bulk hydrogen from a merchant plant by tube trailer or by liquefaction; (b) on-site steam methane reforming of natural gas, the standard for anything above about 100 Nm3/h; and (c) electrolysis of demineralised water for the last, and highest, purity.

###### Steam methane reforming `facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming`

Natural gas is desulphurised to under 0.5 ppm sulphur, mixed with steam at 3:1 and passed over a nickel-molybdenum or chromite catalyst at 800-850 C and 15-25 bar. This gives hydrogen plus CO, and the CO is shifted over an iron-chrome catalyst to CO2 and more hydrogen. Then CO2 is removed by amine scrubbing or molecular sieve.

###### Nickel reforming catalyst `facility.gases.nickel-catalyst` _(medium)_

Nickel oxide on alumina, or the classic nickel-molybdenum on alumina, formed by impregnating a porous pellet with nickel nitrate and calcining. Ends at the laterite and the bauxite.

###### Nickel laterite ore `facility.gases.laterite`

The dominant world nickel ore in 1983 - a limonite/garnierite blanket over ultramafic rock in New Caledonia, Cuba, the Philippines and Indonesia, usually smelted in a ferronickel plant. The Philippines connection is the direct one to the C64's subcontractor geography.

###### Laterite open pit `facility.gases.laterite-mine`

Weathered ultramafic mantle rock, strip-mined by shovel and truck. Ends at the saprolite profile in the ground.

###### Electrolysis of demineralised water `facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis`

In a diaphragm or, from the 1970s, an alkaline cell, a nickel-plated or activated-titanium cathode makes hydrogen while a nickel anode makes oxygen. Fed with conductivity-grade water at 20-25 C. Output purity is 99.99% once the cell gas is passed over a palladium diffuser or an oxygen getter - the 'deoxo' step that killed the last 0.1% of oxygen.

###### Where hydrogen went in a 1980s electronics plant `facility.gases.hydrogen.uses` _(medium)_

Hydrocarbon and silicone greasing, hydrogen annealing of the copper and the metallisation, the reducing atmosphere in the diffusion furnace and the epitaxial reactor, and - for the tie-in with this story - the hydrogen atmosphere in the case of a lamp or a nickel/plated through-hole fill was not yet standard practice.

##### Bulk liquid storage and tube trailers `facility.gases.nitrogen-purge-system` _(medium)_

The logistics layer of the gases: a merchant ASU on the edge of the industrial park with bulk tanks, or a fleet of tube trailers on a shift schedule, delivering 24 hours' supply into a customer's own cryogenic tank.

##### Carbon dioxide (dry ice) `facility.gases.carbon-dioxide` _(medium)_

Used in the plant for refrigerant cargo, for the dry-ice shipping of perishables, and - in the electronics plant - for nothing much; the two dry-ice applications in a 1980s C64 supply chain were chilling the shipped goods and cleaning moulds of frost. Skipping the beverage-carbonation story as instructed.

###### Ammonia-synthesis CO2 (fertiliser plant) `facility.gases.co2-ammonia` _(medium)_

A large part of the 1980s merchant CO2 came from hydrogen- and ammonia-based fertiliser plants, where the shift reactor CO2 is captured and dried. Ends at natural gas and air.

#### Instrument air and plant air `facility.compressed-air`

Every factory ran on compressed air. Instrument air was dried, oil-free air fed to the air-line and to the logic valves; plant air was for the pneumatic tools, the automated insertion machines and the ejectors. The classic 1980s split was a dedicated compressor for instrument air and one or more dirty machines for everything else.

##### Air compressor `facility.compressed-air.compressor`

Reciprocating or, from the 1960s onward, oil-injected rotary screw machines. A large electronics plant ran several 100-300 kW screw units; a small sub-contractor ran one 30 kW reciprocating machine under a concrete acoustic enclosure.

###### Intake silencer and inlet filter `facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer`

An intake filter-silencer combination that kept the machine from eating the dust and the unfiltered outside air. In a coastal site (Kaohsiung, Hong Kong, Long Beach) the sea salt went straight onto the rotors if this was neglected.

###### Drive motor `facility.compressed-air.motor`

A TEFC or, in a corrosive coastal plant, an explosion-proof motor. 400 V three-phase induction motor with a direct-on-line or star-delta starter; speed control only by pole changing.

##### Aftercooler `facility.compressed-air.aftercooler`

A water-cooled or finned-air heat exchanger that takes the discharge air from ~100 C down to ~40 C. Without it the machine would not hold pressure in a hot climate and the separator would not work.

##### Water (and oil) separator `facility.compressed-air.separator`

An automatic drain pot or cyclone knock-out that removes the condensed water and, in an oil-injected screw machine, the injected oil. This vessel was the source of most of the 'the air is wet' complaints in the shop.

##### Air dryer `facility.compressed-air.dryer`

Two chemistries in 1983. Refrigerant (absorption or adsorption, e.g. a zeolite unit chilled to 1-3 C) gave a pressure dew point of about 2-10 C, good enough for most pneumatic machinery and marginal for instrument air. Desiccant (two alternating towers of silica gel or molecular sieve with a heatless regeneration on the off-line tower) got the dew point down to -40 to -70 C, which was what a pneumatic logic valve or a moisture-sensitive process needed.

###### Refrigerant (CFC-11/12, or ammonia) `facility.compressed-air.refrigerant`

The refrigeration for an absorption dryer. CFC-11 and CFC-12 were the universal choices and are the ozone-depleting gases the 1987 Montreal Protocol eventually banned - so this node is both a 1983 fact and a direct cause of later environmental regulation.

###### Fluorspar (CaF2) for the HF needed to make CFCs `facility.compressed-air.fluorspar` _(medium)_

Metallurgical-grade fluorspar for the anhydrous hydrofluoric acid that reacts with chloroform to make the chlorofluorocarbons. A large share of the 1980s HF demand, and a distinct little industry with its own mine (Fluorspar, Derbyshire; Kerimsi, Turkey; San Luis Potosi, Mexico). Ends at the fluorite vein.

###### Fluorspar mine `facility.compressed-air.fluorspar-mine`

Vein or replacement deposit of fluorite in limestone, often with a metre-scale overburden, worked by open pit or by shallow shaft. Ends at the ore body.

##### Air receiver (accumulator) `facility.compressed-air.receiver`

A vertical ASME code air vessel, 1-10 m3, acting as a buffer so the compressor could unload on a pressure switch. It also stored enough air to ride through a power cut for a few minutes - which in a fab meant keeping the wet-bench exhaust and the compressors together.

##### Ring main and distribution `facility.compressed-air.ring-main`

Black steel pipe - galvanised or, better, painted steel - in a ring around the plant with drop-legs to each machine. A ring rather than a spine so that a single closed valve could isolate a section for maintenance. Drops went through a service unit with a tap, a pressure regulator, a filter and a flowmeter at each bench.

##### Nitrogen purge of the air system `facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge`

Before opening a vessel, a line, or a tank that had held flammable or reactive material, it was purged with nitrogen and tested with an oxygen analyser. The purge itself was fed from the nitrogen header or, in a small plant, from a bottled cylinder.

##### Process exhaust (fab wet-bench and furnace) `facility.compressed-air.fab-exhaust` _(medium)_

A separate, larger system from the instrument air: a scrubbed chemical exhaust ducting the acid, base, solvent and furnace exhaust out of the building, usually to an alkaline scrubber on the roof. See facility.hazardous-waste for the emissions and liquid side.

###### Alkaline scrubber packing `facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing` _(medium)_

A packed column of plastic Raschig or saddle rings on a support grid, fed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate, stripping acid mist and the base-mist equivalent out of the exhaust. Discharge is a neutral brine sent to the effluent system.

###### PVC / PP packing media `facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing`

Moulded plastic ring or saddle packing, chemically inert to acid and alkali where ceramic or metal would be attacked. The same vinyl chloride monomer chain that makes the conduit and the cable in the plant.

###### Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) `facility.compressed-air.caustic-soda`

Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH, with the hydrogen and chlorine sold and the caustic sold. The most-used industrial chemical on the site. Ends at salt and electricity.

###### Chlor-alkali membrane cell `facility.compressed-air.membrane-cell` _(medium)_

From the late 1980s the diaphragm cell gave way to the cation-exchange membrane cell, which makes caustic soda pure enough to go straight into a transistor wet bench instead of being evaporated. In 1983 most plants still used diaphragm or mercury cells, which made their caustic soda full of salt - a real problem for a photoresist developer.

###### Brine (concentrated sodium chloride) `facility.compressed-air.salt-brine`

Either evaporated sea salt or a solution of mined rock salt, brined to saturation and clarified with lime and salt cake. Ends at the salt field or the sea.

###### Rock salt mine `facility.compressed-air.rock-salt-mine`

Bedded evaporite salt (halite) mined by room-and-pillar in shafts or by solution mining in the brine field, in Permian or Silurian formations. Ends at the salt body in the rock.

#### Hazardous and industrial waste, 1980s practice `facility.hazardous-waste`

The part of the story usually left out. A 1980s electronics plant generated, per fab, tens of thousands of gallons of spent acid, spent solvent, cyanide-bearing rinse, and metal-bearing sludge a year, plus a smaller amount of contaminated equipment and packaging. What happened to it was loosely governed - in the US by RCRA, which had only been in force for three years in 1983 - and often not well.

##### RCRA: the cradle-to-grave regime `facility.hazardous-waste.rcra`

The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act became law on 21 October 1976. Its Subtitle C hazardous waste regulations were promulgated 26 February and 19 May 1980 and took effect 19 November 1980 - so in 1983 the whole American electronics industry was three years into the most consequential change in waste handling since the Clean Air Act. Generators must determine whether a waste is hazardous, accumulate it in a closed, labelled, inspected area for no more than 90 days, describe it on a manifest, and ship it only to a permitted treatment, storage or disposal facility.

##### What a plant actually generated `facility.hazardous-waste.generation`

Spent sulfuric and hydrochloric acid from etching; spent developer (tetramethylammonium hydroxide from positive photoresist) and stripper; acetone, xylene, toluene, IPA and cellosolve acetate; arsenic-containing waste from the diffusion furnaces; cyanide-bearing waste from the gold and tin plating; and copper/nickel/chromium-bearing rinse. Small generators - which in 1983 was most of Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base - had almost no obligations at all beyond a monthly manifest.

##### Acid neutralisation with lime `facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation`

The cheapest and by far the most common treatment: slaked lime or limestone slurry is dosed into a reaction tank, the acid is neutralised, the metal hydroxides precipitate out, and the tank is then settled and the supernatant discharged. It converts an acid into a sludge - which is still a hazardous waste, just a solid one.

###### Heavy-metal hydroxide sludge `facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide-sludge`

A wet, low-solids sludge of iron, aluminium, chromium, copper, nickel, zinc and cadmium hydroxides, filtered on a plate-and-frame or belt press to 15-25% solids and trucked to a hazardous landfill in a lined, covered cell. In 1983 this was the default destination and the reason so many US sites are now Superfund sites.

###### Settling pond / lagoon `facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond`

An unlined or clay-lined earthen basin into which treated effluent was discharged and solids allowed to settle, with the supernatant decanted to a stream or a municipal sewer. Thousands of these existed in 1983; the liner requirements came later. The pond was often the plant's cheapest and worst idea.

###### Hazardous waste landfill `facility.hazardous-waste.landfill`

In 1983 a hazardous landfill was typically a clay-lined cell with a leachate collection system and groundwater monitoring wells, licensed under RCRA or operating under interim status. Because the Land Disposal Restrictions did not yet exist, most of it received untreated sludge and incinerator ash.

##### Incineration of solvent vapours `facility.hazardous-waste.incineration`

Vapour incineration (afterburner / thermal oxidiser) for the xylene, toluene and trichloroethane vapour from the resist track and the degreaser, plus a wet scrubber or a carbon absorber on the cool side. By the time the air came out it passed an oxidiser at 800-1000 C with a residence time of about one second.

##### The RCRA manifest `facility.hazardous-waste.manifest`

A multi-part paper form - the shipping paper, the generator certification and the transporter and facility certifications - carried with the load from generator to treatment, storage or disposal facility, with signed copies returned to the generator. This is the paper trail that later made it possible to reconstruct where Commodore's waste went.

##### Ocean outfall `facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall` _(medium)_

In the coastal Far East - Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines - dilute effluent was and is discharged through a permitted outfall diffuser into the sea, often at a designated ocean disposal zone beyond the territorial limit. The dilution argument is real; so is the fact that the 1980s outfalls had almost no metals monitoring.

##### Commodore's own solvent site: the CSG Superfund case `facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site`

The clearest documented example in this whole story. A 250-gallon underground concrete tank at the MOS Technology site at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania - installed with the building in 1970 - leaked in 1974. It stored the trichloroethene and other solvents used to clean silicon wafers. MOS replaced it with an unlined steel tank, which leaked too. In 1978 the Audubon Water Company, which supplied the public water system, detected trichloroethene in its wells. PADER concluded by 1979 that the contamination could not be excavated. A ground-water recovery well and a spray/treatment system began in November 1981; an air stripper began in February 1984. The site went on the Superfund National Priorities List on 4 October 1989 and the fab was closed in 1992.

###### Trichloroethene (TCE) `facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene`

A chlorinated solvent, 1,1,2-trichloroethene, once the standard vapour-degreasing and wafer-cleaning solvent in the semiconductor industry. A suspected carcinogen; a common groundwater contaminant; the specific reason the Norristown site is on the National Priorities List.

###### Ethylene from the steam cracker `facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock`

The chlorination of ethylene, or the oxychlorination of 1,2-dichloroethane, which is itself from the chlorination of ethylene. The ethylene came from naphtha steam cracking - the same petrochemical chain as everything else on this tree. Ends at the crude oil still.

#### The semiconductor fab building `facility.cleanroom`

Where the C64's five custom chips were made. A 1-micron NMOS fab: a raised access floor over a service plenum, a ceiling of HEPA filters feeding laminar-flow hoods and open cleanroom, Class 100 in the process bays and Class 1000 in the support areas, and a yellow-lit room for photolithography. Air changed 100-1000 times an hour and consumed most of the plant's electricity.

##### Raised floor and plenum `facility.cleanroom.raised-floor`

A 600 mm or 900 mm void under a load-rated pedestal floor, with all the process exhaust, the cold water, the nitrogen, the vacuum and the electrical cabling running underneath. The whole architectural idea of the fab is that the floor is a duct. This is also why the 1980s fabs needed full basements and 4.5-6 m ceilings.

##### Access floor panel `facility.cleanroom.access-floor`

A 600 mm square steel or aluminium-frame panel with a steel or cast-iron skin, on adjustable pedestals with seismic and electrical bonding. The panel had to be load-rated for a 1000 kg diffusion furnace cart and still be light enough for two people to lift.

##### HEPA (absolute) filter `facility.cleanroom.hepa`

Deep pleated borosilicate glass-fibre media in a galvanised steel casing, rated 99.97% efficient at 0.3 micrometres - the most penetrating particle size, hence 'most penetrating diameter'. A 2.4 m x 1.2 m filter was the ceiling module of every 1980s fab, ceiling and laminar-flow bench alike.

###### Borosilicate glass microfibre `facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre`

Glass melted at 1400 C and blown into fibres a few micrometres across, then laid into a paper and fired at 800-900 C to set a bonding agent, and chopped into slivers. Every 1980s fab consumed tens of thousands of these filters a year and changed them on a schedule rather than on condition.

###### High-purity silica `facility.cleanroom.silica`

The same raw material as the fused-quartz diffusion tube, the photomask substrate and the ceramic package: high-purity SiO2. In 1983 most came from Brazil or from the US inland deposit, and by the mid-80s the industry moved to synthetic vapour-deposited silicon tetrafluoride because natural high-purity quartz was getting scarce.

##### Fan filter unit and laminar flow `facility.cleanroom.ffu`

A 2.4 x 1.2 m fan-filter unit or a fan coil with an integral HEPA, blowing filtered air down through perforated ceiling tiles at 0.3-0.5 m/s to give unidirectional ('laminar') flow. Open cleanroom used ceiling FFUs over the whole floor; the 1980s move was to a 'minienvironment' - a small FFU box over each process tool inside a Class 1000 room - which was the direct ancestor of today's SMIF pods.

##### Class 100 and Class 1000 zoning `facility.cleanroom.classes`

Federal Standard 209E Class 100 in the lithography, etch and metallisation bays; Class 1000 in the diffusion, cleaning and packaging areas; Class 10,000 in the corridors, the airlock and the material store. The class was maintained by air pressure differentials - the Class 100 room slightly positive to the Class 1000 room, which was positive to the corridor - which is why the doors of a 1980s fab always felt like they were being blown open.

##### Amber (yellow) room for photolithography `facility.cleanroom.amber-room` _(medium)_

The lithography bay was lit only through yellow filters - either yellow-lens fluorescent fixtures or, later, a laminated film - so that no light below about 500 nm reached the photoresist. The 1980s specification was that irradiance from 350 to 500 nm should stay below roughly 0.5 W/m2 at the work surface, with the rest of the spectrum unrestricted. Resists of the period were sensitive to the mercury g-line (436 nm), h-line (405 nm) and i-line (365 nm).

##### Photolithography area `facility.cleanroom.litho-area`

Mask aligners, coat/develop tracks, bake ovens and the mask storage cabinets. In a 1980s 1-micron NMOS fab the lithography bay was Class 100 with the amber lighting, the operators wore yellow-room coats and face shields, and the photoresist was spun from a solvent (Shipley AZ1350, based on a novolak resin sensitised with a diazonium salt) with xylene or cellosolve acetate.

##### Passivation and packaging areas `facility.cleanroom.passivation`

Passivation (the final silicon nitride or phosphosilicate glass over the completed aluminium) and then the back-end: wafer probe, dice, die attach, wire bond, and the moulding of the ceramic or plastic package. The back end in 1983 was Class 10000 to Class 1000, not Class 100 - the contaminating work (bonding, moulding compound) happened there.

##### Make-up air and air change rate `facility.cleanroom.makeup-air`

The fab's single largest utility load. Because the Class 100 rooms were almost entirely recirculating, the make-up air was only the leakage plus the exhaust: the acid and solvent fume hoods, the furnace exhaust, the ion-implant exhaust. Even so, a 1980s fab typically ran 100-1000 air changes per hour in the clean bays and 20-60 in the support areas, and the air-handling plant cost tens of millions of dollars and dominated the energy bill.

##### Temperature and humidity control `facility.cleanroom.hvac`

20-22 C and 40-60% relative humidity, tighter than any other building of the era, and the single most expensive thing in the building to get right. The 1980s control was a system of pneumatic controllers and a mechanical chart recorder; a modern fab uses thousands of sensors and a BMS.

##### Gowning and airlock `facility.cleanroom.airlock`

A two-stage airlock - a 'dirty airlock' for incoming components and personnel in street clothes, and a 'clean airlock' with a cross-over bench for gowning. The costume of the era was a hooded coverall plus boots; in the amber room a yellow-coated garment as well.

##### What the building cost (1983 dollars) `facility.cleanroom.cost`

For scale: a small 4-inch fab cost about $4 million in 1970 (about $31 million in 2024 money); a full production fab in 1983 ran from roughly $100 million to several hundred million dollars - National Semiconductor announced a $100 million, 290,000 sq ft plant in August 1983, and UMC spent about $200 million on a 1.2 micron fab in the same year. That is why owning a fab was only ever available to very large firms.

##### Pre-filter bank `facility.cleanroom.prefilter`

Bag or panel filters (2-5 micrometre) ahead of the HEPA units, on the make-up air ducts and on the return air. The 1980s standard pre-filter was a 5-ply disposable bag of coarse glass fibre in a steel frame, or a V-bank of 1-inch washable aluminium-header panels. It existed because a HEPA that gets loaded with dust is an expensive mistake.

###### Coarse glass-fibre filter media `facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media`

Glass melted and blown into coarse fibres and felted into a mat. The same glassfibre technology as the HEPA medium but 100-1000x coarser and far cheaper. Ends at the glass batch.

##### Garment and consumable supply `facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies` _(medium)_

Garments were not laundryable in the era - a hooded coverall was worn once and destroyed. The plant bought enormous quantities of spun-bonded polypropylene garments, hoods, overshoes, gloves, wipes and tacky mats, and washed nothing. One 1980s 5,000-person fab burned something like a million garments a year.

###### Spun-bonded polypropylene `facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp`

Polypropylene melt-spun into continuous filaments and laid down in a random web, then bonded by heat or needle punching. Cheapest possible cleanroom garment material, and the raw material for the 'tacky mat' that caught shoe-borne particles at every airlock.

##### Wafer handling and shipping hardware `facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools`

In 1983 a wafer still travelled in a quartz boat inside a plastic carrier, or hand-carried in a PTFE-wafer cassette from process to process. The SMIF FOUP - the sealed nitrogen-purged single-wafer container that made the whole modern fab possible - arrived with SEMI E10 in the early 1990s. Before that, every transfer was an opportunity for a particle, and a large fraction of the total defect budget.

###### Fused-quartz wafer boat `facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat`

A slotted quartz holder that carries 25-50 wafers through the diffusion furnace. Fused quartz is used because it survives 1000 C, expands predictably, and is chemically inert to the dopants. Made from high-purity synthetic quartz rod, ground and flame-polished.

##### Fab workforce, 1980s `facility.cleanroom.workforce` _(medium)_

A large 1983 fab ran 5,000-10,000 employees, of whom the majority working on the wafer lines were women - the largest single female industrial workforce in many of the regions where the plants went, because the tool operators and the wafer handling were culturally coded as women's work even though they were skilled and tightly controlled.

#### The Commodore supply-chain geography `facility.foundries`

Where a C64 physically came from. Commodore owned one fab, in Pennsylvania. The boards were printed in Hong Kong. The boxes were assembled in Hong Kong, Japan, West Germany, the United States and - from 1984 - Britain. The corporate records that survived the bankruptcy are unusually detailed and are the best source for this branch.

##### The corporate chain that owned all of it `facility.foundries.corporate-structure`

From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top; Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas); Commodore Electronics Ltd (CEL, Bahamas) as the principal operating corporation; Commodore Business Machines Inc (CBM, West Chester PA) as the US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division; Commodore Japan Ltd (CJL); Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd (CE(HK)L) and, after April 1982, the Hong Kong branch of CEL; Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH (West Germany); and CBM International Sales Inc, the DISC. MOS Technology was merged into CBM on 1 January 1981 and carried on as a division - which is why all the chips were still stamped with the MOS logo until 1989.

###### Vertical integration as a strategy `facility.foundries.vertical-integration`

Tramiel's thesis, and the reason the whole tree looks the way it does: if you own the chip, you do not pay a merchant supplier's margin, you control the schedule, and nobody can raise your price. The concrete results: a $135 initial production cost against a $595 retail price, and a production cost driven down to $35-50 by 1985.

##### MOS Technology / Commodore Semiconductor Group fab, Norristown PA `facility.foundries.mos`

The fab that made the 6510, the 6567/6569 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, the 6526 CIA and the ROMs. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 by John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin as a second source for Texas Instruments' calculator chips, was majority-owned by Allen-Bradley from 1970, and built its own plant on 14 acres of the Valley Forge Corporate Center, 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania. It was a 1-micron NMOS fab running 4-inch wafers, and it is the only place the C64's silicon came from - none of the five custom chips could ever be second-sourced. Commodore bought MOS outright for a 9.4% stake in CBM in November 1976 and merged it in 1981. The fab was closed in 1992 after Commodore's bankruptcy.

###### The captive fab as a prototyping advantage `facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototyping`

The reason Commodore could design a chip in nine months: the fab was not full, the mask shop and the processing line were on site, and a designer could pull a test chip in a few weeks - or, in an emergency, four days. Ziembicki's line is the whole story of Commodore's speed: 'We were using people who were there anyway... You waste a little bit of silicon, but silicon's pretty cheap. It's only sand.'

###### After Commodore: GMT Microelectronics `facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor` _(medium)_

The fab was bought out of bankruptcy in December 1994 for about $4.3 million plus $1 million of liabilities (including the EPA licence), reopened in 1995, ran a 1-micron process for third parties, and was shut down by the EPA in 2000-01. 183 employees and $21 million of revenue in 1999. It is a rare, well-documented instance of a 1970s fab surviving the death of its owner.

##### CBM Santa Clara, California `facility.foundries.santa-clara`

Commodore's US assembly line, where production of the C64 began in late summer 1982. It had automated component-insertion equipment. It went badly: excessive video and audio noise, excessive heat, and semiconductors incompatible with the design, so yield was low, cost high and returns came back. Only a limited number of units came out of Santa Clara before responsibility was shifted to Commodore Japan in the autumn of 1982.

###### The automated-insertion board layout fight `facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute`

Commodore's US plant used automatic component insertion; the Japanese plant did not, and the two wanted different component spacing. Charpentier's group won: the C64 board was laid out for automated insertion, and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools. This single decision is why every C64 motherboard was made in Hong Kong.

##### The Hong Kong operation (CE(HK)L and the CEL Hong Kong branch) `facility.foundries.hong-kong`

Where the C64 really got built. Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd had been making watches and calculators since 1979, and manufactured VIC-20 units from April 1982; later the Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd took over. Mass production of the production-redesigned 'C-64A' began at the Hong Kong branch in March 1983, and that branch employed approximately 2,500 people. Commodore's Hong Kong operation bought or produced watches, calculators and computers, and by 1983 it was the assembly centre for the whole company's output. Commodore had Hong Kong subsidiaries listed as Commodore Business Machines Ltd (Hong Kong) and Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd.

###### Hong Kong PCB fabricator `facility.foundries.hk-pcb`

All sixteen versions of the C64 motherboard were manufactured in Hong Kong. Hong Kong in the early 1980s was a genuine centre of bare-board fabrication - dozens of small plants doing gold-impregnated or tin-lead plated FR-4 double-sided boards on a 0.3-0.4 mm grid with the pads drilled and plated by a subcontractor. Commodore did not own one; it bought them.

###### Hong Kong / Taiwan injection moulding sub-contractor `facility.foundries.hk-injection` _(medium)_

The ABS case, the keyboard keycaps and the cassette-port door were moulded by a sub-contractor, not by Commodore. Hong Kong and Taiwan each had hundreds of small toolrooms and presses in 1983, and Commodore used both. The case cost an estimated $1-2 in 1983 prices.

###### Power supply / transformer sub-contractor `facility.foundries.psu-maker` _(medium)_

The linear power supply inside the C64 - the big orange or black transformer, the rectifier and the linear regulators - came from outside suppliers, cost an estimated $5-10 including connectors, and one of Ziembicki's complaints was that a supplier that had passed engineering approval then quietly changed the design without telling anybody.

##### Kentron Co., Ltd., Ina, Japan `facility.foundries.kentron`

The small Japanese production-engineering company that Commodore Japan acquired in October 1982 and that actually fixed the C64. Kentron had about 150 employees at its height and expertise in production engineering, quality control, work standards, purchasing and materials control. Commodore Japan substantially redesigned the machine into the 'C-64A' with Kentron's help; Kentron produced prototypes in late 1982 and began mass production in January 1983. Kentron was a CJL subsidiary from October 1982 to June 1986, when it was sold to an unrelated party.

##### Japanese assembly vendors for the VIC-20 `facility.foundries.japan-vendors` _(medium)_

The VIC-20 - the machine whose case, board size and BASIC the C64 inherited - was first built in Japan by Shinwa Electric Company, then by Japanese Cash Register (JCR), both assembling and manufacturing to Commodore Japan Limited's specifications and under its direction. Japanese Cash Register also owned a factory on Ina road; CJL's engineering headquarters was at Isaka.

##### Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH, Braunschweig, West Germany `facility.foundries.braunschweig`

The European production base. Commodore launched production for the European market in Braunschweig in 1980 and it once employed up to 2,000 people. Commodore GmbH also designed products. The PET had been imported from Braunschweig, and Commodore UK in the 1970s bought calculators at a factory on Teesside. After the 1983 Corby decision, the more expensive business systems stayed in Braunschweig.

##### Commodore Business Machines (UK), Corby `facility.foundries.corby`

The British end. Commodore UK's head office was in Slough and it built calculators at a factory on Teesside; in 1983 it announced a new GBP 20 million home computer factory at Corby, Northamptonshire, as the European manufacturing and distribution centre for the C64 and VIC-20, expecting 300 jobs by the end of 1984 and 700,000 units a year by then. The Corby plant was in place by September 1984 with 850 jobs on a ten-acre site, ran flat out sixteen hours a day, and was closed as a manufacturing base in January 1986.

##### The rest of the manufacturing map, 1983 `facility.foundries.other-sites`

By 1983 Commodore described itself as an international company with manufacturing in Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany, the UK, Pennsylvania and California in the United States, and Scarborough in Metropolitan Toronto. C64 units carried the MADE IN HONG KONG, West Germany or England marks, and were assembled in at least 11 factories worldwide over the model's life. Commodore did not, at this stage, have a Commodore Taiwan plant - the Taiwanese supply chain in this story is the sub-contractor base, not a Commodore factory.

##### The sub-contractor geography: Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines `facility.foundries.subcontract-network` _(medium)_

Commodore's own factories were few; its supply base was enormous. Japan supplied the disks and a great deal of the precision mechanics and passives. Taiwan and Korea supplied the display-grade passives, the transformers, the coils, the keyboards and the power supplies, through the export processing zones. The Philippines and Malaysia supplied the switching power supplies and the magnetics by the late 1980s. Hong Kong was the assembly and test node, sitting between them, with the boards printed locally and the chips arriving from Pennsylvania.

#### Moving 100,000 C64s `logistics.shipping` _(medium)_

The C64 was assembled in East Asia and sold in North America and Europe. In 1983 that was containerised cargo on liner services, not break-bulk: a 40-foot box holds 250-350 C64s depending on how they were packed, and the whole industry's economics were shaped by the 1966-1980s transition from weight/measurement cargo to box rates.

##### Containerisation (40-foot box) `logistics.shipping.containerisation` _(medium)_

ISO 40-foot general purpose container: 12.192 m x 2.438 m x 2.591 m internal, holding up to about 32-36 tonnes. One TEU is a 20-foot box; a 40-foot box is two. Box rates had replaced weight rates on the main east-west lanes by the end of the 1970s, so a low-density, high-value cargo like a C64 paid per box rather than per tonne.

##### The volume Commodore was moving `logistics.shipping.c64-count` _(medium)_

By March 1983 the C64 was shipping at about 25,000 units a month and had passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales; roughly half a million had sold in the first six months. At 300 units a 40-foot box, that is about 83 TEU a month - about four to five ships' worth of containers a month, which sounds trivial until you remember it was compounding 20-30% a month.

##### The ports `logistics.shipping.ports`

Kaohsiung was Taiwan's largest container port and was ranked the world's fifth-largest container port in 1982; its first container terminal was built 1969-70 and Container Terminal No. 4 in the Zhongxing Commercial Harbor Area was built from 1983. Keelung, on the northern approach to Taipei, opened the first Taiwanese container ship movements in January 1972 and worked on a filled jetty because of the terrain. Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour terminals, Rotterdam, and Long Beach or Oakland on the US West Coast, plus New York and Newark on the East Coast, completed the set.

##### Route times: transpacific and Europe-Asia `logistics.shipping.routes` _(medium)_

Kaohsiung or Hong Kong to Long Beach is about 4,500-5,000 nautical miles via the Luzon Strait and the great circle; at 16-18 knots that is roughly 12-14 days port to port, plus 3-7 days in the terminal on each end. Hong Kong to Rotterdam via the Suez Canal is about 11,000 nautical miles, 22-26 days, with 5-7 days of canal transit and waiting. These were the numbers that set Commodore's inventory position: eight weeks of sea transit each way on the Pacific route, eleven to twelve weeks each way on the Europe route.

##### The bill of lading `logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading`

The negotiable document that made containerised trade possible: a carrier-issued contract of carriage naming the shipper, the consignee, the port of loading and discharge, the freight terms, and the description of the goods. Without it the goods did not move; with it, the bank paid on presentation. The 1983 electronic BOL did not exist - the paper document was the mechanism.

##### Air freight for the high-value parts `logistics.shipping.air-freight` _(medium)_
