Customs values tell the story: a box of 300 C64s entered at, say, $150-200 declared value each would carry $45,000-60,000 of electronics inside a container whose ocean freight was a few hundred dollars. The ICs were the opposite case: a 6510 and a VIC-II at internal transfer value were a tiny fraction of the customs value of the finished case, so nobody flew the chips - the chips came by sea inside the container, and the container moved once. Air freight was for prototypes, for a replacement part in an emergency, and for the tape and the spares.

##### Demurrage, detention and the inventory cost `logistics.shipping.demurrage` _(medium)_

Two separate costs. Demurrage is the charge for leaving a container on the terminal beyond the free time; in 1983 free time was commonly four to five days and the daily charge escalated. Detention is the charge for keeping the container beyond the time allowed at the other end. On top of both sat the real cost: eight to twelve weeks of sea transit each way meant Commodore had to hold inventory in transit and in the destination warehouse, which is exactly the cost structure that rewarded the 'just-in-time' port-to-port discipline and punished Commodore's famous spotty availability in 1983.

##### US import duty on a computer in 1983 `logistics.shipping.import-duty` _(medium)_

The C64 entered the United States under the Tariff Schedules of the United States (the TSUS - the HTS did not exist until 1989), classified as an accounting, computing and other data processing machine incorporating a calculating mechanism, item 676.15, dutiable at 5.5% ad valorem. Separately, item 807.00 gave a duty allowance for the US components shipped out for assembly abroad - which for Commodore meant a deduction for the value of the MOS chips and the case shipped to Hong Kong, so only the value added in Hong Kong paid duty.

##### Customs valuation and the paper trail `logistics.shipping.customs-valuation`

US customs value was the transaction value - the price actually paid or payable - which is why Commodore's transfer-pricing between Commodore Electronics Ltd (Bahamas), Commodore Japan Ltd and the Hong Kong branch became the subject of a US Tax Court case that ran from 1991 and shifted $116 million of income between entities. The same transfer prices determined the duty. The documentation for a 1983 shipment would have included a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and, in a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal, a certificate of origin.

#### The labour content of a C64 `logistics.people`

Two labour populations with almost nothing in common: a tiny, very senior, very expensive American engineering team in Pennsylvania and Japan, and a large, low-paid, mostly female production workforce in Hong Kong and Japan. The design labour is amortised over millions of units and is invisible in the $35-40 BOM; the assembly labour is a few dollars per unit and is the reason Commodore could hit a $135 production cost.

##### The bill of materials (1983 estimate) `logistics.people.bom`

Brian Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks gave the most-cited contemporaneous breakdown, used as a production cost of $35-50 by 1985: three ROMs at $1 each; eight 64K DRAMs at $1.85 each; SID and VIC-II at $4 each; RF modulator $3; 6510 at $1-2; TTL, buffers, regulators and capacitors together $5; keyboard under $10; PC board $1-2; plastic case $1-2; power supply and connectors $5-10; packaging and manual $1-2. Note what this says: the eight DRAM chips alone were $14.80, more than the case, the board and the modulator combined.

##### Direct assembly labour per machine `logistics.people.direct-labour` _(low)_

Roughly 0.5-1.5 person-hours per machine across population, insertion (automated), wave-solder, assembly, test and packing, plus a share of the test and rework. At 1983 Hong Kong and Japanese electronics wage levels of roughly HK$9-14 or JPY 500-700 per hour, that is about US$1-3 per machine of direct labour - between 3% and 8% of the $35-50 production cost. Direct labour is genuinely tiny compared with the IC content, which is exactly the point Commodore's vertical integration strategy rested on.

##### Hong Kong electronics wages, 1983 `logistics.people.hk-wages` _(medium)_

The Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's Quarterly Report of Wages, Salaries and Employee Benefits Statistics carried explicit occupational breakdowns for the electronics industry in 1983 - assembler, soldering worker, tester/aligner, quality control operator, packer, machine operator - with average daily wages and normal hours, and it separately flagged that piece rates were common in manufacturing and that the survey therefore reported them on a time basis. Operative daily wages across manufacturing generally sat around HK$60-100 in 1983, so an assembler earned roughly HK$9-14 per hour at a 7-8.5 hour day. Hong Kong had no statutory minimum wage at all in 1983.

##### The international wage gap that placed the work in Hong Kong `logistics.people.wage-index`

The cleanest comparative number available: ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics hourly compensation costs for production workers in electronic and electrical equipment (SIC 36), indexed to the United States at 100. In 1975 Hong Kong was 15-16, Korea 16, Taiwan 18-19, Japan 84, Israel 75. By 1984 Hong Kong was 19, Korea 23, Taiwan 22, Japan 82. The Asian plants ran at roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of American labour cost, and that gap - not the technology - was the reason the assembly was where it was.

##### The worker at the wave-solder line `logistics.people.wave-solder-worker` _(medium)_

The single most recognisable job in a 1980s electronics factory. She stood or sat at one end of a 2-3 m wave-solder machine, fed pre-inserted boards into the conveyor, watched for bridging and dry joints, pulled the rejects, and often did the visual inspection and the component-insertion handwork at the same station. Almost always female, usually in her twenties or thirties, on a piece rate or a small hourly premium for yield, and living within an hour's bus ride of the plant in a New Territories squatter village or a public housing block. Hong Kong's 1983 wage survey listed 'soldering worker' as a distinct occupational category for exactly this reason.

##### Commodore's Hong Kong workforce `logistics.people.hk-headcount`

The Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd employed approximately 2,500 people when mass production of the production-redesigned C-64A began there in March 1983. That is the single best-documented headcount in the whole Commodore manufacturing story.

##### The C64 chip design team `logistics.people.design-team`

A team of about seven people, working in parallel on two chips, in nine months. Al Charpentier designed the VIC-II with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Bob Yannes designed the SID with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Charles Winterble, then director of worldwide engineering, authorised and managed the project. The whole effort began in January 1981, spent about two weeks studying the Mattel Intellivision, the TI 99/4A and the Atari 800, and finished with first-pass silicon in November 1981 that worked except for one bad sprite. The chips were designed in a modular, deliberately uncompact style - Yannes built one oscillator module and repeated it rather than multiplexing - because design time was the scarce resource, not die area. Neither designer had a modern CAD workstation; logic was simulated by hand.

##### The C64 system design team `logistics.people.c64-system-team`

After Tramiel decided in late November 1981 that the VIC-II and SID would go into a 64 KB home computer rather than a game console, the machine itself was designed in about five weeks. The architecture was laid out on paper in two days; five working prototypes were finished just before the new year. The team was Bob Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki, with Yash Terakura of Commodore Japan involved on the Japanese variant. They worked over Thanksgiving and Christmas. Charlie Winterble had set the deadline; Tramiel had decided the machine had to be at the January 1982 CES.

##### Nobody knows what the C64 cost to develop `logistics.people.development-cost`

Winterble's answer to the question was direct: 'I had no formal budget accountability, other than Jack watching me. Jack said that budgets were a license to steal.' The reason the answer was 'nothing much' is that the fab was not running at full capacity and the design chips were absorbed into existing overhead with no supplier margin at all. Ziembicki: 'We were using people who were there anyway.' Software, per Charpentier, 'wasn't tangible - you couldn't hold it, feel it, or touch it - so it wasn't worth spending money for.'

##### The production engineers who fixed it `logistics.people.production-engineering`

The unsung labour in Commodore's story: David Ziembicki (production engineer, then Commodore West Chester), Bruce Crocket and Charles Winterble, who had to debug the project and bring it into production, and Robert H. Lane, who became president of Commodore Business Machines Inc in November 1982 and was fired by Tramiel after the June 1983 CES. Kentron's 150 Japanese engineers and technicians - brought in specifically because Commodore Japan's production engineering had worked on the VIC-20 - are the documented reason the C64 was eventually manufacturable at all.

##### The labour cost of the quality problems `logistics.people.qa-defects`

Commodore's labour did not just build machines, it found and reworked other people's mistakes. The 'sparkle' defect was traced after three weeks to a ROM - not the VIC-II - with a pre-charging circuit that was sensitive to a bus contention spike; three million such ROMs were already in service. A logic error put 64 clock cycles on a scanline instead of 65 and took about five months into production to fix. Assembly-line workers over-adjusted the colour potentiometer until it saturated the colour and wiped out the luma. Electric screwdrivers cut traces on the disk-drive connector, and because those traces went to a connector nobody tested, they passed final inspection. Charles Winterble: 'It takes a very tough person to say I'm not shipping these because they're not as good as they could be - especially when people are clamoring to buy them.'

#### Factory and engineering test equipment `facility.test-equipment`

Short branch. Every C64 that left the Hong Kong line had been through a functional test, and the boards had been tested electrically before population and after soldering. In-circuit testers and flying probes were the technology of the era; the ATE and flying-probe industry of the 1990s did not exist yet.

##### In-circuit tester (ICT) `facility.test-equipment.ict`

A bed-of-nails fixture pressing 1000 or so spring-loaded probes onto the bare board's pads, measuring resistance, capacitance, diode voltage and, at an increasing share, functional signatures at each node - all in a few seconds. By 1983 the analogue resistance-only tester was giving way to the analogue-plus-functional 'in-circuit functional tester' that could catch an unpopulated IC or a wrong-orientation part without a board-level functional test.

##### Functional tester `facility.test-equipment.functional` _(medium)_

A powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM. On a Commodore line this was a dedicated fixture with a monitor and a keyboard, and the operator's job was to load, run, read the result, box or quarantine.

##### Test ROM in the final-test fixture `facility.test-equipment.test-rom`

A dedicated test ROM - the '501' diagnostic ROM is the one most C64 owners meet - loaded into the machine's own ROM socket during factory final test so the machine could self-test its own RAM, character ROM, CIA timers and VIC registers. It is the same object a user later used to prove the machine worked.

##### Burn-in oven and sockets `facility.test-equipment.burn-in` _(medium)_

A forced-air oven at 70-100 C with burn-in sockets, holding hundreds of boards for 24-72 hours so that early-life component failures - bad solder joints, marginal ICs, leaky capacitors - showed up on the line instead of in the customer's house. Commodore's 1982-83 quality record suggests it was not always run long enough.

##### Bare-board test and flying probe `facility.test-equipment.bare-board`

Bare PCB test came first: a bed-of-nails grid fixture to prove every net was etched and plated correctly, catching a shorts-heavy board before it was populated and therefore before the parts were on it. The flying probe - a robot or CNC head with a moving needle that touched nets individually without a fixture - existed by the early 1980s as an engineering diagnostic, and only later became the standard production tester once it got fast enough.

###### Spring probe and tungsten needle `facility.test-equipment.needle-probe` _(medium)_

The bed-of-nails is a field of sprung tungsten-rhenium or beryllium-copper pins on a 2.54 mm grid, each pressing a few grams onto a pad to make contact. The 1980s fixtures were drilled and wired by hand or on a numerical-control machine from the Gerber artwork - which is why a board layout change meant a new fixture.

### Published but unlinked materials `unlinked.catalogue` _(medium)_

These 9 nodes were written as canonical, reusable subtrees — a fragment's "made from" chains in full detail — but no other branch ended up referencing them, so nothing linked them into the tree. They are collected here rather than deleted. Where a component subtree inlines its own shorter version of the same material chain, this is the long one.

#### Glass fibre (E-glass) for laminate and filter media `chem.glass-fiber`

Continuous drawn glass filaments a few microns thick, bundled into strand and woven into cloth. A C64 needs it twice: as the reinforcing cloth in the FR-4 mainboard laminate, and — if you follow the machine out to a television — as the fine filter media in an air-cleaning system. E-glass is the workhorse composition, named for its electrical resistivity, and it is made in enormous tonnage.

##### Batch mixing `chem.glass-fiber.batch`

The raw oxides are weighed and dry-mixed in a batch charger to about +/-1% on each constituent. A modern batch is tens of tonnes; the tolerance matters because the melt is what fixes the composition, and composition fixes the viscosity, which fixes whether 5 micron fibre can be drawn at all.

##### Melting in a regenerative tank furnace `chem.glass-fiber.melt`

The batch is charged into a regenerative furnace held around 1400-1500 C. The glass is not just melted: it must then be refined (bubbles larger than a few microns rise out or are broken by a rotating mechanical stirrer) and conditioned (held just above the liquidus so beta-eucryptite crystallises, which is what stops the finished fibre devitrifying into a crystalline, brittle, unusable mass). Conditioning is slow — tens of hours — and it is the step that makes continuous fibre possible at all.

##### Forehearth and bushings `chem.glass-fiber.bushing`

Glass travels from the furnace through a refractory forehearth to a bushing plate — a small alloy block drilled with 200 to several thousand holes of 10-40 microns, usually gold-platinum alloy because it resists corrosion at 1400 C. Pressure pushes the melt through each hole; surface tension then draws it out, and gravity plus attenuation stretches it to a fiber diameter a fiftieth of the hole.

##### Attenuation and sizing `chem.glass-fiber.attenuation`

Air jets at high velocity and constant pressure stretch the molten filament to 3-10 microns. As it passes a sizing apron a thin film of starch or oil is applied; for laminate grade this is usually replaced after weaving by a silane or acrylate coupling agent, which is what lets the glass bond chemically to the epoxy instead of merely sitting in it.

##### Spinning to strand, roving and woven cloth `chem.glass-fiber.packaging` _(medium)_

The attenuated strand is wound onto a rotating package at high traverse speed — a single package can hold tens of kilometres of strand — then combined into rovings and woven on a air-jet loom into plain-weave cloth. The loom matters: a plain weave with square fill is what gives an FR-4 laminate its isotropic behaviour, which is why PCB cloth is woven rather than chopped.

##### Fine and ultrafine grades for air filtration `chem.glass-fiber.filter-media` _(medium)_

Air-purification media use a much finer fibre than the 5 micron laminate grade: 0.1-1 micron fibres are produced by reducing the number and size of bushing holes and, for HEPA grades, by a flash or steam-blowing process that collapses the fibre into mats. This branch exists because a semiconductor fab and a television both need filtered air, and the same silica-and-limestone feedstocks are involved.

#### Chromate conversion coating `metal.chromate-passivation`

A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.

#### Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel `metal.chromium.aod`

The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

##### Chromium in the C64's stainless parts `metal.chromium.stainless-use` _(medium)_

AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.

##### The AOD lance and its tuyere block `metal.chromium.aod.lance` _(medium)_

The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.

###### The refractory ladle lining `metal.refractory-ladle` _(medium)_

The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.

#### Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum `metal.chromium.metal` _(medium)_

Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.

##### Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath `metal.hex-chrome-plating`

The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.

##### Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm `metal.chromium.metal.cell` _(low)_

Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.

###### The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance `metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm` _(low)_

The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.

#### Cryolite (Na3AlF6), the electrolyte solvent `metal.cryolite`

The white, insoluble, water-repellent mineral that makes aluminium electrolysis possible at all. Pure alumina melts at 2072 C; a bath of cryolite with excess aluminium fluoride and some calcium fluoride is liquid at 950-970 C, and the alumina dissolves in it at 6-10%. The other crucial property is that cryolite is not consumed stoichiometrically - it is a solvent - and only the fluorine lost as HF and in the fume has to be replaced. Correcting the brief: consumption was roughly 0.5-1.0 t of cryolite per tonne of aluminium in 1980s practice (theoretical about 0.5 t, higher in practice because of fluoride loss), not 'four tonnes of aluminium per tonne of cryolite'.

##### Synthetic cryolite from hydrofluoric acid `metal.cryolite.synthesis`

Because natural cryolite was one mine in Greenland, the industry made its own. Sodium carbonate or caustic soda reacts with hydrofluoric acid and aluminium hydroxide at 60-90 C: 6HF + 3Na2CO3 + Al(OH)3 -> 2Na3AlF6 + 3CO2 + 3H2O. So the electrolyte solvent of the aluminium pot is manufactured from fluorspar, caustic soda and alumina - three of this file's other endpoints in one reaction.

##### Aluminium fluoride and the bath `metal.aluminium-fluoride` _(medium)_

The excess AlF3 in the bath is not a deliberate additive so much as the consequence of the water and the fluorides in the alumina; smelters add it back to hold the bath at the composition that gives the best current efficiency, which is somewhere between 8 and 14% excess AlF3. Too little and the bath's freezing point rises and the pot freezes; too much and the current efficiency falls and the crust gets hard. Getting this balance right is the potline operator's entire job, and it is checked by sampling the frozen bath and analysing it in a laboratory.

      - *Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath* `metal.hex-chrome-plating` *(seen above)*
#### Natural quartz crystal `metal.quartz` _(medium)_

Vein and pegmatite quartz, of which Brazil's Minas Gerais was the world source for the resonator industry. Only used where natural material beat synthetic on Q - high-stability resonators - and as the seed for hydrothermal growth. Included because it is a genuine geological leaf for the clock crystal branch, unlike the industrial silica sand and the silicon-grade quartzite, which are both processed rocks.

#### Rosin (colophony) from pine `metal.rosin`

The flux, and it is not synthetic: it is the sticky, yellow-brown, semi-solid fraction of pine resin tapped from living trees or distilled out of pine stumps and mill residues. Chemically it is a mixture of resin acids - abietic acid and its relatives - which at soldering temperature decompose to a mild organic acid that dissolves the copper and tin oxides and floats them away in a non-conductive film. Electronics rosin is gum or wood rosin, bleached pale, dissolved in the flux. It is one of the few places in the electronics chain where the feedstock is a forest product rather than a mine, and it is combustible, which is why rosin-fluxed boards must be cleaned before conformal coating.

##### Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill `metal.pine-resin`

The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.

###### Turpentine from the same stump `metal.turpentine` _(medium)_

When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.

##### The halide activator in the flux core `metal.rosin.activator` _(medium)_

Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.

#### Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995% `metal.zinc.ingot`

Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. This is a deliberate convergence node with four branches: the electrowinning route, the die-cast alloy branch, the electroplating and chromate branch, and the brass branch.

##### Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip `metal.zinc.galvanising`

Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.

###### Ashes and dross recovery from the galvanising kettle `metal.zinc.dross-recovery` _(medium)_

The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.

##### Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster `metal.zinc.die-cast`

Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.

###### Zinc alloy melting furnace `metal.zinc.ingot-furnace` _(medium)_

The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air. A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.

##### Electrolytic zinc plating of steel `metal.zinc.electroplate` _(medium)_

For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.

          - *Chromate conversion coating* `metal.chromate-passivation` *(seen above)*
##### Brass (Cu-Zn) and the alloying of zinc `metal.zinc.brass`

Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

##### Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp `metal.zinc-oxide-varistor`

The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

###### Zinc oxide powder from high-purity zinc `metal.zinc-oxide-powder` _(medium)_

Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.
